Explain how psychology grew out of philosophy and physiology into a laboratory science, and name the founders, methods and central ideas of Wundt's voluntarism, Titchener's structuralism and the functionalism of James and the American pioneers. 1.2 Schools and Systems, the Cognitive Revolution and Indian Psychology : Trace psychology's rival schools (behaviourism, Gestalt, psychoanalysis, humanistic and existential psychology) through the cognitive revolution to today's perspectives, and explain the core ideas of Indian psychology: its pioneers, Samkhya, the three gunas, Patanjali's yoga and the Vedantic self. 1.3 Sensation and Psychophysics : Explain how physical energy becomes sensation, how thresholds, the psychophysical laws and signal detection theory measure it, and how vision, hearing, the chemical senses, the skin senses and the body senses work. 1.4 Perception: Organising and Interpreting the World : Explain how the brain organises and interprets sensory input, from the bottom-up and top-down theories, Gestalt laws, depth cues and constancies to illusions, motion, pattern recognition, perceptual set and perception without awareness. 1.5 Attention and Consciousness : Explain how attention selects, divides and sustains processing (the filter and attenuation models, automaticity, the Stroop effect and vigilance), and describe consciousness and its states: biological rhythms, sleep stages and disorders, dreams, hypnosis, meditation and psychoactive drugs. 1.6 Learning: Conditioning, Cognition and Observation : Define learning and explain habituation, classical and operant conditioning, the conditioning therapies, schedules of reinforcement, and cognitive and observational learning, naming who showed what and when. 1.7 Memory: Encoding, Storage, Retrieval and Forgetting : Explain how memories are encoded, stored, organised, retrieved, distorted and forgotten, using the multi-store and working memory models, the systems of long-term memory, the theories of forgetting and the classic amnesic cases. 1.8 Thinking, Problem Solving, Reasoning, Decision Making and Language : Explain how people form concepts, solve problems, reason, judge, decide and create, and how language is structured, acquired and related to thought, naming the classic studies and their traps. 1.9 Intelligence: Theories, Measurement, Heredity and Environment : Define intelligence, calculate ratio and deviation IQs, describe the Wechsler, Stanford-Binet, culture-fair and Indian tests, compare the factor, multiple, triarchic and emotional intelligence theories, interpret heritability correctly and classify intellectual disability and giftedness. 1.10 Motivation : Explain why people and animals act, from instinct, drive, arousal and incentive theories through Maslow's hierarchy, achievement motivation and self-determination theory, and apply these ideas to conflict, hunger, sex and work. 1.11 Emotion and Stress : Explain what an emotion is, compare the classic theories and brain systems of emotion, and describe how stress arises, how the body responds to it, and how coping, support and personality shape its effects on health. Weightage. 815 of the 815 questions mapped in this book (100.0%) test this chapter, 402 of them from real past papers. 3 of its 11 sections are High yield. Leipzig, in the winter of 1879. In a small room of an old university building known as the Konvikt, a doctoral student named Max Friedrich sits in front of a Hipp chronoscope, a clockwork timer that measures intervals in thousandths of a second. A stimulus is presented; Friedrich presses a telegraph key. Then the rule changes: now he must press not the instant he senses the stimulus, but only once he has clearly grasped what it is. The second reaction takes longer, and the extra time, Friedrich and his supervisor reasoned, is the time the mind needs to apperceive , to bring an impression into the clear focus of attention. Trial after trial, the numbers go into a notebook. His supervisor was a 47-year-old professor of philosophy, Wilhelm Wundt. When Wundt arrived in Leipzig four years earlier, the university had given him this room to store the apparatus he used in lecture demonstrations. By the winter of 1879 it had become something new: a place where students carried out original experiments on the mind and published them as research. Friedrich's study of the duration of apperception became the first dissertation to come out of that room, and historians who later combed the Leipzig archives dated the start of the work to the last weeks of 1879. That is why textbooks, and nearly every entrance paper in India, treat Leipzig in 1879 as the birth of psychology as a science. Look closely and that one small act holds this whole chapter. The stimulus had to be sensed and then perceived as something; attention had to seize it; practice changed the times; the instruction had to be remembered; a decision released the press; and the readiness and strain of waiting were motivation and feeling in miniature. Remember Max Friedrich pressing his key. Each section that follows takes one step of that act and asks how it works. 1.1 Psychology as a Science: Roots, Founders and the First Schools Lower yield · 46 Qs "Psychology has a long past, but only a short history," wrote Hermann Ebbinghaus in 1908. The long past is philosophy and physiology; the short history, set out in Figure 1.1, begins in Wilhelm Wundt's Leipzig laboratory in 1879. What psychology is The word joins the Greek psyche (soul) and logos (study); Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE) wrote the first treatise on the soul, De Anima . Later schools redefined the subject: mind for the philosophers, conscious experience for Wundt ("the Science of Mental Life" for William James in 1890), then behaviour for William McDougall (1905, 1908) and John B. Watson (1913). Woodworth's definition was the individual's activities in relation to the environment; the one Indian textbooks quote, "the scientific study of behaviour", is Norman L. Munn 's. Today psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes : behaviour is overt (speaking, blushing), mental processes internal and covert (perceiving, remembering). Its goals are to describe, explain, predict and control (or influence); basic research seeks understanding for its own sake, applied research solves practical problems. Among its fields, clinical psychology assesses and treats psychological disorders, counselling psychology helps people in the normal range with adjustment problems, and abnormal psychology studies the causes of disorders. Animal behaviour across species is the field of comparative psychology ; evolutionary psychology explains behaviour as inherited adaptations shaped by natural selection, and differential psychology studies individual differences. Health, developmental, social, industrial-organisational, educational, forensic, experimental and neuropsychology study illness, the lifespan, people among others, work, schooling, the law, basic processes and the brain. Exam trap Mental processes are internal and covert, not outward behaviour, overt actions or animal behaviour. The bank credits Munn with "the scientific study of behaviour" ("J. B. William" is no known psychologist). Animal behaviour is comparative psychology, not social, abnormal or differential. Clinical psychology is the assessment and treatment of mental illness , not industry or organisations. "Behaviour in relation to genetic inheritance" is keyed evolutionary psychology . Roots: 1850 to 1890 Schools and institutions: 1892 to 1925 1850 Helmholtz times the nerve impulse; Fechner's insight (22 October) 1859 Darwin, On the Origin of Species 1860 Fechner, Elements of Psychophysics 1861 Broca: speech area (patient Tan) 1869 Galton, Hereditary Genius 1873/74 Wundt, Principles of Physiological Psychology 1879 Wundt's Leipzig laboratory: research begins 1883 Hall: first US research laboratory (Johns Hopkins) 1885 Ebbinghaus, On Memory 1890 James, Principles of Psychology; Cattell coins "mental test" 1892 APA founded at Clark; Hall first president 1894 Washburn: first woman PhD in psychology 1896 Witmer's clinic (Pennsylvania); Dewey's reflex arc paper 1898 Titchener names structuralism 1905 Calkins: first woman APA president 1906 Angell, The Province of Functional Psychology 1913 Watson's behaviourist manifesto 1915/16 Calcutta: first Indian laboratory and department 1922 Bose founds the Indian Psychoanalytic Society 1925 Indian Psychological Association founded Figure 1.1 The short history of psychology at a glance. Notice how the roots (left) cluster in German physiology and British biology, and how quickly the institutions (right) followed once Wundt's laboratory opened in 1879. Philosophical roots Philosophy asked where knowledge comes from: some is inborn, says nativism ; all comes through the senses, says empiricism ; reason is the chief route, says rationalism . Plato (about 427 to 347 BCE) saw learning as the recollection of inborn knowledge. Aristotle, an empiricist, gave the laws of association , similarity, contrast and contiguity: "Sachin" calls up "Tendulkar" by contiguity. Rene Descartes (1596 to 1650) saw the body as a machine run by the reflex, yet gave humans a separate thinking mind that interacts with the body through the pineal gland: dualism . He also held innate ideas (God, self, infinity). His reflex led to behaviourism, and his nativism, through Kant, to Gestalt psychology. John Locke (1632 to 1704) answered in 1690 that the mind at birth is "white paper", a tabula rasa , filled by sensation and reflection. Simple ideas combine into complex ones; primary qualities (size, shape, motion) lie in objects, secondary qualities (colour, taste, warmth) in the perceiver. Building all mental life from such links became the doctrine of associationism , founded by David Hartley (1749). James Mill (1773 to 1836) held a complex idea to be the sum of its parts, mental mechanics; his son John Stuart Mill (1806 to 1873) held that parts fuse into something new, as hydrogen and oxygen make water: mental chemistry . Before Locke, Thomas Hobbes (1588 to 1679) was a materialist; after him, George Berkeley (1685 to 1753) held that to be is to be perceived, David Hume (1711 to 1776) gave the laws of resemblance, contiguity and cause and effect, and Alexander Bain founded the journal Mind (1876). German rationalists made the mind active. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646 to 1716), who built reality from active units called monads, held that unnoticed petites perceptions (each wave in the sea's roar) add up to clear awareness, which he called apperception. Johann Friedrich Herbart (1776 to 1841) added a threshold of consciousness and the apperceptive mass , the existing ideas that must absorb a new idea for it to be understood. Immanuel Kant (1724 to 1804) gave the mind innate categories and denied that psychology could be a science. On mind and body, interactionism (Descartes) lets each act on the other; psychophysical parallelism (Leibniz, Wundt) has them run in step without causation; epiphenomenalism ( Thomas Henry Huxley , 1825 to 1895) makes mind a by-product of the brain; and monism admits one substance, or, in the double-aspect theory of Baruch Spinoza (1632 to 1677), one reality with two faces. Ontology asks what exists; epistemology, how we know. Exam trap Tabula rasa is Locke ; Plato, Descartes and Kant were nativists. Empiricists draw knowledge from sensory experience ; logical reasoning and contemplation are rationalist routes, and theories are products of knowledge. A practice key says Descartes' dualism influenced behaviourism and Gestalt psychology , not empiricism and rationalism. Post-positivism treats knowledge as fallible; scientific realism holds unobservables real. The apperceptive mass (Herbart's term, credited to Wundt by IHBAS 2025) is pure perception and pre-existing ideas , not associated elements (associationism), "sensation and pure perception" or Helmholtz's unconscious inference. Physiological and biological roots The Bell-Magendie law ( Charles Bell , 1811; Francois Magendie , 1822) split the spinal nerve roots into sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral). By the doctrine of specific nerve energies of Johannes Muller (1801 to 1858; Handbook of Human Physiology , 1833 to 1840), a sensation's quality depends on the nerve excited: press on the eye and you see light. Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894) timed the nerve impulse at about 27 metres per second (1850), called perception unconscious inference, and built the 1802 idea of Thomas Young into the trichromatic theory of colour vision. Localisation ran from the phrenology of Franz Joseph Gall and Johann Gaspar Spurzheim (character read from skull bumps, about 1800) through the ablation studies of Pierre Flourens (1820s) to Paul Broca 's speech area (1861), Carl Wernicke 's comprehension area (1874) and the motor cortex of Gustav Fritsch and Eduard Hitzig (1870). Charles Darwin (1809 to 1882; On the Origin of Species , 1859; The Expression of the Emotions , 1872) gave psychology continuity between species, the question of function and an interest in variation. Francis Galton (1822 to 1911) measured that variation, founding the study of individual differences: Hereditary Genius (1869), twin studies, an anthropometric laboratory (1884), correlation, the questionnaire, word association and eugenics. George John Romanes founded comparative psychology on anecdotes (1882), and Conwy Lloyd Morgan 's canon (1894) demanded parsimony: never a higher faculty where a lower one will do. Exam trap Helmholtz is keyed for the trichromatic theory ; the JND is Weber's, the law of effect Thorndike's, the unconscious mind Freud's. Measuring the mind Kant was answered at Leipzig. Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795 to 1878) found that the just noticeable difference is a constant fraction of the standard stimulus. Gustav Theodor Fechner (1801 to 1887), after an insight on 22 October 1850, made sensation grow with the logarithm of intensity (S = k log I) and founded psychophysics in Elements of Psychophysics (1860). (Seeing a contour needs a minimum intensity and exposure time, not a minimum reaction time; Section 1.3.) In 1868 Franciscus Cornelis Donders (1818 to 1889) subtracted the time of a simple reaction from that of one with an added stage, such as identifying the stimulus, founding mental chronometry . Hermann Ebbinghaus (1850 to 1909), working alone, measured memory with nonsense syllables (1885; Section 1.7). Exam trap The founder of psychophysics is Fechner , not Weber, Wundt or Ebbinghaus. Ebbinghaus, Galton and Freud each worked independently as pioneers and each devised new methods (nonsense syllables; the questionnaire and word association; free association), but Freud founded no laboratory. The Panwar bank keys (d), "(a) and (c)"; RML 2020 keyed (a), "pioneers", alone. Both statements are true, so prefer (d). Wundt and the Leipzig laboratory Wilhelm Maximilian Wundt (1832 to 1920), a physician who had assisted Helmholtz, announced a new science in Principles of Physiological Psychology (1873 to 1874), "physiological" meaning borrowed experimental method. At Leipzig his students began original research in 1879, the conventional birth of psychology, and the journal Philosophische Studien followed in 1881. Weber, Fechner and Helmholtz were precursors; Wundt founded the discipline by giving it a laboratory, a journal and students. He studied immediate experience , sensations and simple feelings that the mind actively organises through attention and will; hence voluntarism . Contents in the broad field of consciousness are perceived, those in its focus apperceived: the ceiling fan is perceived, the question paper apperceived. By creative synthesis a whole gains new properties, as a melody exceeds its notes. His tridimensional theory of feeling (1896) has three axes: pleasure-displeasure, tension-relaxation and excitement-depression. His method was introspection under experimental control ( innere Wahrnehmung ), short judgements of signalled stimuli, not armchair self-observation ( Selbstbeobachtung ). Language, myth and custom he studied in the ten-volume Volkerpsychologie (folk psychology, 1900 to 1920). His students included Hall, Cattell, Titchener, Kulpe, Witmer, Munsterberg, Emil Kraepelin (1856 to 1926; psychiatric classification), Charles Spearman (1863 to 1945; factor analysis) and Vladimir Bekhterev (1857 to 1927; reflexology). Exam trap The first laboratory is Wundt's , at Leipzig , not Vienna, Paris or Cambridge; Galton's (1884) was anthropometric, Weber founded none, Jung used word association clinically, and James's 1875 Harvard room was for demonstration. The Principles of Psychology (1890) is James's . Introspection belongs to Wundt (Watson attacked it; Wertheimer founded Gestalt) and to structuralism (functionalism added tests, behaviourism rejected it, psychoanalysis used free association). Spearman is to factor analysis as Wundt is to introspection (humanism: Maslow, Rogers). Folk psychology (RML 2024) is Wundt's ; Pavlov found conditioning, Roentgen X-rays. Structuralism and its rivals Edward Bradford Titchener (1867 to 1927) took a stricter version to Cornell and named it structuralism (1898): consciousness analysed into elements, aiming at a "periodic table" of the mind. Its elements were sensations, images and affections, varying in quality, intensity, duration, clearness and extensity; of Wundt's three feeling dimensions he kept only pleasantness-unpleasantness. Introspection was "a highly specialised form of self-observation"; its cardinal sin, the stimulus error , was naming the object ("an apple") instead of describing the experience (a glossy red patch). By his context theory of meaning , perception is a complex of sensory and imaginal processes. His society, the Experimentalists (1904), barred women. At Wurzburg Oswald Kulpe (1862 to 1915) found imageless thought , thought without images, and showed that the task ( Aufgabe ) steers thought through what Narziss Ach called a determining tendency, creating a set ( Einstellung ): "Mysuru" brings "palace" if you want a building, "Karnataka" if a state. The act psychology of Franz Brentano (1874) studied mental acts and their intentionality, their pointing at objects; Carl Stumpf (1848 to 1936) taught the Gestalt founders; Georg Elias Muller (1850 to 1934) extended memory research at Gottingen. Structuralism died with Titchener in 1927: introspection could not settle disputes, and the school excluded animals, children and applied work. Its topics returned in cognitive psychology. Exam trap Introspection is self-observation , not self-perception (a later social-psychology theory), self-thinking or attention. "Sensory and imaginal" perception is Titchener ; Bruner and Schafer were "New Look" perception researchers, Kimble a learning theorist. Structuralism aimed at a periodic table of elements ; "understanding consciousness" is too general and "behaviour, not mind" is behaviourism. Its heir is cognitive psychology , not neuroscience, behaviourism or functionalism. Functionalism and the American pioneers Americans asked what the mind is for . Their answer, functionalism , studies the mind as it functions in adapting the organism to its environment; it drew on Darwin, on pragmatism (ideas judged by their consequences) and on a demand for useful science. William James (1842 to 1910), father of American psychology and inspiration of functionalism, wrote The Principles of Psychology (1890). It described the stream of consciousness ("It is nothing jointed; it flows"), personal, changing, continuous and selective; habit, "the enormous fly-wheel of society"; the self, split into the material, social and spiritual "Me" and the knowing "I" or pure ego; and, with Carl Lange (1885), the James-Lange theory of emotion (Section 1.11). At Chicago, John Dewey (1859 to 1952) attacked the reflex arc in 1896: stimulus and response are not separate links, since a child's burn changes how the next flame is seen. James Rowland Angell (1869 to 1949) defined functional psychology (1906) and taught Watson; Harvey A. Carr (1873 to 1954) took the adaptive act as its unit. At Columbia, James McKeen Cattell (1860 to 1944) measured reaction time and individual differences and coined mental test (1890), Robert Sessions Woodworth (1869 to 1962) wrote Dynamic Psychology (1918) and added the organism to stimulus and response (S-O-R), and Edward Lee Thorndike (1874 to 1949) studied animal learning (Section 1.6). Granville Stanley Hall (1844 to 1924) earned the first American doctorate in psychology (1878), opened the first American research laboratory (Johns Hopkins, 1883), founded the American Journal of Psychology (1887) and was first president of the American Psychological Association (APA, 1892); he called adolescence "storm and stress", explained by recapitulation (each child relives human evolution). Lightner Witmer (1867 to 1956) opened the first psychological clinic (Pennsylvania, 1896) and first printed "clinical psychology" (1907). Hugo Munsterberg (1863 to 1916) founded forensic and industrial psychology. Mary Whiton Calkins (1863 to 1930), refused a Harvard doctorate as a woman, became the first woman APA president (1905); Margaret Floy Washburn (1871 to 1939) was the first woman PhD in psychology (1894) and wrote The Animal Mind ; Leta Stetter Hollingworth (1886 to 1939) disproved claims of female inferiority. Key study: The first case at the first clinic (1896) A teacher brought Witmer a fourteen-year-old "chronic bad speller". Testing his vision, memory and reading rather than labelling him, Witmer found poor eyesight behind part of the problem; corrected vision and individual teaching helped. Assess first; seek the simplest cause. Functionalism dissolved into the mainstream: Angell's student Watson dropped consciousness to found behaviourism (Section 1.2), and the functional question passed to evolutionary psychology. Exam trap Functionalism ("how people work, play and adapt") is William James , not Titchener, Watson, Hall or "William Wundt"; Darwin inspired it but led no school, and Dewey or Angell is right only for the formal Chicago school. It studies the mind adapting the organism , grew from Darwin's evolution (not Freud, Pavlov or Gestalt laws) and gave rise to the evolutionary perspective . Dewey's arc is the reflex arc ; "efferent" is only the outgoing half; "association" and "dynamic" arcs are invented. "Clinical psychology" in print: Witmer , not Freud, Erikson or Cattell. APA: 1892 , not 1896. First woman APA president: Calkins , not Washburn, Hollingworth or the psychoanalyst Karen Horney. Zeitgeist, great persons and "fathers" Why credit one man and one year? The great-person theory ( Thomas Carlyle , 1841) credits exceptional individuals; the Zeitgeist ("spirit of the times") view, championed by Edwin Garrigues Boring (1886 to 1968), credits ripe times, pointing to multiple discovery, as when Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace reached natural selection independently (1858). "Father" may mean founder, namer, chief influence or first in a country, so read the qualifier (Table 1.1). Psychology's arrival in India, through N. N. Sengupta at Calcutta (1915, 1916), is told in Section 1.2. Table 1.1 Who is the "father" of what. N. Sengupta G. Bose; M. V. Gopalaswamy Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Thinking and remembering are internal, covert processes. Locke called the mind at birth a tabula . Herbart's store of existing ideas is the mass. Wundt's system, stressing will and attention, is . Naming "an apple" instead of describing the experience is the error. Dewey's 1896 paper attacked the concept. The first psychological clinic (1896) was opened by Lightner . Answers: (1) mental, (2) rasa, (3) apperceptive, (4) voluntarism, (5) stimulus, (6) reflex arc, (7) Witmer. 1.2 Schools and Systems, the Cognitive Revolution and Indian Psychology High yield · 112 Qs Section 1.1 ended with structuralism and functionalism. This section meets the rival schools that followed (about 1900 to 1960), the mind's return in the cognitive revolution, and the Indian traditions, which asked the same questions two thousand years earlier. Schools, paradigms and the four forces A school of thought is a group of psychologists sharing assumptions about subject matter, method and explanation. Thomas Samuel Kuhn (1922 to 1996), in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), argued that a mature science works within one paradigm, a shared framework of problems and methods, until anomalies force a paradigm shift; a field of competing schools, as psychology was, is a preparadigmatic science . The humanists later numbered the schools as "forces": psychoanalysis first, behaviourism second, humanistic psychology third, transpersonal psychology fourth. The schools divided on enduring issues, which the historian Robert Irving Watson (1909 to 1980) called prescriptions (1967): mind-body, nature-nurture, free will-determinism, mechanism-vitalism, molar-molecular, nomothetic-idiographic (general laws or the unique individual), objectivism-subjectivism and empiricism-rationalism. Rene Descartes fed two schools: his reflexes led to behaviourism, his innate ideas to Gestalt nativism. Exam trap The fourth force is transpersonal psychology; "experiential" is not a force. Two Watsons : John B. founded behaviourism (1913); Robert I. proposed the prescriptions (1967). Behaviourism: Watson, the neobehaviourists and Skinner Behaviourism threw consciousness out of psychology altogether. Animal psychology (Thorndike's puzzle-box cats, 1898) and Russian objective psychology had prepared the ground: Pavlov's conditioned reflexes and the reflexology of Vladimir Mikhailovich Bekhterev (1857 to 1927), who conditioned movements. Key study: Watson's manifesto (1913) John Broadus Watson (1878 to 1958) launched behaviourism with "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It": psychology is "a purely objective experimental branch of natural science", its subject matter behaviour, not consciousness, and "introspection forms no essential part of its methods". Its goal is prediction and control: given the stimulus, to predict the response, and given the response, the stimulus. The same laws hold for humans and animals. Watson treated thinking as subvocal speech, tiny movements of the larynx; this peripheralism puts mental life in the muscles rather than the brain. Such implicit (covert) responses cannot be seen but can be measured with instruments, so covert behaviour is "measurable but not observable", and the "mental processes" in today's definition of psychology are internal, covert processes. Infants, he held, have only three unlearned emotions, fear, rage and love; the rest are conditioned, as he and Rosalie Rayner tried to show with Little Albert (1920). His boast "give me a dozen healthy infants" (1925) is environmentalism at its purest. The neobehaviourists (about 1930 to 1960) drew on logical positivism (only statements that observation can verify are meaningful) and on operationism , proposed by the physicist Percy Williams Bridgman (1882 to 1961) in 1927: a concept means the operations used to measure it, hence the operational definition. Edward Chace Tolman (1886 to 1959) studied molar, purposive acts and inferred intervening variables between stimulus and response, above all the cognitive map , a mental representation of the environment. His evidence was latent learning : rats that explored a maze unrewarded for ten days matched rewarded rats the day after food appeared (Tolman and Honzik, 1930). Clark Leonard Hull (1884 to 1952) built a hypothetico-deductive system of drive reduction in which reaction potential is habit strength multiplied by drive; John Dollard and Neal Elgar Miller (1950) recast Freud in his terms. Edwin Ray Guthrie (1886 to 1959) needed only contiguity and one-trial learning. Burrhus Frederic Skinner (1904 to 1990; Walden Two , 1948; Verbal Behavior , 1957; Beyond Freedom and Dignity , 1971), who studied operant behaviour, was a radical ("thoroughgoing") behaviourist: thoughts are real behaviour but not causes, whereas methodological behaviourism simply sets them aside. Zing-Yang Kuo (1898 to 1970) rejected instinct outright. From the late 1950s Chomsky's attack (1959, below), instinctive drift (1961) and Kohler's insight weakened behaviourism; it left operational definitions and behaviour therapy, such as Joseph Wolpe 's systematic desensitisation by reciprocal inhibition (1958). Exam trap Watson founded behaviourism (not rationalism) and defined psychology as the science of behaviour (not soul, mind or consciousness). One Panwar item keys N. L. Munn , whose textbooks popularised "the scientific study of behaviour": prefer Watson if offered, else Munn (not Woodworth, of the S-O-R formula, or Wundt). Cognitive map and latent learning are Tolman's, not Kohler's (insight), Harlow's (learning sets), Skinner's, Gould's (he only tested the idea in honeybees, 1986) or Bandura's. Dollard and Miller = early social learning; Bandura and Walters (1963) = later. Gestalt psychology and Kurt Lewin A second rebellion, in Germany, kept consciousness but denied that experience is built from elements. Key study: Wertheimer's phi phenomenon (1912) At Frankfurt, Max Wertheimer (1880 to 1943) flashed two lines in quick succession. About 30 milliseconds apart they looked simultaneous, about 200 apart successive, but at about 60 a single line seemed to move: the phi phenomenon . The motion lay in neither stimulus, so no sum of sensations could produce it. The paper founded Gestalt psychology. Gestalt means an organised whole, and the school's slogan is that the whole is different from (popularly, greater than) the sum of its parts: a square has closedness and an inside that none of its four lines has. Field theory holds that perception, thought and behaviour are set by the whole field of forces present at the moment. Against the elements of structuralism and the reflexes of behaviourism, Gestalt studied wholes and relations and leaned nativist; its laws of organisation (Pragnanz, figure and ground) are in Section 1.4. Wolfgang Kohler (1887 to 1967), stranded on Tenerife from 1913 to 1920, saw the chimpanzee Sultan join two sticks to reach a banana: insight , a sudden reorganisation of the perceptual field (German 1917; The Mentality of Apes , 1925). His hens learned the relation "darker" rather than a shade ( transposition ), and his isomorphism matched the structure of experience to brain fields. Kurt Koffka (1886 to 1941; Growth of the Mind , 1921; Principles of Gestalt Psychology , 1935) separated the geographical environment from the behavioural one, the world as perceived. Wertheimer's Productive Thinking (1945) set understanding against rote. Wertheimer, Kohler and Lewin fled the Nazis to America, where Koffka had settled in 1927. Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947) carried field theory into motivation and social life. In B = f(P, E), behaviour is a function of the person and the environment, together the life space : the totality of facts determining behaviour at a moment, the environment being psychological, as it exists for that person. Topological psychology maps its regions and boundaries, hodological space its paths; valences attract or repel, and vectors push. His students found that interrupted tasks are better recalled ( Bluma Zeigarnik , 1927) and spontaneously resumed ( Maria Ovsiankina , 1928). He coined group dynamics, compared autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire leaders (Social chapter), and founded action research , a cycle of planning, acting, observing and reflecting with the people affected; he is the father of modern social psychology. Gestalt therapy is different: an experiential, here-and-now therapy of Frederick Salomon Perls (Fritz Perls, 1893 to 1970), Laura Perls and Paul Goodman, famous for the empty chair, in which the client addresses an imagined person or a disowned part of the self. Exam trap Founders : Wertheimer, Kohler, Koffka (not Watson, James, Pavlov or Lewin); the school most important for perception. Empty chair = Gestalt therapy, not psychoanalysis, cognitive-behavioural or dialectical behaviour therapy, or person-centred therapy. Loose keys stretch "Gestalt" to cover the therapy: "here-and-now" is keyed to Gestalt psychology, and "Perls was a proponent of the Gestalt perspective" is accepted because "Gestalt focuses on wholeness in the present moment". A management stem adding that the parts relate to each other and to the whole means systems theory . Life space = person plus psychological environment, not groups. Lewin founded action research , not psychoanalysis, psychophysics or functionalism. Psychoanalysis: the first force Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) began as a neurologist treating hysteria (paralysis or blindness without nerve damage). In Paris in 1885 Jean-Martin Charcot (1825 to 1893) showed him hysterical symptoms appearing and vanishing under hypnosis; Pierre Janet (1859 to 1947) explained hysteria as dissociation, and Hippolyte Bernheim (1840 to 1919) of Nancy saw hypnosis as suggestion. Josef Breuer (1842 to 1925) found that his patient Anna O. lost symptoms by talking about their origins, the "talking cure" or cathartic method, and their Studies on Hysteria (1895) began psychoanalysis. Freud turned to free association, called dreams "the royal road" to the unconscious ( The Interpretation of Dreams , 1900) and lectured at Clark University in 1909. His topographic model divides the mind into conscious, preconscious and unconscious; his structural model (1923) into the id (impulsive, irrational, seeking immediate gratification), the ego (reality) and the superego (conscience), the ego guarding against anxiety with defence mechanisms such as repression. (Freud's neurotic anxiety is the fear that id impulses will break through.) Dissenters and neo-Freudians (Personality chapter) stressed relationships and culture: Adler (individual psychology), Jung (analytical psychology, the collective unconscious), Karen Horney ( basic anxiety , a pervasive loneliness and helplessness), Fromm (humanistic psychoanalysis), Sullivan (interpersonal psychiatry), Erikson (psychosocial stages), Anna Freud (ego defences) and Melanie Klein (object relations). From psychoanalysis, the first force, descends the psychodynamic perspective, which explains behaviour, and many disorders, by unconscious urges and the hidden struggle over their expression. Exam trap Freud began as a neurologist . Father of psychoanalysis : Freud, not Bernheim, Adler or Jung. Psychoanalytic theory is Freud's, psychosocial theory Erikson's. Gratification, irrational, impulsive = id . Horney's basic anxiety is not Freud's neurotic anxiety, existential anxiety or "innate anxiety" (no such technical term). Humanistic, existential and positive psychology Against the determinism of psychoanalysis (instinct) and behaviourism (reward), Abraham Harold Maslow (1908 to 1970) launched a third force and studied self-actualisation, the fulfilment of one's potential (Section 1.10); Carl Ransom Rogers (1902 to 1987) described an innate actualising tendency that thrives on unconditional positive regard. Charlotte Buhler (1893 to 1974) added a lifespan view and Rollo May (1909 to 1994) existentialism. The Association for Humanistic Psychology formed in 1961 or 1962 (sources differ), and the Old Saybrook conference (1964) marked the movement's formal birth. Humanistic psychology emphasises free will, the whole person, an innate tendency to grow and reaching maximum potential, understood from inside the person's experience: phenomenology , after Edmund Husserl (1859 to 1938), describes experience by bracketing assumptions about its causes. Disorder means blocked growth; healing comes from acceptance, respect and belief in the person's potential, not from reinforcement or uncovering unconscious conflict. Critics call humanistic and phenomenological approaches vague and blind to the wider social and cultural contexts of experience. Existential psychology starts from the givens no one escapes, which Irvin David Yalom (1980) named the four ultimate concerns: death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness. Soren Kierkegaard (1813 to 1855) called anxiety the dizziness of freedom; Martin Heidegger (1889 to 1976) named human existence Dasein , being-in-the-world (1927); Jean-Paul Sartre (1905 to 1980) held that existence precedes essence, so each person must keep recreating himself and meaning is never fixed. Ludwig Binswanger (1881 to 1966) and Medard Boss (1903 to 1990) built Daseinsanalysis on Heidegger. Viktor Emil Frankl (1905 to 1997) founded logotherapy : the will to meaning is the primary human motive, and its frustration brings an existential vacuum or a noogenic neurosis . May ( The Meaning of Anxiety , 1950) separated normal, usable anxiety, existential anxiety included, from neurotic anxiety. Maslow later foresaw a fourth force (1968), transpersonal psychology , the study of peak experiences, meditation and self-transcendence. Positive psychology, the science of positive experiences, traits and institutions, was launched by Martin Elias Peter Seligman (born 1942) as President of the American Psychological Association in 1998, with Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (1934 to 2021), known for flow. Its themes include the PERMA model of well-being (Seligman, 2011; positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning and accomplishment), C. R. Snyder's hope (the will and the ways to reach a goal), which its interventions promote, and savouring , deliberately enhancing the enjoyment of positive experiences. Exam trap Third force = humanism (Maslow, Rogers), not cognitivism or the biopsychosocial model. "Uncovering unconscious fears" is psychoanalytic, not existential. Dasein and noogenic anxiety belong to the existential school. Will to meaning = logotherapy, not Ellis's rational emotive behaviour therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy or the broader existential-humanistic therapy. Positive psychology was founded by Seligman , not Gardner (multiple intelligences), Pinker (language and evolutionary psychology) or Bandura; its interventions promote hope ; savouring is not avoidance, relaxation or trauma work. The cognitive revolution and today's perspectives Other critics charged behaviourism with leaving out the mind. Tolman's maps, Kohler's insight and Karl Spencer Lashley 's (1890 to 1958) argument of 1948 that rapid sequences such as speech need central plans were anomalies, and the computer made inner states respectable. The symbolic birth year of the cognitive revolution is 1956: Allen Newell and Herbert Alexander Simon 's Logic Theorist modelled problem solving, Noam Chomsky (born 1928) presented formal models of language, George Armitage Miller (1920 to 2012) gave "the magical number seven, plus or minus two", and the Dartmouth project launched artificial intelligence. Donald Eric Broadbent (1926 to 1993) produced the first major information-processing theory (1958); Chomsky's 1959 review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior argued that children produce sentences never reinforced; and Ulric Neisser (1928 to 2012), the father of cognitive psychology, named the field in Cognitive Psychology (1967). Cognitive psychology studies internal mental processes such as attention, memory and problem solving through the information-processing approach , which treats the mind as a computer passing information through stages of limited capacity. Its forerunners were Frederic Charles Bartlett (schemas, 1932) and Jean Piaget (1896 to 1980), who studied children's thinking from the 1920s. Cognitive neuroscience asks how the brain does it, and connectionism , or parallel distributed processing (David Rumelhart and James McClelland, 1986), stores knowledge as weights across many units working at once. Albert Bandura 's (1925 to 2021) self-efficacy (1977), belief in one's capacity to act, and the cognitive therapies of Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck, which target maladaptive thoughts and cognitive distortions, fed cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT; Clinical chapter). By the 1970s schools had given way to coexisting perspectives (Table 1.2, applied to Ravi, a Mysuru student anxious before every examination). Some lists add a developmental perspective, the study of change as people mature. Cross-cultural psychology compares processes across cultures, cultural psychology studies how culture and mind make each other up, indigenous psychology builds theory from within one culture, and eclecticism selects concepts and techniques from several schools to fit the problem. Table 1.2 The contemporary perspectives, applied to one case of examination anxiety. Perspective Explains behaviour through Ravi's anxiety comes from Biological (neurobiological) Brain, nervous system, genes An over-reactive threat system Evolutionary Natural selection An ancient alarm misfiring Psychodynamic Unconscious conflict, early childhood Fear of parental disapproval Behavioural Stimulus-response conditioning Failure paired with humiliation Cognitive Internal mental processes Catastrophic thoughts Humanistic Free will and growth Worth conditional on marks Sociocultural Culture and social context Competitive family pressure Biopsychosocial (George Engel, 1977) All three levels together All of these, interacting Exam trap First major information-processing theory : Broadbent, 1958 (not Treisman, about 1960; Chomsky, 1957; or Watson, 1920). Pioneer of cognitive psychology against Kohler, Chomsky and Kohlberg (moral development): Piaget . "Behaviour is governed by the brain and nervous system" = neurobiological , not psychophysical (Fechner's stimulus-sensation measurement, Section 1.3) or neo-behaviouristic. Cultural differences are studied by cross-cultural psychologists (a Panwar key says social psychologists, the vaguer answer). Indian psychology: the idea and its pioneers Psychology in India is the discipline as practised here, long mostly Western psychology on Indian soil. Indian psychology is an approach that integrates the classical Indian traditions with psychological concepts. It is consciousness-centred; holistic, treating body, mind, spirit, family and community as one system; transformative; open to disciplined first-person methods such as meditation; and value-laden. In mental health it combines traditional practices such as yoga with modern therapy. Modern psychology entered India at Calcutta. Narendra Nath Sengupta (1889 to 1944) set up the first laboratory there in 1915 and the first Department of Psychology in 1916, and founded the Indian Psychological Association (1925), whose Indian Journal of Psychology began in 1926; he is the father of modern psychology in India. Girindrasekhar Bose (1887 to 1953) founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society (1922) and corresponded with Freud; the father of psychoanalysis in India, he proposed the theory of opposite wishes , in which every wish is paired with its opposite, one expressed and one repressed. M. V. Gopalaswamy began psychology at Mysore in 1924; Madras (1943) and Pune (1950) followed. Durganand Sinha (1922 to 1998) urged indigenisation , making psychology's concepts and methods fit Indian culture, either from without, by adapting Western tools (as in Uma Chowdhury 's Indian Thematic Apperception Test, about 1960), or from within, from the culture's own traditions. Jai B. P. Sinha proposed the nurturant-task leader (1980), whose warm care depends on hard work; Udai Pareek (1925 to 2010) studied role stress; and Sudhir Kakar (born 1938) applied psychoanalysis to Indian childhood and society. The Indian Psychology movement dates from the Pondicherry Manifesto (2002). Matthijs Cornelissen founded the Indian Psychology Institute; Koneru Ramakrishna Rao , Anand C. Paranjpe and Ajit K. Dalal edited the Handbook of Indian Psychology (2008); and Cornelissen, Girishwar Misra and Suneet Varma edited Foundations of Indian Psychology (2011). Exam trap Indian psychology is not Western theory applied exclusively, folklore, or meditation without psychological context. Keys naming Bose (IHBAS) or Uma Chaudhuri (Panwar) for the first laboratory are wrong: it was Sengupta's; without Sengupta, choose Bose (Mangal and A. K. Singh are textbook authors; neither they nor Rathi founded a laboratory). Sequence : Calcutta (1916), Mysore (1924), journal (1926), Madras, Pune; a key putting the journal before Mysore is wrong. Bose's theory is opposite wishes (not repression, dharma-sankata or "guilt theory"). "Amitosh Mukherjee" garbles Asutosh Mookerjee, a Calcutta vice-chancellor. Kakar is keyed for Horney's basic anxiety only as the sole psychoanalyst offered ("Kamala Chaudhuri" there probably garbles Uma Chowdhury). "G. R. S. Rao" as father of Indian psychology (RML 2025) probably means K. Ramakrishna Rao. Samkhya, the three gunas and the inner instrument Indian philosophies (darshanas) are astika if they accept the Vedas (Nyaya, logic; Vaisheshika; Samkhya; Yoga; Mimamsa, ritual; Vedanta) and nastika if not (Buddhism, Jainism, the materialist Charvaka); Sufism, Islamic mysticism, lies outside the scheme. Samkhya, attributed to the sage Kapila and set out in Ishvarakrishna's Samkhya Karika , is a dualism of purusha , pure consciousness, the passive, unchanging witness, and prakriti , primordial matter, unconscious, active and ever-changing, from which all forms of life emerge. In purusha's presence prakriti evolves, down to the five great elements (pancha mahabhutas), as Figure 1.2 shows. We suffer by mistaking prakriti's activity for the self ("I am angry"); discriminating the seer from the seen brings liberation, kaivalya. Purusha pure consciousness, witness Prakriti matter: sattva, rajas, tamas presence upsets balance Mahat or buddhi (intellect) Ahamkara (the I-maker) Inner instrument (antahkarana): buddhi + ahamkara + manas sattvic side Manas (sensory mind) 5 jnanendriyas (senses) 5 karmendriyas (organs of action) tamasic side 5 tanmatras (subtle elements) sound, touch, form, taste, smell 5 mahabhutas (gross elements) space, air, fire, water, earth Rajas supplies the energy for both lines of evolution Purusha + prakriti + 23 evolutes = the 25 tattvas Figure 1.2 Samkhya's map of mind and matter. In the presence of purusha, prakriti evolves into intellect, the I-maker, the sensory mind, the ten organs and the elements. Notice that everything below the top row, including thinking, feeling and the sense of "I", is a product of prakriti; only purusha is conscious. Prakriti is woven of three strands, the gunas , always mixed in varying proportions: sattva (clarity, calm, harmony, balance), rajas (activity, passion, desire, restlessness) and tamas (inertia, lethargy, darkness, dullness, ignorance). The Bhagavad Gita (chapters 14, 17 and 18) made them a psychology of personality. Before the same examination, Ananya keeps her plan and sleeps on time (sattva), Rohan flits between six guidebooks and lies awake racing (rajas), and Karthik sleeps till noon, telling himself there is no point (tamas). Nobody is pure; diet, routine and practice shift the balance. The mind's working part is the antahkarana , the inner instrument: manas, the sensory mind that attends and doubts; ahamkara, the I-maker or ego; buddhi, the intellect that decides; and, in later Vedanta, chitta, the store of memory impressions. Exam trap Purusha is not dynamic or ever-changing; prakriti is not pure consciousness, unchanging or the intelligent self. The gunas belong to prakriti (not purusha, atman, Brahman, samadhi or samskara) and come from Samkhya with the Gita (not Nyaya, Charvaka or Mimamsa). Bavisha, who has stopped eating and cannot act, shows tamas alone (yama is a yoga limb, not a state). Not gunas: vata (a dosha), ahimsa, prakriti, ahamkara, or "karma, dharma, moksha". The ego is ahamkara ; the Gita 's three elements of mind are manas, buddhi and ahamkara, not "prakriti, purusha, kshetra" (kshetra, the field, is the body that the self knows) or "dharma, artha, kama". Yoga, the self and other Indian paths Samkhya says what the mind is made of; yoga says how to change it. Patanjali 's Yoga Sutras adopt Samkhya's map, and sutra 1.2 defines yoga as chitta-vritti-nirodha , the stilling of the mind's fluctuations; the goal is liberation (kaivalya). The five fluctuations (vrittis) are valid cognition, error, verbal imagination, sleep and memory. They are stilled by practice (abhyasa) and non-attachment (vairagya), and driven by five afflictions (kleshas): ignorance (avidya), egoism, attachment, aversion and clinging to life. The method is the eight limbs, in fixed order (Table 1.3). Table 1.3 The eight limbs of Patanjali's yoga, in order. Limb Meaning 1. Yama Ethical restraints, such as non-violence (ahimsa) 2. Niyama Personal observances, such as purity 3. Asana Steady, comfortable posture 4. Pranayama Breath regulation 5. Pratyahara Withdrawal of the senses inward 6. Dharana Concentration on one point 7. Dhyana Meditation: an unbroken flow of attention 8. Samadhi Absorption in the object A student meditating on a candle flame turns her senses away from the hostel's noise and smells (pratyahara), fixes on the flame and brings attention back whenever it drifts (dharana), finds it flowing unbroken (dhyana), and for a moment loses even "I am meditating" (samadhi). The Gita 's principle of disinterestedness is nishkama karma , acting without attachment to the fruits. It drives karma yoga, beside the paths of knowledge (jnana) and devotion (bhakti), and answers Arjuna's dharma-sankata, a dilemma in which every action breaks some duty. The Upanishads call the true self atman , eternal consciousness distinct from the body and from passing states of mind; Adi Shankaracharya 's Advaita Vedanta (eighth century CE) makes it one with Brahman, ultimate reality, and calls the world of many things maya, appearance. The Mandukya Upanishad 's four states are waking (jagrat), dreaming (svapna), deep sleep (sushupti) and turiya , "the fourth", the consciousness that witnesses the other three. The Taittiriya Upanishad 's five sheaths ( panchakosha ), outer to inner, are annamaya (the food body), pranamaya (breath), manomaya (mind and senses, the sheath of perception), vijnanamaya (intellect) and anandamaya (bliss); the middle three form the subtle body (linga sharira). Buddhism ( Siddhartha Gautama , the Buddha, traditionally 563 to 483 BCE) teaches four Noble Truths: suffering, its cause in craving, its cessation and the Noble Eightfold Path. Its anatta denies a permanent self, its Abhidhamma catalogues states of mind, and vipassana (insight meditation) trains sati, mindfulness. Sufi psychology refines the nafs, the lower self, from the commanding ammara to the tranquil mutma'inna and the ego's passing away (fana). Sri Aurobindo (1872 to 1950) put the psychic being , the evolving soul, at the centre of integral yoga, behind an outer being of body, vital (life-energy, desire and emotion) and mind. Ayurveda's three doshas (vata, pitta, kapha) govern the body. Karma's impressions (samskaras) work like habits, and dharma, the order of duties, heads the four aims of life (purusharthas): dharma, artha (wealth), kama (pleasure) and moksha (liberation). Clinical link Buddhist mindfulness underlies third-wave CBT, such as Marsha Linehan 's dialectical behaviour therapy, which blends CBT with Zen mindfulness and dialectical philosophy (Clinical chapter). Psychoanalysis is no wave of CBT. Exam trap Goal of yoga : control of the mind and kaivalya, not fitness, cognitive enhancement or emotion regulation only. Last four limbs : pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi. One point = dharana ; senses turned inward = pratyahara (not pranayama or niyama); karma and jnana are not limbs. Nishkama karma is the principle , karma yoga the path. Atman is not the body, a passing state or Jung's collective unconscious; turiya is not deep sleep. Annamaya is outermost, manomaya perceptual; the atman is never a sheath, so a key adding it to the subtle body is wrong. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. Kuhn called a field of competing schools a science. Tolman's unrewarded rats showed learning. Lewin's life space is the person plus the environment. Frankl called neurosis from frustrated meaning neurosis. India's first psychology laboratory (1915) was set up by . The guna of inertia and ignorance is . The yoga limb that withdraws the senses inward is . Answers: (1) preparadigmatic, (2) latent, (3) psychological, (4) noogenic, (5) Narendra Nath Sengupta, (6) tamas, (7) pratyahara. 1.3 Sensation and Psychophysics Lower yield · 40 Qs Everything you know about the world arrives as physical energy. This section follows that energy into experience, shows how sensation is measured, and then takes each sense in turn. From energy to experience In sensation the sense organs detect physical energy and convert it into neural signals; in perception the brain organises and interprets those signals. Optical illusions therefore distort perception, not sensation: in the Muller-Lyer figure the receptors register the lines correctly (Section 1.4). The structuralist Edward Bradford Titchener (1867 to 1927) defined a perception as a complex of sensory and imaginal elements. A receptor is a cell specialised for one form of energy, and its conversion of that energy into neural signals is transduction . Because all impulses look alike, Johannes Peter Muller (1801 to 1858) proposed the doctrine of specific nerve energies (today, labelled-line coding): the quality of a sensation depends on which nerve is stimulated, not on what stimulates it, so pressing a closed eyelid makes you see light. Intensity is coded differently. By the all-or-none law an action potential fires at full size once threshold is reached; a stronger stimulus never makes a bigger impulse, and a sub-threshold one makes none, not a miniature or graded one. Intensity is therefore carried by rate coding (faster firing) and by recruiting more neurons. Every sense except smell relays to the cortex through the thalamus (vision via its lateral geniculate nucleus, hearing via the medial). Finally, sensory adaptation is the fading of response to an unchanging stimulus, which is why you soon stop feeling your wristwatch. Exam trap Illusions distort perception ; "translation" and "adaptation" are bait. "Sensory and imaginal" is Titchener , not Bruner (Section 1.4). Specific nerve energies is Muller , not Helmholtz. The relay for every sense but smell is the thalamus , not the hypothalamus (drives), medulla (breathing), corpus callosum (joins the hemispheres), basal ganglia (movement) or hippocampus (memory). Thresholds and the psychophysical laws Gustav Theodor Fechner (1801 to 1887) founded psychophysics , the measurement of the relation between stimuli and sensations, with his Elements of Psychophysics (1860). The absolute threshold (or limen) is the minimum intensity a person can detect. It is not a switch: as a faint tone grows stronger, "yes" answers climb gradually along an S-shaped psychometric function, since neurons fire spontaneously. The threshold is therefore defined as the intensity detected on 50 percent of trials; weaker stimuli are subliminal. Eugene Galanter (1962) gave the classic examples: a candle flame 48 kilometres away on a dark night, a watch ticking at 6 metres. The difference threshold, or just noticeable difference (JND), is the smallest change detected 50 percent of the time. Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795 to 1878), comparing lifted weights in 1834, found the JND to be a constant fraction of the standard: Weber's law , ΔI / I = k . If k for weights is 0.02, 500 grams needs 10 grams more to feel heavier, but 5 kilograms needs 100. The fraction is finest for pitch and among the coarsest for taste and smell. Fechner then assumed that every JND is an equal unit of sensation; counting JNDs gives Fechner's law , S = k log I , so each doubling of light adds about one equal step of brightness. Stanley Smith Stevens (1906 to 1973) instead had people give each stimulus a number proportional to its strength ( magnitude estimation ) and found Stevens' power law (1957), S = kI n : exponents below 1 compress (brightness, about 0.33), exponents above 1 expand (electric shock, about 3.5). Cross-modality matching (squeezing a hand grip as hard as a sound is loud) confirmed them (Table 1.4). Table 1.4 The three psychophysical laws compared. Law Formula Main limitation Weber (1834) ΔI / I = k Fails near threshold Fechner (1860) S = k log I Assumes equal JNDs; no expansion Stevens (1957) S = kI n Swayed by range and number habits Exam trap Minimum detectable stimulus: absolute threshold ; smallest detectable change: difference threshold . "Sensory adaptation point", "perceptual boundary" and "signal detection of response" are invented; response bias is a signal detection term, and the phi phenomenon is apparent movement (Section 1.4). Weber's JND is a constant fraction , not a fixed amount. The equal-JND assumption is Fechner's , not Weber's. The father of psychophysics is Fechner, not Ernst Weber (whose JND he built on), Wilhelm Wundt (experimental psychology), Hermann Ebbinghaus (memory, inspired by Fechner) or Edward Tolman (learning). Measuring thresholds and signal detection Fechner's method of limits changes the stimulus in steps, in alternating ascending and descending series. Its errors of habituation (keeping an answer too long) and anticipation (switching too early) are cancelled by counterbalancing. The method of constant stimuli presents fixed values many times in random order: most accurate, but slow. In the method of adjustment (average error) the observer sets the stimulus: fastest, but least precise. Modern staircases weaken the stimulus after each "yes" and strengthen it after each "no". Yet a threshold mixes what an observer can sense with how readily the observer says "yes", as wartime radar operators showed; signal detection theory (SDT), set out by David M. Green and John A. Swets in 1966, separates the two. Noise alone and signal plus noise produce overlapping distributions of internal evidence, and the observer says "yes" above a cut-off, the criterion. "Yes" to a signal is a hit , "no" a miss ; "yes" to noise alone is a false alarm , "no" a correct rejection . Sensitivity, or d prime (d′), is the distance between the distributions, z (hit rate) minus z (false alarm rate): zero when hits equal false alarms, larger as hits outnumber them. The criterion ( β or c ), or response bias , follows expectations and payoffs. A liberal observer (a smoke alarm) gives many hits and false alarms; a conservative one (a court) few false alarms but more misses. A4 PDF of the whole book, colour (821 pages) A4 PDF, black and white (821 pages) Chapter 1 Psychology as a Science: Roots, Founders and the First Schools In this chapter 1.1 What Is Psychology? : define psychology as it has been defined across history, state its four goals, separate basic from applied work and name the main fields, including the one that studies animals. 1.2 Philosophical Roots: A Long Past : trace nativism, rationalism, empiricism and associationism from Plato to Kant, and lay out the classic positions on the mind-body problem. 1.3 Physiological and Biological Roots : explain how nerve physiology, brain localisation, Darwin's evolution and Galton's study of individual differences prepared the ground for a laboratory science. 1.4 Measuring the Mind: Psychophysics and Mental Chronometry : show how Weber, Fechner, Donders and Ebbinghaus proved that mental events could be measured. 1.5 Wilhelm Wundt and the Founding of Experimental Psychology : describe Wundt's laboratory, his voluntarism, his theory of feeling, his method and his folk psychology, and name his famous students. 1.6 Structuralism and Its European Rivals : explain Titchener's structuralism, its method and its errors, and the challenges from Wurzburg, Brentano, Stumpf and G. E. Muller. 1.7 Functionalism and the American Pioneers : explain why functionalism arose, what James, Dewey, Angell, Carr and Woodworth contributed, and who built American psychology's institutions. 1.8 Reading the History: Zeitgeist, Great Persons and "Fathers" : compare the two ways of explaining history, master the "father of" and "first" questions, and trace the arrival of psychology in India. Weightage. 46 of the 819 questions mapped in this book (5.6%) test this chapter, 12 of them from real past papers. 1 of its 8 sections is High yield. Leipzig, in the winter of 1879. In a small room of an old university building known as the Konvikt, a doctoral student named Max Friedrich sits in front of a clockwork timer called a Hipp chronoscope, a machine built to measure intervals in thousandths of a second. A stimulus is presented; Friedrich presses a telegraph key. Then the procedure is changed: now he must press the key not the instant he senses the stimulus, but only once he has clearly grasped what it is. The second kind of reaction takes longer, and the extra time, Friedrich and his supervisor reasoned, is the time the mind needs to apperceive , to bring an impression into the clear focus of attention. Trial after trial, the numbers go into a notebook. His supervisor was a 47-year-old professor of philosophy, Wilhelm Wundt. When Wundt had arrived in Leipzig four years earlier, the university had given him this room to store the apparatus he used in lecture demonstrations. By the winter of 1879 it had become something new: a place where students carried out original experiments on the mind and published them as research. Friedrich's study of the duration of apperception became the first dissertation to come out of that room, and historians who later combed the Leipzig archives dated the start of the work to the last weeks of 1879. Here is the puzzle that should bother you. Almost nothing in that room was new. The chronoscope had been built for physicists and astronomers. The idea of measuring the time taken by mental acts came from a Dutch physiologist. The word apperception came from a German philosopher who had died in 1716. And at Harvard, in 1875, the same year Wundt got his room, an American named William James had also been given space for psychological apparatus. So why does every textbook in the world, and nearly every entrance paper in India, treat Leipzig in 1879 as the moment psychology was born? The answer to that question is the subject of this chapter. To find it you need to know where the parts in that room came from: the philosophers who argued for two thousand years about where knowledge comes from, the physiologists who timed nerves and mapped brains, the naturalists who put human beings back among the animals, and the physicists who dared to measure sensation. Then you need to see what Wundt and his students built from those parts, and what the next generation, in Germany and in America, did with it. Remember Max Friedrich pressing his key; we will come back to him at the end of the chapter. 1.1 What Is Psychology? Medium yield · 5 Qs Ask ten people at a chai stall what psychology is and you will hear ten answers: reading minds, treating madness, understanding why people do what they do. Ask ten textbooks and you will get fewer answers, but you will notice something odd: the textbooks of 1890, 1920 and today do not agree with one another either. The definition of psychology has changed several times, and each change tells you which school was in charge. Entrance papers love these definitions, so we start with them. From soul to behaviour: a definition that kept changing The word itself is Greek: psyche (breath, soul) and logos (study or reasoned account). Literally, then, psychology began as "the study of the soul". The Greek philosophers did not use the word as the name of a subject; it first appears in Latin book titles of the sixteenth century (the German scholar Rudolf Goclenius used it in 1590), and the philosopher Christian Wolff (1679 to 1754) made it standard with two books, Psychologia empirica (1732) and Psychologia rationalis (1734). For the Greeks and the medieval scholars, the soul was the principle of life and reason; Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE) wrote the first systematic treatise on it, De Anima ( On the Soul ), which is why some older Indian textbooks call him the "father of psychology". From the seventeenth century, philosophers spoke less of the soul and more of the mind : its ideas, its reasoning, its sensations. When psychology became a laboratory science in the nineteenth century, the definition narrowed again. For Wundt and his student Titchener, psychology was the science of conscious experience , studied by trained observers looking inward. William James, in 1890, opened his great textbook with the sentence "Psychology is the Science of Mental Life, both of its phenomena and of their conditions." Then came the revolt. In 1905 and again in 1908 the British psychologist William McDougall (1871 to 1938) defined psychology as the positive science of the conduct or behaviour of living creatures, and in 1913 John B. Watson declared that psychology should drop consciousness altogether and study only behaviour , by which he meant anything an organism does that can be observed and measured from outside. (Watson and behaviourism are the subject of Chapter 2.) The new definition spread through the textbooks. Robert Sessions Woodworth (1869 to 1962), whom you will meet again in Section 1.7, defined psychology as the scientific study of the activities of the individual in relation to the environment. The definition you will most often find credited in Indian textbooks, "psychology is the scientific study of behaviour", is attributed to the American textbook writer Norman L. Munn . Watson's definition won battles but lost the war. By the 1960s psychologists were again studying memory, imagery and thinking, and today's standard definition reunites the two halves: psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes . Each phrase in that definition is doing work. Behaviour is overt: speaking, walking, blushing, pressing a key. By contrast, mental processes are internal and covert: perceiving, remembering, thinking, dreaming, feeling. You cannot see a student remembering the year of Wundt's laboratory, but you can infer it from what he writes. And scientific means that claims are tested against systematic, public observation that someone else could repeat, not against authority or intuition. An old classroom quip sums up the whole story: first psychology lost its soul, then it lost its mind, then it lost consciousness, and now it has behaviour, of a sort. The four goals: describe, explain, predict, control Every science tries to do four things with the events it studies, and psychology is no exception. Take one example and push it through all four: a student who "blanks out" in the examination hall at Mysuru even though he knew the material the night before. Describe. First we must say exactly what happens, and to whom: racing heart, sweaty palms, a mind that will not retrieve answers, perhaps in the first ten minutes only. Careful description separates this from simple lack of preparation. Explain. Next we ask why. Perhaps very high arousal and catastrophic thoughts ("If I fail, everything is over") compete with retrieval for limited attention. An explanation is a cause that can be tested. Predict. A good explanation lets us forecast who will blank out and when: students with high scores on a test-anxiety scale, under time pressure, on high-stakes papers. Control (many textbooks now say influence or change ). Finally we use the knowledge to change the outcome: practice under timed conditions, relaxation training, rehearsing realistic self-statements. This goal is where clinical psychology lives. Some textbooks add a fifth goal, improving the quality of life, but the four above are the classic list. Watson put prediction and control at the very centre of his definition, a point we will return to in Chapter 2. Basic and applied research Psychologists who study a problem only to understand it are doing basic research ; those who study it to solve a practical problem are doing applied research . When Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised lists of meaningless syllables in the 1880s to discover how quickly memories fade, he was doing basic research; when Lightner Witmer opened a clinic in 1896 to help a boy who could not learn to spell, he was doing applied work. The line is not a wall: Witmer's clinic drew on the basic science of the laboratory, and applied problems constantly raise new basic questions. You will see in Section 1.7 that the split between "pure" and "applied" psychology was one of the main arguments between the first two schools. The fields of psychology Modern psychology is a family of specialities. You will study several of them in other books of this series, so here we need only a map (Table 1.2). Two of them deserve a sentence more, because entrance papers test the boundary between them. Put simply, clinical psychology is the assessment, diagnosis and treatment of psychological disorders and distress; its practitioners work with conditions ranging from anxiety to schizophrenia, in hospitals, clinics and private practice. counselling psychology overlaps heavily but has traditionally focused on people in the normal range who face adjustment problems: career choice, relationships, study difficulties, life transitions. In India, the Rehabilitation Council of India licenses clinical psychologists, not counsellors, to work with psychiatric disorders, which is one reason your interviewers will care whether you understand the difference. The branch that studies the behaviour of animals is comparative psychology : it compares species, often in the laboratory, to understand how behaviour and learning evolved and what is common to humans and other animals. Its biological cousin, ethology , studies animal behaviour in natural settings and is associated with the zoologists Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen. You will see in Section 1.3 that comparative psychology grew directly out of Darwin's work. Three more names in Table 1.2 are easily confused. The first, evolutionary psychology , explains present-day behaviour and mental mechanisms as adaptations shaped by natural selection, that is, as part of our genetic inheritance from ancestors who faced recurring problems of survival and reproduction. The second, behaviour genetics , asks a narrower question: how much of the variation among people in a trait is due to differences in their genes, studied mainly through twins, families and adoption. The third, differential psychology , is the study of individual differences in abilities and personality; the German psychologist William Stern (1871 to 1938) named it in 1900, but its founder in practice was Francis Galton (Section 1.3). The German memory researcher Hermann Ebbinghaus put the answer in one famous sentence in 1908: "Psychology has a long past, but only a short history." The long past is two thousand years of philosophy and a century of physiology; the short history begins in rooms like Wundt's.
