Notice how the roots (left) cluster in German physiology and British biology, and how quickly the institutions (right) followed once Wundt's laboratory opened in 1879. 1.2 Philosophical Roots: A Long Past Medium yield · 5 Qs Long before anyone measured a reaction time, philosophers had asked the three questions that still organise much of psychology. Where does knowledge come from? How are ideas connected to one another? And how is the mind related to the body? Psychology inherited all three, and the answers given between ancient Athens and eighteenth-century Germany are examined every year in Indian entrance papers. Let us define the main positions first, then meet the people who held them. On the first question, there are two classic answers. The first, nativism , holds that some knowledge, ideas or abilities are inborn, present before any experience. The second, empiricism , holds that all knowledge comes from experience, delivered through the senses. A third term, rationalism , is often paired with nativism: it holds that reason, not the senses, is the chief source of knowledge, and that the senses can deceive. Keep the two contrasts apart. Nativism versus empiricism is a question about origins (inborn or learned?). Rationalism versus empiricism is a question about the route to knowledge (reasoning or sensing?). In practice the rationalists were usually nativists, and the empiricists were nearly always anti-nativists, which is why exam setters sometimes treat the pairs as one. Plato and Aristotle Plato (about 427 to 347 BCE) was a nativist and a rationalist. In his dialogue Meno , Socrates draws a theorem of geometry out of an uneducated slave boy simply by asking him questions, and concludes that the boy was not learning but recollecting knowledge his soul already possessed. For Plato, the senses show us only shifting copies of the true, unchanging Forms; real knowledge comes from reason turning inward. He also divided the soul into three parts (reason, spirit and appetite), an early model of conflict within the mind that you may hear echoed when you study Freud. Plato's student Aristotle disagreed. In De Anima he treated the soul not as a separate thing trapped in the body but as the form or function of a living body, the way seeing is the function of an eye. And he was an empiricist: the mind at birth, he wrote, is like a writing tablet on which nothing has yet been written, and knowledge begins with the senses. (Hold on to that tablet; John Locke will pick it up two thousand years later.) Aristotle also gave psychology its first theory of how one idea leads to another. In his short work On Memory and Recollection he observed that when we try to recall something we start from a thing that is similar to it, contrary to it, or was contiguous with it (close to it in time or place). These are the laws of association : similarity , contrast and contiguity , to which later writers added frequency (ideas experienced together often are linked more strongly). Try it on yourself. Hear the name "Sachin" and "Tendulkar" follows by contiguity, because you have always met the two words together; "Virat Kohli" may follow by similarity (another great Indian batsman); and the thought of the slowest batsman you ever watched may follow by contrast. Exam trap Aristotle is the empiricist of the pair and Plato the nativist ; students often reverse them because Aristotle is called the "father of psychology" (for De Anima ) and they assume he must have founded everything. Aristotle's three laws are similarity, contrast, contiguity . David Hume's three laws (below) are resemblance, contiguity in time or place, and cause and effect . If a question lists "contrast", it is Aristotle; if it lists "cause and effect", it is Hume. Rene Descartes: the body as a machine As a young man early in the seventeenth century, Rene Descartes (1596 to 1650) walked in the royal gardens at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, near Paris, where hydraulic statues moved, played music and even sprayed water at visitors who stepped on hidden plates in the path. The statues seemed alive, yet they were only pipes, water and valves. Descartes drew a bold conclusion: perhaps the living body is the same kind of machine. Nerves could be tubes, and "animal spirits", a fine fluid stored in the brain's cavities, could flow through them to inflate the muscles. Using this model, Descartes gave the first clear description of the reflex : an automatic, unlearned response to a stimulus that needs no mind at all. Put your hand near a fire, he said, and the heat moves particles in the skin, which tug on a thread inside the nerve, which opens a tiny valve in the brain, which releases animal spirits that flow back down to the arm muscles and pull the hand away. The details were wrong, but the idea that much behaviour is mechanical stimulus and response would run, through the Russian physiologists, all the way to behaviourism. The body, then, is a machine, and animals, which Descartes believed had no souls, are nothing but machines (automata). But the human being has something more: a mind, a thinking thing that has no size or location and cannot be doubted. "I think, therefore I am" (in French, je pense, donc je suis ), he wrote in his Discourse on Method (1637). This is dualism : mind and body are two different kinds of substance, the thinking substance and the extended (physical) substance. And because the two plainly affect each other (a pinprick causes pain; a decision moves an arm), Descartes was an interactionist. He placed the meeting point in the pineal gland , a small structure deep in the brain, chosen because, unlike most brain structures, it is single rather than paired and sits near the centre of the brain. His last book, The Passions of the Soul (1649), described how bodily events stir the emotions through this gland. Descartes was also a rationalist and a nativist. He held that certain innate ideas are not learned from experience but are built into the mind: the ideas of God, of the self, of infinity, and the axioms of geometry. You will see why this matters when we reach Kant and, in Chapter 2, the Gestalt psychologists. Remember Descartes left psychology four legacies: (1) mechanism and the reflex, which led through reflex physiology to Pavlov and behaviourism; (2) innate ideas , which led through Kant to the nativism of the Gestalt school; (3) dualism , which created the modern mind-body problem; and (4) rationalism , against which the British empiricists reacted. A practice question asks what Descartes' dualism "influenced" and keys behaviourism and Gestalt psychology on exactly this reasoning. "Empiricism and rationalism" is the wrong pairing because Descartes was himself a founder of modern rationalism, and empiricism was the reaction against him. The British empiricists: Hobbes, Locke, Berkeley and Hume Across the English Channel a very different tradition grew up, one that insisted the mind contains nothing that did not come in through the senses. Thomas Hobbes (1588 to 1679), best known for his political book Leviathan (1651), was its blunt forerunner. Hobbes was committed to materialism , the view that only matter exists; he held that sensations are motions in the body caused by motions outside it, and that thinking is a "train of thoughts" in which one motion follows another in the order in which they were first experienced. He also argued that human action is driven by the pursuit of pleasure and the avoidance of pain. Many historians call him the founder of British empiricism. The philosopher who made empiricism a full theory of mind was John Locke (1632 to 1704). Locke tells us that his great book began when a group of five or six friends met in his rooms to discuss a philosophical problem and got nowhere; it struck him that before arguing about what we know, they ought to examine what the human understanding is capable of knowing. Nearly twenty years later he published An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690). Its central claim is that the mind at birth is "white paper, void of all characters", the idea usually summed up by the Latin tabula rasa (blank or scraped tablet). There are no innate ideas. Every idea comes from one of two sources: sensation (experience of the outside world) or reflection (the mind's experience of its own operations, such as thinking and doubting). Locke divided ideas into simple ideas , which cannot be broken down further (the redness, sweetness and roundness of an apple), and complex ideas , which the mind builds by combining simple ones (the idea "apple" itself). This is the beginning of the "mental chemistry" that runs through the rest of this chapter: complex mental life built from simple elements. He also distinguished two kinds of qualities in objects. The primary qualities (solidity, extension or size, shape, motion and number) exist in the object itself, and our ideas of them resemble the object. The secondary qualities (colour, sound, taste, smell and warmth) exist only as powers to produce sensations in a perceiver. Locke's own demonstration is worth doing. Put one hand in hot water and the other in cold water for a minute; then plunge both into a bowl of lukewarm water. The same water feels cold to the first hand and warm to the second. Since the water cannot be both hot and cold, warmth must be in the perceiver, not in the water. Its size and shape, by contrast, feel the same to both hands. Finally, in the fourth edition of the Essay (1700) Locke added a chapter titled "Of the Association of Ideas", giving psychology the phrase. Interestingly, he used association mainly to explain irrational connections: ideas joined by chance or custom (a room where something terrible happened becomes unbearable) that produce prejudice and what he did not hesitate to call a kind of madness. Indian context In 1688 the Irish scientist William Molyneux wrote to Locke with a puzzle: if a man born blind, who had learned to tell a cube from a sphere by touch, were suddenly given sight, could he tell which was which by looking alone? Locke, a good empiricist, said no: the link between seen and felt shape must be learned. For three centuries "Molyneux's problem" could not be tested. Then, in a study published in 2011, Richard Held, Pawan Sinha and colleagues working with Project Prakash in India tested children who had been blind from birth with treatable cataracts. Immediately after surgery the children could see the shapes clearly but could not pick out by sight the shape they had just felt; within days, the link appeared. Locke's answer was largely right, and the learning was fast. George Berkeley (1685 to 1753), an Irish bishop, pushed Locke's argument to a startling end. If colour and warmth exist only in the perceiver, why not size and shape too? All we ever know are our own perceptions. To exist, for any object, is to be perceived: in Latin, esse est percipi . This position is called subjective idealism or mentalism. Berkeley also made a lasting contribution to the psychology of perception. In An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision (1709) he argued that we are not born able to see distance; we learn it, by associating visual cues (such as the feeling of the eyes converging on a near object, or blur) with the experience of reaching and walking. This is the first empiricist theory of depth perception, and the nativist reply to it is one of the threads of Chapter 4. David Hume (1711 to 1776), a Scot, published A Treatise of Human Nature in 1739 and 1740. He divided the contents of the mind into impressions (vivid, immediate experiences) and ideas (faint copies of impressions, as when you remember a taste). Ideas are joined, he said, by three laws of association: resemblance, contiguity in time or place, and cause and effect. He thought of association as a kind of gentle mental force, the mind's equivalent of Newton's gravity. Then he turned the analysis on causation itself and found that we never see one event make another happen; we see only that the two have always been joined (constant conjunction), and the mind forms the habit of expecting one after the other. Even the self, Hume said, is nothing but "a bundle or collection of different perceptions". Hume's scepticism woke the German philosopher Immanuel Kant, as we shall see. Associationism: Hartley, the two Mills and Bain Out of British empiricism grew a doctrine with a name of its own. Its name, associationism , refers to the view that complex mental life, including memory, thought and emotion, is built up by linking simple elements (sensations and ideas) according to a few laws, above all contiguity and frequency. Four writers turned it into a system. David Hartley (1705 to 1757), a physician, published Observations on Man in 1749. He was the first to give association a physiological basis: sensations are vibrations in the nerves and brain, and they leave behind miniature vibrations, which he called vibratiuncles , that are ideas. When two vibrations occur together often, they become linked, so that one later sets off the other. Contiguity, strengthened by repetition, was for Hartley the master law, and he distinguished simultaneous from successive associations. Historians usually credit him with founding associationism as a formal doctrine. James Mill (1773 to 1836) took the doctrine to its most mechanical extreme in Analysis of the Phenomena of the Human Mind (1829). For him a complex idea is nothing more than the sum of the simple ideas that compose it: the idea of a house is the ideas of bricks, mortar, windows and so on, added together, and the idea of "everything" is all the other ideas at once. This view is called mental mechanics . His son, John Stuart Mill (1806 to 1873), saw the flaw. In A System of Logic (1843) he argued that ideas can fuse into a whole with properties that none of the parts possessed, just as hydrogen and oxygen combine into water, which is like neither gas. His favourite example was Newton's colour disc: paint the colours of the spectrum on a wheel and spin it, and you see white, which is not experienced as "seven colours added". This is mental chemistry . Think of masala chai. James Mill would say your idea of its taste is tea plus milk plus ginger plus cardamom plus sugar; John Stuart Mill would say the taste of good chai is a new whole that is in none of the ingredients. The younger Mill's idea anticipates both Wundt's creative synthesis (Section 1.5) and the Gestalt slogan that the whole is different from the sum of its parts (Chapter 2). The last of the associationists, the Scot Alexander Bain (1818 to 1903), brought the tradition to the edge of modern psychology. His The Senses and the Intellect (1855) and The Emotions and the Will (1859) were the standard British textbooks of psychology for half a century, and they tied every mental process to what was then known of the nervous system. Bain described how a random ("spontaneous") movement that happens to bring pleasure is retained and repeated, a trial-and-error account of learning that anticipates Thorndike. In 1876 he founded Mind , the first journal devoted to psychology and philosophy. Exam trap Mental mechanics belongs to the father, James Mill; mental chemistry to the son, John Stuart Mill. Do not mix up James Mill with William James, or John Stuart Mill with John Locke. "Tabula rasa" is Locke , not Plato (nativist), Descartes (innate ideas) or Kant (innate categories). If asked the source of knowledge "as per empiricists", the answer is sensory experience ; "logical reasoning" and "contemplation" are the rationalists' routes. The continental rationalists: Leibniz, Herbart and Kant While the British were building the mind out of sensations, philosophers in Germany insisted that the mind is active, organised and partly unconscious. Their ideas reached Wundt directly, so we need them in some detail. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646 to 1716), co-inventor of the calculus, pictured reality as made of countless monads : simple, indivisible, active units of force, each of which mirrors the whole universe from its own point of view. Monads do not act on one another (they are "windowless"); they are kept in step by a harmony that God arranged in advance. Applied to mind and body, this "pre-established harmony" is a form of parallelism, which we will meet below. More important for psychology was Leibniz's theory of consciousness. He argued that we receive many perceptions too weak to notice individually, which he called petites perceptions (small perceptions). Standing on a beach, you hear the roar of the sea, yet that roar is made of the sounds of thousands of single waves, none of which you could hear on its own. When enough small perceptions add up, they cross into clear awareness, a step Leibniz called apperception . Consciousness is therefore a matter of degree, not all or none, and much mental activity goes on below awareness. Against Locke he wrote, in his New Essays on Human Understanding , that there is nothing in the intellect that was not first in the senses, "except the intellect itself". Johann Friedrich Herbart (1776 to 1841), who succeeded to Kant's chair at Konigsberg, turned Leibniz's ideas into a kind of mental mechanics with mathematics. Ideas, he said, have strength, and they compete: incompatible ideas push each other down. An idea that is pushed down does not vanish; it sinks below a boundary he called the threshold of consciousness (a limen), where it remains active and strives to return. Fechner would borrow the idea of a threshold for psychophysics, and Freud's repressed ideas that push to return to awareness have a family resemblance to it. The ideas currently in consciousness form an organised body that Herbart called the apperceptive mass . A new idea is understood, or apperceived, only by being taken up into this mass of existing ideas; an idea that finds nothing related to attach to is not grasped at all. Herbart was also a great educational theorist, and the classroom lesson follows directly: teach new material by linking it to what the child already knows. (His followers later turned this into the "formal steps" of lesson planning, which teacher-training colleges in India still teach.) You have experienced this yourself: the term "apperception" is far easier to learn now, attached to Leibniz's sea and Herbart's competing ideas, than it would be as an isolated word in a list. Herbart said psychology could be empirical and mathematical, but he did not believe it could be experimental, and he kept it separate from physiology. Within forty years both claims would be overturned in Leipzig. Exam trap An IHBAS 2025 question asks what the "apperceptive mass" constitutes and keys pure perception and pre-existing ideas , meaning a new perception taken up into the store of ideas already in the mind. The term is Herbart's ; Wundt took over and reworked the idea of apperception, which is why the question names him. The distractors each belong to someone else: "a compound of elemental processes bound by association" is the associationist (and structuralist) picture of the mind; "sensation and pure perception" leaves out the existing ideas that are the whole point; "sensation plus unconscious inference" is Helmholtz's theory of perception (Section 1.3). Apperception as a word was coined by Leibniz. The most influential German philosopher of all, Immanuel Kant (1724 to 1804), answered Hume in his Critique of Pure Reason (1781). Hume had shown that experience alone can never give us necessary connections such as causality. Kant replied that the mind does not wait passively for experience to write on it; it imposes its own built-in forms on whatever the senses deliver. Space and time are the forms through which we must perceive anything, and categories such as causality, unity and substance are the frames through which we must think about it. We never know things as they are in themselves, only as our minds organise them. This is nativism of a sophisticated kind, and it passed through the perceptual nativists of the nineteenth century into Gestalt psychology. Kant also issued a challenge. Psychology, he argued, could never be a true natural science, because mental events cannot be measured, cannot be put to experiment, and are distorted by the very act of observing them. The history in the rest of this chapter can be read as a series of replies to Kant: Herbart made psychology mathematical, Fechner made it measurable, and Wundt made it experimental. The answers given over the next three centuries form a small set of positions that every psychology student must be able to name (Figure 1.2). The first, interactionism , is Descartes' own answer: mind and body are different substances that causally affect each other. Its weakness is the one Descartes never solved, namely how something with no physical properties can push on something physical. Some of his followers, notably Nicolas Malebranche, proposed occasionalism : mind and body never act on each other, and God produces the bodily event on each occasion of the mental one, and the reverse. The second, psychophysical parallelism , holds that mental events and bodily events run side by side, perfectly correlated, but neither causes the other. Leibniz's picture was two clocks that keep identical time because they were set together at the start, not because one drives the other. Parallelism was attractive to the first experimental psychologists because it let them correlate mental events with physiological ones without worrying about causation; Wundt and Titchener both held versions of it. The third, epiphenomenalism , holds that bodily (brain) events cause mental events, but mental events cause nothing; consciousness is a by-product. Its best-known advocate, the English biologist Thomas Henry Huxley (1825 to 1895), compared consciousness to the whistle of a steam engine: it accompanies the work of the engine but does nothing to drive it. Finally, monism denies that there are two substances at all. Materialist monism (Hobbes) says only matter exists and mind is a process of the body. Idealist monism (Berkeley) says only minds and their perceptions exist. And double-aspect theory , associated with the Dutch philosopher Baruch Spinoza (1632 to 1677), says there is one underlying reality that shows itself in two ways: seen from the inside it is mind, seen from the outside it is body, as the same curved line is concave from one side and convex from the other. Fechner, the founder of psychophysics, held a view close to this one. A word on the philosophy of science Questions about the mind sit inside larger philosophical questions about what exists and how we can know it, and a few terms from the philosophy of science turn up in psychology papers. The term ontology (from the Greek for "being") names the branch of philosophy that deals with existence: what kinds of things are real? Is the mind a thing, a process, or an illusion? By contrast, epistemology deals with knowledge: how do we know what we know, and what counts as good evidence? The nativist-empiricist debate above is an epistemological debate. In the nineteenth century the French philosopher Auguste Comte (1798 to 1857) founded positivism , the view that genuine knowledge comes only from observable, verifiable facts, and that speculation about unobservable causes should be abandoned. Comte rejected introspection on the ground that the mind cannot observe itself, any more than the eye can see itself, an objection you will meet again when Wundt's method comes under fire. Post-positivism , associated with the twentieth-century philosopher Karl Popper, accepts that all scientific knowledge is fallible and provisional, so that theories are tested by trying to refute them rather than by piling up confirmations. Scientific realism holds that the unobservable entities described by our best theories (electrons, genes, perhaps memory traces) really exist. Of these terms, only ontology is defined by the question of existence. Philosophy, then, handed psychology its questions and some brilliant guesses. What it could not supply was a way to settle the arguments. For that, psychology had to borrow the methods of a different parent: experimental physiology. 1.3 Physiological and Biological Roots Lower yield · 1 Q By the middle of the nineteenth century, physiologists in Germany, France and Britain were doing something philosophers never had: cutting, stimulating, timing and measuring living nervous systems. Their findings did two things for the future psychology. They showed that the machinery of mind could be studied by experiment, and they gave Wundt, who trained as a physiologist, his methods and his confidence. Nerves carry the message The first great discovery was about the wiring. In 1811 the Scottish anatomist Charles Bell (1774 to 1842) described, in a privately printed pamphlet, evidence that the nerve roots entering the spinal cord at the front and at the back have different functions. In 1822 the French physiologist Francois Magendie (1783 to 1855) showed it decisively in experiments on young animals. The result is the Bell-Magendie law : the dorsal (back) roots of the spinal nerves carry sensory information in, and the ventral (front) roots carry motor commands out. The nervous system, in other words, has separate input and output channels, an anatomical basis for the distinction between sensation and movement, and ultimately for the stimulus-response unit. (The two men's quarrel over who deserved credit is a classic example of simultaneous discovery, which we discuss in Section 1.8.) The most influential physiologist of the age was Johannes Muller (1801 to 1858) of Berlin, whose Handbook of Human Physiology (published in parts from 1833 to 1840) summarised the field for a generation. Muller's best-known idea is the doctrine of specific nerve energies : the quality of a sensation depends not on the stimulus but on which nerve is stimulated. The optic nerve, however it is excited, produces only sensations of light; the auditory nerve only sound. You can test this now: close your eyes and press gently on the outer corner of one eyelid. You will see a patch of light, though no light has entered your eye; pressure on the optic pathway is "read" as light. A blow to the head makes a boxer "see stars" for the same reason. Muller's idea meant that we never perceive the world directly, only the state of our own nerves, a physiological version of the philosophers' point that experience is not the same as the object (the modern form of the idea, "labelled lines", is covered in Chapter 3). Muller's students included Hermann von Helmholtz and Emil du Bois-Reymond, and Wundt himself spent a semester in his Berlin laboratory. Muller believed that the speed of the nerve impulse was so great that it might never be measured. His student proved him wrong within a decade. Key study: Helmholtz times the nerve impulse (1850) Question. Is the nerve impulse effectively instantaneous, like light, or does it take measurable time? Method. Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894) used a frog's nerve with the muscle still attached. He stimulated the nerve first at a point far from the muscle and then at a point near it, and timed the delay before the muscle twitched. Result. Stimulation farther from the muscle produced a later twitch, and dividing the difference in distance by the difference in time gave a speed of only about 27 metres per second, roughly the speed of a car on a highway. Conclusion. Nervous activity is a physical process that takes time. If nerve conduction takes time, so may perceiving and deciding, and those times can be measured. Caveat. When Helmholtz tried to measure reaction times in human beings, the results varied so much from trial to trial and person to person that he gave up, an early hint of the individual differences that Galton and Cattell would later study. Helmholtz was perhaps the greatest scientist of the century, and three more of his ideas reach psychology. First, his theory of unconscious inference : perception is not a simple copy of sensation but a conclusion the mind draws, quickly and without awareness, from sensory data and past experience. When you see a distant elephant as huge though its image on your retina is tiny, you are "inferring" its size from its distance. This made Helmholtz an empiricist about perception, and it is the ancestor of modern ideas of perception as hypothesis-testing (Chapter 4). Second, building on a suggestion made by the English physician Thomas Young (1773 to 1829) in 1802, Helmholtz developed the trichromatic theory of colour vision, the Young-Helmholtz theory, which holds that colour vision depends on three types of receptor, most sensitive to different parts of the spectrum. Third, he proposed a resonance (place) theory of hearing. All three are developed in Chapters 3 and 4. For this chapter, remember that Wundt worked as Helmholtz's assistant at Heidelberg for several years. Exam trap "Helmholtz gave the trichromatic theory of colour vision" is the keyed answer to the bank question about him. The distractors are carefully chosen. The just noticeable difference belongs to Weber and Fechner (Section 1.4); the law of effect to Thorndike (Chapter 6). "Proposed the concept of the unconscious" is a trap because Helmholtz did propose unconscious inference , but the concept of the unconscious mind in the psychodynamic sense belongs to Freud (and its philosophical roots to Leibniz and Herbart). Mapping functions onto the brain If the nerves are wires, is the brain a single organ that does everything everywhere, or a collection of specialised parts? The modern answer, localisation of function , emerged through a strange mixture of quackery and careful science. The quackery came first. The Viennese physician Franz Joseph Gall (1758 to 1828) was a skilled brain anatomist, but he is remembered for a bolder claim: that the brain is made up of separate organs for separate mental faculties (such as acquisitiveness, combativeness or love of offspring), that a well-developed faculty means a larger organ, and that a larger organ pushes out the skull above it. By feeling the bumps on a person's head, therefore, one could read his character. Gall's collaborator Johann Gaspar Spurzheim (1776 to 1832) popularised the system under the name phrenology and carried it across Europe and America, where "phrenological parlours" read heads for a fee. Phrenology was wrong in its method (skull shape does not reflect the brain beneath, and Gall chose his evidence selectively), but it was right in its central assumption that different parts of the brain do different things. Phrenology's first scientific critic was the French physiologist Pierre Flourens (1794 to 1867). In the 1820s he used the method of ablation (also called extirpation): surgically removing a part of the brain of an animal, usually a pigeon or rabbit, and observing what behaviour was lost. He found real localisation at the level of large structures: damage to the cerebellum disrupted the coordination of movement, damage to the medulla stopped breathing and heartbeat, and removal of the cerebral hemispheres abolished perception and voluntary action. But within the cerebral hemispheres he found no faculties in particular places: the effects of damage seemed to depend on how much tissue was removed, and the cortex seemed to act as a whole. Flourens' ablation method became standard in physiological psychology, and his view of the cortex as acting as a whole was revived a century later by Karl Lashley (covered in the Physiological Psychology book). Localisation within the cortex was finally demonstrated through language. In 1861 the French surgeon Paul Broca (1824 to 1880) examined a patient named Leborgne, known in the hospital as "Tan" because that was nearly the only syllable he could say. Tan understood much of what was said to him but could not produce speech. When he died, Broca's autopsy found damage in the left frontal lobe, in a region now called Broca's area, and by 1865 Broca had concluded that "we speak with the left hemisphere". In 1874 the 26-year-old German neurologist Carl Wernicke (1848 to 1905) described the opposite pattern: patients with damage to the left temporal lobe who spoke fluently but meaninglessly and could not understand speech. Broca's aphasia is effortful, non-fluent speech with relatively preserved comprehension; Wernicke's aphasia is fluent speech with poor comprehension. (The aphasias, including the transcortical and conduction forms, are covered in the Physiological Psychology book.) Meanwhile, in 1870, the German physicians Gustav Fritsch (1838 to 1927) and Eduard Hitzig (1838 to 1907) applied weak electric currents to the exposed cortex of dogs and found a strip of the frontal lobe where stimulation produced movements of specific body parts on the opposite side of the body: the motor cortex. Electrical stimulation now joined ablation and clinical autopsy as a method of mapping the brain. Table 1.4 brings the localisation story together. Table 1.4 The localisation pioneers. Who When Method Finding Gall and Spurzheim about 1800 to 1830 Skull bumps (phrenology) Faculties have brain "organs"; method wrong, idea of localisation right Flourens 1820s Ablation in pigeons and rabbits Cerebellum: coordination; medulla: vital functions; cortex acts as a whole Broca 1861 Clinical case plus autopsy ("Tan") Left frontal area for speech production Fritsch and Hitzig 1870 Electrical stimulation in dogs Motor cortex; movements on the opposite side Wernicke 1874 Clinical cases plus autopsy Left temporal area for understanding speech Clinical link Phrenology is the clinical psychologist's cautionary tale. It had a plausible theory, confident practitioners, satisfied customers and an apparently huge body of supporting cases, yet it was false, because its evidence was gathered selectively and never put to a fair test. Every assessment tool you will learn to use, from an intelligence test to a projective test, must earn its place by evidence of reliability and validity (the Assessment book), not by the confidence of the person using it. Charles Darwin: the human animal Physiology showed that the mind had machinery. Biology showed where the machinery came from. When Charles Darwin (1809 to 1882) published On the Origin of Species in 1859, he proposed that species change over generations through natural selection : individuals vary, some variations help their owners survive and reproduce, and those variations become more common in later generations. In The Descent of Man (1871) he applied the theory to human beings, and in The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals (1872) he argued that facial expressions of emotion are inherited and universal, shared with other animals because they once served adaptive purposes (baring the teeth in anger is a remnant of preparing to bite). He even published a diary of his infant son's development (1877), one of the first "baby biographies". Darwin gave psychology three gifts, and each grew into a branch of the discipline. Continuity between species. If humans evolved from other animals, then animal minds differ from ours in degree, not kind, and studying animals can tell us about ourselves. This is the foundation of comparative psychology and of all later animal research on learning. Function. If a trait exists because it helped survival, then the right question to ask about any mental process is what it is for . This question is the heart of functionalism (Section 1.7), and through functionalism, of today's evolutionary psychology. Variation. Natural selection works on differences between individuals, so those differences are worth measuring. This idea was taken up by Darwin's own half-cousin. Francis Galton and the measurement of individual differences Francis Galton (1822 to 1911) shared a grandfather, the physician-poet Erasmus Darwin, with Charles Darwin. Independently wealthy, he never held a university post, and he could not see anything without wanting to count it: he once tried to make a "beauty map" of Britain by secretly tallying attractive and unattractive women he passed in different towns. After reading the Origin , he devoted himself to human variation, and in doing so he founded the study of individual differences . His first major book, Hereditary Genius (1869), traced the families of eminent judges, statesmen, scientists and others, and found that eminence ran in families far more than chance would predict. Galton concluded that ability is inherited. The flaw is obvious to you now: eminent families also pass on wealth, education and connections, so his data could not separate heredity from environment. Galton saw the problem himself and, in 1875, proposed studying twins to separate the effects of "nature and nurture" (a phrase he popularised). He was the first to use twin studies for this purpose. Key study: Galton's anthropometric laboratory (1884) Question. How much do people differ in basic physical and mental capacities? Method. At the International Health Exhibition in London in 1884, Galton set up an anthropometric laboratory where, for threepence, visitors were measured on height, weight, arm span, breathing capacity, strength of grip, swiftness of a blow, keenness of sight and hearing, colour discrimination, reaction time and the highest pitch they could hear (tested with a whistle he designed). More than 9,000 people passed through. Reasoning. Following the empiricist logic that all knowledge enters through the senses, Galton assumed that people with sharper senses and quicker reactions would be more intelligent. Result. He obtained the first large body of data on human individual differences, and to analyse it he had to invent new statistics. Criticism. The assumption linking sensory keenness to intelligence turned out to be wrong, as Cattell's followers discovered (Section 1.7); intelligence testing had to wait for Binet's very different approach (Chapter 9). The statistics may be Galton's greatest legacy. Studying the heights of parents and children (and, earlier, the sizes of sweet-pea seeds), he noticed that very tall parents tend to have children who are tall but less extreme than themselves, a phenomenon now called regression to the mean (1886). From this he developed the idea of correlation , a measure of how closely two variables vary together (1888); his younger colleague Karl Pearson (1857 to 1936) later produced the formula for the correlation coefficient that you will use in the Research Methodology book. Galton also pioneered the questionnaire (asking people to describe the vividness of their mental image of that morning's breakfast table), and in 1879 he devised the word association test: he read a word and noted the first association it called up, and was startled to find how many of his own associations reached back to childhood and revealed thoughts he would rather not publish. Carl Jung later developed word association into a clinical technique (the Personality book). There is a darker side. In 1883 Galton coined the word eugenics for the programme of improving the human stock by encouraging the "fit" to have more children and discouraging the "unfit". Eugenics was later used to justify forced sterilisation and, in Nazi Germany, mass murder. Galton's statistics are permanent tools of psychology; his eugenics is a permanent warning. Animal minds: from anecdote to Morgan's canon Darwin's idea of continuity invited a new question: how intelligent are animals? Darwin's young friend George John Romanes (1848 to 1894) set out to answer it, and his Animal Intelligence (1882) is usually treated as the first book of comparative psychology. Romanes gathered stories, from naturalists, pet owners and newspaper readers, of animals doing clever things: a cat that opened a door latch, a dog that seemed to plan. This anecdotal method had two weaknesses. Anecdotes are selected (no one writes in to report a dog doing something stupid), and they invite anthropomorphism , reading human thoughts and feelings into animal behaviour

In 1913 a twenty-six-year-old German psychologist named Wolfgang Kohler sailed to Tenerife, in the Canary Islands, to take charge of a small research station that the Prussian Academy of Sciences kept there for the study of chimpanzees. He expected a short posting. Then the First World War broke out, the sea lanes closed, and he stayed until 1920. For six years he had little to do but watch apes think. His most gifted subject was a chimpanzee called Sultan. One day Kohler placed a banana outside the bars of Sultan's cage, beyond reach. Inside the cage lay two hollow bamboo sticks, one thin enough to slide into the other, but each too short to reach the fruit on its own. Sultan tried one stick, then the other. He pushed one stick out with the second, so that the first touched the banana, but he could not draw it in. After more than an hour Kohler gave up and left a keeper to watch. Sultan sat on a box, idly playing with the two sticks. By chance he found himself holding them in a line, and he pushed the thin one into the end of the thick one. According to Kohler's record, he jumped up at once, ran to the bars and raked in the banana with his new long stick. When the sticks came apart, he joined them again without hesitation. What had happened inside Sultan? Kohler was sure he knew: the ape had suddenly seen the situation in a new way, the two sticks reorganised in his perception into one tool. But in the very year Kohler reached Tenerife, a young American at Johns Hopkins University, John B. Watson, was telling psychologists that "inside" questions of this kind had no place in a science at all; all that could be studied was what the animal did. In Vienna, Sigmund Freud would have asked a different question again: what hidden wish does the behaviour serve? Forty years later, a cognitive psychologist would describe Sultan as an information-processing system searching a "problem space", and today a researcher trained in the Indian tradition might ask about the state of attention in which the solution arrived. Same ape, same sticks, five different stories. That is what this chapter is about. Between about 1900 and 1960 psychology was divided into rival schools , each with its own idea of what psychology should study, how it should study it, and what a human being is. You will meet each school in turn, see why it arose, what it discovered, and why it declined or was absorbed. Remember Sultan; you will meet him again at the end of the chapter. 2.1 Schools, Systems and Paradigms Lower yield · 3 Qs Chapter 1 ended with the first two schools of scientific psychology, structuralism and functionalism. This chapter picks up the story where they left it. Before we meet the newcomers, though, it helps to be clear about what a "school" actually is, because the word is used loosely, and the vocabulary of the field matters as much as its content. What makes a school of thought A school of thought is a group of psychologists who share a common set of assumptions about what psychology should study (its subject matter), how it should study it (its method), and what kind of explanation counts. A school usually has a recognisable founder or leader, a statement of its programme (often called its manifesto), a university or laboratory that serves as its home, a journal in which its members publish, a stream of students who carry its ideas into other institutions, and, just as important, a rival school against which it defines itself. Behaviourism, for example, had Watson as its founder, his 1913 paper as its manifesto, and structuralism's introspection as its enemy. Two classic books gave the age of schools its shape. Robert Sessions Woodworth (1869 to 1962) of Columbia University surveyed the rivals in Contemporary Schools of Psychology (1931), and Edna Heidbreder (1890 to 1985) described Seven Psychologies (1933). Notice their dates. The schools flourished roughly between the 1890s and the 1950s; after that, as you will see in Section 2.7, psychology gradually traded rival schools for overlapping "perspectives". Two related words are worth separating. A system of psychology is an organised and internally consistent body of assumptions, methods and theory that tries to cover the whole field; a theory is narrower, an explanation of one set of facts (a theory of forgetting, a theory of colour vision). Courses called "Systems and Theories" study both: the great systems, and the theories they produced. Kuhn's paradigms and a preparadigmatic science Why did psychology split into warring schools when physics and chemistry did not? A helpful answer comes from a physicist turned historian, Thomas Samuel Kuhn (1922 to 1996). In The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), Kuhn argued that a mature science works within a paradigm : a shared framework of assumptions, problems, methods and model solutions that all workers in the field accept. Under a paradigm, scientists do what Kuhn called normal science : puzzle-solving within the accepted framework. Over time, results accumulate that the paradigm cannot explain (anomalies). When they pile up, the field enters a crisis; a new framework appears; and if it wins, the result is a scientific revolution, or paradigm shift . Newton's physics giving way to Einstein's is Kuhn's model case. A field that has no single accepted paradigm, but several competing schools, each with its own problems and methods, is in Kuhn's term a preparadigmatic science . Kuhn himself noticed this in the social sciences. In the preface to his book he recalled a year spent among social scientists and how struck he was by the number and extent of their open disagreements about what the legitimate problems and methods even were. The age of schools in psychology fits that description well: a structuralist and a behaviourist did not merely disagree about results, they disagreed about what counted as data. Whether psychology has since acquired a paradigm (or whether the cognitive revolution was a true Kuhnian revolution) is still debated, and we return to the question at the end of Section 2.7. The four forces You will often read that psychology has had three or four "forces". The numbering comes from the humanistic psychologists of the 1960s, above all Abraham Maslow, who called their own movement the third force to set it against the two forces that, in their view, dominated mid-century psychology. Table 2.1 sets out the sequence. Notice that the numbers describe a sequence of influence in the eyes of the humanists, not strict dates of birth: psychoanalysis (from the 1890s) is the first force and behaviourism (1913) the second. Table 2.1 The forces in psychology. Force School Key figures Picture of the person First Psychoanalysis Freud and his successors Driven by unconscious conflict and early childhood Second Behaviourism Watson, Skinner Shaped by the environment through conditioning Third Humanistic psychology Maslow, Rogers Free, growth-seeking, capable of self-actualisation Fourth Transpersonal psychology Maslow, Sutich, Grof Capable of experiences that go beyond the individual self Figure 2.1 lays the schools out in time, so that you can see which ones overlapped and which ones replaced each other. Keep it in mind as you read; each bar is the subject of one part of this chapter. Structuralism (1879) Functionalism (1890s) Psychoanalysis, the first force (1890s) Gestalt (1912) Behaviourism (1913) Neobehaviourism Humanistic (third force) Cognitive (1956) Transpersonal (1969) Positive psychology (1998) Indian Psychology movement (2002) 1880 1900 1920 1940 1960 1980 2000 Figure 2.1 The schools of psychology in time. Each bar runs from a school's founding event to the point where it stopped being a dominant, separate school (bars reaching the right edge are still active traditions). Notice how Gestalt and behaviourism were born a year apart, and how the cognitive and humanistic movements grew up side by side in the 1950s. Exam trap "Which is the fourth force?" The answer is transpersonal psychology . In counselling textbooks, however, Paul Pedersen (1991) called multiculturalism the "fourth force" in counselling. If both appear in the options, read the stem: "in psychology" points to transpersonal; "in counselling" may point to multiculturalism. "Experiential" psychology is not one of the numbered forces. 2.2 Behaviourism: From Watson's Manifesto to Skinner Medium yield · 9 Qs In 1913, structuralism (Wundt and Titchener) and functionalism (James, Dewey and Angell) were still arguing about consciousness: what its elements were, or what it was for. Both relied on introspection, the trained observation of one's own experience. A young professor at Johns Hopkins decided that the whole argument was a mistake. Psychology, he said, should stop studying consciousness altogether. To understand how anyone could say such a thing in 1913, and be applauded for it, you need to see the ground that had been prepared. The ground prepared: animal psychology and Russian objective psychology The first preparation came from the study of animals. After Charles Darwin (1809 to 1882) argued for continuity between humans and other species, animal minds became a serious topic. George John Romanes (1848 to 1894) collected stories of clever animals (his anecdotal method), and Conwy Lloyd Morgan (1852 to 1936) answered with his canon of 1894: never interpret an action as the result of a higher mental faculty if it can be explained by a lower one (both are covered in Chapter 1). Jacques Loeb (1859 to 1924), a physiologist who taught Watson at Chicago, went further and explained animal movement as tropisms , forced, mechanical orientations toward or away from light, gravity and chemicals, with no mind required. And Edward Lee Thorndike (1874 to 1949), in his 1898 dissertation Animal Intelligence , put hungry cats in puzzle boxes and showed that they escaped not by reasoning but by gradual trial and error, stamped in by satisfying consequences: his law of effect (Chapter 6). If animal behaviour could be studied so precisely without asking what the animal was conscious of, why not human behaviour too? The second preparation came from Russia, where a tradition of objective psychology had grown out of physiology. Ivan Mikhailovich Sechenov (1829 to 1905), in Reflexes of the Brain (1863), argued that all acts of conscious and unconscious life are reflexes in their origin. Ivan Petrovich Pavlov (1849 to 1936), who won the 1904 Nobel Prize for his work on digestion, discovered around the turn of the century that his dogs began to salivate to signals that preceded food; he called these conditioned reflexes and spent the rest of his life studying them (Chapter 6). Vladimir Mikhailovich Bekhterev (1857 to 1927) studied what he called association reflexes, conditioning motor responses such as withdrawing a limb from an electric shock, and named his whole approach reflexology ; his Objective Psychology appeared between 1907 and 1912. Bekhterev's motor conditioning, more than Pavlov's salivation, gave Watson a method he could use on people. The third preparation was home-grown. American functionalism had already pulled psychology toward practical questions (education, testing, industry) and toward the study of what organisms do to adapt. Behaviourism, in a sense, was functionalism with the mind removed. Watson's manifesto (1913) John Broadus Watson (1878 to 1958) grew up poor in South Carolina, earned his doctorate at the University of Chicago in 1903 with a study of learning in rats, and moved to Johns Hopkins in 1908. He had never been comfortable with introspection; he later admitted that he hated serving as a subject in introspective experiments and preferred animals, which could not be asked what they were experiencing. Early in 1913 he gave a lecture at Columbia University, published that March in Psychological Review as "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It". It is the founding document of behaviourism , the school that defines psychology as the science of observable behaviour. Key study: "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It" (1913) Watson's paper opens with a sentence every student of the history of psychology should know almost by heart: psychology as the behaviourist views it "is a purely objective experimental branch of natural science. Its theoretical goal is the prediction and control of behavior. Introspection forms no essential part of its methods." He added that the behaviourist "recognizes no dividing line between man and brute". The paper made four claims. (1) Subject matter : behaviour, not consciousness. (2) Method : objective observation, never introspection. (3) Goal : prediction and control, which made psychology useful to education, business and medicine. (4) Continuity : the same principles apply to humans and animals. In later books Watson phrased the goal precisely: given the stimulus, to predict the response, and given the response, to identify the stimulus that produced it. Watson was elected President of the American Psychological Association in 1915, only two years later; the manifesto had found an audience ready for it. What methods did Watson allow? Four: observation, with or without instruments; testing (he liked tests as samples of behaviour, not as measures of mental capacities); the verbal report method, in which speech is treated as behaviour, so that what a person says counts as data but is not taken as a window on consciousness; and, from 1915, the conditioned reflex method borrowed from Pavlov and Bekhterev. Watson's programme: thinking, emotion and the "twelve infants" A science of behaviour has to say something about the things introspectionists cared about, such as thought and feeling. Watson had an answer for each, and his answers show you the spirit of the school. Thinking as subvocal speech. Watson argued that thinking is nothing but talking to oneself so quietly that the movements cannot be seen: thought is subvocal speech , small movements of the tongue and larynx (he called them laryngeal habits). This view is called peripheralism , because it locates mental life in the peripheral muscles rather than in central brain processes. It led Watson to divide behaviour into explicit (overt) responses that anyone can see, and implicit (covert) responses such as subvocal speech, which cannot be seen by an observer but can, in principle, be measured with instruments. This is exactly the sense in which modern textbooks say covert behaviour is measurable but not directly observable, and why the "mental processes" in today's definition of psychology (the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes) are internal, covert processes. Was Watson right about thought? A dramatic test came in 1947, when Scott Smith and his colleagues at the University of Utah gave Smith himself a dose of curare large enough to paralyse every skeletal muscle, keeping him alive on a respirator. If thinking were movement of the speech muscles, Smith should have been unable to think. He reported afterwards that he had remained fully aware, had understood what was said to him and could remember it. Peripheralism did not survive. Emotion. Watson held that infants show just three unlearned emotional reactions: fear (to loud noises and sudden loss of support), rage (to hampering of movement) and love (to stroking and gentle handling). Every other emotion, he argued, is built from these three by conditioning. Environmentalism. Watson's most quoted words appeared in his popular book Behaviorism (1925). "Give me a dozen healthy infants, well-formed, and my own specified world to bring them up in and I'll guarantee to take any one at random and train him to become any type of specialist I might select: doctor, lawyer, artist, merchant-chief and, yes, even beggar-man and thief, regardless of his talents, penchants, tendencies, abilities, vocations, and race of his ancestors." This is environmentalism in its purest form: the belief that behaviour is shaped almost entirely by experience rather than heredity. What is usually left out is the next sentence, in which Watson conceded that he was "going beyond my facts", adding that so had the advocates of the contrary view, and they had been doing it for thousands of years. Consistent with this, Watson first accepted, and then by the mid-1920s rejected, the idea of human instincts. Little Albert. To show that emotions are conditioned, Watson and his graduate student Rosalie Rayner (1898 to 1935) conditioned fear in an eleven-month-old infant, "Albert B.", in 1920, pairing a white rat with a loud noise made by striking a steel bar behind his head. Albert came to fear the rat, and the fear generalised to a rabbit, a dog, a fur coat and a Santa Claus mask. The study, its method and its ethical problems are told in full in Chapter 6. The same year, Watson's affair with Rayner became public; he was forced to resign from Johns Hopkins, married Rayner, and spent the rest of his working life in advertising at the J. Walter Thompson agency. His academic career had lasted barely twenty years, but the school he named outlived him by decades. Exam trap Who defined psychology as the science of behaviour? Watson (1913) made behaviour the subject matter of psychology, so for "founder of behaviourism" and "Watson defined psychology as the science of ..." the answers are behaviourism and behaviour (not soul, mind or consciousness: the soul was the subject matter of the ancient philosophers, the mind that of later philosophers, and consciousness that of Wundt and Titchener). One Panwar item, however, keys N. L. Munn as the first to establish psychology as "the scientific study of behaviour": Norman Leslie Munn's widely used textbooks popularised that wording. If Watson is an option, prefer Watson; if the options are Munn, Woodworth and Wundt, the key is Munn. Woodworth is remembered for the S-O-R formula and a quip often credited to him: psychology first lost its soul, then its mind, then consciousness. Rationalism is a philosophical position (Descartes), not a school Watson founded. Functionalism belongs to James, Dewey and Angell; structuralism to Titchener. Three meanings of "behaviourism" As the school matured, it became clear that "behaviourism" could mean three different things, and the three are easily confused. The difference lies in what each says about the mind. Table 2.2 Three kinds of behaviourism. Kind What it says about mental events Typical figures Metaphysical (eliminative) Minds and conscious states do not exist as anything other than behaviour Watson in his most extreme statements Methodological Mental events may exist, but they are private and cannot be studied scientifically; only public behaviour counts as data Watson in practice; most neobehaviourists Radical Private events (thoughts, feelings) are real and are themselves behaviour, obeying the same laws; but they are not the causes of overt behaviour Skinner, who adopted the term in 1945 (Mary Whiton Calkins had first used it, for Watson's view, in 1921) The word "radical" in radical behaviourism does not mean "extreme". Skinner meant it in its root sense: thoroughgoing, going to the roots. Ironically, radical behaviourism is the only one of the three that lets thoughts and feelings into the science; methodological behaviourism simply sets them aside. Neobehaviourism: logical positivism and operationism Watson's crusading behaviourism dominated American psychology from about 1913 to 1930. Historians of psychology usually describe what followed as a second stage, neobehaviourism (about 1930 to 1960), and a third, sociobehaviourism or social learning theory (about 1960 onward). The neobehaviourists, Tolman, Hull, Guthrie and Skinner, kept Watson's demand for objectivity but wanted to make behaviourism more rigorous and more theoretical. They drew on two ideas from the philosophy of science. The first was logical positivism , the philosophy of the Vienna Circle of the 1920s, which held that a statement is meaningful only if it can be verified by observation (or is true by definition). Talk of unobservable "minds" was therefore not false but meaningless unless it could be tied to observables. The second was operationism , proposed by the American physicist Percy Williams Bridgman (1882 to 1961) in The Logic of Modern Physics (1927): a scientific concept means nothing more than the set of operations used to measure it. The psychologist S. S. Stevens brought the idea into psychology in 1935. The legacy is the operational definition that every research methods course still teaches: "hunger" in a rat experiment is defined as "twenty-three hours without food", and "intelligence" as "the score on this test". Edward Chace Tolman's purposive behaviourism. Edward Chace Tolman (1886 to 1959) of the University of California at Berkeley was the behaviourist who let cognition in by the back door. He called his system purposive behaviourism and set it out in Purposive Behavior in Animals and Men (1932), a book he dedicated, with typical humour, to the white rat. Tolman insisted on studying molar behaviour , whole goal-directed acts such as a rat running a maze or a person going home, rather than Watson's molecular behaviour , the individual muscle twitches and glandular secretions that make up an act. Molar behaviour, Tolman observed, "reeks of purpose": a rat that finds its usual route blocked takes another, so what it has learned is not a chain of movements but where the food is. To explain this without returning to introspection, Tolman introduced the intervening variable in the mid-1930s: an unobserved process inferred between the observable stimulus and the observable response and defined operationally by the conditions that produce it. Hunger, expectancy and demand are intervening variables. On one side sit the independent variables (environmental stimuli, hours of deprivation, heredity, previous training, age); on the other, behaviour; in between, the processes that link them. In effect, Watson's S-R formula became S-O-R, the formula Woodworth had used to insert the organism between stimulus and response. Tolman's most famous intervening variable was the cognitive map , a mental representation of the layout of the environment, which he described in "Cognitive Maps in Rats and Men" (1948). The best evidence for it was latent learning , learning that occurs without reinforcement and stays hidden until there is a reason to show it. In the classic experiment of Tolman and Charles Honzik (1930), rats that explored a maze for ten days without food made many errors; once food appeared in the goal box on day 11, their errors fell by the very next day to the level of rats rewarded from the beginning. They had been learning the maze all along (the full study is in Chapter 6). For Tolman, rats learn what leads to what (expectancies), not stimulus-response habits. Clark Leonard Hull's hypothetico-deductive system. If Tolman was the playful neobehaviourist, Clark Leonard Hull (1884 to 1952) of Yale University was the system-builder. Hull admired Newton's Principia and wanted a psychology built the same way, by the hypothetico-deductive method : state a small set of postulates, deduce precise testable predictions (theorems) from them, test the predictions experimentally, and revise the postulates when they fail. His Principles of Behavior (1943) made him for two decades the most cited psychologist in the world. At the centre of Hull's theory is drive reduction . A biological need (for food, water, relief from pain) produces a drive (D), an aroused state that energises behaviour; any response that reduces the drive is reinforced. Reinforced repetitions build habit strength , written S H R , the strength of the learned bond between a stimulus and a response, which grows with the number of reinforced trials. Habit alone does not produce behaviour; it must be energised by drive. Hull's 1943 formula for reaction potential , the tendency to make the response, was therefore multiplicative: S E R = S H R × D The multiplication matters: if either habit or drive is zero, there is no behaviour, however strong the other. A well-trained but completely satiated rat does not run the maze. Later versions added incentive motivation (K, the size of the reward) and stimulus intensity (V), and subtracted inhibition (fatigue-like reactive inhibition and conditioned inhibition). Hull's students, especially Kenneth Spence, Neal Elgar Miller and O. Hobart Mowrer, carried his ideas into many fields. One famous offshoot was John Dollard and Neal Miller's Personality and Psychotherapy (1950), which translated Freud's ideas into Hull's vocabulary of drive, cue, response and reinforcement; it is usually called the early social learning theory, as distinct from the later social learning theory of Albert Bandura and Richard Walters (1963). Edwin Ray Guthrie's contiguity theory. Edwin Ray Guthrie (1886 to 1959) of the University of Washington offered the simplest theory of all, in The Psychology of Learning (1935). His one law was contiguity : a combination of stimuli that has accompanied a movement will, on its recurrence, tend to be followed by that movement. Reinforcement is not needed; what matters is only that stimulus and movement occur together. Learning is one-trial learning : a stimulus-movement association reaches full strength on its first pairing. Why, then, does practice help? Because a skill is made of many movements, each attached to many stimuli, and practice attaches the act to more and more of the situations in which it must occur. Guthrie also gave practical advice on breaking habits (the threshold, fatigue and incompatible-response methods, Chapter 6). Burrhus Frederic Skinner's radical behaviourism. Burrhus Frederic Skinner (1904 to 1990) of Harvard became the most famous psychologist of the twentieth century; a 2002 survey ranking the most eminent psychologists placed him first, ahead of Piaget and Freud. Skinner distinguished respondent behaviour, elicited by a preceding stimulus as in Pavlov's experiments, from operant behaviour, emitted by the organism and controlled by its consequences. His tools (the operant chamber or "Skinner box", the cumulative recorder) and findings (reinforcement schedules, shaping) are covered in Chapter 6. Here what matters is his system. Skinner was a radical behaviourist (Table 2.2) and also an anti-theorist. In a 1950 paper he asked whether theories of learning were necessary at all and answered no: psychology should describe functional relations between environmental events and behaviour, without inventing intervening variables, drives or cognitive maps. This is why Skinner's approach is sometimes called descriptive behaviourism, or the "empty organism" approach (a description Skinner disliked, since he never denied that the organism has insides; he denied that inner events explain anything). His major books are worth knowing by title and year: The Behavior of Organisms (1938); Walden Two (1948), a novel about a utopian community run on reinforcement principles; Science and Human Behavior (1953); Verbal Behavior (1957), which treated language as operant behaviour shaped by a verbal community; and Beyond Freedom and Dignity (1971), which argued that the idea of an autonomous, free person is a pre-scientific fiction we can no longer afford. Zing-Yang Kuo, the behaviourist who abolished instinct. The most extreme environmentalist of all was a Chinese psychologist trained at Berkeley, Zing-Yang Kuo (1898 to 1970). In "Giving Up Instincts in Psychology" (1921) he argued that the concept of instinct explains nothing. He backed the claim with an elegant experiment (1930): kittens reared alone, kittens reared watching their mothers kill rats, and kittens reared together with rats. Most of the kittens that watched their mothers became rat-killers, while only a small minority of those raised alongside rats ever killed one, and some seemed to treat rats as companions. "Rat-killing instinct," Kuo concluded, depends on rearing. Table 2.3 sets the main behaviourists side by side. Table 2.3 The behaviourists compared.
