Thorndike's "connectionism" (stimulus-response bonds) is not the connectionism of modern neural-network models (Section 2.6). Criticism, decline and legacy By the 1950s behaviourism had won American psychology, and it was beginning to lose. The criticisms came from several directions at once. It could not explain language: Noam Chomsky's 1959 review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior , discussed in Section 2.6, argued that children produce sentences they have never heard and never been reinforced for. It ignored biology: two of Skinner's own former students, Keller and Marian Breland, reported in 1961 that the animals they trained for commercial shows kept "misbehaving", drifting back toward instinctive food-getting actions (instinctive drift), and John Garcia showed that rats learn some associations far more easily than others (Chapter 6). Its central concepts strained against its own evidence: Tolman's rats seemed to carry maps in their heads, and Kohler's apes seemed to reason. And it seemed to many to leave out exactly what makes us human: purpose, meaning and freedom. The humanists (Section 2.5) attacked from that side, the cognitive psychologists (Section 2.6) from the other. Yet behaviourism did not so much die as dissolve into the rest of psychology. Its demand for objective, operationally defined, replicable measurement became simply the way psychology is done. Its laws of learning remain the core of Chapter 6. And it gave clinical psychology one of its most effective toolkits. Clinical link Behaviour therapy applies learning principles to psychological problems. Mary Cover Jones (1896 to 1987) removed a small boy's fear of rabbits in 1924 by gradually bringing a rabbit closer while he ate. Joseph Wolpe (1915 to 1997), in Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition (1958), developed systematic desensitisation : relaxation, which is incompatible with anxiety, is paired with an imagined hierarchy of feared situations. (The method is Wolpe's, not Skinner's, Watson's or Pavlov's.) Skinner's operant principles produced token economies and applied behaviour analysis, now widely used with children with autism. The therapies themselves are taught in the Clinical book. 2.3 Gestalt Psychology and Kurt Lewin High yield · 16 Qs Behaviourism rebelled against structuralism by throwing out consciousness. A second rebellion, in Germany, began a year earlier and took the opposite route: it kept consciousness but threw out the idea that consciousness is built from elements. Where Titchener had analysed experience into sensations, images and feelings, and Watson analysed behaviour into reflexes, the Gestalt psychologists argued that both had made the same mistake. They had taken the whole apart and assumed that the parts were more real than the whole. Wertheimer and the phi phenomenon (1912) Max Wertheimer (1880 to 1943) was born in Prague and trained under Oswald Kulpe at Wurzburg. As the story is usually told, in the summer of 1910 he was travelling by train to a holiday in the Rhineland when an idea about seen motion struck him so forcefully that he got off at Frankfurt, bought a toy stroboscope (a device that creates the impression of movement from a series of still pictures), and began experimenting in his hotel room. Historians suspect the story has been polished over the years, but what followed is well documented. At the Psychological Institute in Frankfurt, Wertheimer used a tachistoscope (an instrument that flashes visual displays for precisely controlled intervals) to study apparent motion. His two main observers were younger psychologists, Wolfgang Kohler and Kurt Koffka. The three of them became the founders of Gestalt psychology, and Wertheimer's 1912 paper on the experimental study of seen motion is the school's founding document. The experiment was simple. Two lines were flashed one after the other in slightly different positions. When the interval between them was very short (around 30 milliseconds), observers saw two lines at once; when it was long (around 200 milliseconds), they saw one line and then the other. But at intervals in between (around 60 milliseconds), they saw a single line move from one position to the other. Wertheimer called this apparent movement the phi phenomenon . (He distinguished "pure phi", a sense of motion without any moving object, from the smooth movement of the object itself, later called beta movement; the details belong to Chapter 4.) Why did such a small effect launch a school? Because the motion was not in either stimulus. Each line, analysed on its own, was stationary. An elementist, adding up two static sensations, could never arrive at movement. The perceived motion was a property of the whole pattern of stimulation in time, and it was as real in experience as anything else. If something as basic as seen motion could not be built from elements, perhaps nothing in perception could. The idea was not entirely new. In 1890 the Austrian philosopher Christian von Ehrenfels (1859 to 1932), whose lectures Wertheimer had attended in Prague, had described form qualities (Gestaltqualitaten): a melody played in a different key consists of entirely different notes, yet we hear the same melody. The melody, then, is something more than its notes. Ehrenfels, however, treated the form quality as an extra element added to the sensations. Wertheimer's radical step was to reverse the order: the whole comes first, and the parts get their character from their place in it. The German word Gestalt means form, shape or configuration, an organised whole. Kohler: insight, transposition and isomorphism Wolfgang Kohler (1887 to 1967), born in Reval (now Tallinn in Estonia), took his doctorate in Berlin under Carl Stumpf and was the school's scientist and chief spokesman. You have already met him on Tenerife (1913 to 1920). His observations there, published in German in 1917 and in English as The Mentality of Apes (1925), challenged Thorndike's trial-and-error account of animal problem-solving. Thorndike's cats, Kohler argued, had been put in puzzle boxes whose mechanisms they could not see; of course they fumbled. Give an animal a problem whose elements are all in view, and it may solve it by insight : a sudden reorganisation of the perceptual field so that the relations needed for a solution are seen. Sultan's two sticks, and the boxes his companions stacked to reach fruit hung from the roof, were Kohler's showpieces. Insightful solutions, he noted, appear suddenly, are carried out smoothly once found, are retained, and transfer readily to similar problems. Insight learning as a type of learning is treated in Chapter 6. Key study: Kohler's chickens and transposition (1918) The question. When an animal learns to choose one of two stimuli, does it learn the absolute properties of the stimulus (this particular shade of grey) or a relation between stimuli (the darker of the two)? The method. Kohler trained hens to peck grain from the darker of two grey papers; grain on the lighter one was out of bounds. Then he gave them a test pair: the old "correct" darker grey, now beside an even darker new grey. The result. Most of the time the hens pecked at the new, darker grey, the one they had never been rewarded on, and ignored the shade that had been reinforced. Kohler found the same with chimpanzees. The conclusion. The animals had learned a relation ("the darker one"), not an absolute stimulus. Kohler called this transposition , by analogy with a melody transposed to a new key. It was a direct challenge to the stimulus-response view that a specific stimulus becomes bonded to a response. The criticism: Kenneth Spence (1937) later showed that a stimulus-response account combining generalisation gradients of excitation and inhibition could predict transposition too, and that transposition breaks down when the test pair is far from the training pair. Kohler's most ambitious idea was physiological. In Die physischen Gestalten ("Physical Gestalten", 1920) he proposed isomorphism : the organisation of experience corresponds in structure (not in literal copy) to the organisation of electrical field processes in the brain. A perceived circle does not mean a circle drawn on the cortex, but a pattern of brain activity with the same relational order. The theory was tested in the 1950s. Karl Lashley and his colleagues laid strips of gold foil across the visual cortex of monkeys (1951), and Roger Sperry inserted mica plates and tantalum wires into the cortex of cats (1955), to short-circuit or block any such electrical fields. Perception was essentially unaffected. The field version of isomorphism did not survive, although the broader idea that experience and brain activity share a structure lives on in cognitive neuroscience. Kohler became director of the Psychological Institute at the University of Berlin in 1922, the most prestigious post in German psychology. When the Nazis began dismissing Jewish professors in 1933, he published a newspaper article in their defence, one of the last openly critical pieces to appear in Germany, and resisted the regime's interference with his institute until he resigned and emigrated in 1935. He spent the rest of his career at Swarthmore College in Pennsylvania and was President of the American Psychological Association in 1959. Koffka: development and the behavioural environment Kurt Koffka (1886 to 1941) was the school's great communicator. His Growth of the Mind (German 1921, English 1924) applied Gestalt ideas to child development, arguing that infants perceive organised wholes from the beginning rather than assembling them from sensations. In 1922 he introduced Gestalt psychology to American readers in an article in the Psychological Bulletin titled "Perception: An introduction to the Gestalt-theorie". The article was so influential that for years Americans assumed Gestalt psychology was only about perception, which the founders found frustrating. Koffka moved to Smith College in Massachusetts in 1927, and his Principles of Gestalt Psychology (1935) is the school's most systematic textbook. Koffka's most memorable lesson is a German legend he retold in the Principles . On a winter evening, in a driving snowstorm, a man on horseback rode across a wide, wind-swept plain and arrived at last at an inn. The innkeeper, astonished, asked where he had come from. The rider pointed back across the plain. "Do you know," said the innkeeper, "that you have ridden across Lake Constance?" The rider dropped dead at his feet. In what environment, Koffka asks, did the rider's behaviour take place? In the geographical environment , the physical world, he crossed thin ice over deep water. But he behaved as if he were crossing solid ground, because his behavioural environment , the world as perceived, was a frozen plain. Behaviour, Koffka argued, is governed by the behavioural environment. It is one of the cleanest arguments in psychology for studying the world as the person experiences it. The three founders, together with the neurologist Kurt Goldstein and the psychiatrist Hans Gruhle, launched the school's journal, Psychologische Forschung ("Psychological Research"), in 1921. The central ideas of Gestalt psychology The whole is different from the sum of its parts. This is the school's slogan, and it is usually quoted as "the whole is greater than the sum of its parts". Koffka himself thought "greater" was the wrong word: in the Principles he wrote that it is more correct to say the whole is something else than the sum of its parts, because summing is a meaningless procedure, whereas the whole-part relationship is meaningful. A square drawn with four lines is not "more" than four lines; it is a different kind of thing, with properties (squareness, closedness, an inside) that none of the lines possesses. Textbooks use both versions for the Gestalt principle. Field theory. The Gestalt psychologists borrowed the concept of a field from nineteenth-century physics, where Faraday and Maxwell had shown that electrical and magnetic events are properties of a whole field of forces rather than of isolated particles. Field theory in psychology holds that perception, thought and behaviour are determined by the whole field of interacting forces present at the moment, not by isolated stimuli. Iron filings around a magnet do not each "decide" where to go; the field organises them. Organisation and Pragnanz. Because experience is organised into wholes, the Gestalt psychologists set out the laws by which the organisation happens. Wertheimer's 1923 paper on the laws of perceptual organisation described proximity, similarity, closure, good continuation and common fate, all governed by an overarching law of Pragnanz : perceptual organisation will always be as "good" (simple, regular, symmetrical, stable) as the conditions allow. Figure-ground organisation, first analysed by the Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin (1886 to 1951) in 1915, was adopted as a cornerstone: the figure is seen as a thing, nearer, with a clear contour and shape, usually smaller and more memorable, whereas the ground seems shapeless, diffuse, farther away and to continue behind the figure. The laws themselves, with demonstrations, are taught in Chapter 4. Productive thinking. Wertheimer's last book, Productive Thinking (published in 1945, two years after his death), brought Gestalt ideas to problem-solving and education. He distinguished reproductive thinking , the blind application of a memorised method, from productive thinking , in which the thinker grasps the structure of the problem and sees why a solution works. His favourite example came from a school classroom. Children taught the formula for the area of a parallelogram (base times height) by rote could apply it to the textbook figure but were helpless when the figure was turned on its side. A child who saw that the triangle "sticking out" at one end could be moved to fill the gap at the other, turning the parallelogram into a rectangle, understood the formula and could never be fooled by a rotation. Wertheimer also interviewed Albert Einstein at length about how the theory of relativity had been discovered. Karl Duncker's work on functional fixedness (1945) continued this line (Chapter 8). Notice the method row. The Gestalt psychologists did not use Titchener's trained introspection, which taught observers to report sensations and to avoid the "stimulus error" of naming the object. They wanted exactly what Titchener forbade: a description of experience as it naturally presents itself to an untrained observer, a book as a book and not as patches of colour. This descriptive approach is called phenomenological, and it links Gestalt psychology to the phenomenology of Husserl (Section 2.5). Exam trap Founders. The Gestalt trio is Wertheimer (founder), Kohler and Koffka. Watson, William James and Pavlov are favourite distractors. Lewin is Gestalt-influenced but is not one of the founders. Most important school for perception? Gestalt psychology. "The whole is greater than the sum of its parts and the parts are related to each other and to the whole" in a management or organisational stem refers to systems theory , associated with Ludwig von Bertalanffy's general systems theory, not to Gestalt psychology, motivation theory, contingency theory or Fayol's administrative theory. Read the options. The Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test (Lauretta Bender, 1938) borrowed its designs from Wertheimer's 1923 figures, but it is a test of visual-motor integration (Assessment book), not a Gestalt theory. Kurt Lewin: field theory applied to the person The Gestalt founders worked mainly on perception and thinking. It was a younger colleague at the Berlin Institute, Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947), who carried field theory into motivation, personality and, finally, social life. Lewin's starting point was that behaviour at any moment is a function of the whole psychological situation. He expressed it in a formula that appears in his Principles of Topological Psychology (1936): B = f(P, E) Behaviour (B) is a function (f) of the person (P) and the environment (E). The person and the environment are not independent: they form one interdependent field, which Lewin called the life space (LSp), the totality of facts that determine a person's behaviour at a given moment. So the formula is often written B = f(LSp). The life space contains the person and the psychological environment, the environment as it exists for that person (Koffka's behavioural environment again), not the physical world as a geographer would map it. A rule a student has never heard of is not in her life space; an exam she fears is, even though it is a week away. To describe the life space, Lewin borrowed from a branch of mathematics called topology, which deals with regions, boundaries and connections rather than distances and sizes; hence topological psychology . The life space is divided into regions (activities, goals, groups) separated by boundaries, some of which act as barriers. Movement from one region to another, in thought or action, is called locomotion. Because topology alone cannot express direction and strength, Lewin added two dynamic concepts. A valence is the attracting (positive) or repelling (negative) quality a region has for the person; a vector is a force acting on the person, with a direction and a strength, toward or away from a region. Lewin later added hodological space (from the Greek hodos , path), a geometry of paths that represents the routes, including detours, by which a person can reach a goal. Figure 2.2 puts these terms together. The person and the psychological environment together make up the life space. The goal has positive valence and exerts a force (vector) on the person; a barrier blocks the direct route, so the person must find a detour path; a region of negative valence pushes the person away. Notice that everything in the diagram is the situation as the person sees it. Tension systems and the Zeigarnik effect. Lewin proposed that an intention to reach a goal sets up a tension system within the person, which is discharged only when the goal is reached. One prediction follows directly: unfinished tasks should leave tension behind them and so stay active in the mind. According to a story told by his students, Lewin noticed this one evening at a Berlin restaurant, where a waiter remembered every detail of the unpaid orders but could not recall what had been ordered at a table that had already settled its bill. His student Bluma Zeigarnik (1900 to 1988) tested the idea in 1927. Participants were given a series of simple tasks, half of which were interrupted before completion. Afterwards they recalled the interrupted tasks nearly twice as often as the completed ones. Better memory for interrupted than for completed tasks is the Zeigarnik effect . A second student, Maria Ovsiankina (1898 to 1993), showed in 1928 that people given the chance spontaneously go back to interrupted tasks and finish them, the Ovsiankina effect . Remember the pair this way: Zeigarnik, people remember unfinished tasks; Ovsiankina, people resume them. Contemporaneity. A further principle of Lewin's field theory is that only the present field can influence present behaviour. The past matters only to the extent that it has left traces in the life space now; the future, only as present expectations. This principle of contemporaneity is the most direct "here-and-now" idea in Gestalt-derived psychology. Lewin also analysed conflict as a balance of valences (approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance and approach-avoidance, Chapter 10). Group dynamics and action research. Lewin, who was Jewish, left Germany in 1933, worked briefly at Cornell University and then at the Iowa Child Welfare Research Station, and in 1945 founded the Research Center for Group Dynamics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. There he turned field theory to groups, which he saw as dynamic wholes whose properties are not the sum of their members'. He coined the term group dynamics . With Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White (1939) he compared boys' clubs run under autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire leadership (Social book). He also founded action research , research carried out in partnership with the people affected by a social problem, in a repeating cycle of planning, acting, observing the results and reflecting, then planning again. A summer workshop he led in 1946 gave rise to the T-group (training group) and the National Training Laboratories. His three-stage model of change (unfreezing, moving, refreezing) is still taught in management courses. Lewin is widely called the father of modern social psychology, and his motto summarises his career: "There is nothing so practical as a good theory." Exam trap Life space = the person plus the psychological environment (not society and group, not person and group, not environment and group). Lewin founded action research, group dynamics and modern experimental social psychology; he did not found psychoanalysis (Freud), psychophysics (Fechner) or functionalism (James, Dewey, Angell). Zeigarnik = recall of interrupted tasks; Ovsiankina = resumption of interrupted tasks. Topological = regions and boundaries; hodological = paths. Emigration, legacy, and a different "Gestalt" With the rise of the Nazis, all four leading figures, Wertheimer (1933, to the New School for Social Research in New York), Koffka (already at Smith from 1927), Kohler (1935) and Lewin (1933), ended up in the United States. There they met a psychology dominated by behaviourism, taught at small colleges rather than major research universities, and wrote in a second language. Gestalt psychology never became a dominant American school. Its influence, however, was enormous and lasting. Its account of perceptual organisation is still taught almost unchanged. Its insistence on insight and understanding prepared the ground for cognitive psychology (Section 2.6). And through Lewin, his students (Leon Festinger among them) and Gestalt-minded social psychologists such as Fritz Heider and Solomon Asch, it shaped modern social psychology. One thing Gestalt psychology did not produce is Gestalt therapy. Gestalt therapy was developed in the 1940s and 1950s by Frederick Salomon Perls (Fritz Perls, 1893 to 1970), a German-born psychoanalyst, with his wife Laura Perls and the writer Paul Goodman; the book Gestalt Therapy (1951) was written by Perls, Ralph Hefferline and Goodman. It is an experiential, humanistic therapy that emphasises awareness in the here and now, personal responsibility, and the completion of "unfinished business" (a phrase that echoes Zeigarnik's interrupted tasks). Its best-known technique is the empty chair , in which the client speaks to an imagined person, or a disowned part of the self, placed in an empty chair, and then changes seats to answer. Perls had worked with the holistic neurologist Kurt Goldstein, and he borrowed the word Gestalt and a general holism, but little else. The Gestalt-trained psychologist Mary Henle published a careful comparison in 1978 and concluded that the connection between the two is largely one of name. The therapy itself is taught in the Clinical book. Exam trap Gestalt psychology (Wertheimer, Kohler, Koffka) is not Gestalt therapy (Perls). The empty chair technique belongs to Gestalt therapy, not to psychoanalysis, CBT or person-centred therapy. Questions sometimes blur the two. An assertion-reason item states "Fritz Perls was a proponent of the Gestalt perspective" with the reason "Gestalt focuses on the wholeness of individuals' experiences in the present moment"; the key treats both as true and the reason as the correct explanation, because "Gestalt perspective" is used loosely there to include the therapy. Similarly, one Panwar item keys "here-and-now" to Gestalt psychology : the idea is most at home in Gestalt therapy (and in existential-humanistic therapy), and within Gestalt psychology proper it corresponds to Lewin's principle of contemporaneity. If the options separate Gestalt psychology from Gestalt therapy, choose the therapy. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. A field with competing schools and no shared framework is, in Thomas Kuhn's term, a science. Watson's view that thinking is subvocal speech located in the muscles of the larynx is called . The three unlearned emotions Watson described in infants were fear, rage and . Skinner's position that private events are behaviour but not causes is called behaviourism. The physicist Percy Bridgman argued that a concept means the set of operations used to measure it, a doctrine called . Tolman demonstrated learning without reinforcement, which he called learning, and explained it with the concept of a cognitive . In Hull's 1943 formula, reaction potential equals habit strength multiplied by . The apparent movement that Wertheimer studied in 1912 is called the phenomenon. Kohler's hens chose the darker of two greys even when the shade had changed, showing . Lewin's life space consists of the person and the environment. Answers: (1) preparadigmatic, (2) peripheralism, (3) love, (4) radical, (5) operationism, (6) latent, map, (7) drive, (8) phi, (9) transposition, (10) psychological. 2.4 Psychoanalysis as a School: The First Force Medium yield · 6 Qs Behaviourism and Gestalt psychology were both born in university laboratories, as quarrels with structuralism about how to study normal minds. Psychoanalysis came from somewhere else entirely: the consulting room of a Viennese doctor treating patients whose symptoms made no medical sense. It never really belonged to academic psychology, yet it changed the way the whole twentieth century thought about the mind. This section tells its history as a school; Freud's theory of personality (the stages, defences and dynamics) is taught in full in the Personality book. From neurology to hysteria: Charcot, Bernheim and Breuer Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) did not set out to be a psychologist. He qualified in medicine at the University of Vienna in 1881 after years of research in the physiological laboratory of Ernst Brucke, a leader of the mechanistic school of German physiology, where he studied the nerve cells of fish and other animals under the microscope. Unable to support a family on a researcher's pay, he went into private practice in 1886 as a neurologist , a specialist in diseases of the nerves. Many of the patients who came to him suffered from hysteria , a condition (today classed among the conversion and dissociative disorders) in which people developed paralyses, blindness, loss of feeling or fits with no detectable damage to the nervous system.
