On the morning of 22 October 1850, a forty-nine-year-old former professor of physics lay in bed in Leipzig and worked out how to measure the mind. His name was Gustav Theodor Fechner, and for most of the previous decade he had been too ill to work at all. In the late 1830s Fechner had been studying afterimages, the ghostly colours that linger in your vision after you stare at a bright light, and he had used his own eyes as the instrument, gazing at the sun through coloured glass. The experiments damaged his eyes. A long breakdown followed: he could not bear light, could hardly eat, and could not read. He gave up his chair of physics and spent about three years withdrawn from the world, much of the time in darkened rooms. When he recovered, Fechner turned to an old philosophical puzzle: how are mind and body related? The great philosopher Immanuel Kant had argued that psychology could never become a true natural science, because mental events cannot be measured, and without measurement there is no mathematics and no science. Fechner's insight that October morning was a way around Kant. You cannot hold a ruler against a sensation. But you can measure the physical stimulus that produces it, and you can find out how much that stimulus must change before a person notices any difference at all. If every just-noticeable step in sensation is treated as one unit, sensation can be counted, and the relation between the physical world and the mental world can be written as an equation. Fechner spent the next decade testing the idea, lifting weights, comparing lights and judging distances, thousands of judgements at a time. He found that his Leipzig colleague Ernst Heinrich Weber had already discovered the key regularity, and he generously named it Weber's law. In 1860 Fechner published Elemente der Psychophysik ( Elements of Psychophysics ), and with it founded a new science. Nineteen years before Wilhelm Wundt opened his laboratory, Fechner had shown that the mind could be measured. Psychophysicists still celebrate 22 October as Fechner Day. This chapter explores the territory Fechner opened. It asks how the sense organs turn energy into experience, how weak a stimulus can be before you miss it, how small a change you can notice, and why a "threshold" turns out to be a decision as much as a sensation. It then walks through each sense in turn: vision, hearing, taste, smell, touch, temperature, pain, body position and balance. Keep Fechner's damaged eyes in mind. At the end of the chapter you will see that the afterimages that injured him are now well understood, and that his famous law has been both honoured and revised. 3.1 Sensation and perception: from energy to experience Medium yield · 10 Qs Look up from this page for a moment. You see a room full of objects, each with a colour, a shape and a place. You probably hear something too: a fan, traffic, a voice in the next room. It all seems effortless and immediate, as if the world simply pours into your head. It does not. What actually reaches you is a shower of physical energy (photons striking the back of your eyes, pressure waves in the air, molecules drifting into your nose), and everything you experience is built by your nervous system out of that raw material. This section introduces the first steps of that construction. Sensation versus perception Psychologists traditionally divide the process into two stages. sensation is the process by which sense organs detect physical energy from the environment and convert it into neural signals. perception is the process by which the brain organises and interprets those signals so that they become meaningful objects and events. Think of a batsman at the crease. Light reflected from the ball forms an image on his retinas, and receptors there fire: that is sensation. Recognising, in a fraction of a second, that the ball is a googly spinning the other way: that is perception. The boundary between the two is not sharp, and many modern researchers treat them as one continuous process. But the distinction is useful, and examiners like it, because it tells you where an error happens. Consider an optical illusion such as the Muller-Lyer figure, in which two lines of identical length look unequal because one carries outward-pointing fins and the other inward-pointing fins. Your receptors register the two lines accurately; the image of each line on your retina really is the same length. The error arises later, when the brain interprets the lines in the light of the fins. Optical illusions are therefore distortions of perception, not of sensation (Chapter 4 explains why the brain makes such errors). The idea that experience can be broken into sensory building blocks has a long history. The structuralists, led in America by Edward Bradford Titchener (1867 to 1927), treated sensations as the elements of consciousness and hoped to catalogue them the way chemists catalogue elements, a "periodic table" of the elements of sensation; Titchener counted more than 44,000 distinguishable sensation qualities, most of them visual or auditory. For Titchener, a perception was a complex of sensory and imaginal elements: sensations, plus the images that past experience attaches to them, with meaning supplied by this context (Chapter 1 tells the full story of structuralism). A modern descendant of this idea treats perception as inference. Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894), whose work runs through this chapter, argued in the 1860s that perception involves unconscious inference: the brain draws conclusions about the world from incomplete sensory evidence, using past experience. Today this view is formalised in the Bayesian approach to perception , named after the eighteenth-century mathematician Thomas Bayes. According to it, every perceptual experience combines two ingredients: prior beliefs (what you already expect to be out there, learned from experience) and sensory evidence (what the receptors are reporting now). When the evidence is clear, it dominates; when it is weak or ambiguous, the prior carries more weight. Walking down a dimly lit lane at night, you may "see" a dog lying by a gate when it is really a sack of cement, because dogs by gates are common (a strong prior) and the light is poor (weak evidence). Genes, culture and emotional states can all shape a person's priors, but the Bayesian formula itself has just those two inputs: prior beliefs and sensory evidence. Exam trap "Optical illusions result from distortion in ..." The answer is perception , not sensation: the receptors register the stimulus correctly, and the error is in interpretation. "Translation" and "adaptation" are bait. Likewise, "according to the Bayesian approach, perception is influenced by ..." has the answer prior beliefs and sensory evidence ; options naming only genes, culture or emotions describe things that can shape priors, not the approach itself. Receptors and transduction Every sense begins with a receptor , a specialised cell (or the specialised ending of a neuron) that responds to one particular form of energy. The receptor's job is transduction : the conversion of physical energy into the electrical and chemical language of the nervous system. Light, sound and molecules cannot travel along nerves; only neural signals can. So in the eye, light changes the shape of a pigment molecule, which changes the receptor's electrical state; in the ear, the bending of tiny hairs opens ion channels; in the nose, an odour molecule binds to a receptor protein. Each is a different trick for the same task. Table 3.1 groups the receptors by the energy they transduce. Table 3.1 Receptors classified by the energy they transduce. Receptor class Energy detected Examples Sense Photoreceptors Light (electromagnetic) Rods and cones of the retina Vision Mechanoreceptors Mechanical bending, pressure, stretch Hair cells of the cochlea and vestibular organs; skin corpuscles; muscle spindles Hearing, balance, touch, kinesthesis Chemoreceptors Dissolved or airborne molecules Taste receptor cells; olfactory receptor neurons Taste, smell Thermoreceptors Temperature change Warm and cold free nerve endings Temperature Nociceptors Actual or threatened tissue damage Free nerve endings in skin, muscle and organs Pain Receptors can also be classified by where their information comes from. The British physiologist Charles Scott Sherrington (1857 to 1952), in The Integrative Action of the Nervous System (1906), distinguished exteroceptors , which report on the outside world (eyes, ears, skin), interoceptors , which report on the internal organs (a full bladder, a churning stomach), and proprioceptors , which report on the position and movement of the body itself (Section 3.11). Once a receptor has transduced its stimulus, the signal travels toward the central nervous system along afferent (sensory, incoming) nerve fibres. Commands travel outward to muscles and glands along efferent (motor, outgoing) fibres. The simplest complete loop, from receptor through afferent fibre to the spinal cord and back out along an efferent fibre to a muscle, is the reflex arc: the knee jerk is the textbook example. (The philosopher-psychologist John Dewey famously criticised the reflex arc as a model of behaviour in 1896; Chapter 1 explains why.) Sensory coding: specific nerve energies and labelled lines Here is a puzzle that troubled nineteenth-century physiologists. Every sensory nerve carries the same kind of signal: brief electrical impulses called action potentials. An impulse from the eye looks exactly like an impulse from the ear. So how does the brain know whether a message means "red" or "middle C" or "sour"? The German physiologist Johannes Peter Muller (1801 to 1858) gave the classic answer in his Handbook of Human Physiology (1833 to 1840). His doctrine of specific nerve energies states that the quality of a sensation depends on which nerve is stimulated, not on what stimulates it. Each sensory nerve, however it is excited, produces its own characteristic sensation. You can test this yourself. Close your eyes and press very gently on the outer corner of one eyelid: you will see a spot of light (a phosphene), although no light has entered the eye. The pressure excited the optic nerve's receptors, and the optic nerve can only "speak" light. A hard blow to the back of the head makes people "see stars" for the same reason. Muller drew a startling conclusion: we are never directly aware of objects in the world, only of the activity of our own nerves. Helmholtz, Muller's student, later extended the idea within a single sense, proposing that different fibres in the eye and ear carry different colours and pitches (an idea you will meet again in his theories of colour and hearing). Modern neuroscience keeps the core of Muller's insight under the name labelled-line coding : the quality of a sensation is signalled by which neurons are active, because each pathway is wired to a particular brain region, as if each line carried a label. Activity in the visual pathway to the occipital lobe is experienced as sight; activity in the auditory pathway to the temporal lobe is experienced as sound. Within a sense, however, quality is often coded by the pattern of activity across many receptor types rather than by single labelled lines. This across-fibre pattern coding is especially important in taste and smell, where each receptor type responds to many chemicals and a particular flavour or odour corresponds to a particular profile of activity across the whole population. What about intensity? A dim light and a bright light, a whisper and a shout, must also be told apart. Here a basic fact of neurophysiology matters. An action potential obeys the all-or-none law: once a neuron's threshold is reached, the impulse fires at full, constant size and travels along the axon without shrinking, and a stronger stimulus does not produce a bigger impulse. A stimulus too weak to reach threshold produces no action potential at all, not a "miniature" one (only small graded changes in voltage that fade away). Intensity therefore cannot be coded by the size of impulses. It is coded instead by rate coding (stronger stimuli make each neuron fire more often) and by recruitment (stronger stimuli activate more neurons, including less sensitive ones). Note one curiosity: signals can also be carried by a decrease in activity. The rods and cones of your retina are most active in darkness, and light actually reduces their activity (Pinel and Barnes's textbook makes this point with some relish). A final piece of wiring is worth knowing for general psychology. Before reaching the cerebral cortex, almost every sensory pathway relays through the thalamus, the brain's sensory switching station: vision through its lateral geniculate nucleus, hearing through its medial geniculate nucleus, and touch, pain and taste through its ventral posterior nuclei. Smell is the exception: olfactory signals run from the olfactory bulb straight to the olfactory cortex and the amygdala without a thalamic relay on the way (Section 3.9). The details belong to the Physiological Psychology book. Explaining experience and behaviour through the workings of the brain and nervous system in this way is the neurobiological (biological) approach to psychology, whose main premise is that behaviour is governed by the brain and nervous system. It differs from the psychophysical approach that fills most of this chapter, which studies the lawful relation between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce without needing to know what the neurons are doing (Chapter 2 compares the approaches). Exam trap The doctrine of specific nerve energies belongs to Johannes Muller , not Helmholtz (Helmholtz extended it) and not Fechner. "The principal sensory relay to the cortex for every sense except smell" is the thalamus ; the hypothalamus regulates drives such as hunger and temperature, the medulla controls breathing and heart rate, the corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres, the basal ganglia help to control movement, and the hippocampus serves memory. The lateral geniculate nucleus is visual; the medial geniculate nucleus is auditory ("M for music"). Sensory adaptation When you put on a wristwatch in the morning you feel it on your skin. Ten minutes later you do not, although it is still pressing on exactly the same spot. When you walk into a home where a garland of Mysuru jasmine hangs by the door, the scent is striking; the family who have been sitting there all evening hardly notice it. This is sensory adaptation : a decline in sensitivity (and in receptor response) to a stimulus that remains constant. Adaptation is built into the receptors and the early stages of each sensory pathway, and it is automatic. The English philosopher John Locke (1632 to 1704) described a neat demonstration in 1690. Put one hand in a bowl of hot water and the other in a bowl of cold water for a minute, then plunge both into a bowl of lukewarm water. The same lukewarm water feels cool to the first hand and warm to the second. Each hand has adapted to its starting temperature, so each judges the new water relative to that adapted level. Why should the senses be designed to fade out unchanging stimulation? Because change is what usually matters. A constant stimulus (the pressure of your clothes, the hum of a refrigerator) rarely carries new information, whereas a change (a touch on the shoulder, a sudden silence) may signal something important. Adaptation frees the senses to respond to change. Vision is the dramatic case: if an image is held perfectly still on the retina, it fades from view within seconds, and your eyes avoid this only by moving constantly (Section 3.6). Exam trap Do not confuse sensory adaptation with habituation . Adaptation is a reduced response of the sensory system itself to a constant stimulus. Habituation is a learned decrease in behavioural response to a stimulus that is repeated and proves unimportant (you stop jumping at the ticking clock), and it can be reversed instantly if the stimulus changes (dishabituation). Habituation is the simplest form of learning and is covered in Chapter 6. Adaptation to light and dark is called visual adaptation , not "visual accommodation" (accommodation is the focusing of the lens, Section 3.6). 3.2 Thresholds: how weak a stimulus, how small a difference Lower yield · 2 Qs Fechner's new science, psychophysics , is the study of the quantitative relationship between the physical properties of stimuli and the sensations they produce. It asks two basic kinds of question. The first is about detection: what is the weakest stimulus a person can detect? The second is about discrimination: what is the smallest change in a stimulus a person can notice? The answers are called thresholds. The absolute threshold The absolute threshold is the minimum intensity of a stimulus that a person can detect. The older term for a threshold is limen (Latin for "threshold"), which survives in two words you should know. A stimulus below the absolute threshold is subliminal (below the limen); one above it is supraliminal . At first sight the absolute threshold sounds like a simple switch: below a certain intensity you detect nothing, above it you always detect the stimulus. Experiments show that no such switch exists. If you present a faint tone many times at each of several intensities, there is no single intensity at which "never heard" suddenly becomes "always heard". Instead, the percentage of "yes, I heard it" responses climbs gradually, tracing an S-shaped curve called the psychometric function (Figure 3.1). Why the gradual climb? Because the nervous system is never silent. Neurons fire spontaneously, attention wanders, receptors vary slightly from moment to moment, and even the stimulus itself fluctuates (a very dim light delivers a variable number of light particles from one flash to the next). So the same faint tone is sometimes detected and sometimes missed. Psychophysicists therefore define the absolute threshold statistically: it is the stimulus intensity that is detected on 50 percent of the trials on which it is presented. Not 100 percent, and not "the first time it is noticed", but half the time. 0 25 50 75 100 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 Stimulus intensity (arbitrary units) Percentage of yes responses 50 percent yes = absolute threshold Real observer (ogive) Fixed threshold (step) Observed data Figure 3.1 The psychometric function for detection. If thresholds were fixed switches, detection would jump from 0 to 100 percent at one intensity (dashed step). Real observers produce a gradual S-shaped curve (an ogive), so the absolute threshold is defined as the intensity detected on 50 percent of trials. The dots show data of the kind collected by the method of constant stimuli (Section 3.4). How sensitive are human senses at their absolute thresholds? Eugene Galanter (1962) gave a set of everyday approximations that appear in almost every introductory text (Table 3.2). They are rough, but they make the point that our senses, at their best, are astonishingly sensitive. Table 3.2 Approximate absolute thresholds for five senses (after Galanter, 1962). Sense Approximate absolute threshold Vision A candle flame seen from about 48 km (30 miles) on a dark, clear night Hearing The tick of a watch from about 6 metres (20 feet) under very quiet conditions Taste One teaspoon of sugar dissolved in about 7.5 litres (two gallons) of water Smell One drop of perfume diffused through a six-room apartment Touch The wing of a bee falling on your cheek from a height of 1 centimetre Key study: How few particles of light can you see? (Hecht, Shlaer and Pirenne, 1942) Question. Light comes in tiny packets called quanta (photons). What is the smallest number of quanta a fully dark-adapted human can detect? Method. Selig Hecht , Simon Shlaer and Maurice Pirenne, working in New York, flashed a very brief spot of blue-green light (wavelength 510 nanometres, close to the peak sensitivity of the rods) onto a rod-rich region of the retina about 20 degrees from the centre of gaze. Observers, including the authors themselves, sat in darkness and reported whether they had seen each flash. Result. At threshold, the flash delivered only about 54 to 148 quanta to the front of the eye. After allowing for light lost in the eye's media and for light that passed through the retina unabsorbed, they calculated that only about 5 to 14 quanta were actually absorbed by rods. Spread across hundreds of rods, this meant that no single rod could have absorbed more than one quantum. Conclusion. A single rod responds to a single quantum of light, and the coincidence of a handful of such events produces the experience of seeing. The human eye at threshold works close to the limit set by physics. Why it matters here. Because the number of quanta in a dim flash fluctuates randomly from flash to flash, some of the variability in "seeing" a threshold flash lies in the light itself. The threshold is probabilistic by its very nature. The difference threshold and the JND Detection is only half of psychophysics. Much of the time we need to tell whether something has changed: whether the dal needs more salt, whether the music has been turned up, whether one mango is heavier than another. The difference threshold (or difference limen) is the smallest difference between two stimuli that a person can detect 50 percent of the time. The amount of change at that threshold is called the just noticeable difference (JND). The terms are effectively interchangeable in examinations: the difference threshold is the JND. Difference thresholds are measured by comparing a fixed standard stimulus with a variable comparison stimulus . If you hold a 100-gram standard weight in one hand and a series of comparison weights in the other, you might find that you can tell 102 grams from 100 grams half the time; the JND at that standard is then 2 grams. Along the way you will find a comparison value that feels exactly equal to the standard; this is the point of subjective equality (PSE), and it need not coincide with the true physical equality point. (A systematic gap between the PSE and the standard is called a constant error.) Ernst Heinrich Weber measured one especially elegant kind of difference threshold on the skin. Touch the skin with the two points of a pair of compasses. If the points are far apart, you feel two touches; bring them closer and, at some separation, the two touches merge into one. The smallest separation at which two points are felt as two is the two-point threshold . Weber found that it varies enormously across the body, from about 2 millimetres on the fingertips and lips to several centimetres on the back and thigh (Section 3.10 explains why). It was while measuring such thresholds, and the JNDs for lifted weights, that Weber noticed the regularity that bears his name. Exam trap "The minimum level of a stimulus that can be detected" is the absolute threshold ; "the smallest change that can be detected" is the difference threshold (JND). "Sensory adaptation point" and "perceptual boundary" are invented distractors, and so is "signal detection of response". A question defining "the point at which a stimulus is strong enough to trigger a response only 50 percent of the time" wants threshold ; response bias is a signal detection term for a person's readiness to say "yes" (Section 3.5), and the phi phenomenon is the illusion of movement produced by lights flashing in sequence, described by Max Wertheimer in 1912 (Chapter 4). 3.3 The psychophysical laws: Weber, Fechner and Stevens Lower yield · 3 Qs Thresholds tell us where sensation begins and how finely it can be graded. The next question is more ambitious: is there a general law relating the size of a stimulus to the size of the sensation it produces? Three answers have been proposed, by Weber, Fechner and Stevens. Each was a real advance, each captures something true, and each fails somewhere. Learn them as a sequence, because each one grew out of the one before. Weber's law: the JND is a constant fraction Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795 to 1878) was a professor of anatomy and physiology at Leipzig. In studies of touch and the muscle sense published in 1834 ( De Tactu ) and 1846, he asked people to compare lifted weights. He noticed, among other things, that discrimination was finer when people actively lifted the weights than when the weights simply rested on a passive hand. His enduring discovery, however, was this: the JND is not a fixed amount. With a light standard weight, a small extra amount is noticed; with a heavy standard, a much larger amount is needed. What stays constant is the ratio of the JND to the standard. In symbols, Weber's law is ΔI / I = k where I is the intensity of the standard stimulus, ΔI (read "delta I") is the increase needed to produce a just noticeable difference, and k is a constant for that sensory dimension, called the Weber fraction (or Weber's constant). A small Weber fraction means fine discrimination; a large one means coarse discrimination. A worked example shows how the law works. Suppose the Weber fraction for lifted weights is about 0.02 (one-fiftieth). Then with a 500-gram standard, the JND is 0.02 × 500 = 10 grams: you will just notice the difference between 500 and 510 grams. With a 5-kilogram standard, the JND is 0.02 × 5,000 = 100 grams. Ten grams added to the heavier load would go completely unnoticed. Or take your morning chai. If a cup sweetened with two teaspoons of sugar needs roughly an extra half teaspoon before anyone notices it is sweeter, then a cup with four teaspoons needs roughly an extra whole teaspoon. The absolute amount needed doubles; the proportion stays the same. The everyday consequences are everywhere. A single candle transforms a dark room but is invisible in sunlight. A shopkeeper knows that a fifty-rupee discount feels generous on a two-hundred-rupee item and trivial on a fifty-thousand-rupee phone. In each case what we notice is proportional change, not absolute change. Table 3.3 gives approximate Weber fractions for several dimensions. Table 3.3 Approximate Weber fractions in the middle range of intensities. Values differ considerably between sources and methods; learn the pattern rather than the decimals. Frequency (pitch) is discriminated most finely; the chemical senses are usually among the coarsest. Dimension Approximate Weber fraction Change needed on a standard of 100 units Pitch (frequency of a middle tone) About 0.003 (about 1/333) About 0.3 Electric shock About 0.01 About 1 Heaviness of lifted weights About 0.02 (1/50) About 2 Brightness of light About 0.02 to 0.08 About 2 to 8 Loudness (sound intensity) About 0.05 to 0.1 About 5 to 10 Pressure on the skin About 0.14 (1/7) About 14 Taste (salt) and smell About 0.08 to 0.3 About 8 to 30 Where does Weber's law fail? It holds well across the middle range of intensities for most senses, but it breaks down at the extremes. Near the absolute threshold, the Weber fraction rises sharply: when a stimulus is barely detectable, a proportionally much larger change is needed before any difference is noticed. It can also drift at very high intensities, and for pure tones the fraction for loudness declines slowly as intensity increases, a small but systematic departure known as the "near miss" to Weber's law. Weber's law is best regarded as an excellent approximation over the range in which we usually live. Fechner's law: sensation grows with the logarithm of the stimulus Gustav Theodor Fechner (1801 to 1887) took Weber's finding and built it into a law of sensation itself. Weber's law tells you how big a JND is; it says nothing about how strong a sensation is. Fechner's bridge was a single bold assumption: every JND represents the same increase in sensation, no matter where on the scale it occurs . The step from 100 to 102 grams and the step from 1,000 to 1,020 grams are both one JND, so, Fechner assumed, both add one equal unit to the felt heaviness. With that assumption, the strength of any sensation can be measured simply by counting how many JNDs it lies above the absolute threshold. Now combine this with Weber's law. Start at the threshold and climb one JND at a time. Because each JND is a constant fraction of the current intensity, the physical intensities at successive JNDs form a geometric series (each one multiplied by the same factor), while the sensation steps form an arithmetic series (1, 2, 3, 4 units). A quantity that rises arithmetically while another rises geometrically is a logarithm. The result is Fechner's law : S = k log I where S is the magnitude of the sensation, I is the physical intensity (strictly, measured in multiples of the threshold intensity) and k is a constant that depends on the sense. Because it rests on Weber's law, it is often called the Weber-Fechner law. A worked example makes the logarithm concrete. Picture a dark room on Diwali night. Light one diya and the room is transformed. Light a second and the room gets noticeably brighter. To get the same sized step again, Fechner's law says you will need not three diyas but four; then eight; then sixteen; then thirty-two. Each doubling of the physical light adds roughly one equal step of brightness. By the time sixty-four diyas are burning, adding one more makes no visible difference at all. Scales of this kind are familiar from science and engineering: the astronomers' magnitude scale for the brightness of stars (much older than Fechner) and the decibel scale for sound (introduced by telephone engineers in the 1920s; Section 3.8) are both logarithmic, and both fit how our senses actually grade intensity. Fechner's achievement went beyond the equation. In the Elemente of 1860 he coined the word psychophysics, set out the experimental methods for measuring thresholds (Section 3.4), and distinguished "outer psychophysics" (the relation between the stimulus and sensation, which he could study) from "inner psychophysics" (the relation between brain activity and sensation, which he could not). For founding the field he is called the father of psychophysics, and his work showed the young science of psychology that mental events could be measured. One reader who took that lesson to heart was Hermann Ebbinghaus (1850 to 1909), who came across a second-hand copy of the Elemente and set out to measure memory with the same rigour (Chapter 7). Fechner's method of scaling sensation is called indirect scaling , because it measures sensation indirectly, through discrimination (counting JNDs), rather than by asking people how strong a sensation feels. Where does Fechner's law fail? Its weak point is its founding assumption. There is no direct evidence that all JNDs are subjectively equal, and when people are asked to judge sensory magnitudes directly, their judgements often do not follow a logarithmic curve. For some dimensions, such as electric shock, sensation grows faster than intensity, which no logarithmic law can describe. That is where Stevens enters the story. Stevens' power law: ask people directly Stanley Smith Stevens (1906 to 1973) of Harvard University argued that there was no need to count JNDs: people can judge the magnitude of their sensations directly, and their judgements are lawful. His main method, magnitude estimation , works like this. The experimenter presents a standard stimulus (called the modulus) and assigns it a number, say 10. The observer is then given other stimuli and asked to assign each a number proportional to how intense it seems: a light that looks twice as bright as the standard gets 20; one that looks half as bright gets 5. Across hundreds of studies, Stevens found that the results for every continuum he tested were described by a power function. In 1957 he set out what is now called Stevens' power law : S = k I n where S is the judged magnitude of the sensation, I is the physical intensity, k is a scaling constant and the exponent n is characteristic of each sensory continuum. Taking logarithms of both sides gives log S = log k + n log I : plotted on log-log axes, every power function becomes a straight line whose slope is the exponent. That is how exponents are measured in practice. The exponent tells you how sensation grows. When n is less than 1, sensation grows more slowly than intensity, a pattern called response compression : brightness has an exponent of about 0.33, so to double the apparent brightness of a light you must increase its physical intensity about eightfold (because 2 raised to the power 1/0.33 is 8). When n equals 1, sensation grows in proportion to intensity, as it does for the apparent length of a line. When n is greater than 1, sensation grows faster than intensity, a pattern called response expansion : electric shock has an exponent of about 3.5, so doubling the current makes the shock feel roughly eleven times as intense (2 raised to the power 3.5 is about 11). Figure 3.2 shows the three cases and Table 3.4 lists classic exponents. 0 0 2 2 4 4 6 6 8 8 10 10 Stimulus intensity (arbitrary units) Magnitude estimate Electric shock: n = 3.5 Line length: n = 1.0 Brightness: n = 0.33 n above 1: expansion n equal to 1: proportional n below 1: compression Figure 3.2 Stevens' power functions for three continua. Brightness (exponent 0.33) shows response compression, line length (1.0) is proportional, and electric shock (3.5) shows response expansion. On logarithmic axes each curve would become a straight line whose slope is its exponent. Table 3.4 Representative exponents of Stevens' power law (approximate values reported by Stevens). Continuum Exponent (n) Type of growth Brightness (large target, dark-adapted eye) 0.33 Compression Smell (coffee odour) 0.55 Compression Loudness (3,000 Hz tone, measured as sound pressure) 0.67 Compression Apparent length of a line 1.0 Proportional Taste (sugar) 1.3 Expansion Heaviness of lifted weights 1.45 Expansion Electric shock (through the fingers) 3.5 Expansion Why should the senses differ like this? A plausible functional answer is that compression lets the eye and ear handle an enormous range of physical intensities (the brightest light we can tolerate is billions of times more intense than the dimmest we can see) within a manageable range of experience, whereas expansion makes potentially harmful stimuli, such as electric current, feel alarming quickly. Stevens strengthened his case with cross-modality matching . Instead of using numbers, observers match the intensity of one sense to another: for example, they squeeze a hand grip until the effort feels as strong as a sound is loud. If both senses follow power laws with known exponents, the power law predicts the exponent of the matching function (it should equal the ratio of the two exponents), and the matches came out close to the predictions. This showed that the power law was not merely an artefact of how people use numbers. Stevens was a productive figure in other ways too: in 1946 he proposed the four scales of measurement (nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio) taught in the Research Methodology book, and in 1936 he defined the sone, a unit of loudness. Where does Stevens' law fail? Magnitude estimates are affected by the range of stimuli presented, by the choice of modulus, by the order of presentation and by individual habits with numbers, so exponents vary from study to study. Some critics argue that magnitude estimation measures how people map sensations onto numbers rather than sensation itself. Even so, the power law describes direct magnitude judgements far better than Fechner's logarithm, and in 1961 Stevens titled a famous paper "To honor Fechner and repeal his law". The two laws are best seen as answers to different questions: Fechner's law describes discriminability (how many just noticeable steps lie between two stimuli), while Stevens' law describes apparent magnitude (how big a sensation seems). Table 3.5 sets the three laws side by side. Table 3.5 The three psychophysical laws compared. Law Formula What it says Method behind it Main limitation Weber's law (Weber, 1834) ΔI / I = k The JND is a constant fraction of the standard Discrimination of weights and touches Fails near threshold and at extremes Fechner's law (Fechner, 1860) S = k log I Sensation grows with the logarithm of intensity Indirect scaling: counting JNDs Assumes all JNDs are equal in sensation; cannot describe expansion Stevens' power law (Stevens, 1957) S = k I n Sensation is a power function of intensity; exponent varies by sense Direct scaling: magnitude estimation, cross-modality matching Judgements are sensitive to range, context and number use Exam trap Weber gave the law of the JND as a constant fraction ; Fechner gave the logarithmic law and the assumption that every JND adds an equal unit of sensation ; Stevens gave the power law and magnitude estimation . "Who assumed that every just noticeable difference is a constant increment in sensation?" is Fechner, not Weber, even though it is Weber's JND. The founder (father) of psychophysics is Fechner, author of Elements of Psychophysics (1860), not Weber, not Wundt (father of experimental psychology) and not Ebbinghaus (pioneer of memory research, inspired by Fechner). Tolman, sometimes offered as a distractor, was a learning theorist (Chapter 6). Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. The conversion of physical energy into neural signals by a receptor is called . The doctrine that the quality of a sensation depends on which nerve is stimulated was proposed by Johannes . Because of the all-or-none law, stimulus intensity is coded largely by the of neural firing. The decline in sensitivity to an unchanging stimulus is called sensory . The absolute threshold is the intensity detected on percent of trials. The smallest detectable change in a stimulus is the difference threshold, also called the . Weber's law states that ΔI / I equals a . Fechner's law states that sensation is proportional to the of stimulus intensity. Stevens measured sensation directly by the method of magnitude . An exponent greater than 1 in Stevens' law, as for electric shock, produces response . Answers: (1) transduction, (2) Muller, (3) rate (frequency), (4) adaptation, (5) 50, (6) just noticeable difference (JND), (7) constant (the Weber fraction), (8) logarithm, (9) estimation, (10) expansion. 3.4 The classical psychophysical methods Lower yield · not asked yet A threshold is defined as a 50 percent point, but how do you actually find it? Fechner's Elemente described three procedures, and with small changes they are still in use in every vision clinic, hearing clinic and perception laboratory in the world. Each involves a trade-off between speed and accuracy, and each is vulnerable to particular errors. Understanding those errors, and how they are controlled, is as important for examinations as knowing the procedures. A few terms first. In threshold work the experimenter presents stimuli in a series , which may be ascending (starting well below threshold and increasing step by step) or descending (starting well above threshold and decreasing). The point in a series at which the observer's response changes (from "no" to "yes", or the reverse) is the transition point . When two stimuli are compared, the observer may also show a time-order error : a systematic tendency to judge the second of two equal stimuli as different from the first, simply because it comes second. A similar space error arises when a stimulus is judged differently because it appears on the left rather than the right. Errors of this kind are controlled by counterbalancing : arranging the order (or position) of conditions so that each occurs equally often in each place, so that the errors cancel out. The method of limits In the method of limits (Fechner called it the method of just noticeable differences; it is also called the method of minimal changes), the experimenter changes the stimulus in small steps, in alternating ascending and descending series, and records where the observer's response changes. To find the absolute threshold for a faint tone, for example, a descending series starts with a clearly audible tone and lowers it step by step until the observer first says "no"; an ascending series starts with an inaudible tone and raises it until the observer first says "yes". The threshold for each series is taken as the midpoint between the last two responses, and the overall threshold is the average across all series. Table 3.6 shows a worked example. Table 3.6 A worked example of the method of limits for the absolute threshold of a tone (intensity in arbitrary steps). The overall threshold is the mean transition point, 4.0. Notice that ascending transitions are higher than descending ones, the signature of the error of habituation. Series Direction and start Responses Transition point 1 Descending from 9 "Yes" from 9 down to 4, "no" at 3 3.5 2 Ascending from 1 "No" from 1 up to 4, "yes" at 5 4.5 3 Descending from 8 "Yes" from 8 down to 4, "no" at 3 3.5 4 Ascending from 2 "No" from 2 up to 4, "yes" at 5 4.5 The method of limits is quick and intuitive, but it suffers from two opposite errors, both caused by the predictable order of the stimuli. In the error of habituation (also called the error of perseveration), the observer falls into the habit of giving the same response and keeps giving it after the true threshold has been crossed: continuing to say "no" too long in an ascending series (so the ascending threshold comes out too high) and continuing to say "yes" too long in a descending series (so the descending threshold comes out too low). In the error of anticipation (or expectation), the observer, knowing that a change is coming, switches response too early: saying "yes" prematurely in an ascending series and "no" prematurely in a descending series. The two errors push the transition points in opposite directions. The cure is counterbalancing. Ascending and descending series are alternated in equal numbers, so that whatever error inflates the ascending thresholds is balanced by the corresponding error in the descending ones, and the starting point of each series is varied so that the observer cannot simply count steps to the expected change. The same logic applies to other order effects in psychophysical experiments, such as primacy and recency effects: they are controlled by counterbalancing the order of presentation. The method of limits can also measure difference thresholds. The observer compares each comparison stimulus with the standard and responds "greater", "equal" or "less". The range of comparison values judged "equal" is called the interval of uncertainty; its midpoint gives the point of subjective equality, and half its width gives the difference threshold. The method of constant stimuli The method of constant stimuli (Fechner's method of right and wrong cases, also called the frequency method) removes the predictable order altogether. The experimenter first chooses a small set of fixed ("constant") stimulus values, usually five to nine, spaced so that the weakest is almost never detected and the strongest almost always is. Each value is then presented many times, often fifty or a hundred times, in a random order. The proportion of "yes" responses is calculated for each value and plotted against stimulus intensity to give the psychometric function (Figure 3.1). The absolute threshold is the intensity that corresponds to 50 percent detection, read off (interpolated from) the curve. For difference thresholds, each comparison is paired with the standard and the observer says whether it is "heavier" or "lighter" (or "louder", "brighter" and so on). The comparison value judged "heavier" 50 percent of the time is the point of subjective equality. The difference threshold is conventionally taken as half the distance between the 75 percent and 25 percent points. Because the stimuli arrive in random order, the observer cannot anticipate a change or settle into a habit, so the errors of habituation and anticipation disappear. The method of constant stimuli is therefore regarded as the most accurate and reliable of the classical methods. Its cost is time: many trials are needed, and many are spent on stimuli far from threshold, which tell the experimenter little. It also requires pilot work to choose a sensible set of values. The method of adjustment In the method of adjustment (Fechner's method of average error, also called the method of reproduction), the observer controls the stimulus. To measure an absolute threshold, the observer turns a knob until a tone is just audible; to measure a point of subjective equality, the observer adjusts a comparison line until it looks equal in length to a standard. The procedure is repeated many times. The average setting gives the threshold or the point of subjective equality, and the variability of the settings (their average deviation or standard deviation, the "average error" that gives the method its name) is an index of the difference threshold: the more finely a person can discriminate, the more tightly the settings cluster. The method of adjustment is fast and engaging, and it is the natural way to measure the size of an illusion: observers adjust a plain line until it matches the apparent length of the Muller-Lyer line, and the difference between the setting and the true length (the constant error) measures how strong the illusion is. Its weakness is precision. The stimulus changes continuously under the observer's own control, so motor skill, impatience and the observer's beliefs can all creep into the settings, and the experimenter loses control over exactly which stimuli are presented. Table 3.7 sets the three classical methods side by side. Table 3.7 The three classical psychophysical methods. Method Other names Procedure Strengths Weaknesses Limits Method of just noticeable differences; minimal changes Stimulus changed in small steps in alternating ascending and descending series Quick, simple Errors of habituation and anticipation; needs counterbalancing Constant stimuli Method of right and wrong cases; frequency method Fixed set of values, each presented many times in random order Most accurate; no order errors; gives full psychometric function Slow; many wasted trials Adjustment Method of average error; reproduction Observer adjusts the stimulus until it is just detectable or matches the standard Fastest; ideal for measuring PSE and illusions Least precise; observer controls the stimulus Staircases and forced choice: the modern refinements Modern laboratories and clinics mostly use adaptive procedures that combine the speed of the method of limits with the efficiency of concentrating trials near threshold. In a staircase method , the stimulus is made weaker after every "yes" (or correct) response and stronger after every "no" (or incorrect) response. The intensity therefore climbs and descends around the threshold like a person walking up and down a staircase, and the threshold is estimated as the average of the reversal points, the intensities at which the direction changed. The method was popularised in psychophysics by Tom Cornsweet in 1962. Refinements change the rule to target a particular percentage: in the widely used "two-down, one-up" staircase, the stimulus is made harder only after two correct responses in a row, which makes the staircase settle at about 71 percent correct. To stop observers from guessing the rule, experimenters often interleave two staircases, one starting high and one low, at random. A close cousin is the tracking method that Georg von Bekesy (1899 to 1972) built into an audiometer in 1947. The listener holds down a button whenever the tone is audible; while the button is pressed the intensity falls, and when it is released the intensity rises. The result is a zigzag trace that hugs the listener's threshold as the frequency sweeps from low to high, an audiogram drawn by the listener's own responses. Many modern procedures also replace "yes or no" with a forced-choice procedure . In two-alternative forced choice, the stimulus appears in one of two intervals (or locations) and the observer must say which, even when guessing. Chance performance is 50 percent, so the threshold is usually set at the 75 percent correct point, halfway between chance and perfection. The great advantage of forced choice is that it removes the observer's willingness to say "yes" from the measurement. A cautious person and a bold person can no longer differ simply because one says "yes" more readily. That problem, the contamination of thresholds by the observer's decision style, is exactly what signal detection theory was invented to solve. Clinical link Every routine sensory assessment is a psychophysical experiment. Pure-tone audiometry finds the absolute threshold for tones of different frequencies, usually with an ascending method of limits or a staircase. An eye chart measures a visual threshold for detail. Automated perimetry, used to detect glaucoma, maps detection thresholds across the visual field. When a clinical psychologist tests a patient's two-point threshold or pain threshold as part of a neuropsychological examination, the same principles (50 percent points, counterbalanced series, attention to response bias) decide whether the result can be trusted. Exam trap Match the names: method of limits = method of just noticeable differences = minimal changes; method of constant stimuli = method of right and wrong cases = frequency method; method of adjustment = method of average error = reproduction. In the method of limits, the error of habituation means continuing the previous response too long, and the error of anticipation means changing the response too early. Both, along with primacy, recency and time-order effects, are controlled by counterbalancing (alternating ascending and descending series), not by "randomisation", "pairing" or a "double-blind technique". Randomisation is the cure in a different method: constant stimuli. 3.5 Signal detection theory Medium yield · 4 Qs During the Second World War, radar operators sat for hours in front of screens watching for the faint blip that meant an enemy aircraft. The screen was never clean. It sparkled with "noise": random flecks produced by the equipment and the atmosphere. A real aircraft at long range produced a blip barely stronger than the noise. Every few seconds the operator had to make a decision under uncertainty: is that an aircraft or just noise? Say "aircraft" too readily and fighters are scrambled for nothing; say it too reluctantly and the bombers arrive unannounced. Two operators with equally good eyes could perform very differently because they set different standards for raising the alarm. The classical idea of a threshold had no room for this. It assumed that a stimulus is either above the threshold (and detected) or below it (and missed), with the observer passively reporting the result. Yet experimenters had long noticed awkward facts. If they slipped "catch trials" into a detection experiment (trials on which no stimulus was presented), some observers said "yes" anyway. Observers who were paid for each detection reported more stimuli, and their measured thresholds fell, although their eyes and ears had not changed. A threshold, it seemed, measured not only what an observer could sense but also how willing the observer was to say so. The origins of the theory signal detection theory (SDT) began in engineering. In the early 1950s, W. Wesley Peterson, Theodore G. Birdsall and W. C. Fox at the University of Michigan developed a mathematical "theory of signal detectability" for radar and radio receivers, published in 1954. In the same year Wilson P. Tanner Jr. and John A. Swets applied it to human observers in a paper titled "A decision-making theory of visual detection". The definitive statement for psychology came in the 1966 book Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics by David M. Green and John A. Swets. The central claim is simple and powerful: performance in any detection task depends on two independent things, the observer's sensitivity and the observer's decision criterion , and the two can be measured separately. Noise, signals and the four outcomes SDT starts by admitting that the observer's internal state is never quiet. noise , in SDT, is all the random background activity that is present whether or not a signal occurs: static on a screen, hum in a room, and above all the spontaneous firing of the observer's own neurons. On every trial the observer experiences some amount of internal "evidence" for a signal. On trials with no signal, this evidence comes from noise alone, and it varies from trial to trial, forming the noise distribution . On trials with a signal, the signal adds to the noise, so the evidence tends to be larger, forming the signal-plus-noise distribution . The two distributions overlap (Figure 3.3a). Some noise-alone trials produce more evidence than some signal trials, and the observer, who experiences only the evidence, cannot tell which kind of trial produced it. So the observer must adopt a rule: if the evidence on this trial exceeds a certain level, say "yes, a signal was present"; otherwise say "no". That cut-off level is the criterion . Every trial then ends in one of four outcomes, set out in Table 3.8. A hit is saying "yes" when a signal is present. A miss is saying "no" when a signal is present. A false alarm is saying "yes" when only noise is present. A correct rejection is saying "no" when only noise is present. Table 3.8 The four outcomes of a detection trial. The hit rate and the false alarm rate together contain all the information, because misses = 1 minus the hit rate and correct rejections = 1 minus the false alarm rate. What was presented Observer says "yes" Observer says "no" Signal present (signal plus noise) Hit Miss Signal absent (noise alone) False alarm Correct rejection Two numbers summarise performance. The hit rate is the proportion of signal trials on which the observer said "yes"; the false alarm rate is the proportion of noise trials on which the observer said "yes". Notice what a hit rate alone cannot tell you. A smoke alarm that rings constantly has a perfect hit rate: it never misses a fire. It is also useless, because its false alarm rate is perfect too. Any honest measure of detection must look at hits and false alarms together. (a) What the observer faces (b) ROC curves Criterion Respond no Respond yes Noise alone Signal plus noise Hits d′ Internal sensory response False alarms Misses 0 0 0.5 0.5 1 1 False alarm rate Hit rate C A B d′ = 2 d′ = 1 d′ = 0 (chance) Figure 3.3 Signal detection theory. (a) On noise trials the internal response follows the noise distribution; on signal trials it follows the shifted signal-plus-noise distribution. The observer says "yes" whenever the response exceeds the criterion. The shaded areas are false alarms (noise beyond the criterion) and misses (signal short of it); the remaining areas are hits and correct rejections. The distance between the two peaks is d′. (b) ROC curves: moving the criterion traces out a curve of hit rate against false alarm rate. Doctors A, B and C from the worked example have the same sensitivity (d′ about 2) but different criteria. Sensitivity: d′ The first quantity SDT measures is sensitivity , the ability to distinguish a signal from noise. It is indexed by d prime (written d′), the distance between the means of the noise and signal-plus-noise distributions, expressed in standard deviation units. When the two distributions lie far apart, signal trials almost always produce more evidence than noise trials, and detection is easy (large d′). When they overlap completely, the observer cannot do better than guess (d′ = 0). Sensitivity depends on the strength of the signal, on the amount of noise and on the acuity of the observer's sensory system. Crucially, it does not depend on how willing the observer is to say "yes". In practice d′ is calculated from the hit rate (H) and the false alarm rate (F) by converting each into a z score from the standard normal table: d′ = z (H) minus z (F). You do not need to compute it in the examination, but you must understand what makes it large or small. If the hit rate equals the false alarm rate, the observer is saying "yes" just as often when nothing is there as when something is, and d′ is zero. The further the hit rate rises above the false alarm rate, the larger d′ becomes, so sensitivity is highest when hits clearly outnumber false alarms. (Some Indian exam notes write this loosely as "d = hits minus false alarms"; the direction is right, but the real formula subtracts the z scores of the two rates, not the raw counts.) If false alarms exceed hits, the observer is doing worse than chance, which signals confusion or a misunderstanding of the task. The criterion: liberal and conservative observers The second quantity is the observer's response bias , the location of the criterion. It is expressed either as β (beta), the ratio of the heights of the signal and noise distributions at the criterion, or as c , the distance of the criterion from the point midway between the two distributions. An observer whose criterion is low, who says "yes" on rather weak evidence, has a liberal criterion (also called lax or risky): such an observer earns m

Weightage. 37 of the 819 questions mapped in this book (4.5%) test this chapter, 25 of them from real past papers. 2 of its 9 sections are High yield. In 1958 a fifty-two-year-old Englishman, known in the scientific literature only by his initials, S.B., had an operation that gave him back his sight. He had been effectively blind since he was about ten months old. He had learned to get about with confidence and to use tools, and he lived a full, independent adult life by touch and hearing. Then a surgeon replaced the clouded cornea of one eye with a graft, the bandages came off, and light from the world reached a working retina for the first time in half a century. What did he see? Not, as almost everyone expected, the world suddenly laid out before him. He heard the surgeon's voice in front of him, turned towards it, and saw a blur. Only because the voice came from it did he decide that the blur must be a face. The psychologist Richard Gregory and his colleague Jean Wallace, who studied him over the following months, recorded a string of puzzles. S.B. could read the time from a large clock almost at once, because as a blind man he had told the time by feeling the hands of a watch with no glass. He could read capital letters, which he had learned by touch at school, but not lower-case ones, which he had never felt. Looking down from his hospital window, which was several storeys up, he thought he could touch the ground with his feet if he hung from the sill by his hands. The most famous episode came at the Science Museum in London. Gregory and Wallace showed S.B. a lathe in a glass case, a machine he had always wanted to understand. He could make nothing of it. He was then allowed to run his hands over it with his eyes shut. When he opened them again he said, "Now that I've felt it I can see." Think about what that sentence means. The light reaching S.B.'s eyes did not change when he touched the lathe. What changed was what his brain could do with that light. This chapter is about that difference: the difference between light arriving at the eye and a person seeing a lathe, a face or a cliff edge. Keep S.B. in mind; you will meet him again at the end of the chapter. 4.1 What Perception Is: From Sensation to Interpretation Medium yield · 5 Qs Open your eyes and the world is simply there: a cup on the table, a friend across the room, the far wall at its proper distance. It feels as if nothing could be more direct. This section shows you why that feeling is misleading, and introduces the great debate about how perception actually works. Sensation, perception and the inverse problem Chapter 3 followed physical energy as far as the sense organs: light focused on the retina, sound waves moving the basilar membrane, and receptors turning that energy into neural signals. That is sensation , the detection of physical energy by the sense organs and its conversion (transduction) into neural activity. Perception is what the brain then does with those signals: it selects, organises and interprets them so that they become meaningful objects and events. Sensation gives you a pattern of light; perception gives you your mother's face. Why should perception be hard? Because the information at the eye is poorer than the world that produced it. The retina is a curved, nearly flat sheet, so the image on it has only two dimensions, yet you see a three-dimensional world. A small coin held close and a large plate held far away can throw exactly the same-sized image on the retina. A white page in shadow can send less light to your eye than a black page in sunshine. In each case many different states of the world could have produced the same retinal image. Working backwards from the image to the world that caused it is called the inverse problem , and every theory of perception is, at heart, a proposal about how the brain solves it. Bottom-up and top-down processing Two kinds of processing help. Bottom-up processing (also called data-driven processing) starts with the stimulus: receptors register features such as edges, colours and movements, and these are built up step by step into more complex descriptions. Information flows in one direction, from the senses upwards. Top-down processing (conceptually driven processing) runs the other way: knowledge, expectations and context, stored in the brain, shape how the incoming data are interpreted. You can feel both at work when you read a doctor's handwriting on a prescription. Some letters are clear enough to be read from their shapes alone (bottom-up). Others are scrawls that you can read only because you know what word is likely to come next, for example that "Paracet..." is probably followed by "amol" (top-down). Almost all real perception mixes the two. The theories that follow differ in how much weight they give to each. Perception as inference: Helmholtz, Gregory and the Bayesian brain The oldest answer to the inverse problem came from Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894), the German physicist and physiologist who measured the speed of the nerve impulse and wrote the great Handbook of Physiological Optics (completed in 1867). Helmholtz argued that perception is the end point of unconscious inference : the brain draws rapid, automatic conclusions about the world from the sensory evidence plus past experience, much as a scientist draws conclusions from data, except that we are not aware of doing it. His likelihood principle states that we perceive the object that is most likely to have produced the pattern of stimulation we receive. A small retinal image of a person is perceived as a normal-sized person far away, not as a tiny person nearby, because that is by far the likelier cause. A century later the British psychologist Richard Langton Gregory (1923 to 2010) turned this idea into the modern constructivist approach (also called the indirect or top-down approach) in books such as Eye and Brain (1966) and The Intelligent Eye (1970). For Gregory, a perception is a perceptual hypothesis : a best guess about what is out there, constructed from fragmentary sensory data and stored knowledge, and tested against further input. The senses supply evidence; the brain supplies the theory. What is the evidence for this view? Gregory's favourite was the hollow-face illusion . Look at the inside of a hollow mask from a metre or so away and you see a normal face bulging towards you, not a hollow one. Your knowledge that faces stick out is so strong that it overrides the depth information from your two eyes. Illusions (Section 4.5), ambiguous figures that flip between two interpretations, and the effects of expectation (Section 4.8) all fit the idea that perception is an active construction that can be wrong. Critics raised two problems. First, if perception is guesswork from poor data, why is it usually so accurate? Second, most illusions persist even when you know the truth; if perception were a hypothesis open to correction by knowledge, knowing that the lines of the Müller-Lyer figure are equal ought to make them look equal, and it does not. The modern descendant of Helmholtz's idea is the Bayesian approach to perception, named after the English clergyman and mathematician Thomas Bayes (about 1701 to 1761), whose theorem shows how to update a belief in the light of new evidence. On this view the brain combines two things: prior beliefs (how likely each possible state of the world is, learned from experience or built in by evolution) and the likelihood (how well each possibility fits the current sensory evidence). The result, the posterior, is the percept. When the sensory evidence is clear it dominates; when it is weak or ambiguous the priors take over. The Indian-born neuroscientist Vilayanur S. Ramachandran (born 1951) gave a neat demonstration in 1988. Shaded discs that are lighter at the top look like bumps and discs that are lighter at the bottom look like dents, and turning the page upside down swaps them. The brain is applying a prior that light comes from above, because for the whole of our evolutionary history it has. The hollow face is the same story: the prior that faces are convex outweighs weak evidence that this one is concave. Exam trap The approach that "emphasises unconscious inference and probabilistic reasoning" is the constructivist approach (Helmholtz, Gregory); its Bayesian form adds that the percept combines prior beliefs and sensory evidence . Do not pick "genetic predispositions", "cultural background" or "emotional states" for the Bayesian question: they can shape priors, but the definition is priors plus evidence. And do not confuse Helmholtz's unconscious inference with Wundt's apperception: the "apperceptive mass" (a term from Johann Friedrich Herbart that Wilhelm Wundt took over) is the store of existing ideas into which a new perception is absorbed (Chapter 1). Direct perception: Gibson's ecological approach The fiercest critic of the inference view was the American psychologist James Jerome Gibson (1904 to 1979). During the Second World War Gibson worked on how to select and train pilots, and he noticed that the cues listed in textbooks, cues taken from flat pictures viewed by a motionless observer, were of little use in explaining how a pilot lands an aircraft. A pilot is moving, and movement creates information. Over three books, The Perception of the Visual World (1950), The Senses Considered as Perceptual Systems (1966) and The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979), he built the theory of direct perception , also called the ecological approach because it studies perception in the animal's real environment rather than in the laboratory. Gibson's central claim is that the light reaching a moving observer is not poor at all. The optic array , the structured pattern of light arriving at the eye from every direction, is rich in information that specifies the layout of the world without any need for inference. Three of his ideas are examined often. Invariants are properties of the optic array that stay constant as the observer moves and so specify the world directly. The texture gradient (Section 4.3) is one: the elements of a surface get smaller and denser with distance in a lawful way. The horizon ratio is another: for objects standing on the same ground, the horizon cuts them at the same proportion of their height whatever their distance, so objects of equal height are seen as equal. Optic flow is the pattern of movement in the optic array as you move through the world. When you walk or drive forward, the scene streams outwards from a single point, the focus of expansion , which marks exactly where you are heading. A pilot landing an aircraft keeps the focus of expansion on the start of the runway. No inference is needed; the information is in the light. Affordances , a word Gibson coined in the 1960s and developed in his 1979 book, are the possibilities for action that an object or surface offers to a particular animal. A chair affords sitting, a handle affords grasping, a ledge at knee height affords climbing for an adult but not for a toddler. Gibson claimed that we perceive affordances directly, so that meaning is picked up from the environment rather than added by the brain. Gibson described the perceiver as "resonating" to this information, as a radio resonates to a broadcast. Because perception is driven by the information in the stimulus and not by stored knowledge, Gibson's theory is the classic example of a bottom-up theory. His approach was a healthy corrective: it put the moving, acting animal back at the centre of perception and inspired work on how we steer, catch and avoid collisions. But it has weaknesses. It has little to say about illusions, which by definition are cases where the information misleads us. It explains poorly how we recognise objects whose meaning depends on culture and learning (a letter box affords posting a letter only to someone who knows what a letter box is). And "resonance" names the process without explaining it. Indian context Watch a fielder at long-on under a skied hit at a cricket match in Bengaluru. He does not calculate the ball's trajectory. Studies of fielders running to catch high balls suggest that they run so as to keep the image of the ball rising smoothly in their field of view; if it starts to accelerate upwards they move back, if it starts to drop they move in. This is Gibsonian perception at its best: action guided directly by a property of the changing optic array. Bringing the two together: Neisser's perceptual cycle and two visual systems Must we choose between Gregory and Gibson? Ulric Neisser (1928 to 2012), whose Cognitive Psychology (1967) gave the new field its name, argued in his later book Cognition and Reality (1976) that we need not. His perceptual cycle joins both directions of processing into a loop (Figure 4.1). A schema , an organised body of knowledge about what to expect, directs exploration: where you look, what you listen for, what you reach out to touch. Exploration samples the information actually available in the object or scene. The information sampled then modifies the schema, which directs the next round of exploration. Perception is not a single event but a continuous cycle in which top-down expectation and bottom-up information keep correcting each other. Schema what you expect Exploration looking, moving, touching Object available information directs (top-down) samples modifies (bottom-up) the cycle never stops Figure 4.1 Neisser's perceptual cycle (1976). Notice that top-down and bottom-up processing are not rivals here: each arrow feeds the next, so expectation and information correct each other continuously. A second reconciliation came from the brain. In 1995 David Milner and Melvyn Goodale proposed that the visual system has two streams with different jobs. A ventral stream, running into the temporal lobe, serves vision-for-perception : recognising what objects are, which needs stored knowledge, just as Gregory said. A dorsal stream, running into the parietal lobe, serves vision-for-action : guiding the hand and body in real time, fast and largely unconscious, very much as Gibson described. Their patient D.F., whose ventral stream had been damaged by carbon monoxide poisoning, could not say whether a slot in a disc was horizontal or vertical, yet could turn her hand correctly and post a card through it. The two classic theories may simply be describing two different visual systems (the anatomy is covered in the Physiological book). Two further labels appear as options in examination questions. The information-processing approach treats perception as a series of stages, each transforming the output of the one before, much as a computer program does. The computational approach , associated above all with David Marr, asks what problem each stage of vision has to solve and what calculations would solve it; you will meet it in Section 4.7. Clinical link Several studies have found that people with schizophrenia are much less fooled by the hollow-face illusion than other people: they are more likely to see the mask as hollow, as it really is. One interpretation is that the balance between top-down expectation and bottom-up evidence is altered in the disorder. It is a reminder that "seeing correctly" in a laboratory task is not always a sign of a healthy brain. 4.2 Perceptual Organisation: The Gestalt Laws Medium yield · 8 Qs Before you can recognise an object you must first decide which bits of the visual field belong together and which belong to something else. That sounds trivial until you try to explain how it is done. The school that took this problem most seriously, and that has contributed more to the study of perception than any other, was Gestalt psychology. The Gestalt starting point Gestalt psychology was founded in Germany in 1912, when Max Wertheimer (1880 to 1943) published his experiments on apparent movement, with Kurt Koffka (1886 to 1941) and Wolfgang Köhler (1887 to 1967) as his first subjects and lifelong collaborators (the history of the school is told in Chapter 2). The German word Gestalt means form, shape or configuration. The school's founding claim, aimed squarely at Wundt's and Titchener's attempt to break experience into elementary sensations, was that the whole is different from the sum of its parts. A melody is still the same melody when every note is changed by transposing it into another key; the "melodiness" lies in the relations between the notes, not in the notes themselves. In perception, said the Gestaltists, the brain spontaneously organises the visual field into wholes according to a small set of innate laws, and in 1923 Wertheimer set these out in a famous paper. Figure and ground The most basic act of organisation is to split the field into a figure , the object that stands out and is attended to, and a ground , the background against which it appears. The Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin (1886 to 1951) studied this figure-ground relationship in his 1915 doctoral work and drew the best-known demonstration of it, Rubin's vase : a white vase on a black background which, as you look, becomes two black faces in profile on a white background. Rubin described how figure and ground differ in experience: The figure has a thing-like quality (it looks like an object) and a definite shape; the ground is shapeless and looks like substance or empty space. The contour between them seems to belong to the figure, not the ground. The figure appears nearer and in front; the ground appears farther away, diffuse, and seems to continue behind the figure. The figure is more vivid, more easily named and better remembered. Certain regions are more likely to become figure: smaller regions, enclosed regions, symmetrical and convex regions, and regions in the lower part of the field. Figure-ground organisation is not only visual. At a noisy wedding reception, the voice of the person talking to you is an auditory figure and the din of the hall is ground. The vase and faces is a reversible figure : either region can be seen as figure, but never both at once, and the percept flips back and forth. Notice what this means. The stimulus never changes, yet the perception does. Organisation is something the perceiver does, not something in the picture. Exam trap "Which is not a characteristic of a figure?" The answer is "appears diffused and spatially distant", because that describes the ground . Smaller size, clear outlines and greater object character (thing-like quality) are all properties of the figure. Camouflage works by breaking figure-ground segregation, so that the animal's contour is lost in the ground. The laws of grouping Once figures are separated from ground, elements must be grouped into larger units. The Gestalt laws of perceptual organisation describe how. Look at Figure 4.2 as you read; each panel lets you watch one law at work in your own perception. By the law of proximity , elements that are close together in space or in time are seen as belonging together. In the first panel the dots are equally spaced vertically but not horizontally, so you see three pairs of columns rather than four rows. Proximity in time works the same way: the taps of a drum heard close together form a rhythm group. By the law of similarity , elements that look alike (in colour, shape, size or orientation) are grouped together; in the second panel equal spacing would favour columns, but similarity makes you see rows of filled and open dots. By the law of closure , we tend to complete figures that have gaps, so that the broken outline in the third panel is seen as a circle, not as four separate arcs. The law of good continuation (also called the law of continuity) holds that elements that follow a smooth line or curve are grouped together, so that the fourth panel shows a straight line crossing a curve rather than two odd angular shapes meeting at a point. By the law of common fate , elements moving together in the same direction are grouped together: a flock of birds or a column of marching soldiers is seen as one unit, and in the sixth panel the arrows split the row into two sets. The Gestaltists also described a law of symmetry (symmetrical regions are grouped together and tend to be seen as figure), and Wertheimer added a law of past experience or familiarity (elements that together form a familiar object tend to be grouped). Modern researchers have added two laws. The law of common region , proposed by Stephen Palmer in 1992, states that elements inside a common enclosed region are grouped together, even when proximity says otherwise (fifth panel, top row). The law of connectedness (element connectedness), described by Palmer and Irvin Rock in 1994, states that elements physically joined by lines are seen as a unit (fifth panel, bottom row). In the same 1994 paper Palmer and Rock proposed uniform connectedness: any connected region of uniform colour, texture or lightness is organised as a single perceptual unit. Both kinds of connectedness, and common region, are powerful enough to override proximity and similarity. Table 4.2 brings all the laws together.
