It states that every stimulus pattern is seen in such a way that the resulting structure is as simple, regular, stable and complete as the conditions allow. Two overlapping rings could in principle be seen as three oddly shaped pieces, but you see two circles because that is the simplest description. The other laws can be seen as special cases of this one, which is why Prägnanz is called the master law of Gestalt organisation and why a question about a figure "perceived not in parts but organised in the best possible whole form" is answered by Prägnanz. The power of these laws shows most clearly when they create something that is not there. In 1955 the Italian psychologist Gaetano Kanizsa (1913 to 1993) drew three black discs, each with a wedge cut out, arranged so that the wedges face each other. Observers see a bright white triangle lying on top of the discs, complete with sharp edges across empty paper. These illusory contours (subjective contours) show closure and Prägnanz at work: the simplest interpretation of three cut discs is one triangle covering three whole discs. A related process, amodal completion , makes us perceive an object partly hidden behind another as continuing, complete, behind it. How good are the Gestalt laws? They are excellent descriptions; every textbook of design, typography and advertising still uses them. But they are descriptions, not explanations. They do not say why the brain groups this way, and they are vague about what happens when two laws conflict. The Gestaltists' own physiological explanation, that perceptual organisation reflects electrical fields in the brain with the same shape as the percept (Köhler's isomorphism), was not supported by later experiments in which the cortex of animals was filled with metal strips or wires to disrupt any such fields without destroying perception. And research since then has shown that grouping is partly learned: what counts as "similar" or "familiar" depends on experience, as you will see in Section 4.8. Exam trap The tendency to complete a figure is closure , not continuity or continuation (continuity is about smooth paths, not gaps). Items close together in space and time group by proximity . The figure "organised in the best possible whole form" is Prägnanz . The school that contributed most to perception is Gestalt psychology , not structuralism, behaviourism or psychoanalysis. And Gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls) has nothing to do with Gestalt psychology except the name. Exam trap Do not confuse interposition (a depth cue: a nearer object blocks a farther one, Section 4.3) with interpolation (filling in between known points, as the visual system does when it completes a contour hidden behind an occluder) or extrapolation (extending a trend beyond the known points). One past paper also used structuring for working out a rule or organising principle from incomplete evidence and then picking out the items that satisfy it; that keyed answer fits the Gestalt idea that perception imposes structure on incomplete input. Clinical link In 1938 the American child psychiatrist Lauretta Bender built a test from nine of Wertheimer's grouping designs. The Bender Visual-Motor Gestalt Test asks the person to copy the designs; distortions, rotations and failures of integration can point to visuoconstructive or organic difficulties. Answers: (1) inverse, (2) top-down, (3) unconscious, (4) hypothesis, (5) prior, (6) affordances, (7) expansion, (8) schema, (9) reversible, (10) Prägnanz. 4.3 Depth and Distance Perception High yield · 9 Qs Reach out and pick up the cup in front of you. Your hand opens to the right width and stops at exactly the right distance, without a moment's thought. Yet the image of the cup on each retina has no depth at all. How does a flat image give you a world in three dimensions? The problem of the flat retina The problem was posed clearly in 1709 by the Irish philosopher George Berkeley (1685 to 1753) in An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision . Berkeley pointed out that a point at any distance along a line of sight falls on the same point of the retina, so distance cannot be "seen" directly. He concluded that we learn to judge distance by associating visual sensations, such as the strain of turning the eyes inwards, with the experience of reaching and walking. Modern research has replaced Berkeley's short list with a long list of depth cues , sources of information that correlate with distance and that the brain combines to give depth perception , the ability to see the world in three dimensions and to judge how far away things are. The cues fall into families according to what they need: two eyes, one eye, movement, or feedback from the eye's own muscles. Binocular cues: disparity and convergence Binocular cues are depth cues that require both eyes working together. The most important is retinal disparity (also called binocular disparity). Your eyes are about 6 centimetres apart, so each receives a slightly different view of the world. Hold a finger about 20 centimetres in front of your nose and close each eye in turn: the finger jumps from side to side against the background. The difference between the positions of an object's images on the two retinas is its disparity, and the nearer the object, the larger the disparity. Objects at the fixation distance fall on corresponding points of the two retinas and have zero disparity; the imaginary curved surface through all such points is called the horopter . Objects nearer than the horopter have crossed disparity and objects beyond it have uncrossed disparity, so the sign of the disparity tells the brain whether an object is in front of or behind the point being looked at. The vivid impression of solid depth produced by fusing the two images is called stereopsis . The English physicist Charles Wheatstone (1802 to 1875) proved the point in 1838 with his stereoscope , which presented a slightly different drawing to each eye; viewers saw a single solid object. Every 3-D film works the same way, using special glasses to send a different image to each eye. In 1960 the Hungarian-American engineer Béla Julesz (1928 to 2003) went further with random-dot stereograms: two fields of random dots, identical except that a central square of dots is shifted slightly in one of them. Each image alone looks like television snow. Viewed in a stereoscope, a square floats out in depth. Because there is no square to recognise in either image alone, Julesz showed that stereopsis can work before any object is recognised, a purely bottom-up process. The second binocular cue is convergence (vergence): the inward turning of the two eyes to fixate a near object. Look at your fingertip as you bring it towards your nose and you can feel your eyes cross. The brain registers how much the eyes are turned in, from the commands sent to the eye muscles and feedback from them, and the greater the convergence, the nearer the object. Convergence is a binocular cue, because it needs two eyes, and also an oculomotor cue, because it comes from the eye muscles; it is useful only for objects within a couple of metres. Binocular cues can work only where the fields of the two eyes overlap. Each human eye sees roughly 160 degrees horizontally (about 60 degrees towards the nose and about 100 degrees towards the temple); the two together cover roughly 200 degrees, and the central overlap where both eyes see, the binocular field, is about 120 degrees wide. Predators such as cats and owls, and primates such as ourselves, have forward-facing eyes with a large overlap and good stereopsis; prey animals such as rabbits and deer have eyes on the sides of the head, a nearly all-round view, and little binocular overlap. Exam trap A past paper asked for the "approximate visual field covered by each human eye" and keyed 180 degrees . The better textbook figure for one eye is about 160 degrees horizontally; 180 to 200 degrees is the field of both eyes together, and about 120 degrees is the binocular overlap. If you meet that exact item, be aware that the paper's key was 180; if the question clearly says "both eyes", 180 to 200 is right. Monocular cues: what a painter knows Monocular cues are depth cues available to one eye alone. People who have lost an eye still judge depth well, and a flat painting or photograph can look deep, because of them. Most are pictorial cues , so called because artists since the Renaissance have used them to put depth on a flat canvas. Figure 4.3 shows the main ones in a single scene. Relative size : if two objects are known or assumed to be the same size, the one casting the smaller retinal image is seen as farther away. A row of identical lamp posts seems to shrink into the distance. Familiar size : when we know an object's real size, its retinal size tells us its distance. A tiny-looking autorickshaw is seen as a normal autorickshaw far away. Interposition (also called overlap or occlusion): when one object partly blocks the view of another, the blocked object is seen as farther away. Interposition gives only order (nearer or farther), not distance. Linear perspective : parallel lines, such as railway tracks or the edges of a road, appear to converge as they recede, meeting at a vanishing point on the horizon. Texture gradient : a surface with an even texture (pebbles, grass, the sleepers of a railway track, bricks in a courtyard) shows its elements as larger, coarser and more widely spaced nearby, and smaller, finer and more densely packed farther away. This was Gibson's favourite cue, because it specifies distance and the slant of a surface directly. Aerial perspective (atmospheric perspective): distant objects look hazier, less sharp, lower in contrast and often bluer, because light from them passes through more air, dust and moisture. On a clear day after the monsoon, the Nilgiri hills seem nearer than they do in hazy summer. Height in the visual field (relative height or elevation): for objects on the ground below the horizon, those higher in the visual field, that is, closer to the horizon, are seen as farther away; for objects above the horizon, such as clouds, the reverse holds. Shading (light and shadow): the pattern of light and shadow on an object reveals its three-dimensional shape, and shadows cast on the ground show where an object stands. As Section 4.1 showed, the brain assumes the light comes from above. Relative brightness: of two identical objects, the brighter is usually seen as nearer. Aerial perspective: far hills look hazy Linear perspective: edges converge Texture gradient: stripes crowd together Interposition Relative size and height in the field Figure 4.3 Pictorial depth cues in one scene. The road's edges converge (linear perspective), the cross stripes crowd together with distance (texture gradient), the three identical trees shrink and rise towards the horizon (relative size and height in the field), the near house hides part of the far one (interposition), and the distant hills are pale (aerial perspective). Road engineers use these cues deliberately. Stripes painted across the approach to a toll plaza or an exit ramp, with the gaps between them getting smaller, create an exaggerated texture gradient and a heightened sense of speed, so that drivers slow down without being told. Cues from movement and from the eye's own muscles Gibson's complaint that textbook cues were taken from frozen pictures applies with special force to the cues that need movement. The most powerful is motion parallax : when you move, objects at different distances move across your retina at different speeds. Look out of the side window of a moving train. The electric poles beside the track flash past in the direction opposite to your travel, the trees beyond move more slowly, the distant hills crawl, and the moon seems to travel along with you. The relative speed of the images tells you their relative distance. Motion parallax is a monocular cue (one eye is enough) but not a pictorial one, because a still picture cannot show it. A related cue is deletion and accretion: as you move, a nearer surface progressively covers (deletes) and uncovers (accretes) the texture of a farther one, which is interposition in motion. Accommodation is the change in the shape of the lens, controlled by the ciliary muscles, that focuses the image of near or far objects on the retina (Chapter 3). The brain can use the state of these muscles as a rough distance cue for objects within about two metres. Accommodation, like convergence, is an oculomotor cue , but unlike convergence it works with one eye. Everything else, including accommodation and motion parallax, is monocular. So "a monocular cue" from convergence, retinal disparity, assimilation and interposition is interposition ; "requires both eyes" from motion parallax, aerial perspective, convergence and accommodation is convergence ; and retinal disparity is a binocular cue, not a pictorial, static monocular or motion parallax cue. Assimilation is not a depth cue at all: in Piaget's theory it means fitting new experience into an existing schema (Developmental book), and in perception it names the opposite of contrast, when a colour or grey looks more like its surroundings. Increasing density of stones, pebbles or painted stripes with distance is texture gradient , not aerial perspective (haze) or interposition (overlap). Is depth perception innate? The visual cliff Berkeley thought depth perception had to be learned. Is he right? In the 1950s Eleanor Jack Gibson (1910 to 2002) and Richard Walk (1920 to 1999), at Cornell University, built an apparatus to find out. Key study: The visual cliff (Gibson and Walk, 1960) Question. Can infants and young animals perceive depth before they have had a chance to learn it through falls and bumps? Method. The visual cliff is a large table topped by a sheet of strong glass. Under one half a checkerboard pattern is fixed directly beneath the glass (the shallow side); under the other half the same pattern lies far below the glass (the deep side), so that the table appears to end in a sheer drop, although the glass makes it perfectly safe. A narrow centre board separates the two sides. Thirty-six infants aged 6 to 14 months were placed on the centre board and their mothers called them from the shallow side and from the deep side in turn. Results. Twenty-seven infants moved off the board. All of them crawled onto the shallow side at least once, but only three crept, hesitantly, onto the deep side. Many crawled away from their mothers when called from the deep side, or cried because they could not reach them, and some patted the glass yet still refused to cross. Newly hatched chicks, young goats and lambs placed on the apparatus within a day of birth also avoided the deep side. Conclusion. By the time human infants can crawl, they can perceive depth, and in species that walk from birth, depth perception is present from birth. Criticism. Human infants cannot be tested until they crawl, at around six months, by which time they have had months of visual experience, so the study cannot show that depth perception in humans is innate. Later work divided the question. When Joseph Campos and his colleagues in 1970 lowered infants of about two to three and a half months directly onto the deep side, their heart rate slowed, the sign of interest and attention, not the speeding up that signals fear. Young infants therefore detect the difference in depth long before they fear it. Fear of the drop appears with experience of moving about on one's own: infants of the same age who have begun crawling, or who have been given experience in baby walkers, show fear on the deep side sooner than those who have not. The most balanced conclusion is that the ability to detect depth appears very early and may well be largely built in, while the meaning of a drop, the knowledge that it is dangerous, is learned through self-produced movement. Exam trap The visual cliff was devised by Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk (1960) to study depth perception and whether it is innate. It did not study object permanence (Piaget), colour perception, imprinting (Lorenz) or language. The infants were 6 to 14 months old (crawling age), not newborns and not "3 to 6 months", as some revision notes say. The best summary of the human results is "depth perception is present by the time infants can crawl", not "fully developed at birth" and not "only after age two". Clinical link Children whose eyes are misaligned (strabismus) or who have a lazy eye (amblyopia) in early childhood often grow up stereoblind, because the brain never learns to combine the two eyes' images. The neurobiologist Susan Barry , cross-eyed from infancy, gained stereoscopic vision in her late forties after intensive vision therapy, a case made famous by the neurologist Oliver Sacks (1933 to 2015). Her experience, of suddenly seeing snowflakes floating in depth, shows both how much the brain depends on early experience and how much plasticity remains in adulthood. 4.4 Perceptual Constancy Lower yield · 3 Qs As a friend walks away from you down a corridor, the image of her on your retina shrinks steadily; at twice the distance it is half the height. Yet she does not seem to shrink. When a door swings open, the image it casts changes from a rectangle to a narrower and narrower trapezoid; yet you see a rectangular door turning. This stability is called perceptual constancy : the tendency to perceive objects as having stable, unchanging properties (size, shape, lightness, colour, position) despite large changes in the sensory input they produce. Without constancy the world would be a chaos of swelling, shrinking, stretching, darkening shapes. Size constancy and size-distance invariance Size constancy is the perception of an object as remaining the same size even though the size of its retinal image changes with distance. Try this. Hold one hand at arm's length and the other halfway to your face. The retinal image of the far hand is only about half the size of the near one, yet both look like normal hands of the same size. How is it done? The brain takes account of distance. The size-distance invariance hypothesis states that perceived size is proportional to retinal image size multiplied by perceived distance. If the retinal image halves while the perceived distance doubles, perceived size stays the same. It follows that size constancy should depend on depth cues, and should break down when they are removed. Key study: Holway and Boring (1941) Question. Does size constancy depend on information about distance? Method. Alfred Holway and Edwin Garrigues Boring (1886 to 1968) seated observers at the junction of two long corridors. Down one corridor, at distances from 10 to 120 feet, they placed test discs whose physical size was increased with distance so that every disc cast exactly the same retinal image (one degree of visual angle). In the other corridor was a comparison disc whose size the observer adjusted until it matched the test disc. Observers did this under four conditions: with both eyes, with one eye, with one eye through a small peephole, and finally through a peephole and a long black tunnel that hid almost every cue to distance. Results. With both eyes and full cues, observers matched the discs' physical sizes almost perfectly: size constancy was excellent. As cues were removed, their settings moved steadily towards the retinal size; with the peephole and tunnel, all the discs looked nearly the same size. Conclusion. Size constancy depends on information about distance, just as the size-distance invariance hypothesis predicts. Emmert's law You can test size-distance invariance on yourself with an afterimage. Stare for about thirty seconds at a bright lamp or a coloured square, then look at a sheet of paper in your hand, and then at a distant wall. The afterimage, which is a fixed patch of fatigued retina and therefore has a fixed retinal size, looks small on the paper and large on the wall. This is Emmert's law , described by the Swiss ophthalmologist Emil Emmert (1844 to 1911) in 1881: the perceived size of an afterimage is proportional to the perceived distance of the surface on which it is projected (Figure 4.4). Emmert's law is the size-distance relationship laid bare, because the retinal size is held perfectly constant and only perceived distance varies. Perceived size = retinal size × perceived distance Eye Near wall afterimage looks small Far wall afterimage looks large same retinal image Figure 4.4 Emmert's law. The dashed lines mark one fixed visual angle, the size of the afterimage on the retina. Projected onto a near wall the afterimage looks small; onto a far wall it looks large, because the brain scales retinal size by perceived distance. Size constancy is not perfect, and it depends on experience of distance. From the top of a tall building, people on the street look like ants, because we have little practice in judging vertical distances. In Section 4.8 you will meet a forest dweller who had never seen across open country and who took distant buffalo for insects. And when distance is misjudged, size is misjudged too; this is the key to several famous illusions (Section 4.5). Shape constancy Shape constancy is the perception of an object as keeping its shape even when its orientation to us changes, so that the retinal image changes shape. A round dinner plate on a table casts an elliptical image unless you look straight down on it, and an opening door casts a trapezoid, yet the plate looks round and the door rectangular. The British psychologist Robert Thouless (1894 to 1984) showed in 1931 that constancy is usually a compromise: when observers drew the shape of a tilted circle as it appeared to them, they drew an ellipse that was rounder than the retinal image but not fully round. He called this tendency for perception to lie between the retinal image and the real object phenomenal regression to the real object . Brightness and colour constancy A lump of coal in bright sunlight sends more light to your eye than a sheet of white paper in the shade, yet the coal still looks black and the paper white. Brightness constancy (more precisely, lightness constancy) is the perception of an object's lightness (its whiteness, greyness or blackness) as constant despite changes in the amount of light falling on it. The key, as Hans Wallach (1904 to 1998) showed in 1948, is the ratio principle : perceived lightness depends on the ratio of light reflected from an object to the light reflected from its surroundings. When the illumination changes, object and surroundings change together and the ratio stays the same. White paper reflects about 80 to 90 percent of the light falling on it and coal only a few percent, whatever the lighting. The ratio principle also explains simultaneous contrast : a grey square on a black background looks lighter than an identical grey square on a white background, because the ratio to the surround differs. Part of the neural basis lies in lateral inhibition , the tendency of active neurons in the retina to suppress the activity of their neighbours. Lateral inhibition exaggerates differences at borders and so enhances edge perception. It explains Mach bands , the illusory light and dark stripes seen at the boundaries of a graded strip, described by the Austrian physicist Ernst Mach (1838 to 1916) in 1865, and the grey smudges seen at the intersections of the white lines of the Hermann grid , described by Ludimar Hermann (1838 to 1914) in 1870 (the retinal circuitry is in Chapter 3 and the Physiological book). Colour constancy is the perception of an object's colour as constant under different coloured lights. A ripe banana looks yellow under the bluish light of a tube light, the orange light of a sodium street lamp and the reddish light of sunset, although the light it reflects changes greatly. The brain compares the light from the banana with the light from the rest of the scene and discounts the colour of the illuminant; adaptation of the cones to the prevailing light also helps. Edwin Land (1909 to 1991), the inventor of the Polaroid instant camera, built his retinex theory on demonstrations of this kind. Colour constancy can fail when the brain cannot tell what the illumination is. In February 2015 a photograph of a striped dress divided the internet: some people saw it as blue and black, others as white and gold. The two groups seemed to differ in whether their brains assumed the dress was lit by bluish daylight or by yellowish artificial light, and so discounted different illuminants. Location constancy Every time you move your eyes, the image of the world sweeps across your retina, yet the world stays still. Location constancy (position constancy) is the perception of stationary objects as remaining in the same place despite movements of the eyes, head and body. You can break it yourself with a demonstration that Helmholtz described. Close one eye and press very gently on the outer corner of the other eyelid with a fingertip: the world jumps. When you move your eyes in the normal way, the brain sends a copy of the motor command to the visual system, called a corollary discharge by Roger Sperry (1913 to 1994) and an efference copy by Erich von Holst , both in 1950, and uses it to cancel the expected movement of the retinal image. When your finger moves the eye, there is no command and nothing to cancel, so the movement of the image is attributed to the world. The same mechanism underlies the perception of real motion (Section 4.6). How often does the brain have to make this correction? Several times every second. When you read or scan a scene your eyes do not glide smoothly; they jump from point to point in rapid movements called saccades, separated by brief pauses called fixations, during which information is taken in. Even during a fixation the eyes are never perfectly still: they make a fine tremor, slow drifts and tiny rapid flicks called microsaccades. These small movements are not a flaw. In the 1950s researchers devised ways of keeping an image fixed on the same receptors however the eye moved (a stabilised retinal image), and the image faded from view within seconds, because receptors stimulated without change adapt (sensory adaptation, Chapter 3). By constantly refreshing the image on the retina, saccades and microsaccades ensure constant perception, while the corollary discharge keeps the world from seeming to jump with every one of them. Table 4.4 summarises the five constancies. Table 4.4 The perceptual constancies. Constancy What changes at the eye What we perceive Main explanation Size Retinal image size with distance Constant size Size-distance invariance; depth cues (Holway and Boring, 1941) Shape Retinal shape with orientation Constant shape Perceived slant; phenomenal regression (Thouless, 1931) Brightness (lightness) Amount of light reflected Constant whiteness or blackness Ratio principle (Wallach, 1948) Colour Wavelengths reflected under different lights Constant colour Discounting the illuminant; adaptation; retinex (Land) Location (position) Image movement when the eyes move A stable world Corollary discharge (Sperry; von Holst, 1950) Exam trap Your outstretched hand looks the same size as your near hand because of size constancy , not shape constancy, motion parallax or "depth perception" in general (depth perception is what size constancy uses, not the name of the effect). Emmert's law concerns afterimages and their apparent size. Lateral inhibition enhances edges; it does not dull them, lower overall brightness or improve colour vision. Tiny rapid eye movements that keep the retinal image from fading are saccades (strictly, microsaccades), and they ensure constant perception ; a fixation is the pause between saccades, not a movement, and sensory adaptation is the fading they prevent. Constancy is a property of perception, not of sensation: the sensory input changes; the percept does not. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. The difference between the images of an object on the two retinas is called retinal . The vivid impression of depth produced by fusing the two eyes' images is called . The inward turning of the eyes to look at a near object is , a binocular cue. Stones that look smaller and more densely packed with distance illustrate the cue of texture . Near objects flashing past a train window faster than distant ones illustrate motion . The visual cliff was devised by Eleanor Gibson and Richard in 1960. Perceived size equals retinal size multiplied by perceived . An afterimage looks larger on a distant wall than on a near page, as stated by law. Thouless called the compromise between retinal shape and real shape phenomenal to the real object. Wallach explained lightness constancy by the principle. Answers: (1) disparity, (2) stereopsis, (3) convergence, (4) gradient, (5) parallax, (6) Walk, (7) distance, (8) Emmert's, (9) regression, (10) ratio. 4.5 Illusions: What Perception's Mistakes Reveal High yield · 7 Qs Everything in this chapter so far has been a success story: a flat retina yields a deep world, a shrinking image yields a friend of constant size, a scatter of dots yields tidy groups. But a system that works by inference, as Helmholtz and Gregory argued, must sometimes infer wrongly. Those failures are far more than curiosities for puzzle books. A slip of the tongue tells you something about how speech is planned; in the same way, a visual illusion tells you which rules the visual system is following, because it catches the system applying a sensible rule in a place where the rule does not fit. What an illusion is An illusion is a perception that does not correspond to the physical properties of the stimulus: a misinterpretation of a stimulus that really exists in the outside world. Three features mark an illusion in the psychologist's sense. First, there is a real external stimulus; the lines of the Müller-Lyer figure are really there on the page. Second, the error is systematic. Nearly everyone who looks makes the same mistake, in the same direction and by roughly the same amount, so illusions can be measured with the psychophysical methods of Chapter 3. Third, most illusions are stubborn. You can measure the lines with a ruler, satisfy yourself that they are equal, look again, and still see them as unequal. This was the second objection to Gregory's hypothesis theory that you met in Section 4.1, and it tells you that much of the machinery behind illusions runs automatically, below the level that knowledge can reach. Where exactly does the error happen? Not in the eye. Photograph the Müller-Lyer figure and the two lines in the photograph are equal; the image on your retina is just as faithful. The receptors register the light correctly, so sensation is not distorted. What goes wrong is the interpretation of that light, the organising and inferring that turn a retinal image into a seen world. Optical illusions are therefore distortions of perception , not of sensation, which is why textbooks reach for them whenever they want to make the difference between sensation and perception concrete. Illusions are not only visual. Cross your index and middle fingers, close your eyes and roll a small marble between the two fingertips: you feel two marbles (Aristotle's illusion, described more than two thousand years ago). Lift a small box and a large box of exactly the same weight and the small one feels clearly heavier; this size-weight illusion was measured by the French physician Augustin Charpentier in 1891.
