In the early 1950s Eugene Aserinsky (1921 to 1998) was a graduate student in physiology at the University of Chicago, nearly thirty years old, short of money and living with his wife and young son in a converted army barracks. His supervisor, Nathaniel Kleitman (1895 to 1999), was the most senior sleep researcher in the world, and he had given Aserinsky a modest job: watch the eyes of sleepers and see what they do. Most scientists of the day thought that sleep was simply the brain switching off, a long quiet night of nothing, so the project did not look promising. Aserinsky found an old, temperamental recording machine in a basement, repaired it as best he could and began taping electrodes around the eyes of anyone who would sleep in his laboratory. One of his first volunteers was his eight-year-old son, Armond. As the boy slept, the pens of the machine scratched out slow, lazy lines, exactly as expected. Then, deep into the night, the pens began to jerk sharply from side to side, the tracing of eyes darting about as if the sleeper were wide awake and watching something. Aserinsky assumed that his old machine had failed again. But the boy was asleep, and the jerking pens came back, in bursts, at regular intervals through the night. They came back in adult volunteers too. Aserinsky then did the obvious thing that nobody had done before: he woke people up during these bursts of eye movement and asked them what had been going on in their minds. Most of them described vivid, story-like dreams. Woken at other times, they usually reported nothing much. In 1953, Aserinsky and Kleitman published their discovery in the journal Science : sleep contains recurring periods of rapid eye movement, and these periods are when we dream. That short paper did something larger than add a fact to physiology. It showed that consciousness does not simply switch on in the morning and off at night. The mind changes state, many times a night, and each state has its own brain activity and its own kind of experience. This chapter is about those states. It begins with attention, the process that decides which tiny part of the world reaches awareness at all, and then moves to consciousness itself, the body's daily clocks, sleep, dreams, hypnosis, meditation and the changes that drugs produce. Keep Armond's dancing eyes in mind; you will meet them again in Section 5.7. 5.1 Attention: what it is, how it behaves and what captures it Lower yield · 1 Q Sit for a moment in a busy chai stall near the Mysuru bus stand. Buses roar past, the stove hisses, two men argue about cricket, a radio plays a film song, your tea is too hot, your shoe pinches and a crow is calling from the roof. All of this reaches your sense organs at once, yet at any instant you are clearly aware of only a small part of it. If your friend starts telling you about tomorrow's exam, the cricket argument fades into a murmur. Then someone at the next table says your name, and suddenly you are listening to them instead. The process that is doing this choosing is attention. Defining attention The most quoted definition comes from William James (1842 to 1910), the American philosopher-psychologist, in his Principles of Psychology of 1890: "Everyone knows what attention is. It is the taking possession by the mind, in clear and vivid form, of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought. Focalization, concentration, of consciousness are of its essence. It implies withdrawal from some things in order to deal effectively with others." Notice the two halves of that definition. Attention is a process of selection (one object out of several) and of concentration (that object is held clearly and vividly while others are withdrawn from). Modern textbooks say much the same thing in plainer words: attention is the process by which we select some information from the vast amount available to the senses and to memory, and concentrate mental resources on it. Why do we need such a process at all? Because the brain's capacity to process information fully is limited. You can register a great deal at the level of the sense organs, but you cannot analyse it all for meaning, remember it all or act on it all. Attention is the gatekeeper between the flood of sensation and the narrow channel of awareness, which is why Indian exam notes often summarise the sequence as sensation, then attention, then perception. (Sensation and perception have their own chapters, Chapters 3 and 4.) Psychologists have classified attention in several ways. A classic classification, set out by Edward Bradford Titchener (1867 to 1927), separates involuntary attention (his "primary" attention), which is pulled by the stimulus without effort (a sudden bang), from voluntary attention (his "secondary" attention), which you direct deliberately and with effort (forcing yourself to read a dull chapter), and adds a third, habitual attention (his "derived primary" attention), which began as voluntary but has become effortless through long practice and interest (the cricket fan who notices a score flashing on a distant shop television without trying). A clinical classification, proposed by McKay Moore Sohlberg and Catherine Mateer in 1987 for rehabilitating brain-injured patients, describes five levels: focused attention (responding to a single stimulus at all), sustained attention (keeping that response going over time), selective attention (holding focus in the presence of distractors), alternating attention (switching back and forth between tasks) and divided attention (responding to two tasks at the same moment). You will meet each of these again in this chapter. The characteristics of attention Classical general psychology describes attention by five characteristics. Each is a simple observation about how attention behaves, and each is a favourite source of exam questions. Selectivity. Attention picks out a few stimuli and neglects the rest. The mother asleep through traffic noise but awake at her baby's faintest whimper shows selectivity at work even during sleep. Shifting. Attention moves from one object to another, often several times a second, as when your eyes and mind move between the teacher, the blackboard and your notes. Shifting can be voluntary or forced by a new stimulus. Span. Attention can take in only a limited number of items in a single glance. This limit is called the span of attention, and it is examined in detail below. Fluctuation. Even when you try to keep attention on one unchanging stimulus, its clarity waxes and wanes. This is different from shifting: in fluctuation the object stays the same but your hold on it rises and falls. Division. Under some conditions attention can be shared between two activities at once, such as walking and talking. How far it can be divided, and why it often cannot, is the subject of Section 5.4. The span of attention The span of attention (also called the span of apprehension) is the number of separate objects that can be clearly perceived in a single brief exposure, too short for the eyes to move or for counting. The question is old. The Scottish philosopher Sir William Hamilton (1788 to 1856) remarked in his lectures that if you throw a handful of marbles on the floor, you will find it difficult to see more than six, or seven at most, at one view without confusion. Key study: Jevons and the beans (1871) The English economist and logician William Stanley Jevons (1835 to 1882) turned Hamilton's remark into an experiment, with himself as the only participant. He threw random handfuls of black beans into a shallow box, glanced at them for an instant, called out an estimate of how many there were, and then counted them. Over about a thousand trials he was never wrong with three or four beans; errors began at five, and his accuracy fell steadily as the number rose. He published the result in Nature in 1871. Later laboratory work used the tachistoscope , an apparatus that flashes a display for a fraction of a second, and arrived at the figure that general psychology textbooks still give: for unrelated items, the adult span of attention is about six to eight, usually summarised as "about seven". For perfectly accurate, effortless enumeration the limit is lower, about four; this rapid, error-free judgement of small numbers was named subitising by E. L. Kaufman and colleagues in 1949. The span of attention explains a lot of everyday design. An Indian vehicle registration number is not printed as one long string such as KA09AB1234. It is broken into short groups (a two-letter state code, a two-digit district code, a letter series and a number of no more than four digits), so that a witness to an accident can take in each group at a glance. The same reason lies behind short telephone groupings and four-digit PINs. The closely related limit on how much we can hold in mind for a few seconds, George Miller's "magical number seven, plus or minus two" of 1956, belongs to short-term memory and is taught in Chapter 7. Exam trap When a question asks why number plates carry only about four digits with a few letters, the answer is span of attention , not selective, divided or sustained attention. Do not confuse the span of attention (how many items can be apprehended in one glance; Jevons, tachistoscope studies) with the memory span of Miller (how many items can be held and repeated back). The numbers are similar; the processes are not. Fluctuation of attention Hold a watch at the distance where its ticking is just audible and listen carefully. You will notice that the ticking seems to fade out and come back, although the watch has not changed. The classical laboratory demonstration of this fluctuation of attention used the Masson disc , a white disc carrying a broken line of small grey segments that, when the disc is spun, forms faint grey rings at the threshold of visibility. A person who fixes the disc steadily reports that the faint rings appear and disappear, again and again. Ambiguous figures, such as Rubin's vase-faces figure (see Chapter 4), show something similar: attention cannot be held on one organisation for long and keeps flipping between them. Part of the fluctuation has peripheral causes (small eye movements and the adaptation of receptors), and part is central. The broader lesson is that attention is never static. It needs constant renewal, and when a task gives it nothing new, it drifts. That drift, as you will see in Section 5.5, is where daydreams come from. The determinants of attention What decides which stimulus wins? The determinants of attention are traditionally divided into two groups. External determinants (also called objective factors) are properties of the stimulus itself, and they explain why advertisers do what they do. Internal determinants (subjective factors) are properties of the person: motives, interests, expectations and attitudes. Table 5.1 sets them out. Table 5.1 The determinants of attention. Determinant What it means Everyday example Intensity Stronger stimuli capture attention more than weaker ones A loud horn; a bright floodlight Size Larger stimuli are noticed before smaller ones A full-page newspaper advertisement Contrast A stimulus that differs from its background stands out One person in white at a wedding of bright silks Change A sudden change, including sudden silence, is noticed The fan stopping during a power cut Movement Moving stimuli capture attention over still ones Blinking and scrolling shop signs Novelty New or unusual stimuli attract attention A camel walking down a Bengaluru road Repetition A repeated stimulus is more likely to be noticed (up to a point) A jingle repeated in every IPL break Motives Needs direct attention toward what satisfies them A hungry person notices every food stall Interests We attend to what we care about A cricket fan spots a score from across a room Mental set Readiness to perceive a particular stimulus A runner waiting for the starter's gun Attitudes and emotions Beliefs and feelings bias what we notice An anxious student notices every frown Two of these deserve a further word. Mental set is a temporary readiness to perceive or respond in a particular way, created by instructions, expectation or recent experience. A student waiting for exam results online sees her roll number leap out of a long list because she is set for it. Repetition, meanwhile, cuts both ways. A stimulus repeated a few times gains attention, but a stimulus repeated endlessly without change loses it, because the nervous system habituates to it. This is why advertisers keep changing the details of a campaign while keeping the brand the same, and why external and internal determinants usually work together: the size and colour of the hoarding get your eyes there, and your hunger or interest decides whether you stay. Exam trap Learn which list each determinant belongs to. Intensity, size, contrast, change, movement, novelty, repetition, colour and position are external (objective). Motives, interests, mental set, attitudes, emotions and habit are internal (subjective). "Fluctuation" and "span" are not determinants at all; they are characteristics of attention. Also keep shifting (attention moves to a different object) apart from fluctuation (attention to the same object waxes and wanes). 5.2 Selective listening: filters, attenuators and late selection Medium yield · 5 Qs The chai stall showed you a puzzle. You can follow your friend's voice through a wall of noise, and yet your name, spoken by a stranger, still gets through. How can the mind be ignoring the other voices and also listening to them? This puzzle drove the first great theoretical debate of cognitive psychology, and it was fought with headphones. The cocktail party problem and dichotic listening The British engineer Colin Cherry (1914 to 1979), working on problems of communication, named the puzzle in 1953. He called it the cocktail party problem : how do we manage to follow one conversation when many people are talking at once? The everyday experience of hearing your own name across a crowded room, even though you were not listening to that conversation, is called the cocktail party phenomenon (or cocktail party effect). Key study: Cherry's shadowing experiments (1953) Cherry invented the method that dominated attention research for twenty years. In dichotic listening , a person wears headphones and a different message is played to each ear. To make sure they really attend to one ear, they must repeat the attended message aloud, word for word, as it arrives, a technique called shadowing . Afterwards they are asked what they noticed in the other, unattended ear. The results were striking. People could report almost nothing about the content of the unattended message. They did not notice when it switched from English to German, or when the speech was played backwards. But they almost always noticed physical changes: a switch from a male to a female voice, or a pure tone in place of speech. Cherry concluded that the unattended message is processed only for its physical features, not for meaning. A few years later the British psychologist Neville Moray added two findings that pulled in opposite directions. First, in 1959 he showed that a short list of words repeated 35 times in the unattended ear left no trace in memory: people did not recognise the words afterwards. That supported Cherry. Second, about a third of his participants noticed when an instruction in the unattended ear was preceded by their own name. Your name, it seems, can break through a channel you are not listening to. This is the laboratory version of the cocktail party phenomenon, and any theory of attention has to explain both halves of Moray's result. Broadbent's filter model (1958): early selection The first theory came from Donald Eric Broadbent (1926 to 1993), a British psychologist who had served in the Royal Air Force and studied the problems of pilots and air traffic controllers swamped with radio messages. In his book Perception and Communication (1958) he proposed the filter model of attention. This was the first major theory to treat the mind explicitly as an information-processing system, a sequence of stages through which information flows, like messages through a telephone exchange, and it is often described as the starting point of the information-processing approach in cognitive psychology. Broadbent's model has three parts (see the top row of Figure 5.1). All incoming messages first enter a sensory buffer , a brief store that holds them for a second or two. Next comes a selective filter , which lets through only one message, chosen on the basis of a physical characteristic such as which ear it arrives at, the pitch of the voice or its loudness. Everything else is blocked. Finally, the selected message passes into a limited-capacity channel where it is analysed for meaning and can enter awareness and memory. Because the filter works on physical features before any analysis of meaning, Broadbent's is the classic early selection model, and because the filter passes one channel and blocks the other completely, like a railway switch, it is sometimes called an all-or-none or "switch" model. The filter is also the first bottleneck in attention theory: a narrow point in the system through which only a little information can pass at once. Broadbent supported his model with the split-span experiment (1954). Three pairs of digits were played simultaneously, one digit of each pair to each ear (for example 7 to the left ear and 2 to the right, then 4 and 9, then 3 and 6). People found it much easier to recall the digits ear by ear (743, then 296) than pair by pair (72, 49, 36). Broadbent's explanation was that the filter is set to one ear at a time; recalling by ear means switching the filter only once, while recalling by pairs means switching it back and forth. The model fitted Cherry's findings well, but it could not survive long. If the unattended message is blocked before meaning is analysed, how could Moray's participants hear their own names? And there was more trouble. Jeffrey Gray and A. A. I. Wedderburn (1960) played "Dear 7 Jane" to one ear and "9 Aunt 6" to the other; people reported "Dear Aunt Jane", grouping by meaning across the ears, not by ear as the filter predicts. Anne Marie Treisman (1935 to 2018) found in 1960 that when the story being shadowed suddenly switched to the other ear, people often followed the story into the "wrong" ear for a word or two before catching themselves: meaning in the unattended ear was guiding them. And in 1972 Robert Corteen and B. Wood conditioned people to expect a mild electric shock when they heard certain city names; later, when those names (and even other city names never paired with shock) were played in the unattended ear, the participants showed a galvanic skin response, although they could not report hearing the words. Something in the unattended channel was being analysed for meaning. Broadbent (1958): early selection Two messages Sensory buffer Filter (all-or-none) Meaning analysis Response Unattended message is blocked at the filter, before its meaning is analysed Treisman (1964): attenuation Two messages Sensory buffer Attenuator (turns down) Dictionary units Response Unattended message passes weakly; low-threshold words (your name) still fire Deutsch and Deutsch (1963): late selection Two messages Sensory buffer Full analysis of both Selection (late) Response Both messages are analysed for meaning; selection happens just before response Figure 5.1 Three answers to "where is the bottleneck?". Broadbent places a complete block early, Treisman turns the unattended message down instead of off, and Deutsch and Deutsch let everything be analysed for meaning and select only at the response. Treisman's attenuation model (1964) Treisman's answer, set out fully in 1964, kept Broadbent's idea of an early stage that works on physical features but changed what that stage does. In her attenuation model , the filter is not a switch but a volume control, an attenuator . The attended message passes at full strength; unattended messages are not blocked but turned down, so that a weakened version still travels on to the next stage (middle row of Figure 5.1). The next stage is a mental dictionary of dictionary units , one for each word you know, and each unit has its own threshold , the amount of activation it needs before it fires and the word reaches awareness. Thresholds are not equal. Words that are personally important (your own name, "fire", "help") have permanently low thresholds, so even an attenuated signal is enough to fire them. Words that are made probable by the context of the attended message have their thresholds temporarily lowered too, which is why Treisman's participants followed the story into the wrong ear: the next word of the story was expected, so its unit fired even from the weakened channel. Treisman also proposed that analysis runs through a hierarchy, from physical cues to syllable patterns to individual words to grammar and meaning, and that when capacity runs short, the later stages of analysis are simply not carried out for the unattended message. The attenuation model explains everything that troubled Broadbent: Moray's own-name effect, Gray and Wedderburn's grouping by meaning, Corteen and Wood's skin responses and Treisman's own ear-switching. That is why it is the standard answer when a question asks which model best explains the cocktail party phenomenon. It is also why Treisman's theory is called a filter-attenuation theory: it is a modified filter theory, still early selection in spirit, but leaky. Exam trap "Filter-attenuation theory" is Treisman , not Broadbent (pure filter), Johnston or Heinz (multimode theory). The attenuation model is dated 1964 (her ear-switching experiment was 1960). Some Indian notes give 1980 for the attenuation model; 1980 is the year of a different Treisman theory, feature integration theory (Treisman and Gelade), taught in Section 5.3. If a question asks which model "better explains the cocktail party effect", the answer is the attenuator model; Broadbent's switch model cannot explain why your name gets through. Late selection: Deutsch and Deutsch (1963) and Norman (1968) At the opposite extreme, J. Anthony Deutsch and Diana Deutsch argued in 1963 that there is no early filter at all. In their late selection model, every incoming message is fully analysed, including for meaning, automatically and without capacity limits. The bottleneck comes only at the end, when the system must decide which analysed message to respond to, remember or become aware of (bottom row of Figure 5.1). Selection is based on importance : the most pertinent message wins the response. On this view you do understand the cricket argument at the next table; you simply do not respond to it, and you will not remember it, unless it becomes more important than your friend's voice. Donald Arthur Norman (born 1935) refined the late-selection view in 1968. He proposed that what gets selected depends on two things added together: the strength of the sensory input (how loud and clear it is) and its pertinence (how relevant it is to current goals and expectations). A faint word that is highly pertinent can beat a loud word that is irrelevant. Norman's idea gives a late-selection account of the own-name effect: your name is so pertinent that it is selected even though the voice saying it is faint. So which is right, early or late? The evidence pointed both ways. Treisman and Riley (1969) found that people detected target words far more often in the shadowed message than in the unattended one, which is awkward for a theory in which both are fully analysed. Yet the skin-response and own-name findings show some analysis of meaning in the unattended channel. The debate was eventually resolved not by declaring a winner but by asking a better question: when does selection happen early, and when late? Flexible selection: Johnston and Heinz (1978) and Lavie's perceptual load theory William A. Johnston and Steven P. Heinz proposed in 1978 that the bottleneck has no fixed position. In their multimode theory (flexible multimode model), selection can occur at any of three stages: at the stage of sensory representation (early, on physical features), at the stage of semantic representation (late, on meaning), or after both have been built and are entering consciousness. The listener chooses the mode, but there is a price: the later the selection, the more mental effort and capacity it consumes. Johnston and Heinz showed that when two messages differed physically (one male voice, one female), people selected early and had capacity left for a secondary task; when the messages could be told apart only by meaning, selection had to be late and secondary-task performance suffered. Attention is, in their phrase, flexible but costly. The most influential modern resolution is the perceptual load theory of Nilli Lavie , developed in the mid-1990s (with Yehoshua Tsal in 1994, and in her own paper of 1995). Lavie argued that perception has limited capacity and that it runs automatically until that capacity is full. When the main task carries a high perceptual load (many items, hard discriminations), it uses up all the capacity, so nothing is left over for distractors and they are not processed at all: selection looks early. When the main task is easy ( low perceptual load ), spare capacity spills over automatically onto the distractors, which are then processed and can interfere: selection looks late. The early-late debate, on this view, was a debate about task difficulty. A practical prediction follows: if you want to stop being distracted, a harder, more absorbing task helps more than willpower does. (Lavie added that a high load on working memory, a cognitive load, has the opposite effect and makes distraction worse, because it weakens the control needed to ignore distractors.) Table 5.2 sets the six theories of selective listening side by side. Table 5.2 Theories of selective auditory attention. Theory Theorist and year Where selection happens What happens to the unattended message Filter (switch) model Broadbent, 1958 Early, on physical features Blocked completely; meaning never analysed Attenuation model Treisman, 1964 Early but leaky Weakened; important or expected words still reach awareness Late selection Deutsch and Deutsch, 1963 Late, at the response Fully analysed for meaning, then not responded to Pertinence model Norman, 1968 Late Selected if sensory strength plus pertinence is high enough Multimode theory Johnston and Heinz, 1978 Flexible: early, late or after both Depends on the mode chosen; late selection costs more effort Perceptual load theory Lavie, 1994 to 1995 Depends on load Ignored under high load; processed under low load Exam trap Three dating traps cluster here. Deutsch and Deutsch's late selection ( 1963 ) came before Treisman's full attenuation model ( 1964 ), although textbooks usually teach Treisman first. Broadbent ( 1958 ) is the answer to "the first major theoretical effort in information-processing psychology". And "bottleneck" in an attention question refers to the narrow stage in processing; it is not a name for the cocktail party phenomenon (the "bottleneck effect" in biology is something else entirely, a sharp fall in a population's genetic variety). 5.3 Visual attention: spotlights, binding and blindness to the obvious Lower yield · 1 Q The early debate was conducted with the ears, but vision is our dominant sense, and from the 1970s most attention research moved to the eyes. The questions changed shape. What is visual attention like : a beam that sweeps across the scene, or something more flexible? What is it for , beyond picking one thing out? And how much of the visual world do we actually see when we are not attending to it? The answer to the last question turned out to be: far less than you think. The spotlight and the zoom lens You can attend to something without looking straight at it. Fix your eyes on this word, and without moving them, notice the margin of the page. Moving attention with the eyes is overt attention ; moving attention while the eyes stay still is covert attention . Michael I. Posner (born 1936), whose experiments are described below, likened covert attention to a spotlight : a beam of limited width that illuminates one region of space, so that whatever falls inside it is processed faster and better, and that can be moved from place to place independently of the eyes. William James had anticipated the idea in 1890 when he described consciousness as having a bright focus , surrounded by a dimmer margin or fringe . A real spotlight has a fixed beam. Charles Eriksen and James St James argued in 1986 that visual attention is more like a zoom lens : you can widen the attended area to take in a whole scene or narrow it to a single letter, but there is a trade-off. The wider the area, the lower the resolution; the same amount of processing power is spread more thinly. A batsman watching the bowler's hand narrows his zoom lens to a tiny patch of space; a fielder at deep midwicket keeps it wide to watch the whole ground. Later work found that under some conditions attention can even be split between two separate locations, like two spotlights, so both metaphors are best treated as approximations of a flexible system. Posner's cueing task: endogenous and exogenous attention Key study: Posner's spatial cueing paradigm (1980) Posner asked people to keep their eyes on a central point and press a key as soon as a light appeared in a box to the left or right. Before the light, a cue appeared. Sometimes it was a central cue, an arrow at fixation pointing left or right; sometimes it was a peripheral cue, a brief brightening of one of the boxes. Most cues were valid (the target appeared where the cue indicated), some were invalid (the target appeared on the other side) and on some trials a neutral cue gave no information. Responses were fastest after valid cues, slowest after invalid cues and in between after neutral cues. Because the eyes never moved, the benefit and the cost could only mean that attention itself had moved, covertly, to the cued location. The two kinds of cue revealed two systems. An arrow at fixation must be interpreted and used deliberately; this is endogenous attention (also called voluntary, goal-directed or top-down attention), controlled by the person's intentions. It takes a few hundred milliseconds to deploy and, crucially, people ignore central arrows if they learn the arrows are usually wrong. A flash in the periphery grabs attention whether you want it to or not; this is exogenous attention (reflexive, stimulus-driven or bottom-up), and it is fast and automatic, pulling attention even when the flash predicts nothing. You use endogenous attention when you search a crowded railway platform for your friend's red bag; exogenous attention takes over when a pigeon suddenly flaps up beside you. Later imaging work by Maurizio Corbetta and Gordon Shulman (2002) mapped these onto a dorsal fronto-parietal network for goal-directed attention and a right-hemisphere ventral network that acts as a "circuit breaker", redirecting attention to unexpected events. Posner himself, with Steven Petersen in 1990, went on to describe three attention networks: alerting (getting ready), orienting (moving attention to a location) and executive control (resolving conflict). The peripheral flash has one more surprise. If the target appears very soon after an uninformative flash (within about a quarter of a second), responses at the flashed location are faster. If it appears later than about 300 milliseconds, responses at that location become slower than elsewhere. Attention, having been pulled to the spot and found nothing, is now biased against going back. Posner and Yoav Cohen described this inhibition of return in 1984. Its likely function is to make visual search efficient: once you have checked a location, you are discouraged from wasting time checking it again, rather like a person searching a house who does not reopen a cupboard she has just looked in. Feature integration theory (Treisman and Gelade, 1980) Look at a ripe red tomato. Its redness is analysed by colour-sensitive neurons, its roundness by shape-sensitive neurons, its position by yet other circuits, in different parts of the visual brain. Yet you see one red, round object in one place, not a floating redness next to a floating roundness. How are the separate features put back together? This is the binding problem , and Anne Treisman's second great theory, developed with Garry Gelade in 1980, proposed that attention is the solution. Feature integration theory divides visual processing into two stages. In the first, preattentive stage , simple features (colour, orientation, size, curvature, motion) are registered automatically, in parallel, across the whole visual field, each in its own feature map. No attention is needed and no effort is felt. In the second, focused attention stage , attention is directed to one location at a time and acts as a kind of glue: it combines the features found at that location into a single object. Because the glue can be applied to only one location at a time, this stage is serial. The theory makes a clear prediction about visual search, tested by Treisman and Gelade. Suppose you must find a target among distractors. In feature search the target differs from every distractor by a single feature: a red letter among green letters, a vertical line among horizontals. The target is found at the preattentive stage and seems to leap out of the display, a phenomenon called pop-out , and search time hardly changes whether there are 5 distractors or 30. In conjunction search the target is defined only by a combination of features, say a green T among green X's and brown T's. No single feature map can find it; attention must visit items one by one, binding features at each, so search time rises in a straight line with the number of items. Figure 5.2 shows the pattern. Treisman and Gelade also found that when the target was absent, the conjunction slope was about twice as steep as when it was present, exactly what a serial, self-terminating search predicts: on average you find a present target halfway through, but you must check every item to be sure it is absent. 400 800 1200 1 5 15 30 Number of items in the display Search time (ms) Conjunction search (serial: about 29 ms per item) Feature search (parallel pop-out: nearly flat) Figure 5.2 Feature versus conjunction search (target-present trials, approximate values in the pattern reported by Treisman and Gelade, 1980). A target defined by one feature pops out, so search time stays almost flat as the display grows; a target defined by a conjunction of features needs serial attention to each item, so search time climbs steadily. If attention is the glue, then features that are not attended should sometimes be glued wrongly. They are. Treisman and Hilary Schmidt (1982) flashed displays of coloured letters very briefly while people's attention was occupied by a second task. Participants often reported seeing, with confidence, combinations that were not there, such as a red X when the display contained a red T and a green X. These illusory conjunctions are strong evidence that features are registered separately and combined only with attention. Patients with damage to both parietal lobes (Balint's syndrome), who have severe difficulty directing spatial attention, produce illusory conjunctions even with long, leisurely displays. Later research qualified the theory (Jeremy Wolfe's guided search model showed that feature information can guide the serial stage, so many conjunction searches are faster than pure serial search), but the distinction between parallel feature detection and attention-dependent binding remains one of the most important ideas in the field. Exam trap Anne Treisman gave us two theories: the attenuation model of auditory selection (1964) and feature integration theory of visual binding (1980, with Gelade). Questions mixing them up are common. In feature integration theory, the preattentive stage is automatic and parallel (features), the focused attention stage is serial and binds features into objects; pop-out belongs to feature search, linear search slopes to conjunction search, and illusory conjunctions are the error that occurs when attention is unavailable. Blind to the obvious: inattentional blindness and change blindness Most people believe that they see everything in front of their eyes and that anything unusual would immediately catch their attention. Two families of experiments show that this belief is false. Key study: the invisible gorilla (Simons and Chabris, 1999) Daniel J. Simons and Christopher F. Chabris , then at Harvard University, filmed two teams of students, one in white shirts and one in black, passing basketballs among themselves. Viewers were asked to count the passes made by the white team, a task that demands close attention. Partway through the clip a woman in a full gorilla suit walks into the middle of the players, turns to the camera, thumps her chest and walks off; she is in full view for several seconds. Around half of the viewers did not see her at all, and many refused to believe she had been there until the clip was replayed. When viewers counted the black team's passes instead, far more of them (83 per cent) noticed the black gorilla, because her colour now matched what they were attending to. The gorilla study is the best-known demonstration of inattentional blindness : the failure to notice a fully visible but unexpected object or event because attention is engaged elsewhere. The term was introduced by Arien Mack and Irvin Rock , whose 1998 book reported that many people failed to see an unexpected shape flashed near the point they were fixating while they judged which arm of a cross was longer. The lesson is that seeing is not just a matter of light reaching the retina; without attention, an object may never reach awareness at all. Change blindness is a related but different failure: the failure to notice that something in a scene has changed , even a large change, when the change happens during a brief interruption such as an eye movement, a blink, a cut in a film or a flicker. Ronald Rensink, Kevin O'Regan and James Clark (1997) showed that people can stare for many seconds at two alternating photographs, separated by a brief blank, without spotting that a large object (a jet engine on an aeroplane, for example) appears in one and not the other; this is the flicker paradigm . In a famous field version by Simons and Daniel Levin (1998), an experimenter stopped pedestrians on a university campus to ask for directions; while they talked, two workmen carried a door between them, and behind the door the experimenter was replaced by a different person in different clothes. About half the pedestrians carried on giving directions to the new person without noticing the switch. Continuity errors in films, which audiences almost never spot, are everyday change blindness. Keep the two apart. In inattentional blindness, an unexpected object is present and is not seen at all. In change blindness, the person may well see both versions of the scene but fails to notice the difference between them, because noticing a change requires attending to the changed item and comparing it across time. Neither should be confused with perceptual constancy , the tendency to see objects as having stable size, shape and colour although their image on the retina changes (taught in Chapter 4); constancy is a success of perception, not a failure of attention. Exam trap "Failing to notice significant changes in the environment, even obvious ones" is change blindness (Rensink and colleagues; the Simons and Levin door study). Failing to see an unexpected object that is in plain view while busy with another task is inattentional blindness (Mack and Rock; the gorilla). If the question stresses change , choose change blindness; if it stresses an unexpected object , choose inattentional blindness. The attentional blink Attention is limited not only in space but in time. In 1992 Jane Raymond, Kimron Shapiro and Karen Arnell used rapid serial visual presentation : letters flashed one after another in the same place at about ten per second. Participants had to identify a first target (say, a white letter among black ones) and then report whether a second target (say, the letter X) appeared later in the stream. If the second target came within roughly 200 to 500 milliseconds after the first, it was very often missed; before and after that window it was seen well. This brief "blindness" after a target is called the attentional blink . The usual explanation is that attention is still busy consolidating the first target into memory when the second arrives, so the second decays before it can be processed. (Curiously, a second target that comes immediately after the first, with no item between, is often spared, apparently because it slips into the same attentional episode.) Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. The number of objects that can be apprehended in a single brief glance is the of attention. Jevons estimated handfuls of thrown into a box and published his results in 1871. Intensity, contrast and movement are determinants of attention; motives and mental set are internal determinants. In dichotic listening, repeating the attended message aloud is called . Broadbent's 1958 model, in which unattended messages are blocked on the basis of physical features, is an selection model. In Treisman's model, unattended messages are weakened by an rather than blocked. Deutsch and Deutsch (1963) argued that all messages are analysed for meaning and selection occurs . Responses slowed at a recently cued location after about 300 milliseconds show of return. In feature integration theory, a target that differs by a single feature shows and is found in parallel. Failing to see a gorilla while counting basketball passes is an example of blindness. Answers: (1) span, (2) beans, (3) external, (4) shadowing, (5) early, (6) attenuator, (7) late (at the response stage), (8) inhibition, (9) pop-out, (10) inattentional. 5.4 Divided attention, automaticity, the Stroop effect and vigilance High yield · 10 Qs Selective attention asks how we keep one thing in and other things out. Divided attention asks the reverse question: how far can we do two things at once? You can walk and talk, and an experienced driver can drive and hold a conversation. But a learner driver cannot, and nobody can hold two conversations at the same time. Why do some pairs of tasks combine easily and others not at all? Three answers have been proposed: that we have one limited pool of capacity, that we have several pools, and that practice makes some processes stop needing capacity at all. Kahneman's capacity model (1973) In his book Attention and Effort (1973), Daniel Kahneman (1934 to 2024), later a Nobel laureate in economics, replaced the bottleneck with a different picture. Attention, he proposed, is a single, limited pool of mental effort, or capacity , that can be shared out among activities. This is the capacity model (also called resource or central capacity theory). Two tasks can be performed together as long as their combined demand does not exceed the capacity available; when it does, performance on one or both suffers. The amount of capacity is not fixed: it rises and falls with arousal, so that a drowsy person has less to share out and a moderately alert one has more. How the capacity is divided depends on an allocation policy , which is shaped by four influences: enduring dispositions (built-in tendencies to attend to novel or moving stimuli, or to one's own name), momentary intentions (what you are trying to do right now), the evaluation of demands (the system's judgement of how much each task needs) and the current level of arousal. Kahneman measured effort through the size of the pupil, which widens as a mental task becomes harder. The capacity model explained why difficult tasks interfere more than easy ones, and why practice, which makes tasks easier, makes them easier to combine. But it had a weakness: it predicts that two equally difficult tasks should interfere equally with a third, and they do not. What matters is how similar they are. Multiple resource theory and dual-task interference The study of what happens when people perform two tasks together is called the dual-task paradigm , and its main finding is that interference depends heavily on similarity. In a striking demonstration, Alan Allport, Barbara Antonis and Patricia Reynolds (1972) found that skilled pianists could sight-read music while shadowing speech with little loss on either task, although shadowing two spoken messages would have been impossible. Christopher Wickens captured this in his multiple resource theory (1984, refined in later work). Instead of a single pool, Wickens proposed several separate pools of resources, defined along a few dimensions: the stage of processing (perceptual and cognitive processing versus responding), the modality of input (visual versus auditory), the code of processing (spatial versus verbal) and, within vision, focal versus peripheral (ambient) vision. Two tasks that draw on different pools can be time-shared well; two tasks that compete for the same pool interfere. Driving (visual, spatial, manual) combines reasonably well with listening to the radio (auditory, verbal), and badly with reading a text message (visual, verbal, manual). Practice also changes what can be combined. In a famous study, Elizabeth Spelke, William Hirst and Ulric Neisser (1976) trained two students for several months to read short stories while writing down words dictated to them. At first their reading speed and comprehension collapsed; after weeks of practice they read as fast and understood as well as when reading alone, while writing to dictation. Practice had apparently turned one of the tasks into something that no longer needed much capacity. Multitasking and the phone in the car What people call multitasking is, for most tasks, rapid switching between them. Every switch has a switch cost : responses are slower and more error-prone just after a switch than when the same task is repeated, as Robert Rogers and Stephen Monsell showed in 1995. The real-world consequences are serious. David Strayer and William Johnston (2001) had people perform a simulated driving task while talking on a mobile phone; they missed nearly twice as many red lights and braked more slowly than when driving alone, and a hands-free phone was no better than a hand-held one. Listening to the radio or a recorded book did not have this effect. The problem is the conversation, not the hands. Later work by Strayer's group found that drivers talking on phones were impaired about as much as drivers at the legal limit for alcohol, and that they looked straight at roadside objects and then failed to remember them: inattentional blindness at the wheel. A two-wheeler rider in Bengaluru with a phone wedged inside his helmet is not doing two things well; he is doing two things badly. Automatic versus controlled processing Spelke's students point to the third answer. Some mental processes demand attention and effort; others run off by themselves. In 1975 Michael Posner and Charles Snyder proposed three criteria for an automatic process : it occurs without intention, it occurs without conscious awareness, and it does not interfere with other ongoing mental activity. Two years later Richard M. Shiffrin and Walter Schneider (1977) made the distinction the basis of a major theory. Controlled processes are slow, serial, effortful, limited by capacity, open to awareness and flexible: you can change them at once when the situation changes. Automatic processes are fast, run in parallel, need little or no capacity, are hard to stop once triggered and are inflexible. Table 5.3 lists the contrasts. Key study: Shiffrin and Schneider's search experiments (1977) Participants memorised a set of up to four characters and then searched rapidly presented displays for any of them. In the consistent mapping condition, targets and distractors never swapped roles (for example, targets were always consonants and distractors always digits). In the varied mapping condition, the same characters served as targets on some trials and distractors on others. With consistent mapping, search speed hardly depended on how many items had to be compared: search had become automatic and parallel. With varied mapping, every extra item added time: search was controlled and serial. When participants were trained for 2,100 trials with one set of letters as targets and another as distractors, search became automatic; when the roles were then reversed, it took nearly 1,000 trials before performance recovered even to its starting level. Automatic processes, once learned, are fast but stubborn. Table 5.3 Automatic versus controlled processing (Posner and Snyder, 1975; Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977). Feature Automatic processing Controlled processing Effort and capacity Little or none Effortful; limited by capacity Speed and organisation Fast, parallel Slow, serial Intention Triggered without intention; hard to stop Deliberate; can be started and stopped Awareness Usually outside awareness Conscious Flexibility Rigid; hard to modify once learned Flexible; adapts to new situations How acquired Extensive consistent practice Needed for novel or variable tasks Examples Reading a word, an expert's gear change A learner driver, solving a new problem The distinction reaches well beyond the laboratory. Patricia Devine (1989) applied it to prejudice: because cultural stereotypes are learned by everyone in a society, they are activated automatically in high- and low-prejudiced people alike when a member of the group is encountered; what distinguishes low-prejudiced people is that they use controlled processing to override the activated stereotype and replace it with their own egalitarian beliefs. (The social psychology of prejudice is taught in the Social Psychology book.) And the stubbornness of automatic processes produces the most famous interference effect in psychology. The Stroop effect (1935) Key study: Stroop's colour-word experiments (1935) John Ridley Stroop (1897 to 1973), an American psychologist, published "Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions" in 1935, based on his doctoral research at George Peabody College. In one experiment, people simply read aloud colour words printed in conflicting ink colours (the word RED printed in green ink) and were barely slower than when reading the same words printed in black. In another, they had to name the ink colour of such words, saying "green" to RED printed in green, and here performance collapsed: naming the ink colours of 100 conflicting words took about 74 per cent longer than naming the colours of plain coloured patches, and errors rose. A third experiment showed that days of practice reduced the interference but did not abolish it. Stroop himself soon left experimental work to teach the Bible, never knowing that his dissertation would become one of the most cited studies in psychology. The Stroop effect is the slowing of colour naming (and the rise in errors) when the word and the ink colour conflict. Notice its asymmetry. Words interfere strongly with naming colours, but colours hardly interfere with reading words. Why? The most widely accepted explanation is in terms of automaticity. For a literate adult, reading is so overlearned that it is automatic: you cannot look at a familiar word and not read it. Naming an ink colour, by contrast, is a controlled process that needs attention. When the two conflict, the automatically produced word ("red") competes with the deliberately produced colour name ("green") at the stage of choosing a response, and resolving that conflict takes time. A related account, the relative speed of processing explanation, says that words are simply processed faster than colours, so the word's name arrives at the response stage first and must be suppressed. Later connectionist models (Jonathan Cohen, Kevin Dunbar and James McClelland, 1990) recast both ideas in terms of the strength of the pathways involved: the word-reading pathway, trained by years of practice, is stronger. What, then, does the Stroop effect demonstrate? Above all, a limit on selective attention : we cannot completely filter out a stimulus dimension whose processing is automatic, even when we are told to ignore it and it hurts our performance to attend to it. Within a single stimulus, one attribute (the word) dominates the other (the ink colour) in controlling the response. It is also a measure of interference in reaction time due to conflicting information, and of the ability to inhibit a dominant response, which is why the Stroop task is one of the standard tests of the inhibition component of executive function and why it is used clinically to assess frontal lobe and attention problems. The emotional Stroop task applies the same logic: people name the ink colour of emotional and neutral words, and anxious individuals are slower with words related to their worries (a person with a spider phobia slows down on "web" and "hairy"), revealing an attentional bias toward threat. Exam trap The Stroop effect is an attention phenomenon: specifically, a failure of selective attention caused by interference from automatic word reading. It is not primarily about long-term memory retrieval, working memory, procedural memory, perception or language development, which are the usual distractors, and it does not show improved recall for related items or better accuracy under divided attention. One past paper (RML 2024) asks what the Stroop effect is "an account of" and keys stimulus dominance : one dimension of the stimulus (the printed word) dominates the other (its ink colour). "Semantic dominance" is the tempting wrong option because the intruding word is meaningful, but the keyed term describes one attribute of the stimulus overpowering another; "instructional" and "conceptual" dominance are not terms used for this effect. Vigilance and sustained attention Some jobs require attention not to many things at once but to one thing for a very long time, while waiting for something rare to happen. Air traffic controllers watching radar screens, radar operators, airport baggage screeners, lifeguards and nurses monitoring intensive-care displays all depend on sustained attention , the ability to keep attention on a task over a prolonged period; when the events to be detected are infrequent and unpredictable, it is usually called vigilance . Key study: the Mackworth clock (1948) During the Second World War, the Royal Air Force noticed that radar operators hunting for enemy submarines missed more signals as their watches went on. Norman Mackworth built a laboratory model of the problem. A pointer moved around a blank clock face in small regular jumps; occasionally, and unpredictably, it made a double jump, and the observer had to press a key whenever this happened. Over a two-hour watch, detection fell sharply, with the largest drop within the first half hour; a short break or a telephone message restored it. Mackworth had demonstrated the vigilance decrement : the decline in detection over time on a monotonous monitoring task. Two kinds of explanation have been offered for the decrement. One is that boring, understimulating tasks lower arousal, so the observer becomes less alert. The other, now more favoured, is that vigilance is hard mental work that steadily depletes attentional resources; people rate vigilance tasks as surprisingly effortful and stressful. Signal detection analysis (Chapter 3) adds that part of the decrement is a shift in criterion: tired observers become more cautious about saying "yes, there it is". Clinically, sustained attention is measured with the Continuous Performance Test (respond to a rare target letter in a long stream), and it is one of the first functions to suffer from sleep loss, as you will see in Section 5.8. Brain recordings provide another window: when a rare target appears among frequent non-targets (the oddball task), the brain produces a positive event-related potential about 300 milliseconds later, the P300, which indexes the allocation of attention to the target and is reduced in conditions such as schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. Exam trap Air traffic controllers and radar readers are the textbook example of sustained attention (vigilance) , not selective attention (choosing one input among several), divided attention (two tasks at once) or "perceptual attention" (not a standard category).
