The baby in the old film is calm, almost stolid. In the published report he is simply "Albert B.", the son of a wet nurse at the Harriet Lane Home for Invalid Children, a hospital attached to Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. When Albert was about nine months old, two psychologists, John B. Watson and his graduate student Rosalie Rayner, brought him a parade of things to look at: a white rat, a rabbit, a dog, a monkey, masks with and without hair, cotton wool, even a burning newspaper. Albert reached for some of them and stared at others. He was afraid of none of them. Only one thing reliably upset him. When a long steel bar was struck sharply with a hammer just behind his head, Albert startled violently; at the second blow his lips puckered and trembled; at the third he broke into a sudden fit of crying. Watson and Rayner had found what they were looking for: a stimulus that produced fear without any learning at all. When Albert was eleven months old the experiment proper began. The white rat was taken from its basket and offered to him, and just as his hand touched it the bar was struck behind his head. Albert jumped violently and fell forward, burying his face in the mattress. The pairing was repeated once more that day, and he began to whimper. A week later the rat and the noise were paired five more times, seven pairings in all. Then the rat was shown alone, in silence. The instant he saw it, Albert began to cry, toppled over, raised himself on all fours and crawled away so fast that he was caught only just before he reached the edge of the table. Five days later he was tested again. Now he whimpered and withdrew from things that had never been paired with the noise: a rabbit, a dog, a sealskin coat, cotton wool, a Santa Claus mask. His wooden blocks, offered between the tests, he played with happily. Soon afterwards Albert left the hospital, and the fears that had been built into him were never removed. A healthy, placid baby had been taught to be afraid, and the fear had spread well beyond the animal that started it. How could this happen in a week? Why did the fear spread to the rabbit and the fur coat but not to the blocks? Could the same process be run backwards to cure a fear? Keep Albert in mind. These questions run through the whole chapter, and we will return to him at the end. 6.1 What Learning Is, and What It Is Not Medium yield · 6 Qs Almost everything that makes you a particular person rather than a generic human being was learned: your language, your taste in chai, your fear of a certain teacher, your skill at a cricket cover drive, the way your stomach tightens when you walk into an exam hall. Psychologists have studied learning more intensively than almost any other topic, and for the first half of the twentieth century the study of learning very nearly was experimental psychology. Before we look at how learning happens, we need to be precise about what it is. A working definition The definition most textbooks use descends from Gregory Kimble , who in 1961 revised a classic text on conditioning. In modern form: learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour, or in the potential for behaviour, that results from experience. Each phrase does work. Relatively permanent excludes passing states. If you perform badly because you are sleepy, nothing has been learned; when you wake up, the change is gone. "Relatively" is there because learned things can be forgotten or extinguished; learning is durable, not eternal. Behaviour or the potential for behaviour acknowledges that learning can be silent. You may learn the route to a new friend's house in Kuvempunagar while riding pillion and show no sign of it until the day you have to drive there yourself. Results from experience excludes changes caused by growth, injury, drugs or disease. Kimble's own wording said "reinforced practice"; later writers dropped the word "reinforced" because, as you will see in Sections 6.7 and 6.8, a great deal is learned without any reward at all. The second point leads to one of the most important distinctions in this chapter. Performance is what an organism actually does on a given occasion; learning is the change in knowledge or capacity that we infer from performance. The two can come apart. A student who knows the answer but freezes in the exam has learned but not performed. As you will see, Edward Tolman's rats (Section 6.7) and Albert Bandura's children (Section 6.8) both showed that learning can occur without being displayed until there is a reason to display it. Changes that are not learning Several kinds of behavioural change look like learning but are not, and examiners like to use them as distractors. Maturation is change that unfolds according to a biological timetable, largely independent of specific experience. A baby does not learn to walk in the way she learns to ride a bicycle; she walks when her muscles, bones and nervous system are ready, and practice before that point achieves little. Fatigue, illness, injury and drugs also change behaviour, but temporarily or without experience being the cause. So do motivational states: a hungry rat runs faster than a satiated one, but it has not learned anything new. Finally, much behaviour is innate. Ethologists, biologists who study animal behaviour in natural settings, describe the fixed action pattern : an unlearned, stereotyped sequence of behaviour that is the same in every member of a species and, once triggered, runs to completion. The trigger is a sign stimulus (also called a releaser), a simple feature of the environment to which the animal is tuned from birth. Nikolaas (Niko) Tinbergen (1907 to 1988) found that a male three-spined stickleback in breeding season attacks crude models of fish as long as they have a red underside, the sign stimulus of a rival male, while ignoring a realistic model with no red. A greylag goose that sees an egg outside its nest stretches out and rolls it back with its bill; if the egg is removed halfway, the goose completes the rolling movement anyway. Fixed action patterns are instinctive; they are the result of evolution, not of the individual's experience. Exam trap "Fixed action patterns result from ..." The answer is innate (unlearned) behaviour, not classical or operant conditioning. Also watch the word "permanent": learning is relatively permanent. And do not confuse habituation (below) with sensory adaptation , the reduced firing of receptors under constant stimulation (Chapter 3). Adaptation happens in the sense organ and is not reversed by an unrelated stimulus; habituation happens in the nervous system and is. The simplest learning: habituation and sensitisation The simplest forms of learning involve only one stimulus. Because nothing is being associated with anything else, they are called non-associative learning . There are two. Habituation is a decrease in response to a stimulus that is presented repeatedly and turns out to be harmless. The first night in a hostel room near a railway line, every passing train wakes you; by the end of the week you sleep through them. Habituation is adaptive: an organism that kept reacting to every irrelevant event would have no attention left for the ones that matter. It has three diagnostic features. It is stimulus-specific (you still wake if your phone rings). It shows spontaneous recovery (after a long gap without trains, the first train wakes you again). And it shows dishabituation : if a new, strong stimulus occurs, the habituated response returns to the old stimulus. Dishabituation is the clearest proof that habituation is a form of learning and not simple fatigue of the muscles or receptors. Sensitisation is nearly the opposite: an increase in response, usually to a wide range of stimuli, after exposure to a strong or noxious stimulus. After a near-miss with a bus on the Mysuru ring road, every horn makes you jump for the rest of the day. Unlike habituation, sensitisation is not specific to the stimulus that caused it. The dual-process theory proposed by Philip Groves and Richard F. Thompson in 1970 holds that every stimulus sets off both processes at once, and what you observe is their sum. These two simple forms of learning were the first to be traced to the level of individual neurons. Eric Kandel (born 1929) chose the sea slug Aplysia , whose nervous system has only about 20,000 neurons, many of them large enough to record from one at a time. Touching the slug's siphon makes it withdraw its gill. With repeated gentle touches the withdrawal habituates, because the sensory neurons release less transmitter onto the motor neurons. A shock to the tail sensitises the reflex, because interneurons release serotonin onto the sensory neurons' terminals and increase their transmitter release. This work earned Kandel a share of the Nobel Prize in 2000 (the cellular details are in the Physiological Psychology book). Habituation is also one of developmental psychology's most useful tools. Infants cannot tell you what they can distinguish, but they can get bored. Robert Fantz showed in 1964 that babies look less and less at a pattern shown repeatedly and look longer at a new one. If an infant habituated to one picture recovers its looking when a second picture appears, the infant must be able to tell the two apart. The habituation-dishabituation paradigm is therefore used to study discrimination and categorisation in babies long before they can speak. Imprinting: learning on a biological timetable Between instinct and ordinary learning lies imprinting , the rapid formation of a lasting attachment to the first suitable moving object a young animal encounters. The phenomenon was described in chicks by Douglas Spalding in 1873, but it is linked forever with the Austrian ethologist Konrad Lorenz (1903 to 1989). In a 1935 paper Lorenz reported that greylag goslings hatched in an incubator, whose first sight was Lorenz himself, followed him about as if he were their mother, and showed no interest in their real mother. Photographs of a line of goslings marching behind the bearded scientist made the finding famous. Imprinting differs from ordinary learning in four ways. It happens fast, often within minutes of exposure. It needs no reward: the gosling is not fed for following. It is relatively irreversible: Lorenz's geese continued to prefer humans, and some later directed courtship at them (sexual imprinting). And it can occur only during a critical period , a limited window of development in which a particular kind of learning is possible. Eckhard Hess found the window peaked about 13 to 16 hours after hatching in mallard ducklings. Later research showed the window is less rigid than Lorenz believed, and many researchers now prefer the term sensitive period. Lorenz shared the 1973 Nobel Prize with Tinbergen and Karl von Frisch, and John Bowlby borrowed the idea of imprinting for his theory of human attachment (Developmental Psychology book). Exam trap Imprinting is rapid, largely irreversible, confined to a critical period and independent of reward. Options describing it as "slow and reversible across the lifespan", "operant conditioning with food reward" or "a purely visual recognition system unrelated to attachment" are all wrong. The classic species is the greylag goose (Lorenz); the 13 to 16 hour peak comes from Hess's mallard ducklings. The map of the chapter Habituation and sensitisation concern a single stimulus. Most learning, by contrast, is associative learning : learning that two events go together. Two broad kinds dominate. In classical conditioning the organism learns that one stimulus predicts another (the rat predicts the noise). In operant conditioning it learns that a response produces a consequence (pressing a lever produces food). Most of this research was done on animals, within comparative psychology , the branch of psychology that studies animal behaviour and compares species (its history is in Chapter 2). Later, cognitive psychologists showed that animals and people also learn maps, insights and concepts (Section 6.7), and Albert Bandura showed that people learn a great deal simply by watching others (Section 6.8). We begin, as psychology did, with a Russian physiologist and his dogs. 6.2 Pavlov and the Language of Classical Conditioning Medium yield · 7 Qs A physiologist and his "psychic secretions" Ivan Petrovich Pavlov (1849 to 1936) did not set out to study learning. He was a physiologist, and in 1904 he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his research on digestion. To measure digestive secretions in living animals he developed surgical techniques of great elegance; for the salivary work, the duct of a dog's salivary gland was redirected through a small opening (a fistula) in the cheek so that every drop of saliva could be collected through a tube and counted. In the late 1890s Pavlov and his co-workers noticed something that spoiled their measurements. Dogs that had been in the laboratory for a while began to salivate before food reached their mouths: at the sight of the food, at the sight of the dish, even at the sound of the attendant's footsteps. Pavlov at first called these "psychic secretions". Instead of treating them as a nuisance, he realised that they offered an objective way to study how the brain forms new connections, and from about 1897 he and his students studied them systematically. He described the work publicly at a congress in Madrid in 1903, and his lectures appeared in English in 1927 as Conditioned Reflexes . The procedure was simple. A hungry dog stood in a harness in a quiet room. A neutral stimulus, often the ticking of a metronome, a buzzer or a bell, was presented, and a few seconds later meat powder was delivered to the dog's mouth. After a number of such pairings the metronome alone made the dog salivate. Pavlov called the new reflex "conditional", because it depended on the conditions of the dog's experience; the English translation "conditioned" stuck. Pavlov was not quite the only discoverer. In 1902 the American graduate student Edwin Burket Twitmyer , studying the knee-jerk reflex, noticed that his participants' legs began to jerk when they heard the bell that warned of the hammer tap, even without the tap. He reported it to the American Psychological Association in 1904, where it was ignored. Discovery in science belongs partly to the person who sees what a finding means. The five terms Classical conditioning (also called Pavlovian or respondent conditioning) is learning in which a neutral stimulus, through repeated pairing with a stimulus that already produces a response, comes to produce a similar response itself. Its vocabulary has five terms, and exam questions test them constantly. The unconditioned stimulus (UCS, or US) is a stimulus that produces a response without any prior learning: food in the mouth. The unconditioned response (UCR, or UR) is the unlearned, reflexive response to the UCS: salivation to food. The neutral stimulus (NS) is a stimulus that, before conditioning, does not produce the response of interest. It is not completely without effect: the first time the metronome ticks, the dog pricks up its ears and turns towards it, the orienting response that Pavlov called the "what-is-it?" reflex. But it does not produce salivation. The conditioned stimulus (CS) is the formerly neutral stimulus after it has been paired with the UCS and has come to produce a response. The conditioned response (CR) is the learned response to the CS: salivation to the metronome. Notice two things. First, the same physical stimulus changes its name: the metronome is a neutral stimulus before conditioning and a conditioned stimulus after it. Second, the same physical response also changes its name according to what produces it. Salivation to food is a UCR; salivation to the metronome is a CR. The CR is usually similar to the UCR but not identical: Pavlov's dogs produced less saliva to the metronome than to food, and with a different chemical composition. What makes the whole thing work is association : the pairing of two stimuli close together in time. Figure 6.1 shows the three stages. Before conditioning Food (UCS) Salivation (UCR) Metronome (NS) No salivation During conditioning (many pairings) Metronome (NS) Food (UCS) Salivation (UCR) After conditioning Metronome (CS) Salivation (CR) Figure 6.1 The three stages of classical conditioning. Notice that the metronome changes its label from NS to CS, and that salivation is called a UCR when food produces it but a CR when the metronome produces it. The best way to master the five terms is to push real cases through four questions. What produced the response before any learning took place? That is the UCS. What was that unlearned response? The UCR. What stimulus was present, neutral at first, and paired with the UCS? The CS. What does that stimulus now produce on its own? The CR. Table 6.1 applies the four questions to five situations, including Albert's. Table 6.1 Five classical conditioning situations broken into their parts. Situation UCS UCR CS CR Pavlov's dog Meat powder Salivation Metronome Salivation to the metronome Little Albert Loud clang Startle and fear White rat Fear of the rat Child at the clinic Injection pain Crying, fear Doctor's white coat Crying at a white coat Student who lost a match Defeat and humiliation Distress The sports ground Anxiety at the ground Cancer patient Chemotherapy drug Nausea Hospital smell Nausea on arrival (anticipatory nausea) The last two rows are worth pausing over. Nobody chooses to become anxious at a cricket ground or nauseated at the smell of a hospital corridor; the response is elicited, automatic and emotional. That is the signature of classical conditioning: it attaches involuntary responses, especially emotional and bodily ones, to new stimuli. Your racing heart when you see the exam timetable was learned the same way Pavlov's dogs learned to drool. Exam trap "In Pavlov's experiment the bell was ..." The answer is: a neutral stimulus before it was associated with food and a conditioned stimulus after . It is never an unconditioned stimulus, and never an "operant stimulus". Likewise, a neutral stimulus becomes a CS "when it is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus", not when it is "reinforced with a reward" (that is operant language) or "occurs randomly". If a question asks for the "fundamental element" of classical conditioning, the answer is association. Some question writers loosely say the pairing brings out an "unconditioned behaviour"; read past the slip and answer classical conditioning. Timing: which arrangement conditions best? Pavlov and his successors quickly found that the order and spacing of the CS and UCS matter enormously. Four arrangements are distinguished (Figure 6.2). In delay conditioning , the CS comes on first and stays on until the UCS arrives, so the two overlap. The metronome starts, keeps ticking, and the food arrives while it is still ticking. This is the most effective arrangement and the standard laboratory procedure. The word "delay" refers to the delay between CS onset and UCS onset, not to any weakness. For fast reflexes such as the eyeblink, conditioning is best when the CS leads by about half a second; for slower responses, longer intervals work. In trace conditioning , the CS comes on and goes off before the UCS begins, leaving a gap. The organism must keep a memory "trace" of the CS across the gap. Trace conditioning works if the gap is short, but it is weaker than delay conditioning and gets weaker as the gap lengthens. Because the CS precedes the UCS in both delay and trace conditioning, both are sometimes grouped together as forward conditioning. In simultaneous conditioning , the CS and UCS begin and end together. Conditioning is weak, because the CS gives no advance warning; the UCS is already there. In backward conditioning , the UCS comes first and the CS follows. This produces little or no excitatory conditioning. If anything, the CS comes to signal that the UCS is over, so it may become a signal for safety (a conditioned inhibitor). Delay (forward) Strongest; most used CS UCS Trace Weaker; short gap only CS gap UCS Simultaneous Weak CS UCS Backward Weakest; often inhibitory CS UCS Time Figure 6.2 The four timing arrangements. In each row the upper bar shows when the CS is on and the lower bar when the UCS is on. Conditioning is strongest when the CS comes first and is still present when the UCS arrives (delay conditioning). Why should the order matter so much? Because, as Section 6.4 will show, classical conditioning is not really about two things happening together; it is about one thing predicting another. A stimulus that comes before the UCS can serve as a warning. A stimulus that comes with it or after it predicts nothing. Exam trap "Which is most effective in conditioning?" The answer is delayed (delay) conditioning. Students who think "delay" means "slow" pick trace conditioning instead; trace is the one with the gap. Backward conditioning is the least effective. The one famous exception to the short-interval rule is taste aversion, which forms even when illness follows the taste by hours (Section 6.4). 6.3 The Phenomena of Classical Conditioning Medium yield · 6 Qs Once Pavlov had a reliable way to create a conditioned reflex, he and his students spent three decades finding out what could be done to it. They discovered that a conditioned response can be strengthened, weakened, revived, spread to new stimuli, narrowed to one stimulus and even used to build further conditioned responses. These phenomena are the grammar of classical conditioning, and most of them reappear, under the same names, in operant conditioning. Acquisition, extinction and the return of the response Acquisition is the stage in which the CS-UCS pairing is repeated and the CR grows stronger. Plotted against trials, it rises steeply at first and then levels off: each pairing adds less than the one before (Figure 6.3, left). Acquisition is faster when the UCS is intense, when the CS is noticeable, when the timing is right (delay conditioning with a short interval) and, as Section 6.4 will show, when the CS reliably predicts the UCS. What happens when the UCS stops coming? If the metronome is sounded again and again with no food, the dog salivates less and less until it stops. This is extinction : the gradual weakening and disappearance of a conditioned response when the CS is repeatedly presented without the UCS. Pavlov called the UCS the "reinforcement" of the conditioned reflex, so in his language extinction occurs when reinforcement is withdrawn. Do not let that word mislead you into thinking of operant conditioning; in a classical-conditioning question, "withdrawing reinforcement" simply means omitting the UCS. It would be natural to assume that extinction erases what was learned. Pavlov showed that it does not, and his evidence is still the core of every modern account. Spontaneous recovery . If the extinguished animal is given a rest, say a day, and the CS is presented again, the CR reappears, weaker than before, with no further pairings (Figure 6.3, right). Something was suppressing the response, and the suppression faded with time. Disinhibition . If a novel, unrelated stimulus (a sudden noise) occurs during extinction, the extinguished CR temporarily comes back. Pavlov reasoned that extinction is an active inhibitory process and that the distraction disrupted the inhibition. Rapid reacquisition (savings). If CS-UCS pairings are resumed after extinction, the CR returns much faster than it was first acquired. This is the classical equivalent of finding that you relearn a forgotten poem in fewer readings than it took the first time. Reinstatement . After extinction, a few presentations of the UCS on its own, with no CS, are enough to bring the CR back to the CS. Robert Rescorla and Donald Heth demonstrated this in 1975 (you will meet Rescorla again in Section 6.4). Renewal . Extinction is tied to the context in which it happens. If fear is conditioned in one room (context A) and extinguished in another (context B), the fear returns when the animal is put back in room A, or into any new room. Mark Bouton has shown in many experiments that what extinction produces is a new, context-dependent memory ("the CS is safe here ") that competes with the old one. Acquisition CS + UCS Extinction CS alone Rest no trials Spontaneous recovery High Zero Strength of CR Trials (presentations of the CS) Figure 6.3 Acquisition, extinction and spontaneous recovery. Each pairing adds less strength than the last (a negatively accelerated curve). After extinction and a rest, the CR returns without any new pairings, which shows that extinction had suppressed the response rather than erased it. Clinical link Spontaneous recovery, reinstatement and renewal are the laboratory faces of relapse. A client whose fear of lifts was extinguished in the therapist's building may find the fear back when she steps into the lift at her own office (renewal), or after an unrelated frightening event (reinstatement). This is why modern exposure therapy is carried out in several settings and why therapists warn clients that a brief return of fear is expected and is not failure. Exam trap Keep the four "comeback" terms apart. Spontaneous recovery needs only the passage of time. Disinhibition needs a novel distracting stimulus. Reinstatement needs a presentation of the UCS alone. Reconditioning (rapid reacquisition) needs new CS-UCS pairings. Sensitisation is not a comeback at all; it is the non-associative increase in responding from Section 6.1. "If the UCS is subsequently omitted, the CR will undergo ..." Extinction. Generalisation and discrimination Pavlov's dogs, conditioned to one tone, also salivated to other tones, the more so the more similar they were to the original. This is stimulus generalisation : the tendency for a CR to be produced by stimuli similar to the CS. If you plot the strength of the response against the similarity of the test stimulus to the original CS, you get a hump-shaped generalisation gradient , highest at the original CS and falling off on either side. In 1937 Carl Hovland demonstrated such a gradient in humans: participants conditioned to show a skin-conductance response to one tone responded less and less to tones further away from it in pitch. Albert's fear of the rabbit, the dog and the sealskin coat was generalisation from the white rat; things that were furry and rat-like produced fear, while wooden blocks, which shared nothing with the rat, did not. Generalisation is adaptive. A gazelle that has been chased by one lion does well to be wary of a lion of slightly different size or colour. But generalisation that goes too far is costly, and so organisms also learn stimulus discrimination : the learned ability to respond to the CS but not to similar stimuli that have never been followed by the UCS. Pavlov trained it by differential conditioning. One tone (called CS+) was always followed by food; a similar tone (CS-) never was. At first the dog salivated to both; gradually it salivated only to CS+. A child who was frightened by a large black dog but still plays happily with her grandmother's small tabby cat, or a child who avoids one furry black cat but cuddles another, is showing discrimination. Key study: Experimental neurosis in Pavlov's laboratory (1921) Question. What happens when a discrimination becomes impossible? Method. In Pavlov's laboratory, Shenger-Krestovnikova projected a circle and an ellipse onto a screen in front of a dog. The circle was always followed by food; the ellipse never was. Once the dog discriminated them, the ellipse was made rounder step by step, until the ratio of its two axes was 9 to 8, almost a circle. Result. The dog's discrimination broke down; worse, the formerly placid animal began to squeal and wriggle in its stand, bit through the tubes and barked violently whenever it was brought to the room, and even easy discriminations it had previously mastered were lost. Conclusion. Pavlov called this state experimental neurosis : a lasting emotional disturbance produced by an unresolvable conflict between excitation and inhibition. Significance. It was the first laboratory model of anxiety, and it pointed toward the idea, developed later by Joseph Wolpe, that neurotic anxiety is learned and can therefore be unlearned. A second, accidental "experiment" convinced Pavlov that his dogs could be traumatised. In September 1924 the River Neva flooded Leningrad, and the dogs in the laboratory's kennels were trapped as the water rose almost to the tops of their cages before they were rescued. Afterwards several of the dogs had lost their carefully trained conditioned reflexes, and some showed lasting fear: a trickle of water allowed to run under the door of the room was enough to throw them back into agitation. Pavlov devoted much of his final decade to these "neuroses" and to applying conditioning ideas to psychiatry. Exam trap Generalisation is responding to similar stimuli; discrimination is responding differently to similar stimuli. A child who avoids a furry black cat but plays with a short-haired tabby is showing discrimination, not extinction (the fear of the black cat has not gone), not successive approximation (that is shaping, Section 6.5), and not negative transfer (old learning interfering with new learning, Section 6.10). Building on conditioning: higher-order conditioning and sensory preconditioning Food, pain and loud noises are rare in daily life, yet adults have strong emotional reactions to words, logos, places and faces that have never been directly paired with any of them. How? Pavlov's laboratory found one answer. Once a metronome has become a strong CS for salivation, it can itself be used in place of food to condition a second stimulus. Pair a black square with the metronome, with no food anywhere, and after some trials the black square alone produces salivation. This is higher-order conditioning (second-order conditioning when there are two links): an established CS serves as the UCS for conditioning a new stimulus. Third-order conditioning is very weak or absent, partly because during second-order training the first CS is repeatedly presented without food and so begins to extinguish. Higher-order conditioning helps explain why a word like "exam" can make a student's heart race. The word was never itself painful, but it was paired, over years, with the anxious waiting and the stern invigilator that had themselves become conditioned stimuli for fear. A related procedure reverses the order of training. In sensory preconditioning , two neutral stimuli are first paired with each other when neither means anything. Only afterwards is one of them paired with a UCS. The other then produces the CR too, even though it was never paired with the UCS or with a CS. W. J. Brogden demonstrated this in dogs in 1939: a light and a bell were presented together many times; then the bell alone was paired with a shock to the leg until it produced leg flexion; finally the light alone, never paired with shock, also produced some flexion. The finding mattered because it showed that animals learn associations between neutral stimuli that have no consequences at the time; the learning stays silent until later events reveal it, a point Edward Tolman would make about rats in mazes (Section 6.7). Table 6.2 sets the two procedures side by side. Table 6.2 Higher-order conditioning versus sensory preconditioning (S1 and S2 are two neutral stimuli). Procedure Phase 1 Phase 2 Test Higher-order conditioning (Pavlov's laboratory) S1 + UCS, so S1 becomes a CS S2 + S1 (no UCS) S2 alone produces the CR Sensory preconditioning (Brogden, 1939) S2 + S1 (both neutral) S1 + UCS S2 alone produces the CR A final point completes the picture. Not every CS signals that something is coming; some signal that something is not coming. If a light is always followed by shock except when a tone accompanies it, the tone comes to inhibit fear. Such a stimulus is a conditioned inhibitor . Conditioned inhibitors are the laboratory version of safety signals, such as a trusted friend whose presence lets an anxious person enter a crowded mall. Exam trap "Using an already-established CS to condition a new neutral stimulus" is higher-order (second-order) conditioning. It is not backward conditioning (UCS before CS), not stimulus discrimination, and not counterconditioning (replacing one response to a stimulus with an incompatible response, Section 6.4). If the two neutral stimuli were paired before any UCS appeared, it is sensory preconditioning. Scan Your Brain Fill in the blanks. The answers are below; cover them first. A decrease in responding to a repeated, harmless stimulus is called ; its near opposite is . The return of a habituated response when a novel strong stimulus occurs is called . Lorenz's goslings followed the first moving object they saw during a limited window called the period. In Pavlov's work, the metronome was a stimulus before conditioning and a stimulus after it. The most effective timing arrangement, in which the CS begins first and overlaps the UCS, is conditioning. When an extinguished CR reappears after a rest, with no new pairings, the phenomenon is called . Shenger-Krestovnikova's dog, unable to tell a circle from a near-circular ellipse, developed experimental . Pairing two neutral stimuli first and only then pairing one of them with a UCS is called . Fear that returns when a client goes back to the context in which it was originally learned is an example of . Answers: (1) habituation, sensitisation, (2) dishabituation, (3) critical, (4) neutral, conditioned, (5) delay (forward), (6) spontaneous recovery, (7) neurosis, (8) sensory preconditioning, (9) renewal. 6.4 Fear, Prediction and Preparedness High yield · 29 Qs For its first half-century, classical conditioning was thought of as a simple, mechanical process: pair two stimuli often enough, close enough together in time, and the first will come to produce the response to the second. This section tells how that picture was enriched in three directions. Conditioning was applied to human emotion, first to create fears and then to remove them. It was shown to depend on prediction, not mere pairing. And it was shown to be shaped by evolution, so that some associations are learned in a single trial and others hardly at all. Little Albert and conditioned emotional responses John Broadus Watson (1878 to 1958) had launched behaviourism in 1913 with the claim that psychology should study only observable behaviour (Chapter 2). He believed that most adult emotional life consisted of conditioned versions of a few innate emotional reactions, and the study you read about at the opening of this chapter, published with Rosalie Rayner in 1920 under the title "Conditioned emotional reactions", was meant to prove it. In the terms of Table 6.1, the loud clang was the UCS, the startle and fear it produced was the UCR, the white rat became the CS, and Albert's fear of the rat was the CR. His fear of the rabbit, the dog, the coat and the mask was stimulus generalisation. A fear or other emotional reaction acquired through classical conditioning is called a conditioned emotional response . In animal laboratories it is usually measured indirectly. In a procedure introduced by William Estes and B. F. Skinner in 1941, rats press a lever for food; a tone is then paired with a mild shock; afterwards, whenever the tone sounds, the rats stop pressing. The degree of this conditioned suppression measures how much fear the tone produces, and you will meet the procedure again in Kamin's experiments below. Fear conditioning depends critically on the amygdala, a structure in the temporal lobe that receives information about the CS and organises the bodily fear response ( Joseph LeDoux 's work on these circuits is covered in the Physiological Psychology book). The Albert study made Watson's case vividly, but it is a weak experiment by modern standards. There was one participant, no control condition, and the fear was measured by informal description; the fear also faded between sessions and had to be "freshened" with extra pairings. Ethically it could not be done today: the researchers deliberately frightened an infant and made no attempt to remove the fear. As you will see in the revisit at the end of the chapter, even Albert's identity is disputed. Peter, counterconditioning and the conditioning therapies If fear can be conditioned, can it be unconditioned? Four years after Albert, Mary Cover Jones (1897 to 1987), working with Watson's advice, answered yes. Her 1924 report "A laboratory study of fear: The case of Peter" described a boy of almost three who was intensely afraid of rabbits, and also, by generalisation, of a fur coat, feathers and cotton wool, much as Albert had been. Jones used two methods. In one, Peter played alongside other children who were not afraid of the rabbit. In the other, while Peter sat eating a favourite food, the rabbit in its cage was brought a little closer each day, never so close that he became upset. Over many sessions Peter came to tolerate the rabbit, then to touch it, and finally to let it nibble his fingers. His fears of the related objects declined as well. The method is counterconditioning : replacing a conditioned response to a stimulus with a new response that is incompatible with it. Eating and contentment cannot easily coexist with terror, so the rabbit, paired with eating, gradually came to signal something that was no longer threatening. Jones is often called the mother of behaviour therapy. The idea was developed into a systematic treatment three decades later by the South African psychiatrist Joseph Wolpe (1915 to 1997). Wolpe first made cats anxious by giving them mild shocks in an experimental cage; afterwards the cats were too anxious to eat in it. He then fed them first in a room quite unlike the cage, where their anxiety was weak enough for them to eat, and then in rooms that resembled the cage more and more closely, until eating, a response incompatible with anxiety, had overcome the anxiety even in the cage itself. He borrowed the physiologist Charles Scott Sherrington 's term for the principle: reciprocal inhibition , the idea that if a response incompatible with anxiety can be made to occur in the presence of an anxiety-provoking stimulus, it will weaken the bond between that stimulus and anxiety. In Psychotherapy by Reciprocal Inhibition (1958) he described the treatment that grew out of it, systematic desensitisation , which has three steps. Relaxation training . The client learns deep muscle relaxation, usually a shortened form of the progressive relaxation developed by the American physician Edmund Jacobson (1888 to 1983), in which muscle groups are tensed and then released one by one. Relaxation is the response that will compete with anxiety. Constructing an anxiety hierarchy . Client and therapist list situations involving the feared object, from the mildest to the most frightening, and the client rates each on the Subjective Units of Disturbance Scale (SUDS), a 0 to 100 rating of felt anxiety that Wolpe introduced in The Practice of Behavior Therapy (1969). Desensitisation proper . While deeply relaxed, the client imagines (or, in vivo, actually encounters) the lowest item. Only when it no longer produces anxiety does the therapist move up to the next item, and so on to the top. Systematic desensitisation is one of several treatments that grew directly out of classical conditioning. In flooding , the client is exposed to the most feared situation at full intensity, without gradual steps or relaxation, and is kept there until the anxiety subsides on its own; a person afraid of heights stands on a high balcony and does not leave. Flooding works by extinction: the CS (height) is presented without any UCS (falling), and escape, which would otherwise prevent extinction, is blocked. Implosive therapy, developed by Thomas Stampfl in the 1960s, is flooding carried out in imagination with deliberately exaggerated scenes. In aversion therapy the logic is reversed: a stimulus linked to an unwanted behaviour (the taste of alcohol) is paired with an aversive UCS (a nausea-producing drug) so that the stimulus becomes unpleasant. In covert sensitisation , introduced by Joseph Cautela in 1967, both the behaviour and the unpleasant consequence are only imagined: the client pictures reaching for a cigarette and then vividly imagines being violently sick. And in exposure and response prevention, the standard treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder developed by Victor Meyer in 1966, the client is exposed to the obsessional cue (touching a "contaminated" doorknob) and prevented from performing the compulsion (washing). The anxiety rises, peaks and falls; the treatment works through habituation and extinction. The full clinical details of all these treatments are in the Clinical Psychology book; Table 6.10 in Section 6.6 sorts them by the learning principle on which each rests. Exam trap Systematic desensitisation is Wolpe's , and its principle is reciprocal inhibition (counterconditioning), not operant extinction, not habituation, not the law of effect and not catharsis. Relaxation comes from Jacobson . The anxiety ratings are SUDS . Graded steps plus relaxation means desensitisation; full intensity with no escape and no relaxation means flooding; imagined unpleasant consequences of an imagined behaviour means covert sensitisation (Cautela). Exposure and response prevention rests on habituation and extinction . And do not confuse Wolpe's reciprocal inhibition with Bandura's reciprocal determinism (Section 6.8). Symptom substitution , sometimes offered as an option, is not a technique at all: it is the psychoanalytic prediction that removing a symptom without resolving its supposed underlying cause will simply produce a new symptom, a criticism of behaviour therapy that outcome research on desensitisation has generally not supported. Contiguity is not enough From Pavlov to the 1960s, almost everyone assumed that the key to conditioning was contiguity , the occurrence of the CS and UCS close together in time. Four findings from the late 1950s and 1960s, summarised in Table 6.3, showed that contiguity is not sufficient. What matters is whether the CS gives the animal new information about the UCS. The first came from Robert Rescorla (1940 to 2020) in 1968. He gave groups of rats the same number of tone-shock pairings, but varied how often shocks also occurred when the tone was absent. When shocks came only with the tone, the rats developed strong fear of the tone. When shocks were just as likely without the tone as with it, the rats showed no fear of the tone at all, even though they had experienced exactly as many tone-shock pairings. Rescorla concluded that conditioning depends on contingency : the degree to which the CS predicts the UCS, that is, how much more likely the UCS is in the presence of the CS than in its absence. A positive contingency produces excitatory conditioning; zero contingency produces none; a negative contingency (UCS less likely when the CS is present) produces conditioned inhibition. The second finding, blocking , was reported by Leon Kamin (1927 to 2017) in 1969. Kamin first conditioned rats to fear a noise by pairing it with shock. Then he presented the noise together with a light, followed by the same shock. Finally he tested the light alone. Rats that had had the first phase showed almost no fear of the light; control rats that had experienced only the noise-plus-light pairings feared the light strongly. Prior conditioning of the noise had blocked conditioning of the light. The light was perfectly contiguous with the shock, but it was redundant: the noise already predicted the shock, so the light added no information. The third, overshadowing , had been noted by Pavlov himself. When two stimuli are presented together as a compound CS, the more salient one (the louder, brighter or more noticeable) acquires most of the conditioning and the weaker one acquires little, even though either would have been conditioned well if presented alone. The fourth, latent inhibition , was described by Robert Lubow and A. U. Moore in 1959. If a stimulus is presented many times on its own before conditioning begins, it is later much harder to condition. The animal has learned that the stimulus is irrelevant. Latent inhibition explains a useful clinical fact: a child who has had many uneventful visits to the dentist is less likely to develop a dental phobia after one painful visit than a child whose first visit is the painful one. Table 6.3 Four findings showing that pairing alone does not produce conditioning. Finding Who, when What was done What it shows Contingency Rescorla, 1968 Equal CS-UCS pairings; UCS also given without the CS No conditioning unless the CS predicts the UCS Blocking Kamin, 1969 Noise trained first, then noise plus light A redundant CS is not conditioned Overshadowing Pavlov Strong and weak stimuli presented as a compound The more salient stimulus takes most of the learning Latent inhibition Lubow and Moore, 1959 CS presented alone many times before conditioning A familiar, meaningless stimulus conditions slowly The Rescorla-Wagner model: learning from surprise In 1972 Rescorla and Allan Wagner (1934 to 2018) proposed a simple mathematical model that captures most of these findings. The Rescorla-Wagner model says that on every trial the associative strength of a CS changes in proportion to how surprising the outcome is. In words: the animal learns only when what happens differs from what it expected. In symbols: ΔV = αβ(λ − ΣV) Here V is the associative strength of the CS (roughly, how strongly it predicts the UCS); ΔV is the change in that strength on this trial; α is the salience of the CS (how noticeable it is); β is a learning-rate value set by the UCS; λ (lambda) is the maximum associative strength the UCS can support, which is set to zero on trials when the UCS is absent; and ΣV is the sum of the associative strengths of all the stimuli present on the trial, which is the animal's total expectation. The term in brackets, (λ − ΣV), is the surprise, or prediction error . Push some numbers through it. Let αβ = 0.3 and λ = 100. On trial 1 the CS has no strength, so ΔV = 0.3 × (100 − 0) = 30, and V becomes 30. On trial 2, ΔV = 0.3 × (100 − 30) = 21, so V becomes 51. On trial 3, ΔV = 0.3 × 49 = 14.7, so V becomes 65.7. Each increment is smaller than the last because the UCS is becoming less surprising; that is why acquisition curves are negatively accelerated (Figure 6.3). Now blocking: after many noise-shock trials the noise has V close to 100. When the light is added, ΣV = 100 (noise) + 0 (light) = 100, so the prediction error is 100 − 100 = 0, and the light gains nothing. Extinction follows too: on a CS-alone trial λ = 0, so ΔV = 0.3 × (0 − 65.7), a negative change. The model is not perfect. It treats extinction as unlearning, which cannot explain spontaneous recovery or renewal, and it predicts no effect of presenting a CS alone before conditioning, so it cannot explain latent inhibition. Later models added attention to deal with these problems. But its central idea proved extraordinarily fruitful. In the 1990s Wolfram Schultz recorded from dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra of monkeys. The neurons fired in a burst to an unexpected reward; once a light reliably predicted the reward, they fired to the light and not to the reward; and if the predicted reward failed to arrive, their firing dipped below baseline at the moment it should have come. The neurons were signalling prediction error, the quantity in the Rescorla-Wagner brackets. The same idea now drives the reinforcement-learning algorithms used in artificial intelligence. Exam trap The brain's reward "prediction error" signal is carried by dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area (and substantia nigra), not by serotonin release, GABA inhibition or acetylcholine release. Blocking is Kamin's; contingency is Rescorla's; the model is Rescorla and Wagner's (1972); latent inhibition is Lubow and Moore's. Latent inhibition (pre-exposure slows conditioning) is a different thing from latent learning (Tolman, Section 6.7). What is learned: a substitute stimulus or a signal? Pavlov held a stimulus substitution theory : through pairing, the CS comes to activate the same brain centre as the UCS, so it becomes a substitute for the UCS and produces the same response. The theory predicts that the CR should be a copy of the UCR, and often it is not. Rats shocked through the floor jump and run (the UCR), but to a tone that predicts shock they freeze (the CR). The most striking evidence comes from drug tolerance. Shepard Siegel showed that the cues that regularly accompany a drug (the room, the syringe, the ritual) come to produce a compensatory response, opposite to the drug's effect, that prepares the body for it. This is part of why tolerance develops. It also explains a grim finding: rats given a large dose of heroin in a familiar drug context survived more often than rats given the same dose in an unfamiliar context, where the protective compensatory response was not triggered. Many human "overdoses" occur at doses the person usually tolerates, but in an unusual setting. The modern view, which Rescorla championed, is an information or expectancy view: in classical conditioning the organism learns that one event predicts another, and the CR is whatever response best prepares it for the predicted event. On this view the CS is a signal, not a substitute. The idea that conditioning depends on prediction and surprise fits the evidence from contingency, blocking and the dopamine neurons. Biological constraints: Garcia's rats and the idea of preparedness Behind classical learning theory lay an assumption that was rarely stated because it seemed obvious. It was called equipotentiality : the view that any stimulus can be associated with any response or UCS with equal ease, so that the laws of learning are the same whatever stimuli and responses are used. Pavlov's dogs and the metronome were assumed to be a convenient example of a universal process. In the 1960s an American psychologist overturned this assumption. Key study: Garcia and Koelling's "bright, noisy, tasty water" (1966) Question. Are all stimuli equally easy to associate with all consequences? Method. John Garcia (1917 to 2012) and Robert Koelling let thirsty rats drink from a spout. The water was flavoured with saccharin (taste), and every lick also produced a flash of light and a click (bright, noisy). Some rats were then made ill (by X-irradiation or a toxic drug); others received electric shocks to the feet. Later each rat was tested with tasty water (flavour, no light or click) and with bright-noisy water (plain water with light and click). Result. Rats made ill avoided the tasty water but drank the bright-noisy water freely; rats shocked avoided the bright-noisy water but drank the tasty water freely. Conclusion. Rats readily associate taste with illness and sights and sounds with external pain, but not the reverse. The cue and the consequence must "belong" together. Criticism and fate. The findings so contradicted accepted theory that Garcia had great difficulty getting them published; they are now among the most cited in the field. Garcia's broader work on conditioned taste aversion , the avoidance of a taste that has been followed by illness, broke three accepted principles at once. It showed one-trial learning: a single pairing of a new taste with illness is enough, whereas a metronome needs many pairings with food. It showed long-delay learning: the aversion forms even when the illness follows the taste by several hours, which flatly contradicts the rule that the CS and UCS must be close in time. And it refuted equipotentiality, as the key study shows. The adaptive logic is obvious once stated: in the wild, poisoned food makes an animal ill hours after eating, and an animal that could learn from a single such experience would survive to reproduce. Martin Seligman (born 1942) generalised the point in 1970 as the principle of preparedness : through evolution, each species is prepared to learn some associations easily, unprepared for others (they can be learned with effort), and contraprepared for still others (they are learned with great difficulty or not at all). In 1971 he applied the idea to human phobias. People commonly develop phobias of snakes, spiders, heights, the dark and enclosed spaces, which were dangers to our ancestors, but rarely of guns, electric sockets or cars, which are far more dangerous today. Preparedness may also explain why Albert's fear attached so readily to a furry animal: when Elsie Bregman tried, in 1934, to condition infants to fear wooden blocks and cloth objects, she largely failed. Taste-aversion learning has practical uses. Ilene Bernstein showed in 1978 that children receiving nausea-producing chemotherapy developed aversions to an unusual ice cream eaten shortly before treatment; later work found that giving patients a novel "scapegoat" food before chemotherapy can protect their usual diet from becoming aversive. Ranchers in the western United States have reduced coyote attacks on sheep by leaving out lamb meat laced with lithium chloride, which makes the coyotes ill and gives them an aversion to lamb. Aversion therapy for alcohol use, described above, uses the same principle. Advertisers apply classical conditioning constantly. A brand (the CS) is shown again and again with a beloved film star, a cricket hero, attractive people or pleasant music (the UCS), in the hope that the warm feelings these produce will transfer to the brand. The transfer of liking or disliking through pairing is called evaluative conditioning. In a well-known 1982 experiment, the marketing researcher Gerald Gorn found that students who saw a pen of one colour while hearing music they liked were more likely to choose a pen of that colour afterwards. Exam trap Taste aversion is an example of classical conditioning (taste = CS, illness = UCS, nausea = UCR, aversion = CR), not operant conditioning, not second-order conditioning, and not a "spurious association" (a statistical term for a coincidental link). The Garcia effect best illustrates biological preparedness (constraints on learning) . It contradicts two textbook rules: that all stimuli are equally easy to associate (equipotentiality) and that conditioning needs near-simultaneous events (contiguity). 6.5 Thorndike, Skinner and the Consequences of Behaviour High yield · 41 Qs Classical conditioning explains how stimuli come to trigger reflexive and emotional responses. But most of what you do is not triggered in that way. You choose to study, to message a friend, to order masala dosa rather than idli. These actions are not elicited by a stimulus; they are emitted, and whether you repeat them depends on what happened the last time you did them. The study of how consequences shape behaviour began, a few years before Pavlov's first reports, with an American graduate student and a houseful of cats. Thorndike's puzzle boxes and the law of effect Edward Lee Thorndike (1874 to 1949) began his animal work as a student of William James at Harvard, training chicks to run through mazes; when his landlady objected, James let him keep the chicks in the cellar of his own house. Thorndike then moved to Columbia University, and his doctoral dissertation, Animal Intelligence (1898), became one of the founding documents of comparative psychology. His best-known apparatus was the puzzle box: a slatted wooden crate from which a hungry cat could escape, to reach a piece of fish placed outside, only by performing a particular action such as pulling a loop of string, pressing a lever or stepping on a platform. Placed in the box, the cat clawed at the bars, squeezed at the gaps, bit and scrambled, until by accident it operated the release and got out. On the next trial it went through much the same frantic routine, but it hit the release a little sooner. Over many trials the useless movements dropped out and the escape time fell, but gradually and irregularly, not suddenly. When Thorndike plotted escape time against trials he produced some of the first learning curves in psychology, and their gradual slope persuaded him that the cats were not reasoning their way out. He called the process trial-and-error learning (he also called it learning by "trial and accidental success"). To explain it, Thorndike proposed the law of effect , stated in its classic form in 1911: of several responses made to the same situation, those that are accompanied or closely followed by satisfaction to the animal will, other things being equal, be more firmly connected with the situation, so that when the situation recurs they will be more likely to recur; those followed by discomfort will have their connections with the situation weakened. Thorndike defined "satisfaction" behaviourally, as a state of affairs the animal does nothing to avoid and often acts to attain. In plain words: behaviour followed by pleasant consequences is more likely to be repeated, and behaviour followed by unpleasant consequences is less likely to be repeated. Weightage. 111 of the 819 questions mapped in this book (13.6%) test this chapter, 72 of them from real past papers. 5 of its 11 sections are High yield. In March 1985, Clive Wearing was at the top of his profession. He was a British musician and musicologist, a producer of music programmes for BBC radio and an authority on the Renaissance composer Orlande de Lassus. Then he fell ill with what looked like a bad flu and a headache that would not go away. It was herpes simplex encephalitis: the same virus that causes ordinary cold sores had invaded his brain, and within days it had destroyed the hippocampus on both sides and damaged large parts of his temporal and frontal lobes. Clive survived, but the man who woke up was trapped inside a moment that lasted only seconds. He could hold a conversation as long as it kept moving, and he could follow a sentence to its end. But a short while after any experience ended, it was gone, and with it any sense that it had ever happened. He felt, continuously, as if he had just regained consciousness for the first time. His diary filled with page after page of entries, each giving the time and announcing that he was now, at last, truly awake; every earlier entry, which he had no memory of writing, was angrily crossed out. When his wife Deborah stepped out of the room for a few minutes and came back, he greeted her with tears of joy, as if they had been apart for years. The damage reached backwards as well as forwards. Almost every particular episode of his earlier life had become inaccessible to him. He knew certain facts, that he was a musician and that he was married to Deborah, but he could bring back almost no specific event from the decades he had lived. And yet some things survived untouched. Seat Clive at a piano or in front of a choir and he could still sight-read, play and conduct with his old skill; the music carried him from one bar to the next for as long as it lasted. Nor did he ever lose his love for Deborah or his recognition of her, although he could not remember a single conversation with her from one visit to the next. Clive Wearing's case raises nearly every question this chapter tries to answer. How can a person hold a thought for a few seconds but not for a minute? How can someone lose his whole personal past and still remember how to play the piano? Is there one memory or many? Where do memories go when we forget them, and why do some of them come back changed? Keep Clive in mind; you will meet him again at the end of the chapter. 7.1 What Memory Is, and How Ebbinghaus Measured It Medium yield · 5 Qs You use memory in everything you do. Reading this sentence requires you to hold its first words in mind until you reach its last ones; understanding it requires the meanings of words you learned years ago; and if you can answer a question about it next week, it is because something of it was kept. memory is the capacity to retain information over time and to use it later. Notice that this definition says nothing about consciousness: as Clive Wearing's piano playing shows, much of what we retain is expressed in what we can do rather than in what we can report. Three processes: encoding, storage and retrieval Psychologists find it useful to break remembering into three processes, an idea that grew out of the information-processing approach of the 1950s and 1960s, which treated the mind as a system that takes in, transforms, stores and outputs information, much as a computer does. The study of mental processes such as attention, memory and problem solving through this information-processor metaphor is cognitive psychology, whose rise is told in Chapter 2. encoding is the transformation of incoming information into a form, or code, that the memory system can hold. storage is the maintenance of encoded information over time. retrieval is the recovery of stored information when it is needed. A library is a fair analogy: books must be acquired and catalogued (encoding), kept on the shelves (storage), and found again when a reader asks for them (retrieval). A book can be missing because it was never bought, because it was lost from the shelf, or because it was shelved under the wrong number and cannot be found; in the same way, a failure to remember can be a failure at any of the three stages. The first stage depends heavily on attention. What you do not attend to is usually never encoded at all. In 1979 Raymond Nickerson and Marilyn Adams asked American adults to pick out the correct drawing of a one-cent coin from fifteen versions; fewer than half chose correctly, although every one of them had handled thousands of such coins. You can try the same test on yourself with a ten-rupee coin. The failure is not forgetting in the ordinary sense but encoding failure : the details were never encoded, because nothing in daily life requires you to attend to them, and what was never stored cannot later be retrieved. Attention itself is the subject of Chapter 5. Ebbinghaus and the first experiments on memory For most of the nineteenth century, memory was a subject for philosophers. Even Wilhelm Wundt, who founded the first psychology laboratory in 1879, doubted that the higher mental processes could be studied by experiment. The person who proved otherwise was Hermann Ebbinghaus (1850 to 1909), a young German scholar working alone, without a laboratory, who had been inspired by Gustav Fechner's demonstration that sensations could be measured (Chapter 3). If sensations could be measured, Ebbinghaus reasoned, why not memories? His first problem was material. Real words and poems come loaded with associations: a word you already know is not learned from scratch, and some words are far easier than others. So Ebbinghaus invented the nonsense syllable , a pronounceable but meaningless consonant-vowel-consonant combination such as DAX, BUP or ZOL. He built a pool of about 2,300 of them, drew lists at random, and, acting as his own and only participant, read each list aloud at a steady rate until he could recite it without error. Then, after a delay that ranged from twenty minutes to a month, he learned the same list again to the same standard. His measure of what remained was ingenious. Even when he could not recall a single syllable, relearning a list was faster than learning it had been the first time. The savings method expresses this as a percentage: savings equals the time (or number of trials) for original learning minus the time for relearning, divided by the time for original learning, multiplied by 100. Here is a worked example. Suppose a list took 20 readings to learn on Monday and 12 readings to relearn on Friday. The savings are (20 minus 12) divided by 20, multiplied by 100, which is 40 per cent. Forty per cent of the original work did not have to be repeated, so something of Monday's learning survived, even if Friday's attempt at recall produced nothing at all. Key study: Ebbinghaus, Memory (1885) Ebbinghaus published his results in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (On Memory; translated into English in 1913). His central result was the forgetting curve : savings fell steeply at first and then levelled off. After twenty minutes he had already lost about 42 per cent of the original learning; after an hour, more than half; after a day, about two thirds. But after that the loss slowed dramatically, and a month later about a fifth of the learning still survived (Figure 7.1). He also found that a list of about seven syllables could be repeated after a single reading but that the number of readings needed rose steeply for longer lists; that extra repetitions beyond the point of mastery increased later savings; that repetitions spread over several days were more efficient than the same repetitions crowded into one sitting; that syllables at the beginning and end of a list were learned before those in the middle; and that meaningful material (stanzas of poetry) needed far fewer readings than nonsense syllables. The criticisms are obvious and Ebbinghaus knew most of them: one participant, who was also the experimenter; artificial material stripped of meaning; and syllables that were not, in fact, equally meaningless (later researchers measured the "association value" of each syllable). Frederic Bartlett would later argue that by removing meaning Ebbinghaus had removed the most important thing about human memory (Section 7.9). Even so, his curves have been replicated many times, and his work showed that memory could be studied with the same precision as sensation. 0 25 50 75 100 Savings (%) 0 6 12 18 1 10 20 31 Hours after learning Days after learning 58% at 20 minutes 44% at 1 hour 36% at 9 hours 34% at 1 day 28% at 2 days 25% at 6 days 21% at 31 days Figure 7.1 Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, plotted from his 1885 savings data. The time axis is broken: hours on the left, days on the right. Notice how much is lost in the first hour and how little is lost between the sixth and the thirty-first day. Two features of Figure 7.1 are worth fixing in your mind, because examiners return to them. First, the curve is negatively accelerated: forgetting is fastest immediately after learning and slows as time passes. Second, it never reaches zero; Ebbinghaus's savings method detected traces of learning long after recall had failed. Ebbinghaus also left psychology one of its best-known sentences, from a textbook of 1908: "Psychology has a long past, but only a short history." Exam trap A question asks what Hermann Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud have in common. All three worked largely independently and were pioneers, and each devised a new method for studying the mind (Ebbinghaus the nonsense syllable and savings, Galton questionnaires and word association, Freud free association). None of them founded a formal psychology laboratory in the sense that Wundt did (Galton's Anthropometric Laboratory, opened in London in 1884, measured physical and sensory traits of the public rather than running psychological experiments). The RML 2020 key gives "each worked independently and were pioneers" alone, while the Panwar bank keys "(a) and (c)". The difference turns on the word "observational": Ebbinghaus's method was experimental, not observational, which is the likely reason the RML key stops at (a). Read the options carefully and choose the statement that is true of all three without qualification. Measuring retention: recall, recognition, relearning and reconstruction Ebbinghaus measured savings, but memory can be measured in several ways, and the same memory can look strong on one test and absent on another. All of the methods below are explicit tests: the person knows that memory is being tested and tries to remember. (Implicit tests, where memory shows itself without any attempt to remember, are described in Section 7.5.) recall requires the person to reproduce information with few or no hints. It comes in three forms. In free recall the person reports the items in any order, as when you list the films you saw last year. In serial recall the items must be reproduced in the order presented, as when you repeat a phone number. In cued recall a hint is given, such as a category name or the first letter. A special and historically important form of cued recall is paired-associate learning , introduced by Mary Whiton Calkins (1863 to 1930) in 1894: the person learns pairs of items (HOUSE and 47, or a Kannada word and its English meaning) and is later given the first member of each pair as a cue for the second. Learning the vocabulary of a new language is paired-associate learning in everyday life. recognition requires the person only to identify previously encountered items among new ones, called distractors or lures. It may take a yes or no form ("Was this face in the set?") or a forced-choice form, like the multiple-choice questions in your exam. A police line-up is a recognition test. Recognition is usually easier than recall, because the item itself is supplied and the person need only judge its familiarity. relearning is Ebbinghaus's savings method: the person learns the material again, and the reduction in time or trials is the measure of what was retained. It is the most sensitive of the measures, because it detects traces too weak to support either recall or recognition. Finally, the reconstruction method presents items in a particular order, then hands them back shuffled and asks the person to put them back into the original order. The score reflects memory for order rather than for the items themselves, which are all in front of the person. Table 7.1 sets the methods side by side. "Reconstructive memory" (Bartlett's idea that remembering rebuilds the past from schemas, Section 7.9) is a theory. A question describing items presented in order, then scrambled, then put back in order by the participant is asking for the reconstruction method, not recall, recognition or relearning. And when asked which measure is most sensitive, the answer is relearning (savings); recall, with no cues to help, is the least sensitive. 7.2 The Multi-Store Model High yield · 17 Qs Ebbinghaus studied memory as a single thing that weakens over time. The idea that memory might be made of several different stores is older than experiments on it. William James (1842 to 1910), in his Principles of Psychology (1890), distinguished primary memory, the small amount of information that is still present in consciousness (the sentence you are reading), from secondary memory, the vast store of knowledge that must be brought back into consciousness. In 1965 Nancy Waugh and Donald Norman revived James's terms in an experimental model. Three years later came the version that every textbook teaches. Atkinson and Shiffrin's modal model (1968) In 1968 Richard C. Atkinson and Richard M. Shiffrin proposed the multi-store model of memory. Because so many theorists of the period proposed something similar, it is also called the modal model (the most typical model). It has two kinds of parts. The structural features are three stores through which information passes: sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory. The control processes are strategies that the person can choose to use, such as attending, rehearsing, coding information in a particular way, and searching memory during retrieval. As Figure 7.2 shows, information from the environment enters the sensory stores; what is attended to passes into short-term memory; what is rehearsed there is transferred to long-term memory; and information can be retrieved from long-term memory back into short-term memory when it is needed.
