Sensory memory Wave a lit sparkler in a circle on Diwali night and you see a circle of light, not a moving dot. The circle exists only in your memory: the image of each position persists for a fraction of a second after the sparkler has moved on. sensory memory (also called the sensory register) is a very brief store that holds a large amount of raw, unprocessed sensory information, one store for each sense, just long enough for attention to select some of it for further processing. Its contents are pre-categorical: they are a record of the stimulus, not yet of its meaning. The visual sensory store is iconic memory and the auditory store is echoic memory ; both terms were coined by Ulric Neisser (1928 to 2012) in his book Cognitive Psychology (1967), which gave the new field its name. A tactile store, sometimes called haptic memory, has been studied far less. Key study: Sperling's partial-report experiments (1960) When people see an array of twelve letters (three rows of four) flashed for 50 milliseconds, they can report only about four or five of them. Yet they insist that they saw more, and that the rest faded while they were reporting. George Sperling (born 1934) tested this claim with the partial-report procedure . Immediately after the flash, a tone told the participant which row to report: a high tone for the top row, a medium tone for the middle row, a low tone for the bottom row. Because the participant could not know in advance which row would be cued, the proportion of the cued row reported must be true of the whole array. Participants reported about three of the four letters in whichever row was cued, which means that about nine of the twelve letters, roughly 75 per cent, were available at the moment of the tone, about twice as many as the whole-report method suggested. Then Sperling delayed the tone. With every fraction of a second of delay the partial-report advantage shrank, and by about one second it had vanished: performance fell to the level of whole report. Sperling concluded that a rich visual image persists for a few hundred milliseconds after the stimulus ends and fades rapidly, so that whole report underestimates what was seen simply because the image decays while the first letters are being named. A bright visual stimulus that follows the array (a mask) wipes the icon out even faster. Iconic memory therefore lasts roughly 250 to 500 milliseconds (a quarter to half a second, a little longer in some conditions). Echoic memory lasts longer. In 1972 Christopher Darwin, Michael Turvey and Robert Crowder ran an auditory version of Sperling's experiment, the "three-eared man" study: participants heard three different lists of letters and digits at once over headphones, one in the left ear, one in the right ear and one in both ears (which is heard as coming from the middle of the head). A visual cue then indicated which "ear" to report. A partial-report advantage appeared again, and it lasted for up to about four seconds. Echoic memory is generally put at about two to four seconds. You use it every time someone speaks to you while your attention is elsewhere: you say "What did you say?" and then realise you can replay the last few words yourself before they repeat them. The longer life of the echo makes sense, because speech unfolds over time and the end of a word can only be understood together with its beginning. Exam trap Two past papers ask about "the largest capacity" and get different answers. If a question says "largest capacity but shortest duration" (JEMAS 2025), the answer is sensory memory: it registers almost everything that reaches the senses, far more than short-term memory can hold, but for under a second (icon) or a few seconds (echo). If a question asks only which store has "the largest capacity" in the Atkinson and Shiffrin model, the answer is long-term memory, whose capacity has no known limit. Read the second half of the stem. Also note that "icon and echo" belong to sensory memory, never to short-term or working memory; that iconic memory is shorter than echoic memory; and that when a question says "lasts only a few seconds" and offers sensory memory, sensory memory is the intended answer, not eidetic imagery (Section 7.5), which is a rare, long-lasting visual image. Short-term memory: capacity and chunking Information that is attended to passes into short-term memory (STM), a store of very limited capacity that holds information for a matter of seconds unless it is rehearsed. Its capacity is measured by the memory span : the longest sequence of items that a person can repeat back in the correct order immediately after hearing it. Joseph Jacobs measured digit span systematically as early as 1887, and digit span remains part of every major intelligence and memory scale (Psychological Assessment book). In 1956 George Armitage Miller (1920 to 2012) published a paper with one of the most famous titles in psychology, "The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information." Across many tasks, he noted, people could hold about seven items (between five and nine) in immediate memory. But Miller's deeper point was that the limit applies to meaningful units, not to raw items. He called these units chunks, and the process of grouping items into larger meaningful units chunking . Try to hold this string: I N D I A I I T I S R O. Twelve letters is beyond most people's span. Read it as INDIA, IIT, ISRO and it becomes three chunks, well within span. You chunk your mobile number into groups (98450 12345), and your twelve-digit Aadhaar number into three groups of four, for the same reason. Chunking depends on knowledge already stored in long-term memory: IIT is a chunk only for someone who knows what it is. The most dramatic demonstration came from a student known as S.F., studied by Anders Ericsson, William Chase and Steve Faloon (1980). S.F. began with an ordinary digit span of about seven. Over more than 200 hours of practice spread across about twenty months he raised it to around 80 digits, by recoding groups of digits as running times (he was a keen club runner, so 3492 became "3 minutes 49.2 seconds, a near world-record mile"). His span for letters, which he did not practise, stayed at about six. His short-term store had not grown; he had learned to chunk. In the same way, chess masters glancing at a board from a real game for five seconds can reconstruct it almost perfectly, but are no better than novices when the pieces are placed at random (Chase and Simon, 1973). When rehearsal and chunking are prevented, the true capacity of short-term memory appears to be smaller than seven. In 2001 Nelson Cowan reviewed this evidence and argued for "the magical number 4": about four chunks, plus or minus one. Modern textbooks therefore give both figures: Miller's seven plus or minus two for memory span, and Cowan's four for the pure capacity of the store. Short-term memory: duration, forgetting and coding How long does information last in short-term memory if you are prevented from rehearsing it? Two studies answered almost simultaneously: John Brown in Britain in 1958 and, in a paper that every student learns, Lloyd and Margaret Peterson in the United States in 1959. Key study: The Brown-Peterson technique (1958, 1959) Lloyd Peterson and Margaret Peterson read a consonant trigram (such as CHJ) to each participant, followed at once by a three-digit number. The participant had to count backwards by threes from that number (506, 503, 500 ...) until a signal, then recall the trigram. Counting backwards prevented rehearsal. The retention interval varied from 3 to 18 seconds. Recall fell rapidly: from about 80 per cent after 3 seconds to about 10 per cent after 18 seconds. This method of filling the retention interval with a distracting task became known as the Brown-Peterson technique . The Petersons interpreted the result as decay: an unrehearsed trace simply fades in under half a minute, which is the origin of the textbook figure of "about 18 to 30 seconds" for the duration of short-term memory. But the decay interpretation did not survive. In 1962 Geoffrey Keppel and Benton Underwood looked at the very first trial each participant received and found almost no forgetting at all, even after 18 seconds. Forgetting grew only over successive trials, as trigrams from earlier trials piled up and competed with the current one. That is proactive interference (Section 7.8), not decay. Further evidence pointed the same way. Delos Wickens and his colleagues showed in the 1960s and early 1970s that if several Brown-Peterson trials use items from one category (say, fruits), recall declines from trial to trial; but if the category is then switched (to professions), recall jumps back up. This release from proactive interference shows that the earlier items were interfering with the new ones, and, incidentally, that items in short-term memory carry some meaning. Waugh and Norman (1965) presented digits at fast or slow rates and found that forgetting depended on how many items came after the target, not on how much time had passed: new items displace old ones from a store with few slots. The modern view is that short-term forgetting is mostly due to interference and displacement, with decay playing a role, if at all, only over the first few seconds. What form does information take in short-term memory? In 1964 Reuben Conrad showed people strings of letters visually and recorded their recall errors. The errors were acoustic: people wrote V when the letter had been B, or S when it had been X, letters that sound alike but look different. Even visual material, it seemed, was held as sound. Two years later Alan Baddeley (born 1934) gave people short lists of words to recall immediately. Lists of words that sounded alike (man, mad, cap, can, map) were recalled very poorly; lists of words with similar meanings (big, huge, large, broad, great) caused little difficulty. When recall was delayed by twenty minutes, so that it depended on long-term memory, the pattern reversed: similarity of meaning now caused confusion, and similarity of sound did not. The classic conclusion is that acoustic coding dominates in short-term memory and semantic coding in long-term memory. "Dominates" is the right word: short-term memory can also hold visual codes for a second or two, and Wickens's release effect shows that meaning is present too. Long-term memory long-term memory (LTM) is the relatively permanent store of information. Its capacity has no known limit: nobody has ever been turned away from learning a new face because the store was full. Its duration ranges from minutes to a lifetime. Harry Bahrick and his colleagues (1975) tested nearly four hundred American adults on the names and faces of their high-school classmates; even 34 years after graduation, people recognised about 90 per cent of their classmates' faces, although their ability to recall names freely was far poorer and declined steadily. In a later study, Bahrick (1984) found that much of the Spanish people had learned at school was still there fifty years later; he called this stable residue permastore. Information in long-term memory is coded mainly by meaning. Jacqueline Sachs (1967) found that people who had heard a passage could not tell, after a short delay, whether a test sentence matched the exact wording they had heard, but readily detected any change in its meaning: we keep the gist and lose the words. Long-term memory also holds sounds (a song, a voice), images (a face) and movements (how to ride a bicycle), so semantic coding is the typical, not the only, code. Not the middle ones. Plot the probability of recall against each word's position in the list and you get a U-shaped curve, the serial position effect , also called the primacy-recency effect (Figure 7.3). The superior recall of the first few items is the primacy effect ; the superior recall of the last few is the recency effect . Bennet Murdock (1962) showed how reliable this curve is in free recall across lists of different lengths and presentation rates. The multi-store model explains it neatly. The first items receive more rehearsal than later ones, because each of them is rehearsed alone and then together with the next few, so they are more likely to be transferred to long-term memory: primacy is a long-term memory effect. The last items are still sitting in short-term memory at the moment of recall and are simply read out first: recency is a short-term memory effect. Dewey Rundus (1971) confirmed the first claim by asking people to rehearse aloud; the early items were rehearsed far more often than the rest, and the number of rehearsals predicted recall. Key study: Glanzer and Cunitz (1966) If primacy and recency come from different stores, it should be possible to change one without touching the other. Murray Glanzer and Anita Cunitz did exactly that. When recall was delayed by 30 seconds filled with counting (which empties short-term memory), the recency effect disappeared, but the primacy effect was unchanged. When words were presented more slowly (allowing more rehearsal), recall of early and middle items improved, but recency was unaffected. The second line of evidence comes from brain damage. Patients with the classic amnesic syndrome, such as H.M. (Section 7.10) and Clive Wearing, have normal digit spans and normal recency effects, but cannot transfer new information into long-term memory: short-term memory intact, long-term learning destroyed. If the stores are truly separate, the opposite pattern should also exist. It does. In 1970 Tim Shallice and Elizabeth Warrington described K.F., a man who had injured the left side of his brain in a motorcycle accident. His digit span was only about two items, and his recency effect was almost absent, yet his long-term learning was essentially normal. When one patient shows damage to function A with function B intact, and another shows the reverse, the result is a double dissociation , the strongest kind of neuropsychological evidence that two functions depend on different systems. Exam trap Who first observed the primacy-recency effect? Ebbinghaus noted in 1885 that the beginning and end of a list were learned first, and many textbooks credit him with the first observation of the serial position effect. The RML 2024 key, however, gives "McCray and Hunter", which refers to J. W. McCrary and W. S. Hunter, who published influential serial position curves for serial learning in 1953. If Ebbinghaus and McCrary and Hunter both appear, remember that the official key for that paper chose McCrary and Hunter, and that the historically earlier observation is Ebbinghaus's. Two more confusables: primacy and recency effects in impression formation and persuasion belong to the Social book, and primacy and recency as order effects in a psychophysics experiment are controlled by counterbalancing (Research Methodology book). Criticisms of the multi-store model The modal model gave memory research a common map, and the distinction between a small, fragile short-term store and a vast, durable long-term store has survived. But nearly every detail has been challenged. First, the stores are not unitary. Short-term memory turned out to have separate verbal and visual parts and an attentional controller, which is why it was replaced by the working memory model (Section 7.3); long-term memory turned out to contain several systems (Section 7.5). Second, rehearsal is not the royal road to long-term memory that the model assumed: simply repeating an item can keep it in short-term memory for as long as you like without making it much more memorable later (Section 7.4). Third, K.F. is a problem as well as a support: if information could reach long-term memory only by passing through short-term memory, his damaged short-term store should have crippled his long-term learning, and it did not. Fourth, the order of the stores is wrong in an important way: we can chunk IIT in short-term memory only because long-term memory has already been consulted, so long-term knowledge acts on information before and during its stay in short-term memory, not merely after it. Finally, the model treats short-term memory as a passive waiting room, when in daily life it is where we calculate, reason and understand. Exam trap "Which of the following is NOT a store in the stage model of memory?" The stage (multi-store) model has three stores: sensory, short-term and long-term. Working memory is not one of them; it is the separate model of Baddeley and Hitch (1974). A related question asks which store information must pass through before reaching long-term memory in the Atkinson and Shiffrin model: short-term memory, which some practice papers write as "short-term (working) memory" because Atkinson and Shiffrin themselves described the short-term store as a working memory. You must hold the numbers, carry out the steps, store the partial result (140) while you calculate the next one (28), and then combine them. Short-term memory in the Atkinson and Shiffrin sense, a passive box where items wait to be rehearsed or lost, does not capture what your mind just did. In 1974 Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch proposed that short-term memory is better thought of as a working memory : a limited-capacity system for temporarily holding and manipulating information while we carry out complex tasks such as reasoning, comprehension, mental arithmetic and learning. The dual-task method and the case against a single store Baddeley and Hitch's main tool was the dual-task method : give people two tasks at once and see whether they interfere. The logic is simple. If two tasks need the same limited resource, doing them together will impair one or both; if they draw on different resources, they can be combined with little cost. In their key experiments, participants held a list of up to six digits (a full short-term memory load, by the multi-store account) while solving reasoning problems, such as deciding whether "A follows B" correctly describes the pair BA. If short-term memory were a single store, filling it with six digits should have wrecked the reasoning. It did not. Reasoning slowed somewhat, but accuracy held up. Baddeley and Hitch concluded that short-term memory has several components: a store that was occupied by the digits, and something else, which was still available to do the reasoning. The model that resulted originally had three components, a controlling central executive and two "slave" systems, the phonological loop and the visuospatial sketchpad. In 2000 Baddeley added a fourth, the episodic buffer. Figure 7.4 shows the model in its current form. Central executive attentional controller Visuospatial sketchpad visual cache and inner scribe Episodic buffer (added in 2000) binds information into episodes Phonological loop phonological store and articulatory control process Long-term memory visual semantics episodic long-term memory language Figure 7.4 Baddeley's working memory model (Baddeley and Hitch, 1974; episodic buffer added by Baddeley, 2000). The central executive directs attention but stores nothing; the three subsidiary systems hold information and exchange it with long-term memory. The phonological loop The phonological loop holds and rehearses speech-based, auditory-verbal information. It has two parts. The phonological store, sometimes called the inner ear, holds speech sounds for about two seconds before they fade. The articulatory control process, the inner voice, refreshes the contents of the store by silent rehearsal (the way you repeat a phone number under your breath) and converts written material into a speech code so that it can enter the store. Four findings support this account. The phonological similarity effect : lists of similar-sounding items (B, G, V, P, T) are recalled worse than dissimilar ones (F, W, K, R, Y), because similar sounds are confused in the store. This is Conrad's and Baddeley's finding from Section 7.2, now given a home. The word-length effect : memory span is greater for short words than long ones. Baddeley, Neil Thomson and Mary Buchanan (1975) found that people could recall about as many words as they could say in roughly two seconds, so span for words like "wit, sum, harm" is larger than for "university, opportunity, constitutional". Even words with the same number of syllables but longer spoken durations (Friday, harpoon) are recalled worse than quick ones (bishop, wicket). Digit span depends on language for the same reason: Nick Ellis and Richard Hennelly (1980) showed that Welsh-English bilingual children had smaller digit spans in Welsh, whose digit names take longer to say, than in English. articulatory suppression : if people repeat an irrelevant word aloud ("the, the, the") while studying a list, the articulatory process is occupied. Suppression abolishes the word-length effect, and with visually presented items it also abolishes the phonological similarity effect, because written items can no longer be recoded into sound and so never reach the store. With spoken items, the similarity effect survives, because heard speech enters the store directly. The irrelevant speech effect: background speech, even in a language the listener does not know, impairs serial recall of visually presented digits, whereas non-speech noise of the same loudness does not (Pierre Salamé and Baddeley, 1982). Speech gains automatic access to the phonological store. What is the loop for? Not, mainly, for remembering phone numbers. Baddeley and his colleagues argue that it evolved as a language-learning device: to learn a new word, you must hold its unfamiliar sound sequence long enough to build a long-term representation. A patient known as P.V., whose phonological store was damaged, could learn pairs of words in her own language normally but was almost unable to learn words in Russian, which offered nothing familiar to lean on. The visuospatial sketchpad The visuospatial sketchpad holds and manipulates visual and spatial information: the route from your hostel to the exam hall, the layout of your room in the dark, an image you rotate in your mind. Robert Logie (1995) divided it into a visual cache, which stores form and colour, and an inner scribe, which handles spatial and movement information and rehearses the contents of the cache. When Roger Shepard and Jacqueline Metzler (1971) showed that the time needed to decide whether two drawings show the same object increases steadily with the angle through which one must be mentally rotated, they were measuring the sketchpad at work; any question about the component of working memory that "mentally rotates an object" is asking for the visuospatial sketchpad. The dual-task evidence for a separate sketchpad is elegant. Lee Brooks (1968) asked people to imagine a block capital F and to move around its corners in their mind, classifying each corner as "yes" if it was on the extreme top or bottom and "no" otherwise. They could respond either by saying "yes" or "no" or by pointing to Y and N letters scattered over a sheet of paper. Pointing, which needs spatial control, made the imagery task much slower than speaking. With a verbal task (classifying the words of a remembered sentence), the reverse was true: speaking was slower than pointing. Spatial responses interfere with spatial memory and verbal responses with verbal memory, which is what separate visuospatial and phonological systems predict. Clinically, visuospatial span is measured with the Corsi block-tapping test, in which the examiner taps a sequence of blocks and the patient copies it. The central executive The central executive is the most important and least understood component. It is an attentional control system with no storage of its own. Baddeley (1996) listed its functions as focusing attention, dividing attention between tasks, switching attention, and linking working memory with long-term memory. He modelled it on Donald Norman and Tim Shallice's supervisory attentional system, which takes over from habit whenever a situation is new, difficult or dangerous. Later work by Akira Miyake and colleagues (2000) separated three related executive functions: inhibition of unwanted responses, shifting between tasks, and updating the contents of working memory. The best-known measure of inhibition is the Stroop task (John Ridley Stroop, 1935): naming the ink colour of a colour word printed in a conflicting colour (RED in blue ink) is slow because automatic reading competes with the controlled task of colour naming. The Stroop effect is therefore interference in selective attention, not the interference between memories that causes forgetting (Section 7.8); it is taught fully in Chapter 5. The classic way to load the central executive is random generation. Try saying a random sequence of digits for a minute: you must constantly monitor what you have said, suppress the habitual sequences (1, 2, 3 or your phone number) and decide what to say next. Random number or letter generation disrupts reasoning, planning and the selection of chess moves, and the more demanding the main task, the more random generation suffers. Damage to the frontal lobes, especially the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, produces what Baddeley and Barbara Wilson (1988) called the dysexecutive syndrome: poor planning, distractibility and perseveration, with memory stores themselves intact (Physiological book). Note too that the central executive stores nothing; if an option says it "holds verbal information", it is wrong. The episodic buffer By the late 1990s the three-part model had a problem. People can repeat back a meaningful sentence of fifteen or sixteen words, far more than the five or six unrelated words the phonological loop can hold. Some densely amnesic patients can recall a short prose passage immediately, at normal levels, although they will have forgotten it entirely an hour later. Where is all this information held, and where are words, images and meaning combined into a single experience? In 2000 Baddeley proposed the episodic buffer : a limited-capacity store, holding perhaps four chunks, that uses a multidimensional code to bind information from the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad and long-term memory into integrated episodes. It is "episodic" because it holds integrated scenes or episodes, and a "buffer" because it serves as an interface between systems that use different codes. It is controlled by the central executive and is thought to be the place where we are consciously aware of the bound result. Exam trap The four components of working memory are the central executive, the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad and the episodic buffer. Distractors invent plausible-sounding parts: "visual executive loop", "verbal sketchpad", "semantic buffer". The phonological loop handles auditory-verbal information; the sketchpad handles visual and spatial information (including mental rotation); the episodic buffer integrates information into coherent episodes and was the one added in 2000. The original 1974 model had three components. Working memory versus short-term memory Are working memory and short-term memory just two names for the same thing? Not quite. Short-term memory refers to the temporary storage of information, measured by simple span tasks: hear a list, repeat it back. Working memory refers to storage combined with processing, measured by complex span tasks. In the reading span task of Meredyth Daneman and Patricia Carpenter (1980), for example, people read a series of sentences aloud and then try to recall the last word of each one; they must store words while processing sentences. Simple digit span repeated forwards is the classic short-term memory test; digit span repeated backwards requires the person to hold the sequence and reverse it, so it is treated as a working memory test. Working memory capacity, measured by complex span, predicts reading comprehension, reasoning and fluid intelligence far better than simple span does (Chapter 9). In short, short-term memory is a component of the larger working memory system; the multi-store model's single box became Baddeley's set of interacting parts. Clinical link Working memory tasks are central to cognitive assessment. The Wechsler intelligence scales combine forward, backward and sequenced digit span into a working memory index, and the Wechsler Memory Scale, Fourth Edition (WMS-IV), reports five index scores: Auditory Memory, Visual Memory, Visual Working Memory, Immediate Memory and Delayed Memory. Working memory deficits are prominent in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, schizophrenia and frontal lobe injury, and tests of executive function such as the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test tap the central executive. (Test details are in the Psychological Assessment book.) 7.4 Levels of Processing and the Quality of Encoding Medium yield · 4 Qs The multi-store model said that what gets into long-term memory depends on how long an item is rehearsed in short-term memory. Think about your own studying for a moment. Have you ever read a page five times and remembered nothing, and heard a single striking story once and remembered it for years? If so, you already suspect that the amount of rehearsal is not the whole story. In 1972 Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart turned that suspicion into a theory. Craik and Lockhart's framework (1972) Craik and Lockhart argued that memory is not a series of boxes but a by-product of the way information is processed. Incoming information can be analysed at different depths. At the shallowest level, structural (or orthographic) processing, we attend to physical appearance: is the word printed in capital letters? At an intermediate level, phonemic processing, we attend to sound: does the word rhyme with "weight"? At the deepest level, semantic processing, we attend to meaning: is it a kind of fish? Would it fit the sentence "He met a ___ in the street"? According to the levels of processing framework, deeper processing produces more elaborate, longer-lasting and stronger memory traces. Memory is what is left behind by the analyses that perception and comprehension perform, so the crucial question is not "How long did you rehearse it?" but "What did you do with it?" An important consequence is that the intention to learn matters very little. Thomas Hyde and James Jenkins (1973) gave people word lists with different orienting tasks: some rated each word for pleasantness (a semantic task), others checked whether the word contained the letters E or G (a structural task). Some participants in each condition were warned of a later memory test; others were not. Recall depended strongly on the orienting task and hardly at all on the warning: people who rated pleasantness without trying to learn remembered about as well as people who were deliberately trying to learn. What you do with information determines what you remember, whether or not you mean to remember it. Key study: Craik and Tulving (1975) Fergus Craik and Endel Tulving presented words, each preceded by a question that required one of three levels of processing: a structural question ("Is the word in capital letters?"), a phonemic question ("Does the word rhyme with WEIGHT?") or a semantic question ("Would the word fit the sentence 'He met a ___ in the street'?"). Participants did not know that a memory test would follow. On a later surprise recognition test, memory rose steadily from structural to phonemic to semantic questions, with semantic processing producing performance more than three times as good as structural processing. Words that received a "yes" answer were remembered better than "no" words, especially at the semantic level, because a "yes" word fits into a meaningful structure. Was depth just a disguise for time? Semantic questions take a little longer to answer. Craik and Tulving checked by devising a slow but shallow task (judging the pattern of consonants and vowels in a word). It took longer than the semantic task and still produced poorer memory. In a further experiment, words judged against complex sentence frames ("The great bird swooped down and carried off the struggling ___") were recalled about twice as well as words judged against simple frames ("She cooked the ___"): within the same level, more elaborate processing helped too. Maintenance versus elaborative rehearsal Craik and Lockhart drew a distinction that every student should use. maintenance rehearsal (which they called Type I processing) is the simple repetition of information at the same level, like repeating a phone number until you dial it. It keeps information available in short-term memory but adds little to long-term memory. elaborative rehearsal (Type II processing) links the information to other knowledge: thinking about what it means, how it relates to what you already know, what example illustrates it. It is elaborative rehearsal that builds durable memories. Craik and Michael Watkins (1973) demonstrated the difference neatly. Participants heard lists of words and had to keep in mind the most recent word beginning with a target letter, say G, so that some G-words were held in mind for a long time and others only briefly. On a surprise final recall test, the time a word had spent being maintained made almost no difference to whether it was remembered. Repetition kept words in mind; it did not make them memorable. Two further ideas extend the levels framework. Elaboration refers to the richness of processing within a level, as the complex sentences in Craik and Tulving's study showed. Distinctiveness refers to how different a trace is from other traces; a distinctive memory has fewer competitors at retrieval. Michael Eysenck and Christine Eysenck (1980) asked people to pronounce words with silent letters as they are spelled (the "b" in comb). This was shallow, phonemic processing, yet because it was distinctive it produced recognition as good as semantic processing. (The classic demonstration of distinctiveness, the von Restorff effect, is described in Section 7.8.) The self-reference, generation and dual-coding effects If semantic processing beats phonemic processing, is there anything deeper than meaning? In 1977 T. B. Rogers, Nicholas Kuiper and W. S. Kirker added a fourth orienting question to the classic three: "Does this word describe you?" Adjectives judged in relation to the self were recalled about twice as well as adjectives judged for meaning alone. This self-reference effect , the finding that information is remembered better when it is related to oneself, has been confirmed many times. The usual explanation is that the self is the richest, most organised and most often used body of knowledge each of us has, so linking a word to it provides both elaboration and organisation. Interestingly, in some collectivist cultures, relating words to one's mother produces almost as large an advantage as relating them to oneself, which suggests that what matters is an elaborate, well-organised knowledge structure rather than the self as such. The generation effect is the finding that information you produce yourself is remembered better than information you merely read. Norman Slamecka and Peter Graf (1978) had people either read word pairs (HOT and COLD) or generate the second word from a rule and a cue (an opposite of HOT beginning with C). Generated words were remembered better. The lesson for study is direct: an answer you work out for yourself is worth more than an answer you highlight. A third principle concerns images. Allan Paivio (1925 to 2016) proposed his dual coding theory in 1971: information can be represented in a verbal code and in an imagery code (in his later terms, by logogens and imagens). Concrete words such as "elephant" are easily coded both ways, so they have two routes to retrieval; abstract words such as "truth" are coded mainly verbally. Dual coding explains why concrete words are remembered better than abstract ones and why pictures are remembered better than words (the picture superiority effect), and it underlies the imagery mnemonics of Section 7.11. Exam trap The self-reference effect was demonstrated by Rogers, Kuiper and Kirker (1977); exam keys often write "Rogers and Kuiper". It is not Craik and Lockhart's, although it extends their framework. The other names offered in the RML 2024 question have their own claims: Allan Paivio is dual coding theory; Michael Posner is known for attention research and the letter-matching task (Chapter 5). And the "self-reference effect" is a memory phenomenon; the "sum of a person's impressions of himself", "the beliefs we hold about what we are like" and "the knowledge that we exist as separate individuals" describe self-concept, self-schema and self-awareness (Social and Personality books). Criticisms and transfer-appropriate processing The levels framework was enormously productive, but three criticisms stuck. The first is circularity. How do we know that a task involves deep processing? Because it produces good memory. Why does it produce good memory? Because it involves deep processing. Without an independent measure of depth, the theory cannot be tested properly; Alan Baddeley made this point forcefully in a 1978 critique. The second is that depth, elaboration and distinctiveness were never clearly separated or measured. The third, and most important, is that the framework looked only at encoding and ignored the conditions of retrieval. The third criticism came with an experiment by Donald Morris, John Bransford and Jeffery Franks (1977). Participants answered semantic or rhyme questions about words, as in the levels experiments. Then half of them took a stand
