Weightage. 63 of the 819 questions mapped in this book (7.7%) test this chapter, 22 of them from real past papers. 1 of its 8 sections is High yield. In 1904 the French Ministry of Public Instruction had a problem that any Indian school inspector would recognise. The education laws of the early 1880s had made primary schooling free and compulsory, so every child in Paris now sat in a classroom, and some of them could not keep up. Which of these children were slow because they lacked the capacity to learn at the ordinary pace, and which were simply badly taught, mischievous, often absent or disliked by their teachers? Teachers' opinions were no help: the same child could be called "backward" by one teacher and "lazy" by the next. The ministry set up a commission to study the education of what it called "abnormal" children, and one of its members was a 47-year-old psychologist named Alfred Binet. Binet had spent years watching children think, including his own two young daughters, and he had become convinced that the measures then in fashion (reaction times, the sharpness of hearing, the size of the head) told you almost nothing about a child's mind. Intelligence, he argued, shows itself in judgement: in understanding a question, keeping a goal in mind and noticing your own mistakes. So, with a young physician named Théodore Simon, he did something disarmingly simple. They collected dozens of small tasks, tried them on children in Paris schools and institutions, and kept the ones that older children passed more often than younger children. The result, published in 1905, was a ladder of 30 tasks. At the bottom, a child had only to follow a lighted match with the eyes; near the top, the child had to explain how two abstract words differed or build a sentence around three given words. How far up the ladder a child climbed, compared with other children of the same age, was the measure. Binet was proud of the scale and wary of it. It was, he insisted, a practical tool for picking out children who needed special help, not a ruler that measured some fixed quantity inside the head. He prescribed "mental orthopaedics", classroom exercises in attention and self-control, to help slow children improve, and in 1909 he protested against "the brutal pessimism" of those who claimed that a person's intelligence is a fixed quantity that cannot be increased. Binet died in 1911. Within a decade his ladder had crossed the Atlantic and been turned into something he had warned against. In the United States it was used to label newly arrived immigrants as "feeble-minded", to rank well over a million army recruits, and to argue that intelligence is simply inherited and that whole nations were born less able. Remember Binet's two claims: that intelligence is complex and a test can only sample it, and that it can be raised. By the end of this chapter you will be able to judge, with a century of evidence in hand, how right he was. 9.1 What Is Intelligence? Lower yield · 3 Qs Everyone uses the word, and everyone believes they recognise intelligence when they see it: the classmate who solves a puzzle in seconds, the grandmother who keeps the household accounts in her head, the cricket captain who reads a match two overs ahead of everyone else. Yet when psychologists have tried to pin the word down, they have disagreed for more than a century. It is worth starting with the disagreements, because they shape every theory and every test in this chapter, and because examiners love to ask who said what. Definitions from Binet to the Experts Alfred Binet (1857 to 1911) put judgement at the centre: "to judge well, to comprehend well, to reason well, these are the essential activities of intelligence." He also called it good sense, practical sense, initiative and the faculty of adapting oneself to circumstances, and in 1909 he compressed it into four words: comprehension, invention, direction (holding a goal in mind) and censorship (criticising one's own attempts). Binet's view is sometimes classified as a unifactor theory , the idea that intelligence is one general, undivided capacity, because his scale produced a single overall level; the label is also attached to Lewis Terman and William Stern, whom you will meet in Section 9.2. In 1921 the Journal of Educational Psychology asked more than a dozen leading American psychologists to define intelligence. The replies varied revealingly. Lewis Madison Terman said it was the ability to carry on abstract thinking. Edward Lee Thorndike called it "the power of good responses from the point of view of truth or fact." Others stressed the capacity to learn or to adapt to relatively new situations. Two years later, exasperated, the Harvard historian of psychology Edwin Garrigues Boring (1886 to 1968) wrote that intelligence is "what the tests test." He was making a serious point about method. Until psychologists agree on a theory, the only definition anyone can check is an operational definition , one that defines a concept by the procedure used to measure it. The definition most often quoted in Indian examinations is that of David Wechsler (1896 to 1981): intelligence is "the aggregate or global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, to think rationally and to deal effectively with his environment." It is usually dated 1944, from the third edition of his book The Measurement of Adult Intelligence ; almost the same words appear in the 1939 first edition, so you may see either year. Notice the two key words. Aggregate means that intelligence is made of many distinct abilities; global means that they work together as a whole. That double view, many parts but one whole, is exactly how his tests are built: separate subtests whose scores are summed into one full-scale score. Sixty-five years after the 1921 symposium, Robert Jeffrey Sternberg and Douglas Detterman repeated the exercise, putting the same question to about two dozen experts and publishing the replies as What Is Intelligence? (1986). The overlap with 1921 was considerable: higher-level abstract reasoning, problem solving and the capacity to learn appeared in both. But the 1986 experts gave more weight to metacognition (knowing about, and controlling, one's own thinking) and to the culture that decides which abilities count as intelligent. Sternberg's own definition makes the cultural point explicit: intelligence is mental activity directed toward purposive adaptation to, and selection and shaping of, real-world environments relevant to one's life. Hold on to the three verbs adapt, select and shape; they return as the "contextual" part of his triarchic theory in Section 9.5. Finally, after the storm over the book The Bell Curve (Section 9.7), Linda Gottfredson drafted a statement signed by 52 researchers and published in December 1994. Its definition is the working definition most researchers use today: "a very general mental capability that, among other things, involves the ability to reason, plan, solve problems, think abstractly, comprehend complex ideas, learn quickly and learn from experience." It is, the statement added, "not merely book learning, a narrow academic skill, or test-taking smarts." What do these definitions share? Three themes recur: the capacity to learn from experience, the capacity to reason abstractly, and the capacity to adapt to the environment. Where they part company is on two questions. Is intelligence one thing or many? And how much of it can a test capture? Those two disagreements organise the rest of this chapter. Table 9.1 collects the definitions you are most likely to be asked about. Table 9.1 Classic definitions of intelligence. Who When Intelligence is ... Alfred Binet 1905 to 1911 Judgement, good sense, adapting to circumstances; comprehension, invention, direction, censorship Lewis Terman 1921 The ability to carry on abstract thinking Edward Thorndike 1921 The power of good responses from the point of view of truth or fact Edwin Boring 1923 What the tests test (an operational definition) David Wechsler 1944 (1939) The aggregate or global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment Robert Sternberg 1985 Mental activity directed toward adapting to, selecting and shaping real-world environments Linda Gottfredson and 51 cosignatories 1994 A very general mental capability to reason, plan, solve problems, think abstractly, learn quickly and learn from experience Intelligence, Aptitude and Achievement Three words are often used loosely, and examiners exploit the looseness. Achievement is what a person has already learned through a specific course of instruction; an achievement test, such as a Class 10 board examination in mathematics, looks backwards at the effects of known teaching. An aptitude is a capacity to acquire, with training, some specific knowledge or skill. Walter Van Dyke Bingham (1880 to 1952) defined it in 1937 as a condition or set of characteristics regarded as symptomatic of a person's ability to acquire, with training, some knowledge, skill or set of responses, such as the ability to speak a language or produce music. An aptitude test therefore looks forwards: it predicts how well someone will learn to fly, to type or to study engineering before the training begins. The classic battery is the Differential Aptitude Tests of George Bennett, Harold Seashore and Alexander Wesman (1947). Because they predict how well a student will do in different courses and careers, aptitude tests are central tools of educational and vocational guidance. Intelligence tests sit between the two. They sample broad abilities that schooling influences but does not directly teach, and they predict learning and problem solving in general rather than in one field. The boundary is fuzzy (a vocabulary subtest is partly an achievement measure), so the difference is best understood as one of breadth and purpose, as Table 9.2 shows. Table 9.2 Achievement, aptitude and intelligence tests compared. Type of test What it measures Time orientation Example Achievement Effects of a specific, known course of learning Past School board examination; reading attainment test Aptitude Potential to learn a specific skill with training Future, specific Differential Aptitude Tests; clerical or mechanical aptitude tests Intelligence Broad reasoning and learning ability Future, general Wechsler scales; Stanford-Binet; Raven's matrices Exam trap The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) is an intelligence test, not an aptitude, achievement or attitude test. An attitude test measures a person's evaluative stance towards an object (the Social book). One paper (RML 2022) keyed the aptitude test as "the heart of the guidance programme". The standard phrase in guidance textbooks is that counselling is the heart of the guidance programme, so if counselling is offered, choose it; when counselling is not among the options, as in that paper, the aptitude test is the expected answer, because guidance decisions about courses and careers rest on it. The other usual options are guidance tools of a different kind: the case study is an intensive study of one person's history and circumstances, the interview is a face-to-face conversation to gather information and build rapport, and the cumulative record is a running file of a student's marks, test results, health and activities kept across the school years. Implicit Theories: What Ordinary People and Cultures Believe The definitions above are explicit theories , formal theories built by psychologists and tested against data. Ordinary people carry implicit theories of intelligence , beliefs about what intelligence is that guide how they judge themselves and others. In 1981 Sternberg and his colleagues simply asked people in a railway station, a supermarket and a college library to list the behaviours of an intelligent person. Three clusters emerged: practical problem-solving ability (reasons logically, sees all sides of a problem), verbal ability (speaks clearly, reads widely) and social competence (accepts others for what they are, admits mistakes). Laypeople, in other words, already included the social and practical abilities that the psychometric tests left out. Implicit theories also differ in a way that changes behaviour. Carol Susan Dweck (born 1946) distinguished an entity theory of intelligence, the belief that intelligence is a fixed quantity you either have or lack, from an incremental theory , the belief that it can be developed through effort and good strategies. In her popular book Mindset (2006) these became the fixed mindset and the growth mindset . Children who hold an entity theory tend to avoid challenges and give up after failure, because failure seems to reveal a permanent lack; children with an incremental theory treat failure as information and persist. Praise can push a child towards one theory or the other. In a well-known series of experiments with American fifth-graders, Claudia Mueller and Dweck (1998) praised some children for being clever ("you must be smart at this") and others for working hard; after a later failure, the children praised for ability chose easier tasks, enjoyed the work less and performed worse than those praised for effort. The mindset research therefore recommends praising effort and strategy, not innate ability. Large school studies of brief mindset interventions have found real but small average effects on grades, with larger effects for low-achieving students, so the idea is useful but not magic. Indian context The Indian-born psychologist J. P. Das (Section 9.5) has pointed out that the closest Indian word, buddhi , is broader than the Western test-based idea. It includes discrimination between right and wrong, self-knowledge, determination and feeling, not only speed and accuracy of reasoning. Studies of everyday Indian conceptions likewise give a large place to social competence, responsibility and wisdom. This is one reason a test built on one culture's implicit theory can misjudge people from another. Exam trap "Incremental" belongs to Dweck's entity versus incremental theories, not to Sternberg's triarchic theory, whose three parts are componential, experiential and contextual. Options such as "incremental" and "experimental" in a Sternberg question are bait. A "growth mindset" is the belief that intelligence is malleable and can be developed through effort. 9.2 From Galton to Binet: The Birth of Mental Testing Medium yield · 5 Qs Binet's 1905 scale is usually called the first intelligence test, and it was. But it was a reaction against an earlier attempt that had failed, and you cannot understand why Binet succeeded without knowing why his predecessors did not. Francis Galton and the Anthropometric Laboratory Francis Galton (1822 to 1911), a half-cousin of Charles Darwin, was fascinated by the fact that eminent men seemed to come from a small number of families. In Hereditary Genius (1869) he traced the family trees of judges, statesmen, scientists and poets and concluded that "natural ability" was inherited. (The obvious objection, that eminent families also pass on wealth, schooling and connections, did not trouble him much.) In 1874 he popularised the phrase "nature and nurture", in 1875 he proposed comparing twins as a way of separating the two, and in 1883 he coined the word eugenics for the programme of improving the human stock by selective breeding, an idea that later did great harm. How was natural ability to be measured? Galton followed the empiricist logic that all knowledge enters through the senses, so the people with the keenest senses and quickest reactions should be the most intelligent. At the International Health Exhibition in London in 1884 he opened an anthropometric laboratory (anthropometry is the measurement of the human body) where, for a small fee, about 9,000 visitors had their head size, grip strength, reaction time, visual acuity and highest audible pitch measured. To analyse such data he developed the ideas of regression and correlation, later put into mathematical form by his protégé Karl Pearson. For this work Galton is often called the father of differential psychology , the study of individual differences, and of psychometrics. He had, however, measured the wrong things. James McKeen Cattell and the "Mental Test" The American James McKeen Cattell (1860 to 1944) took his doctorate under Wilhelm Wundt in Leipzig and then worked with Galton in England. In an 1890 paper in the journal Mind , "Mental Tests and Measurements", he coined the term mental test and proposed a battery of ten: grip pressure, rate of hand movement, two-point touch threshold, the pressure needed to cause pain, the smallest noticeable difference in weight, reaction time to sound, time to name colours, bisection of a 50-centimetre line, judgement of a ten-second interval, and the number of letters remembered after one hearing. At Columbia University he tested entering students every year. The test of these tests came in 1901. Cattell's own student Clark Wissler correlated the scores of Columbia students with their college grades and with one another. The correlations with grades were close to zero, and the tests barely correlated with each other. If reaction time and pitch discrimination were measures of one underlying intelligence, they should have hung together and predicted academic success; they did neither. The sensory approach collapsed, leaving the field open for someone who would measure higher mental processes directly. Binet and Simon: Measuring Judgement That someone was Binet, working with the physician Théodore Simon (1873 to 1961; a few sources give 1872). Their approach differed from Galton's in two decisive ways. First, they measured complex functions (comprehension, reasoning, memory, judgement) rather than simple sensations. Second, they chose items empirically: a task stayed in the scale only if older children passed it more often than younger children, so success on the scale tracked mental development. Key study: The Binet-Simon scales (1905, 1908, 1911) Question. Could an objective test pick out schoolchildren who needed special education, without relying on teachers' impressions? Method. In 1905 Binet and Simon published 30 items arranged in order of increasing difficulty, from following a lighted match with the eyes to defining abstract words. In the 1908 revision they grouped the items by the age at which most normal children passed them (ages 3 to 13). A child's mental age was the age level of the items the child could pass (Binet's own term was "mental level"). A 7-year-old who passed the items typical of 9-year-olds had a mental age of 9. The 1911 revision, published the year Binet died, extended the scale into the adult range. Result. For the first time a single, standardised procedure could rank children's intellectual development. Conclusion and criticism. Binet regarded the score as a practical sample of performance, not a measure of fixed inborn capacity, and he warned against using it to label children for life. Those warnings were largely ignored once the test reached America. There is a footnote to this story that examiners enjoy. Around 1920 a young Swiss biologist named Jean Piaget worked in Simon's laboratory in Paris, standardising reasoning tests on Parisian children. He became less interested in whether the children got the answers right than in the systematic ways they got them wrong, and that curiosity grew into his theory of cognitive development (the Developmental book). So Piaget came out of the Binet tradition, but he did not create the first intelligence test. Across the Atlantic: Goddard, Stern and Terman Henry Herbert Goddard (1866 to 1957), research director of the Vineland Training School for "feeble-minded" children in New Jersey, translated the Binet-Simon scale into English in 1908. He grouped people with intellectual disability into idiots (the most severe), imbeciles, and a new category he named in 1910: the moron , from a Greek word for foolish, for people with mental ages of roughly 8 to 12. His book The Kallikak Family (1912) claimed to trace "feeble-mindedness" down two branches of one family, and from 1913 his team tested immigrants arriving at Ellis Island in New York, classifying many as feeble-minded on the strength of a translated test given through interpreters to frightened, exhausted travellers. These terms are now purely historical, but they appear as options in exam questions. Meanwhile, in Germany, William Stern (1871 to 1938) saw a problem with mental age. A child who is two years behind at age 4 is much more retarded in development than one who is two years behind at age 14. In 1912 he proposed dividing mental age by chronological age to give a "mental quotient", in German the Intelligenzquotient . Stern therefore coined the term and the ratio of the intelligence quotient (IQ) . It was Lewis Madison Terman (1877 to 1956) of Stanford University who made the IQ famous. His 1916 American revision of the Binet-Simon scale, the Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale , multiplied Stern's quotient by 100 to remove the decimal and reported the result as the IQ: IQ = (mental age ÷ chronological age) × 100 This is the ratio IQ . Work two cases through. A 10-year-old with a mental age of 8 has an IQ of (8 ÷ 10) × 100 = 80. A 10-year-old with a mental age of 12 has an IQ of 120. A child performing exactly at age level always scores 100, whatever the age, which is what made the number so appealing. Terman's Stanford-Binet became the standard American test for decades, and Terman, unlike Binet, believed it measured an inherited capacity. Testing Goes to War: Army Alpha and Army Beta When the United States entered the First World War in 1917, Robert Mearns Yerkes (1876 to 1956), then president of the American Psychological Association (and the same Yerkes as the Yerkes-Dodson law of Chapter 10), led a committee, with Terman and Goddard among its members, that built the first large-scale group intelligence tests. The Army Alpha was a written, verbal test for recruits who could read English. The Army Beta was a non-verbal, pictorial test, given by demonstration and mime, for recruits who were illiterate or did not speak English. About 1.75 million men were tested. Group testing had arrived: one examiner could now test hundreds of people at once. The aftermath is a lesson in the misuse of data. In A Study of American Intelligence (1923) the psychologist Carl Brigham used the army results to rank immigrant groups, with northern Europeans on top, ignoring the obvious fact that recent immigrants scored lower the fewer years they had lived in the United States, that is, the less English and American schooling they had. Such arguments were cited in the debates that led to the restrictive Immigration Act of 1924. Brigham publicly retracted his conclusions in 1930. Table 9.3 gathers the milestones of this history, together with the later tests you will meet in Section 9.3. Clinical link The Ellis Island and army episodes are the origin of three rules every clinical psychologist follows: test a person in a language and format they understand, interpret the score against norms from a comparable population, and never treat a single score as a verdict on a person's worth or future. In India, with its many languages and very unequal schooling, these rules decide which test you choose (Section 9.3). Table 9.3 Milestones in the measurement of intelligence. William Stern coined "intelligence quotient" (1912); Terman multiplied it by 100 and popularised it in the Stanford-Binet (1916). "Who invented the term IQ?" is Stern. Two Cattells. James McKeen Cattell coined "mental test" (1890); Raymond Bernard Cattell, unrelated and a generation later, gave us fluid and crystallised intelligence, the Culture Fair Intelligence Test and the 16PF. Galton versus Binet. Galton founded the study of individual differences and ran the first mental-measurement laboratory; Binet (with Simon) built the first practical intelligence test. Alpha versus Beta. Alpha is for the literate (verbal); Beta is for the illiterate (non-verbal). 9.3 The IQ and the Modern Tests High yield · 32 Qs The ratio IQ had a fatal flaw, and the way it was fixed gave us the IQ we use today. To see the flaw, push an adult through the formula. From Ratio IQ to Deviation IQ Mental age grows quickly in childhood, slows in adolescence and stops growing in the mid to late teens. Chronological age keeps climbing. Take a perfectly ordinary 40-year-old whose mental age, like that of most adults, levelled off at about 16: the ratio formula gives (16 ÷ 40) × 100 = 40, a score that would label an average adult as severely impaired. Terman patched the problem by treating every adult as if he or she were about 16 years old, but the patch hid a second flaw. Even in childhood, the spread of ratio IQs differs from age to age, so an IQ of 115 might put a 6-year-old in a different position relative to his age-mates than a 12-year-old with the same number. A score that means different things at different ages is a poor score. David Wechsler's solution, introduced with the Wechsler-Bellevue Intelligence Scale in 1939, was to abandon mental age altogether. A person's raw score is compared with the scores of a large, representative sample of people of the same age (the norms ), and the IQ simply reports how far above or below the average of that age group the person falls. This is the deviation IQ ; because it is a standard score, some books call it the "standard IQ". The mean of every age group is set at 100 and the standard deviation (SD) , the typical distance of scores from the mean, is set at 15. In formula form, if z is the number of standard deviations a person scores above or below the age-group mean (a z score ): deviation IQ = 100 + 15 z A 40-year-old who scores exactly at the mean of 40-year-olds gets 100; one who scores one standard deviation above them gets 115. The meaning of 115 is now the same at every age: better than about 84 per cent of one's age-mates. Study guides sometimes describe Wechsler's method as "the actual score divided by the expected mean score for the person's age"; that is a loose way of saying the same thing, that the person is compared with the expected performance of his or her own age group, and if you meet that wording as an option, it is the one intended. Other standard scores work the same way with different numbers: the T score used by many personality and neuropsychological tests has a mean of 50 and an SD of 10, and the Wechsler subtest scaled scores have a mean of 10 and an SD of 3. A percentile rank is different again; it is not a standard score but simply the percentage of the norm group scoring below a person. Because IQ scores are approximately normally distributed, the familiar properties of the normal curve let you translate any IQ into a percentile, the percentage of people scoring below it. As Figure 9.1 shows, about 68 per cent of people score between 85 and 115 (within one SD of the mean) and about 95 per cent between 70 and 130 (within two SDs). 85 to 115: about 68% of people 70 to 130: about 95% of people 34.1% 34.1% 13.6% 13.6% 2.1% 2.1% IQ SD Percentile 55 −3 0.1 70 −2 2nd 85 −1 16th 100 0 50th 115 +1 84th 130 +2 98th 145 +3 99.9 Figure 9.1 The distribution of deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15). Read across the bottom rows to convert an IQ into standard deviations and percentiles: 85 is the 16th percentile, 115 the 84th, 130 about the 98th, and 70 about the 2nd. Work two examples. On a Wechsler scale an IQ of 85 is one SD below the mean, so 16 per cent of people score below it (the 16th percentile); an IQ of 100, the mean, is by definition the 50th percentile. Now an older Stanford-Binet style question: on a test with a mean of 100 and an SD of 16, a person scores 136. Then z = (136 − 100) ÷ 16 = 2.25, and the normal-curve table gives about 0.987 of the area below z = 2.25, so about 98.7 per cent of people score lower. The SD matters. The Stanford-Binet adopted the deviation IQ in its 1960 revision (Form L-M) with an SD of 16, kept 16 in the fourth edition (1986), and moved to 15, in line with the Wechsler scales, only in the fifth edition (2003). Always check which SD a question gives you. Exam trap Ratio IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100, from Stern (1912) and Terman (1916); the original Stanford-Binet used it. Deviation IQ is a standard score with mean 100 and SD 15, comparing a person with same-age peers; Wechsler introduced it in 1939, and modern tests (including the SB5) use it. The deviation IQ is not "only for adults", it does not use raw scores without standardisation, and the ratio IQ is not the more reliable of the two (its meaning shifts from age to age, which is why it was abandoned). The old Stanford-Binet SD was 16, not 15. The Wechsler Scales Wechsler, a Romanian-born American who had tested army recruits in 1918, was chief psychologist at Bellevue Psychiatric Hospital in New York when he built his first scale. He set out to correct several faults he saw in the Stanford-Binet: it was designed for children, so its items had little appeal for adults; it leaned heavily on verbal, word-manipulation tasks; it placed too much weight on speed; and it rested on the concept of mental age, which made no sense for adults. His answer had four features that still define the Wechsler tests. They are point scales rather than age scales : items are grouped by type into subtests, and points are earned within each subtest, rather than items being grouped by the age at which they are passed, as in Binet's ladder. They combine verbal subtests with non-verbal performance tests (block designs, picture puzzles) that require little or no language. They yield subtest and part scores as well as a total, so a clinician can see a profile of strengths and weaknesses. And they use the deviation IQ. The family has grown with every generation (Table 9.4). Until the 2000s each test produced a Verbal IQ , a Performance IQ and a Full Scale IQ (FSIQ) . The newer editions replaced the verbal-performance split with index scores built on factor-analytic research (Section 9.4). Table 9.4 The Wechsler family of intelligence scales. Scale First edition Current edition Age range of current edition Wechsler-Bellevue 1939 (replaced by the WAIS) Adolescents and adults Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) 1955 WAIS-IV (2008); WAIS-5 (2024) 16 years to 90 years 11 months Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC) 1949 WISC-V (2014) 6 years to 16 years 11 months Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence (WPPSI) 1967 WPPSI-IV (2012) 2 years 6 months to 7 years 7 months The WAIS-IV, still the most widely used adult test in India, has 15 subtests: 10 core subtests that produce the scores and 5 supplemental subtests that can substitute for them. They are organised into four indices (Table 9.5). The Verbal Comprehension Index (VCI) measures verbal reasoning and acquired knowledge. The Perceptual Reasoning Index (PRI) measures non-verbal, fluid and visual-spatial reasoning. The Working Memory Index (WMI) measures the ability to hold information in mind and manipulate it, that is, to attend, concentrate and exert mental control. The Processing Speed Index (PSI) measures the speed and accuracy of simple visual scanning and copying. The four indices combine into the FSIQ. An optional General Ability Index (GAI) , computed from the six verbal and perceptual core subtests alone, gives an estimate of reasoning ability less affected by working memory and speed, which is useful when, say, a patient's attention has been disrupted by a head injury or depression. Table 9.5 The structure of the WAIS-IV (2008). Index Core subtests Supplemental subtests Verbal Comprehension (VCI) Similarities, Vocabulary, Information (3) Comprehension Perceptual Reasoning (PRI) Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles (3) Picture Completion, Figure Weights Working Memory (WMI) Digit Span, Arithmetic (2) Letter-Number Sequencing Processing Speed (PSI) Symbol Search, Coding (2) Cancellation The WISC-V for children went further, splitting perceptual reasoning in two. It has five primary indices: Verbal Comprehension, Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, Working Memory and Processing Speed. The WAIS-5 (2024) adopted the same five-index structure for adults. For examination purposes, though, "the four WAIS-IV indices" (VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI) remain the most frequently tested fact in this whole area. Do not confuse any of these with the Wechsler Memory Scale (WMS), first published by Wechsler in 1945, which is a memory test rather than an intelligence test. Its early editions summarised performance as a single memory quotient (MQ) on the IQ metric; the WMS-IV (2009) gives five index scores instead: Auditory Memory, Visual Memory, Visual Working Memory, Immediate Memory and Delayed Memory. An option listing "Verbal IQ, Performance IQ, Full Scale IQ and Memory Quotient" therefore mixes the old WAIS with the old WMS and is not the WAIS-IV. Exam trap The WAIS-IV has 3 core verbal (VCI) and 3 core perceptual (PRI) subtests, plus 2 core working-memory and 2 core processing-speed subtests: 10 core in all. The Working Memory Index, built from Digit Span and Arithmetic, is the one that reflects attention, concentration and mental control. One paper asked which subtest is "core in the WAIS-IV but not found in the WISC-V" and keyed Letter-Number Sequencing. Strictly, Letter-Number Sequencing is a supplemental subtest in the WAIS-IV (it was part of the Working Memory Index in the WAIS-III) and a secondary subtest in the WISC-V; but it is still the best of the options offered, because Digit Span, Symbol Search and Matrix Reasoning are core in both tests. The WISC-V covers 6 years to 16 years 11 months. The Stanford-Binet Today, and Other Individual Tests The Stanford-Binet was revised in 1937 (by Terman and Maud Merrill), in 1960, in 1986 and most recently as the Stanford-Binet Fifth Edition (SB5) (in full, the Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales, Fifth Edition), developed by Gale Roid and published in 2003. The SB5 covers ages 2 to 85 and over and is organised around five factors drawn from the hierarchical Cattell-Horn-Carroll model of Section 9.4, with the working-memory factor also drawing on Alan Baddeley's working-memory model (Chapter 7): Fluid Reasoning, Knowledge, Quantitative Reasoning, Visual-Spatial Processing and Working Memory. Each factor is measured once in a verbal and once in a non-verbal form, giving 10 subtests and a Full Scale IQ, a Verbal IQ and a Nonverbal IQ, all with mean 100 and SD 15. Like the earlier Stanford-Binets, it uses a basal level (the level at which the person passes all items, so easier items need not be given) and a ceiling level (the level at which the person fails all or most items, so testing stops). Several other individual tests appear in questions. Alan and Nadeen Kaufman's Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (K-ABC, 1983) was one of the first major tests built on Luria's neuropsychology (Section 9.5); their Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test, second edition (KBIT-2, 2004), is a 20-minute screening test with just two scales, a Verbal or crystallised scale and a Nonverbal or fluid scale. For infants, intelligence in the adult sense cannot yet be measured, so developmental scales are used instead: the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development (Nancy Bayley; the current edition covers roughly the first 42 months) assess cognitive, language and motor development, and the McCarthy Scales of Children's Abilities (Dorothea McCarthy, 1972) cover about 2½ to 8½ years. Developmental scales express results as a developmental quotient (DQ) , developmental age divided by chronological age, times 100, a ratio exactly like Stern's. Detailed administration and scoring belong to the Assessment book. Classifying IQ Scores Test publishers attach descriptive labels to ranges of IQ (Table 9.6). The labels have softened over the decades: the WAIS-IV's "borderline" has become "very low" in the WISC-V and WAIS-5, and the old psychiatric category of borderline intellectual functioning , which DSM-IV-TR placed at IQ 71 to 84, overlaps the "low average" and "borderline" bands. An IQ in the 70 to 84 region therefore falls into "low average or borderline, depending on the edition." Table 9.6 IQ classification bands (deviation IQ, mean 100, SD 15). DSM-5 requires deficits in adaptive functioning as well, and sets severity by adaptive functioning, not by IQ (Section 9.8). On the WAIS-IV a score of exactly 70 falls in the "borderline" band (70 to 79), one point above "extremely low"; so a question asking how to classify an FSIQ of 70 wants "borderline, and intellectual disability only if adaptive functioning is also impaired". With measurement error, scores of about 65 to 75 are compatible with intellectual disability only if adaptive deficits are present. Culture-Fair Tests A vocabulary item asks, in effect, "Have you met this word?", and whether you have met it depends on your home, school and language. Psychologists have therefore tried to build tests whose content is equally familiar, or equally unfamiliar, to everyone. The early hope was a culture-free test , one entirely free of cultural influence; that turned out to be impossible, because even the habit of sitting quietly, working against a clock and treating abstract shapes as a meaningful problem is learned. The realistic goal is a culture-fair test (also called culture-reduced), one that minimises language, reading, specific knowledge and speed so that people from different backgrounds are on a more equal footing. The most famous is Raven's Progressive Matrices , devised by the British psychologist John Carlyle Raven (1902 to 1970), a student of Spearman. Each item shows a pattern of figures arranged in a matrix with one piece missing, and the examinee chooses the piece that completes it. Solving an item requires working out the rule that governs the rows and columns, which is what Spearman called the eduction of relations (Section 9.4). The Standard Progressive Matrices (SPM), published in 1938 (Raven had drafted it by 1936, so some books give that year), has 60 items in five sets of 12 that grow progressively harder, hence the name. The Coloured Progressive Matrices (36 items) are for children and older or impaired adults, and the Advanced Progressive Matrices (48 items) for high-ability adults. Raven's matrices are the classic measure of fluid intelligence, the ability to reason with novel material (Section 9.4), and they are also the best single marker of Spearman's general factor. Raymond Bernard Cattell's Culture Fair Intelligence Test (CFIT), first issued around 1940 as a "culture-free" test and soon renamed, is a group test in three scales for different ages and abilities. Its subtests (series completion, classification, matrices and "conditions", a topological task) use only figures. Other non-verbal and performance tests that reduce the role of language include Florence Goodenough's Draw-a-Man test (1926), the Leiter International Performance Scale, the Porteus Maze Test, Kohs block designs and Alexander's Pass-Along test; the Army Beta was an early example of the same idea. Exam trap Raven's Progressive Matrices measure fluid intelligence; choose "fluid" over "crystallised", "verbal" or "social". If "general intelligence (g)" is offered alongside "fluid", the expected answer is still fluid, although Raven's is also the best single measure of g, because Gf and g are very closely related. Raven's is called culture-fair because it is non-verbal, with minimal language demands; it is not culture-free, and schooling still affects scores. Intelligence Tests in India Most Western tests cannot simply be translated for Indian use: the vocabulary, the general-information items ("Who wrote Hamlet ?") and even the pictures assume a particular culture, and many children who need assessment have had little or no schooling. Indian psychologists responded in two ways: by adapting the Binet and Wechsler tests with Indian content and norms, and by building performance batteries that need no reading at all. Table 9.7 lists the tests that appear in examinations; full detail belongs to the Assessment book. Table 9.7 Intelligence and related tests developed or adapted in India. Malin Adaptive behaviour: social age and social quotient (Section 9.8) Now apply the principle. A 10-year-old from a village, who has never been to school and cannot read, is brought for assessment because he struggles to learn. Which test? The WISC-IV and the SB5 depend heavily on verbal knowledge built by schooling and were normed on other populations. Malin's MISIC is an Indian test but half of it is verbal, built on the WISC's information, comprehension, arithmetic and vocabulary items. Bhatia's Battery, a set of performance tasks that need no reading, with rural norms, is the most appropriate choice to minimise cultural and educational bias. Exam trap Bhatia's Battery was developed by C. M. Bhatia; the other names often offered, Girishwar Misra, Durganand Sinha and J. B. P. Sinha, are distinguished Indian psychologists known for cultural and indigenous psychology, social psychology and organisational leadership, not for this test. Some notes date the Battery to the 1940s, when Bhatia did the work; 1955 is the commonly cited publication year. Do not confuse Malin's two contributions: MISIC (an intelligence test) and the Indian adaptation of the Vineland Social Maturity Scale (an adaptive-behaviour scale). Are IQ Tests Reliable and Valid, and What Do They Predict? A test is useful only if it is reliable (it gives consistent scores) and valid (it measures what it claims to measure). The major individual IQ tests are among the most reliable instruments in psychology: the internal-consistency reliability of the WAIS-IV Full Scale IQ is about .98, and retesting after a few weeks typically gives correlations around .9. Individual subtests are much less reliable than the total, which is why clinicians interpret composite scores first. Validity comes in several kinds (the Assessment and Research Methodology books treat them fully). Content validity asks whether the items sample the domain adequately. Criterion-related validity asks whether scores relate to an outside criterion; it is called concurrent validity when test and criterion are measured at about the same time, and predictive validity when the criterion comes later. Construct validity asks whether the test behaves as the theory of the construct predicts, for example correlating with other measures of reasoning but not with unrelated traits. So if a new intelligence test is given alongside a well-established one, and the two sets of scores are correlated, the researcher is checking concurrent validity. What does IQ predict? A great deal, though far from everything. IQ correlates about .5 with school grades and about .55 with the number of years of education completed. In a famous 1998 review of 85 years of research, Frank Schmidt and John Hunter found that general mental ability predicts job performance with a validity of about .5, higher for complex jobs than for simple ones, which makes it the single best predictor of job performance across occupations. Childhood IQ even predicts health and lifespan: in Scotland, people who had been tested at age 11 in the Scottish Mental Survey of 1932 were more likely to be alive decades later if they had scored higher. But a correlation of .5 means IQ accounts for only about a quarter of the variation in grades (.5 squared is .25); motivation, conscientiousness, teaching, opportunity and luck account for the rest. Clinical link Clinical psychologists use intelligence tests to diagnose intellectual disability, to identify specific learning disabilities (where achievement falls well below what ability predicts), to document cognitive decline after brain injury or in dementia, to plan rehabilitation and education, and to establish eligibility for benefits such as a disability allowance or disability certificate. For adults the WAIS is used; for children with special educational needs, the WISC or an Indian equivalent. Every such use rests on current, local norms: a test normed decades earlier inflates scores (the Flynn effect, Section 9.7), which can wrongly deny someone a diagnosis or support. Scan Your Brain Fill in each blank with the most appropriate term. The answers are below; cover them first. Edwin Boring's statement that intelligence is "what the tests test" is an example of an definition. Wechsler defined intelligence as the aggregate or capacity to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment. The term "mental test" was coined in 1890 by . Binet and Simon's first scale (1905) contained items. The term intelligence quotient was coined in 1912 by . A 10-year-old with a mental age of 8 has a ratio IQ of . The Army was the non-verbal test for illiterate recruits. On a Wechsler scale, an IQ of 85 corresponds to the percentile. The WAIS-IV index built from Digit Span and Arithmetic is the Index. For an illiterate rural Indian child, the most culture-fair of the Indian tests is Battery of Performance Tests. Answers: (1) operational, (2) global, (3) James McKeen Cattell, (4) 30, (5) William Stern, (6) 80, (7) Beta, (8) 16th, (9) Working Memory, (10) Bhatia's. 9.4 The Structure of Intelligence: Factor Theories Medium yield · 9 Qs Once there were tests, a new question could be asked with data rather than opinion. If intelligence is one thing, people who do well on one test should do well on all of them. If it is many things, a person could be strong in one and weak in another. The tool for deciding between these possibilities was invented for the purpose, and it shaped the next hundred years of theory. Factor Analysis in Plain Words Suppose 200 Class 9 students take tests in English, Hindi, mathematics, physics and drawing. You correlate every test with every other and lay out the correlations in a table, a correlation matrix. You notice that English and Hindi correlate highly with each other, mathematics and physics correlate highly with each other, and every test correlates at least a little with every other. Factor analysis is a family of statistical methods that asks how few underlying variables, called factors , are needed to explain such a pattern of correlations. Each test's correlation with a factor is its factor loading . Here you might find one factor on which all five tests load (a general ability), plus a "language" factor and a "mathematics-science" factor. The method does not tell you what the factors mean; the researcher names them by looking at which tests load on them, and different methods of extracting and rotating factors can give different-looking answers from the same data. That is why factor analysts have argued for a century. Spearman's Two-Factor Theory The British psychologist Charles Edward Spearman (1863 to 1945) invented the first form of factor analysis. In 1904, in a paper titled "General Intelligence, Objectively Determined and Measured", he analysed the school marks and sensory-discrimination scores of English schoolchildren (in classics, French, English, mathematics, pitch discrimination and music). He found that all the measures correlated positively with one another, a pattern now called the positive manifold . Moreover, the correlations fell into a neat hierarchy, a regularity Spearman later expressed as "tetrad differences" close to zero, which is exactly what you would expect if a single common factor ran through every measure. He called this common factor general intelligence (g) . Every test, he proposed, measures g plus a specific factor (s) peculiar to that test: the ability to do arithmetic depends partly on g and partly on a specific arithmetical skill. Because it has exactly two kinds of factor, general and specific, this is called the two-factor theory (Figure 9.2). Tests differ in how heavily they are "saturated" with g; Spearman found that tasks requiring abstract reasoning were the most saturated, and simple sensory tasks the least. He interpreted g as a kind of general mental energy, and in 1923 he described three "noegenetic" (knowledge-creating) principles that he thought defined it: the apprehension of experience, the eduction of relations (seeing the relationship between two things) and the eduction of correlates (applying a relationship to generate a new item). Raven's matrices, built by his student, are a direct test of eduction. In The Abilities of Man (1927) Spearman admitted that some tests also share narrower group factors, such as verbal or mechanical ability, but g remained the centre of his theory. Spearman (1904): g plus s g Classics s1 French s2 Maths s3 Music s4 each test score = g + its own s Thurstone (1938): 7 primary abilities Verbal comprehension (V) Word fluency (W) Number (N) Space (S) Associative memory (M) Perceptual speed (P) Reasoning or induction (R or I) Later: the seven correlate (a higher g) Figure 9.2 Two early answers to "one or many?". In Spearman's two-factor model every test draws on the same general factor g plus its own specific factor s. In Thurstone's model there are seven separate primary abilities and no g, although Thurstone later found that the seven themselves correlate, which brings a general factor back at a higher level. Exam trap Spearman's g is a general factor underlying performance on all cognitive tasks; s is the specific factor of each task. Neither is "group factors" (that is Thurstone, Burt and Vernon) nor "genetic predisposition". The two-factor theory is not the triarchic model (Sternberg), multiple intelligences (Gardner), seven primary abilities (Thurstone) or fluid and crystallised intelligence (Cattell). The same Spearman gave us the rank-order correlation coefficient (rho) and, with William Brown, the Spearman-Brown formula used in reliability. Thorndike's Multifactor Theory Edward Lee Thorndike (1874 to 1949), the learning theorist of Chapter 6, rejected g. For him intelligence was the product of a vast number of separate stimulus-response connections, and a person was more intelligent simply by having more of them. This multifactor theory is sometimes called the "anarchic" theory, because it allows no governing general factor. Thorndike distinguished three broad kinds of intelligence: abstract intelligence (dealing with ideas and symbols), mechanical intelligence (also called concrete intelligence: dealing with things and tools) and social intelligence (dealing with people). In 1920 he defined social intelligence as the ability to understand and manage men and women, boys and girls, and to act wisely in human relations. His later test, the CAVD (1927), combined four kinds of item, sentence Completion, Arithmetic, Vocabulary and following Directions, and he described intelligence along four dimensions: level (the difficulty of tasks one can solve), range (the number of tasks one can solve at a given level), area (the total of the ranges across levels) and speed. A related idea came from the English-born psychologist Godfrey Hilton Thomson (1881 to 1955), who spent most of his career at Newcastle and then Edinburgh. His sampling theory (first proposed in 1916 and developed in The Factorial Analysis of Human Ability , 1939) showed that the positive manifold does not prove that a single g exists. Suppose the mind contains a huge number of small, independent "bonds" or elementary abilities, and every test calls on a random sample of them. Any two tests will then share some bonds by chance, and so will correlate, even though nothing general exists. Correlation among tests, Thomson pointed out, could come from overlapping samples rather than from one common cause. Versions of this argument are still debated today. Thurstone's Primary Mental Abilities Louis Leon Thurstone (1887 to 1955) of the University of Chicago developed a more powerful method, multiple factor analysis, designed to find several factors at once. In Primary Mental Abilities (1938) he gave 56 tests to 240 university students and extracted seven factors that he called the primary mental abilities : verbal comprehension (V), word fluency (W), number (N), space (S), associative memory (M), perceptual speed (P) and reasoning, also called induction (R or I). Thurstone argued that these seven were distinct abilities, not reflections of g, and he built the Primary Mental Abilities tests (1941, with his wife Thelma Gwinn Thurstone) to give each person a profile across them. Because it replaces one ruler with a small number of group factors, his view is called a group-factor theory (sometimes "oligarchic", rule by a few). The story has a twist. When the Thurstones tested schoolchildren, whose abilities are less differentiated than those of university students, the seven factors correlated substantially with one another. And a set of correlated factors can itself be factor-analysed, yielding a "second-order" general factor. Spearman and Thurstone were, in the end, both partly right: there are several distinct broad abilities, and there is something general that they share. The hierarchical models below formalise that compromise. Exam trap Count carefully. Thurstone: seven primary mental abilities (1938). Gardner: seven intelligences in 1983, eight after the naturalist was added in 1999. Do not mix the lists: "spatial" appears in both, but "word fluency", "perceptual speed" and "associative memory" are Thurstone's, while "musical", "bodily-kinaesthetic" and "intrapersonal" are Gardner's. Thurstone is also the Thurstone of attitude scaling (the method of equal-appearing intervals) in the Social book. In the Indian textbook classification, the unifactor or "monarchic" theory is Binet's (one general ability), the "oligarchic" theory is Thurstone's (a few group factors) and the "anarchic" theory is Thorndike's (many independent abilities). Guilford's Structure of Intellect Joy Paul Guilford (1897 to 1987), who had worked on the selection of aircrew during the Second World War, went furthest in the direction of many abilities. His structure of intellect (SOI) model , set out fully in The Nature of Human Intelligence (1967), classifies every intellectual task along three dimensions, pictured as a cube (Figure 9.3): Operations , the kind of mental process involved (five): cognition, memory, divergent production (generating many possible answers to an open problem, the basis of creativity), convergent production (arriving at the one correct answer) and evaluation. Contents , the kind of material the process works on (four): figural, symbolic, semantic and behavioural. Products , the form the information takes (six): units, classes, relations, systems, transformations and implications. Every combination of one operation, one content and one product defines a separate ability, so the model contains 5 × 4 × 6 = 120 abilities. For example, knowing what words mean is the cognition of semantic units; thinking up as many uses as possible for a brick is the divergent production of semantic units. Guilford later split the figural content into visual and auditory, giving 5 × 5 × 6 = 150 abilities (sources date this to 1977 or 1982), and in 1988 he split memory into memory recording and memory retention, giving 6 × 5 × 6 = 180. OPERATIONS (5), front slice to back slice: cognition, memory, divergent production, convergent production, evaluation PRODUCTS (6) Units Classes Relations Systems Transformations Implications Figural Symbolic

incentive and goal, trace the motivational cycle, and classify motives as primary or secondary and as intrinsic or extrinsic. 10.2 Instinct Theories : explain the instinct theories of James, McDougall and Freud, the ethologists' fixed action patterns, and why instinct theory declined. 10.3 Drives, Homeostasis and Arousal : describe homeostasis, Hull's drive-reduction theory and its limits, optimal arousal, the Yerkes-Dodson law and sensation seeking. 10.4 The Pull of the Goal: Incentives, Expectancies and Opponent Processes : contrast push and pull theories, explain expectancy-value thinking, and describe the opponent-process theory of acquired motivation. 10.5 Hierarchies of Need: Maslow, Alderfer and Other Lists : state Maslow's hierarchy precisely, distinguish deficiency from growth needs, evaluate the theory, and compare it with Alderfer's ERG theory and other lists of needs. 10.6 Psychosocial Motives and Achievement : explain Murray's needs and press, McClelland's three needs, Atkinson's theory of achievement motivation, fear of success and Weiner's attribution theory. 10.7 Intrinsic Motivation, Competence and the Self : explain curiosity, competence, self-efficacy, the overjustification effect, self-determination theory, flow and the consistency motive. 10.8 Conflict and Frustration : classify motivational conflicts, use Miller's gradients to predict behaviour, and describe the sources of frustration and the ways people react to it. 10.9 Biological Motives: Hunger, Thirst, Sex and Others : explain what starts and stops eating and drinking, how the hypothalamic "centre" theory was revised, and the classic findings on sexual and maternal motivation. 10.10 Motivation in Practice: Work, School and Clinic : apply Herzberg, Vroom, Adams and Locke to work, apply motivation research to the classroom, and describe motivational interviewing. Weightage. 76 of the 819 questions mapped in this book (9.3%) test this chapter, 36 of them from real past papers. 3 of its 10 sections are High yield. In a primate laboratory at the University of Wisconsin in Madison, at the end of the 1940s, a young rhesus monkey sat in its home cage fiddling with a small wooden board. Screwed to the board was a puzzle made of three pieces of hardware: a metal pin, a hook and a hasp. To undo the hasp, the monkey had to pull the pin first, then lift the hook, and only then swing the hasp open. There was nothing behind the hasp. No raisin, no peanut, no sip of juice. The monkey had been fed and watered as usual. Yet it worked at the puzzle, again and again, and when the experimenters put the pieces back together it took them apart again. The experimenters were Harry Harlow, Margaret Kuenne Harlow and Donald Meyer, and in 1950 they reported what they had seen. Monkeys left with assembled puzzles for about two weeks became fast, nearly error-free solvers. Monkeys given the same puzzles already taken apart, so that there was nothing to solve, did not. Harlow even reported that bringing food into the test tended to disrupt the monkeys' smooth performance rather than improve it. The monkeys, the authors concluded, were driven by the activity itself. They called it a manipulation drive. Why should this small observation have caused such a stir? Because in 1950 the most powerful theory in American psychology said it should not happen. According to that theory, an animal learns a response only when the response reduces a biological need: hunger, thirst, pain. Harlow's monkeys were not hungry, not thirsty and not in pain. What need was being reduced? If you have ever done the newspaper Sudoku on a bus to Mysuru, or stayed up past midnight to finish a crossword that nobody will ever check, you already know the answer the theory could not give. This chapter is about that puzzle: why animals and people do what they do. You will meet instincts, drives, arousal, incentives, needs, expectancies and the self, roughly in the order psychology met them. Keep Harlow's monkeys in mind as you read; we will come back to them at the end of the chapter. 10.1 What Motivation Is Medium yield · 7 Qs The word motivation comes from the Latin movere , "to move". In psychology it refers to the processes that start behaviour, give it direction, set its intensity and keep it going until it ends. Notice the four parts of that definition, because questions are built on them. Activation is the starting of behaviour (you get up from your desk). Direction is the choice of one goal over others (you walk to the kitchen, not the television). Intensity is how much effort goes in (you stride, you do not stroll). Persistence is how long the behaviour continues in the face of obstacles (you keep searching after finding the biscuit tin empty). No one has ever seen a motive. You see a student studying until 2 a.m., and you infer that something inside is pushing or pulling him. Motivation is therefore a hypothetical construct, an intervening variable placed between what we can observe (hours without food, a promised reward) and what we can measure (speed, effort, persistence). This is why the history of motivation is a history of competing guesses about what that invisible something is. Need, drive, motive, incentive and goal Five words recur in every theory in this chapter, and the exam treats them as distinct. Take one example, thirst, and follow it through. A need is a state of deficiency or lack within the organism. After a long afternoon in a Mysuru summer, your body is short of water. That shortage is a physiological need, and it exists whether or not you feel it. A drive is the aroused, tense psychological state that a need produces and that energises behaviour. You feel thirsty, restless and irritable. Need is the biological condition; drive is its psychological consequence. The two are not perfectly correlated: a person can have a need without a strong drive (old people can become dangerously dehydrated without feeling very thirsty), and a drive can outlast the need. A motive is the broader term for any internal state that arouses and directs behaviour towards a goal. In practice "drive" is reserved for biologically based states and "motive" for learned, psychological and social ones, such as the motive to achieve or to be liked. John Atkinson used "motive" in a narrower sense still: a stable personality disposition that a person carries from situation to situation. An incentive is an external stimulus or object that attracts (positive incentive) or repels (negative incentive) the organism. A cold bottle of water in a shop window is an incentive; so is the thought of the chai stall after the exam. A goal is the end state towards which motivated behaviour is directed, the incentive as it is represented and pursued: reaching the water and drinking it. The commonly taught shorthand is that drives push from inside and incentives pull from outside. The motivational cycle Put the five terms in order and you get the motivational cycle : a need gives rise to a drive; the drive energises instrumental behaviour , that is, goal-directed activity that is a means to an end; the behaviour reaches the goal or incentive; reaching the goal reduces the drive and brings relief; and after a while the need builds up again and the cycle restarts. Figure 10.1 draws the cycle for thirst. The cycle is a useful teaching device, but notice that it is drawn from one theory, drive reduction, which you will meet in Section 10.3. Much of the rest of the chapter is about behaviour that does not fit it. 1 Need body short of water 2 Drive felt thirst, tension 3 Behaviour walk to the water tap 4 Goal (incentive) drinking water 5 Relief drive reduced, rest The motivational cycle (example: thirst; the need returns later) Figure 10.1 The motivational cycle. A need produces a drive, the drive energises instrumental behaviour, the behaviour reaches the goal, and the drive is reduced until the need builds up again. Notice that this picture is drive-reduction theory in miniature. Classifying motives The most common classification divides motives by their origin. The primary motives , also called biological, physiological or unlearned motives, are rooted in the body's survival needs and are present without learning: hunger, thirst, the need for oxygen, sleep, avoidance of pain, temperature regulation, elimination, sex and, in many textbooks, the maternal drive. Most of them are homeostatic (they correct a bodily imbalance); sex and the maternal drive are the usual exceptions, because no tissue is depleted when they are unsatisfied. The secondary motives , also called psychosocial, social, acquired or learned motives, develop through experience and culture: achievement, affiliation, power, approval, aggression, curiosity about a particular subject, the wish for money. They vary enormously between people and between cultures. Between the two sits a group that some textbooks (following Clifford Morgan and Richard King) call general or unlearned non-homeostatic motives: curiosity, activity, manipulation and the need for contact comfort. They seem to be inborn, like primary motives, yet they repair no tissue deficit. Harlow's monkeys belong here. Table 10.1 sets out the three classes side by side. The personality theorist Henry Murray (you will meet him properly in Section 10.6) drew the same line with his own words. His viscerogenic needs are the primary needs tied to bodily events (air, water, food, sex, urination, avoidance of heat, cold and harm). His psychogenic needs are the secondary needs that arise from mental life and are only loosely connected to the body (achievement, affiliation, dominance, autonomy, order). Motives can also be classified by awareness: conscious motives are ones the person can report, and unconscious motives (the core of Freud's theory) drive behaviour without the person knowing why. Finally, the American personality psychologist Gordon Willard Allport (1897 to 1967) pointed out in 1937 that a learned motive can cut loose from its origins. A man who went to sea to earn a living may, when rich, still long for the sea. Allport called this functional autonomy : a means can become an end in itself, so today's motive need not be explained by the need that started it. Table 10.1 A working classification of motives. Class Other names Examples Key feature Primary Biological, physiological, unlearned, viscerogenic Hunger, thirst, sleep, pain avoidance, sex, maternal drive Rooted in body; mostly homeostatic General Unlearned non-homeostatic, stimulus motives Curiosity, exploration, manipulation, activity, contact comfort Inborn but repair no tissue deficit Secondary Psychosocial, social, learned, acquired, psychogenic Achievement, affiliation, power, approval, gregariousness Learned; vary by person and culture Exam trap Gregariousness , the tendency to seek the company of others, is classed as a social motive (RML 2022 keyed "social motive" over biological, psychological and personal). The bait is that William McDougall listed gregariousness as one of his instincts (Section 10.2). In the textbook classification of motives, the answer is still "social". Similarly, "psychological motive" and "personal motive" are not standard class names; do not be drawn to them. Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation A second, cross-cutting distinction concerns where the reward lies. The desire to do something for its own sake, because the activity itself is interesting, enjoyable or satisfying, is called intrinsic motivation . The desire to do something for a separable outcome (money, marks, praise, or the avoidance of punishment) is called extrinsic motivation . A child who reads comics under the blanket is intrinsically motivated; the same child reading the prescribed textbook to escape a scolding is extrinsically motivated. A classic past-paper example: a toddler goes to great lengths to open a box that she knows is empty. Nothing is inside, so there is no external payoff; the opening is the reward. That is intrinsic motivation. It is not homeostasis (no bodily balance is being restored), not extrinsic motivation (there is no separable reward) and not secondary motivation (nothing learned or social is being served). The two kinds of motivation can interact in surprising ways, and Section 10.7 shows how an external reward can sometimes kill an internal interest. Clinical link The intrinsic-extrinsic distinction is used diagnostically. In malingering a person deliberately produces or exaggerates symptoms for an obvious external incentive (money, avoiding duty, obtaining drugs). In factitious disorder the person also deliberately produces symptoms, but in the absence of obvious external rewards; the motive is internal, typically to occupy the sick role. Same behaviour, different motive, different diagnosis. (The disorders themselves are covered in the Psychiatric Disorders book.) Five ways of explaining motivation Before we take the theories one by one, it helps to see the whole map. Each major school of psychology produced its own answer to "why do we do what we do?", and examiners love questions that ask which school said what.
