The cognitive model emphasises thinking and beliefs; the behavioural model emphasises conditioning and reinforcement; "statistical norms" belong to the statistical definition of abnormality (Psychiatric Disorders book), not to any school of motivation. Do not confuse "humanistic" with "existential": Maslow and Rogers are the humanistic pair; Frankl, May and Yalom are the existential names. 10.2 Instinct Theories Medium yield · 5 Qs The first scientific answer to the motivation question was the oldest folk answer dressed in new clothes: we do things because we are born to do them. A spider spins a perfect web the first time it tries; a newly hatched turtle heads for the sea. Darwin's theory of evolution (1859) made such inborn behaviour respectable, because a behaviour that helped ancestors survive could be inherited just as a beak or a wing could. Around 1900 it seemed natural to explain human motivation the same way. What counts as an instinct An instinct is a complex, unlearned pattern of behaviour that is characteristic of every member of a species and that appears in full form the first time the triggering situation arises. Four criteria follow from the definition: the behaviour is unlearned (it appears in animals reared in isolation), species-specific or universal within the species, stereotyped (performed the same way each time) and complex (more than a simple reflex such as the knee jerk). Keep these criteria in mind; you will see that most of what was called "instinct" in human beings fails them. William James (1842 to 1910), in his Principles of Psychology of 1890, defined instinct as "the faculty of acting in such a way as to produce certain ends, without foresight of the ends, and without previous education in the performance." James then made a claim that surprised his readers: human beings do not have fewer instincts than animals, they have more . His list included sucking, crying, imitation, rivalry, pugnacity, sympathy, fear, acquisitiveness, constructiveness, play, curiosity, sociability, shyness, modesty, jealousy and parental love. Humans look less instinctive, James argued, because our many instincts conflict with one another and because habit quickly modifies them; an instinct, once acted on, gets bound to particular objects and loses its blind quality. McDougall's hormic psychology The theorist most closely tied to the instinct theory of motivation is the British-born psychologist William McDougall (1871 to 1938), who moved to Harvard in 1920 and later to Duke University. In An Introduction to Social Psychology (1908) McDougall argued that instincts are the prime movers of all human activity: without them, he wrote, the organism would be like a clock without a mainspring. For McDougall an instinct was an inherited disposition with three aspects, corresponding to the old three-part division of mind. It has a cognitive aspect (the animal perceives and pays attention to certain objects), an affective aspect (perceiving the object arouses a particular emotion) and a conative aspect (the animal feels an impulse to act). Each major instinct was paired with a primary emotion, and Table 10.3 shows the famous pairs. Over time, emotions organise around particular objects into sentiments (love of one's country, hatred of a rival), and the most important of these, the self-regarding sentiment, gives character its unity. Table 10.3 McDougall's principal instincts and their primary emotions (1908). Instinct Primary emotion Instinct Primary emotion Flight Fear Self-abasement (subjection) Negative self-feeling Repulsion Disgust Self-assertion (self-display) Positive self-feeling (elation) Curiosity Wonder Parental Tender emotion Pugnacity Anger Also listed Gregariousness, acquisition, construction, reproduction McDougall's list grew across the many editions of his book; by the time of The Energies of Men (1932) he preferred the word "propensities" and listed eighteen of them, which is the figure (18 instincts) you will find in most Indian textbooks. His system is called hormic psychology , from the Greek horme , meaning an urge or impulse, because it put purposive striving at the centre of psychology. McDougall insisted that behaviour is purposive : it is directed towards goals, it persists, it varies its means when blocked, and it stops when the goal is reached. This put him in open conflict with John B. Watson's behaviourism, and the two men debated publicly in 1924. Exam trap "The instinct theory of motivation was developed by" has the keyed answer William McDougall , even though William James also wrote about instincts and Freud built his theory on them. James described instincts; McDougall made them the systematic foundation of motivation and social behaviour. Maslow is the bait from the wrong school (humanistic). A second trap: McDougall's purposive (hormic) psychology is not Edward Tolman's purposive behaviourism . Both stress goals; McDougall explained goals by instincts, Tolman by learned expectancies (Section 10.4). Freud's instincts: life and death Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) also put inborn forces at the root of motivation, though his are better described as drives. His German word was Trieb , a driving force or impulse, which his English translators rendered as "instinct". Freud said every instinct has four features: a source (a bodily need or excitation), an aim (to remove the excitation, which is felt as pleasure), an impetus (the amount of force or pressure it exerts) and an object (the thing or person through which the aim is achieved). Of the four, only the object is learned and changeable, which is why the same hunger can be satisfied by idli in Mysuru and bread in Vienna. In his final theory, set out in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920), Freud grouped all instincts into two classes. The life instincts (Eros) serve the survival of the individual and the species: hunger, thirst and above all sex. Their energy is the libido . The death instinct , which his followers named Thanatos, is an unconscious wish to return to the inorganic state; turned outwards it appears as aggression and destructiveness. Freud developed the idea after the slaughter of the First World War, and he read war and violence as evidence of it. The investment of psychic energy in an object, person or idea he called cathexis . The reservoir of all these unorganised instinctual drives is the id , which operates on the pleasure principle. (The id, ego and superego, the defence mechanisms and the psychosexual stages are taught in the Personality book; here we need only Freud's view of motivation.) Exam trap "According to Freud, human beings are motivated by powerful innate forces known as" has the answer instincts , not needs (Maslow, Murray), not drives (Hull's term, though it is a fair translation of Trieb ) and not the id (the id is the reservoir of the instincts, not the forces themselves). "Wars and violence are evidence of" the death instinct ; libido is the energy of the life instincts. Freud himself did not use the word Thanatos in his published writing; it was popularised by his followers. Ethology: fixed action patterns and sign stimuli While instinct theory was fading in human psychology, it was reborn in zoology. The new discipline was ethology , the study of animal behaviour in the natural environment, with an emphasis on its evolution and function. Its founders, the Austrian Konrad Lorenz (1903 to 1989), the Dutch-born Nikolaas Tinbergen (1907 to 1988) and the Austrian Karl von Frisch (1886 to 1982), shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973. The ethologists replaced the vague word "instinct" with precise terms. A fixed action pattern is an unlearned, stereotyped sequence of movements that, once started, runs to completion. A sign stimulus (or releaser) is the simple, specific feature of the environment that triggers it, and the hypothesised neural detector that responds to the sign stimulus was called the innate releasing mechanism . Tinbergen found that a male three-spined stickleback in breeding season attacks crude models of fish as long as their underside is red, while ignoring a realistic model without the red belly. Lorenz and Tinbergen showed that a greylag goose that sees an egg outside its nest stretches its neck and rolls the egg back with the underside of its bill; if the egg is removed mid-roll, the goose finishes the rolling movement over empty ground. A herring gull chick pecks at the red spot on its parent's bill, and the pecking brings up food. Lorenz also described imprinting , the rapid attachment of newly hatched geese to the first moving object they see, during a brief sensitive period (taught in the Learning and Developmental chapters). Why instinct theory declined As an explanation of human motivation, instinct theory had collapsed by the late 1920s, for three reasons. First, naming is not explaining . Why do people form groups? Because of a gregarious instinct. How do we know there is a gregarious instinct? Because people form groups. The argument is circular: the "instinct" is simply the behaviour renamed and then offered as its own cause. Second, the lists grew out of control. Every new behaviour seemed to earn its own instinct, and in 1924 the sociologist Luther Lee Bernard surveyed the literature and counted nearly six thousand proposed human instincts, a reduction to absurdity. Third, the evidence pointed to learning. Anthropologists showed that supposedly universal "instincts" such as pugnacity or acquisitiveness varied enormously between cultures, and the Chinese psychologist Zing-Yang Kuo (1898 to 1970) showed in 1930 that even a cat's "instinctive" killing of rats depended on rearing: most kittens that watched their mothers kill rats became rat killers, while few kittens reared together with rats ever killed one. The idea did not die completely. Ethology showed that fixed action patterns are real in many animals, and modern evolutionary psychology asks how natural selection shaped human motives such as mate preferences and fear of snakes. But psychologists stopped treating a list of instincts as an explanation, and looked for a mechanism. The mechanism they found was the drive. Remember Instinct theory explained behaviour by naming it. Its replacement, drive theory, tried to say how a bodily need turns into action. Whenever a question asks why instinct theory fell, the expected answer is circularity (naming is not explaining), followed by cultural variability and the role of learning. 10.3 Drives, Homeostasis and Arousal Medium yield · 7 Qs Drive theory begins not in psychology but in physiology, with a simple observation: the inside of a healthy body stays remarkably constant while the world outside changes. The air around you may be at 45 degrees on a Rajasthan afternoon or at 5 degrees on a Shimla morning, yet your core temperature stays near 37 degrees Celsius. How? Homeostasis The French physiologist Claude Bernard (1813 to 1878) argued in the second half of the nineteenth century that the cells of the body live in an internal sea of fluids, which he called the milieu intérieur (internal environment). The constancy of this internal environment, he wrote, is the condition for a free and independent life. The American physiologist Walter Bradford Cannon (1871 to 1945) of Harvard gave the idea its modern name: he coined the term homeostasis in 1926 and popularised it in his book The Wisdom of the Body (1932). (Some books date the term to 1932, the year of the book; the word itself first appeared in print in 1926.) Homeostasis is the tendency of the body to maintain a stable internal state by detecting deviations and correcting them. The usual model is a thermostat. A set point is the value the system tries to maintain (the temperature you dial in). When a sensor detects a deviation from it, a correction is switched on (the heater), and when the set point is restored the correction is switched off. This is negative feedback : the output of the system feeds back to reduce the deviation that produced it. Some corrections are automatic and need no behaviour at all (sweating, shivering). Others require the whole organism to act: you put on a sweater, walk into the shade or drink water. Those behavioural corrections are what a motivation theory must explain, and that is where Clark Hull came in. Hull's drive-reduction theory The word "drive" entered psychology in 1918, when Robert Sessions Woodworth (1869 to 1962) of Columbia University used it in Dynamic Psychology for the energy that powers behaviour, as distinct from the mechanisms that steer it. The theory built on the word belongs to Clark Leonard Hull (1884 to 1952) of Yale, whose Principles of Behavior (1943) was for a decade the most influential book in American psychology. Hull's drive-reduction theory runs as follows. A physiological need (a departure from homeostasis) creates a drive, an aroused state of tension that energises behaviour. The organism becomes active, and any response that happens to reduce the drive is reinforced , that is, strengthened, so that it is more likely to occur the next time the drive appears. Reinforcement, for Hull, simply is drive reduction. The goal of motivated behaviour is a return to a state of low tension. Two features of the theory are often examined. First, drive energises but does not direct . What decides which response the hungry rat makes is habit strength , the learned stimulus-response connection built up by past reinforcement; drive only multiplies it. Second, drive is general: Hull believed that the energy from any drive pooled together and energised whatever habit was strongest at the moment. Hull expressed all this in a formula. In its later form (by 1952) it reads, in simplified notation: Reaction potential S E R = S H R × D × K × V (minus inhibition) Because the terms multiply, if any one of them is zero the response does not occur. A rat that has learned a maze perfectly (high habit strength) but has just eaten (drive near zero) will sit in the start box. Hull added that reaction potential must exceed a minimum value, the reaction threshold ( S L R ), before any response appears at all, and that above the threshold its strength shows in four measurable ways: a shorter response latency, a greater response (reaction) amplitude , meaning the vigour or size of the response, a higher probability of responding and greater resistance to extinction. Table 10.4 lists the symbols. Table 10.4 The terms in Hull's equation. Symbol Name What it stands for S E R Reaction (excitatory) potential The tendency to make the response S H R Habit strength Learned S-R bond; grows with reinforced trials D Drive Energy from need, for example hours without food K Incentive motivation Size and quality of the reward V Stimulus-intensity dynamism Stronger stimuli evoke the response more readily J Delay of reinforcement Longer delays weaken the response I R and S I R Reactive and conditioned inhibition Fatigue from responding, and learned not-responding Exam trap "The greater the intensity of a stimulus, the greater the probability that a learned response will be elicited" is Hull's stimulus-intensity dynamism (V). Incentive motivation (K) is about the size of the reward, not the strength of the stimulus. Some coaching notes wrongly gloss V as "need"; need belongs to D. Response amplitude and reaction threshold are genuine Hullian terms too, but they name a measure of the response and the minimum reaction potential needed to produce it, not the effect of stimulus intensity. Also note that the word "drive" was introduced by Woodworth (1918) , but drive-reduction theory is Hull's (1943) , and homeostasis is Cannon's term (Bernard's concept was the milieu intérieur). Primary and secondary drives Hull distinguished primary drives , which arise from tissue needs (hunger, thirst, pain, temperature, sex), from secondary drives , which are acquired through learning when a neutral stimulus is repeatedly associated with a primary drive. The clearest demonstration came from Neal Elgar Miller (1909 to 2002), Hull's colleague at Yale, in 1948. Rats were shocked in a white compartment and escaped through a door into a black one. Later, with no shock at all, the rats still hurried out of the white compartment, and they learned a completely new response (turning a wheel to open the door) to get out. Fear had become a learned drive, and reducing it was reinforcing enough to teach new behaviour. The same logic underlies Orval Hobart Mowrer 's (1907 to 1982) two-factor theory of avoidance learning (1947). Factor one is classical conditioning: a warning signal paired with shock comes to evoke fear. Factor two is operant conditioning: the avoidance response is reinforced because it reduces that fear. Mowrer's theory explains why phobic avoidance is so persistent: each escape from the feared situation reduces anxiety, and so strengthens the avoidance (the Learning chapter develops this). What drive reduction cannot explain Drive-reduction theory works well for thirst after a cricket match. It works badly for much else, and the failures pushed psychology towards new ideas. Animals and people seek stimulation. Harlow's monkeys took puzzles apart for nothing (the opening story). Robert Butler showed in 1953 that rhesus monkeys in a closed box would learn a discrimination task for the sole reward of opening a small window and looking out at the laboratory, and would keep doing so for hours. Rewards need not reduce any need. Fred Sheffield and Thornton Roby reported in 1950 that rats learned a maze to obtain saccharin, a sweetener with no nutritional value whatever. Reducing stimulation can be unbearable. At McGill University in 1954, in Donald Hebb's laboratory, Woodburn Heron and his colleagues (Bexton, Heron and Scott) paid students a generous daily wage to lie in a quiet cubicle wearing translucent goggles, gloves and cardboard cuffs, with almost nothing to see, hear or touch. By drive-reduction logic this should have been bliss. Most students quit within two or three days, and many reported difficulty thinking and vivid hallucinations. We eat when we are not hungry , as anyone who has accepted a second sweet at a wedding knows. And people deliberately raise their tension : they climb mountains, ride roller coasters and watch horror films. These findings did not abolish the concept of drive; they showed that tension reduction is only half the story. Sometimes organisms want less stimulation, and sometimes more. The next idea took that seriously. Optimal arousal theory Psychologists use arousal to mean the general level of physiological and psychological activation of the organism, running from deep sleep at one end to frantic excitement at the other. It is regulated by the brainstem's reticular activating system (the Attention and Consciousness chapter, Chapter 5, covers its anatomy). The optimal arousal theory holds that each organism tries to maintain a moderate, optimal level of arousal: when arousal is too low (boredom) it seeks stimulation, and when arousal is too high (anxiety, overload) it seeks to reduce it. The theory was set out most influentially by the Canadian psychologist Donald Olding Hebb (1904 to 1985) in a 1955 paper, "Drives and the C.N.S." (the initials punned on "central nervous system" and "conceptual nervous system"). Hebb argued that arousal acts as a general drive and that performance is best at an intermediate level of it. The theory explains sensory-deprivation distress, curiosity and thrill seeking in one stroke, which drive reduction could not. Optimal arousal theory found its classic evidence in a study that was forty years old by the time Hebb wrote. Key study: Yerkes and Dodson's dancing mice (1908) Question. Does stronger motivation always produce faster learning? Method. Robert Mearns Yerkes (1876 to 1956) and John Dillingham Dodson (1879 to 1955) at Harvard trained "dancing mice" to choose the white compartment of a discrimination box and avoid the black one; a wrong choice brought an electric shock of weak, medium or strong intensity. They also varied how hard the brightness discrimination was. Result. Learning was fastest at an intermediate shock, not the strongest one, and the harder the discrimination, the weaker the shock that produced the fastest learning. Conclusion. The relation between motivation and performance is not linear but rises and then falls, and its peak depends on task difficulty. Criticism. The original study was about shock strength in mice, not "arousal" or "anxiety" in people; the name "Yerkes-Dodson law" and the arousal interpretation came decades later, and the human evidence for a neat inverted U is weaker than textbooks suggest. The Yerkes-Dodson law , as it is now taught, has two parts. First, the relation between arousal (or anxiety) and performance is an inverted U : performance improves as arousal rises from low to moderate, peaks, and then declines as arousal rises further. Second, the optimal level depends on the task: for simple or well-learned tasks the optimum is relatively high, while for complex, difficult or new tasks the optimum is lower. Figure 10.2 shows both curves. In everyday terms, a little exam anxiety sharpens you, and a lot wrecks you, and it wrecks you sooner on a hard numerical problem than on writing your roll number. Simple or well-learned task Complex or new task best for simple task best for complex task high low Performance low high Arousal or anxiety too little: drowsy, careless too much: tense, disorganised Figure 10.2 The Yerkes-Dodson law. Performance is an inverted-U function of arousal, and the peak for a complex or new task (dashed) lies at a lower arousal level than the peak for a simple or well-learned task (solid). Why does too much arousal hurt? One answer came from J. A. Easterbrook in 1959: as arousal rises, attention narrows to fewer cues (his cue-utilisation hypothesis ). At moderate arousal, irrelevant cues are dropped and performance improves; at high arousal, relevant cues are dropped as well and performance falls, and complex tasks, which need more cues, suffer first. The same arousal logic explains a social phenomenon. Norman Triplett noticed in 1898 that cyclists rode faster when racing others than when racing the clock. Robert Zajonc (1923 to 2008) explained such social facilitation in 1965 with a drive theory: the mere presence of others raises arousal, and arousal strengthens the dominant response , the response most likely in that situation. On an easy or well-learned task the dominant response is the correct one, so an audience improves performance; on a new or difficult task the dominant response is often an error, so an audience impairs it. (Social facilitation and social loafing are developed in the Social Psychology book.) Exam trap "The Yerkes-Dodson law states that between performance and anxiety there is" an inverted-U shaped relationship . "Curvilinear" is not false (an inverted U is a kind of curve), but it is less specific, and when both appear the precise answer wins. "Linear" and "M-shaped" are simply wrong. The second half of the law is examined too: on a complex task, performance is best at a moderate arousal level, with the optimum lower than on a simple task. Never choose "very high arousal" or "independent of task difficulty". An option such as "punishment severity and learning rate" describes what the 1908 mouse experiment actually varied, but when "arousal and performance as an inverted U" is offered, that is the law as it is taught. Sensation seeking If each of us has an optimal arousal level, it need not be the same level for everyone. Marvin Zuckerman (1928 to 2018) built a research programme on that idea. In his definition, sensation seeking is the tendency to seek varied, novel, complex and intense sensations and experiences, and to take physical, social, legal and financial risks for the sake of them. Zuckerman's Sensation Seeking Scale (first version 1964) measures four components: thrill and adventure seeking (desire for risky physical activities such as skydiving), experience seeking (novel experiences through the mind, travel, music and a non-conforming lifestyle), disinhibition (seeking release through parties, drinking and varied sexual partners) and boredom susceptibility (intolerance of repetition and routine). High sensation seekers are over-represented among extreme-sport enthusiasts, early drug users and people who drive fast; biologically they tend to have low levels of the enzyme monoamine oxidase (MAO). Yet a well-fed guest still eats the gulab jamun because it is there. The theories in this section shift the spotlight outwards, to the goal, and then inwards again to what the person expects about the goal. Incentive theory: push versus pull The incentive theory of motivation holds that behaviour is motivated primarily by the pull of external rewards and the push away from external punishments, rather than by internal tension. Drives push; incentives pull. The theory explains why behaviour depends on the quality of what is on offer, and not only on how deprived the organism is. Two classic observations showed incentives at work. In 1928 Otto Tinklepaugh let monkeys watch while he hid a piece of banana under a cup; then, out of sight, he swapped it for lettuce, which monkeys normally eat readily. When a monkey lifted the cup and found lettuce, it searched about, shrieked and refused the lettuce. The monkey had been working for a specific expected incentive, not for "food". In 1942 Leo Crespi trained rats to run for different amounts of food and then switched them. Rats shifted from a large to a small reward ran more slowly than rats that had always received the small reward, and rats shifted upwards ran faster than rats always given the large one. These contrast effects forced Hull to add K, incentive motivation, to his equation. Pinel and Barnes (Biopsychology) apply the same idea to eating with their positive-incentive perspective : we are drawn to eat mainly by the anticipated pleasure of eating, which depends on the food's taste, our past experience with it, the time since we last ate, and the presence of other people, rather than by energy deficits. Section 10.9 returns to it. Modern neuroscience has refined the idea further. Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson distinguish the "wanting" of an incentive (its motivational pull, which depends on dopamine) from its "liking" (the pleasure actually felt). Their incentive-sensitisation theory of addiction (1993) proposes that drugs progressively increase wanting without increasing liking, which is why people with addiction can crave a drug they no longer enjoy. Exam trap "In incentive theory, motivation is primarily driven by" external rewards . The baits each belong to another theory: intrinsic satisfaction (self-determination theory), biological drives (Hull), self-efficacy beliefs (Bandura). Likewise "drive theory primarily explains motivation as a process to" reduce physiological needs ; seeking external rewards is incentive theory, setting long-term goals is goal-setting theory, and increasing social connections is affiliation. Expectancy-value theories Incentives do not pull equally hard on everyone. A promotion pulls hard on someone who thinks he can get it and who wants it, and hardly at all on someone who has given up or who does not care. The label expectancy-value theory covers the family of theories holding that the strength of motivation depends on two things multiplied together: the person's expectancy that an action will lead to an outcome, and the value the person places on that outcome. Because the terms multiply, motivation is zero if either is zero: a highly valued goal that seems impossible does not motivate, and neither does a certain outcome that nobody wants. The idea has several authors. Edward Chace Tolman (1886 to 1959) argued against Hull that animals learn expectancies about what leads to what (his "purposive behaviourism"), and that incentives decide whether this knowledge is shown in performance (latent learning is covered in the Learning chapter). Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947) described goals as having positive or negative valence in a person's psychological field. Julian Bernard Rotter (1916 to 2014), in Social Learning and Clinical Psychology (1954), wrote the most quotable version: the potential for a behaviour to occur in a given situation is a function of the person's expectancy that the behaviour will be reinforced and the reinforcement value of the outcome to that person. Rotter's full theory has four variables: behaviour potential , expectancy, reinforcement value and the psychological situation (the situation as the person perceives it). The same multiplicative logic reappears in John Atkinson's theory of achievement (Section 10.6), in Victor Vroom's expectancy theory of work (Section 10.10) and in Jacquelynne Eccles's model of students' choices, in which value is split into interest, importance, usefulness and cost. Exam trap A bank item reads: "The ______ framework is based on the expectancy, demand and incentive concepts", with the options behavioural, cognitive, social learning and supportive. The wording comes from organisational-behaviour textbooks, which describe three frameworks for explaining behaviour at work: the cognitive framework (built on Tolman's expectancies), the behaviouristic framework (built on reinforcement) and the social learning or social cognitive framework (Rotter, Bandura), which combines the two. The bank keys social learning ; because expectancy is also the defining idea of Tolman's cognitive approach, "cognitive" has its defenders, so read the options carefully. "Supportive" is not a framework at all but one of Keith Davis's models of organisational behaviour (autocratic, custodial, supportive, collegial). Whatever the key, expectancy and incentive are the shared ideas of Tolman, Rotter and every expectancy-value theory in this section. The opponent-process theory of acquired motivation Why do people keep doing things that hurt at first, like parachuting or running marathons, and keep taking drugs that have stopped giving them pleasure? In 1974 Richard Lester Solomon (1918 to 1995) and John D. Corbit proposed an answer in their opponent-process theory , which Solomon later (1980) called the opponent-process theory of acquired motivation. The theory assumes that the brain is built to resist strong emotional departures from neutrality. Any stimulus that produces a strong feeling arouses a primary process (the a-process), which produces the initial state, called state A (pleasant or unpleasant). The a-process automatically triggers an opponent process (the b-process), which produces the opposite feeling, state B. The two have different time courses. The a-process is quick, closely tied to the stimulus and does not change with repetition. The b-process is sluggish: it starts late, builds slowly and decays slowly after the stimulus stops. What we feel is the difference between them. So during the stimulus, state A peaks and then settles to a lower level (as the b-process grows), and when the stimulus ends, the a-process stops at once and the lingering b-process is felt on its own as an after-reaction in the opposite direction. The crucial assumption is that the b-process, unlike the a-process, grows stronger with use : with repeated exposure it starts sooner, becomes larger and lasts longer. Figure 10.3 shows the consequence. After many exposures, state A becomes weak (this is tolerance ), and state B becomes strong and long-lasting (this is withdrawal , or in the case of frightening activities, exhilaration). Motivation shifts from seeking A to escaping B. First few exposures After many exposures A state B state A state B state strong A weak A weak, brief B strong, lasting B baseline stimulus on stimulus on Figure 10.3 The opponent-process theory (after Solomon and Corbit, 1974). The line shows the feeling actually experienced (state A above the baseline, state B below it) while the stimulus is on (black bar) and after it ends. With repetition the opponent b-process grows, so A shrinks (tolerance) and the after-reaction B becomes larger and longer (withdrawal). Solomon and Corbit's favourite examples make the theory concrete. A novice parachutist is terrified during the first jump (state A) and dazed and stony-faced on landing; a veteran feels only tense eagerness during the jump and, afterwards, an exhilaration that lasts for hours (a strengthened state B). A first dose of an opiate brings intense euphoria (A) followed by mild craving (B); after hundreds of doses the euphoria is faint and the withdrawal is agonising, so the person takes the drug mainly to escape B. The same pattern, the theory claims, describes the comfort of a loved one's presence and the grief of separation, and the relief after a sauna. Clinical link Opponent-process theory gives the clinician a vocabulary for addiction: tolerance is a growing b-process, withdrawal is the b-process exposed when the drug wears off, and craving is the motive to escape B. It also explains why the risk of relapse peaks during early abstinence, when B is strongest. Siegel's conditioned-tolerance research (in the Learning chapter) adds that the b-process can become conditioned to the cues that usually accompany the drug. Exam trap There are two "opponent-process theories" in psychology. Ewald Hering's opponent-process theory (1878) is a theory of colour vision (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white; see the Sensation chapter). Solomon and Corbit's (1974) is a theory of acquired motivation and emotion . Match the author to the domain. In Solomon's theory it is the b-process , not the a-process, that strengthens with repetition. 10.5 Hierarchies of Need: Maslow, Alderfer and Other Lists High yield · 17 Qs By the 1950s American psychology had two grand theories of human nature. Psychoanalysis, the "first force", saw people as driven by unconscious sexual and aggressive instincts; behaviourism, the "second force", saw them as products of conditioning. Both, critics complained, had built their pictures of humanity from neurotic patients and hungry rats. The self-styled "third force", humanistic psychology , set out to study healthy, growing people, and to put free will, personal growth and the innate tendency to fulfil one's potential at the centre of psychology. Its two founders were Abraham Harold Maslow (1908 to 1970) and Carl Rogers (whose self theory is taught in the Personality book). Of the two, Maslow is the motivation theorist. There is a neat link to the opening of this chapter. Maslow did his doctoral research at the University of Wisconsin under Harry Harlow, studying dominance in monkeys. He left convinced that motivation had to be studied in its highest as well as its lowest forms. The hierarchy of needs Maslow first set out his theory in the paper "A Theory of Human Motivation" in Psychological Review (1943) and developed it in the book Motivation and Personality (1954). His hierarchy of needs arranges human needs in five levels, from the most basic to the most distinctively human: Physiological needs : food, water, oxygen, sleep, warmth, sex. These are the most powerful of all when unmet. Safety needs : security, stability, protection, order, freedom from fear and chaos. Maslow pointed to children's preference for routine and adults' preference for a steady job and insurance. Belongingness and love needs : friends, a partner, children, membership in a group, acceptance. (Some exam questions call this level "social needs".) Esteem needs : self-respect (competence, mastery, independence) and respect from others (status, recognition, appreciation). Self-actualisation : the need to become everything one is capable of becoming. "What a man can be, he must be," Maslow wrote. The organising principle is prepotency : lower needs are stronger than higher needs whenever they are unmet, so they must be at least partly satisfied before the higher needs take over the direction of behaviour. A starving man dreams of food, not of fame. Once food is reliable, safety becomes the dominant concern; once safety is secure, loneliness begins to hurt, and so on upwards. The lower a need stands in the hierarchy, the greater its strength and priority, so physiological and safety needs, at the base, are the lower needs (management writers call them the lower-order needs, and belongingness, esteem and self-actualisation the higher-order needs); the four levels below self-actualisation together form the deficiency needs described below. Maslow called all five levels basic needs , and he described them as instinctoid : inborn in a weak, instinct-like way, although the behaviours used to satisfy them are learned. Two points of precision are often lost in retelling. First, the hierarchy is not all-or-none. In the 1943 paper Maslow suggested that an average person might be about 85 per cent satisfied in physiological needs, 70 per cent in safety, 50 per cent in love, 40 per cent in esteem and 10 per cent in self-actualisation. A higher need emerges gradually as lower ones are partly met. Second, Maslow himself acknowledged exceptions, such as the martyr who gives up life for an ideal, or the creative person who pursues work through poverty. The familiar pyramid diagram, incidentally, is not Maslow's own drawing; it was added later by management writers. Figure 10.4 uses it because it is how the theory is examined. Self- actualisation Esteem respect, achievement Belongingness and love friends, family, acceptance Safety security, order, no danger Physiological food, water, sleep, warmth Deficiency (D) needs Growth or being (B) needs Higher needs Lower needs Figure 10.4 Maslow's hierarchy of needs (1943, 1954). The four lower levels are deficiency (D) needs; self-actualisation is a growth or being (B) need. Lower needs are prepotent: when unmet they dominate behaviour, and they must be largely met before higher needs take charge. Exam trap Memorise the order bottom to top: physiological, safety, belongingness and love (social), esteem, self-actualisation . Distractors swap safety and physiological, or put esteem above self-actualisation. "Which is NOT a level of Maslow's hierarchy?" has the answer ego , which belongs to Freud's structural model. "Maslow considers physiological and safety needs as" lower needs . The bait "greatest potency needs" is cleverly half-true: Maslow did call the lower needs prepotent (strongest when unmet), but the category name for physiological and safety needs is lower (lower-order) needs. "Transformational" is a leadership term (Burns, Bass), not Maslow's. Exam trap RML 2025 asked which need "must be mostly fulfilled before an individual seeks esteem needs". The level immediately below esteem is belongingness and love (social belonging) , so that is the correct answer. The key printed for this question gives physiological needs . Physiological needs must indeed be met first, but so must safety and belonging; the question asks which need precedes esteem, and on Maslow's ladder that is belonging. If the same wording appears, choose social belonging; if only physiological appears among lower levels, choose it. Deficiency needs, growth needs and metamotivation In Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) Maslow drew his most important distinction. The deficiency needs (D-needs) are the four lower levels. They arise from a lack, their satisfaction removes tension, and once satisfied they stop motivating; a fed person is not motivated by food. Behaviour driven by them is D-motivation , and it works much like Hull's drive reduction. The growth needs or being needs (B-needs) are different. They arise not from a lack but from the wish to grow; their satisfaction does not reduce tension but often increases it, and the more they are satisfied, the stronger they become. Maslow called the motivation of self-actualising people metamotivation (also B-motivation): they are not striving to fill a gap but are drawn towards states of being he called metaneeds or B-values, such as truth, goodness, beauty, wholeness, aliveness, uniqueness, justice, order, simplicity, playfulness and meaningfulness. When metaneeds are frustrated, the result is not a neurosis in the ordinary sense but a metapathology : cynicism and mistrust when truth is denied, apathy and loss of zest, a feeling of meaninglessness and despair. Maslow also described the Jonah complex , the fear of one's own greatness that keeps people from attempting to reach their potential. Later Maslow added to his list. In Motivation and Personality he discussed cognitive needs (to know and to understand) and aesthetic needs (for order, symmetry and beauty), which some textbooks insert between esteem and self-actualisation to make a seven-level hierarchy. And in his late writing (around 1969, and in the posthumous The Farther Reaches of Human Nature , 1971) he wrote of self-transcendence : a level beyond self-actualisation at which a person seeks to serve something beyond the self, such as others, a cause, nature or the sacred. An eight-level version (adding cognitive, aesthetic and transcendence needs) circulates widely. Self-actualisers and peak experiences The term self-actualisation was coined by the German neurologist Kurt Goldstein (1878 to 1965) in The Organism (1939), for the single master motive of any organism to realise its capacities. Maslow made it famous. He studied people he judged to be self-actualising, including historical figures such as Abraham Lincoln, Thomas Jefferson, Albert Einstein, Eleanor Roosevelt, William James, Jane Addams and Albert Schweitzer, and concluded that they made up 1 per cent or less of the population. They shared characteristics such as an efficient perception of reality, acceptance of self and others, spontaneity, a focus on problems outside themselves, a need for privacy, autonomy, a continued freshness of appreciation, deep relationships with a few people, a democratic character, a philosophical sense of humour and creativity. They also reported peak experiences : moments of intense ecstasy, wonder and awe, resembling mystical experiences, in which the sense of self is transcended. (A questionnaire measure of self-actualisation, Shostrom's Personal Orientation Inventory, is described in the Assessment book.) Exam trap "The striving for fulfilment of one's potential is called" self-actualisation . Its look-alikes: self-concept (one's organised picture of oneself, Rogers), ideal self (who one thinks one should be, Rogers), self-efficacy (belief in one's ability to perform a task, Bandura). The motivation proposed for self-actualisers is metamotivation , not D-motivation (and "E-motivation" and "F-motivation" are invented options). Goldstein coined "self-actualisation"; Maslow popularised it; Rogers spoke of an "actualising tendency" in all organisms. Evaluating Maslow Maslow's hierarchy is probably the best-known motivation theory in the world, and one of the least well supported. Four criticisms recur. Method : his self-actualisers were chosen by Maslow himself, according to his own values, so the description of self-actualisers partly describes Maslow's heroes. Evidence : in 1976 Mahmoud Wahba and Lawrence Bridwell reviewed the research and found little support for the ranking of the needs or for the idea that satisfying one level activates the next. Counter-examples : starving artists, hunger strikers and soldiers who die for comrades put higher needs before lower ones. Culture : the ladder reflects an individualistic, Western ideal in which personal fulfilment is the summit; in collectivist cultures, belonging and duty to the group may rank higher, and self-actualisation may be understood in relational terms. A survey of 123 countries by Louis Tay and Ed Diener (2011) found that the needs Maslow named are indeed universal and do predict we
