title: Cognitive Psychology (Eysenck & Keane), in full depth
text: Cognitive Psychology (Eysenck & Keane), in full depth Eysenck and Keane's Cognitive Psychology: A Student's Handbook , rewritten as real explanatory prose instead of bullet fragments. Every concept is built from scratch in full sentences, every mechanism is walked through step by step, the experiment or the patient behind each claim is named, the theorist is named wherever there is one, and each chapter closes with a worked example that pushes a real case through the machinery rather than restating it. Read a chapter cold and you should finish it understanding the concept, not merely recognising the words. How to read this The chapter order is Eysenck and Keane's own, so it doubles as a map of the book. Chapter 1 is the load-bearing one: it sets out the four approaches (cognitive psychology, cognitive neuropsychology, cognitive neuroscience, computational cognitive science) whose arguments then recur in every later chapter, and if you do not have those four straight, half the disputes further in will look like people disagreeing about facts when they are really disagreeing about method. Chapters 2 to 5 are visual perception and attention. Chapters 6 to 8 are memory. Chapters 9 to 11 are language. Chapters 12 to 14 are thinking and reasoning. Chapters 15 and 16 broaden out to emotion and consciousness. On the artwork. The figures are not yet here. The PDF of this book on file is a text-only conversion: all 281 figure boxes in it are empty, and the only image anywhere in the file is a 16×16 placeholder repeated on every page. The rule set on the Pinel book (every figure and every table, cropped from the source and placed at the paragraph that explains it) holds for this one too, and it will be applied the moment a PDF with the artwork intact turns up. Nothing here has been redrawn to fill the gap, because a redrawn diagram is not the book's diagram. The sixteen chapters Approaches to human cognition Basic processes in visual perception Object and face recognition Perception, motion and action Attention and performance Building: 6 Learning, memory and forgetting · 7 Long-term memory systems · 8 Everyday memory · 9 Reading and speech perception · 10 Language comprehension · 11 Language production · 12 Problem solving and expertise · 13 Judgement and decision making · 14 Reasoning and hypothesis testing · 15 Cognition and emotion · 16 Consciousness. Shipped in tranches, same as Pinel was, so you can start Part I while the rest is written. 1. Approaches to human cognition Cognitive psychology is the study of the internal processes that stand between a stimulus arriving and a response coming out: attending, perceiving, recognising, remembering, understanding language, reasoning, deciding. The word that does the work in that definition is internal . Nobody has ever observed a memory trace or a decision rule directly. What is observed is that someone was shown a word list and later recalled eleven of the twenty items, or that they named a picture 80 milliseconds faster when it had been primed. Everything cognitive psychology claims about the machinery in between is an inference from such measurements, and the whole methodological argument of this chapter is about which kinds of inference are trustworthy. That is why Eysenck and Keane open not with content but with four approaches . Each is a different way of getting evidence about an invisible process, each has a characteristic strength, and each has a characteristic blind spot. When two researchers disagree about, say, whether there are two visual systems or one, the disagreement is very often not about the data at all: it is about which approach's data should be allowed to settle the matter. Get the four straight now and the rest of the book stops looking like a list of controversies. The historical starting point: behaviourism and why it broke From roughly 1920 to 1950, North American psychology was dominated by behaviourism , whose founding claim ( John B. Watson , 1913) was that psychology should confine itself to observable stimuli and observable responses, because anything in between is unobservable and therefore unscientific. This was a genuinely reasonable position at the time. Introspection, the main alternative, had produced decades of disputes that no experiment could settle: when Wilhelm Wundt's laboratory and the Würzburg school disagreed about whether thought could be imageless, there was no way to check. Behaviourism broke on several problems at once. Edward Tolman 's rats learned the layout of a maze while being rewarded for nothing (latent learning), which meant learning had happened with no reinforced response to point to; the rats had built something like a cognitive map . Noam Chomsky 's 1959 review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior argued that language could not be a chain of reinforced responses, because speakers routinely produce and understand sentences that they have never heard and that have therefore never been reinforced. And the arrival of the digital computer supplied something behaviourism had lacked: a way of talking about internal processing that was not mystical. A computer plainly has internal states, plainly transforms input into output through a sequence of operations, and is plainly a physical machine. If that is respectable for a computer, it can be respectable for a person. High-yield The cognitive revolution is usually dated to the mid-1950s and given three landmarks: Noam Chomsky 's generative grammar and his 1959 demolition of B. F. Skinner; Allen Newell and Herbert Simon 's Logic Theorist, the first program to prove theorems in the way a human might; and Donald Broadbent 's filter theory of attention (1958), the first flow-diagram model of a mental process. Miller 's "magical number seven" paper (1956) belongs on the same list. Approach 1: experimental cognitive psychology This is the oldest of the four and still the default. Its method is to run behavioural experiments on healthy participants and infer the internal processing from the pattern of results, usually reaction times and error rates. The theoretical framework it grew up inside is the information-processing approach : the mind is treated as a series of stages, each taking an input, doing something to it, and passing the result on. Stimulus, then attention, then perception, then thought, then decision, then response. That early version carried two strong assumptions worth naming, because most of the subsequent history of the field consists of weakening them. The first is seriality : one stage at a time, each finishing before the next begins. The second is that processing is bottom-up (also called stimulus-driven), meaning it is determined by the input rather than by what the perceiver already knows. Both turned out to be too strong. Processing is now generally accepted to be substantially parallel , with stages overlapping in time, and heavily top-down : expectations, context and prior knowledge shape perception rather than merely decorating it. Read a smudged handwritten word in a sentence and you will read it correctly because the sentence told you what to expect; that is top-down processing doing visible work. The great strength of this approach is control. You can manipulate one variable, hold everything else fixed, and draw a causal conclusion. Its great weakness is that reaction times are a very indirect readout. Two quite different architectures can predict the same millisecond pattern, so behavioural data frequently underdetermine the theory. A related problem is paradigm specificity : a finding may hold for the particular laboratory task used and not generalise, which is a serious charge when the task is something like naming a letter in a briefly flashed array, an activity nobody performs outside a laboratory. Eysenck and Keane also flag lack of ecological validity and, more subtly, the fact that theories in this tradition are often stated vaguely enough that they are hard to falsify. Approach 2: cognitive neuropsychology Cognitive neuropsychology studies patients with brain damage in order to work out the structure of normal cognition. The logic is not "find out what the damaged area does"; it is subtler than that, and the difference matters. The reasoning runs: if brain damage can knock out ability A while leaving ability B intact, then A and B cannot depend on exactly the same machinery. Damage is being used as a natural experiment that cuts the system apart at joints an intact brain never reveals. Four theoretical assumptions underlie it, and they are examinable as a set. Modularity : the cognitive system consists of relatively independent modules or processors, each doing one job, so that one can be damaged without the others going down. Anatomical modularity : each module is localised in a reasonably circumscribed brain region, which is what makes brain damage selective rather than global. Uniformity of functional architecture across people : the patient's cognitive system was organised like yours before the damage, otherwise nothing generalises. Subtractivity : brain damage impairs or removes processes but does not cause the system to develop new ones, so the patient is the normal system minus a part, not a different system. Single and double dissociation A single dissociation is one patient who is impaired on task A but normal on task B. It is weak evidence on its own, because task A might simply be harder, and a general loss of resources would produce the same picture. A double dissociation is two patients showing the opposite pattern: patient 1 impaired on A but not B, patient 2 impaired on B but not A. Task difficulty can no longer explain both, so the two tasks must draw on at least partly separate mechanisms. This is the single most powerful inferential tool in neuropsychology and it recurs throughout the book: amnesia (episodic memory impaired, procedural learning intact) against Huntington's or Parkinson's patients (the reverse); Broca's aphasia (production impaired, comprehension relatively spared) against Wernicke's (the reverse); prosopagnosia (faces impaired, objects spared) against visual object agnosia. The limitations are equally important. Brain damage from stroke, tumour or trauma does not respect module boundaries, so patients almost always have several impairments and it is a matter of judgement which is the one of interest. Patients also compensate : by the time they are tested, months may have passed and they may be performing the task by an unusual route, which straightforwardly violates subtractivity. Numbers are small, often a single case, which makes generalisation delicate. And the whole enterprise presupposes modularity, which is at best partly true; a great deal of cognition looks distributed rather than modular, and for those parts the method has little purchase. Approach 3: cognitive neuroscience Cognitive neuroscience uses evidence from the brain, in healthy people, to constrain theories of cognition. It is best understood as a toolbox, and the single most useful thing to hold in your head is the trade-off between spatial and temporal resolution , because it explains why researchers use several techniques on the same question. Single-unit recording pushes a microelectrode next to a single neuron and records its firing. Resolution is superb in both space (one cell) and time (milliseconds), but it is invasive and therefore almost entirely an animal method. EEG records electrical activity from scalp electrodes; averaging the EEG over many trials time-locked to a stimulus yields event-related potentials (ERPs) , whose temporal resolution is of the order of a millisecond but whose spatial resolution is poor, because the inverse problem (working back from a scalp voltage pattern to the generators inside) has no unique solution. MEG records the magnetic fields produced by the same neural currents; magnetic fields are less distorted by skull and scalp than electrical ones, so MEG buys somewhat better spatial resolution while keeping the millisecond timing. PET and fMRI work the other way round. fMRI measures the BOLD signal (blood oxygen level dependent): active neurons consume oxygen, local blood flow over-compensates, and the resulting change in the ratio of oxygenated to deoxygenated haemoglobin is detectable magnetically. Spatial resolution is good, around a millimetre, but the haemodynamic response is sluggish, peaking several seconds after the neural activity, so temporal resolution is measured in seconds. fMRI tells you where with confidence and when only crudely; ERP tells you when with confidence and where only crudely. Used together they complement each other, which is exactly why they are used together. Two further techniques are worth naming. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) delivers a brief magnetic pulse through the skull that transiently disrupts processing in the cortex beneath, creating what is often called a "virtual lesion". This matters because it converts correlation into causation: fMRI can only show that a region is active during a task, whereas TMS can show that interfering with the region impairs the task. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) tracks the diffusion of water along white-matter tracts and so maps connections rather than regions, which suits the increasingly common view that cognition depends on networks rather than isolated areas. Trap The standard criticism of neuroimaging is not that it is inaccurate but that it is often merely correlational and merely locational . Showing that the fusiform gyrus is active during face processing does not by itself decide any psychological question. There is also the reverse-inference fallacy: observing amygdala activity and concluding the participant was afraid is invalid, because the amygdala is active in many conditions besides fear. Cognitive neuroscience earns its keep when a brain measure decides between two psychological theories that make identical behavioural predictions, and not when it simply adds a colourful picture to a result already established behaviourally. Approach 4: computational cognitive science The fourth approach builds computational models: programs whose behaviour is compared with human behaviour. The discipline this imposes is severe and is the main argument for the approach. A verbal theory can say "the word is activated by context" and get away with it; a program cannot, because activated by how much, from what, on what time course, and what happens when two contexts conflict must all be specified before it will run at all. Vagueness that survives in prose dies in code. Two families dominate. Production-system architectures such as ACT-R (John Anderson) represent knowledge as IF-THEN rules operating on a declarative memory, and are strong on complex, strategic, multi-step tasks such as problem solving and skill acquisition. Connectionist networks represent knowledge as patterns of activation across simple units joined by weighted connections; nothing is stored at an address, and knowledge lives in the weights. Connectionist models learn by gradually adjusting those weights (typically by back-propagation), degrade gracefully when units are removed rather than failing outright, and generalise to new inputs automatically because similar inputs produce similar activation patterns. Those three properties are also properties of human cognition, which is the substantive argument in their favour. A newer and increasingly important framework is the Bayesian or predictive-processing one, associated with Karl Friston 's free-energy formulation and with Andy Clark 's exposition of it. Here the brain is not a passive stimulus processor but a prediction machine: it continually generates top-down predictions about incoming input and only the prediction error , the mismatch, is passed forward for further processing. This turns the classic bottom-up picture upside down and provides a principled account of why top-down effects are everywhere rather than being occasional exceptions. Keep it in mind for the perception chapters, where it reappears constantly. The limitations of computational modelling are real. A model that fits the data does not thereby prove the human system works that way, since other models may fit equally well; models typically have free parameters that can be tuned until they fit, which weakens the evidential force of the fit; and models are usually built for one narrow task rather than for cognition as a whole. Comparing the four, and why nobody wins Set the four side by side and their strengths are close to complementary. Experimental cognitive psychology gives tight causal control over behaviour but indirect evidence about mechanism. Cognitive neuropsychology gives strong dissociative evidence about the separability of components but depends on messy lesions and small samples. Cognitive neuroscience gives direct measures of the brain but has to resist the temptation to treat a location as an explanation. Computational modelling forces precision but at the price of narrowness and free parameters. What follows methodologically is converging operations : a claim is credible when it is supported from more than one of these directions at once. The clearest case in this book is the two-visual-systems theory of Chapter 2. It was proposed on behavioural and anatomical grounds, then supported by a double dissociation between two patients (DF and the optic-ataxia cases), then localised by neuroimaging, then made causal by TMS to the relevant parietal region. No single one of those would have been decisive. Together they are hard to dismiss, and that is the pattern the good arguments in the rest of the book follow. Trap Do not treat the four approaches as a historical sequence in which each replaced the last. They are contemporaneous and all four are in active use. An exam answer that says cognitive neuroscience superseded experimental cognitive psychology has the relationship wrong: the experiments still supply the tasks, and without a decent behavioural paradigm there is nothing worth imaging. Worked example Take a concrete question and push it through all four approaches: is recognising a face done by the same machinery as recognising a chair? Experimental cognitive psychology notes that faces suffer far more from inversion than objects do (the face-inversion effect ) and that the parts of a face are hard to judge in isolation (the composite effect ), suggesting faces are processed holistically while objects are processed more part by part. Strong control, but everything rests on inferring a mechanism from a reaction-time difference. Cognitive neuropsychology supplies the double dissociation. Patients with prosopagnosia cannot recognise familiar faces, sometimes including their own in a mirror, while recognising objects normally; other patients with visual object agnosia show the reverse. Difficulty cannot explain both directions, so at least partly separate mechanisms exist. Cognitive neuroscience localises it: the fusiform face area responds far more to faces than to objects, and ERP work finds the face-selective N170 component at around 170 ms, telling you the separation happens early rather than at a late decision stage. TMS over the relevant occipitotemporal site selectively impairs face discrimination, which upgrades the claim from correlation to causation. Computational modelling asks what "holistic" would actually mean in a working system, and shows that a network trained to discriminate many individuals within one visually homogeneous category naturally develops representations sensitive to the whole configuration rather than to parts, which explains why faces would be special without having to stipulate a face module by fiat. The answer that survives all four is not "there is a face module" but something more careful: face recognition depends on configural or holistic processing that object recognition uses much less, this shows up early, it can be lost selectively, and it may arise from expertise with a homogeneous category rather than from a genetically specified face box. Notice that each approach on its own would have supported a cruder conclusion. That is the argument for using all four. 2. Basic processes in visual perception Vision feels effortless and immediate, and that feeling is the main obstacle to studying it. What actually arrives at the eye is a two-dimensional, constantly moving, ambiguous pattern of light intensities; what is experienced is a stable three-dimensional world of coloured objects at definite distances. Everything in between has to be constructed, and this chapter is about how the construction is done and where it can be caught out. One framing point before the machinery. David Marr 's influential analysis proposed that any information-processing system can be described at three levels: the computational level (what problem is being solved and why), the algorithmic level (what representations and procedures solve it), and the implementational level (how that is realised in neurons). Much apparent disagreement in perception research is disagreement across levels rather than within one, and Marr's point was that a complete account needs all three. Vision and the brain: the route from retina to cortex Light reaches the retina, where two classes of photoreceptor transduce it. Cones are concentrated in the fovea, need good light, and support colour vision and fine detail. Rods dominate the periphery, work in dim light, and are colour-blind. The functional consequence is that acuity and colour are excellent where you are looking and poor everywhere else, which is why the eye must move constantly; visual experience feels uniformly detailed only because you never catch the periphery being vague. From the retina, ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve. At the optic chiasm the fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross, with the result that everything in the left visual field, from both eyes, ends up in the right hemisphere and vice versa. Most fibres then synapse in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus and project to primary visual cortex (V1) , also called the striate cortex, at the occipital pole. This is the retino-geniculate-striate pathway and it carries the great majority of the traffic. A smaller retinotectal pathway runs via the superior colliculus, and it matters more than its size suggests, because it is the route that survives V1 damage and is the leading explanation of blindsight later in this chapter. Two channels run in parallel within the main pathway, distinguishable from the retina onwards. The parvocellular (P) channel has small, colour-sensitive cells with fine spatial resolution and sluggish responses; it carries detail and colour. The magnocellular (M) channel has large, colour-blind cells with coarse spatial resolution and fast, transient responses; it carries motion and rapid change. Hold this distinction: it maps roughly (not perfectly) onto the two cortical streams that dominate the rest of the chapter. High-yield David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel 's single-unit recordings in cat and monkey V1 (Nobel Prize 1981) identified cells tuned not to spots of light but to oriented edges . Simple cells respond to a bar of a particular orientation at a particular retinal position. Complex cells respond to the same orientation anywhere within a larger region, and often prefer a direction of movement. The architecture is columnar: cells in a vertical column share an orientation preference, and a hypercolumn contains a full set of orientations plus both ocular-dominance columns for one patch of the visual field. The theoretical significance is that the very first cortical stage is already extracting features rather than transmitting a picture, and it does so with position invariance increasing as you ascend. Beyond V1, processing becomes increasingly specialised: V4 is strongly implicated in colour and in shape, and V5/MT in motion. The evidence for functional specialisation is not merely correlational. Damage to V4 can produce achromatopsia , in which the world is seen in shades of grey while form and motion are intact; damage to V5/MT can produce akinetopsia , in which motion perception is lost while colour and form survive. The best-documented akinetopsia case, patient LM, described the world as a series of still snapshots, saw the coffee appear to freeze in the air while pouring, and found crossing roads dangerous because a car that was far away seemed suddenly to be close. Colour lost with motion spared, and motion lost with colour spared, is a double dissociation, and it is why functional specialisation is not seriously disputed. Two visual systems: perception and action The most important theoretical claim in this chapter is that vision serves two different jobs and does so through two anatomically distinct cortical streams. The formulation to know is Milner and Goodale 's (1992, and revised repeatedly since). The ventral stream runs from V1 down into the inferotemporal cortex and is the vision-for-perception system. It is concerned with identifying and recognising what an object is. It works in an allocentric frame, meaning object-relative or scene-relative coordinates, which is the right choice for recognition because an object's identity should not change when you move. It relies on stored knowledge, is relatively slow, and its products are available to consciousness. The dorsal stream runs from V1 up into the posterior parietal cortex and is the vision-for-action system. It is concerned with locating objects and with the visual control of movements towards them. It works in an egocentric frame, in coordinates centred on the actor's hand or eye, because to grasp something you need to know where it is relative to you . It is fast, operates largely without conscious awareness, and its representations are short-lived, since information about where something was two seconds ago is useless for a movement made now. The defining double dissociation Patient DF suffered carbon monoxide poisoning producing bilateral damage to the lateral occipital complex in the ventral stream, leaving her with visual form agnosia. Asked to report the orientation of a slot, or to rotate a card to match it, she performed at chance. Asked to post the card through the same slot, she rotated her hand accurately as she reached. She could not see the orientation, yet she could act on it. Optic ataxia patients, with damage to the posterior parietal cortex in the dorsal stream, show the reverse: they can describe an object's size, shape and orientation perfectly well but misreach for it and shape the hand badly as they grasp. Perception intact, action impaired. Two patients, opposite patterns, same tasks. Task difficulty cannot explain both, so perception and action must depend on at least partly separate systems. Converging support comes from healthy participants via visual illusions. In the Ebbinghaus (Titchener) illusion , a disc surrounded by large circles looks smaller than an identical disc surrounded by small circles. Ask people to judge the sizes and they are fooled. Ask them to reach out and pick the disc up, and the maximum grip aperture as the hand opens in flight is scaled to the disc's real size, or very nearly. Perception is fooled while action is not, which is what the two-systems account predicts. Trap The grasping-versus-illusion evidence is genuinely contested, and a good answer says so. Franz and others argued that the perceptual and grasping tasks were not properly matched: perceptual judgements were often made with both discs visible while grasping was directed at one, and grasping benefits from visual feedback from the hand that judgement does not get. When the tasks are equated more carefully, the dissociation shrinks and sometimes disappears. The safest position is that the anatomical and neuropsychological evidence for two streams is strong, while the claim that action is wholly immune to illusion is not. Milner and Goodale themselves revised the theory towards more interaction between the streams, which is why "two streams, extensively interacting" is a better summary than "two independent systems". Colour vision Colour is a construction, not a property of light. Light has wavelengths; colour is the visual system's response to them, and the mapping is many-to-one, which is why two physically different spectra can look identical. Two classical theories were long treated as rivals and are now understood as descriptions of successive stages. Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory holds that there are three cone types with peak sensitivities in the short (blue, around 420 nm), medium (green, around 530 nm) and long (red, around 560 nm) wavelengths, and that colour is coded by the ratio of activity across the three. This is straightforwardly correct at the receptor level and explains why three primaries suffice to match any colour, and why most colour deficiency involves one cone class being absent or shifted. Ewald Hering's opponent-process theory holds that colour is coded by three opponent channels, red-green, blue-yellow and black-white, each signalling one member of the pair by increased activity and the other by decreased activity. This explains what trichromatic theory cannot: negative afterimages (stare at red, look away, see green, because the red-green channel adapts and rebounds), the fact that no colour is ever described as reddish-green or bluish-yellow, and the pattern of the common colour deficiencies, which come in red-green and blue-yellow varieties rather than in single-colour ones. Opponent cells with exactly this organisation were later recorded in the LGN. The resolution is that trichromatic coding happens at the cones and opponent coding at the ganglion cells and beyond. The deeper problem is colour constancy : a banana looks yellow in daylight and under a tungsten bulb, although the wavelength composition reaching the eye differs enormously. Since the light reaching the eye is the product of the illuminant and the surface reflectance, and only the product is available, recovering the reflectance requires discounting the illuminant, which is formally an underdetermined problem. The visual system solves it approximately using several cues: chromatic adaptation (receptors adapt to the prevailing illumination), the relations between a surface and its surround rather than absolute values, familiarity with the object's typical colour, and specular highlights, which tend to carry the illuminant's own colour. Land 's retinex theory is the best-known formal proposal, computing lightness separately in each of three wavebands by comparing across the whole scene. Constancy is good but not perfect, which is exactly what you would expect from a system using approximate cues; the viral disagreement about "the dress" was a case where the cues to the illuminant were unusually ambiguous and different observers' visual systems settled on different assumptions. Depth perception The retinal image is two-dimensional and depth must be inferred. The cues divide cleanly and are worth memorising by group. Monocular (pictorial) cues are available to one eye and are the ones painters use. Linear perspective : parallel lines converge with distance. Texture gradient (Gibson's favourite): a uniformly textured surface projects finer, denser texture as it recedes. Interposition or occlusion : a partly hidden object is further away. Relative size : with two objects known to be the same size, the smaller image is more distant. Familiar size : knowing the real size lets image size specify distance. Aerial perspective : distant objects are hazier and bluer because of atmospheric scattering. Shading : patterns of light and shadow specify three-dimensional shape, under a default assumption that light comes from above. Height in the visual field : objects nearer the horizon are further away. Motion-produced cues require movement. Motion parallax : when you move, near objects sweep across the retina faster than far ones and in the opposite direction relative to the fixation point. This is a powerful cue and available to one eye, which is why people with one eye judge depth far better while moving. Binocular and oculomotor cues require two eyes or feedback from the eye muscles. Convergence : the eyes turn inwards for near objects, and the muscular signal indicates distance, though only usefully within about two metres. Accommodation : the lens changes shape to focus, another muscular signal with a similarly short range. Binocular disparity : the eyes are about 6.5 cm apart, so each receives a slightly different image, and the magnitude of the difference specifies depth. This is stereopsis and it is the most precise depth cue at close range. High-yield Julesz 's random-dot stereograms settled an old question. Each eye is shown a field of random dots containing no recognisable form whatever; a central region is shifted horizontally in one eye's image. Viewed one eye at a time there is nothing to see. Viewed binocularly, the central region floats clearly in front of the background. Since there is no monocular form to recognise, stereopsis cannot depend on first identifying objects and then comparing them: disparity is computed early, on unstructured input, before recognition. This is a clean demonstration that a process happens earlier than intuition suggests. Real perception uses cue combination , and the modern account of it is Bayesian: cues are weighted by their reliability in the current conditions and combined, which is why depth judgements degrade gracefully rather than collapsing when one cue is removed. Size constancy follows from the same machinery. Perceived size is a function of retinal size and perceived distance, so when distance is registered correctly an object retains its apparent size as it recedes. The Ponzo and Müller-Lyer illusions and the Ames room are all cases where the distance information is manipulated and size perception follows it obediently, which is evidence that the constancy mechanism is real rather than evidence that perception is unreliable. Perception without awareness The claim that stimuli can be processed without being consciously perceived has a poor reputation because of the subliminal-advertising folklore, so the evidence has to be assessed carefully; but the careful evidence is good. Blindsight is the strongest case. Patients with damage to V1 report no conscious vision in the corresponding part of the field, yet when forced to guess they perform above chance at locating a stimulus, discriminating its orientation or direction of motion, and sometimes at detecting emotional expression. The best-known case, DB , studied by Weiskrantz , was consistently astonished to be told his guesses had been correct. The standard explanation is the retinotectal pathway via the superior colliculus, which bypasses V1 and can support crude discrimination without generating conscious experience. The standard sceptical alternative is that small islands of spared V1 tissue support degraded normal vision, and this is why later work concentrated on demonstrating qualitatively different performance rather than merely weaker performance in the blind field. Subliminal perception in healthy people is demonstrated with masked priming: a prime word is presented for a few tens of milliseconds and immediately masked, so that participants cannot report it or even reliably detect its presence, yet it speeds responses to a semantically related target. The methodological issue that dominates this literature is how to establish that awareness was genuinely absent. An objective threshold (chance performance on a forced-choice detection task) is a stricter criterion than a subjective threshold (the participant says they saw nothing), and effects that survive the objective threshold are the ones worth citing. The honest summary is that unconscious processing is real, that it extends at least to simple semantic properties, and that its effects are small and short-lived, which is precisely why subliminal advertising does not work as advertised. Worked example Reach out and pick up the mug on your desk. Trace what the chapter says just happened. Light from the mug falls on the retina; cones in the fovea handle the detail and colour of the part you are looking at, rods contribute nothing much in office lighting. Signals split into the P channel (the mug's colour and the fine detail of the handle) and the M channel (any movement, including the movement produced by your own hand). Fibres from the left half of each retina reach the right hemisphere. In V1, simple and complex cells extract the oriented edges of the rim and handle. Now the two streams diverge. The ventral stream identifies it as your mug, using stored knowledge, in allocentric coordinates that do not change as you lean; this is the part you are aware of, and the part patient DF has lost. The dorsal stream computes where it is in relation to your hand, in egocentric coordinates that must be updated as you move; this is the part optic-ataxia patients have lost, and the part you are not aware of, which is why you cannot introspect the size your hand is opening to. Depth comes from several cues at once: binocular disparity is precise at desk range, convergence adds a coarse distance signal, the mug occludes the papers behind it, and motion parallax updates continuously as you lean in. The mug's colour stays constant as your hand shadows it, because chromatic adaptation and surround comparison are discounting the change in illumination. Meanwhile your grip aperture is scaled to the mug's real size, not to its retinal size, which is size constancy operating on the dorsal side; if a colleague had surrounded the mug with large circles, your judgement of its size would have shifted while your grip would have shifted much less. The whole thing takes about a fifth of a second and feels like nothing at all. That gap between the effort involved and the effort experienced is the reason the chapter exists. 3. Object and face recognition Chapter 2 got as far as edges, colour and depth. That is nowhere near recognition. Recognising a chair means assigning a two-dimensional retinal pattern to a category despite the fact that the pattern changes completely with viewpoint, distance, lighting and partial occlusion, and despite the fact that no two chairs are alike. The problem is called invariance , and it is the reason object recognition was one of the hardest problems in artificial intelligence for fifty years while remaining something a three-year-old does without noticing. Pattern recognition: why templates fail The simplest possible theory is template matching : a stored template for each pattern, and recognition is finding the template that matches. It fails immediately. The letter A comes in countless fonts, sizes, orientations and handwritings, and a stored template will not match any of them exactly. You could store more templates, but the number required explodes, and the theory has no account of novel instances. Feature theories improve on this. Instead of whole templates, store a list of features, and recognise by detecting the features and combining them: an A is two oblique lines meeting at the top plus a horizontal crossbar, however it is drawn. This is far more economical and inherits real support from David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel's feature detectors in V1. Evidence includes visual search data, where finding a target defined by a feature the distractors lack is fast and roughly independent of the number of distractors. The weakness is that features alone do not fix an identity: the same features arranged differently make a different letter, so the relations between features must be represented as well. Feature theories also struggle with context effects,

title: Foundations of Clinical Psychology and Positive Psychology
text: Foundations of Clinical Psychology and Positive Psychology Built off the four references on your course reading list: Pomerantz, Trull and Phares, Lopez and Snyder, Baumgardner and Crothers. Sixteen chapters, taught from scratch. Your course named four books you can't afford. This is the ground those four books cover, written out as a textbook you can learn from cold. Part I is clinical psychology : what it is, where it came from, the models clinicians think with, diagnosis, the interview and the mental status examination, assessment, psychotherapy, ethics and law, and the specialties and culture. That is the ground of Pomerantz and of Trull and Phares. Part II is positive psychology : what it is, happiness and well-being, positive emotions, strengths and flow, optimism and resilience, relationships and meaning, and positive psychology in the clinic. That is the ground of Baumgardner and Crothers and of the Oxford Handbook. Part I: Clinical psychology 1 What clinical psychology is, and who does it Every professional subject has to begin by saying what the profession is, and clinical psychology finds this harder than most. The public confuses it with psychiatry, with counselling and with "talking to someone", and even psychology graduates often cannot say how a clinical psychologist differs from a counselling psychologist, or what legally entitles a person in India to the title. This chapter builds the answer from the ground up: the formal definition, read word by word; what Lightner Witmer originally meant by "clinical"; what clinical psychologists do and where; how the profession differs from its neighbours; and how it is regulated in India through the Rehabilitation Council of India. It also introduces the idea that runs through this whole book: clinical psychology is meant to be a science and a helping profession at once, and holding the two together is genuinely hard. The chapter ends with a day in the life of a clinical psychologist in an Indian hospital. This is the ground of the opening chapters of the clinical textbooks on your list (Pomerantz; Trull and Phares), and definitions, professional comparisons and the Indian regulatory position are among the most frequently examined topics in the subject. 1.1 The formal definition, read word by word The American Psychological Association is organised into numbered divisions, each representing a specialty. Clinical psychology is Division 12, the Society of Clinical Psychology, and its definition is the one most often quoted in textbooks: "The field of Clinical Psychology integrates science, theory, and practice to understand, predict, and alleviate maladjustment, disability, and discomfort as well as to promote human adaptation, adjustment, and personal development. Clinical Psychology focuses on the intellectual, emotional, biological, psychological, social, and behavioral aspects of human functioning across the life span, in varying cultures, and at all socioeconomic levels." "Integrates science, theory, and practice." Science means the systematic gathering of evidence through controlled study and measurement. Theory means organised explanations of why people think, feel and behave as they do, such as the psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive and humanistic accounts of later chapters. Practice means the applied work of assessing and helping real people. The key word is "integrates". Theory without evidence hardens into dogma; practice without science becomes habit and guesswork; science without practice drifts away from the people it is meant to serve. The clinical psychologist is trained in all three and expected to let each correct the others. "Understand, predict, and alleviate." To understand a problem is to explain how it developed and what keeps it going, which is the job of assessment and of the case formulation (the clinician's working explanation of one person's difficulties). To predict is to forecast: whether a patient is at risk of suicide, whether an offender will reoffend, whether a client will respond to a treatment. Prediction is where the field's claim to be scientific is tested most directly, because predictions can be checked against what later happens. To alleviate is to reduce suffering; notice that the word is not "cure", since schizophrenia, intellectual disability or chronic pain are rarely cured in any simple sense, yet much can be done to lighten them. "Maladjustment, disability, and discomfort." The three targets are deliberately broad. Maladjustment is a poor fit between a person's behaviour and the demands of their life, such as constant conflict at home or repeated failure at work. Disability is a limitation in functioning, from intellectual disability, head injury, long-standing psychosis or dementia. Discomfort is subjective distress: anxiety, sadness, grief, shame. They can occur separately: a man may work well while privately tormented by intrusive thoughts (discomfort without maladjustment), and a child with a moderate intellectual disability may be perfectly content (disability without discomfort). By naming all three, the definition avoids saying "mental illness"; the field serves people who meet a diagnosis and people who meet none but still need help. "To promote human adaptation, adjustment, and personal development." The field is about building as well as repairing: helping people adapt, adjust to change and develop their potential. This clause is easy to skip, but it is the seed from which positive psychology, the second half of this course, grew. The scope clause then says that no single level of explanation is enough (a problem may involve brain, thinking, feelings, relationships and habits at once), that the field spans infancy to old age, that it must understand distress as the client's own culture expresses it, and that it serves all socioeconomic levels, not only those who can pay. Key. Learn the definition as two triplets plus a clause: three verbs (understand, predict, alleviate), three targets (maladjustment, disability, discomfort), and the growth clause (promote adaptation, adjustment and personal development), all resting on the integration of science, theory and practice. Trap. Clinical psychology is not "the study of abnormal behaviour". That is abnormal psychology, a body of knowledge. Clinical psychology is a discipline and a profession that uses that knowledge, with assessment, therapy and research methods, to help real people. Nor is it the same as psychotherapy, which is one of its activities and is also practised by people who are not clinical psychologists. 1.2 Lightner Witmer and the original meaning of "clinical" Who gave us this. Lightner Witmer (1867 to 1956) took his doctorate under Wilhelm Wundt at Leipzig in 1892, opened the first psychological clinic at the University of Pennsylvania in 1896, and in 1907 founded the journal The Psychological Clinic , in whose first issue he introduced and explained the term "clinical psychology". In 1896 academic psychology meant laboratory psychology in the tradition of Wilhelm Wundt, who had opened his experimental laboratory at Leipzig in 1879. Psychologists measured sensations and reaction times; they did not try to help individuals with practical problems. That year a schoolteacher brought Witmer a boy who had unusual difficulty learning to spell. Witmer examined him carefully to find where exactly the difficulty lay, designed remedial teaching, and followed his progress to see whether it worked: he had turned the methods of the laboratory on a single individual, for that individual's benefit. When he proposed the idea of a psychological clinic to the American Psychological Association later that year, most colleagues were indifferent, believing psychology should remain a pure science. The clinic grew nonetheless, seeing mainly children with learning and behavioural difficulties referred by schools. When Witmer explained his term in 1907 he made a point students often miss. He had borrowed "clinical" from medicine, but it named a method , not a place or a kind of patient: the close study of one individual through observation and experiment, followed by remedial or educational treatment to bring about change in that individual, whether a child who could not spell, a gifted child or an adult. So "clinical" did not originally mean "sick" or "in a hospital". Two lasting ideas come from Witmer: that psychological science should be used to help individual people, the root of the scientist-practitioner identity; and that assessment exists for the sake of intervention, so a person is studied in order to be helped, not merely labelled. Much has changed since. Witmer's clinic did not practise psychotherapy with adults in the modern sense, and in the early twentieth century clinical psychologists were known mainly as testers, especially after Alfred Binet produced the first practical intelligence scale in France in 1905. Psychotherapy became central only after the Second World War, when the United States Veterans Administration needed large numbers of professionals to treat returning soldiers and funded the training of clinical psychologists. Trap. Wilhelm Wundt founded experimental psychology (Leipzig, 1879). Lightner Witmer founded clinical psychology (first psychological clinic, University of Pennsylvania, 1896; the term in 1907). Sigmund Freud, a Viennese physician, founded psychoanalysis; his ideas shaped clinical psychology, but he did not found it as a profession. 1.3 What makes clinical psychology distinct The clinical textbooks agree on five distinguishing features. The first is the integration of science and practice in one person . A psychiatrist is trained first as a physician, a psychiatric social worker as a social worker, an experimental psychologist as a researcher who treats no one. The clinical psychologist is the one mental health professional whose training deliberately combines research with clinical work; in India both the older and the newer training routes require a research dissertation alongside hundreds of hours of supervised practice. The second is a focus on the individual case , often called the clinical attitude. Gordon Allport, in his 1937 book on personality, popularised two useful terms. A nomothetic approach seeks general laws that hold across many people, such as the finding that cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) reduces depression on average. An idiographic approach tries to understand one person in their own pattern: why this woman became depressed now, and what keeps it going in her family and job. The core clinical skill is translation from the average to the individual. The third is expertise in measurement : psychologists are the mental health professionals trained in how tests are constructed, standardised and validated, and in when a score should not be trusted, and in Indian hospitals testing is often the first thing a team asks of them. The fourth is breadth : the same profession works with a toddler with developmental delay, a student with examination anxiety and a man with chronic schizophrenia. The fifth, which Andrew Pomerantz makes a pillar of his textbook alongside science and practice, is culture . In India distress is often expressed through bodily complaints such as weakness and fatigue rather than as sadness, families commonly expect to share treatment decisions, and some presentations, such as Dhat syndrome (a preoccupation with the supposed loss of semen), are recognised mainly in South Asia. A clinician who ignores these meanings will misread the person. Why it matters. A weak answer to "what distinguishes clinical psychology?" lists activities. A strong answer names the features: science and practice integrated in one professional, the individual case approach, expertise in measurement, breadth, and cultural awareness. 1.4 What clinical psychologists actually do Textbooks conventionally list six activities. Very few clinical psychologists do only one, and the mix changes across a career. Assessment is the gathering and integration of information to answer a question about a person: diagnosis, intellectual ability, personality, neuropsychological functioning after a stroke, risk of self-harm, or suitability for a treatment. The clinician combines interview, observation, standardised tests, questionnaires, reports from family and teachers, and records, and produces a report and formulation with recommendations. Following Lightner Witmer, assessment should guide what happens next, not end in a label. Psychotherapy and intervention covers every planned attempt to bring about change: psychotherapy with individuals, couples, families or groups, but also psychoeducation (teaching patients and families about an illness), skills training, relapse prevention, crisis intervention, rehabilitation and prevention programmes. Indian clinical psychology has a strong tradition in behaviour therapy, and the Rehabilitation Council's curriculum requires supervised hours in both psychotherapy and behaviour therapy. Research asks what causes psychological problems, how they can be measured and which treatments work for whom; even clinicians who never publish must be able to judge whether a study's conclusions follow from its methods. Teaching and supervision includes university teaching and the training of nurses, teachers and health workers; supervision, in which a senior clinician oversees a trainee's cases, is how clinical skill passes between generations, and it carries shared responsibility for the trainee's clients. Consultation means giving expert advice to another professional or organisation, who remains responsible for the decision, as when a physician asks whether a patient refusing treatment is depressed. Administration means running departments, clinics and training programmes; it is rarely what students imagine, yet senior clinicians often spend much of their time on it. How is the time split? Surveys of the American Psychological Association's clinical division, repeated since the 1970s and in later rounds associated especially with John Norcross and colleagues, consistently find that most clinical psychologists combine several activities, that psychotherapy takes the largest share of the average clinician's time with assessment next, and that private practice became the most common primary setting in the United States. Academics do more teaching and research, senior clinicians more supervision and administration. Indian hospital posts lean towards assessment, while posts at the major training institutes combine clinical work with teaching, supervision and research. 1.5 The scientist-practitioner identity in daily work Clinical training still reflects a decision taken in the United States after the Second World War. Needing many clinicians quickly, the Veterans Administration and the Public Health Service asked the American Psychological Association to define proper training. A committee chaired by David Shakow reported in 1947, and a conference at Boulder, Colorado, in 1949 adopted its central idea: the scientist-practitioner or Boulder model, in which the clinical psychologist is trained as both scientist and practitioner so that each role informs the other. Later alternatives include the practitioner-scholar model endorsed at Vail, Colorado, in 1973, which puts practice first and trains students as informed consumers of research, and the clinical scientist model of Richard McFall's 1991 "Manifesto for a science of clinical psychology". Training models are treated fully later in this book. In daily work the identity shows up as five habits: choosing interventions partly by evidence of what works for a given problem; measuring progress, with a brief questionnaire each session or a behaviour chart kept by a parent, instead of relying on impression; treating the formulation as a hypothesis to be tested and revised; checking fallible judgement against structured tools; and, where possible, contributing back to knowledge through audits and case series. It has often been pointed out that the model is easier to endorse than to live, since many graduates publish little research and many practitioners find research of limited use with their clients. That gap is the central tension of the field, taken up in section 1.10. 1.6 Where clinical psychologists work Internationally, clinical psychologists work in general hospitals (psychiatry, and increasingly neurology, paediatrics, oncology and pain services); psychiatric hospitals ; outpatient clinics and community mental health services ; private practice ; universities and medical colleges ; schools , usually as consultants alongside school psychologists and counsellors; forensic and correctional settings , assessing fitness to stand trial, mental state at the time of an offence, risk of violence and child custody; rehabilitation centres for brain injury, substance dependence and developmental disabilities; and industry , through employee assistance and occupational health programmes. In India the pattern is shaped by the public health system and by the scarcity of trained clinical psychologists. In the public sector the largest group works in general hospital psychiatry units , the psychiatry departments of medical college and district hospitals, alongside psychiatrists, psychiatric social workers and psychiatric nurses. The national and regional institutes are both treatment and training centres. The National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS) in Bengaluru is the country's leading institution, with a department of clinical psychology running child and adolescent, neuropsychology, family and addiction services and training students through a competitive entrance examination. The Central Institute of Psychiatry at Ranchi, founded in 1918, is one of the country's oldest psychiatric institutions and a long-standing training centre. Others include the Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences in Delhi and the Lokopriya Gopinath Bordoloi Regional Institute of Mental Health in Tezpur. At community level, the District Mental Health Programme , launched in 1996 under the National Mental Health Programme of 1982 and built on a pilot in Bellary district of Karnataka, aims to bring care to each district through a team that includes a psychiatrist, a clinical psychologist, a psychiatric social worker and a psychiatric nurse; many of these posts have been hard to fill. The national tele-mental-health service, Tele-MANAS, launched in 2022, is a newer public setting. Indian clinical psychologists also work in private practice, increasingly online; in special schools, rehabilitation and de-addiction centres; in community mental health organisations; in courts and child welfare; and in corporate wellness. They contribute to the assessments through which intellectual disability and specific learning disability are formally certified. 1.7 How clinical psychology differs from its neighbouring professions Several professions work in the same territory, often with the same patient. They differ in training, in the questions they are equipped to answer, in the methods they may use, and in how they are regulated. Psychiatry. A psychiatrist is a medical doctor: in India, a Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery followed by a postgraduate qualification in psychiatry such as the Doctor of Medicine. As physicians, psychiatrists can prescribe medication, order investigations, admit patients and give physical treatments such as electroconvulsive therapy (Ugo Cerletti and Lucio Bini, 1938). The clinical psychologist holds a psychology degree, does not prescribe, and specialises in psychological assessment, psychological treatment and research. The two overlap, since some psychiatrists practise psychotherapy and every clinical psychologist must understand diagnosis and medication, but the core of one is medicine and of the other psychology. In a good team they are colleagues with different tools. Counselling psychology. Its roots lie in the vocational guidance movement, usually traced to Frank Parsons, who opened a vocation bureau in Boston in 1908 and whose Choosing a Vocation appeared in 1909, and in student counselling. It was later shaped by Carl Rogers, whose 1942 book Counseling and Psychotherapy gave it a humanistic emphasis on the relationship and the client's capacity for growth. Historically counselling psychologists worked with the normal range of adjustment (careers, life transitions, relationship strain), emphasised strengths and prevention, and worked in settings such as university counselling centres, while clinical psychologists worked more with severe disorder, in hospitals, using formal testing. In the United States the difference has narrowed greatly, and both are licensed as psychologists. In India the difference is also legal: counselling psychology is taught through master's degrees but is not a category the Rehabilitation Council registers. School psychology. School psychologists assess children with learning and behavioural difficulties, plan special educational provision and consult with teachers and parents. In the United States they usually hold a specialist-level or doctoral degree. In India school psychology has not developed as a separate licensed profession; schools usually employ counsellors, and children with suspected learning disabilities are commonly assessed by clinical psychologists in hospitals and clinics. Health psychology. Health psychology applies psychology to physical health: why people smoke or skip medication, how stress affects the body, how people cope with chronic illness and pain. It rests on the biopsychosocial model proposed by the physician George Engel in 1977; the American Psychological Association created its health psychology division in 1978, with Joseph Matarazzo a leading figure in defining the field. Many health psychologists are researchers; the clinical branch overlaps with clinical psychology in medical settings. Psychiatric social work. In India the established qualification has been a Master of Social Work followed by a two-year Master of Philosophy in Psychiatric Social Work, and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 defines psychiatric social workers by that qualification and provides for their registration as mental health professionals. Their focus is the person in their social world: family work, social and economic circumstances, community resources and welfare entitlements, discharge planning and rehabilitation. They are not trained in psychological testing. Psychiatric nursing. Psychiatric nurses are trained nurses specialised in mental health, in India through qualifications such as a Master of Science in Psychiatric Nursing, registered through the nursing councils. They provide round-the-clock ward care, monitor patients, administer prescribed medication, manage risk, provide psychoeducation and increasingly work in the community. Psychotherapists and counsellors without licensing. In many countries, India included, "psychotherapist" and "counsellor" have not been protected titles, so people with anything from a short certificate to a master's degree may offer therapy, and clients have little way to judge competence and no regulator to complain to. This differs from planned task sharing , in which community health workers are trained to deliver a specific structured treatment under supervision, an approach tested in careful trials, including in India. The problem is unregulated practice, not non-psychologists helping. India's National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions Act of 2021 brought psychologists other than clinical psychologists, and various counsellors, into a new regulatory framework, but its machinery has been slow to take shape, so check the current position before relying on it.
