Psychiatrist versus psychologist: the psychiatrist has a medical degree and can prescribe; the clinical psychologist has a psychology degree, does not prescribe in India, and is the specialist in psychological testing. Clinical versus counselling psychologist: historically the range of clients (severe disorder versus normal-range adjustment) and the roots (testing and hospitals versus vocational guidance); in India also a legal difference, since only the clinical psychologist is registered by the Rehabilitation Council. 1.8 The prescription privileges debate "Prescription privileges" means limited legal authority for psychologists, after substantial extra training, to prescribe psychiatric medication. In the United States the movement gained momentum through a Department of Defense demonstration project in the 1990s that trained a small number of military psychologists to prescribe. New Mexico became the first state to grant such authority in 2002, followed by Louisiana in 2004 and later a handful of others, including Illinois, Iowa and Idaho. The extra training typically involves a postdoctoral master's degree in clinical psychopharmacology, supervised practice and an examination, and prescribing is usually done in collaboration with the patient's physician. The American Psychological Association has supported the movement. The case for it rests on access and integration : rural areas have too few psychiatrists, one clinician who understands both the psychology and the medication might offer more coherent care, and other non-physicians such as nurse practitioners already prescribe. The case against comes from two directions. Medical organisations argue that psychiatric drugs act on the whole body, interact with other medicines and are given to patients whose physical illnesses may themselves cause psychological symptoms, so safe prescribing needs a full medical education. Some psychologists object that the profession would lose its identity as the discipline of psychological treatment, drift into the medical model it has long criticised, and become more exposed to the pharmaceutical industry. In India the debate is not live: prescribing is restricted to registered medical practitioners, and clinical psychologists work alongside psychiatrists who prescribe. 1.9 Clinical psychology as a profession in India The Rehabilitation Council of India and its Act The body that regulates the training and registration of clinical psychologists in India is the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) . Set up in 1986 as a registered society, it became a statutory body through the Rehabilitation Council of India Act, 1992 , amended in 2000 to broaden its role, and functions under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment through the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities. It regulates the training of rehabilitation professionals, recognises institutions and courses, standardises syllabi, maintains the register of qualified professionals, and promotes research and continuing education. Students are often puzzled that clinical psychologists fall under a disability council rather than a health council. The reason is historical: the Council registers the range of professionals who work with persons with disabilities, such as special educators, audiologists and speech therapists, and psychologists were included because psychological assessment and intervention are central to identifying and rehabilitating intellectual disability, learning disability, mental illness and other disabilities. The consequence is clear: in India it is the Council's recognition that makes a clinical psychology qualification a professional one. The Central Rehabilitation Register and why registration matters A person who completes a Council-recognised course may be entered on the Central Rehabilitation Register and receives a registration number. Under the Act, only a professional with a recognised qualification who is enrolled on the register may practise as a rehabilitation professional, hold such a post in government or publicly run institutions, sign certificates the law requires from such a professional, or give expert evidence in court in that field, and contravening these provisions is an offence. Registration must be renewed periodically, with renewal tied to the Council's continuing rehabilitation education programmes. In practice, registration is what allows appointment to government hospital posts, makes a psychologist's report acceptable in official processes such as disability certification, and lets the public check whether someone calling themselves a clinical psychologist is qualified. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 India's main mental health law points to the same gate. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 defines a clinical psychologist by reference to a clinical psychology qualification recognised by the Rehabilitation Council, or a master's in psychology followed by a two-year full-time Master of Philosophy in Clinical Psychology (or in Medical and Social Psychology) with supervised clinical training, approved by the Council. It then provides for clinical psychologists, psychiatric social workers and mental health nurses to be registered by the State Mental Health Authority to work as "mental health professionals", the category, alongside psychiatrists, to which the Act's provisions refer. The training routes For decades the route was long and narrow: a three-year bachelor's degree, a two-year master's in psychology, then a competitive entrance examination for a handful of seats on a two-year, full-time Master of Philosophy (MPhil) in Clinical Psychology at a Council-approved centre such as NIMHANS, the Central Institute of Psychiatry, the Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences or a medical college psychiatry department. It combined theory papers with intensive supervised clinical work and a dissertation, and led to registration. That route is being replaced. The National Education Policy 2020 recommended discontinuing the MPhil, and the University Grants Commission's regulations of 2022 stopped universities from offering it. The Council responded with a professional two-year RCI-regulated Master of Arts (or Master of Science) in Clinical Psychology , which from the 2025 to 2026 academic year serves as the licensing route at the major centres; NIMHANS calls its version the Master's in Clinical Psychology. Under the Council's programme document, entry rests on a four-year bachelor's degree in psychology, with alternative routes for students from the older three-year system; there are six papers over two years, with roughly half the marks from practical work, case records and a research thesis; trainees must complete minimum numbers of supervised case histories, interviews and psychodiagnostic and neuropsychological assessments, and supervised hours in psychotherapy and behaviour therapy; and selection is prescribed as entrance test and interview weighted 70 percent and 30 percent, though institutions have adopted this at different speeds. Seats stay few because each trainee needs a steady flow of supervised cases. Route Entry requirement Status Leads to registration? Two-year MPhil in Clinical Psychology Master's in psychology Being phased out after the 2022 regulations Yes, from a Council-approved centre Two-year Council-regulated master's in clinical psychology Four-year bachelor's in psychology, or an equivalent route in the regulations The current professional route Yes Ordinary master's in psychology, or a "clinical psychology" master's not regulated by the Council Bachelor's degree Widely offered No Trap. Some universities offer two degrees both called "Master of Arts in Clinical Psychology": an ordinary academic master's and the Council-regulated professional master's. Only the second leads to registration. The degree's name proves nothing; what matters is whether that programme at that campus is on the Rehabilitation Council's list of approved institutions. 1.10 Science and practice: the central tension Researchers study groups under controlled conditions and report what happens on average. Practitioners face one person, now, with several problems at once, a family with its own views, and circumstances no study sampled. Researchers are tempted to see practitioners as relying on intuition; practitioners are tempted to see research as irrelevant. Much of the history of clinical psychology is the history of attempts to bring the two together. Two episodes show why science matters to practice. In 1952 Hans Eysenck argued that about two thirds of neurotic patients improved within two years with or without psychotherapy, so there was no convincing evidence that therapy helped. Decades of research followed, and in 1977 Mary Lee Smith and Gene Glass combined hundreds of outcome studies using the then new technique of meta-analysis and concluded that psychotherapy was, on average, clearly more effective than no treatment: the question was settled by evidence, not by therapists' conviction. In 1954 Paul Meehl's Clinical versus Statistical Prediction reviewed studies in which simple statistical rules predicted outcomes as well as or better than experienced clinicians using the same information. His point was not that clinicians are useless but that judgement is fallible, prone to seeing what one expects and to overconfidence, and should be checked against structured methods. The modern expression of the scientific side is evidence-based practice . David Sackett and colleagues described evidence-based medicine in 1996 as the conscientious and judicious use of the best current evidence in decisions about individual patients. In psychology, a Society of Clinical Psychology task force in the mid-1990s, whose work is associated with Dianne Chambless, drew up criteria and lists of empirically supported treatments, and in 2006 an American Psychological Association task force defined evidence-based practice in psychology as "the integration of the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture, and preferences". All three parts matter. Critics note that trial patients are often selected for a single clear diagnosis while real patients rarely have one, that short manual-based treatments are easier to test and so dominate the lists, and that factors common to all therapies, such as the therapeutic relationship, may matter more than specific techniques. A useful bridge was proposed by George Stricker and Steven Trierweiler in 1995: the clinician as a local clinical scientist , who brings the scientific attitude, not only the published findings, to each case, treating hunches as hypotheses, gathering information in the session to test them, considering alternative explanations, watching for their own biases, and attending to features of the client and culture that no general study captured. Case. A 19-year-old student has stopped attending college. The psychologist's first hunch is depression, but she holds it as one hypothesis among several: depression, social anxiety about a new English-medium college after schooling in Tamil, a substance problem, or bullying. She gives brief depression and social anxiety questionnaires and asks him to record when he avoids college and what he is thinking. He attends happily when unlikely to be asked to speak, and avoids exactly the classes with presentations. Her hypothesis shifts to social anxiety linked to language, the plan changes, and she keeps measuring to check she was right. This is why a foundations course starts here: the identity sets the standard by which everything later is judged, tests by reliability and validity, therapies by evidence of what works for whom, conduct by ethics and registration. The same standard applies to positive psychology. Martin Seligman, during his 1998 presidency of the American Psychological Association and in a 2000 special issue of the American Psychologist edited with Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, argued that after the Second World War, with funding flowing through the Veterans Administration and the new National Institute of Mental Health into treating illness, psychology had become largely a science of repairing damage and had neglected building strengths. The growth clause in the Division 12 definition was always there; positive psychology asked the field to act on it, and later chapters show that some of its own famous claims did not survive scrutiny, which is why the scientific standard must apply there too. Key. Being a scientist-practitioner does not mean every clinician runs studies. It means every clinician thinks like a scientist about their own practice: choosing treatments by evidence, measuring outcomes, treating formulations as hypotheses, checking judgement against structured tools, and fitting the evidence to the particular person and culture. 1.11 A day in the life: the roles made concrete Case. Ananya (a composite, not a real person) is a clinical psychologist registered with the Rehabilitation Council, seven years into work in the psychiatry department of a government medical college hospital in a mid-sized Indian city. This is an ordinary Tuesday. At 8.30, in the case conference, the team discusses a 24-year-old man admitted with a first episode of psychosis. The psychiatrist has started medication; Ananya will

title: Psychological Tests: Authors, Versions, Items and Subtests
text: Psychological Tests: Authors, Versions, Items and Subtests Every psychological test the Indian clinical psychology entrances (RCI MA, NIMHANS, IHBAS, RML, JSS, CIP, Amity) keep asking about, one table per test: full name, who built it and when, the current edition and the ones before it, publisher, age range, number of items, every subtest, scale or index, how it is scored and normed, what it measures, its Indian adaptation, and the trap examiners set on it. Each family opens with a from-scratch explanation of how that kind of test works and closes with a comparison table. Where a count or a year genuinely differs between sources, the table says so instead of guessing: an honest "uncertain" is worth more in the hall than a confident wrong number. In this book Intelligence tests (international) Performance tests and Indian intelligence tests Developmental, adaptive behaviour and social maturity scales Objective personality inventories Aptitude, interest, creativity and attitude measures Projective techniques Neuropsychological tests and batteries Clinical rating scales and symptom inventories Structured diagnostic interviews and the mental status examination Index of every test in this book 1. Intelligence tests (international) An intelligence test is a standardised set of tasks, given in exactly the same way to everyone, whose scores are compared with a large reference group (the norm sample ) of people of the same age. The test does not measure "intelligence" directly; it samples behaviour (defining words, copying block patterns, repeating digits) that theory and data say depends on general reasoning ability. The score tells you where a person stands relative to age-mates, which is why the same raw score means something very different at age 7 and at age 70. The modern story starts in Paris. The French government wanted a way to identify children who would not profit from ordinary schooling, and Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon (1905) produced the first practical intelligence scale: 30 tasks arranged in rough order of difficulty. In the 1908 revision Binet and Simon grouped tasks by the age at which typical children pass them, which gave the idea of a mental age (MA) : a child who passes the tasks typical of 8-year-olds has an MA of 8, whatever their actual age. A third revision followed in 1911. Mental age alone is awkward, because being 2 years behind means far more at age 4 than at age 14. The German psychologist William Stern (1912) proposed dividing mental age by chronological age (CA), giving a "mental quotient". Lewis Terman (1916) , in the Stanford revision of the Binet scale at Stanford University, multiplied this by 100 and called it the intelligence quotient : ratio IQ = (MA / CA) x 100 . A 10-year-old with an MA of 12 has a ratio IQ of 120. The ratio IQ breaks down in adolescence and adulthood, because mental age stops growing in the late teens while chronological age keeps rising, so an ordinary 40-year-old would get an absurdly low "IQ". David Wechsler (1939) , working at Bellevue Hospital in New York, solved this with the deviation IQ . Instead of a ratio, the person's score is converted to a standard score that shows how far they sit from the mean of their own age group, on a scale with mean 100 and standard deviation (SD) 15 . An IQ of 115 now means "1 SD above the age mean" (about the 84th percentile) at any age. Every major modern test uses deviation scores. Within Wechsler batteries, individual subtests are reported as scaled scores with mean 10 and SD 3 . Theoretical frameworks evolved alongside: Charles Spearman's (1904) general factor g , Raymond Cattell's (1941, 1963) fluid (Gf) versus crystallised (Gc) intelligence, John Horn's extensions, and John Carroll's (1993) three-stratum model, which merged into the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) model that now organises the indices of the Wechsler, Stanford-Binet and KABC-II. Definition Ratio IQ = (mental age / chronological age) x 100 (Stern 1912 idea, Lewis Terman 1916 formula and name). Deviation IQ = a standard score locating the person relative to same-age peers, mean 100, SD 15 on Wechsler tests (Wechsler 1939). Scaled score = subtest standard score, mean 10, SD 3. T score = mean 50, SD 10. z score = mean 0, SD 1. Exam trap "Who coined IQ?" Stern proposed the quotient (MA/CA) in 1912; Terman added the x 100 and popularised the term "IQ" in the 1916 Stanford-Binet. Wechsler introduced the deviation IQ for adults. The 1960 Stanford-Binet Form L-M also switched to a deviation IQ, but with SD 16 , not 15. Alfred Binet himself never used the IQ. How to read age ranges in this book: Wechsler-style notation "16:0 to 90:11" means 16 years 0 months up to 90 years 11 months. WAIS-IV: Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fourth Edition The WAIS-IV is the standard individually administered adult intelligence test worldwide and the one most often named in Indian entrance papers. The examiner gives a series of subtests (verbal questions, block puzzles, digit repetition, symbol copying), converts each raw score to an age-scaled score, and combines these into four index scores and a Full Scale IQ. Interpretation moves from the global score (FSIQ) to the indices to individual subtests, looking for statistically significant strengths and weaknesses. The fourth edition is the one that dropped the old Verbal IQ and Performance IQ in favour of four indices. Field Detail Full name Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fourth Edition Author(s), year David Wechsler (original Wechsler-Bellevue Intelligence Scale, 1939). WAIS-IV (2008) was developed by the publisher's research team after Wechsler's death (1981), still under his name. Versions Wechsler-Bellevue Form I (1939), Wechsler-Bellevue Form II (1946), WAIS (1955), WAIS-R (1981), WAIS-III (1997), WAIS-IV (2008), WAIS-5 (2024, see next entry) Publisher Pearson (formerly The Psychological Corporation) Age range 16:0 to 90:11 Items Item counts are per subtest (they differ widely, and testing stops at discontinue rules); a single total item count is not a meaningful or standard figure. 15 subtests in all. Subtests / scales / indices 10 core subtests : Verbal Comprehension: Similarities, Vocabulary, Information. Perceptual Reasoning: Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles. Working Memory: Digit Span (forward, backward and the new sequencing task), Arithmetic. Processing Speed: Symbol Search, Coding. 5 supplemental subtests : Comprehension (VCI), Picture Completion and Figure Weights (PRI), Letter-Number Sequencing (WMI), Cancellation (PSI). Figure Weights, Letter-Number Sequencing and Cancellation are normed only for ages 16 to 69. 4 indices : Verbal Comprehension Index (VCI), Perceptual Reasoning Index (PRI), Working Memory Index (WMI), Processing Speed Index (PSI). Full Scale IQ (FSIQ) from the 10 core subtests. Optional composites : General Ability Index (GAI = VCI + PRI subtests, less affected by working memory and speed) and Cognitive Proficiency Index (CPI = WMI + PSI subtests). New in WAIS-IV: Visual Puzzles, Figure Weights, Cancellation. Dropped from WAIS-III: Object Assembly and Picture Arrangement. Scoring and norms FSIQ and indices mean 100, SD 15; subtest scaled scores mean 10, SD 3. US standardisation sample 2,200. FSIQ 130 and above: very superior; 69 and below: extremely low (WAIS-IV classification labels). Measures General intellectual ability (g) and four broad abilities: verbal reasoning and knowledge, nonverbal and fluid reasoning, working memory, processing speed Indian adaptation Pearson has marketed an India edition with Indian norms (reported as WAIS-IV INDIA); year and sample details uncertain. In routine Indian practice, especially for certification, the older Indian performance scale WAPIS (Ramalingaswamy, 1974) and Indian norms of other tests are still widely used. Exam trap WAIS-IV has no VIQ or PIQ (those ended with WAIS-III). It has 4 indices, not 5 (5 primary indices belong to WISC-V and WAIS-5). The core-versus-supplemental split is 10 + 5 = 15 . Comprehension and Picture Completion are supplemental in WAIS-IV, while Visual Puzzles is core. GAI is built from VCI and PRI; CPI from WMI and PSI: examiners swap these. WAIS-5: Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fifth Edition The WAIS-5 is the 2024 revision of the adult Wechsler. Its main structural change is to bring the adult test into line with WISC-V: the old Perceptual Reasoning Index is split into a Visual Spatial Index and a Fluid Reasoning Index , giving five primary indices. It was designed for both paper and digital (Q-interactive tablet) administration and shortened the subtests needed for an FSIQ. Because it is very new, Indian clinics and most Indian textbooks still teach WAIS-IV; treat WAIS-5 details below as current but verify against the manual. Field Detail Full name Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fifth Edition Author(s), year David Wechsler (original scale 1939); WAIS-5 developed by Pearson's research team, published 2024 Versions WAIS-5 (2024); previous: WAIS-IV (2008), WAIS-III (1997), WAIS-R (1981), WAIS (1955), Wechsler-Bellevue (1939) Publisher Pearson Age range 16:0 to 90:11 Items Per subtest; total subtest count reported as about 20 across primary, secondary and complementary groupings (exact count and grouping: uncertain, check the manual) Subtests / scales / indices 5 primary indices : Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Visual Spatial (VSI), Fluid Reasoning (FRI), Working Memory (WMI), Processing Speed (PSI). New subtests (as reported): Running Digits, Set Relations, Spatial Addition (Spatial Addition previously appeared in the Wechsler Memory Scale, WMS-IV), and Digit Span is split into separately scored tasks such as Digit Sequencing (details uncertain). Retained subtests include Similarities, Vocabulary, Information, Block Design, Visual Puzzles, Matrix Reasoning, Figure Weights, Arithmetic, Coding, Symbol Search. Which older subtests (for example Comprehension, Picture Completion, Cancellation, Letter-Number Sequencing) were dropped or moved: uncertain. FSIQ is derived from a reduced set of about 7 subtests (exact composition uncertain). Ancillary indices such as GAI and CPI are available. Scoring and norms FSIQ and indices mean 100, SD 15; subtest scaled scores mean 10, SD 3. US norms. Measures General intelligence and five CHC-aligned broad abilities Indian adaptation None standard (as of this writing) Exam trap The key conceptual change from WAIS-IV to WAIS-5 is PRI split into VSI + FRI , mirroring the WISC-V change of 2014. If a question asks which adult Wechsler has a Perceptual Reasoning Index, the answer is WAIS-IV (and WISC-IV), not WAIS-5. Note the naming: WAIS-5 uses an Arabic numeral, WAIS-IV a Roman one. WISC-V: Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fifth Edition The WISC-V is the children's version of the Wechsler, used for school-age assessment of intellectual disability, giftedness and specific learning disorder. It was the first Wechsler to split perceptual reasoning into separate visual-spatial and fluid reasoning indices, producing five primary indices. Subtests are organised in three tiers (primary, secondary, complementary), and the FSIQ comes from just 7 primary subtests, which shortens testing. Field Detail Full name Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fifth Edition Author(s), year David Wechsler (WISC, 1949); WISC-V published 2014 (US), developed by Pearson's research team Versions WISC-V (2014); WISC-IV (2003); WISC-III (1991); WISC-R (1974); WISC (1949) Publisher Pearson Age range 6:0 to 16:11 Items Per subtest. 21 subtests in all: 10 primary, 6 secondary, 5 complementary (the 16 primary plus secondary subtests are the ones that yield the classic scores). Exam trap WISC-IV (2003) had 4 indices (VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI) and 15 subtests (10 core + 5 supplemental), the same architecture as WAIS-IV. WISC-V has 5 primary indices, 10 primary subtests and FSIQ from 7. Picture Span (visual working memory) is new to WISC-V. Do not confuse "10 primary subtests" with "10 subtests for FSIQ". WPPSI-IV: Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Fourth Edition The WPPSI is the Wechsler for preschoolers. Because a 3-year-old cannot do what a 6-year-old can, the WPPSI-IV uses two age bands with different batteries: the younger band gets fewer, simpler subtests and fewer indices. It uses child-friendly working-memory tasks (remembering pictures, placing animal cards in a zoo) and picture-based processing-speed tasks. Field Detail Full name Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Fourth Edition Author(s), year David Wechsler (WPPSI, 1967); WPPSI-IV published 2012 Versions WPPSI-IV (2012); WPPSI-III (2002); WPPSI-R (1989); WPPSI (1967, original ages about 4 to 6:6) Publisher Pearson Age range 2:6 to 7:7, in two bands: 2:6 to 3:11 and 4:0 to 7:7 Items Per subtest; 15 subtests in total Subtests / scales / indices Band 2:6 to 3:11 : primary indices VCI, VSI, WMI (3) plus FSIQ. Band 4:0 to 7:7 : primary indices VCI, VSI, FRI, WMI, PSI (5) plus FSIQ. Scoring and norms FSIQ and indices mean 100, SD 15; scaled scores mean 10, SD 3 Measures Early cognitive ability, school readiness, early identification of developmental delay and giftedness Indian adaptation None standard Exam trap Age boundaries: WPPSI-IV ends at 7:7 and WISC-V begins at 6:0 , so ages 6:0 to 7:7 overlap and the examiner chooses. WAIS-IV begins at 16:0 and WISC-V ends at 16:11, another overlap. The youngest WPPSI-IV band has only 3 primary indices. SB5: Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales, Fifth Edition The Stanford-Binet is the direct descendant of the 1905 Binet-Simon scale and the test that gave the world the IQ. The fifth edition measures five CHC-type factors, each through one verbal and one nonverbal subtest, which allows a Verbal IQ and a Nonverbal IQ as well as an FSIQ. Testing starts with two routing subtests that estimate the person's level so that later subtests begin at the right difficulty. It is valued for its very wide age range and good floor and ceiling, useful in assessing both intellectual disability and high giftedness. Each factor is tested in a nonverbal and a verbal domain, giving 10 subtests . Routing subtests : Nonverbal Fluid Reasoning (Object Series/Matrices) and Verbal Knowledge (Vocabulary); together they give the Abbreviated Battery IQ (ABIQ) . Composites : Full Scale IQ, Nonverbal IQ, Verbal IQ, 5 factor index scores. SB4 Standard Age Score mean 100, SD 16 (subtests mean 50, SD 8). 1916 and 1937: ratio IQ. SB5 norm sample about 4,800. Also gives change-sensitive scores. Measures General intelligence (g) plus five CHC broad abilities, verbal and nonverbal Indian adaptation Binet-Kamat Test (V. V. Kamat, 1934; revised 1967), based on the 1916 Stanford-Binet; see section 2 Exam trap SD 16 versus SD 15 : the Stanford-Binet used SD 16 from Form L-M (1960) through SB4 (1986); SB5 switched to SD 15 to match Wechsler. SB5 author is Gale Roid (not Thorndike, who led SB4). SB5 has 5 factors and 10 subtests; SB4 had 4 areas and 15 subtests. The 1937 forms are named L and M after Lewis Terman and Maud Merrill. Raven's Progressive Matrices (SPM, CPM, APM, SPM Plus, Raven's 2) Raven's matrices are nonverbal reasoning tests: each item shows a pattern (a matrix of figures) with one piece missing, and the person chooses the missing piece from 6 or 8 options. Because no reading, speaking or culture-specific knowledge is needed, the test is used across languages and with people who have hearing or language problems. John Raven designed it to measure Charles Spearman's g , specifically eductive ability (making meaning out of confusion, seeing relations), as distinct from reproductive ability (recalling learned information), which he measured with the companion Mill Hill Vocabulary Scale. Items get "progressively" harder within each set, hence the name. Field Detail Full name Raven's Progressive Matrices: Standard (SPM), Coloured (CPM), Advanced (APM) Author(s), year John C. Raven (developed with Lionel Penrose; Penrose and Raven 1936 paper); SPM published 1938. Later revisions and manuals by John Raven (son), J. C. Raven and J. H. Court. Versions SPM (1938); CPM (1947); APM (1947, revised 1962); SPM Plus (1998, harder items to restore ceiling); Raven's 2 (2018, Pearson, digital and paper, item-bank based) Publisher Originally H. K. Lewis, London; later Oxford Psychologists Press; now Pearson Age range SPM: about 6 years to adulthood (norms extend to old age). CPM: 5 to 11 years, elderly people and people with intellectual or physical disability. APM: adolescents and adults of above-average ability. Raven's 2: reported about 4 to 90 years (uncertain). Items SPM: 60 items in 5 sets (A, B, C, D, E) of 12 each . CPM: 36 items in 3 sets (A, Ab, B) of 12 each , printed in colour to hold children's attention. APM: Set I 12 items (practice/screening) + Set II 36 items . Raven's 2: short computer-generated forms from an item bank (item count per form uncertain). Subtests / scales / indices No subtests; a single total score. Sets are ordered by difficulty. Scoring and norms Raw score (number correct) converted to percentiles and grades (Grade I "intellectually superior" at or above the 95th percentile, through Grade V "intellectually defective" at or below the 5th percentile); IQ-equivalent conversion possible. Untimed (APM can be timed). Score consistency check: the obtained set-wise pattern is compared with the expected composition for that total. Measures Spearman's g, eductive (fluid) reasoning, nonverbal abstract reasoning Indian adaptation Indian norms have been collected in several studies and appear in some Indian manuals; the authorship commonly cited (for example a Deshpande norm set) is uncertain. Widely used in Indian disability certification as a nonverbal measure. Exam trap Count the sets: SPM has 5 sets, A to E, 60 items ; CPM has 3 sets, A, Ab, B, 36 items ; APM has Set I (12) + Set II (36) . Set Ab exists only in the CPM. CPM is "coloured" (for children and elderly), not "complex". Raven measures eductive ability; the Mill Hill Vocabulary Scale measures reproductive ability. CFIT: Cattell Culture Fair Intelligence Test Raymond Cattell built this test to measure fluid intelligence (Gf) , the ability to reason with new material, while minimising the influence of language, schooling and culture. All items are figural (series, odd-one-out, matrices, topology). Cattell first called it "culture free", then admitted no test can be free of culture and renamed it "culture fair". It is timed and group-administrable. Field Detail Full name Culture Fair Intelligence Test (earlier Culture Free Intelligence Test) Author(s), year Raymond B. Cattell (Culture Free Test, 1940); Culture Fair Intelligence Test, Raymond B. Cattell and A. K. S. Cattell (1949; later editions 1950s and 1960s, exact years uncertain) Versions Scale 1, Scale 2, Scale 3; Scales 2 and 3 each have parallel Forms A and B Publisher Institute for Personality and Ability Testing (IPAT), Champaign, Illinois Age range Scale 1: 4 to 8 years and adults with intellectual disability. Scale 2: 8 to 14 years and average adults. Scale 3: high school, college and superior adults. Items Scale 2 commonly reported as 46 items per form (Series 12, Classification 14, Matrices 12, Conditions 8); Scale 3 as 50 items per form (13, 14, 13, 10). Treat exact counts as uncertain. Scale 1 has 8 subtests, some of which require verbal instructions and are not truly culture fair. Subtests / scales / indices Scales 2 and 3: 4 subtests : Series, Classification, Matrices, Conditions (Topology) Scoring and norms Deviation IQ; the CFIT has traditionally been normed with SD 16 (sources differ; some tables give SD 24 for older scales). Timed subtests. Measures Fluid intelligence (Gf) Indian adaptation Indian norms are reported in various studies; no single standard adaptation (uncertain) Exam trap Cattell's test measures fluid , not crystallised, intelligence. It was first called "Culture Free " (1940) and renamed "Culture Fair ". The four Scale 2/3 subtests are Series, Classification, Matrices, Conditions: "Conditions" (topology) is the one examiners use as a distractor. KABC-II: Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children, Second Edition The KABC was built from neuropsychological theory rather than from older IQ tests. Its first edition used Alexander Luria's distinction between sequential processing (handling information in serial order, like digit recall) and simultaneous processing (integrating information all at once, like seeing a whole pattern), and it separated processing ability from acquired knowledge. The second edition offers a dual interpretive model: the examiner chooses Luria (excluding knowledge, fairer to children from deprived or bilingual backgrounds) or CHC (including knowledge) before testing. Kaufman (KABC, 1983; KABC-II, 2004) Versions KABC-II NU (2018, normative update); KABC-II (2004); KABC (1983) Publisher American Guidance Service (AGS) originally; now Pearson Age range KABC-II: 3 to 18 years. The original KABC's theory was Alexander Luria's sequential versus simultaneous processing, which also underlies the Das-Naglieri PASS model. Do not confuse the Kaufmans' KABC with their adolescent and adult test, the KAIT (1993), or the brief KBIT. Leiter-3: Leiter International Performance Scale, Third Edition The Leiter is a fully nonverbal intelligence test: instructions are given by gesture and pantomime and the child responds by placing cards or foam pieces. It exists for people who cannot be tested verbally: deaf and hard-of-hearing children, children with autism or language disorder, and people who do not speak the examiner's language. Russell Leiter developed it in the late 1920s partly while working in Hawaii with a culturally diverse population. CAS2: Das-Naglieri Cognitive Assessment System, Second Edition The CAS operationalises the PASS theory of intelligence (Planning, Attention, Simultaneous, Successive), which J. P. Das, an Indian-born psychologist from Odisha who worked at the University of Alberta, derived from Alexander Luria's three functional units of the brain: arousal and attention (unit 1, brainstem and reticular system), coding as simultaneous and successive processing (unit 2, posterior cortex), and planning (unit 3, frontal lobes). Instead of asking "how much intelligence", it asks "which cognitive processes are weak", which is useful in learning disability and ADHD assessment. Theoretical source: Luria , not CHC. Goodenough-Harris Drawing Test (Draw-a-Man) The child is simply asked to draw a person ("make a picture of a man; make the very best picture you can"). Florence Goodenough noticed that children's drawings acquire details (neck, fingers, correct proportion, clothing) in a regular developmental order, so the number of details correctly included can be scored as an index of intellectual maturity. It is a quick, nonthreatening, nonverbal screening measure, not a projective test (projective human figure drawing, such as Karen Machover's 1949 Draw-a-Person, is a separate tradition). Performance tests and Indian intelligence tests A performance test is an intelligence test in which the person responds by doing something with materials (arranging blocks, fitting shapes into a board, sliding pieces, drawing) rather than by answering in words. Performance tests developed for three reasons. First, the US Army testing programme of World War I (the Army Alpha for literate recruits and the Army Beta for illiterate and non-English-speaking recruits, Robert Yerkes and colleagues, 1917) showed that verbal tests unfairly penalise people without schooling or language. Second, clinicians needed tests for deaf, speech-impaired and non-English-speaking children. Third, verbal and performance tasks seemed to tap partly different abilities: W. P. Alexander (1935) argued for a "practical" factor (F) beyond g, and Wechsler built both Verbal and Performance scales into his tests. India needed performance tests for the same reasons, even more acutely: at independence most of the population was not literate, the country has dozens of languages, and verbal Western tests are culturally loaded. Indian psychologists therefore did two things: they adapted Western tests (Binet-Kamat from the Stanford-Binet; MISIC from the WISC; WAPIS from the WAIS; Indian norms for Raven's and the Draw-a-Man), and they assembled batteries of existing performance tests with Indian norms (the Bhatia Battery). Many of these instruments date from the 1930s to 1970s and use old norms, a limitation examiners like to ask about, yet they remain in daily use in Indian clinics and are named in the government guidelines for certifying intellectual disability. High yield Indian adaptation pairs to memorise: Binet-Kamat (V. V. Kamat) from Stanford-Binet; MISIC (A. J. Malin, Nagpur) from WISC; WAPIS (P. Ramalingaswamy) from WAIS performance scale; Malin's VSMS (A. J. Malin, Nagpur) from Doll's Vineland; DASII (Pramila Phatak, Baroda) from Bayley; Bhatia Battery (C. M. Bhatia) is an Indian battery of mostly Western performance tests. Bhatia Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence C. M. Bhatia assembled five tests, four performance tests and one memory test, and standardised them on Indian school children so that intelligence could be assessed without depending on literacy or a particular language. The tests are given individually with materials, and the scores are converted into an overall index. It remains one of the most-asked Indian tests in entrance MCQs, usually as "name the five subtests" or "who developed it". Field Detail Full name Bhatia Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence (from Bhatia's monograph Performance Tests of Intelligence under Indian Conditions ) Author(s), year C. M. Bhatia (1955) Versions 1955 original; no major revision widely documented (uncertain) Publisher Oxford University Press (1955 monograph); test materials from Indian suppliers (uncertain) Age range Originally standardised on children aged 11 to 16 years (Uttar Pradesh sample, uncertain); used clinically more widely Items Commonly cited: Koh's Block Design 10 designs, Alexander Pass-Along 8 designs, Pattern Drawing 8 cards, Picture Construction 5 pictures, Immediate Memory for digits forward and backward. Treat individual counts as uncertain (sources differ). Subtests / scales / indices 5 subtests : (1) Koh's Block Design Test; (2) Alexander Pass-Along Test; (3) Pattern Drawing Test; (4) Immediate Memory (auditory digit span, forward and backward); (5) Picture Construction Test. A shorter battery (omitting tests for illiterate groups) is also described (uncertain which). Scoring and norms Raw scores (with time credits on several tests) converted from tables to a performance quotient / IQ equivalent; separate norms reported for literate and illiterate groups (uncertain) Measures Nonverbal, practical (performance) intelligence; visuospatial reasoning, planning, short-term memory Indian adaptation It is itself an Indian battery Exam trap The Bhatia Battery's memory subtest is Immediate Memory (digits), the only one that is not a performance task. Seguin Form Board is NOT in the Bhatia Battery , nor is Cube Construction or Picture Completion; these are common distractors. Bhatia's Koh's Block Design uses only part of the original 17 designs. Kohs Block Design Test The person is given coloured cubes and a printed design card and must arrange the blocks so that their top faces reproduce the design. Success requires analysing the whole design into parts (analysis) and putting the blocks together again (synthesis), so it measures visuospatial reasoning and nonverbal abstract ability. Wechsler borrowed it as the Block Design subtest, which is still one of the best single measures of g in the Wechsler batteries and is sensitive to right parietal brain damage. Field Detail Full name Kohs Block Design Test Author(s), year Samuel C. Kohs (1920 article; 1923 book Intelligence Measurement: A Psychological and Statistical Study Based upon the Block-Design Tests ) Versions Original 1920/1923; adapted into the Wechsler Block Design subtest (1939 onward), Bhatia Battery (1955), Alexander's battery Publisher Stoelting (original materials; uncertain) Age range Originally about 5 years to adult (uncertain) Items 17 designs (original), using up to 16 blocks . Cube faces: red, white, blue, yellow, red/white diagonal, blue/yellow diagonal. Bhatia uses 10 designs (sources commonly cite). Subtests / scales / indices Single test Scoring and norms Accuracy and time (time credits); mental age in the original Measures Visuospatial analysis and synthesis, nonverbal reasoning, visuomotor construction Indian adaptation Included in the Bhatia Battery (1955) Exam trap 16 is the number of blocks; 17 is the number of designs in the original Kohs test. Examiners offer both. The author is Samuel Kohs (often printed "Koh's" in Indian texts). Alexander Pass-Along Test The person is given a shallow tray containing coloured (red and blue) wooden blocks and must reach a target pattern shown on a card by sliding blocks along the tray, without lifting any piece out. It requires planning several moves ahead, so it measures practical problem solving and foresight. Alexander believed tests like this tap a practical ability (his "F" factor) that matters for technical and vocational success. Field Detail Full name Alexander Pass-Along Test Author(s), year W. P. Alexander (1932); part of the Alexander Performance Scale (with Kohs Block Design and Cube Construction) described in Intelligence, Concrete and Abstract (1935) Versions Original 1932; Bhatia Battery version (1955) Publisher Uncertain Age range Children and adolescents, about 8 years upward (uncertain) Items Original: 9 designs (uncertain); Bhatia version: 8 designs (commonly cited) Subtests / scales / indices Single test Scoring and norms Success within time limit plus time credits Measures Planning, practical intelligence, visuospatial problem solving Indian adaptation Included in the Bhatia Battery (1955) Exam trap The rule is "slide, do not lift". Alexander's Performance Scale = Pass-Along + Kohs Block Design + Cube Construction ; Bhatia replaced Cube Construction with other tests. Seguin Form Board Test The child is shown a wooden board with 10 recesses of different shapes; the shapes are removed and stacked, and the child must put them back as quickly as possible. It is repeated over three trials. It is one of the oldest psychological instruments, originally a training device in Edouard Seguin's physiological method of educating children with intellectual disability, later turned into a timed test. In Indian clinics it is used as a quick nonverbal measure for young children and people with intellectual disability, with results expressed as a mental age. Field Detail Full name Seguin Form Board Test (SFB) Author(s), year Edouard Seguin (form board in his 1866 book Idiocy and its Treatment by the Physiological Method ; used earlier in the 1840s). Standardised as a test by Henry H. Goddard (about 1912; year sources differ), the "Goddard form board". Versions Goddard's version is the standard; Indian norms in use (author uncertain) Publisher Various Indian suppliers (uncertain) Age range About 3 to 14 years (Indian norms commonly up to about 11 or 14; sources differ) Items 10 shapes (for example circle, square, triangle, star, cross, oval, semicircle, hexagon, rectangle, diamond or similar; exact set varies by version) Subtests / scales / indices Single test, 3 trials Scoring and norms Time per trial; shortest time (and sometimes total time) converted to mental age; ratio IQ Measures Visual discrimination of form, visuomotor coordination, speed, nonverbal ability Indian adaptation Indian norms widely used and listed in the Indian ID certification guidelines; norm author uncertain Exam trap Seguin = 10 shapes, 3 trials, shortest time . Seguin was a French physician-educator of the intellectually disabled (pupil of Jean Itard), not a psychometrician. Seguin is not part of the Bhatia Battery. Gesell Drawing Test The child copies a series of simple geometric figures (circle, cross, square, triangle, diamond and similar) from cards. Arnold Gesell observed that the ability to copy each shape appears at a typical age (for example a circle around 3 years, a cross around 4, a square around 4 to 5, a triangle around 5, a diamond around 7), so the most complex figure copied correctly gives a developmental level. It is used in Indian clinics as a quick visuomotor and developmental screen. MISIC: Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children MISIC is the Indian adaptation of the original WISC (1949), developed by Arthur J. Malin at the Child Guidance Centre, Nagpur. Items were changed to suit Indian children's experience, and Indian norms were developed. Like the original WISC, it gives a Verbal Quotient, a Performance Quotient and a Full Scale IQ. It is still a standard test for school-age children in Indian clinics and for ID and learning disability certification. MISIC is based on the WISC , not the WAIS or the Stanford-Binet. Binet-Kamat Test of Intelligence The Binet-Kamat is the Indian adaptation of the 1916 Stanford-Binet, prepared by V. V. Kamat for Kannada- and Marathi-speaking children in the Bombay-Karnataka region. Like its parent, it is an age scale: items are grouped by age level, the examiner finds the basal age (level where all items are passed) and adds months of credit for items passed above it to get a mental age, then computes a ratio IQ. It is one of the tests named for ID assessment in India. Field Detail Full name Binet-Kamat Test of Intelligence (BKT) Author(s), year V. V. Kamat adapted the Stanford-Binet ; Malin adapted the WISC. WAPIS: Wechsler Adult Performance Intelligence Scale (Indian adaptation) WAPIS is P. Ramalingaswamy's Indian adaptation of the performance half of the WAIS. Because the performance subtests depend less on language and schooling, they were judged more suitable across India's linguistic groups. It yields a Performance IQ for adolescents and adults and is commonly used in Indian adult assessment, including disability certification. Author: Ramalingaswamy . Its 5 subtests are the 5 WAIS performance subtests, including Picture Arrangement and Object Assembly, which were dropped from WAIS-IV. Draw-a-Man Test: Indian norms (Phatak) Pramila Phatak (often printed Pathak), of the M. S. University of Baroda, collected Indian norms for Goodenough's Draw-a-Man test, so that Indian children's drawings are judged against Indian age-mates. Administration and point scoring follow Goodenough's method (see section 1). Phatak's Baroda group is also responsible for the Baroda norms of the Bayley scales (DASII, section 3). Do not attribute either to Malin (Nagpur) or Kamat. Other Indian intelligence measures Several other names circulate in Indian test catalogues and old question papers. Their details are less well documented, so treat this list as orientation, not as exam-grade fact. Raven's Progressive Matrices, Indian norms : SPM and CPM norms for Indian samples exist in several studies and in Indian supplements; the author most often cited for one norm set (Deshpande) is uncertain, and different clinics use different norm tables. WISC-IV INDIA and WAIS-IV INDIA : Pearson India editions with Indian norms have been marketed; years and sample details uncertain. Bhatt's Nonverbal Test of Intelligence : named in some Indian catalogues; author details, year and structure uncertain. Do not rely on any specific fact about it without the manual. Kamat : see Binet-Kamat above; there is no separate widely used "Kamat's" test beyond the Binet-Kamat. No reliable source was found for an Indian WISC adaptation by "Bhatnagar"; it is left out deliberately. The exact list in the current notification should be checked, but this cluster is what examiners mean by "Indian tests for ID".
