Developmental, adaptive behaviour and social maturity scales An IQ test asks "how well can this person reason when tested?". A developmental scale asks "has this infant or young child reached the milestones expected for their age?", and an adaptive behaviour scale asks "how well does this person actually manage everyday life: dressing, eating, communicating, getting along with others, handling money?". These questions matter because intellectual disability is defined by two criteria, deficits in intellectual functioning and deficits in adaptive functioning, both beginning in the developmental period. A child can score 65 on an IQ test yet function independently at home and school; under DSM-5 that child may not meet criteria. Most developmental and adaptive scales are completed by observation and informant interview (usually a parent or caregiver) rather than by testing the person directly, which makes them usable with infants and with severely disabled people who cannot be tested. Scores are typically expressed as an age equivalent (developmental age, social age) and a quotient: Developmental Quotient (DQ) = developmental age / chronological age x 100 , and Social Quotient (SQ) = social age / chronological age x 100 . Modern scales (Vineland-3, Bayley-4) use deviation standard scores with mean 100, SD 15 instead. A further distinction is screening versus diagnostic assessment . Screening tests (Denver II, TDSC) are short, used on many children (for example in paediatric clinics), and only flag children who need further evaluation; they do not give a diagnosis or a reliable quotient. Diagnostic scales (Bayley, Gesell schedules, DASII) take longer and give a quantified developmental level. Definition Adaptive behaviour : the conceptual, social and practical skills people learn and perform in their everyday lives (AAIDD definition). Social age (SA) : the age level of a person's social competence on the VSMS. SQ = SA / CA x 100. DQ = developmental age / CA x 100. VSMS: Vineland Social Maturity Scale (Doll) Edgar Doll, at the Vineland Training School in New Jersey, wanted to measure what intelligence tests missed: how far a person can look after themselves and take part in social life. The VSMS is a list of everyday competencies arranged in order of the age at which they are typically achieved (from "crows, laughs" in infancy to managing others' affairs in adulthood). An informant who knows the person well is interviewed, each item is marked as habitually performed or not, and the total gives a social age and a social quotient. It was the first standardised adaptive behaviour scale. Field Detail Full name Vineland Social Maturity Scale Author(s), year Edgar A. Doll (1935); revised manual 1947, 1953 ( The Measurement of Social Competence ), 1965 Versions 1935 original, 1965 revision; superseded in the US by the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales (1984) Publisher Educational Test Bureau / American Guidance Service (uncertain) Age range Birth to adulthood (items go to "25+ years"; sources state birth to 25 years or birth to 30 years) Items 117 items Subtests / scales / indices 8 categories : Self-Help General (SHG), Self-Help Eating (SHE), Self-Help Dressing (SHD), Self-Direction (SD), Occupation (O), Communication (C), Locomotion (L), Socialization (S) Scoring and norms Items passed give a total score converted to Social Age ; SQ = SA / CA x 100 Measures Social competence, self-help, adaptive behaviour Indian adaptation A. J. Malin, Nagpur (see next entry) Exam trap Doll's original VSMS has 117 items and 8 categories; Malin's Indian version has 89 items . The VSMS is given to an informant , not to the child. Self-Help is split into three (General, Eating, Dressing), which is why there are 8 categories and not 6. VSMS (Indian adaptation, Malin) A. J. Malin adapted Doll's VSMS for Indian children at the Child Guidance Centre, Nagpur, removing or changing items that did not fit Indian life and restricting the range to childhood. It is the standard Indian measure of social age and social quotient and is listed in the Indian guidelines for certifying intellectual disability, where SQ is used alongside IQ. Field Detail Full name Vineland Social Maturity Scale, Indian adaptation (Malin) Author(s), year A. J. Malin (1965; published manual 1971, sources differ), adapting Edgar Doll (1935) Versions Malin's Indian adaptation; a later Indian revision by J. Bharath Raj (Mysore, about 1992) is also reported (details uncertain) Publisher Indian Psychological Corporation / Nagpur (uncertain) Age range 0 to 15 years Items 89 items Subtests / scales / indices Same 8 categories as Doll (Self-Help General, Self-Help Eating, Self-Help Dressing, Self-Direction, Occupation, Communication, Locomotion, Socialization) Scoring and norms Social Age and SQ; Indian norms Measures Social competence and adaptive behaviour in children Indian adaptation This entry is the Indian adaptation Exam trap Malin VSMS: 89 items, 0 to 15 years . Bharath Raj DST: 88 items, 0 to 15 years . These two numbers are deliberately placed side by side in MCQs. VSMS gives SQ; DST gives DQ. Vineland-3: Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, Third Edition The Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales replaced Doll's VSMS with a modern, multidimensional instrument. Adaptive behaviour is divided into domains (communication, daily living skills, socialization, motor), each with subdomains, and scored with deviation standard scores. It can be given as a semi-structured interview with a caregiver, or as parent or teacher rating forms. It is the most widely used adaptive behaviour

title: Requested Topics
text: Requested Topics Five topics you asked for by name, each written to be learned cold from this page alone: the diathesis-stress model and its descendants, Eugen Bleuler's four A's and how the idea of schizophrenia was built, the theory of planned behaviour, every kind of brain scan an examiner can ask about, and the nine concepts you asked about after the NIMHANS paper on 31 May (dissociation, desensitization, habit reversal, flashbulb memory, paradoxical intention, ICD-11 gender incongruence, the gunas, dharana and Kegels). Theorists and years sit inside the explanations where they belong, the exam traps are flagged as you go, and each chapter closes with a self-check written the way the entrance papers write their questions. In this book The diathesis-stress model Bleuler's four A's and the history of the schizophrenia concept The theory of planned behaviour Types of brain scanning and imaging tests NIMHANS 31 May: the nine you asked about (Qs 36-41, gunas, dharana, Kegels) 1. The diathesis-stress model Why do two people who go through the same divorce, the same job loss or the same childhood poverty end up so differently, one with a major depressive episode and the other with a bad few months? And why do identical twins, who share all their genes, so often differ on whether they develop schizophrenia? The diathesis-stress model is psychology's oldest and most widely used answer to both questions. It is less a single theory than a template for explaining how a disorder comes about, and almost every modern theory of depression, anxiety and psychosis is built on it. Definition A diathesis is a predisposition or vulnerability to a disorder that a person carries before the disorder appears. The word comes from the Greek diathesis , meaning "disposition" or "arrangement" (from diatithenai , to arrange or dispose), and was used in older medicine for a constitutional tendency to a disease (for example the "gouty diathesis"). The diathesis-stress model states that a disorder develops when a diathesis is combined with sufficient stress (an adverse environmental event or condition), and that neither the diathesis alone nor the stress alone is usually sufficient. 1.1 The core idea, built from scratch Think of three ingredients: The diathesis : something relatively enduring that the person brings to the situation. It can be biological (genes, neurodevelopmental damage, a reactive stress hormone system), psychological (a negative thinking style, dysfunctional schemas, a personality trait such as neuroticism) or social and developmental (early loss, insecure attachment). It is usually latent : you cannot see it in daily behaviour until something activates it. The stress : an environmental challenge, usually after the diathesis is in place. Classic examples are negative life events (bereavement, failure, migration), chronic strain (poverty, caregiving, a hostile family) and biological insults (cannabis use, infection, sleep loss). The interaction : the outcome depends on the combination . A high-diathesis person may break down after a modest stressor; a low-diathesis person may need an extreme stressor, or may never break down at all. The statistical word for this is interaction : the effect of stress on outcome is not the same for everyone, it depends on (is "moderated by") the level of diathesis. In plain words, stress hurts the vulnerable much more than the non-vulnerable. This is why the model is often written as vulnerability x stress rather than vulnerability + stress. Exam trap The diathesis is the predisposition , never the stressor. If an option says "diathesis refers to the precipitating life event", it is wrong. The stressor is the precipitant (trigger); the diathesis is the predisposing factor. In the familiar "4 P" case formulation, diathesis maps onto predisposing factors and stress onto precipitating (and sometimes perpetuating) factors. 1.2 History: from Meehl to Zubin and Spring Paul E. Meehl (1962): schizotaxia, schizotypy, schizophrenia The modern model is usually traced to Paul E. Meehl (1962) , whose presidential address to the American Psychological Association was published in the American Psychologist as "Schizotaxia, schizotypy, schizophrenia". Meehl proposed a chain of three levels: Schizogene : Meehl hypothesised a single dominant gene (the "schizogene") as the inherited starting point. This specific single-gene claim has not been supported; schizophrenia is now understood as highly polygenic. Schizotaxia : the gene produces a subtle neural integrative defect , a fault in how the nervous system integrates information (Meehl spoke of a defect he called "hypokrisia" at the level of neuronal functioning). Schizotaxia is purely the inherited neurological vulnerability. Schizotypy : almost any schizotaxic person, growing up in any ordinary social learning environment, develops a characteristic personality organisation called schizotypy: cognitive slippage (mild thought disorder), anhedonia, interpersonal aversiveness and ambivalence. Schizotypy is learned on top of schizotaxia. Schizophrenia : only a minority of schizotypes decompensate into clinical schizophrenia, and this happens when they meet adverse environmental conditions (Meehl, writing in 1962, gave the much-criticised example of a "schizophrenogenic" mother). Most schizotypes remain compensated for life. In his later reformulation (Meehl, 1990) he gave rough figures, often quoted as about 10 percent of the population being schizotypal in his sense and about 10 percent of those developing clinical schizophrenia. Treat these as Meehl's speculative estimates, not epidemiological facts. Exam trap Schizotaxia = inherited neural integrative defect (biology). Schizotypy = the personality organisation that develops from it through social learning (psychology). Schizotypal personality disorder = a DSM diagnostic category (DSM-III, 1980, onward), partly inspired by the schizotypy concept and by the Danish adoption studies of relatives of people with schizophrenia, but not the same thing as Paul Meehl's schizotypy. Also note: in ICD-10 schizotypal disorder sits in the schizophrenia chapter (F21), whereas DSM places schizotypal personality disorder among personality disorders and also lists it in the schizophrenia spectrum chapter. David Rosenthal (1970): popularising the term The exact phrase "diathesis-stress" is often credited to David Rosenthal (1970) , in his book Genetic Theory and Abnormal Behavior , which used it to summarise the genetic and environmental evidence on schizophrenia, including the Danish adoption studies he ran with Seymour Kety and others. Who used the phrase first is uncertain; sources differ, so the safe statement is that Rosenthal popularised it. Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring (1977): the vulnerability-stress model Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring (1977) , in "Vulnerability: a new view of schizophrenia" ( Journal of Abnormal Psychology ), restated the idea in a form that is still the standard textbook diagram. Their key claims: Vulnerability is the enduring trait ; schizophrenia itself is not permanent. What a person carries for life is the vulnerability, not the illness. Episodes are time-limited . An episode occurs when stress pushes the person above their personal vulnerability threshold ; when the stress subsides the person tends to return to their premorbid level. This was a deliberate challenge to the Kraepelinian assumption of inevitable deterioration. Inborn vs acquired vulnerability . Inborn vulnerability lies in the genes and internal environment (neurophysiology). Acquired vulnerability comes from traumas, specific diseases, perinatal complications, family experiences, adolescent peer interactions and other life events. Moderators . Whether stress tips someone over also depends on their social network, ecological niche and premorbid personality. Graphically, Zubin and Spring plotted vulnerability against challenging events: a curved threshold line divides a "well" zone from an "episode" zone. A highly vulnerable person crosses the line with little stress; a person with low vulnerability needs a great deal. Memory hook Zubin and Spring = 1977 , the same year as George Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977) and one year before Kety. Remember "seven-seven: vulnerability and biopsychosocial were born together". But they are different ideas: Engel's model is a general philosophy of medicine (biology, psychology and social context all matter for every illness); the diathesis-stress model is a specific causal claim that a pre-existing vulnerability interacts with later stress. 1.3 Refinements: what form does the interaction take? Scott Monroe and Anne Simons (1991) Scott M. Monroe and Anne D. Simons (1991) , "Diathesis-stress theories in the context of life stress research: implications for the depressive disorders" ( Psychological Bulletin ), is the classic critical review. Their main points: Most theories had been vague about how diathesis and stress combine. Researchers needed to specify the form of the relationship rather than just say "both matter". Stress must be measured carefully . Self-report checklists confound the stressor with the person's reaction to it. They favoured interview-based, contextual ratings of life events (in the tradition of George Brown and Tirril Harris's Life Events and Difficulties Schedule) and the distinction between independent events (outside the person's control, such as an earthquake) and dependent events (partly produced by the person, such as a breakup after repeated arguments). Diathesis and stress are not always independent . The diathesis may shape which stressors the person meets, and stress may change the diathesis over time (a dynamic rather than fixed diathesis). Forms of the model (Ingram and Luxton, 2005) Rick Ingram and David Luxton (2005), in a widely cited chapter on vulnerability-stress models, organised the possible forms. The terms below are the ones exam setters lift: Form What it claims Dichotomous diathesis The diathesis is either present or absent (as in Paul Meehl's single gene). Without it, no amount of stress produces the disorder. Quasi-continuous diathesis The diathesis varies in degree (as with polygenic risk or a graded cognitive style). The more diathesis, the less stress needed. Ipsative (additive) model Diathesis and stress are inversely related: they add up, and disorder appears once the sum crosses a threshold. A very strong diathesis may need almost no stress, and an extreme stressor may produce disorder even in someone with little diathesis. Zubin and Spring's diagram is of this kind. Threshold (interactive) model Stress has an effect only once the diathesis (or stress) passes a certain level; below it, stress makes little difference. The exact labels vary between textbooks, so in an MCQ go by the description rather than the label alone. Stress generation (Constance Hammen, 1991) Constance Hammen (1991) , studying women with depression, showed that depressed people experience more dependent stressful events (especially interpersonal conflicts) than controls, but not more independent ones. In other words, people with a depressive diathesis partly generate their own stress. This breaks the simple assumption that stress just "happens to" the vulnerable person and is a key reason Monroe and Simons called for a dynamic model. Kindling (Robert Post, 1992) Robert M. Post (1992) , in the American Journal of Psychiatry , borrowed the term "kindling" from epilepsy research. In mood disorders the first episodes are usually triggered by major life stress, but later episodes need less and less stress, and eventually may occur almost spontaneously. The diathesis itself is being changed (sensitised) by earlier episodes. Monroe and Kate Harkness (2005) later distinguished two readings: stress sensitisation (smaller stressors become enough) and stress autonomy (episodes occur without stress). Kindling is a related idea, not a version of the original diathesis-stress model: it describes a diathesis that grows over time. 1.4 Examples of diatheses Cognitive diatheses in depression Aaron T. Beck (cognitive theory, 1967 onward): early experience lays down dysfunctional schemas (for example "I am worthless unless I am loved"). They stay latent until a congruent stressor (a rejection) activates them, producing the negative cognitive triad (self, world, future). Beck (1983) added the personality diatheses sociotropy (dependence on relationships) and autonomy (dependence on achievement and independence), with the congruency hypothesis : sociotropic people are vulnerable to interpersonal loss, autonomous people to failure. Hopelessness theory , Lyn Abramson, Gerald Metalsky and Lauren Alloy (1989) , Psychological Review : the diathesis is a negative inferential style , a tendency to explain negative events with stable and global causes, to infer negative consequences, and to infer negative things about oneself. When such a person meets negative events, they are likely to become hopeless, and hopelessness is the proximal sufficient cause of a subtype, "hopelessness depression". This is an explicit diathesis-stress theory, and it revised the earlier learned helplessness reformulation (Abramson, Martin Seligman and Teasdale, 1978). A genetic example: Caspi et al. (2003) and what happened next Avshalom Caspi, Terrie Moffitt and colleagues (2003) , in Science , used the Dunedin (New Zealand) birth cohort and reported that people carrying one or two short alleles of the serotonin transporter promoter polymorphism ( 5-HTTLPR ) were more likely to become depressed after stressful life events than people with two long alleles. It became the textbook example of a gene x environment (G x E) interaction, that is, a molecular diathesis-stress effect. The story did not hold up well. Neil Risch and colleagues (2009) , a meta-analysis in JAMA , found no evidence that 5-HTTLPR moderated the stress-depression link (stress itself strongly predicted depression). A 2011 meta-analysis by Karg and colleagues, using broader inclusion, did report support, so the literature was contested for a while. Then Richard Border and colleagues (2019) , in the American Journal of Psychiatry , tested historical depression candidate genes, including 5-HTTLPR and its interaction with stress, in very large samples and found no support. The lesson for exams: Caspi et al. is the classic G x E example, but it is now regarded as a failed replication story, and polygenic approaches have replaced single candidate genes. Schizophrenia examples Copenhagen high-risk study : begun in 1962 by Sarnoff Mednick and Fini Schulsinger . Children of mothers with schizophrenia (high genetic risk) and matched controls were followed from childhood. Among the high-risk children, those who later developed schizophrenia were more likely to have had obstetric complications and disruptive early rearing (for example separation from the mother), a diathesis-stress pattern where acquired insults act on a genetic predisposition. Finnish Adoptive Family Study of Schizophrenia , led by Pekka Tienari : adopted-away children of mothers with schizophrenia spectrum disorders were compared with adoptees of mothers without them, and the adoptive families' functioning was rated independently. High genetic risk raised the rate of schizophrenia spectrum disorders mainly when the adoptive family was rated as disturbed (dysfunctional communication); in healthy adoptive families the high-risk adoptees did about as well as controls (Tienari et al., 2004, British Journal of Psychiatry ). This is one of the cleanest human demonstrations of genotype x rearing environment interaction. A cousin: Barlow's triple vulnerability theory David H. Barlow (2000, 2002) explained anxiety and related emotional disorders through three vulnerabilities: a generalised biological vulnerability (heritable negative affect, neuroticism), a generalised psychological vulnerability (an early sense that events are uncontrollable and unpredictable) and a specific psychological vulnerability (learning that particular objects or bodily sensations are dangerous, which explains why one person develops panic disorder and another social anxiety). Stress activates these vulnerabilities. It is a diathesis-stress model with the diathesis split into three layers. 1.5 Differential susceptibility: the challenge to diathesis-stress The diathesis-stress model assumes that "vulnerable" people only ever do worse: in a good environment they are at best equal to everyone else. Jay Belsky (1997) proposed, on evolutionary grounds, that some children are simply more plastic (more responsive to rearing) than others. Because parents cannot know which rearing strategy will pay off in an unpredictable future, natural selection would favour having some offspring who are highly shaped by the environment and others who are not. Belsky and Michael Pluess (2009) , in "Beyond diathesis stress: differential susceptibility to environmental influences" ( Psychological Bulletin ), reviewed evidence that the same traits once called vulnerabilities (difficult or negatively emotional infant temperament, certain dopamine and serotonin gene variants, high physiological reactivity) make people do worse in adverse environments but better in supportive ones. The slogan is "for better and for worse" , in contrast to diathesis-stress, which is only "for worse". Biological sensitivity to context : W. Thomas Boyce and Bruce J. Ellis (2005) , Development and Psychopathology , argued that high stress reactivity (autonomic and adrenocortical) reflects heightened sensitivity to context, both harmful and protective. They proposed a U-shaped relation: highly reactive children are over-represented in both very stressful and very protective early environments. Orchid vs dandelion children : a metaphor drawn from the Swedish expression maskrosbarn ("dandelion child", one who thrives anywhere). Dandelion children do reasonably well in almost any environment; orchid children wilt under neglect but flourish spectacularly with good care. Boyce popularised it in his book The Orchid and the Dandelion (2019). Vantage sensitivity : Pluess and Belsky (2013) , Psychological Bulletin , described the positive half on its own: some individuals benefit more than others from positive experiences and interventions (for example psychotherapy or school programmes). Vantage resistance is the failure to benefit. Diathesis-stress describes the negative pole, vantage sensitivity the positive pole, and differential susceptibility combines both. Seeing the difference: the crossover interaction Plot environment quality on the x axis (adverse on the left, supportive on the right) and outcome (well-being, higher is better) on the y axis. Draw one line for the "vulnerable" or "susceptible" group and one for the comparison group. A. Diathesis-stress B. Differential susceptibility Adverse Supportive Adverse Supportive Environment quality Environment quality Well-being Well-being gap only at adverse end lines cross Vulnerable / susceptible Non-vulnerable / less susceptible Panel A (diathesis-stress) : the lines fan out toward the adverse end and converge at the supportive end. In a good environment the vulnerable do as well as everyone else; the diathesis only shows under stress. This is an ordinal (non-crossing) interaction. Panel B (differential susceptibility) : the susceptible line is steeper and crosses the other line. Susceptible people do worst in bad environments and best in good ones. This is a disordinal (crossover) interaction. To claim differential susceptibility, researchers must show the crossover point lies within the realistic range of environments, and that the "better" side is real, not just noise (Glenn Roisman and colleagues, 2012, proposed formal statistical tests for this). Feature Diathesis-stress Differential susceptibility What the trait is A vulnerability (risk factor) A plasticity or sensitivity factor Effect in adverse environment Worse outcome Worse outcome Effect in supportive environment Same as others (no advantage) Better than others Shape of interaction Ordinal, fan-shaped Crossover Key names Paul Meehl 1962, Rosenthal 1970, Zubin and Spring 1977, Monroe and Simons 1991 Belsky 1997, Boyce and Ellis 2005, Belsky and Pluess 2009, Pluess and Belsky 2013 (vantage sensitivity) 1.6 Clinical implications Prevention : if the diathesis can be identified early (family history, high-risk mental states, a negative cognitive style), stress exposure can be reduced or coping strengthened before a first episode. Clinical high-risk (prodromal) services for psychosis rest on this logic. Relapse prevention : in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, medication is understood as lowering biological vulnerability, while psychosocial work reduces stress. Relapse signature plans teach patients and families to spot early warning signs after a stressor. Stress management and coping : problem-solving training, sleep regularity, avoiding cannabis and other drugs, and building social support all aim at the stress side or at the moderators that Zubin and Spring listed. Cognitive therapy : Aaron Beck's therapy tries to modify the diathesis itself (the schemas) so that future stressors do less damage; mindfulness-based cognitive therapy targets the kindling-like reactivation of depressive thinking in recurrent depression. Family expressed emotion (EE) : George W. Brown, J. L. T. Birley and John Wing (1972) , building on Brown's earlier work in the 1950s and 1960s, showed that people with schizophrenia discharged to families high in criticism, hostility or emotional over-involvement relapsed more often. Christine Vaughn and Julian Leff (1976) replicated this using the Camberwell Family Interview and found the risk was greatest when high-EE contact was long (more than about 35 hours a week face to face) and medication was not taken. High EE is an environmental stressor acting on a biological vulnerability. Family psychoeducation and behavioural family therapy (for example Ian Falloon's work) lower EE and reduce relapse. Indian relevance: EE studies in north India (Chandigarh, by N. N. Wig, Leff and colleagues in the 1980s, linked to the WHO Determinants of Outcome study) found that high EE was less common in Indian families than in London samples, one proposed reason for the better course of schizophrenia observed in developing-country WHO centres. High yield Paul Meehl 1962 (schizotaxia, schizotypy, schizophrenia; schizogene). Rosenthal 1970 (popularised "diathesis-stress"). Zubin and Spring 1977 (vulnerability model; episodes time-limited; inborn vs acquired vulnerability). Monroe and Simons 1991 ( Psychological Bulletin review of diathesis-stress and life stress). Hammen 1991 (stress generation). Post 1992 (kindling). Abramson, Metalsky and Alloy 1989 (hopelessness theory). Caspi 2003 (5-HTTLPR x stress), Risch 2009 and Border 2019 (failed). Belsky 1997, Belsky and Pluess 2009 (differential susceptibility). Boyce and Ellis 2005 (biological sensitivity to context). Pluess and Belsky 2013 (vantage sensitivity). Brown, Birley and Wing 1972; Vaughn and Leff 1976 (expressed emotion). Exam trap (1) Diathesis = predisposition, not trigger. (2) Schizotaxia (neural defect) vs schizotypy (personality organisation) vs schizotypal personality disorder (DSM category). (3) Zubin and Spring is 1977 , not 1962 (Meehl) or 1970 (Rosenthal). (4) In Zubin and Spring, the vulnerability is permanent, the episode is time-limited. (5) Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977) is not the diathesis-stress model. (6) Differential susceptibility is "for better and for worse"; diathesis-stress is "for worse only". (7) Stress generation (Hammen) means dependent events increase, not independent ones. (8) Kindling is Post (1992), borrowed from epilepsy research. Self-check The term "diathesis" in the diathesis-stress model refers to: (a) the precipitating life event (b) a pre-existing predisposition or vulnerability (c) the coping response to stress (d) the residual symptoms after an episode Answer: (b). Diathesis is the predisposition; the stressor is the precipitant. In Meehl's (1962) model, the inherited neural integrative defect is called: (a) schizotypy (b) schizotaxia (c) schizoid personality (d) schizophreniform state Answer: (b). Schizotaxia is the neural defect; schizotypy is the personality organisation built on it. "Vulnerability: a new view of schizophrenia", which proposed that episodes are time-limited while vulnerability is enduring, was written by: (a) Paul Meehl, 1962 (b) David Rosenthal, 1970 (c) Joseph Zubin and Bonnie Spring, 1977 (d) Scott Monroe and Anne Simons, 1991 Answer: (c). Zubin and Spring (1977), Journal of Abnormal Psychology . Hammen's (1991) finding that depressed women experience more dependent, interpersonal stressful events is known as: (a) kindling (b) stress generation (c) vantage sensitivity (d) expressed emotion Answer: (b). People with a depressive diathesis partly generate their own (dependent) stress. In the hopelessness theory of Abramson, Metalsky and Alloy (1989), the diathesis is: (a) the short allele of 5-HTTLPR (b) a negative inferential style attributing negative events to stable, global causes (c) high expressed emotion in the family (d) sociotropy Answer: (b). The cognitive diathesis is the negative inferential (attributional) style. The large 2019 study by Border and colleagues concluded that 5-HTTLPR x stress effects on depression: (a) were strongly confirmed (b) were confirmed only in women (c) were not supported (d) were larger than the main effect of stress Answer: (c). Border et al. (2019) found no support for historical candidate gene or candidate G x E hypotheses. A trait that predicts worse outcomes in adverse environments and better outcomes in supportive environments, compared with others, best fits: (a) the diathesis-stress model (b) differential susceptibility (c) the kindling hypothesis (d) the biopsychosocial model Answer: (b). "For better and for worse" with a crossover interaction is differential susceptibility. "Biological sensitivity to context" was proposed by: (a) Belsky and Pluess (2009) (b) Boyce and Ellis (2005) (c) Caspi and Moffitt (2003) (d) Ingram and Luxton (2005) Answer: (b). Boyce and Ellis (2005), Development and Psychopathology . Which component is NOT one of the classic dimensions of expressed emotion rated on the Camberwell Family Interview that predict relapse? (a) critical comments (b) hostility (c) emotional over-involvement (d) thought broadcasting Answer: (d). Thought broadcasting is a Schneiderian first-rank symptom, not an EE dimension. Robert Post's (1992) kindling hypothesis proposes that in recurrent mood disorder: (a) each later episode needs more stress than the first (b) later episodes need less stress and may become autonomous (c) stress plays no role at any stage (d) episodes are caused only by independent life events Answer: (b). Earlier episodes sensitise the system, so the threshold for later episodes falls. 2. Bleuler's four A's and the history of the schizophrenia concept "Schizophrenia" is a little over a century old as a word, and the concept has been reshaped three or four times since. Entrance examiners love this history because it is full of near-identical names, years one apart and symptom lists that sound alike. The way to keep it straight is to see each figure as answering a different question: Emil Kraepelin asked "what is the course?", Eugen Bleuler asked "what is the underlying psychological disturbance?", and Schneider asked "which symptoms can be reliably recognised and used for diagnosis?" 2.1 Before Kraepelin: the pieces Bénédict Augustin Morel (France) used the term démence précoce ("early dementia") for young people who showed early mental deterioration. The usual dates given are 1852 (Études cliniques) and 1860 (Traité des maladies mentales); sources differ on which is the "first" use. Morel worked within his theory of hereditary degeneration . Ewald Hecker (1871) described hebephrenia , an illness beginning in adolescence with silly, incongruous behaviour and rapid deterioration (the name had been suggested earlier by his teacher Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum). Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum (1874) described catatonia ("tension insanity"), with motor symptoms such as stupor, posturing and waxy flexibility. Paranoid states (with delusions as the main feature) were described by several authors as separate conditions. 2.2 Emil Kraepelin: dementia praecox Emil Kraepelin , working in Heidelberg and later Munich, revised his textbook ( Psychiatrie ) repeatedly. He used the Latin term dementia praecox in the 4th edition (1893) , at first for a narrower group among the "degenerative" processes. In the 6th edition (1899) he consolidated hebephrenia, catatonia and paranoid dementia into one disease, dementia praecox, on the grounds that, despite different symptoms, they shared: early onset (praecox = early, typically adolescence or young adulthood), and a deteriorating course ending in a characteristic weakening of mind (the "dementia"). In the same edition he set this against manic-depressive insanity , which ran an episodic course with good recovery between episodes. This Kraepelinian dichotomy (dementia praecox vs manic-depressive insanity, separated by course and outcome) still underlies the split between schizophrenia spectrum and mood disorder chapters in DSM and ICD. Kraepelin's method was longitudinal: he grouped patients by how the illness unfolded over years, recorded on his famous index cards (Zählkarten), rather than by any single symptom. Later editions (the 8th, 1909 to 1915) added further subforms such as simple dementia praecox. Exam trap Emil Kraepelin did not coin the French "démence précoce" (that is Morel). He did not coin "schizophrenia" (that is Bleuler). What Kraepelin did was unify hebephrenia, catatonia and paranoid forms under "dementia praecox" (consolidated in the 6th edition, 1899) and separate it from manic-depressive insanity. If a question asks who first described catatonia, the answer is Kahlbaum (1874); hebephrenia, Hecker (1871). 2.3 Eugen Bleuler: from dementia praecox to "the group of schizophrenias" Eugen Bleuler (1857 to 1939) was director of the Burghölzli , the psychiatric hospital of the University of Zurich, from 1898; Carl Gustav Jung worked there under him. Bleuler lived alongside his patients and was influenced by the associationist psychology of the day and by Sigmund Freud's ideas, which he applied to the content of psychotic symptoms. He introduced the word "schizophrenia" in a lecture in 1908 (to the German Psychiatric Association, Berlin). His great monograph, Dementia Praecox oder Gruppe der Schizophrenien ("Dementia praecox, or the group of schizophrenias"), appeared in 1911 as part of Gustav Aschaffenburg's handbook of psychiatry. It was translated into English only in 1950 , by Joseph Zinkin . Why rename it? "Schizophrenia" comes from Greek schizein (to split) and phren (mind). Bleuler meant the splitting (loosening) of the psychic functions from one another: thought, emotion and will no longer work together as a coherent whole, so a patient might describe a tragedy while smiling. He did not mean a "split personality" in the sense of multiple identities (that is dissociative identity disorder, a completely different condition). He also rejected Emil Kraepelin's name because his own patients showed that the illness was: not always a dementia : many did not deteriorate to a final weakened state, and some recovered, and not always praecox : onset could be later in life. The phrase "group of schizophrenias" shows that he already saw it as a heterogeneous group of conditions, not a single disease. 2.4 The four A's, one by one Eugen Bleuler did not use the phrase "four A's" himself; it is a teaching mnemonic added later by textbook writers to summarise his fundamental symptoms . Each is explained below with a clinical picture. 1. Associations (loosening of associations) For Bleuler this was the central disturbance. In normal thinking, ideas follow one another guided by a goal (the "determining tendency"). In schizophrenia the threads that link ideas are broken, so thoughts follow chance, sound or private links. Example: asked "How are you sleeping?", a patient replies, "Sleep is a bed of roses, roses are red, the Red Army marches at night, I keep watch." Modern terms that descend from this include derailment, tangentiality, incoherence and, in its mildest form, Meehl's "cognitive slippage". Bleuler also included thought blocking (sudden stopping of the train of thought). 2. Affect (affective disturbance) Emotional expression becomes flattened (blunted) or incongruous (inappropriate) to the content of thought. Example: a young man reports, without visible emotion, that his mother died last week, or laughs while describing being persecuted. Bleuler stressed that the inner emotional life might be less impoverished than it looks; what is lost is the integration between feeling and the rest of the mind. 3. Ambivalence Bleuler coined this word too. It means the simultaneous presence of contradictory feelings, wishes or thoughts toward the same object, both held at full strength without resolution. He described three forms: affective ambivalence : loving and hating the same person at the same moment; ambitendency (volitional ambivalence): wanting and not wanting to do something at once, so the patient starts to shake hands, withdraws, extends the hand again; intellectual ambivalence : thinking "I am a man" and "I am not a man" at the same time. Ordinary mixed feelings are not what he meant: in schizophrenia the opposites coexist without the normal pressure to reconcile them. 4. Autism Bleuler coined "autism" (Greek autos , self), around 1910 to 1911 (sources differ on the very first use), for the withdrawal from external reality into an inner world of fantasy , with "autistic thinking" governed by wishes and private logic rather than by reality. Example: a patient sits for hours absorbed in an inner drama, treating reality as less important than the inner world. The word was later borrowed by Leo Kanner (1943) , "Autistic disturbances of affective contact", and Hans Asperger (1944) , "autistic psychopathy", for a developmental condition of childhood. That borrowing is why the same word now names a completely different disorder. Memory hook A ssociations, A ffect, A mbivalence, A utism. None of the four is a hallucination or a delusion. Eugen Bleuler thought the dramatic "positive" symptoms were the surface; the real illness was the loosening underneath. 2.5 Two different axes: fundamental vs accessory, primary vs secondary This is the single most confused point in Bleuler questions, so build it slowly. Eugen Bleuler classified symptoms in two separate ways . Axis 1: fundamental (basic) vs accessory symptoms (a diagnostic axis) Fundamental symptoms are present, at least to some degree, in every case and at every stage, and are characteristic of schizophrenia. They are therefore what the diagnosis rests on. They include the four A's, and Bleuler also listed further fundamental disturbances (of attention, will, the "person" or sense of self, and schizophrenic "dementia" in his special sense). Accessory symptoms may or may not be present, come and go, and also occur in other illnesses. They include hallucinations, delusions , catatonic symptoms, certain disturbances of memory, speech and writing, and acute syndromes. They are often what brings the patient to hospital, yet for Bleuler they were not essential to the diagnosis. Axis 2: primary vs secondary symptoms (a theoretical, causal axis) Primary symptoms are the direct product of the underlying disease process , which Bleuler presumed to be organic. The chief primary symptom in his account was the loosening of associations (along with some others he thought organic, such as certain disturbances of consciousness and physical signs). Secondary symptoms are the person's psychological reactions to the primary disturbance and to their life situation, shaped by complexes and wishes. Much of the clinical picture, including autism, much of the affective change, hallucinations and delusions, was secondary in this sense. Because these are different axes, a symptom can be fundamental but secondary : autism is present in every case (fundamental) yet Bleuler regarded it as a psychological consequence (secondary). Hallucinations are accessory and secondary . Loosening of associations is fundamental and primary . Symptom Fundamental or accessory? Primary or secondary? Loosening of associations Fundamental Primary (the core) Autism Fundamental Largely secondary Hallucinations Accessory Secondary Delusions Accessory Secondary Catatonic symptoms Accessory Mostly secondary in his account Exam trap "Primary" is not a synonym for "fundamental", and "secondary" is not a synonym for "accessory". Many guidebooks blur them; when an MCQ asks specifically about Eugen Bleuler's primary symptom, the safest answer is loosening (disturbance) of associations. When it asks which are accessory , choose hallucinations and delusions. A fifth and sixth A? Some textbooks add Attention (Bleuler did discuss attentional disturbance among fundamental symptoms) and Avolition (or abulia, loss of will) as a fifth and sixth A. These are later teaching extensions, not part of the classic four. Do not confuse them with Nancy Andreasen's negative symptom domains on the SANS (1982): affective flattening, alogia, avolition-apathy, anhedonia-asociality and attention, sometimes called "the five A's of negative symptoms". If a question says "Bleuler's four A's", stick to associations, affect, ambivalence and autism. 2.6 Bleuler's influence: a broad concept and the US-UK gap Because Eugen Bleuler's fundamental symptoms were subtle and not tied to deterioration, his concept was broad : mild, latent and "simple" cases with no hallucinations or delusions could qualify. This broad view became dominant in the United States (helped by psychoanalytic psychiatry and by Harry Stack Sullivan and others), whereas British and European psychiatry stayed closer to Emil Kraepelin and Schneider. US-UK Diagnostic Project (John E. Cooper, Robert Kendell, Barry Gurland and colleagues, 1972, Psychiatric Diagnosis in New York and London ): New York hospital psychiatrists diagnosed schizophrenia far more often than London psychiatrists, including many patients London would have called manic-depressive or personality disordered. When the project team rated the same patients with a standardised interview (the Present State Examination), most of the difference disappeared. The gap was in diagnostic habits , not in the patients. International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia (IPSS) , WHO (1973): nine centres, including Agra in India . Seven centres shared a broadly similar core concept; Washington and Moscow used much broader concepts. The IPSS and its successor, the WHO Determinants of Outcome study (with Chandigarh as an Indian centre), also suggested a better course in developing-country centres. These findings pushed psychiatry toward operational criteria (Feighner criteria 1972, Research Diagnostic Criteria 1978, DSM-III 1980) that narrowed the American concept and leaned on Schneider's symptoms. 2.7 Kurt Schneider: first-rank symptoms Kurt Schneider (Heidelberg) took a pragmatic route. Whatever the underlying process, which symptoms are both easy to recognise and highly characteristic ? He set these out in Klinische Psychopathologie (first edition 1950, developed from earlier work in the late 1930s), translated into English by M. W. Hamilton in 1959 . In the absence of organic brain disease, the presence of a first-rank symptom (FRS) was to be taken as strongly suggestive of schizophrenia. Christopher S. Mellor (1970) l

title: Biopsychology & Neuroscience
text: Biopsychology & Neuroscience The biology of behaviour from first principles: how neurons fire and talk, how the nervous system is built and mapped, the transmitter systems and their drugs, and the circuits behind sensation, movement, memory, hunger, hormones, sleep, stress, emotion, addiction and psychiatric disorders, anchored to Pinel & Barnes and deepened with Carlson, prioritised for MET 2026 and NIMHANS clinical neuropsychology. In this book Biopsychology as a neuroscience Evolution, genetics & experience Anatomy of the nervous system The cranial nerves (I–XII) Neural conduction & the action potential Synaptic transmission & neurotransmitter systems Research methods of biopsychology The visual system Audition & the other senses The sensorimotor system Development of the nervous system Brain damage & neuroplasticity Learning, memory & amnesia Hunger, eating & health Hormones, sex & the HPA axis Sleep, dreaming & circadian rhythms Reward, drugs of abuse & addiction Lateralisation, language & the split brain Emotion, stress & health Biopsychology of psychiatric disorders Clinical neuropsychology: syndromes & batteries Genetic, chromosomal & metabolic disorders Landmark studies, walked through Extended concept bank Fast glossary (A–Z) 1. Biopsychology as a neuroscience The one idea behind the whole field. Biopsychology is the scientific study of the biology of behaviour : how the nervous system produces what we think, feel and do. It is the branch of neuroscience (the larger study of the nervous system) that keeps behaviour at the centre. The recurring lesson is that mind and brain are not two things: every thought is a physical event in tissue. The six divisions of biopsychology The field is split by what you study and how . Learn each by its defining method, because the paper tests "which division does X?". Division What it studies Typical method Physiological psychology Neural mechanisms of behaviour Direct manipulation of the brain in controlled experiments (lesions, stimulation), usually in lab animals Psychopharmacology Effects of drugs on behaviour and the brain Manipulate behaviour with drugs; develop therapeutic drugs Neuropsychology Psychological effects of brain damage in human patients Case studies + standardised tests; the most applied division (NIMHANS leans here) Psychophysiology Relation between physiology and behaviour using non-invasive body measures in healthy humans EEG, heart rate, skin conductance (GSR), pupil size Cognitive neuroscience Neural bases of cognition (thought, memory, attention) Mainly functional brain imaging (fMRI, PET) in humans Comparative psychology Behaviour across species, evolution, genetics, ethology Cross-species comparison, naturalistic + lab study Trap Psychophysiology vs physiological psychology. Both have "physiolog" in the name. Physiological psychology = invasive manipulation of the brain, usually in animals . Psychophysiology = non-invasive recording from the surface of healthy humans . And neuropsychology = the study of human brain-damaged patients. Kinds of research, kinds of inference Pure vs applied. Pure = curiosity-driven knowledge; applied = solving a practical problem. Most real work is a blend. Experiments vs non-experiments. Only a true experiment (the researcher manipulates an independent variable and randomly assigns) can support a causal claim. Quasi-experiments and case studies cannot fully rule out confounds. Converging operations. Because every single method is flawed, biopsychology trusts a conclusion only when several different methods point the same way . This is the field's signature methodological value. Morgan's Canon / law of parsimony: prefer the simplest explanation that fits; do not attribute a higher mental process when a lower one will do. High-yield Human brain-damaged patients = neuropsychology ; drugs = psychopharmacology ; non-invasive measures in healthy humans = psychophysiology ; imaging of cognition = cognitive neuroscience ; animal brain manipulation = physiological psychology ; across species = comparative . Causation needs a true experiment; trust the conclusion many methods agree on. 2. Evolution, genetics & experience The problem this fixes. The old "nature versus nurture" question is a false dichotomy. Genes and experience are not rival causes adding up to 100%; they interact continuously. A trait is a genetic program read out in an environment. You cannot say a behaviour is "60% genetic" for an individual, only how much variation in a population is associated with genetic variation (heritability). Evolution of the brain Natural selection (Charles Darwin): heritable traits that improve fitness (reproductive success) spread. Behaviour evolves too. Larger brains are not automatically "better"; what matters is brain size relative to body size and the expansion of specific regions, especially the cerebral cortex in primates. Convergent evolution = similar traits arise independently (analogous structures). Homologous structures share a common ancestor. Do not read similarity as shared ancestry. Spandrels & exaptations: not every trait is a direct adaptation; some are by-products later co-opted for new uses. Mendelian genetics & the molecular layer Gene = a stretch of DNA on a chromosome. Humans have 23 pairs; the 23rd is the sex pair (XX female, XY male). Dominant vs recessive alleles; homozygous vs heterozygous ; genotype (the genes) vs phenotype (the expressed trait). Dizygotic (fraternal) twins share ~50% of genes (like ordinary siblings); monozygotic (identical) twins share ~100%. Comparing them is the classic heritability tool. Central dogma: DNA → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation) → protein. Epigenetics: experience changes which genes are read Epigenetics is the mechanism that finally dissolves nature-versus-nurture. The DNA sequence does not change, but experience can switch genes on or off via chemical tags, especially DNA methylation (silences genes) and histone modification . These ma

title: Cognitive Psychology — the whole domain, explained cold
text: Cognitive Psychology — the whole domain, explained cold Built from Eysenck & Keane, Cognitive Psychology: A Student's Handbook , the book you listed for cognitive. This is the full-depth version : for every named model you get what it claims, who proposed it, the key experiment (what was done and what was found), and the contrast with its rival in a red trap box. Tables stay as quick-reference, but read the prose around them first. Cognition spans perception, attention, memory, knowledge, language and thinking, so this single page walks the book chapter by chapter. Rebuilt to full depth 2026-05-29. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How cognitive is tested. (1) Name the model from its claim ("we store info in three stores" = multi-store). (2) Pin the model to its author (working memory = Alan Baddeley & Graham Hitch). (3) Tell rival models apart — that's where the distractor lives: Gregory vs Gibson, early vs late selection, episodic vs semantic, prototype vs exemplar, Broca vs Wernicke. Learn each in its contrast pair, and learn the one experiment that decides between them. Jump to: 1. Approaches 2. Visual perception 3. Object & face recognition 4. Attention 5. STM & working memory 6. Long-term memory 7. Forgetting & everyday memory 8. Concepts & knowledge 9. Language 10. Problem solving & expertise 11. Judgement & decision making 12. Reasoning ★ At-a-glance compare ★ MCQ traps ★ Key studies ★ Glossary ★ Self-test 1. Approaches to human cognition Eysenck & Keane open by saying cognitive psychology is not one method but four converging approaches , each with its own logic and limits. The point of knowing all four is that an exam stem will describe a technique and ask which approach it belongs to. Experimental cognitive psychology What it claims: you can infer the hidden stages of mental processing in healthy people by measuring behaviour under controlled conditions — chiefly reaction time (RT) and accuracy/error rate . It is the oldest strand and the historical core of the field. If a manipulation slows people down, that stage must require processing. Key logic: the subtraction/additive-factors idea — compare two tasks differing in one operation, and the RT difference estimates that operation's duration. Limit: behaviour alone is ambiguous about the underlying architecture (many models predict the same RT), and lab tasks may lack ecological validity. Cognitive neuropsychology + modularity What it claims: studying brain-damaged patients reveals the normal architecture of cognition, because damage can knock out one ability while sparing another. The bedrock assumption is modularity (Fodor): the mind contains specialised, domain-specific, informationally encapsulated modules that can be independently impaired. Key logic — the double dissociation : patient A is impaired on task X but fine on Y, while patient B is fine on X but impaired on Y. That pattern is strong evidence the two tasks rely on separate systems (one alone could be explained by task difficulty). Example: H.M. (studied by William Scoville and Brenda Milner, 1957) lost the ability to form new long-term memories yet had normal short-term span; other patients (e.g. K.F.) show the reverse — together a double dissociation of STM and LTM. Limit: damage is rarely clean, the brain reorganises, and single cases generalise poorly. Cognitive neuroscience methods What it claims: by measuring the living brain we can locate where and time when cognition happens. The methods trade off spatial against temporal resolution, and the exam loves to ask which method gives which. Method Measures Strength fMRI Blood-oxygen (BOLD) — indirect metabolic signal Excellent spatial resolution (mm), poor temporal (seconds); shows where . PET Radioactive tracer, blood flow/metabolism Good spatial, very poor temporal; needs injected tracer. EEG / ERP Scalp electrical activity; ERP = signal averaged to an event Excellent temporal resolution (ms), poor spatial; shows when . TMS Magnetic pulse that briefly disrupts a region Creates a "virtual lesion" → tests if a region is necessary (causal, not just correlational). Spatial vs temporal mnemonic: fMRI/PET = WHERE (great space, poor time). EEG/ERP = WHEN (great time, poor space). TMS = whether it's NECESSARY (causal). fMRI and EEG are merely correlational; only TMS and lesions establish that a region is causally required. Computational cognitive science & connectionism (PDP) What it claims: if a theory is precise enough, you can implement it as a running computer program; a model that actually reproduces human performance (including human errors ) is a strong test of the theory. The dominant style is connectionism / parallel distributed processing (PDP) : networks of simple, neuron-like units connected by weighted links, where knowledge is distributed across the pattern of weights rather than stored in one location, and learning happens by gradually adjusting weights (e.g. back-propagation). NIMHANS tests harder — connectionism. Be ready for the contrast with classical "symbolic" models. Symbolic (e.g. Allen Newell & Herbert Simon's physical-symbol-system) manipulates discrete rules and symbols, processing serially. Connectionist/PDP uses distributed sub-symbolic representations and parallel processing; its hallmarks are graceful degradation (partial damage = partial loss, not total crash), generalisation, and learning from examples. NIMHANS may ask which framework explains prototype effects or developmental error patterns (e.g. the U-shaped curve in learning the past tense) — that's connectionism. Bottom-up vs top-down; serial vs parallel Two cross-cutting distinctions run through the whole book. Bottom-up (data-driven) processing starts from the stimulus and works up. Top-down (concept-driven) processing brings expectations, context and stored knowledge to bear. Information processing (the frame Donald Broadbent founded) treats the mind as stages from input → encoding → storage

title: Developmental Psychology
text: Developmental Psychology The lifespan story of how mind, behaviour, and relationships unfold, told through the theorists MET 2026 and NIMHANS love to test: Jean Piaget and Vygotsky on cognition, Bronfenbrenner on context, Erik Erikson, Sigmund Freud, Marcia on identity and psychosocial growth, Lawrence Kohlberg and Gilligan on morality, John Bowlby, Mary Ainsworth, Main, Harlow on attachment, Baumrind on parenting, Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess plus Mary Rothbart and John Bates and Kagan on temperament, plus prenatal development, language, adolescence, and aging. Read top to bottom once, then revise off the tables and the red Trap boxes. In this book Foundational principles Prenatal development and teratogens Piaget: cognitive development Vygotsky: sociocultural theory Bronfenbrenner: ecological systems / bioecological model Erikson: psychosocial stages Marcia: identity statuses Freud: psychosexual stages Kohlberg and Gilligan: moral development Attachment: Bowlby, Ainsworth, Main, Harlow Baumrind: parenting styles Temperament: Thomas & Chess, Rothbart & Bates, Kagan Language development Adolescence Aging and late adulthood Theorist hooks (one line each) Top MCQ traps and 30-second recall 1. Foundational Principles Principle Meaning Example Cephalocaudal Head to toe Head control before walking Proximodistal Center to periphery Trunk control before fine finger movement Continuity vs Discontinuity Gradual growth vs stage jumps Vocab growth (continuous) vs Piaget stages (discontinuous) Nature vs Nurture Genes vs environment; modern view = interactionist Twin studies, behavioral genetics Critical period Rigid window; miss it and the capacity is lost Lorenz imprinting in geese Sensitive period Flexible window; learning easier but still possible later L1 acquisition, depth perception Stability vs Change Do traits persist or shift across life? Temperament (mostly stable), IQ (some plasticity) Active vs Passive child Does the child shape their own development? Bidirectionality (Urie Bronfenbrenner, Bell) Trap Critical = rigid biological window (lost if missed). Sensitive = optimal but flexible. Konrad Lorenz's imprinting = critical. Language learning = sensitive (you can still learn L2 at 30, just harder). 2. Prenatal Development and Teratogens Three prenatal stages Stage Duration Key event Germinal 0-2 weeks Zygote to blastocyst to implantation Embryonic 2-8 weeks Organogenesis; most vulnerable to teratogens Fetal 8 weeks to birth Growth and refinement; viability ~24 weeks Teratogens (high-yield) Alcohol — Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD); FAS = facial anomalies, growth restriction, CNS damage. Most common preventable cause of intellectual disability. Tobacco — low birth weight, prematurity. Thalidomide — limb malformations (1950s-60s, classic teratogen exam case). Rubella — heart, eye, ear defects in 1st trimester. Lead, mercury — CNS damage. Zika — microcephaly. Trap The embryonic period (weeks 2-8) is most vulnerable, not the fetal period. Organs are forming. By the fetal period, organs already exist and growth is the main task. 3. Piaget: Cognitive Development The 4 stages Stage Age Achievements Limits Sensorimotor 0-2 Object permanence (~8mo), goal-directed action, deferred imitation (end) No symbolic thought early on Preoperational 2-7 Symbolic thought, language, pretend play Egocentrism, animism, centration, no conservation Concrete Operational 7-11 Conservation, reversibility, classification, seriation, decentration Tied to concrete reality; abstract is shaky Formal Operational 11+ Abstract, hypothetico-deductive, propositional logic Adolescent egocentrism (imaginary audience, personal fable) Sensorimotor: the 6 substages Reflexive schemes (0-1mo) Primary circular reactions (1-4mo, on own body) Secondary circular reactions (4-8mo, on objects) Coordination of secondary schemes (8-12mo, intentional, object permanence , A-not-B error) Tertiary circular reactions (12-18mo, experimentation) Mental representation (18-24mo, deferred imitation, symbolic thought) Key concepts Schema — mental framework for understanding the world. Assimilation — fitting new info into an existing schema (a horse = a "doggie"). Accommodation — modifying the schema for new info ("ok, that's a horse, not a doggie"). Equilibration — the drive to balance assimilation and accommodation; the engine of cognitive change. Egocentrism — preoperational; can't take another's perspective. Three Mountains task. Animism — preoperational; attributing life to objects. Centration — focus on one feature at a time; blocks conservation. Conservation — quantity stays the same despite a change in form (number, mass, volume). Order: number then mass then liquid then length then area then weight then volume (last, ~11). Trap Object permanence (sensorimotor, ~8mo) is NOT conservation (concrete operational, ~7yr). Different stages, different concepts. Also: "egocentrism" in dev psych is a cognitive limit, not narcissism or a personality trait. Critiques of Piaget Underestimated infants (modern habituation studies show object permanence earlier). Stages less discrete than he claimed ( horizontal décalage = uneven performance within a stage). Underplayed culture (Lev Vygotsky's main attack). Not everyone reaches formal operational, especially for unfamiliar content. 4. Vygotsky: Sociocultural Theory ZPD (Zone of Proximal Development) — the gap between what a child can do alone vs with help from a more knowledgeable other (MKO). Scaffolding — temporary, tailored support, withdrawn as competence grows. This is Jerome Bruner's term , applied to Lev Vygotsky's framework. Private speech — kids talk to themselves while problem-solving. It becomes inner speech and guides cognition. Jean Piaget called this "egocentric speech" and dismissed it; Vygotsky said it is central. Tools of thought — language is the master tool, internalized from social interaction. Higher mental functions are socially mediated . Cultural specificity — cognitive devel

Defining abnormality (the 4 Ds) Deviance — statistical or social norm violation. Distress — subjective suffering. Dysfunction — impairs daily life / role functioning. Danger — risk to self or others. Trap Deviance alone is not abnormal. A genius IQ is statistically deviant but not pathological. You always need at least distress or dysfunction alongside it. High-yield Some textbooks list a 5th D, Duration , used for chronicity criteria (the recurring duration thresholds like ≥ 6 months, ≥ 2 years, etc. that define many disorders below). 2. Historical models & conceptions Era Model Key name(s) Prehistoric / Ancient Supernatural (demons, possession) Trephination Greek / Roman Biological, four humors Hippocrates, Galen Middle Ages Demonological return, witch trials Malleus Maleficarum (1487) Renaissance Asylum reform begins Pinel (Bicêtre, "moral treatment"), Tuke (York Retreat) 19th c. Watson (behaviorism) Mid 20th c. Cognitive-behavioral Aaron Beck (depression / CBT), Albert Ellis (REBT) 1980s+ Biopsychosocial integration Engel (1977) Trap Emil Kraepelin coined dementia praecox (emphasising early onset and a deteriorating course). Eugen Bleuler renamed it schizophrenia ("split mind", referring to fragmented thought, not split personality). Do not confuse with DID. 3. Approaches to psychopathology Approach Cause Treatment Biological Genes, neurotransmitters, brain Meds, ECT, psychosurgery Psychodynamic Unconscious conflict, early experience Psychoanalysis, free association, transference Behavioral Maladaptive learning Conditioning, exposure, reinforcement Cognitive Distorted thoughts, schemas CBT, cognitive restructuring (Aaron Beck), REBT (Albert Ellis) Humanistic Blocked self-actualization Person-centered (Carl Rogers), Gestalt (Fritz Perls) Sociocultural Family, culture, stigma, oppression Family therapy, community psychology Biopsychosocial All three interact ( Engel, 1977 ) Integrative Diathesis-stress Predisposition × stressor Reduce both load 4. The ICD: WHO's classification (full breakdown) Definition The ICD (International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems) is the WHO's global classification of all diseases, not just mental ones. Mental disorders occupy a single chapter of it. DSM (American Psychiatric Association) covers mental disorders only. So: ICD = whole-body, global, free, used for official health statistics; DSM = mental-only, US, paywalled, research-heavy. NIMHANS / India officially codes on ICD . 4.1 What ICD is & who owns it Question Answer Full name International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems Publisher WHO (World Health Organization). DSM is APA, the contrast examiners love. Scope All diseases and health conditions, every body system. Mental & behavioural disorders are just one chapter . Purpose Global standard for mortality & morbidity statistics , billing, epidemiology. Official tool for cause-of-death and disease reporting worldwide. Cost Free , multilingual. DSM is copyrighted and sold by APA. Used where ~194 WHO member states, including India . DSM dominates US clinical research. 4.2 Version history (the dates they ask) Version Year Note ICD-6 1949 First edition to include a section on mental disorders. Common MCQ. ICD-8 1965 ICD-9 1975 US used a clinical modification, ICD-9-CM , for decades. ICD-10 1990 endorsed, 1992 in use Still tested. Mental disorders = Chapter V (F-codes) . Alphanumeric coding introduced here. ICD-11 Adopted 2019, in force 1 Jan 2022 Fully digital "foundation" architecture. Mental disorders = Chapter 06 . High-yield Lock the three dates: ICD-6 (1949) = first mental-disorder section · ICD-10 (1992) = F-codes · ICD-11 (in force 2022) = current. 4.3 Where mental disorders live ICD-10 ICD-11 Chapter Chapter V Chapter 06 Title Mental and Behavioural Disorders Mental, Behavioural or Neurodevelopmental Disorders Code prefix F (F00–F99) Alphanumeric 6 -codes (e.g. 6A20 for schizophrenia) Companion text "Blue Book" (Clinical Descriptions & Diagnostic Guidelines) + "Green Book" (research criteria) CDDR (Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements) High-yield Why "F"? No mnemonic meaning, it is simply the letter assigned to the mental-disorders chapter (Chapter V) in ICD-10's alphanumeric scheme. If asked "F-codes refer to," the answer is mental and behavioural disorders . 4.4 ICD-10 F-codes — the F00–F99 blocks (memorise the ranges) Range Block Examples F00–F09 Organic, incl. symptomatic, mental disorders Dementia (Alzheimer's, vascular), delirium F10–F19 Mental/behavioural due to psychoactive substance

title: Abnormal Psychology — the integrative approach, disorder by disorder (Barlow & Durand + DSM-5-TR + ICD-11)
text: Abnormal Psychology — the integrative approach, disorder by disorder (Barlow & Durand + DSM-5-TR + ICD-11) The Abnormal section built the way Barlow & Durand, Abnormal Psychology: An Integrative Approach teaches it: every disorder opens with a clinical case , then runs the book's four-beat frame — (1) clinical description · (2) statistics (prevalence, onset, sex ratio, course) · (3) causes , read through the multidimensional integrative model (biological × psychological × emotional × social × developmental) · (4) treatment . On top of the book, every disorder's classification is cross-checked against the current criteria so nothing is outdated: DSM-5-TR (APA, 2022) and ICD-11 (WHO, in force Jan 2022), shown side by side where they differ (the ICD-11 reclassifications are exactly what MET/NIMHANS/RCI fish for). Look-alike distinctions MCQs live on are in red trap boxes; where NIMHANS pushes past the book it's in purple . This is the companion to the Ahuja full-book page — same disorders, the integrative/case lens instead of the Indian-psychiatry lens. Built 2026-06-07. Abnormal (Barlow & Durand) Abnormal (Ahuja, full book) Abnormal cheatsheet ICD breakdown High-yield sheet Counselling (Sharf) Lookalikes What is "Barlow & Durand" and why a second abnormal page. The Ahuja page reads the field as Indian psychiatry: definitions, criteria, drugs, fast and exam-tight. Barlow & Durand reads it as integrative science : it refuses any single cause and forces every disorder through a multidimensional model , and it teaches from cases . That's the angle this page adds. Same syllabus, deeper "why does it happen" answers (causes), plus the triple vulnerability theory (Barlow's own) for the anxiety block and the equifinality / multifinality developmental ideas — both pure B&D, both testable. Use Ahuja for the cut-offs and drugs, use this for the model questions ("which approach / what causes it / which dimension"). Two ideas hold the whole book together. (1) The multidimensional integrative model. No disorder has one cause; each is the product of biological (genes, brain circuits, neurotransmitters), psychological (learning, cognition, conditioning), emotional , social/cultural and developmental dimensions interacting. (2) Diathesis-stress run forward in time. A vulnerability (diathesis) only becomes a disorder when life delivers the stress; genes and environment are not separate but reciprocal (your genes shape the environments you pick), and experience switches genes on and off ( epigenetics ). Hold these two and you can reconstruct almost every "what causes X / which model" answer. Jump to: 1. Defining a disorder (the 3 components) 2. The integrative model 3. Assessment & diagnosis 4. Anxiety disorders + triple vulnerability 5. Panic disorder & agoraphobia 6. Specific & social phobia 7. Trauma- & stressor-related (PTSD) 8. OCD & related 9. Somatic symptom disorders 10. Dissociative disorders 11. Mood disorders 12. Suicide 13. Eating disorders 14. Sleep–wake disorders 15. Sexual, gender & paraphilic 16. Substance-related & addictive 17. Personality disorders 18. Schizophrenia spectrum 19. Neurodevelopmental 20. Neurocognitive DSM vs ICD at a glance All the MCQ traps Names & studies roster Fast glossary (A–Z) Self-test (active recall) Part One · Foundations & the integrative model Ch 1. What makes behaviour a disorder, and the three traditions Barlow & Durand do not use a "4 Ds" list. Their working definition of a psychological disorder has three components , and all three usually travel together: (1) psychological dysfunction — a breakdown in cognitive, emotional or behavioural functioning; (2) distress or impairment — it hurts the person or wrecks their day-to-day functioning; (3) an atypical or culturally unexpected response — it deviates from what the culture expects (and is not merely a deviant act society dislikes). They lean on Wakefield's "harmful dysfunction" : a disorder is a failure of an internal mechanism to do what it evolved to do ( dysfunction ) and that failure is harmful to the person by their culture's standards. B&D's 3 vs Ahuja's 4 Ds. If a question cites " dysfunction + distress/impairment + atypical/culturally unexpected ," that's the Barlow & Durand definition (3 components). The "Deviance, Distress, Dysfunction, Danger" 4-D list is the more common Indian-text framing. Danger is NOT one of B&D's three. Both agree dysfunction/impairment is the indispensable core and distress alone is neither necessary nor sufficient (a person in mania feels great). Tradition Core claim · key names Treatment it implies Supernatural Possession, sin, the moon, witchcraft; Malleus Maleficarum (1487); the "mass hysteria"/St Vitus dances Exorcism, prayer, shunning Biological Hippocrates' four humours (imbalance = illness); Galen ; Emil Kraepelin (classification, dementia praecox ); the discovery that general paresis = late-stage syphilis cemented "mental illness can be physical" Rest, drugs, ECT, psychosurgery Psychological Moral therapy (Pinel at Bicêtre, Tuke's York Retreat — humane treatment); Sigmund Freud & psychoanalysis (unconscious, defences); Watson/Pavlov/Skinner behaviourism (learning); humanism (Carl Rogers) Talk therapy, conditioning, person-centred B&D frame the modern clinician as a scientist-practitioner : a consumer and producer of research who treats each case as testable. The whole book is then an argument that the three traditions are not rivals but dimensions of one integrative explanation. Recap Ch 1. B&D disorder = psychological dysfunction + distress/impairment + atypical/culturally unexpected (3 components, NOT 4 Ds; "harmful dysfunction," Wakefield). Three historical traditions — supernatural, biological (humours → Kraepelin → general paresis), psychological (moral therapy → Freud → behaviourism) — converge in the integrative model. How DSM-5-TR is built, and how to use it in an exam Before any disorder, understand the machine. A surprising number of entrance questions are about the classification system itself rather than about any single disorder, and those are free marks because there is nothing to remember except structure. What DSM is, and what it deliberately is not The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders is published by the American Psychiatric Association . It is a categorical, descriptive, atheoretical nosology. Descriptive means it defines disorders by observable signs and reported symptoms, not by presumed cause. Atheoretical means it deliberately refuses to commit to psychoanalytic, behavioural, or biological explanation, so a clinician of any orientation can use the same code. That neutrality was the single biggest change at DSM-III (1980), which is the edition that introduced explicit operational criteria, the multiaxial system, and the abandonment of the psychoanalytic word "neurosis". If a paper asks which DSM edition marked the turn to operational criteria and reliability, the answer is always DSM-III. Edition timeline, memorise the years DSM-I 1952 (106 categories, "reactions", Meyerian). DSM-II 1968 (182 categories, still psychodynamic language). DSM-III 1980 (265 categories, operational criteria, multiaxial, atheoretical, homosexuality already removed as a diagnosis in 1973 from DSM-II's printing). DSM-III-R 1987. DSM-IV 1994, DSM-IV-TR 2000. DSM-5 2013 (Arabic numeral so it can be revised 5.1, 5.2; multiaxial system abolished; dimensional and spectrum thinking added). DSM-5-TR March 2022 . What changed in the 2022 Text Revision, specifically DSM-5-TR is a text revision, so most of the change is in the explanatory text rather than the criteria. The examinable changes are: One entirely new disorder: Prolonged Grief Disorder , placed in the Trauma and Stressor-Related chapter. This is the highest-yield single fact in the whole TR. Unspecified Mood Disorder was brought back, for presentations where you cannot yet tell depressive from bipolar. Suicidal behaviour and non-suicidal self-injury became separate coded conditions (ICD-10-CM codes) that can be recorded alongside any diagnosis, rather than only being criteria inside borderline personality disorder and depression. Terminology. "Intellectual Disability" now carries the parenthetical "(Intellectual Developmental Disorder)"; "neuroleptic" was largely replaced by "antipsychotic"; the term "sexual identity" was dropped; "desired gender" became "experienced gender", "cross-sex medical procedure" became "gender-affirming medical procedure", and "natal male/female" became "individual assigned male/female at birth" in Gender Dysphoria. Culture and racism. Text throughout was rewritten by an Ethnoracial Equity and Inclusion work group; "race" is discussed as a social construct, "racialised" and "ethnoracial" replace older usage, and the impact of racism and discrimination on prevalence and presentation is stated in the text. Prevalence, risk and culture sections were updated across almost every disorder, and ICD-10-CM codes were refreshed. The multiaxial system, and why it is gone DSM-IV-TR used five axes: Axis I clinical disorders, Axis II personality disorders and mental retardation, Axis III general medical conditions, Axis IV psychosocial and environmental problems, Axis V the Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF), a 0 to 100 scale. DSM-5 abolished all of it. Axes I, II and III were merged into a single list of diagnoses; Axis IV was replaced by the ICD Z-codes for psychosocial and contextual factors; Axis V was dropped because the GAF was psychometrically poor (it confounded symptom severity with functioning) and replaced by the WHODAS 2.0 , the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule, a 36-item measure across six domains (cognition, mobility, self-care, getting along, life activities, participation). Trap Questions still ask "on which axis was mental retardation coded?" The answer is Axis II, in DSM-IV-TR, and the correct full answer adds that the multiaxial system no longer exists in DSM-5 or DSM-5-TR and that GAF was replaced by WHODAS 2.0. Answer both halves. The definition of a mental disorder DSM-5-TR defines a mental disorder as a syndrome characterised by clinically significant disturbance in an individual's cognition, emotion regulation, or behaviour that reflects a dysfunction in the psychological, biological, or developmental processes underlying mental functioning. Mental disorders are usually associated with significant distress or disability in social, occupational, or other important activities. Three exclusions are written into that definition and are examined constantly: An expectable or culturally approved response to a common stressor or loss (for example ordinary bereavement) is not a mental disorder. Socially deviant behaviour (political, religious, sexual) and conflicts primarily between the individual and society are not mental disorders, unless the deviance results from a dysfunction in the individual. The disturbance must not be better explained by another condition, including a substance or another medical condition. The clause under almost every disorder Two clauses recur so often that you should assume them unless told otherwise. Clinical significance: "the symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning." Exclusion: "not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition, and not better explained by another mental disorder."
