When a question gives you a person with symptoms but explicitly says work and relationships are unaffected and they are not bothered, the answer is usually "no diagnosis", not the disorder that matches the symptom list. Categorical versus dimensional, and where DSM-5-TR hedges DSM remains categorical: you either meet criteria or you do not. The known problems with that are heterogeneity (two people with the same diagnosis can share almost no symptoms), arbitrary thresholds (five of nine symptoms is a diagnosis, four is not), high comorbidity (a sign the categories are not carving nature at its joints), and heavy use of "other specified" and "unspecified" residual categories. DSM-5 added dimensional elements without abandoning categories: severity specifiers on almost every disorder, cross-cutting symptom measures, the collapse of autism's subtypes into one spectrum , the collapse of substance abuse and dependence into a single graded substance use disorder , and the Alternative Model for Personality Disorders in Section III. The fully dimensional alternatives you should be able to name are HiTOP (Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology), RDoC (Research Domain Criteria, NIMH, organised by domains such as negative valence and positive valence systems crossed with units of analysis from genes to self-report), and the p-factor (a general psychopathology factor). DSM-5-TR versus ICD-11, the comparisons that get asked Publisher and purpose. DSM is by the American Psychiatric Association, primarily a diagnostic manual for clinicians and researchers. ICD-11 (in effect from 1 January 2022) is by the WHO, is a global public-health statistical classification covering all diseases, is free, and is the system India officially uses for reporting. Structure. ICD-11 uses alphanumeric codes; mental, behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders sit in Chapter 06. ICD-11 gives prototypical descriptions with flexible boundaries rather than DSM's counted criteria, on the reasoning that counted thresholds create false precision in general medical settings. Disorders that exist in one and not the other. ICD-11 has Complex PTSD , Gaming Disorder , Prolonged Grief Disorder (DSM added it in the TR), Body Integrity Dysphoria , Compulsive Sexual Behaviour Disorder and Olfactory Reference Disorder ; DSM-5-TR does not have Complex PTSD or Gaming Disorder as full diagnoses (internet gaming disorder is in Section III, conditions for further study). DSM has Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder ; ICD-11 folds that presentation into oppositional defiant disorder "with chronic irritability-anger". Personality. ICD-11 abolished the ten categorical personality disorders entirely and replaced them with a single Personality Disorder diagnosis rated mild, moderate or severe, plus five trait domain qualifiers (negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia) and a borderline pattern qualifier. DSM-5-TR keeps the ten categories in Section II and offers its own trait model only in Section III. Schizophrenia. Both dropped the classical subtypes (paranoid, hebephrenic, catatonic, undifferentiated, residual, simple). ICD-11 requires one month of symptoms; DSM requires six months of total disturbance with at least one month of active-phase symptoms. That six versus one month contrast is one of the most reused questions in the whole syllabus. How to read a vignette fast Four questions, in this order. (1) Duration. Almost every differential in DSM is settled by time: 1 day / 1 month / 6 months / 2 years. Find the duration in the stem first. (2) Onset age. Before 12, before 18, after 60. (3) Is there a substance or medical cause? If the stem mentions steroids, thyroid, stroke, or a drug, that is not decoration. (4) Impairment. If it says functioning is intact, suspect a subthreshold or "no diagnosis" option. 2. Neurodevelopmental disorders Onset in the developmental period, meaning the deficits are present early and are not a decline from a previously normal level. That last phrase is the whole differential against the neurocognitive chapter: neurodevelopmental means never acquired, neurocognitive means acquired and then lost. Intellectual Developmental Disorder (Intellectual Disability) F70-F73 In plain language. The person's reasoning and their ability to run their own life are both below what is expected for their age, and this has been true since childhood. DSM-5 made the important move of deciding severity by adaptive functioning , not by the IQ number, because how well someone copes is what determines the support they need. Deficits in intellectual functions (reasoning, problem solving, planning, abstract thinking, judgment, academic learning, learning from experience), confirmed by clinical assessment and individualised standardised testing. Deficits in adaptive functioning so that the person fails to meet developmental and sociocultural standards for personal independence and social responsibility, across at least one of three domains: conceptual (language, reading, money, time), social (empathy, friendships, gullibility), practical (self-care, job, money management, transport). Onset during the developmental period . Numbers IQ roughly two standard deviations below the mean, about 65 to 75 allowing for the measurement error band, but severity is graded Mild / Moderate / Severe / Profound on adaptive functioning, not IQ. Prevalence about 1 percent overall, about 6 per 1000 for severe. Male to female roughly 1.6:1 for mild. Related Global Developmental Delay is the diagnosis under age 5 when severity cannot yet be reliably assessed; it requires reassessment. Unspecified Intellectual Disability is for over-5s who cannot be assessed because of sensory or physical impairment or severe behaviour. Comorbidity Three to four times the general-population rate of other mental disorders. Commonest: ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, stereotypic movement disorder (with or without self-injury), depressive and bipolar disorders, anxiety disorders, impulse-control disorders. Medically: epilepsy, cerebral palsy, sensory impairment. Differential Major neurocognitive disorder (there the ability was present and was lost; here it was never acquired, though the two can coexist). Specific learning disorder (deficit is confined to one academic domain, general intelligence is normal). Communication disorders (language impaired, non-verbal reasoning intact). Autism (social deficits out of proportion to overall developmental level). Also rule out sensory impairment, deprivation, and poor test-taking due to unfamiliarity with the testing language, which is a real issue in Indian samples. Communication Disorders F80.x In plain language. Five conditions, each about a different part of using language. Language Disorder. Persistent difficulty acquiring and using language across modalities (spoken, written, sign) because of deficits in comprehension or production: reduced vocabulary, limited sentence structure, impaired discourse. Abilities are substantially below age expectation. Onset in the early developmental period. Speech Sound Disorder. Persistent difficulty with speech sound production that interferes with intelligibility. The child is understood poorly, though language content is fine. Childhood-Onset Fluency Disorder (Stuttering). Disturbance in the normal fluency and time patterning of speech: sound and syllable repetitions, prolongations, broken words, audible or silent blocking, circumlocutions, physical tension. Causes anxiety about speaking. Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder. Persistent difficulty with the social use of verbal and non-verbal communication: greeting and sharing information appropriately, changing communication to match the listener or context, following rules of conversation and storytelling (turn taking, rephrasing when misunderstood), and understanding what is not explicitly stated (inference, idiom, humour, metaphor). New in DSM-5. Unspecified Communication Disorder. Numbers Stuttering onset usually between ages 2 and 7, with 80 to 90 percent onset by age 6; recovery in about 65 to 85 percent. Social pragmatic communication disorder is rarely diagnosed under age 4 or 5 because the skills are not yet expected. Comorbidity Specific learning disorder, ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, developmental coordination disorder, social anxiety disorder (especially with stuttering). Differential The examined one is Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder versus Autism Spectrum Disorder . Both have the social communication deficit. Autism additionally requires restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities , and if those are present now or were ever present in the past, the diagnosis is autism, not SPCD. So SPCD is autism's Criterion A without autism's Criterion B, and you must ask about childhood history before settling on it. Also rule out intellectual disability, hearing loss, selective mutism (the child can speak, but does not in specific settings), and normal variation. Autism Spectrum Disorder F84.0 In plain language. Two things together, both from early childhood: the person does not do the ordinary back-and-forth of relating to other people, and the person's behaviour and interests are narrow, repetitive, and sensitive to change. DSM-5 collapsed autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, childhood disintegrative disorder and PDD-NOS into one spectrum, and cut the old triad to a dyad by merging social and communication deficits into one criterion. A. Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across contexts, and all three must be present: (1) deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, from abnormal back-and-forth conversation and failure to share interests or affect through to failure to initiate or respond to social interaction; (2) deficits in non-verbal communicative behaviours, from poorly integrated verbal and non-verbal communication through abnormal eye contact and body language to a total lack of facial expression and gesture; (3) deficits in developing, maintaining and understanding relationships, from difficulty adjusting behaviour to context through difficulty making friends to an absence of interest in peers. B. Restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities , at least two of four : (1) stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects or speech (lining up toys, echolalia, idiosyncratic phrases); (2) insistence on sameness, inflexible routines, ritualised patterns, extreme distress at small change; (3) highly restricted, fixated interests abnormal in intensity or focus; (4) hyper- or hypo-reactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (indifference to pain or temperature, adverse response to sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching, visual fascination with lights or movement). Criterion B4, the sensory criterion, is new in DSM-5. C. Symptoms present in the early developmental period, though they may not fully show until social demands exceed capacity, and may be masked by learned strategies later. D. Clinically significant impairment. E. Not better explained by intellectual disability or global developmental delay; to diagnose both, social communication must be below that expected for general developmental level. Specifiers Severity is coded separately for social communication and for restricted repetitive behaviours, as Level 1 requiring support , Level 2 requiring substantial support , Level 3 requiring very substantial support . Also specify: with or without accompanying intellectual impairment; with or without accompanying language impairment; associated with a known medical, genetic or environmental factor; associated with another neurodevelopmental, mental or behavioural disorder; with catatonia. Numbers Prevalence now reported around 1 in 100 worldwide and higher in US surveillance data (about 1 in 36 in recent CDC estimates). Male to female about 4:1, and girls are under-identified because of camouflaging. Concordance in monozygotic twins is high (roughly 60 to 90 percent for the broader phenotype); heritability is among the highest in psychiatry. Comorbidity Around 70 percent have at least one comorbid mental disorder and about 40 percent have two or more. Commonest: intellectual disability, ADHD (DSM-5 for the first time allowed the two to be diagnosed together, DSM-IV forbade it), anxiety disorders (especially specific phobia and social anxiety), depression, OCD, tic disorders, specific learning disorder, developmental coordination disorder, avoidant restrictive food intake disorder, sleep disorders, epilepsy (about 20 to 30 percent), gastrointestinal problems, and known genetic syndromes such as fragile X, tuberous sclerosis and Rett syndrome. Differential Social (pragmatic) communication disorder : no Criterion B, ever. Intellectual disability without autism : social skills are at the level of the mental age, not below it. Rett syndrome : in DSM-5-TR this is no longer a separate diagnosis but is coded as an associated medical condition; the pattern of regression with hand-wringing between 5 and 48 months is the clue. Selective mutism : normal social reciprocity outside the feared setting. ADHD : inattention and social intrusiveness without the qualitative social-reciprocity deficit or the repetitive behaviours. Schizophrenia with childhood onset : delusions and hallucinations appear after a period of normal development. Stereotypic movement disorder : stereotypies without the social criterion. Reactive attachment disorder : severe social neglect history, and the social deficit improves once care improves. ICD-11 Also uses a single "Autism spectrum disorder" with qualifiers for intellectual and language impairment, so the two systems agree here. ICD-11 kept Rett syndrome out of the mental disorders chapter as well. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder F90.x In plain language. Either the child cannot hold attention, or cannot stay still and cannot wait, or both, to a degree that is out of step with their age and is spoiling their life in more than one place. A. A persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity , with at least six of nine symptoms in the relevant list, present for at least six months , at a level inconsistent with developmental level. From age 17 and older, five of nine is enough. Inattention list (9): careless mistakes and inattention to detail; difficulty sustaining attention; does not seem to listen when spoken to directly; does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish; difficulty organising tasks; avoids tasks requiring sustained mental effort; loses things; easily distracted by extraneous stimuli; forgetful in daily activities. Hyperactivity-impulsivity list (9): fidgets or squirms; leaves seat when remaining seated is expected; runs or climbs inappropriately (in adults, restlessness); unable to play quietly; "on the go" as if driven by a motor; talks excessively; blurts out answers; difficulty waiting turn; interrupts or intrudes. B. Several symptoms present before age 12 . C. Symptoms present in two or more settings (home, school, work, with friends). D. Clear interference with functioning. E. Not occurring exclusively during schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder, and not better explained by another mental disorder. Specifiers Predominantly inattentive presentation , predominantly hyperactive/impulsive presentation , combined presentation . Note the word: DSM-5 says presentation , not subtype, because people move between them over time. Also in partial remission , and severity mild / moderate / severe. Numbers The age-of-onset criterion was raised from 7 in DSM-IV to 12 in DSM-5 , which is the single most examined ADHD fact. Symptom count drops from 6 to 5 at age 17. Prevalence about 5 percent of children and about 2.5 percent of adults. Male to female about 2:1 in children, closer to 1.6:1 in adults; girls present more often with the inattentive picture. Comorbidity Oppositional defiant disorder (about half of combined presentation), conduct disorder (about a quarter), specific learning disorder, anxiety disorders, depressive disorders, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, autism spectrum disorder, tic disorders including Tourette's, substance use disorders in adolescence and adulthood, and antisocial personality disorder in adults. Differential Oppositional defiant disorder : the child refuses because they resist demands, not because they cannot sustain attention. Specific learning disorder : inattention appears only in the academic domain that is hard. Intellectual disability : symptoms must exceed what the mental age predicts. Bipolar disorder : ADHD is chronic and continuous, mania is episodic with a clear change from baseline, and mania brings elevated mood and reduced need for sleep, which ADHD does not. Anxiety : inattention there is driven by worry and rumination. Reactive attachment disorder and medication effects (bronchodilators, thyroid). Also normal high activity in a young child, and an unstimulating classroom. Specific Learning Disorder F81.x In plain language. A child of ordinary intelligence, taught properly, still cannot read, write or do arithmetic at anything like age level. A. Difficulties learning and using academic skills, with at least one of six symptoms persisting for at least six months despite intervention : inaccurate or slow effortful word reading; difficulty understanding what is read; difficulties with spelling; difficulties with written expression; difficulties mastering number sense, number facts or calculation; difficulties with mathematical reasoning. B. The affected academic skills are substantially and quantifiably below those expected for chronological age and cause significant interference, confirmed by individually administered standardised achievement measures (or, over age 17, a documented history). C. Begin during school-age years, though they may not fully appear until demands exceed capacity. D. Not better accounted for by intellectual disability, uncorrected visual or auditory acuity, other mental or neurological disorders, psychosocial adversity, lack of proficiency in the language of instruction, or inadequate educational instruction. Specifiers With impairment in reading (word reading accuracy, reading rate or fluency, reading comprehension; the alternative term dyslexia is retained in the text), in written expression (spelling accuracy, grammar and punctuation, clarity or organisation; dysgraphia ), or in mathematics (number sense, memorisation of arithmetic facts, accurate or fluent calculation, accurate mathematical reasoning; dyscalculia ). Severity mild / moderate / severe. Numbers Prevalence 5 to 15 percent of school-age children across languages and cultures; about 4 percent in adults. Reading is the commonest domain. DSM-5 abolished the old IQ-achievement discrepancy requirement, which is a favourite question: you no longer need a gap between IQ and achievement, you need low achievement plus failure to respond to intervention. Comorbidity ADHD (very high overlap), communication disorders, developmental coordination disorder, autism, anxiety and depressive disorders (secondary to school failure), and conduct problems in adolescence. Differential Normal variation in academic attainment; lack of instruction or schooling disruption, which is common in Indian samples and is an explicit exclusion; intellectual disability (all domains low, not one); ADHD (performance varies with attention and improves with structure); neurocognitive disorder (skills were acquired and lost); psychosocial adversity ; sensory impairment. Motor Disorders and Tic Disorders F82, F98.4, F95.x In plain language. Clumsiness that is out of proportion to age, repetitive purposeless movement, and tics. Developmental Coordination Disorder. Acquisition and execution of coordinated motor skills is substantially below age expectation (clumsiness, slowness and inaccuracy in catching, using scissors, handwriting, cycling, sports). It interferes with daily living and academics, begins in the early developmental period, and is not explained by intellectual disability, visual impairment, or a neurological condition affecting movement (cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy). Stereotypic Movement Disorder. Repetitive, seemingly driven and purposeless motor behaviour (hand shaking or waving, body rocking, head banging, self-biting, hitting own body). Onset in the early developmental period, interferes with activities or results in self-injury. Specify with or without self-injurious behaviour , and whether it is associated with a known medical or genetic condition or environmental factor (for example Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, intellectual disability, intrauterine alcohol exposure). Tic disorders. A tic is a sudden, rapid, recurrent, non-rhythmic motor movement or vocalisation. Tourette's Disorder : multiple motor tics and one or more vocal tics , both present at some time during the illness though not necessarily concurrently, persisting for more than 1 year since first tic onset, with onset before age 18 . Persistent (Chronic) Motor or Vocal Tic Disorder : motor or vocal tics but not both, more than 1 year, onset before 18. Provisional Tic Disorder : single or multiple motor and/or vocal tics present for less than 1 year since first onset. Numbers Tics typically begin between ages 4 and 6, peak in severity between 10 and 12, and decline through adolescence. Tourette's prevalence 3 to 8 per 1000 school-age children; male to female 2:1 to 4:1. Coprolalia occurs in only about 10 percent, which is the standard trap because popular culture treats it as the defining feature. Comorbidity Tourette's with ADHD (about half) and OCD (roughly a third to a half) is the classic triad. Also anxiety, depression, disruptive behaviour, and learning problems. Developmental coordination disorder co-occurs with ADHD (the old "DAMP" concept), specific learning disorder and autism. Stereotypic movement disorder co-occurs with intellectual disability and autism. Differential Tics versus stereotypies : tics are faster, non-rhythmic, preceded by a premonitory urge and can be briefly suppressed; stereotypies are rhythmic, prolonged, fixed, start earlier (before 3) and are not preceded by an urge. Tics versus compulsions : compulsions are performed in response to an obsession or a rule and aim to prevent something; complex tics can look identical, and the two coexist. Chorea (random, flowing, not suppressible), dystonia (sustained), myoclonus , seizures . Also substance-induced (stimulants) and other medical conditions (Huntington's, post-viral). 3. Schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders This chapter is arranged along a gradient of psychopathology , from least to most: schizotypal personality disorder, delusional disorder, brief psychotic disorder, schizophreniform disorder, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder. Everything in it is defined by five domains: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised thinking (speech), grossly disorganised or abnormal motor behaviour including catatonia, and negative symptoms . Learn the five, then learn the durations, because duration is what separates almost every member of this chapter from its neighbour. The duration ladder, the single most examined thing in the chapter Brief psychotic disorder: at least 1 day, less than 1 month, with full return to premorbid functioning. Schizophreniform disorder: at least 1 month, less than 6 months. Schizophrenia: at least 6 months of total disturbance, including at least 1 month of active-phase symptoms. Delusional disorder: at least 1 month of delusions. So: one day, one month, six months. If a stem gives you three months of psychosis, the answer is schizophreniform, and the word "provisional" belongs in the answer if the person has not yet recovered. Delusional Disorder F22 In plain language. One or more fixed false beliefs, for a month or more, and apart from what follows directly from the belief, the person is otherwise entirely normal. The person is not obviously odd, their speech is coherent, they hold down a job. A. One or more delusions of 1 month or longer . B. Criterion A for schizophrenia has never been met. If hallucinations occur they are not prominent and are related to the delusional theme (for example the sensation of insects in delusional parasitosis). C. Apart from the impact of the delusion, functioning is not markedly impaired and behaviour is not obviously bizarre or odd. D. If manic or major depressive episodes have occurred, they have been brief relative to the duration of the delusional periods. E. Not attributable to a substance, another medical condition, or better explained by another disorder such as body dysmorphic disorder or OCD. Subtypes Erotomanic (another person, usually of higher status, is in love with the person), grandiose , jealous (the "Othello syndrome"), persecutory (the commonest), somatic , mixed , unspecified . Also specify with bizarre content . Course specifiers after 1 year: first episode currently in acute episode / in partial remission / in full remission; multiple episodes; continuous. Numbers Lifetime prevalence about 0.2 percent, so it is rare. Onset later than schizophrenia, typically middle to late adult life. The DSM-5 change worth naming: the requirement that delusions be non-bizarre was removed , and "with bizarre content" became a specifier instead. Shared delusional disorder (folie a deux) was also removed as a separate diagnosis; it is now coded as delusional disorder or under other specified schizophrenia spectrum disorder. Comorbidity Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder (especially where insight is absent), depressive disorders (often secondary to the delusion), and paranoid, schizoid and avoidant personality disorders, which often precede the onset. Differential Schizophrenia (Criterion A met, functioning declines, negative symptoms). OCD with absent insight (the belief grew out of an obsession, and the person has compulsions). Body dysmorphic disorder with absent insight . Paranoid personality disorder (suspiciousness that never reaches delusional conviction, and is lifelong and trait-like). Substance or medication induced , and psychotic disorder due to another medical condition . Major depressive or bipolar disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features (the delusion only exists inside the mood episode). Brief Psychotic Disorder F23 In plain language. Psychosis that arrives suddenly, lasts days or a few weeks, and then goes completely, leaving the person as they were. A. Presence of one or more of: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour. At least one must be from the first three (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech), so catatonia alone does not qualify. B. Duration at least 1 day but less than 1 month , with eventual full return to premorbid level of functioning . C. Not better explained by a depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features or another psychotic disorder, and not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. Specifiers With marked stressor(s) (this is the old brief reactive psychosis ), without marked stressor(s), with peripartum onset (during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum), and with catatonia . Severity rated on the 5 psychotic dimensions, 0 to 4. Numbers Accounts for roughly 9 percent of first-onset psychosis in some series. Twice as common in females. Average age of onset in the mid thirties. Suicide risk is elevated, particularly in the acute phase and in younger patients. Comorbidity Personality disorders, especially borderline, schizotypal, paranoid and histrionic, are frequent precursors. Differential Schizophreniform disorder (a month or more). Substance-induced psychotic disorder , which is the leading practical mimic in a young patient, so ask about cannabis and stimulants and take a urine screen. Psychotic disorder due to another medical condition (delirium, epilepsy, thyrotoxicosis, autoimmune encephalitis). Malingering and factitious disorder . Culturally sanctioned response , such as trance or a possession state that is a normal part of a religious practice, which is explicitly excluded. Bipolar or depressive disorder with psychotic features . Personality disorder with transient stress-related paranoia, especially borderline, where the psychotic-like symptoms are brief, stress-triggered, and recur across a long history. Schizophreniform Disorder F20.81 In plain language. Schizophrenia's symptom picture, but the clock has not run long enough yet. It is a provisional label you use while waiting. A. Same as schizophrenia Criterion A: two or more of delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour, negative symptoms, each present for a significant portion of a 1-month period, with at least one being delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech. B. An episode lasting at least 1 month but less than 6 months . If you are diagnosing while the person is still ill, qualify as "provisional" . C. Schizoaffective and depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features ruled out. D. Not substance or medical. Note that unlike schizophrenia, impaired functioning is not required . Specifiers With good prognostic features requires at least two of: onset of prominent psychotic symptoms within 4 weeks of the first noticeable change in usual behaviour; confusion or perplexity; good premorbid social and occupational functioning; absence of blunted or flat affect. Otherwise, without good prognostic features . Also with catatonia. Numbers Roughly a third recover within the 6 months and keep the diagnosis; about two-thirds progress to schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder. Incidence in developed countries is about a fifth that of schizophrenia. Comorbidity As for schizophrenia: substance use, depression, anxiety. Differential Brief psychotic disorder (under 1 month). Schizophrenia (6 months or more, including prodrome and residual). Schizoaffective (a full mood episode runs for the majority of the illness). Substance-induced and medical causes. Schizophrenia F20.9 In plain language. For at least six months the person has been drifting away from ordinary reality and ordinary functioning, and for at least one of those months they have actively had psychotic symptoms. A. Two or more of the following, each present for a significant portion of time during a 1-month period (or less if successfully treated), and at least one must be (1), (

title: Personality — the full book, chapter by chapter
text: Personality — the full book, chapter by chapter Not a summary. This is your Schultz & Schultz, Theories of Personality walked through in the book's own order, one chapter per theorist, with the book's signature recurring frame kept intact for each: the life (how the theorist's own biography shaped the theory), the theory unpacked in full, the book's Questions About Human Nature scorecard, Assessment , Research , and Reflections (the criticisms). After the book's chapters come the four domains the book underweights but NIMHANS tests hard, flagged in purple: object relations & self · existential · type theories · Indian / Triguna · assessment in depth . Built 2026-05-22 · Rewritten as a teaching chapter 2026-05-24 · Poured out to full-book, chapter-by-chapter depth 2026-05-24 . Expanded to full depth 2026-05-24 (added the key studies walked through, an extended concept bank, an A–Z glossary, and a by-chapter self-test). How to read this page. Read it like the textbook, top to bottom, once; then revise off the coloured boxes. Each chapter follows the book: amber = the intuition / why it matters, amber "Human nature" = where the theorist lands on the book's six recurring issues. Green = the line to lock. Red = the MCQ trap. Purple = NIMHANS-specific (clinical / Indian / rival-theory swaps). Grey recap = the chapter in one breath. The one-line testable list lives in Rapid Recall ; the personality tests in depth (MMPI (Starke Hathaway and J. Charnley McKinley, 1943)/16PF (Raymond Cattell)/NEO/projectives, scoring) are on the tests deep-dive . Jump to: 1. What personality theory is 2. Freud 3. Jung 4. Adler 5. Horney 6. Erikson 7. Allport 8. Maslow 9. Rogers 10. Kelly 11. Skinner 12. Bandura 13. The trait approach & Five-Factor Model 14. Facets of personality 15. Personality in perspective S1. Object relations & self S2. The other neo-Freudians S3. Existential S4. Type theories S5. Indian psychology / Triguna S6. Assessment in depth At-a-glance compare All the MCQ traps Key studies, walked through Extended concept bank Fast glossary (A–Z) Self-test (active recall) The one frame that organises the whole book. The book ends every chapter by scoring the theorist on six recurring Questions About Human Nature . Hold these six and you can predict any theorist's "view of the person" answer: (1) free will vs determinism · (2) nature vs nurture (heredity vs environment) · (3) past vs present (does childhood fix us, or does the here-and-now/future drive us) · (4) uniqueness vs universality · (5) equilibrium vs growth (is the basic motive to reduce tension and stay balanced, or to grow ) · (6) optimism vs pessimism . Sigmund Freud is the dark end of all six; the humanists are the bright end. Everyone else sits between. Part One · The study of personality Ch 1. Personality: what it is, and how the book studies it Personality is the relatively enduring, distinctive pattern of thoughts, feelings and behaviours that characterises a person and how they adapt to the world. The word comes from the Latin persona , the mask the Roman actor wore, which already hides the book's central tension: is personality the mask we show, or the real face behind it? Every theory in the book is one answer to four questions: what is personality made of , where does it come from , why do people differ , and can it change . The book groups the theorists into approaches , and that grouping is the spine of the table of contents: the psychoanalytic (Sigmund Freud); the neopsychoanalytic (Carl Jung, Alfred Adler, Karen Horney); the life-span (Erik Erikson); the genetics/trait pioneer (Gordon Allport); the humanistic (Abraham Maslow, Carl Rogers); the cognitive (Kelly); the behavioural (B. F. Skinner); the social-learning (Albert Bandura); the trait approach (Raymond Cattell, Hans Eysenck, the Five-Factor Model); and the facet / limited-domain theories (Julian Rotter, Zuckerman, Martin Seligman). How the book assesses and researches personality The book insists every theory must answer two practical questions, and the recurring "Assessment" and "Research" sections grade each theorist on them: Assessment = how do you measure this theory's constructs? The methods recur: self-report inventories (objective, scored against norms, e.g. MMPI, 16PF, NEO), projective techniques (ambiguous stimuli, e.g. Rorschach, TAT), clinical interviews , behavioural assessment , and idiographic personal documents (diaries, letters). A good test must clear three bars: reliability (consistency), validity (measures what it claims), and standardised norms . Research = how was the theory tested ? Three designs recur: the clinical method (case studies, the dominant psychoanalytic tool, rich but unreliable and unrepresentative), the experimental method (manipulate a variable, the only route to cause and effect), and the correlational method (relate two measured variables, covariation only, never causation). TRAP — method by camp. Case study / clinical method = the psychoanalysts (Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Alfred Adler). Correlational + factor analysis = the trait theorists (Raymond Cattell, Hans Eysenck, FFM). Controlled experiment = the behaviourists and social-learning theorists (B. F. Skinner, Albert Bandura) and Carl Rogers, who pioneered experimental psychotherapy research. The method usually tells you the camp. Recap Ch 1. Personality = the enduring, distinctive pattern of how a person thinks, feels and behaves. The book is organised by approach and grades every theorist on six human-nature issues plus Assessment and Research. Nomothetic (general laws, trait research) vs idiographic (the unique individual, case studies) is the master methodological split. Part Two · The psychoanalytic approach Ch 2. Sigmund Freud — psychoanalysis The life (1856–1939). Born in Moravia, raised in Vienna, the adored eldest son of a young mother (the book notes this shaped his Oedipal theory). Trained as a neurologist; studied hysteria under Charcot in Paris and worked with Josef

title: Social & General Psychology
text: Social & General Psychology One consolidated revision chapter for the whole domain: the foundational ("general") psychology of perception, attention, memory, learning, emotion, motivation, intelligence, cognition, personality, development, consciousness and stress, and the full social-psychology arc from research methods through social cognition, attribution, the self, attitudes, prejudice, attraction, influence, prosocial behaviour, aggression and groups, closing with the landmark experiments walked through and a fast A–Z glossary. Anchored to Baron & Branscombe's Social Psychology and standard general-psychology texts; every named effect, theorist, date, table, mnemonic and MCQ trap from both source sets is preserved. The dominant question type NIMHANS and MET test is which name goes with which effect , so the lookalike pairs are flagged throughout in trap boxes. Read it like a textbook, then drill the traps and glossary. In this book Psychology as a science: methods & perspectives Sensation & perception Attention Memory Learning Cognition: thinking, language & social cognition Emotion Motivation Intelligence Personality Developmental psychology Consciousness & sleep Stress, coping & health Social perception & attribution The self Attitudes & persuasion Stereotyping, prejudice & discrimination Attraction, relationships & love Social influence: conformity, compliance, obedience Prosocial behaviour (helping) Aggression Groups & individuals Landmark studies, walked through Schools & history of psychology The MCQ traps, collected Fast glossary (A–Z) 1. Psychology as a science: methods & perspectives What the field claims. Social psychology is the scientific study of how the thoughts, feelings and behaviour of individuals are influenced by the actual, imagined or implied presence of others (Gordon Allport's classic definition). The key word is scientific : it settles questions by study, not intuition. The governing insight, repeated throughout, is the power of the situation : ordinary people help, conform, obey and aggress far more because of where they are and who is around than because of fixed traits. That theme, situation over disposition, returns in obedience (Stanley Milgram), bystander apathy (Bibb Latané & John Darley) and attribution (the fundamental attribution error is precisely our failure to see it). The role of theory. A theory is an integrated set of principles that explains and predicts observed events. Good science runs a loop: a theory generates a falsifiable hypothesis ; a study tests it; results refine or refute it. A theory is never "proven", only supported or disconfirmed. The core research methods Method What you do Strength / limit Experimental Manipulate one factor (the independent variable, IV ), hold all else constant, measure the effect on the dependent variable, DV . Use random assignment to conditions. The only method that establishes cause and effect . Limit: artificiality, low external validity if over-controlled. Correlational Measure two or more variables as they naturally occur and see if they covary (correlation coefficient, −1 to +1). Good for real-world variables you cannot ethically manipulate. Limit: correlation ≠ causation (direction problem + third-variable problem). Survey Ask a representative sample questions to describe a population's attitudes/behaviour. Cheap, broad. Limit: sampling bias, wording effects, social-desirability responding. Systematic / naturalistic observation Watch and record behaviour as it occurs without intervening (e.g. counting jaywalkers). High realism. Limit: no control, observer effects, no causal claim. High-yield The IV is the cause you dial (the knob), the DV the effect you read off (the dial). Random assignment is what lets you claim the knob, not pre-existing differences between people, moved the dial; correlational work has no knob, so it cannot tell you which dial drives. A mediator is the mechanism between cause and effect, explaining why (frustration → anger → aggression: anger mediates). A moderator changes the strength or direction of a relationship, telling you when / for whom it holds (heat raises aggression more for provoked people). A meta-analysis statistically combines many studies to estimate the true effect size. Ethics, deception and replication Because the true purpose can change behaviour, social psychology often uses deception (a cover story), permitted only under strict safeguards: informed consent , the right to withdraw, minimising harm, and a thorough debriefing that reveals the true purpose and removes any after-effects. An Institutional Review Board / ethics committee must approve the study first. The field also takes its replication crisis seriously: a finding is trusted only when independent labs replicate it, which is why classics (Stanley Milgram, marshmallow studies) are now discussed alongside their replications and failures. The four perspectives Baron uses Perspective Core claim Cognitive To explain social behaviour, study how people think : notice, store, recall, interpret. The dominant modern lens (schemas, heuristics, attribution live here). Evolutionary Some tendencies (mate choice, helping kin, fear of strangers) were shaped by natural selection for survival/reproduction. Social neuroscience Links social behaviour to brain and biology (fMRI, hormones): amygdala in out-group fear, oxytocin in trust. Cultural / multicultural Many findings hold differently across cultures; must test whether an effect is universal or culture-bound (individualist vs collectivist). High-yield The researcher is also a thinker prone to the very biases the field studies, so methods (random assignment, double-blind procedures, pre-registration, replication) exist partly to fence out the researcher's expectancy bias / experimenter effects. NIMHANS asks methods crisply: name the only method that proves causation (experimental), say why correlation cannot (third-variable + directionality), and distinguish medi

title: Psychological Assessment & Testing
text: Psychological Assessment & Testing A psychological test is a measuring instrument, and like any instrument it must be (a) consistent and (b) accurate. Consistent = reliability . Accurate = validity . Everything in this chapter is either a way to estimate reliability, a way to estimate validity, a way to interpret scores against norms, or a real-world test built on those foundations. We measure things we cannot see directly (anxiety, intelligence, personality) by building instruments out of items, like a thermometer made of questions, then deciding things with them: special education, army fitness, diagnosis. This chapter locks the psychometric theory first, then the major intelligence, personality, projective, and clinical instruments, with every author, year, item count, scale, score range, and exam trap in one place. In this book Item analysis & test construction Reliability (the consistency story) Validity (the accuracy story) Norms & standard scores Intelligence theories & IQ mechanics Stanford-Binet family Wechsler family Raven’s Progressive Matrices Kaufman, Cattell CFIT & special-purpose scales Group & infant/developmental scales Indian intelligence tests IQ classification & intellectual disability Objective (self-report) personality tests Projective tests Adjustment, clinical & Indian inventories Aptitude, attitude & interest scales Psychiatric & cognitive rating scales Educational measurement basics Master reference tables & trap list 1. Item analysis & test construction Each test item is a single sensor reading. If a sensor is too easy (everyone passes) it tells us nothing; too hard (no one passes) it tells us nothing; and if it disagrees with the rest of the test, something is wrong with it. That is why every well-built test goes through item analysis. Difficulty index, p The difficulty index is the proportion who got an item right. p = (number correct) / (total attempting) , range 0 to 1. p = 0.50 is the sweet spot for a free-response item because it discriminates the most. For a 4-option MCQ the optimal p is ~0.625 , halfway between chance guessing (0.25) and ceiling (1.00). p above 0.80 = too easy; p below 0.20 = too hard. Both are revision candidates because they cannot separate strong from weak students. Discrimination index, D Do high-scorers on the whole test do better on this item than low-scorers? D = p_upper − p_lower , where p_upper = proportion correct in the top 27% of scorers and p_lower = proportion in the bottom 27%. Range −1 to +1. D above 0.40 = item agrees with the test, a good signal. D near zero = random noise; both groups perform alike. Negative D = the bottom group out-performed the top group: the item is mis-keyed, ambiguous, or has a trick strong test-takers over-think. Trap Read negative discrimination as a mis-keyed / flawed item to discard immediately , NOT as a merely “hard” item. This is asked every cycle. 2. Reliability (the consistency story) Reliability is not about whether a test is correct; it is about whether it is consistent . A bathroom scale that reads 75 kg every time is reliable even if your true weight is 70 (that is a validity problem). A scale bouncing between 60, 90, 80 is unreliable, full stop. If a test is unreliable you cannot trust any single score: the same person retested gives a different answer for reasons unrelated to the trait. You are measuring noise. Definition Classical Test Theory: Observed Score = True Score + Error . Reliability is the proportion of observed-score variance that is true variance, not error. A reliability of 0.80 says 80% signal, 20% noise. There are several reliability methods because there are several ways to think about “consistency”: Across time: test the same person twice (test-retest). Across forms: give two equivalent versions (parallel/alternate forms). Within one administration, across items: check items hang together (split-half, Cronbach alpha, KR-20). Across raters: check two judges agree (Cohen kappa for categorical, ICC for continuous). Test-retest (time stability) Give the test, give it again later, correlate the two scores. High correlation = stable over time. The standard window is two to four weeks . Too long and the trait itself can change (correlation drops, but the test is not at fault); too short and memory carryover inflates the correlation. Split-half + Spearman-Brown Give the test once, split into two halves (often odd vs even items), correlate the halves. By splitting you have halved the test length, and shorter tests are less reliable, so the raw split-half correlation under estimates full-test reliability. Spearman-Brown corrects this: r_full = 2 × r_half / (1 + r_half) . Example: r_half = 0.60 → r_full = 1.20 / 1.60 = 0.75 . Always apply Spearman-Brown after any split. Cronbach alpha Imagine doing every possible split-half and averaging the result: that mean is Cronbach alpha. It is the most common internal-consistency measure for tests with multi-point (e.g. Likert) items. Alpha rises with item count, item homogeneity, and trait variance. Trap Alpha is NOT a measure of unidimensionality. A test can have high alpha and still measure two distinct constructs. The MET loves this. KR-20 (Kuder-Richardson 20) When items are right-or-wrong (dichotomous, 1/0), Cronbach alpha simplifies to KR-20: same idea, adapted for 0/1 items. So “30-item right-wrong vocabulary test, one administration, which reliability?” → KR-20 . Inter-rater: kappa and ICC When humans do the scoring (Rorschach protocols, clinical interviews, essay grades), reliability is about rater agreement. Cohen kappa for categorical decisions (OCD: yes/no), corrects for chance agreement. Kappa ≥ 0.81 = almost-perfect; 0.61–0.80 = substantial. Intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for continuous ratings (a 0–100 severity score); different ICC forms exist depending on whether raters are random or fixed. Trap Kappa is NOT an internal-consistency measure. If a question describes a one-administration internal-structure tes

title: Therapy, Counselling & Ethics
text: Therapy, Counselling & Ethics One consolidated chapter for everything the MET / NIMHANS paper tests on treatment: the learning principles that behaviour therapy is built on, the major schools of psychotherapy & counselling (Sharf's frame, school by school, with the third-wave and integrative models folded in), the common therapeutic factors that cut across schools, and professional ethics . Each concept lives in exactly one place. The exam tests four moves: name the theory from its claim; pin the theory to its founder; pin the named technique to its theory; and tell rival theories apart, because that is where the distractor always hides. Learn every technique in its contrast pair . In this book Learning & conditioning: the foundation How to read any theory (the master frame) Psychodynamic approaches Humanistic & existential approaches Behavioural & cognitive approaches Constructivist, feminist & systemic approaches Third-wave, integrative & specialised models Group therapy (Yalom) Common factors & the therapeutic frame Indications quick-map (what to recommend) Professional ethics Master trap list, rosters & glossary High-yield The single most-tested skill is telling near-identical pairs apart: REBT (Ellis) vs Cognitive Therapy (Aaron Beck) , systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) vs flooding , ERP (OCD) vs EMDR (trauma) , cognitive triad (Beck) vs ABC (Albert Ellis) , DBT modules (4) vs ACT hexaflex (6) , and the four family-therapy founders (Bowen / Minuchin / Haley / Satir). And in learning: shaping vs chaining , fading vs extinction , VR vs VI , latent vs insight learning . Master these pairs and most of the section answers itself. 1. Learning & conditioning: the foundation of behaviour therapy Behaviour therapy is applied learning theory, so the vocabulary below is tested both as 1-mark definition traps and as the mechanism behind clinical techniques. Read this orientation once: classical (Pavlovian) conditioning is about stimulus pairings ; operant (Skinnerian) conditioning is about consequences shaping voluntary behaviour ; priming is about one stimulus making a later one easier to process ; and habituation / sensitization are non-associative (a single stimulus, no pairing). When a question mixes the families, the answer is almost always the term whose family matches the stem. Family Terms inside Classical (Pavlovian) phenomena Extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination, habituation, sensitization Operant (Skinnerian) shaping tools Shaping, chaining, fading, prompting Operant reinforcement schedules FR, VR, FI, VI Cognitive / social learning Latent learning (Edward Tolman), insight learning (Wolfgang Köhler), observational learning (Albert Bandura) Implicit / cognitive priming Priming (semantic, perceptual, affective) 1.1 Operant shaping tools — shaping, chaining, fading, prompting Shaping (B. F. Skinner): reinforcing successive approximations of a target behaviour the organism does not yet emit . Train a rat to press a lever by reinforcing facing it, then approaching, then touching, then pressing. The defining feature is that the reinforcement criterion changes across trials . Clinically: skill acquisition, autism intervention. Chaining : linking a sequence of already-learned behaviours into a longer chain, where each behaviour is the discriminative stimulus (S D ) for the next and only the final link is reinforced (brushing teeth: pick up brush → wet → paste → brush → rinse → put away). Forward chaining teaches step 1 first; backward chaining teaches the last step first, so the learner always reaches the reinforcer at the natural endpoint (often preferred clinically). Used heavily in ABA / ADL skills training. Prompting : an added antecedent stimulus (verbal, gestural, physical, modelled, visual) that helps the learner emit the right response in the presence of the natural cue. Prompt hierarchy, most → least intrusive: physical → modelling → gestural → verbal → visual/positional . "Least-to-most" vs "most-to-least" prompting are classic vignette distractors. Fading : gradually removing the prompt while transferring stimulus control to the natural cue (teach "ball": full model "say ball" → partial "say buh…" → just holding up the ball). Trap Shaping vs chaining: shaping builds a new behaviour ; chaining links existing behaviours . Fading vs extinction: fading removes the prompt (an antecedent) and transfers stimulus control; extinction removes the reinforcer / UCS and eliminates the behaviour. Prompts are antecedents; reinforcement is a consequence — that distinction has been tested directly. 1.2 Classical conditioning phenomena Extinction : reduction and disappearance of a conditioned response when reinforcement (operant) or the UCS (classical) is no longer presented — Ivan Pavlov's dog stops salivating to the unpaired bell; the ignored tantrum fades. Watch for the extinction burst : a temporary increase in frequency/intensity right after reinforcement is withdrawn, before decline. Extinction does not erase learning. Spontaneous recovery : reappearance of a previously extinguished response after a rest period, with no new conditioning trials — proving extinction is suppression, not unlearning . The recovered response is typically weaker , and re-extinction is faster the second time (savings effect). Distinguish from reinstatement (re-emergence after UCS-alone presentation) and renewal (re-emergence in a new context). Generalization vs discrimination. Generalization = responding similarly to stimuli that resemble the CS / S D (Little Albert, conditioned by John B. Watson & Rosalie Rayner to fear a white rat, also feared a white rabbit, cotton wool, a Santa beard). The generalization gradient : response strength drops with distance from the original CS. Discrimination = responding only to the specific stimulus, taught by differential reinforcement (reinforce in presence of S D , withhold for S Δ ). One-liner: generalization is the default; discrimination is traine

title: Research Methods & Statistics
text: Research Methods & Statistics One consolidated, exam-ready treatment built from A. K. Singh ( Tests, Measurements and Research Methods in Behavioural Sciences — strong on measurement, test construction, item analysis) and Coolican ( Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology — design, the logic of inference, which test to run). Read the prose and understand why each statistic does what it does; the tables are then just reminders. Trap boxes flag the exact confusions MCQs are built on. Coverage runs MET 2026 depth with NIMHANS M.Phil clinical extensions where the entrance pushes harder. In this book Research design & methodology Variables, confounds, mediation & moderation Validity & threats in a study Sampling Levels of measurement Reliability & validity in measurement Scaling (attitude measurement) Item analysis & test construction Descriptive statistics Distributions, z-scores & the Central Limit Theorem The logic of inference Parametric tests Non-parametric tests Correlation, regression & special coefficients Degrees of freedom — from scratch Qualitative & mixed methods Clinical trials & reporting standards Research ethics Decision table: which test do I use? Collected MCQ traps Worked intuition Fast glossary Research design & methodology Only an experiment (manipulate the IV and randomly assign participants) can establish causation, because randomisation balances out unknown confounds. Everything else can describe and relate, but not prove cause. Experimental hierarchy — by degree of control Design Manipulate IV? Random assignment? Control group? Internal validity True experimental (RCT) Yes Yes Yes High — gold standard for causation Quasi-experimental Yes No (intact/pre-existing groups: classes, wards) Usually yes Moderate — confounds remain Pre-experimental Loosely No Often none Low — e.g. one-group pretest-posttest; many threats Non-experimental (correlational) No — — No causal claim Between- vs within-subjects (and factorial) Between-subjects (independent groups): different people in each condition. No carry-over, but between-person variability is noise and groups may differ to start. Within-subjects (repeated measures): the same people in every condition. Each is their own control, so it is powerful and economical, but risks order/carry-over effects (practice, fatigue) — fixed by counterbalancing . Factorial: two or more IVs crossed, so you can test their interaction (a 2×2 has 4 cells). Specific designs to know Pretest-posttest control group: the classic two-group RCT. Posttest-only control group: avoids pretest sensitisation entirely. Solomon four-group: combines both. Two groups get a pretest, two do not; half of each get treatment. It detects and separates pretest sensitisation (the interaction of pretest and treatment) from the treatment effect itself. Resource-heavy but the most rigorous design for ruling out testing effects. Crossover design: every subject receives both conditions in different order. Single-case designs (ABA, ABAB, multiple baseline): used in behaviour analysis. Non-experimental & epidemiological designs Correlational: measure variables as they are and relate them; no manipulation, so no causal claim. Cross-sectional: one snapshot in time; reports prevalence . Cheap, but cannot show temporality or change. Longitudinal: the same people followed over time; can show change and causal order, but slow, costly, and bleeds participants through attrition . Cohort study: follow exposed and unexposed groups forward in time; reports relative risk . Case-control: start with cases and controls, look back at exposure; reports odds ratio . Case study: deep dive into one person/unit (rich, hypothesis-generating, not generalisable). Observational: watch behaviour in situ — naturalistic vs structured; participant vs non-participant; covert vs overt. Controlling confounds Randomisation — random assignment spreads unknown confounds evenly across groups (the most powerful control). Counterbalancing — vary the order of conditions across subjects to cancel order effects in within-subjects designs. Matching — pair subjects on a key variable (e.g. IQ) before assigning, removing that variable as a confound. Single-blind (participant unaware of condition) and double-blind (participant and experimenter/assessor unaware) — control expectancy and experimenter effects. Trap Random sampling vs random assignment . Random sampling = who gets into the study (drives external validity/generalisability). Random assignment = which condition they go to (drives internal validity/causation). A study can have one without the other. Trap Counterbalancing (fixes order effects in within-subjects designs) vs matching (controls a specific confound variable in between-subjects designs). Variables, confounds, mediation & moderation Independent variable (IV): what the experimenter manipulates or groups by — the presumed cause. Dependent variable (DV): the measured outcome — the presumed effect. Control variable: a variable deliberately held constant. Confound: a variable tied to both the IV and the DV, creating a spurious link and offering a rival explanation. Controlled by randomisation, matching, or statistical adjustment. Extraneous variable: any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV; it becomes a confound only if it also correlates with the IV. Operationalisation: defining a fuzzy construct in concrete, measurable terms (e.g. "anxiety" = score on the GAD-7). Bad operationalisation sinks construct validity. Mediator vs moderator — the high-frequency trap Both are "third variables," but they do opposite jobs: Mediator explains HOW / WHY the IV affects the DV — the mechanism in the causal chain: IV → Mediator → DV . Stress → cortisol → poorer immunity: cortisol mediates. If you control the mediator, the IV–DV link weakens or vanishes. Tested with Baron-Kenny steps or Hayes PROCESS. Moderator changes WHEN / FOR WHOM / HOW STRONGLY the IV affects the DV — it alters the strength or directio

title: Unit 3 – Psychometrics & Test Construction
text: Unit 3 – Psychometrics & Test Construction The science of measuring the mind: how a psychological test is built, scored and judged. This book teaches the four scales of measurement, the anatomy of a good item and how to analyse one, the full reliability and validity families with their formulae, the meaning of norms and standard scores, and the major families of real tests – intelligence, neuropsychological, personality, interest and aptitude – together with where and why each is applied (education, occupation, military, clinic). It closes with the M.Phil-style exam questions folded in. Sourced from Rodrick Prashanth's Unit 3 decks (Areas of testing, Applications of testing, Interest & aptitude tests, Item writing & item analysis, Reliability/Validity/Norms, Scales) and the M.Phil question bank, deepened to NIMHANS clinical depth. In this book Scales of measurement & attitude scaling Item writing & item analysis Reliability Validity Norms & standard scores Areas of testing: intelligence & creativity Areas of testing: neuropsychological assessment Areas of testing: personality assessment Interest & aptitude tests Applications of testing Structured personality-test construction M.Phil exam questions 1. Scales of measurement & attitude scaling The one idea. Before you can measure a psychological attribute you must decide what kind of number you are assigning. S. S. Stevens' four levels of measurement – nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio – form a ladder: each rung adds one mathematical property and therefore unlocks one more legitimate statistic. Choosing the wrong scale is the commonest hidden error in test interpretation: you cannot average ranks, and you cannot say one IQ is "twice" another. The four levels Level Allows categorising Allows ranking (order) Equal intervals True (absolute) zero Example Nominal Yes – – – Diagnosis codes, gender, jersey numbers Ordinal Yes Yes – – Rank in class, Likert agree/disagree, race finishing order Interval Yes Yes Yes – Temperature in °C, IQ scores, calendar years Ratio Yes Yes Yes Yes Reaction time, weight, number of errors, age Why each property matters. A nominal scale only labels – the numbers are names, so the only legitimate operations are counting frequencies and the mode. An ordinal scale adds order, so you can take a median and percentiles, but the gaps between ranks are unequal (the difference between 1st and 2nd is not the same "amount" as between 2nd and 3rd). An interval scale adds equal spacing, so you can finally add, subtract and compute a mean and standard deviation; but its zero is arbitrary (0°C is not "no temperature"). A ratio scale adds a true zero meaning total absence of the attribute, so ratios become meaningful: 40 errors is genuinely twice 20 errors. High-yield Memorise the ladder of properties: N ominal = categorise; O rdinal = + order; I nterval = + equal intervals; R atio = + true zero. Each level permits everything the levels below it permit, plus one more. Mnemonic NOIR (French for "black") gives the order of increasing power: N ominal → O rdinal → I nterval → R atio. Trap Interval vs ratio. Both have equal intervals; only ratio has a true zero. IQ and Celsius temperature are interval – an IQ of 0 does not mean "no intelligence," so you cannot say IQ 140 is "twice as smart" as IQ 70. Kelvin temperature and reaction time are ratio. Attitude scales Attitude measurement applies these principles to subjective opinion. The deck names four classic formats: Scale Structure Key feature Likert scale Five ordered responses on an agree/disagree or approve/disapprove continuum (e.g. Strongly Agree → Strongly Disagree) Summative; the most widely used attitude format. Strictly ordinal, though usually treated as interval in practice. Guttman scale Items ordered by intensity; a respondent who endorses one statement also endorses all milder statements on the same continuum Cumulative / unidimensional. "Check the statement from each group that is most true of you." Semantic differential (Osgood) A set of bipolar adjective scales (Healthy – Unhealthy, Pleasant – Unpleasant) anchoring a 7-point line Measures the subjective meaning and affective reaction to a concept; classic dimensions are Evaluation, Potency, Activity. Stapel scale A single ( unipolar ) adjective with 10 categories from −5 to +5, no neutral zero A one-adjective alternative to the semantic differential; forces a direction. Trap Semantic differential vs Stapel. Semantic differential uses bipolar adjective pairs with a neutral midpoint; the Stapel scale uses a single (unipolar) adjective on a −5 to +5 line with no neutral point . Guttman is cumulative (endorsing a strong item implies endorsing the weaker ones); Likert is summative. 2. Item writing & item analysis The one idea. A test is only as good as its items. Item construction is part craft (writing clear, unambiguous questions) and part statistics (keeping the items that actually discriminate among people and dropping those that do not). Item analysis is the set of empirical methods for that pruning. Guidelines for item writing (DeVellis, 2012) Define clearly what you want to measure before writing anything. Generate an item pool larger than the final test, so weak items can be discarded. Avoid exceptionally long items – length adds reading load, not information. Keep reading difficulty appropriate to the intended respondents. Avoid "double-barrelled" items that pack two ideas into one statement ("I feel anxious and depressed") – the respondent cannot answer cleanly. Mix positively and negatively worded items to counter acquiescence (yea-saying) response bias. Item formats & correction for guessing The dichotomous format scores an item 0 or 1 (true/false, right/wrong). The polytomous format gives each item more than two alternatives. In a multiple-choice item, the incorrect alternatives are called distractors ; it is usually best to write three or four good distractors per item, and three distractors are about as effectiv

title: Unit 4 — Biological Basis of Behaviour
text: Unit 4 — Biological Basis of Behaviour The full biological machinery of behaviour, built from the ground up: how a single neuron is wired and how it fires, the chemical languages it speaks, how those neurons are assembled into the brain and the rest of the nervous system, and the circuits that drive movement, every sense, hunger and thirst, emotion, the hormones and glands, sleep, heredity, and the methods scientists use to take the whole system apart. Anchored to Carlson & Pinel-level neuroscience and prioritised for MET 2026 and NIMHANS clinical psychology. In this book Neurons: structure, types & the neural impulse Neurotransmitters Structure & functions of the nervous system Divisions of the nervous system (CNS, PNS, ANS) Divisions of the human brain & their functions The motor (sensorimotor) system Sensory systems — vision Auditory & somatosensory systems Chemical & vestibular senses Hunger & thirst Emotions Hormonal regulation of behaviour The glandular (endocrine) system Sleep & biological clocks Genetics & behaviour Invasive & non-invasive research methods 1. Neurons: structure, types & the neural impulse The neuron is the information-processing and information-transmitting element of the nervous system. Everything else in this unit is about how neurons are built, how they fire, how they talk to each other, and how billions of them are wired into the brain. Master the neuron first and the rest of the unit becomes mechanism rather than memorisation. The four regions of a neuron Part What it is Function Cell body (soma) Contains the nucleus and most of the cell's life-support machinery; shape varies widely between neuron types. Keeps the cell alive; integrates incoming signals. Dendrites Branching projections; the major receivers of messages. Receive neural messages transmitted across the synapse (the small gap between a terminal button and the dendrite). Axon A long slender tube, often myelinated; works like an electrical cord. Carries the action potential away from the soma toward the terminal buttons. Terminal buttons Little knobs at the ends of axon branches. When an action potential arrives, they secrete a chemical messenger, the neurotransmitter . Definition Action potential — a brief electrical event that starts at the axon end nearest the cell body (the axon initial segment) and travels toward the terminal buttons. It is the basic message the axon carries. Axoplasmic transport Terminal buttons need molecules that can only be made in the soma, so substances are moved along the axon along microtubule "tracks". This is an active process, separate from the action potential. Anterograde transport (soma → terminal): accomplished by the motor protein kinesin , which "walks" along microtubules carrying cargo. Remarkably fast, up to 500 mm/day. Retrograde transport (terminal → soma): accomplished by the protein dynein ; about half as fast as anterograde transport. Types (classes) of neurons Multipolar neuron — more than two processes extending from the cell body (the most common type). Unipolar neuron — one process extending from the cell body (e.g. sensory dorsal-root neurons). Bipolar neuron — two processes (e.g. in the retina). Interneurons — neurons with a short axon or no axon at all; they integrate neural activity within a single brain structure . Neuroanatomical gross structures Composed of In the CNS In the PNS Mostly cell bodies Nuclei Ganglia Mostly axons Tracts Nerves Trap Cell-body clusters are nuclei in the CNS but ganglia in the PNS; axon bundles are tracts in the CNS but nerves in the PNS. The paper loves to swap these. Glial cells There are roughly equal numbers of neurons and glia in the human brain. Four kinds matter: Oligodendrocytes — paddle-shaped processes that wrap myelin around axons in the CNS . A single oligodendrocyte produces up to 50 segments of myelin. Myelin is 80% lipid, 20% protein and speeds axonal conduction. Schwann cells — perform myelination in the PNS ; one Schwann cell wraps one axon entirely. After PNS injury they digest dead axons and form cylinders that guide axonal regrowth, which is why PNS axons regenerate and CNS axons largely do not (the difference is in the supporting cells, not the axons). Microglia — the brain's immune cells; multiply after injury, engulf debris and dead cells, and trigger inflammation. Astrocytes — the largest glia, star-shaped; provide physical support, clean up debris, supply chemicals neurons need, gate substances between blood and CNS neurons, and contract/relax blood vessels to match local blood-flow demand. The resting membrane potential Recorded with intracellular microelectrodes, the inside of a resting neuron sits at about −70 mV relative to the outside. The neuron is then said to be polarized . Four ions matter: organic anions (A−), chloride (Cl−), sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+). At rest there is more Na+ outside the cell and more K+ inside; organic anions are trapped inside (too big to cross the membrane). Na+ feels strong pressure to enter from both the concentration gradient and electrostatic (electrical) pressure, but Na+ channels are mostly closed at rest. Balance is held by: The sodium–potassium pump — actively pushes 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in . More open K+ channels than Na+ channels, but few K+ actually leave because the negative interior holds them in. Mnemonic Resting potential = "bow and arrow." The membrane has done its work in advance (taut bowstring) so the neuron can fire strongly and rapidly the instant it is stimulated. The action potential, step by step Depolarization to threshold: a stimulus reduces polarization toward zero. If it crosses the threshold of excitation (about −65 mV), voltage-dependent Na+ channels open wide. Rising phase: Na+ rushes in explosively (driven by diffusion + electrostatic pressure). Membrane potential shoots from −70 mV to about +40 mV , overshooting zero to a reversed polarity. Peak (~1 ms): Na+ channels become refractory (blocked) and cannot reopen until

title: Unit 5 — Attention, Perception & Memory
text: Unit 5 — Attention, Perception & Memory The cognitive core of the syllabus, built from Solso-style cognitive psychology and the classic learning systems: how attention selects a trickle from the flood of sensation (Donald Broadbent, Treisman, Deutsch-Norman, Daniel Kahneman), how organisms learn by association and consequence (Ivan Pavlov, B. F. Skinner, Edward Thorndike, Edwin Guthrie, Clark Hull, Spence, Edward Tolman, Albert Bandura), how memory encodes, stores and retrieves (Atkinson-Shiffrin, Alan Baddeley, Endel Tulving, Fergus Craik & Robert Lockhart), why we forget (decay, interference, retrieval failure, repression, motivated forgetting), and how the visual system builds a stable percept of form, depth and pattern (Gestalt, template/feature/prototype, Irving Biederman, Oliver Selfridge) under uncertainty (signal detection theory). Each model is taught for its mechanism and its exam relevance, with theorists, dates and the traps that examiners love. In this book Attention: forms & models Classical & instrumental conditioning Fundamental learning theories Hull, discrimination, latent & observational learning Memory processes & systems Theories of forgetting Perception: approaches, illusions & pattern recognition Distance & depth perception Form perception Signal detection theory 1. Attention: forms & models Solso defines attention as "the concentration of mental effort on sensory or mental events." More fully (Duncan 1999; Motter 1999; Posner & Fernandez-Duque 1999), attention is the means by which we actively process a limited amount of information from the enormous amount available through our senses, stored memories and other cognitive processes. It is a concentration of mental activity that includes both conscious and unconscious processes. Definition Attention = selective concentration of finite mental resources on some stimuli at the expense of others. The central problem it solves is that the sensory world delivers far more information than the system can fully process. Forms of attention Divided attention — attending to several messages simultaneously, responding to each as needed. Performance typically suffers unless the tasks are well practised; practice alters the limits of attentional capacity. Selective attention — focusing on one task/stimulus while disregarding the others. It simplifies our lives because attentional capacity is limited. The Stroop effect is the classic demonstration of the cost of selecting against a dominant response. Sustained attention (vigilance) — the maintenance of selective attention to infrequent events over long periods. There is a reliable vigilance decrement : performance declines as time-on-task wears on, affected by the neurological and physiological state of the person. Filter / bottleneck models — early selection Everyday phenomena like the cocktail-party effect (you can follow one conversation in a noisy room, yet your own name spoken across the room captures you) are explained by filter theories . Early-selection means attention operates early in the information-processing sequence: only one source (the attended one) reaches meaningful processing; unattended information is actively filtered/blocked before it can compete for scarce higher-order resources. Broadbent's switch (filter) model (1958) Donald Broadbent proposed a simple on-off switch : attention directs processing to one input channel, which is fully analysed for meaning and made available to consciousness. Because the switch is all-or-none, additional messages are completely blocked. Attention is attracted and maintained by sensory/physical attributes of messages (e.g., the voice qualities at a party). The switch does not allow unconscious processing: unattended signals left in sensory memory rapidly decay and never receive the extra processing needed for longer-term retention. A subject should therefore be able to report only the physical features of the unattended message, not its meaning. Cherry's dichotic listening & shadowing (1953) Colin Cherry created a paradigm to test early selection: dichotic listening (different messages to each ear at once) combined with shadowing (repeating one message aloud as it occurs). Shadowing forces the subject onto one message so they cannot switch. Findings that strain the strict switch: when the meaning of the shadowed sentence switches to the non-shadowed ear, shadowing is disrupted (Anne Treisman 1960) — the subject follows the meaning rather than the physical cue of ear location, allowing determination of when attention shifts. Treisman's attenuator model (1964) Anne Treisman proposed a more flexible early-selection theory using a different mechanical metaphor: instead of an off/on switch, attention works like an attenuator (regulator) that allows gradations of energy through. Most of the attended message passes through; some unattended information may also reach the level of pattern recognition. Attention thus becomes a matter of degree . Physical cues tune the attenuator, but it can also be influenced by the meaning of previously analysed material, so control is exerted by both sensory and semantic information. It remains an early-selection theory because filtering still occurs prior to full meaningful analysis; partial analysis of all signals occurs. Late-selection models — Deutsch & Deutsch (1963), Norman (1968) Late-selection models propose that all information is recognised: every sensory input activates its corresponding meaning in long-term memory, but attention then selects among the activated meanings , allowing only a limited amount to reach consciousness. Selective attention operates on response output , not input. The non-shadowed information, requiring no overt response, may be rapidly forgotten before testing. The activation of meaning is unconscious; awareness itself is treated as a response . The activity decays quickly unless the activated meaning is selected for conscious processing.
