title: Unit 6 — Intelligence, Creativity & Thinking
text: Unit 6 — Intelligence, Creativity & Thinking The higher cognition syllabus from first principles: what intelligence is and the great factor theories that try to carve it (Charles Spearman's g through CHC), how intelligence is tested, what creativity is and how it is produced and nurtured, and then the machinery of thought itself: how we form concepts and categories, how we reason and where reasoning breaks, how we solve problems and get stuck, and how we make decisions and judge probability with the heuristics Daniel Kahneman & Amos Tversky exposed. Built to NIMHANS/MET clinical-psychology depth, reproducing every named theorist, model and term in the source notes. In this book Intelligence: definitions & theories Creativity Nurturing creativity at the workplace Thinking Concepts & categorization Reasoning Problem solving Factors influencing problem solving Decision making Decision-making styles Heuristics in decision making 1. Intelligence: definitions & theories The one problem behind the whole field. Everyone agrees intelligence exists; nobody agrees what it is . So the topic is really two arguments: (a) how to define intelligence, and (b) how it is structured : one general ability, a handful of group factors, or many independent ones. The factor theories below are best learned as a single conversation in which each thinker reacts to the last. The classic definitions (know the one-liners) Theorist Intelligence is… Spearman (1904, 1923) a general ability involving mainly the eduction of relations and correlates . Binet & Simon (1905) the ability to judge well, understand well, and reason well. Lewis Terman (1916) the capacity to form concepts and grasp their significance. Pintner (1921) the ability to adapt adequately to relatively new situations in life. Edward Thorndike (1921) the power of good responses from the point of view of truth or fact. Wechsler (1939) the aggregate or global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally, and deal effectively with the environment. Jean Piaget (1972) the superior forms of organization/equilibrium of cognitive structuring used for adaptation to the environment. Robert Sternberg (1985) the capacity to automatize information processing and emit contextually appropriate behavior in response to novelty. Hans Eysenck (1986) error-free transmission of information through the cortex. Howard Gardner (1986) the skill to solve problems or fashion products valued within one or more cultural settings. Ceci (1994) multiple innate abilities that develop, fail to develop, or atrophy depending on motivation and exposure. High-yield Match the phrase to the man: eduction of relations = Spearman; judge/understand/reason well = Binet & Simon; aggregate/global capacity = Wechsler; error-free cortical transmission = Hans Eysenck; fashion products valued in a culture = Howard Gardner. Galton and sensory keenness (the false start) The first theories came from the "Brass Instruments" era at the turn of the 20th century. Francis Galton and Cattell promoted a sensory keenness theory: smarter people have sharper senses and faster reactions. This proved a psychometric dead end . (Curiously, Arthur Jensen (1980) later reported reaction-time and movement-time indices correlating as high as .50 with traditional IQ tests, partly rehabilitating the idea of mental speed.) Spearman and the g factor Charles Spearman proposed that intelligence consists of two kinds of factors: a single general factor g plus numerous specific factors (s1, s2, s3…). To test this he helped invent factor analysis : a statistical technique to discern how many underlying factors must exist to account for the observed correlations among many tests. Performance on any homogeneous test is determined mainly by two influences: g (pervasive) and s (specific to that test). Because s differs for every test and is usually weaker than g, Spearman cared little about it. Spearman (1923) held that individual differences in g show up in three principles of cognition : Apprehension of experience Eduction of relations (given two ideas, find the relation between them) Eduction of correlates (given an idea and a relation, find the matching idea) Eduction simply means the process of figuring things out. The hardest problem for his two-factor theory was the stubborn existence of group factors (clusters bigger than s but smaller than g), which the next thinkers seized on. Definition g = a single, pervasive general intelligence loading on all cognitive tasks. Factor analysis = the statistical tool Charles Spearman built to find the latent factors behind a correlation matrix. Thurstone and the Primary Mental Abilities (PMAs) L. L. Thurstone (1931) refined factor analysis to search correlation matrices for group factors and concluded intelligence is not one thing but about a dozen relatively independent Primary Mental Abilities : Verbal Comprehension (best measure: vocabulary; also reading comprehension, verbal analogies) Word Fluency (anagrams; quickly naming words in a category) Number (speed/accuracy of simple arithmetic) Space (visualizing a 3-D object rotated or disassembled) Associative Memory (rote paired-associate learning) Perceptual Speed (clerical checking of visual detail) Inductive Reasoning (finding a rule, e.g. number-series completion) P. E. Vernon (1950) reconciled Spearman and Thurstone with a hierarchical group-factor theory : g sits at the top; below it two major group factors, verbal-educational (v:ed) and practical-mechanical-spatial-physical (k:m) ; below those, minor group factors resembling Thurstone's PMAs; specific factors at the bottom. Trap Spearman = one general factor (g + specifics). Thurstone = many coequal group factors (the PMAs), no dominant g. Vernon = a hierarchy that contains both (g on top, group factors beneath). Cattell–Horn–Carroll: fluid & crystallised, then CHC Raymond Cattell (1941, 1971) split g into two broad abilities: Fluid intelligence (Gf) : on-the-spot reasoning independent

title: Unit 7 — Personality, Emotion & Motivation
text: Unit 7 — Personality, Emotion & Motivation The whole of personality from first principles — the psychodynamic founders (Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Alfred Adler) and the neo-Freudians, the trait and type measurers (Gordon Allport, Cattell's 16PF, Eysenck's PEN, the Big Five and beyond), the humanistic-existential self (Abraham Maslow, Carl Rogers, May), and the behavioural / social-cognitive theorists (Albert Bandura, Julian Rotter, Walter Mischel, Martin Seligman, Kelly) — then how personality is assessed, and finally the affective and developmental engine behind it: theories of emotion, stress and the GAS, theories of motivation, attachment and emotional-social development, and the exploratory/sensation-seeking drive. Built from the Unit 7 source decks and taught to NIMHANS/MET depth, losing no named theorist or term. In this book Freud & the psychoanalytic approach Neo-Freudians: Jung, Adler, Horney, ego & object relations Erikson & lifespan identity Trait & type approaches Humanistic: Maslow & Rogers Existential: Rollo May Behavioural & social-cognitive: Bandura, Rotter, Mischel Cognitive approaches: Kelly, Lewin, Seligman, Kohlberg Assessment of personality Emotion & its physiology; theories of emotion Stress, the GAS & conflict Theories of motivation Emotional & social development Attachment Exploratory behaviour, curiosity & sensation seeking Fast glossary (A–Z) 1. Freud & the psychoanalytic approach The one idea. Sigmund Freud saw the psychological world as a series of opposing tensions (for example the tension between selfishness and society). Underlying every tension were inner pressures that strive for relief. The motor of the whole system is instinct : the German term is Trieb — a driving force or impulse. Instincts are the basic elements of personality, the motivating forces that drive behaviour and determine its direction. Instincts and motivation Life instincts (Eros). Serve the survival of the individual and the species by satisfying needs for food, water, air and sex. They are oriented toward growth and development. The psychic energy of the life instincts is the libido (Latin for desire/lust). Cathexis. The libido can be attached to, or invested in, objects — Sigmund Freud called this cathexis . Death instincts (Thanatos). In opposition to the life instincts, Freud postulated a destructive/death instinct. One component is the aggressive drive — the wish to die, turned outward against objects other than the self. Levels of personality (the topographic model) Level What it holds Conscious All sensations and experiences in immediate awareness. Preconscious / subconscious The storehouse of memories that can be brought to awareness. Unconscious The most important level and the major portion of personality; holds instincts, drives, desires and emotionally charged memories. The structure of the mind (the structural model) Id — operates on the pleasure principle ; strives solely to satisfy desires and reduce inner tension. It can only act through reflex or through wish-fulfilling hallucinatory/fantasy experience, which Sigmund Freud called primary-process thought . Ego — based on the reality principle ; the structure that develops to deal with the real world using perception, recognition, judgement and memory ( secondary-process thought ). Superego — based on the morality principle ; represents society's demands. Through praise/punishment children learn good and bad: punished behaviours form the conscience ; praised behaviours form the ego-ideal . When the ego and especially the superego do not do their job, elements of the id slip out as parapraxes — mistakes that reveal the unconscious. Freudian slips (errors in speech or writing) are more common when a person is tired or distracted, because defences are down and unconscious impulses surface. Psychosexual stages of development Stage Age Erogenous zone / conflict Fixation outcome Oral 0–1 Mouth; pleasure from sucking; id dominant Oral-incorporative (optimism, dependency) vs oral-aggressive/sadistic (pessimism, hostility, aggressiveness) from painful teething Anal 1–3 Toilet training interferes with gratification from defecation Anal-aggressive (hostile, sadistic) vs anal-retentive (stubborn, stingy, hoarding, rigid, compulsively neat, obstinate) Phallic 4–5 Incestuous fantasies; Oedipus/Electra complex; castration anxiety; superego develops Phallic character — strong narcissism Latency 5–puberty Sublimation of the sex instinct — Genital Adolescence–adulthood Sex-role identity, adult social relationships Genital type — finds satisfaction in love and work (work = acceptable sublimation of id impulses) Definition Fixation. An arresting of part of the libido at an earlier psychosexual stage because of excessive frustration or gratification, leaving a characteristic adult personality pattern. Anxiety and the defence mechanisms For Sigmund Freud, anxiety is a feeling of fear and dread without an obvious cause. He proposed three types: reality anxiety (fear of tangible dangers), neurotic anxiety (id–ego conflict), and moral anxiety (id–superego conflict). When anxiety builds, the ego deploys defence mechanisms : Defence What it does Repression Unconscious denial of the existence of something that causes anxiety Denial Denying an external threat or traumatic event Reaction formation Expressing an id impulse that is the opposite of the true one Projection Attributing a disturbing impulse to someone else Regression Retreating to an earlier, less frustrating period and acting childishly Rationalization Reinterpreting behaviour to make it more acceptable, less threatening Displacement Shifting id impulses from a threatening/unavailable object to an available substitute Sublimation Diverting instinctual energy into socially acceptable behaviours Mnemonic Three anxieties map to the three conflicts: Reality = external world; Neurotic = id vs ego; Moral = id vs superego. "RNM = world, ego, conscience." 2. Neo-Freudians: Jung, Adler, Horney, ego

title: Unit 8 — Social Psychology
text: Unit 8 — Social Psychology How the presence, behaviour and existence of other people shape what we think, feel and do: the field's history and grand theories, how we read other people, how groups push us into conformity, obedience and compliance, what happens inside groups, how leaders lead, why we help and why we harm, the roots of prejudice and intergroup conflict, and how all of it is applied to health, the law and the environment. Built file-by-file from the Rodrick Prashanth source decks and deepened to NIMHANS / MET clinical-psychology depth, preserving every named theorist, study, term and proposition. In this book History of social psychology Theories of social psychology Social perception Group & social influence Group dynamics Leadership styles Prosocial behaviour Aggression Theories of intergroup relationship Applying social psychology 1. History of social psychology The one idea. Social psychology is the scientific study of how the actual, imagined or implied presence of others influences an individual's thoughts, feelings and behaviour. Its history is a chain of named "firsts" and named "founders", and the paper loves to test who did what, in what year. The foundation (late 19th to early 20th century) Figure Year Contribution Norman Triplett 1897–1898 Credited with the first research article in social psychology . He noticed cyclists raced faster against others than against a clock, and designed a careful controlled experiment to study it. This is the origin of social facilitation . Max Ringelmann 1880s (published 1913) Found individuals performed worse on simple tasks such as rope-pulling when working with others. This is the origin of social loafing (the "Ringelmann effect"). William McDougall 1908 Published an early social psychology textbook; helps establish the field. Edward Ross 1908 American who published a founding social psychology text the same year. Floyd Allport 1924 His textbook is taken as establishing social psychology as a distinct experimental field. Trap Norman Triplett = social facilitation (first article, 1897–98). Max Ringelmann = social loafing (1880s, published 1913). Don't swap them. Establishing the field as a discipline is attributed to McDougall (1908), Ross (1908) and Floyd Allport (1924). 1930s–1950s: the field finds its problems 1936: Gordon Allport (younger brother of Floyd, the 1924 textbook author) and others formed the Society for the Psychological Study of Social Issues (SPSSI) . Muzafer Sherif published groundbreaking experimental research on social influence (the autokinetic-effect norm-formation studies). Kurt Lewin fled the Nazis and emigrated to the US in the early 1930s. His central contribution: behaviour is a function of the interaction between the person and the environment (the interactionist perspective ), often written B = f(P, E) . 1950s: Gordon Allport (1954) published The Nature of Prejudice . Solomon Asch (1951) demonstrated how willing people are to conform to an obviously wrong majority. Leon Festinger introduced two landmark theories: social comparison (1954, how people learn about themselves by comparing to others) and cognitive dissonance (1957, how attitudes change through one's own behaviour). 1960s–1990s: crisis and pluralism Stanley Milgram's obedience research (early/mid 1960s) linked the post-WWII era to the coming era of social revolution, showing individuals' vulnerability to the destructive commands of authority. Strong disagreements of the period (the "crisis of social psychology") were largely a reaction against the dominant method of the day, the laboratory experiment . Mid-1970s onward = an era of pluralism: laboratory and field experiments used side by side; a "hot" perspective (emotion and motivation) alongside a "cold" perspective (cognition); and the rise of international, cross-cultural and multicultural perspectives. Social psychology in a new century Social cognition dominated the final quarter of the field's first century: the study of how people perceive, remember and interpret information about themselves and others. Social neuroscience emerged as a subfield studying the relationship between neural and social processes. Behavioural genetics (the study of how genes affect behaviour) triggered research on, e.g., whether aggression is heritable and the role of genes in sexual orientation. Evolutionary psychology uses evolutionary principles to understand behaviour (e.g., asking how the psychological mechanisms underlying jealousy may have evolved from natural-selection pressures). Increasing emphasis on testing the universal generality vs cultural specificity of theories via cross-cultural and multicultural research. High-yield Norman Triplett (facilitation, first article) · Max Ringelmann (loafing) · McDougall/Ross 1908 + Floyd Allport 1924 (founding) · Lewin B = f(P,E) · Muzafer Sherif (norm formation) · Solomon Asch 1951 (conformity) · Leon Festinger 1954 social comparison / 1957 dissonance · Milgram 1960s (obedience) · Gordon Allport 1954 Nature of Prejudice . New century: social cognition, social neuroscience, behavioural genetics, evolutionary psychology, cross-cultural work. 2. Theories of social psychology The grand frameworks the field uses to explain social behaviour. Learn each by its core construct and its named author. Field theory (Kurt Lewin) Lewin, whose name is most associated with field theory , was a student of the founders of the Gestalt movement. Others (Edward Tolman 1932, Wheeler 1940, Karl Lashley 1929, Brunswik 1949) have been called field theorists, but none dealt specifically with social behaviour, so Lewin is taken as the best representative. Six principal attributes of field theory: (1) use of a constructive method ; (2) a dynamic approach; (3) emphasis on psychological processes; (4) analysis based on the situation as a whole ; (5) a distinction between systematic and historical issues; (6) a mathematical representation of the psychological situation (Lewin favoured topo

title: Unit 9 — Human Development & Intervention
text: Unit 9 — Human Development & Intervention The arc of a human life and the clinical work built on top of it: how development proceeds from conception to old age across every domain and theory (Sigmund Freud, Erik Erikson, Jean Piaget, Lev Vygotsky, the learning and information-processing views), how language and motor skills unfold, what it means for behaviour to become abnormal and how disorders are described and classified, the full landscape of psychotherapies (psychoanalytic, person-centred, Gestalt, existential, behavioural, REBT/CBT, transactional, family/systems), and the biological and socioemotional theories of successful aging. Built from Rodrick Prashanth's MET source decks and taught to NIMHANS clinical depth, losing no named theorist, term, or stage. In this book Developmental processes, domains & periods Theories of development Piaget's cognitive stages Vygotsky & information-processing Sensorimotor & motor development Language: components, theories, periods The concept of abnormality Describing & assessing disorders Classification (DSM & ICD) & causes Psychoanalytic therapy Person-centred, Gestalt & existential Behaviour therapy REBT & Beck's cognitive therapy Transactional analysis Family & systems therapy Successful aging: biological theories Socioemotional aging & late-life disorders 1. Developmental processes, domains & periods The one idea. Developmental science studies change and stability across the lifespan. Scientists care not only about how people change but about the underlying stability or constancy of personality and behaviour over time. Two kinds of change Quantitative change — a change in number or amount : growth in height, weight, vocabulary, aggressive behaviour, or frequency of communication. Qualitative change — a change in kind, structure, or organisation . Not "more of the same" but a different form altogether. Three domains of development Change and stability occur in various domains (dimensions) of the self. Scientists discuss them separately but treat development as a single unified process . Domain What changes Physical development Growth of body and brain; change or stability in sensory capacities, motor skills, and health. Cognitive development Change or stability in mental abilities: learning, attention, memory, language, thinking, reasoning, and creativity. Psychosocial development Change and stability in emotions, personality, and social relationships. Periods of the lifespan The division of the lifespan into periods (infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, old age) is a social construction : a concept about the nature of reality based on societally shared perceptions or assumptions, not a fixed biological fact. High-yield Quantitative = change in amount (height, vocabulary). Qualitative = change in kind/structure . Three domains: physical, cognitive, psychosocial. Lifespan periods are a social construction . 2. Theories of development The psychoanalytic viewpoint — Freud Sigmund Freud concluded that human development is a conflictual process : as biological creatures we have basic sexual and aggressive instincts that must be served, yet society dictates that many of these drives be restrained. The ways parents manage these urges in the first few years play a major role in shaping personality. Freud held personality was fixed in childhood — essentially formed by age 5 or 6. Psychosexual stages of development Stage Age Characteristics Fixation outcomes Oral 0–1 Mouth is the primary erogenous zone; pleasure from sucking; id is dominant . Oral incorporative (taking in) — optimism, dependency. Oral aggressive/sadistic (during teething) — pessimism, hostility, aggressiveness. Anal 1–3 Toilet training (external reality) interferes with gratification from defecation. Anal aggressive — defecates to defy parents; basis for hostile/sadistic adult behaviour. Anal retentive — stubborn, stingy, hoarding; rigid, compulsively neat, obstinate, overly conscientious. Phallic 4–5 Incestuous fantasies; Oedipus and Electra complex ; castration anxiety; superego development. Phallic character shows strong narcissism . Latency 5–puberty Period of sublimation of the sex instinct. — Genital Adolescence–adulthood Development of sex-role identity and adult social relationships. Genital type finds satisfaction in love and work , work being an acceptable outlet for sublimation of id impulses. Erikson's theory of psychosocial development Erik Erikson renounced Sigmund Freud's idea of fixity, arguing that identity formation is a lifelong process . Personality (Erikson focused on identity ) develops through eight stages as life unfolds. The outcome of each stage depends on the outcome of the previous one, and successful negotiation of each ego crisis is essential for optimal growth. He used Freud's psychosexual stages as his basis; his first five stages reflect ego crises tied to Freud's stages. Trap Sigmund Freud: personality fixed by age 5–6 , five psychosexual stages. Erik Erikson: identity is lifelong , eight psychosocial stages built on Freud's first five. Don't merge the two. The learning viewpoint — Watson & the operant view John B. Watson believed that well-learned associations between external stimuli and observable responses (called habits ) are the building blocks of development. From this perspective children do not progress through distinct biologically dictated stages; development is a continuous process of behavioural change shaped by each person's unique environment, and may differ dramatically from person to person. Operant learning theory claims development depends on external stimuli (reinforcers and punishers) rather than internal forces such as instincts, drives, or maturation. Modern developmentalists agree habits can emerge and disappear over a lifetime depending on their positive or negative consequences. The cognitive viewpoint — Jean Piaget Piaget (1950) defined intelligence as a basic life process that helps an organism adapt to its environment

title: Unit 10 — Emerging Areas
text: Unit 10 — Emerging Areas The newer frontiers of applied psychology, built directly from the Unit 10 source: the psychology of gender and the schools of feminism , feminist psychology and feminist therapy with their critique of traditional treatment, the workplace barriers women face, the psychology of poverty , the positive-psychology science of wellbeing and self-growth (eudaimonia vs hedonia, the major wellbeing models, character strengths and post-traumatic growth), and cyberpsychology (online disinhibition and internet addiction). Every named area, model and theorist in the file is reproduced and taught to NIMHANS depth. In this book Issues of gender Types of feminism Feminist psychology Workplace barriers: glass ceiling & relatives Feminist therapy Issues in traditional therapies Empowerment & feminist techniques The psychology of poverty Wellbeing & self-growth Models of wellbeing Character strengths & virtues Post-traumatic growth Cyberpsychology 1. Issues of gender The one distinction to never blur. The whole topic rests on separating two words the public uses interchangeably. Sex is the biological distinction between male and female, fixed at conception by the chromosomes: the male karyotype is XY and the female karyotype is XX . Gender is the culturally constructed categorisation of maleness and femaleness, that is, the social meanings of masculinity and femininity . Sex is given by biology; gender is built by culture. Definition Gender = the culturally constructed categorisation of maleness and femaleness (masculinity / femininity). Sex = the biological distinction of male (XY chromosome) and female (XX chromosome). Gender stereotypes A gender stereotype is a widely held belief about the abilities, personality traits, and social behaviour of females and males (the source attributes this definition to Weiten, 2001 ). Stereotypes are not the same as differences that actually exist; they are beliefs about the sexes, which may be exaggerated, inaccurate, or self-fulfilling. They feed the discrimination patterns described later in this book (glass ceiling, maternal wall, etc.). Minimalist vs maximalist views of gender differences How big are the psychological differences between men and women? The field splits into two camps: Maximalists believe in huge, fundamental differences between men and women. On this view the sexes are deeply, qualitatively distinct. Minimalists believe there are few fundamental differences between them. On this view the apparent gaps are small, situational, or socially produced rather than essential. Trap Maximalist = MAXimum difference; minimalist = MINimum difference. Maximalists emphasise large, fundamental sex differences; minimalists emphasise that the genuine fundamental differences are few. Do not confuse the camps because the names sound technical. High-yield Sex = biological (XY male, XX female). Gender = cultural construction of masculinity/femininity. Gender stereotype = widely held belief about males'/females' abilities, traits and social behaviour (Weiten, 2001). Maximalists = big differences; minimalists = few fundamental differences. 2. Types of feminism The source lists five branches of feminism . Each answers the same question, "what is the root of women's oppression and how do we end it?", in a different way. Learn them by their diagnosis and their strategy , because that is what is tested. Branch Core idea / diagnosis Strategy Liberal feminism Works within the structure of mainstream society. Its roots reach back to social-contract theory of government, the idea instituted by the American Revolution. Integrate women into the existing structure (equal access, equal rights) rather than overthrow it. Radical feminism Seen by many as the "undesirable" element of feminism, yet it is actually the breeding ground for many of the ideas that other branches shape and pound out. Holds that women's oppression is the deepest, original oppression. Tackle the root system of male domination (patriarchy) directly; the source ties consciousness raising to this branch. Socialist feminism The result of Marxism meeting radical feminism . Marxism recognises that women are oppressed and attributes the oppression to the capitalist / private-property system . The only way to end women's oppression is to overthrow the capitalist system . Cultural feminism Retreated to vanguardism , working instead to build a women's culture . Some of this effort has had real social benefit. Create and value a distinct women's culture rather than fight for integration. Eco-feminism Much more spiritual than political or theoretical in nature. May or may not be wrapped up with Goddess worship and vegetarianism . Its basic tenet: a patriarchal/hierarchical society will exploit its resources without regard to long-term consequences, as a direct result of the attitudes fostered in such a society. Link the domination of women to the domination of nature; resist both. Mnemonic " L iberals L obby (work within), R adicals R oot out patriarchy, S ocialists S mash capitalism, C ultural C reates a women's culture, E co links women & E arth." — L-R-S-C-E. High-yield Socialist feminism = Marxism + radical feminism , blames the capitalist/private-property system. Radical feminism is the "breeding ground" of feminist ideas and is the home of consciousness raising . Liberal feminism = integration within the system. Eco-feminism = spiritual, links patriarchy to environmental exploitation. 3. Feminist psychology Feminist psychology aims to understand the individual within the larger social and political aspects of society . Its defining move is to refuse to study a person in isolation: a woman's distress is read against the background of her social and political situation, not just her internal makeup. title: Research Methods & Statistics
text: Research Methods & Statistics How psychological knowledge is made and judged: the philosophical paradigms beneath every study, the quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods that grow from them, the experimental and non-experimental designs that license (or block) causal claims, and the statistical tests that decide whether a result is real. This book moves from epistemology to inference, builds every parametric test (t, F) from the logic of sampling distributions, extends them to MANOVA and ANCOVA, and closes with the distribution-free family. It is prioritised for MET 2026 and NIMHANS clinical psychology, with assumptions, degrees of freedom and a "which test when" decision table you can recite under pressure. In this book Paradigms & methods of research Research designs & sampling Hypothesis testing & inference Parametric test: the t-test ANOVA & experimental designs MANOVA & ANCOVA Non-parametric tests "Which test when" decision guide 1. Paradigms & methods of research The one idea behind the section. Before any method is chosen, a researcher already holds a paradigm : a way of thinking about and conducting research, a philosophy that guides how the research might be done. Method is downstream of philosophy. Two scientists can study the same phenomenon and reach different designs because they answer two prior questions differently: what is real ( ontology ) and how can we know it ( epistemology ). Definition Ontology = the nature of reality (is there one objective reality, or many constructed realities?). Epistemology = the nature of knowledge and the relationship between the knower and what is known (can the researcher stand apart from what is studied, or are they entangled with it?). Together they shape both the data-collection process and the analysis. The four research paradigms Learn each by its stance on reality, on the researcher, and on the kind of knowledge it produces. Paradigm Ontology / epistemology Typical methods Goal Positivism One objective reality exists and can be measured directly; researcher is detached and value-free Experiments, structured measurement, statistics Discover universal laws; explain and predict Post-positivism Objective reality exists but can only be known imperfectly and probabilistically ; all observation is theory-laden Quantitative methods with a plan fixed before the study; falsification Approximate truth through repeated, fallible testing Constructivism / interpretivism Reality is socially and personally constructed ; multiple realities; knower and known are inseparable Open-ended interviews, observation, narrative documents kept in text form Understand meaning from the participant's perspective Critical / transformative Reality is shaped by power, history, economics; knowledge is political Critical ethnography, participatory and emancipatory designs Expose and change unjust structures; empower Trap Positivism vs post-positivism. Both are "objective-reality" paradigms and both drive quantitative work. The shift is that positivism claims we can know reality directly and with certainty, while post-positivism (the modern stance behind most quantitative social science) says we can only know it imperfectly : every measurement is fallible, theory-laden, and provisional, so we falsify rather than prove. In exam phrasing, "quantitative research = post-positivist approach" and "qualitative research = constructivist approach". Quantitative vs qualitative vs mixed methods The paradigm choice cascades into a whole research stance. The table is high-yield because the paper tests the cascade directly. Feature Quantitative (post-positivist) Qualitative (constructivist) Plan A specific plan is developed prior to the study; tight structure Less structure on specific guidelines; general guidelines only; emergent design Data "Objective": easily classified or quantified (age, gender, test scores, recovery time) "Subjective": interpreted differently by different people (perceptions of pain, feelings about work) Collection Structured interviews / questionnaires, observations, records; scored reliably with little training Open-ended interviews, observation, narrative documents (diaries); data kept in text form Analysis Inferential statistics to generalise from sample to population Coding of themes , assigning meaning to words or images Strength Results across many studies can be combined into a large body of evidence Depth; tools for data, analysis and interpretation that quantitative work lacks Mixed methods. When the two paradigms are blended so that one sets the stage for or leads to the other , the approach is mixed methods. It rests on the pragmatic approach, which focuses on methodological rather than philosophical concerns and combines qualitative and quantitative methods, using exploratory and confirmatory methods. This widens the options for data collection, analysis tools and interpretation. Trap Using two methods in the same study but discussing them separately is not mixed methods, it is just "two methods being used". Mixed methods requires genuine integration where one paradigm feeds the other. Qualitative methods of research, in depth NIMHANS expects you to name each qualitative tradition and its signature. Observation. Being present in a situation and recording one's impressions. The primary research instrument is the self , consciously gathering sensory data. Problems: the enormous complexity of human behaviour, the impossibility of a complete record, and the subjectivity of the researcher. Types: structured (schedules predetermine the categories of behaviour/talk to be observed, e.g. Flanders' Interaction Analysis Categories, FIAC), unstructured (broad decisions made in advance, seen through the researcher's own socio-culturally constructed values), shadow studies (tracking one participant), and participant observation (the researcher joins and participates, gaining unique insight but risking distraction from the research purpose). text: UGC NET Psychology — Past Papers & Syllabus A faithful reference pack for the UGC NET (subject code 04) Psychology paper: the complete official 10-unit syllabus reproduced as a clean outline, a plain-language guide to how the exam works distilled from the NTA FAQ, and three full past papers transcribed question-by-question. The December 2019 paper is reproduced with its official answer key; the June 2019 paper and the 2020 paper are reproduced verbatim from the source documents, and because no official answer key was supplied for them, every question there is marked "Answer: not in key" rather than guessed. Use this to learn the real shape, weight and wording of the exam. In this book The official syllabus (all 10 units) How the exam works December 2019 NET paper (with answer key) June 2019 NET paper 2020 NET paper 1. The official syllabus (all 10 units) This is the University Grants Commission (UGC) NET Bureau syllabus for Psychology, Code No. 04 , reproduced in full. The paper draws its questions from these ten units. Topics are listed exactly as in the official syllabus. High-yield Every NET Psychology question maps to one of these ten units. Knowing the unit a question belongs to is half the battle: it tells you which body of theory the examiner is testing. Units 1 (Emergence/systems), 2 (Methodology & Statistics) and 3 (Testing) are disproportionately heavy in the papers in this book. Unit 1. Emergence of Psychology Eastern systems: Psychological thought in major Eastern systems — Bhagavad Gita, Buddhism, Sufism and Integral Yoga. Academic psychology in India: Pre-independence era; post-independence era; 1970s (the move to addressing social issues); 1980s (Indigenization); 1990s (paradigmatic concerns, disciplinary identity crisis); 2000s (emergence of Indian psychology in academia). Issues: the colonial encounter; post-colonialism and psychology; lack of distinct disciplinary identity. Western: Greek heritage, medieval period and modern period. Structuralism, Functionalism, Psychoanalytical, Gestalt, Behaviorism, Humanistic-Existential, Transpersonal, Cognitive revolution, Multiculturalism. Four founding paths of academic psychology — Wundt, Freud, James, Dilthey. Issues: crisis in psychology due to strict adherence to the experimental-analytical paradigm (logical empiricism); Indic influences on modern psychology. Knowledge paradigms: Essential aspects — ontology, epistemology, and methodology. Paradigms of Western Psychology: Positivism, Post-Positivism, Critical perspective, Social Constructionism, Existential Phenomenology, and Co-operative Enquiry. Paradigmatic controversies. Significant Indian paradigms on psychological knowledge: Yoga, Bhagavad Gita, Buddhism, Sufism, and Integral Yoga. Science and spirituality (avidya and vidya). The primacy of self-knowledge in Indian psychology. Unit 2. Research Methodology and Statistics Research: Meaning, purpose, and dimensions. Research problems, variables and operational definitions, hypothesis, sampling. Ethics in conducting and reporting research. Paradigms of research: Quantitative, Qualitative, Mixed methods approach. Methods of research: Observation, Survey (interview, questionnaires), Experimental, Quasi-experimental, Field studies, Cross-cultural studies, Phenomenology, Grounded theory, Focus groups, Narratives, Case studies, Ethnography. Statistics: Measures of central tendency and dispersion. Normal probability curve. Parametric (t-test) and non-parametric tests (Sign test, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Mann-Whitney test, Kruskal-Wallis test, Friedman). Power analysis. Effect size. Correlational analysis: Correlation (Product Moment, Rank Order), partial correlation, multiple correlation. Special correlation methods: Biserial, Point-biserial, tetrachoric, phi coefficient. Regression: simple linear regression, multiple regression. Factor analysis: assumptions, methods, rotation and interpretation. Experimental designs: ANOVA (one-way, factorial), Randomized Block Designs, Repeated Measures Design, Latin Square, Cohort studies, Time series, MANOVA, ANCOVA. Single-subject designs. Unit 3. Psychological Testing Types of tests. Test construction: Item writing, item analysis. Test standardization: Reliability, validity and norms. Areas of testing: Intelligence, creativity, neuropsychological tests, aptitude, personality assessment, interest inventories. Attitude scales — Semantic differential, Stapel, Likert scale. Computer-based psychological testing. Applications of psychological testing across settings: Clinical, Organizational and business, Education, Counseling, Military, Career guidance. Unit 4. Biological Basis of Behavior Sensory systems: general and specific sensations, receptors and processes. Neurons: structure, functions, types, neural impulse, synaptic transmission. Neurotransmitters. The Central and Peripheral Nervous Systems — structure and functions. Neuroplasticity. Methods of Physiological Psychology: Invasive methods (anatomical methods, degeneration techniques, lesion techniques, chemical methods, microelectrode studies); Non-invasive methods (EEG, scanning methods). Muscular and glandular system: types and functions. Biological basis of motivation: hunger, thirst, sleep and sex. Biological basis of emotion: the limbic system, hormonal regulation of behavior. Genetics and behavior: chromosomal anomalies; nature-nurture controversy (twin studies and adoption studies). Unit 5. Attention, Perception, Learning, Memory and Forgetting Attention: Forms of attention, models of attention. Perception: Approaches to the study of perception (Gestalt and physiological). Perceptual organization (Gestalt, figure and ground, laws of organization). Perceptual constancy (size, shape, colour); illusions. Perception of form, depth and movement. Role of motivation and learning in perception. Signal detection theory: assumptions and applications. Subliminal perception and related factors, information processing approach, culture and perception, perceptual styles, pattern recognition, ecological perspective on perception. Learning process: Fundamental theories (Thorndike, Guthrie, Hull). Classical conditioning: procedure, phenomena, related issues. Instrumental learning: phenomena, paradigms, theoretical issues. Reinforcement: basic variables and schedules; behaviour modification and its applications. Cognitive approaches in learning: latent learning, observational learning. Verbal learning and discrimination learning. Recent trends: neurophysiology of learning. Memory and forgetting: Memory processes (encoding, storage, retrieval). Stages of memory (sensory, short-term/working, long-term — declarative: episodic and semantic; procedural). Theories of forgetting (interference, retrieval failure, decay, motivated forgetting). Unit 6. Thinking, Intelligence and Creativity Theoretical perspectives on thought processes: Associationism, Gestalt, Information processing, Feature integration model. Concept formation: rules, types, strategies; role of concepts in thinking. Types of reasoning. Language and thought. Problem solving: types, strategies, obstacles. Decision-making: types and models. Metacognition: metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive regulation. Intelligence: Spearman; Thurstone; Jensen; Cattell; Gardner; Sternberg; Goleman; Das, Kar & Parrila. Creativity: Torrance, Getzels & Jackson, Guilford, Wallach & Kogan. Relationship between intelligence and creativity. Unit 7. Personality, Motivation, Emotion, Stress and Coping Determinants of personality: biological and socio-cultural. Approaches to personality: Psychoanalytical, Neo-Freudian, Social learning, Trait and Type, Cognitive, Humanistic, Existential, Transpersonal. Other theories: Rotter's Locus of Control, Seligman's explanatory styles, Kohlberg's theory of moral development. Basic motivational concepts: instincts, needs, drives, arousal, incentives, motivational cycle. Approaches to motivation: Psychoanalytical, Ethological, S-R, Cognitive, Humanistic. Exploratory behavior and curiosity. Zuckerman's sensation seeking. Achievement, affiliation and power. Motivational competence. Self-regulation. Flow. Emotions: physiological correlates. Theories of emotion: James-Lange, Cannon-Bard, Schachter and Singer, Lazarus, Lindsley. Emotion regulation. Conflicts: sources and types. Stress and coping: concept, models, Type A/B/C/D behaviors, stress-management strategies (Biofeedback, Music therapy, Breathing exercises, Progressive Muscular Relaxation, Guided Imagery, Mindfulness, Meditation, Yogasana, Stress Inoculation Training). Unit 8. Social Psychology Nature, scope and history of social psychology. Traditional theoretical perspectives: Field theory, Cognitive Dissonance, Sociobiology, Psychodynamic approaches, Social Cognition. Social perception (communication, attributions); attitude and its change within cultural context; prosocial behavior. Group and social influence (Social Facilitation; Social Loafing). Social influence (Conformity, Peer Pressure, Persuasion, Compliance, Obedience, Social Power, Reactance). Aggression. Group dynamics, leadership style and effectiveness. Theories of intergroup relations (Minimal Group Experiment and Social Identity Theory, Relative Deprivation Theory, Realistic Conflict Theory, Balance Theories, Equity Theory, Social Exchange Theory). Applied social psychology: Health, Environment and Law; personal space, crowding, and territoriality. Unit 9. Human Development and Interventions Developmental processes: nature, principles, factors, stages of development. Successful aging. Theories of development: Psychoanalytical, Behavioristic, Cognitive. Various aspects of development: sensory-motor, cognitive, language, emotional, social and moral. Psychopathology: concept, Mental Status Examination, classification, causes. Psychotherapies: Psychoanalysis, Person-centered, Gestalt, Existential, Acceptance Commitment Therapy, Behavior therapy, REBT, CBT, MBCT, Play therapy, Positive psychotherapy, Transactional Analysis, Dialectical Behavior Therapy, Art therapy, Performing Art Therapy, Family therapy. Applications of theories of motivation and learning in school. Factors in educational achievement. Teacher effectiveness. Guidance in schools: needs, organizational set-up and techniques. Counselling: process, skills, and techniques. Unit 10. Emerging Areas Issues of gender, poverty, disability, and migration: cultural bias and discrimination. Stigma, marginalization, and social suffering; child abuse and domestic violence. Peace psychology: violence, non-violence, conflict resolution at the macro level, role of media in conflict resolution. Wellbeing and self-growth: types of wellbeing (Hedonic and Eudemonic), character strengths, resilience and post-traumatic growth. Health: health-promoting and health-compromising behaviors, lifestyle and chronic diseases (Diabetes, Hypertension, Coronary Heart Disease), psychoneuroimmunology (Cancer, HIV/AIDS). Psychology and technology interface: digital learning; digital etiquette; cyber bullying; cyber pornography (consumption, implications); parental mediation of digital usage. 2. How the exam works UGC-NET (the National Eligibility Test) is conducted by the National Testing Agency (NTA) on behalf of the University Grants Commission. It determines eligibility for Assistant Professor only, or for Assistant Professor and Junior Research Fellowship (JRF) both, in colleges and universities. Below is the practical guidance distilled from the official NTA FAQ document. Format and mode Mode: Computer Based Test (CBT) only. Sittings: Two shifts on exam day — roughly 09:00–12:00 and 15:00–18:00. The date and slot are allotted randomly by computer (needed for the normalization process); a candidate cannot choose them. Two papers in one session: Paper 1 (general teaching/research aptitude, common to all subjects) and Paper 2 (the Psychology subject paper based on the 10-unit syllabus above). Both are attempted in the same sitting. Subjects: NET is conducted in roughly 80+ subjects; Psychology is subject code 04. High-yield There is NO negative marking in UGC-NET. The official FAQ states plainly: "No. There is no negative marking for wrong answers." So you should attempt every question — leaving a question blank can only cost you, never protect you. (This is the opposite of many other entrance tests, so do not carry a "skip if unsure" habit into NET.) Marking and result Negative marking: None. Every question carries positive marks only; wrong answers are not penalised. Qualifying criterion: Per UGC policy, the top 6% of candidates who appear in both papers and obtain the minimum qualifying marks (in aggregate of both papers) are declared NET-qualified. No all-India rank: The FAQ states "Rank is not assigned in UGC-NET." Results are pass/qualify based, with JRF allocated subject-wise and category-wise. Challenging the key: After the test, the question paper, recorded responses and the provisional answer key are released. Candidates may challenge an answer by paying a non-refundable fee (Rs 200 per question challenged) within the given window. The final result uses the answer key vetted by subject experts. No re-evaluation or re-checking is done after results. Eligibility and age Subject: Candidates should appear in the subject of their post-graduation. If their PG subject is not in the NET list, they may appear in a related subject. JRF age limit: Not more than 31 years (as on the first day of the month in which the exam concludes), with relaxations for reserved categories. There is no upper age limit for the Assistant Professor eligibility. Category concessions: Candidates in the non-creamy layer whose category is in the central OBC list, and SC/ST/PwD candidates, get fee and (where applicable) qualifying-mark concessions. Fees (as per the cited cycle) Category Fee General / Unreserved Rs. 1100 Gen-EWS / OBC-NCL Rs. 550 SC / ST / PwD / Third gender Rs. 275 Payment is online only (debit/credit card or net banking). Fees are non-refundable and applications cannot be withdrawn. Documents and most details can be edited later through the correction window. Mnemonic Remember the three numbers that define NET: 0 (zero negative marking), 6 (top 6% qualify), 2 (two papers in one session). Attempt everything, aim for the top slice, and budget time across both papers. Trap NET does not give you a "rank" or a "score out of 100" that ranks you nationally for admission the way a CET does. Qualifying is a percentile-style cut-off (top 6%). Do not confuse a NET qualification with an entrance-exam merit rank. 3. title: Statistics and Research Methods for Clinical Psychology Entrances
text: Statistics and Research Methods for Clinical Psychology Entrances Everything from scales of measurement (Stanley Smith Stevens, 1946) to MANCOVA, factor analysis and item response theory, then the whole of research methods (designs, validity, single-case, qualitative, trials, ethics), built from scratch, with a diagram on every idea that has a shape. This is a book, not a cheat sheet. Every concept is built from the ground up: what the thing is, why it exists, the formula with every symbol named, a worked example with real numbers, the assumptions it stands on, what breaks it, and who invented it. Read it cold and you will understand statistics and research design, not just recognise the words. Part I (sections 1 to 17) is statistics; Part II (sections 18 to 27) is research methods. The 64 diagrams are drawn from the actual functions or from real numbers, so the normal curve really is a normal curve, the F distribution really is an F distribution, and every single-case graph, time series and forest plot is computed. 27 sections 64 diagrams 60+ named statisticians 100+ research-methods names Every test with its assumptions Built for IHBAS · CIP · RML · JSS · DIMHANS · Amity · SGT · NIMHANS 1 · Variables and scales of measurement 2 · Frequency distributions and graphs 3 · Central tendency 4 · Dispersion 5 · Skewness and kurtosis 6 · The normal curve and standard scores 7 · Probability, sampling and the sampling distribution 8 · Hypothesis testing, errors, power, effect size 9 · The t tests 10 · ANOVA 11 · ANCOVA, MANOVA, MANCOVA 12 · Correlation 13 · Regression 14 · Non-parametric tests 15 · Psychometrics 16 · Which test to use 17 · Formula sheet and who-did-what index Part II: Research methods 18 · The research process: science, problems, hypotheses and variables 19 · Validity of a study and the control of extraneous variables 20 · Experimental and quasi-experimental designs 21 · Non-experimental designs: correlational, developmental and epidemiological 22 · Single-subject (small-N) designs 23 · Collecting the data: observation, interviews, questionnaires and scaling 24 · Qualitative and mixed-methods research 25 · Clinical trials, evidence and meta-analysis 26 · Research ethics 27 · Which design to use, the research-methods name index, and the traps How to use this book. First pass: read sections 1 to 8 straight through, because everything later is built on them. Second pass: sections 9 to 14 are the test family; do not memorise formulas, memorise the question each test answers and the assumptions it needs , because that is what entrance papers ask. Third pass: section 15 (psychometrics) is worth as many marks as ANOVA in most of these papers and is usually the least prepared. Section 16 is the decision tree; if you can walk it without looking, you can answer any "which test would you apply" item. Section 17 is the night-before page. Part II (sections 18 to 27) is research methods: read 18 to 20 in order, because validity and the threats in 19 are the language every design in 20 to 22 is judged in; 23 to 26 can be read in any order; 27 is the which-design tree, the name index and the traps. 1 Variables and scales of measurement Statistics is a set of tools for one job: getting from what you observed in a handful of people to a defensible statement about people in general. Everything in this book is either describing what you have (descriptive statistics) or generalising beyond what you have (inferential statistics). Keep that split in your head; it is the first line of a hundred exam answers. 1.1 The vocabulary you cannot skip Term Meaning Symbol Population The entire set of people or observations you actually want to talk about. Usually hypothetical and never fully measured. N Sample The subset you actually measured. Statistics exists because samples are all you ever get. n Parameter A number describing the population . Fixed, unknown, written with Greek letters. μ, σ, ρ, π Statistic A number describing the sample . Known, varies from sample to sample, written with Roman letters. M or X̄, s, r, p Variable Any characteristic that takes more than one value. X, Y Constant A characteristic that takes only one value in your study. – Datum / data A single recorded observation / the set of them. Xᵢ The rule that generates half the notation questions: Greek letters are for populations, Roman letters are for samples. μ is the population mean, M (or X̄) is the sample mean. σ is the population SD, s is the sample SD. ρ (rho) is the population correlation, r is the sample correlation. β is the population regression weight, b is the sample one. Types of variable Independent variable (IV): the one the experimenter manipulates or selects. The presumed cause. Also called the predictor (in regression) or the factor (in ANOVA). Its values are called levels . Dependent variable (DV): the one you measure. The presumed effect. Also called the criterion or the outcome. Extraneous variable: anything else that could affect the DV. Controlled by randomisation, matching, holding constant, or statistically (ANCOVA). Confounding variable: an extraneous variable that actually varies systematically with the IV , so its effect is inseparable from the IV's. A confound is an extraneous variable that got away. Mediator: the variable through which the IV acts (X → M → Y). Explains how or why . Tested by Baron and Kenny's (1986) steps or by Sobel / bootstrapped indirect effects. Moderator: a variable that changes the strength or direction of the X–Y relation. Explains when or for whom . Statistically, a moderator is an interaction . Discrete variable: takes only separate whole values (number of children, number of hospital admissions). Continuous variable: can take any value in a range; between any two values another is possible (reaction time, IQ). Measured to a limit of precision, with real limits of ±half the smallest unit: a reported weight of 62 kg means 61.5 to 62.5. Trap: mediator and moderator are the single most confused pair in research-methods sections. Mediator = the mechanism, sits between IV and DV in the causal chain. Moderator = the condition, sits outside and changes the size of the effect. "Stress causes depression through rumination" is mediation. "Stress causes depression more strongly in people with low social support" is moderation. 1.2 The four scales of measurement (S. S. Stevens, 1946) Stanley Smith Stevens , Harvard psychophysicist, published "On the theory of scales of measurement" in Science in 1946. The four-scale taxonomy is his, and it is the single most examined single fact in the statistics section of every one of these papers. Learn it perfectly. Scale What it does Properties Examples Permissible central tendency Permissible statistics Nominal (categorical) Names / labels only. Numbers are arbitrary tags. Identity / difference only. No order, no equal intervals, no true zero. Gender, diagnosis, blood group, jersey numbers, marital status, religion Mode only Frequencies, percentages, mode, χ², phi, contingency coefficient, Cramér's V Ordinal (ranks) Orders cases, but the gaps between ranks are unequal and unknown. Identity + order. No equal intervals, no true zero. Socio-economic status, ranks in a class, Likert-type agreement, Mohs hardness, stage of illness, birth order Mode and median Median, percentiles, quartile deviation, Spearman ρ, Kendall τ, Mann–Whitney U, Kruskal–Wallis Interval Equal units, but the zero point is arbitrary. Identity + order + equal intervals. No absolute zero. Temperature in °C or °F, calendar years, IQ scores, most psychological test scores, z scores Mode, median and mean Mean, SD, Pearson r, t test, ANOVA, regression, factor analysis Ratio Equal units and a true zero meaning "none of it". All four properties. Ratios are meaningful. Height, weight, reaction time, number of errors, income, age, kelvin temperature Mode, median, mean, geometric and harmonic mean Everything, plus coefficient of variation and ratio statements Mnemonic: NOIR (French for black), in order of increasing information: N ominal, O rdinal, I nterval, R atio. Each scale keeps all the properties of the ones before it and adds one. Any statistic legal at a lower scale stays legal at a higher one; the reverse is never true. The two traps that are asked every year. (1) Temperature in Celsius is interval, not ratio , because 0°C is the freezing point of water, not the absence of heat; 40°C is not "twice as hot" as 20°C. Temperature in kelvin is ratio. (2) IQ is interval, not ratio. There is no IQ of zero meaning "no intelligence", so a person with IQ 140 is not twice as intelligent as one with 70. Strictly, IQ is arguably only ordinal, but for exam purposes it is treated as interval. Why the scale decides everything downstream. The scale of your DV is the first branch of the which-test decision tree. Nominal DV means frequencies means chi-square. Ordinal DV means ranks means the non-parametric family. Interval or ratio DV means the mean and the SD are meaningful, which means the parametric family (t, ANOVA, Pearson, regression) becomes available. If you can name the scale you have already narrowed the answer to about four tests. Two more scales worth knowing Absolute scale: a counting scale where the unit is one and cannot be changed (number of children). Some texts treat it as a fifth, strongest scale. Interval-like ordinal (quasi-interval): Likert items are ordinal per item, but a summed Likert scale of many items is conventionally treated as interval. Say this explicitly if asked; examiners like the nuance. 2 Frequency distributions and graphs Raw data is unreadable. The first act of every analysis is to impose order on it, and the tool for that is the frequency distribution. 2.1 Building a grouped frequency distribution Find the range: R = highest score − lowest score (some texts add 1 for the "inclusive range"). Choose the number of class intervals: conventionally 10 to 20. Too few hides the shape, too many defeats the purpose. Find the class interval width (i): i = R / (number of intervals), rounded to a convenient number (2, 3, 5, 10). Set the intervals so they are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, and start the lowest interval at a multiple of i. Tally and count. Term Definition Example (interval 50–59) Apparent (written) limits The limits as printed. 50 and 59 Exact / real limits The true boundaries, extending half a unit each way. Used in all computation. 49.5 and 59.5 Class interval (i) Upper real limit − lower real limit. 59.5 − 49.5 = 10 Midpoint (lower limit + upper limit) / 2. Assumed to represent every score in the interval. 54.5 Cumulative frequency (cf) Running total of frequencies up to the top of that interval. – Relative frequency f / N, usually expressed as a proportion or percentage. – 2.2 The graphs Histogram bars touch: the variable is continuous Frequency polygon midpoints joined, anchored to the baseline 50% → median Ogive (cumulative frequency) always S-shaped; read percentiles off it Same grouped frequency distribution, three standard graphs. A bar diagram differs from a histogram in one way: its bars have gaps, because the variable is categorical. The three graphs of a frequency distribution. Graph Built from Used for Distinguishing feature Bar diagram Categories on X, frequency on Y Nominal or ordinal data Bars have gaps between them, because the categories are discrete Histogram Class intervals on X, frequency on Y Continuous, grouped data Bars touch , because the variable is continuous. Area is proportional to frequency Frequency polygon Midpoints joined by straight lines Comparing two or more distributions on one axis Anchored to the baseline at both ends; area under it equals the histogram's area Frequency curve A smoothed frequency polygon Showing the underlying shape Smooth, no corners; the theoretical limit as N → ∞ and i → 0 Ogive (cumulative frequency curve) Cumulative frequency plotted at the upper real limit Reading percentiles and the median straight off the graph Always S-shaped and never decreasing. The score at 50% cumulative frequency is the median Pie chart Proportions as sectors of a circle Parts of a single whole, nominal data Each 1% = 3.6° Stem-and-leaf plot (Tukey) Leading digits as stems, trailing as leaves Small datasets Shows the shape and preserves every original value Box plot (Tukey) Five-number summary Comparing groups, spotting outliers and skew Built entirely from ranks, so extreme scores cannot distort it Scatterplot / scattergram Paired X and Y values as points Correlation and regression The only honest way to see a relationship before computing r Lower whisker Q1 − 1.5×IQR Q1 (25th %ile) Median (Q2) Q3 (75th %ile) Upper whisker Q3 + 1.5×IQR Outliers Interquartile range, IQR = Q3 − Q1 (semi-interquartile range or quartile deviation Q = IQR/2) Tukey's box-and-whisker plot. Everything in it is a rank statistic, so it is unaffected by extreme scores , that is why it is paired with the median, not the mean. Box plot (John Tukey, 1977): the five-number summary drawn. Reading a box plot for skew: if the median line sits nearer the bottom of the box and the upper whisker is longer, the distribution is positively skewed. Nearer the top with a longer lower whisker means negative skew. A centred median with equal whiskers means symmetry. 3 Central tendency A measure of central tendency is a single value that best represents the whole distribution: the point around which the scores cluster. There are three you must know cold, and two more worth naming. 3.1 The mean (arithmetic average) Definition: the sum of all scores divided by the number of scores. The balance point of the distribution. Formulas. Ungrouped sample mean: M = ΣX / n . Population mean: μ = ΣX / N . Grouped data: M = ΣfXᵐ / N , where Xᵐ is the midpoint of each interval and f its frequency. Assumed-mean (short) method: M = A + (Σfd / N) × i , where A is any assumed mean, d = (Xᵐ − A)/i, and i is the class interval. Worked example Scores: 4, 7, 7, 9, 13. ΣX = 40, n = 5, so M = 40 / 5 = 8 . The six mathematical properties of the mean (each one is an exam item) The sum of deviations about the mean is exactly zero: Σ(X − M) = 0. This is what "balance point" means, and it is why you must square deviations to get a usable measure of spread. The sum of squared deviations about the mean is a minimum: Σ(X − M)² is smaller than Σ(X − any other value)². This is the least squares property , and it is the reason regression, ANOVA and the variance are all built on the mean. Adding a constant c to every score adds c to the mean. Multiplying every score by c multiplies the mean by c. The mean is affected by every single score , so one extreme score moves it. It is not resistant. The mean of a combined group is the weighted mean: Mᵗ = (n₁M₁ + n₂M₂) / (n₁ + n₂). The mean is the most reliable measure across repeated samples , that is, it has the smallest standard error, which is why inferential statistics is built on it. Trap: the mean cannot be computed from an open-ended distribution ("60 and above"), because the top interval has no midpoint. In that situation you must use the median. 3.2 The median Definition: the value that divides the ordered distribution into two equal halves. The 50th percentile, the 2nd quartile, the 5th decile. Formulas. Ungrouped, n odd: the ((n+1)/2)th score. Ungrouped, n even: the mean of the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th scores. Grouped: Md = L + [(N/2 − cf) / f] × i , where L is the exact lower limit of the median class, cf the cumulative frequency below it, f the frequency of the median class and i the interval width. Worked example Scores 4, 7, 7, 9, 13 (n = 5, odd): the (5+1)/2 = 3rd score, so Md = 7 . Add a sixth score of 40: ordered 4, 7, 7, 9, 13, 40; median = (7 + 9)/2 = 8 , while the mean jumps from 8 to 13.3. That single comparison is the whole argument for the median. Properties The sum of absolute deviations from the median is a minimum: Σ|X − Md| is smaller than about any other point. (The mean minimises squared deviations; the median minimises absolute ones.) It is a positional average, so it is unaffected by extreme scores : it is robust or resistant. It can be computed for open-ended distributions and for ordinal data. It cannot be manipulated algebraically the way the mean can, so it is not used in inferential statistics. 3.3 The mode Definition: the most frequently occurring score. The point of maximum density. Grouped formula (crude vs. exact). Crude mode = midpoint of the interval with the highest frequency. Exact (King's) formula: Mo = L + [(f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × i . Empirical relation for a moderately skewed distribution (Karl Pearson): Mo = 3Md − 2M , equivalently M − Mo = 3(M − Md) . A distribution can have no mode, one mode ( unimodal ), two ( bimodal ), or many ( multimodal ). A bimodal distribution usually means two different populations have been pooled, and that is a substantive finding, not a nuisance. It is the only measure of central tendency usable with nominal data. It is the least stable across samples and the least used inferentially. A rectangular or uniform distribution has no mode at all. 3.4 Choosing between them Use the... When Because Mean Data are interval or ratio, distribution roughly symmetrical, and you intend to do further statistics on it Most reliable, uses all the data, algebraically tractable, required by t, ANOVA and regression Median Distribution is skewed, there are outliers, the distribution is open-ended, or the data are ordinal Resistant to extreme scores; still meaningful when the mean is misleading Mode Data are nominal, or you specifically want the most typical or most common case The only legal option at nominal level; identifies the actual peak Classic applied example: income. Income distributions are strongly positively skewed, so the mean income of a country is dragged up by a few very rich people, and the median income is the honest description of the typical person. Same logic for hospital length of stay, reaction times, and number of therapy sessions attended. Two extra means worth naming Geometric mean: the nth root of the product of n scores. Used for rates of change, growth rates and ratio data. GM ≤ AM always. Harmonic mean: n divided by the sum of the reciprocals. Used for averaging rates and, in statistics, for computing the effective sample size in unequal-n ANOVA and post hoc tests. HM ≤ GM ≤ AM always. 4 Dispersion Two distributions can have the same mean and be completely different. Central tendency without dispersion is half a description. Measures of dispersion (variability, scatter, spread) tell you how far the scores stray from the centre. 4.1 Range R = highest score − lowest score. Simplest, crudest, and completely determined by the two most extreme scores, which are also the two least reliable ones. Unstable across samples. Useful only as a quick indication. 4.2 Quartile deviation (semi-interquartile range) Q = (Q₃ − Q₁) / 2 , where Q₁ is the 25th percentile and Q₃ the 75th. The interquartile range (IQR) is Q₃ − Q₁; the quartile deviation is half of it. It covers the middle 50% of scores, so it is unaffected by extreme values. It is the partner of the median : report Md and Q together, always. 4.3 Average deviation (mean deviation) AD = Σ|X − M| / N. The average distance of scores from the mean, ignoring sign. Uses all scores, which is a step up from the range, but the absolute-value operator makes it algebraically useless, so it disappeared from inferential statistics. It is minimised when taken about the median , not the mean. 4.4 Variance and standard deviation Definition: the standard deviation is the root-mean-square deviation from the mean. It is, quite literally, the typical distance a score sits from the mean, in the original units. The variance is its square. Formulas. Population variance: σ² = Σ(X − μ)² / N · population SD: σ = √[Σ(X − μ)² / N] Sample variance (unbiased estimate): s² = Σ(X − M)² / (n − 1) · sample SD: s = √[Σ(X − M)² / (n − 1)] Computational (raw-score) form: s² = [ΣX² − (ΣX)²/n] / (n − 1) The numerator Σ(X − M)² has its own name: the sum of squares (SS) . Remember that, because the whole of ANOVA is bookkeeping about sums of squares. Worked example Scores 4, 7, 7, 9, 13; M = 8. Deviations: −4, −1, −1, +1, +5. (They sum to 0, as they must.) Squared: 16, 1, 1, 1, 25. SS = 44. s² = 44 / (5 − 1) = 11.0 · s = √11 = 3.32 . If these five were the whole population: σ² = 44/5 = 8.8, σ = 2.97. Note that dividing by n gives a smaller , biased-downward answer. 4.5 Degrees of freedom: why n − 1 The idea. Degrees of freedom is the number of values in a calculation that are free to vary once the constraints are imposed. To compute the sample variance you must first compute M from the same data. That fixes one thing: the deviations must sum to zero. So if n = 5 and you know four of the deviations, the fifth is forced. Only 4 of the 5 are free. Hence df = n − 1. The consequence. Dividing SS by n gives a variance estimate that is systematically too small, because the sample mean is always closer to the sample's own scores than the population mean is. Dividing by n − 1 corrects the downward bias, and is called Bessel's correction . It makes s² an unbiased estimator of σ². Degrees of freedom for every test you will meet One-sample t: df = n − 1 · Independent t: df = n₁ + n₂ − 2 · Paired t: df = n(pairs) − 1 One-way ANOVA: df between = k − 1, df within = N − k, df total = N − 1 Two-way ANOVA: df A = a − 1, df B = b − 1, df A×B = (a−1)(b−1), df within = N − ab Repeated measures: df treatment = k − 1, df subjects = n − 1, df error = (k−1)(n−1) Pearson r significance: df = n − 2 · Simple regression: df = n − 2 · Multiple regression: df = n − k − 1 χ² goodness of fit: df = k − 1 · χ² independence: df = (r − 1)(c − 1) A general principle: df = number of observations − number of parameters you had to estimate from the data. 4.6 Coefficient of variation CV = (s / M) × 100. A relative, unit-free measure of dispersion, so it lets you compare the variability of two things measured in different units (heights in cm vs. weights in kg), or two groups with very different means. It requires a ratio scale with a meaningful zero, so it must not be used on IQ or on Celsius temperature. 4.7 Properties of the standard deviation Adding a constant to every score leaves the SD unchanged (the whole distribution shifts, the spread does not). Multiplying every score by c multiplies the SD by |c| and the variance by c². The SD is in the same units as the original scores; the variance is in squared units. That is why you report SD and analyse variance. Variances add; standard deviations do not. This is the reason ANOVA partitions variance . The SD is the most reliable measure of dispersion across repeated samples, and it is the one used in every inferential formula. It is affected by every score, including extreme ones. On badly skewed data, report the quartile deviation with the median instead. Recap of sections 1 to 4: Stevens's four scales (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio) determine which statistics are legal. A frequency distribution and its graphs (histogram, polygon, ogive, box plot) show you the shape. Central tendency locates it: the mean is the balance point and minimises squared deviations, the median is the 50th percentile and resists outliers, the mode is the peak and the only option at nominal level. Dispersion measures how wide it is: range, quartile deviation (partner of the median), average deviation, and the standard deviation (partner of the mean), whose squared numerator SS and denominator n − 1 are the foundation of everything that follows. 5 Skewness and kurtosis Central tendency gives the location, dispersion gives the width. The third and fourth properties of a distribution are its shape : how lopsided it is (skewness) and how peaked it is (kurtosis). Formally these are the third and fourth moments about the mean; the first moment is zero by definition and the second is the variance. 5.1 Skewness Mo Md M Negative skew Mean < Median < Mode long tail to the LEFT Sk < 0 Mo = Md = M Normal (symmetrical) Mean = Median = Mode no tail Sk = 0 Mo Md M Positive skew Mode < Median < Mean long tail to the RIGHT Sk > 0 Skewness. Mo = mode, Md = median, M = mean. The name of the skew follows the tail, not the hump. The mean is dragged furthest because it is the only one of the three that uses every score's value. Definition: the degree of asymmetry of a distribution. A distribution is skewed when one tail is longer than the other. Positive (right) skew Symmetrical Negative (left) skew Tail Long tail to the right, towards high scores Both tails equal Long tail to the left, towards low scores Order Mode < Median < Mean Mode = Median = Mean Mean < Median < Mode Sk > 0 = 0 < 0 Bulk of scores Low; a few very high scores stretch it out Centred High; a few very low scores stretch it out Test example A very difficult test: most people score low A well-constructed test of average difficulty A very easy test: most people score high (a ceiling effect) Real examples Income, reaction time, number of psychiatric admissions, symptom counts in a normal population Height, IQ in the general population Age at death, scores on a mastery test, life satisfaction in a healthy sample The rule that unlocks every skew item: the skew is named for the tail , not the hump, and the mean is always dragged furthest into the tail , because the mean is the only one of the three that uses each score's actual value. So the mean is always on the tail side of the median, and the mode is always at the hump. Get the mean's position and the whole ordering falls out. Formulas. Pearson's first coefficient of skewness: Sk = (M − Mo) / s Pearson's second coefficient (used when the mode is unstable): Sk = 3(M − Md) / s Bowley's quartile coefficient: Sk = (Q₃ + Q₁ − 2Md) / (Q₃ − Q₁) , bounded between −1 and +1 Moment coefficient: g₁ = m₃ / s³ , where m₃ is the third moment about the mean = Σ(X − M)³/N Interpretation rule of thumb: |Sk| under 0.5 is approximately symmetrical, 0.5 to 1.0 is moderately skewed, over 1.0 is substantially skewed. Another common working rule: skew is a problem if it exceeds twice its own standard error. What causes skew, and what to do about it Floor effect: the measure cannot go below a limit and most people are at it. Produces positive skew. Common with symptom counts and error counts in healthy samples. Ceiling effect: the measure cannot go above a limit and most people are at it. Produces negative skew. Common with easy tests. Selection: studying only the extreme end of a population. Transformations to fix positive skew: square root (mild), logarithm (moderate), reciprocal (severe). For negative skew, reflect the variable first (subtract each score from the maximum + 1), then apply the same transformation. Or switch to a non-parametric test , which does not care about the shape. 5.2 Kurtosis Leptokurtic (Ku > 3, excess > 0) Mesokurtic (normal, Ku = 3, excess = 0) Platykurtic (Ku < 3, excess < 0) All three have the same mean and the same total area. They differ in peakedness and tail weight. Excess kurtosis = Ku − 3. Leptokurtic = tall and thin with fat tails; platykurtic = flat and broad. Kurtosis: the peakedness of the distribution. Definition: the degree of peakedness of a distribution relative to the normal curve, and equivalently the heaviness of its tails. Type Shape Ku (moment) Excess kurtosis (Ku − 3) Tails Leptokurtic Tall, thin, sharply peaked ("lepto" = slender, think a leaping narrow peak) > 3 Positive Fat: more extreme scores than a normal curve Mesokurtic The normal curve itself ("meso" = middle) = 3 0 Normal Platykurtic Flat, broad, blunt ("platy" = flat, think a plateau or a platypus) < 3 Negative Thin: fewer extreme scores; in the limit, a rectangular distribution Formula. Moment coefficient of kurtosis g₂ = m₄ / s⁴ , where m₄ = Σ(X − M)⁴/N. Percentile-based: Ku = Q / (P₉₀ − P₁₀) , which equals 0.263 for a normal curve. Most software reports excess kurtosis, so a printed value of 0 means normal, not flat. Trap: SPSS and most statistical software report excess kurtosis (already minus 3). So a reported kurtosis of 0.00 means mesokurtic (normal), while a reported 3.00 means strongly leptokurtic. Exam questions almost always use the raw moment version where normal = 3. Read the question for which convention it wants. Testing normality formally Test Who Use Read it as Shapiro–Wilk Samuel Shapiro and Martin Wilk, 1965 The most powerful normality test for small to moderate n (under about 50, usable to 2000) Non-significant (p > .05) = normal. You want it to fail Kolmogorov–Smirnov Andrey Kolmogorov and Nikolai Smirnov Compares the sample cumulative distribution to the normal one; better for larger n (with the Lilliefors correction) Non-significant = normal Skewness / kurtosis z tests – Divide the coefficient by its standard error |z| > 1.96 means significant departure at .05 Q–Q plot / P–P plot – Visual check Points on the straight diagonal = normal The large-n paradox.
