Shapiro–Wilk and K–S become so powerful with large n that they flag trivial, harmless departures from normality as significant. With n over about 300, trust the histogram, the Q–Q plot and the skew and kurtosis values instead of the p value, and remember that the central limit theorem has already protected you. 6 The normal curve and standard scores The normal curve was derived by Abraham de Moivre in 1733 as the limit of the binomial, developed by Pierre-Simon Laplace , and applied to measurement error by Carl Friedrich Gauss (hence "Gaussian"). Adolphe Quetelet was the first to apply it to human characteristics ("l'homme moyen", the average man), and Sir Francis Galton brought it into psychology, along with the words "regression", "correlation" and "percentile". 34.13% 34.13% 13.59% 13.59% 2.14% 2.14% 0.13% 0.13% z score -4 -3 -2 -1 0 +1 +2 +3 +4 Percentile 0.003 0.1 2.3 15.9 50 84.1 97.7 99.9 99.997 T score (M50, SD10) 10 20 30 40 50 60 70 80 90 Wechsler IQ (M100, SD15) 40 55 70 85 100 115 130 145 160 Stanford-Binet IQ (SD16) 36 52 68 84 100 116 132 148 164 Stanine (M5, SD2) 1 1 1 3 5 7 9 9 9 68.26% of all cases lie within ±1 SD · 95.44% within ±2 SD · 99.74% within ±3 SD (the ±1.96 SD band is exactly 95%, the ±2.58 SD band exactly 99% , those are the numbers used for confidence intervals) Mean = Median = Mode The normal probability curve. Area under the curve = 1.00. The percentages are fixed properties of the curve, which is why one z score converts into every other standard score. 6.1 Properties of the normal probability curve Bell-shaped and perfectly symmetrical about the mean. Skewness = 0. Mean = median = mode , all at the centre. Asymptotic: the tails approach the X axis but never touch it, so the curve extends from −∞ to +∞. Any score has a non-zero probability. Unimodal , with a single maximum ordinate at the mean. The maximum ordinate is 0.3989 (that is, 1/√2π) when expressed in z units. Mesokurtic: kurtosis = 3, excess kurtosis = 0. Total area under the curve = 1.00 (or 100%), which is why areas can be read as probabilities. Points of inflection (where the curve changes from concave-down to concave-up) lie exactly at ±1σ. It is completely defined by two parameters: μ and σ . Change μ and the curve slides; change σ and it widens or narrows. The standard normal curve is the special case with μ = 0 and σ = 1. The quartile deviation Q = 0.6745σ, and the average deviation AD = 0.7979σ. 6.2 The area percentages (memorise these exactly) Band Area inside Area in each tail μ ± 1σ 68.26% (34.13% each side) 15.87% μ ± 2σ 95.44% (adds 13.59% each side) 2.28% μ ± 3σ 99.74% (adds 2.14% each side) 0.13% μ ± 1.96 σ 95.00% exactly 2.5% (this is where α = .05 two-tailed comes from) μ ± 2.58 σ 99.00% exactly 0.5% (this is where α = .01 two-tailed comes from) μ ± 1.645 σ 90.00% 5% (the one-tailed .05 critical value) The three numbers that carry the most marks: 68 – 95 – 99.7 for 1, 2 and 3 SD, and 1.96 and 2.58 as the exact 95% and 99% cut-offs. Every confidence interval and every z test in the paper comes out of these. 6.3 z scores Definition: a z score expresses a raw score as the number of standard deviations it lies above or below the mean. z = (X − M) / s (sample) · z = (X − μ) / σ (population) · to go back: X = M + z·s Worked example A student scores 85 on a test with M = 70 and s = 10. z = (85 − 70)/10 = +1.5 . From the table, the area below z = 1.5 is .9332, so the student is at the 93rd percentile and beat 93% of the group. A second student scores 60: z = −1.0, area below = .1587, so the 16th percentile . Properties of a z distribution The mean of a set of z scores is always 0 and the SD always 1 . Converting to z is a linear transformation. Standardising does not change the shape of the distribution. A skewed distribution converted to z scores is still exactly as skewed. This is the most frequently missed point about z scores. z scores make scores from different tests comparable, which is the whole reason they exist. Roughly 99.7% of z scores fall between −3 and +3. Trap: "z transformation normalises a distribution." False. It standardises it (fixes M = 0, s = 1) but leaves the shape untouched. To actually change the shape into a normal one you need a normalised standard score , which is computed from percentile ranks via the area table, not from the linear z formula. Normalised T scores and stanines are of this second kind. 6.4 The derived standard scores Score Mean SD Formula from z Where you meet it z 0 1 – The base currency of all standard scores T score (McCall) 50 10 T = 50 + 10z MMPI, MCMI, most clinical inventories. Avoids negative numbers and decimals Wechsler IQ (deviation IQ) 100 15 IQ = 100 + 15z WAIS, WISC, WPPSI Stanford–Binet IQ 100 16 IQ = 100 + 16z Stanford–Binet (5th ed. now uses 15) Wechsler subtest scaled score 10 3 = 10 + 3z Individual WAIS/WISC subtests Stanine (standard nine) 5 2 = 5 + 2z, then rounded to 1–9 US school testing. Nine bands, each half an SD wide except the extremes Sten (standard ten) 5.5 2 = 5.5 + 2z Cattell's 16PF CEEB / SAT / GRE 500 100 = 500 + 100z Older SAT and GRE subscales NCE (normal curve equivalent) 50 21.06 = 50 + 21.06z US education, chosen so 1, 50 and 99 match percentiles Conversion recipe. Any standard score converts to any other by going through z. Example: a T score of 70 means z = (70 − 50)/10 = +2.0, so the Wechsler IQ equivalent is 100 + 15(2) = 130 , the percentile is 97.7 , and the stanine is 5 + 2(2) = 9 . That single chain answers a whole family of exam items. Percentile rank is not a standard score Percentiles are ordinal, not interval. A percentile rank says what proportion of the group scored below you. Because scores pile up in the middle of a normal distribution, percentiles are squeezed together at the centre and stretched at the extremes : the difference between the 50th and 55th percentile is a tiny difference in raw score, while the difference between the 94th and 99th is large. So you must not average percentiles or do arithmetic on them. Convert to z first. This is one of the most reliably examined points in the psychometrics section. 7 Probability, sampling and the sampling distribution 7.1 Probability basics Probability p(A) = number of favourable outcomes / total number of equally likely outcomes. Ranges from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). Addition rule (for "or"): mutually exclusive events, p(A or B) = p(A) + p(B). Non-exclusive, p(A or B) = p(A) + p(B) − p(A and B). Multiplication rule (for "and"): independent events, p(A and B) = p(A) × p(B). Dependent, p(A and B) = p(A) × p(B|A). Conditional probability p(A|B): the probability of A given that B has occurred. The basis of Bayes's theorem , and of sensitivity, specificity and predictive value in diagnostic testing. Binomial distribution: the probability distribution of the number of successes in n independent trials each with probability p. Mean = np, variance = npq. As n grows it approaches the normal curve, which is exactly de Moivre's 1733 result. 7.2 Sampling Simple random every case an equal chance Stratified random sample within each stratum Cluster whole intact groups sampled Systematic every kth case from a list Filled = sampled. All four are PROBABILITY methods, so sampling error is calculable. Purposive, quota, snowball, convenience and incidental sampling are NON-probability: cheaper, but no sampling error can be estimated and generalisation is unsafe. The four probability sampling designs. Method How Strength Weakness PROBABILITY sampling: every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection, so sampling error is calculable and generalisation is defensible Simple random Lottery or random-number table; every case has an equal chance Unbiased, the theoretical ideal, the assumption behind every inferential formula Needs a complete sampling frame; may miss small subgroups by chance Stratified random Divide the population into strata (gender, diagnosis, SES), then sample randomly within each. Proportionate or disproportionate More precise than simple random , guarantees representation of every stratum, reduces sampling error You must know the strata in advance Cluster Divide into naturally occurring groups (schools, wards, villages), randomly select whole clusters, study everyone inside Cheap and practical when the population is geographically spread; no full frame needed Largest sampling error of the probability methods, because people within a cluster are alike Systematic Choose a random start, then take every kth case (k = N/n) Simple, spreads the sample evenly through the list Fails badly if the list has a periodicity matching k Multi-stage Cluster sampling applied repeatedly (state → district → school → class) The only feasible design for national surveys Error accumulates at each stage NON-PROBABILITY sampling: selection chance unknown, so sampling error cannot be estimated and inferential statistics are strictly not justified Purposive / judgemental The researcher picks cases judged typical or informative Efficient for expert or rare populations Wide open to researcher bias Quota Fill preset quotas per subgroup, but choose within them non-randomly Gets the demographic profile right cheaply; the non-probability cousin of stratified Selection within quota is biased Snowball / chain referral Participants recruit further participants The standard method for hidden populations: substance users, sex workers, undocumented migrants Heavily networked people are over-represented Convenience / accidental / incidental Whoever is available (the classic undergraduate subject pool) Cheapest and fastest Weakest external validity of all Definitions to be exact about: sampling error is the natural, unavoidable discrepancy between a sample statistic and its population parameter, caused by chance alone; it shrinks as n grows. Sampling bias is a systematic tilt caused by a faulty method; it does not shrink with n, and a bigger biased sample is simply a bigger wrong answer. 7.3 The sampling distribution of the mean This is the pivot of the whole book. Everything inferential rests on one imaginary object. The idea. Take a sample of size n and compute its mean. Put it back, take another sample of size n, compute its mean. Do this endlessly. You now have a distribution, not of raw scores, but of sample means . That is the sampling distribution of the mean . It is theoretical; you never actually build it. But you know its three properties exactly, and that is enough to say how surprising your one real sample is. Its mean equals the population mean: μ M = μ. The sample mean is an unbiased estimator. Its standard deviation is the standard error of the mean: SE M = σ / √n , estimated in practice by s / √n . Its shape approaches normal as n grows, whatever the shape of the parent population. That is the central limit theorem. μ Population (skewed, μ =

title: Systems & Theories of Psychology
text: Systems & Theories of Psychology The whole history of psychology told as a single argument: how the discipline broke away from philosophy in 1879 and then spent a century fighting over one question, what is the right object of study, the mind, behaviour, the whole person, or consciousness itself. This book teaches every major school from the ground up, with the theorists inline, the dates the exam tests, and the traps it sets. Read it top to bottom once to see how each school is a reply to the one before it, then revise off the tables, the red Trap boxes, and the side-by-side comparison at the end. It is the companion notes to the 119-question Systems & Theories mock. In this book Before the schools: roots and the big questions Structuralism (Wundt, Titchener) Functionalism (James, Dewey) Gestalt psychology (Wertheimer, Köhler, Koffka, Lewin) Behaviorism (Watson, Pavlov, Thorndike, Skinner, Bandura) Psychoanalysis and the psychodynamic school (Freud and after) Humanistic and existential psychology (Maslow, Rogers) Cognitive psychology (the cognitive revolution) Indian psychology and Eastern systems The schools side by side: timeline, comparison, and traps 1. Before the Schools: Roots and the Big Questions Psychology did not appear from nowhere in 1879. For more than two thousand years its questions belonged to philosophy , and its tools, later, to physiology . The schools you are about to study are best understood as rival answers to a handful of very old questions that psychology inherited and then tried to settle with experiment. The philosophical inheritance Mind and body — are they two different substances or one? René Descartes' dualism (interactionism via the pineal gland) said two; the monists said one. This is the mind-body problem. Where knowledge comes from — the rationalists (Descartes, Leibniz, Immanuel Kant) held that the mind brings innate structure to experience; the British empiricists ( John Locke's tabula rasa , the blank slate, plus Berkeley, Hume, and the Mills) held that all knowledge is written by experience. The empiricists also gave psychology associationism , the idea that complex ideas are built by associating simple ones, which became the raw material of both structuralism and behaviorism. Nature versus nurture — the same debate in modern dress, still alive in every school. The physiological inheritance In the nineteenth century, physiology made the mind measurable for the first time. Johannes Müller's doctrine of specific nerve energies, Hermann von Helmholtz's measurement of the speed of the nerve impulse and his work on vision and hearing, Ernst Weber and Gustav Fechner's psychophysics (Fechner's 1860 Elements of Psychophysics gave the first true mental measurement, relating stimulus intensity to sensation), and Paul Broca and Carl Wernicke's localisation of speech in the brain all showed that mental events have lawful, measurable physical correlates. Charles Darwin's theory of evolution (1859) supplied the other great engine: it made function and adaptation central and licensed the study of animals, infants, and individual differences (taken up by his cousin Francis Galton , founder of mental testing and the study of individual differences). High-yield Fechner (psychophysics, 1860) and Helmholtz made the mind measurable; Charles Darwin (1859) made it functional and adaptive; Wilhelm Wundt (1879) made it a laboratory science. These four names are the bridge from philosophy to scientific psychology, and they explain why the very first quarrel, structuralism versus functionalism, was about structure versus adaptation. Memory hook Read the schools as a chain of rebellions: Structuralism (study the contents of consciousness) provokes Functionalism (no, study its purpose) and Gestalt (no, study organised wholes); Behaviorism throws consciousness out entirely; Psychoanalysis dives under it to the unconscious; Humanism answers both Sigmund Freud and the behaviorists with the whole, free person; and the Cognitive revolution brings the mind back as an information processor. Indian psychology runs alongside the whole story with a different goal: not explaining the mind but transcending it. 2. Structuralism Psychology as we know it began on a single, much-tested date: 1879 , when Wilhelm Wundt founded the first formal psychology laboratory at the University of Leipzig , Germany. This act is the conventional birth of psychology as an independent science : it stepped out from under philosophy (which had asked about the mind for centuries through reason and argument) and from under physiology (which studied the body but not experience as experience). Wundt's claim was bold: the contents of conscious experience could be studied with the same controlled, measured, repeatable methods that physics and physiology used. He thereby created experimental psychology and trained the first generation of psychologists, many of whom carried the lab model across Europe and to America. Wundt's program was to study the structure of conscious experience : to break down the mind into its basic elements and discover the laws by which they combine. His chosen method was introspection , but a disciplined, laboratory version of it. He distinguished immediate experience (the raw, direct datum of consciousness as it is happening, the proper object of psychology) from mediate experience (experience used as a means to know something else about the outside world, which is what other sciences study). A psychologist, for Wundt, reports the immediate experience itself, not the object it points to. Definition Introspection is the systematic self-observation and reporting of one's own conscious experience (sensations, images, feelings) under controlled conditions. In Wilhelm Wundt's lab it required trained observers giving standardized reports to a measured stimulus, not casual self-reflection. It is a common error to label Wundt a "structuralist." Wundt's own position is better called voluntarism : he held that the mind is active , not a passive mosaic of elements. Through a central process he called apperception , the mind selects, attends to, and creatively organizes elementary contents into a meaningful unified experience, an act of will ( voluntas ). Pure, systematic structuralism , the doctrine that consciousness is to be analyzed into static elements and nothing more, is really the creation of Wundt's student, Edward Bradford Titchener . Beyond his lab method, Wundt's experimental work included mental chronometry : using reaction-time measurements (an idea he took from the astronomer's "personal equation" and from Donders) to time mental operations such as discrimination and choice. Importantly, Wundt did not think introspection could reach the higher mental processes, language, myth, religion, social custom. These, he argued, must be studied historically and culturally in a second great enterprise he called Völkerpsychologie (folk, cultural, or "people's" psychology), to which he devoted ten volumes late in life. Titchener and the systematizing of Structuralism Edward Titchener, an Englishman, took the Leipzig training to Cornell University in the United States, where he coined the term structuralism and radicalized the method into analytic introspection . Trained observers learned to report the raw elements of an experience while strictly avoiding the stimulus error , the mistake of describing the meaningful object ("I see an apple") rather than the bare sensory contents (a red, round, bright patch). For Titchener the mind contained three irreducible elements: Sensations , the elements of perceptions (from sense organs); Images , the elements of ideas (representing experiences not present); Affections , the elements of emotions (feelings such as pleasantness/unpleasantness). Each sensation could be described by its attributes : quality , intensity , duration , and clarity (attensity), with extensity added for some modalities. Titchener also offered a context theory of meaning : meaning is nothing mystical but simply the context of associated sensations and images that a core sensation calls up. The discipline set itself three questions: the what (analyze consciousness into its elements), the how (specify how those elements combine, via the laws of association and synthesis), and the why (explain the experience). Wilhelm Wundt allowed a causal "why," and physiological explanation entered through reaction time; Titchener was stricter, treating physiology only as the parallel substrate and resisting a functional "why." Dimension Wilhelm Wundt E. B. Titchener Place Leipzig, Germany (1879 lab) Cornell, USA School name Voluntarism (often miscalled structuralism) Structuralism (he coined it) View of mind Active; organizes elements via apperception Passive mosaic of elements; pure analysis Introspection Controlled self-observation + reaction time Rigorous analytic introspection; avoid stimulus error Elements Sensations and feelings (tridimensional feeling theory) Sensations, images, affections Higher processes Studied via Völkerpsychologie Largely set aside Trap Do not swap the two men. Wilhelm Wundt = Leipzig, 1879, founder of experimental psychology, a voluntarist . Edward Titchener = Cornell, the man who coined and built structuralism . Exam items deliberately ask "who founded structuralism?" expecting you to wrongly answer Wundt. The system named "structuralism" is Titchener's; Wundt founded scientific psychology. High-yield 1879, Leipzig, Wilhelm Wundt is the single most-tested fact in the entire history-and-systems syllabus. Memorize the trio together: year, place, person. Why Structuralism died Structuralism was attacked and ultimately collapsed for several reasons. Its method was the central weakness: introspection proved unreliable and unreplicable , because different trained labs reported different elements for the same stimulus. The decisive blow was the imageless thought controversy : the Würzburg school under Oswald Külpe reported that thinking can occur without any sensory image, directly contradicting Edward Titchener's claim that every conscious content reduces to sensations and images. Critics also found the school far too narrow : by limiting psychology to the introspection of the normal adult human mind, it excluded animals, children, and the abnormal , and it produced little of practical use, earning the charge of being sterile . When Titchener died in 1927, structuralism essentially died with him, but it had done its historic job: it established psychology as an experimental laboratory science. Memory hook "Wundt Won the lab; Titchener Titled the school." Wundt won psychology its first lab (1879); Titchener gave structuralism its title (and its three elements: Sensations, Images, Affections = "SIA" ). 3. Functionalism While German laboratories dissected consciousness into elements, a very different psychology grew up in the United States as a reaction against structuralism . Where structuralism asked what consciousness is made of, functionalism asked what consciousness is for : what does the mind do , and how does it help the organism survive and adapt? This shift was no accident. The deepest influence was Charles Darwin : if bodily organs evolve because they serve a function in adaptation, then so might mind and consciousness. The practical, problem-solving temper of American life reinforced the move; American psychologists wanted a psychology that worked , one applicable to schools, clinics, and industry. Trap The single most tested contrast in this unit: structuralism studies the WHAT (the structure / contents / elements of consciousness, analysis), whereas functionalism studies the WHY / WHAT-FOR (the function, purpose, and adaptive use of mental processes). Structure vs function; contents vs operations. Do not reverse them. William James, the forerunner William James is called the "father of American psychology." His monumental Principles of Psychology ( 1890 ) framed the questions a whole generation would pursue. James argued that consciousness is not a string of static elements but a stream of consciousness : continuous (no gaps), constantly changing , personal (belonging to a self), and above all selective , attending to some things and ignoring others, which is precisely its adaptive function. Among his lasting ideas are the James-Lange theory of emotion (we feel afraid because we tremble and run; bodily change precedes the felt emotion), his analysis of the self into the I (the knower) and the Me (the known, with its material, social, and spiritual aspects), his classic treatment of habit as the "flywheel of society," and his philosophy of pragmatism (an idea's truth lies in its practical consequences). James, however, founded no formal school; he was more an inspiring precursor than a system-builder, and he largely abandoned psychology for philosophy. The Chicago school, the formal founding Functionalism as an organized movement is usually dated to John Dewey's 1896 paper, "The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology," the field's recognized founding document . Dewey attacked the reflex arc (the stimulus-response unit) for being artificially "chopped up" into separate stimulus, central process, and response. In real behavior, he argued, these form one continuous coordinated act : perception and movement are bound together in a single adaptive circuit, and the "stimulus" and "response" are only roles within an ongoing whole. James Rowland Angell then organized and championed the Chicago school; his 1906 APA presidential address, "The Province of Functional Psychology," laid out its program explicitly. Harvey Carr later consolidated and matured the school. The Columbia school A second center grew at Columbia University, more applied and individual-differences oriented. James McKeen Cattell (who had studied under Wundt yet rejected his approach) pioneered mental tests , in fact coined the term "mental test," and championed the study of individual differences . Robert S. Woodworth developed dynamic psychology and inserted the organism into the equation, expanding S-R into S-O-R (Stimulus-Organism-Response): the organism's drives and state determine the response. Edward L. Thorndike studied animal learning, formulated connectionism and the law of effect (responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in), and in doing so built a clear bridge to behaviorism . Center Key figures Signature contributions Forerunner William James Principles (1890); stream of consciousness; self (I/Me); James-Lange emotion; pragmatism Chicago school John Dewey, J. R. Angell, Harvey Carr Dewey's Reflex Arc (1896, founding paper); Angell's program; mental operations as adaptation Columbia school J. McK. Cattell, R. S. Woodworth, E. L. Thorndike Mental tests / individual differences; dynamic psychology (S-O-R); connectionism / law of effect The functionalist program, taken as a whole, studied mental operations rather than mental contents , treated the mind-body as one functioning whole serving adaptation, and prized individual differences, applied psychology, education (Dewey's lasting influence on schooling), and mental testing . Because it asked what mind is for rather than what it is made of , it had no reason to exclude anyone: it threw psychology's doors open to the study of animals, children, and the abnormal , and to the applied fields, clinical, educational, and industrial psychology, that define so much of the discipline today. High-yield Pin the two anchors: William James = forerunner, Principles of Psychology (1890). John Dewey = "The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology" (1896) is functionalism's founding paper . Chicago = Dewey, Angell, Carr; Columbia = Cattell, Robert Woodworth, Edward Thorndike. Finally, note that functionalism did not "die" the way structuralism did. It had no single dramatic refutation; instead it dissolved into the mainstream of American psychology , becoming so widely accepted that it ceased to be a distinct school. In the process it gave birth to behaviorism (through Thorndike's animal learning and the focus on observable function) and seeded the entire enterprise of applied and clinical psychology . Its very success was its disappearance. Memory hook "Function = For." Functionalism asks what the mind is For , born For -Darwin (adaptation), and is remembered For opening psychology to applied fields. People hook: "James Dreamed, Dewey Arced, Angell Announced" (James inspired, Dewey wrote the Reflex Arc, Angell announced the program). 4. Gestalt Psychology In the opening years of the twentieth century, while Wilhelm Wundt's structuralists were busy dissecting consciousness into sensory elements and the behaviorists were preparing to throw consciousness out altogether, a third movement arose in Germany that rejected both . This was Gestalt psychology . The German word Gestalt has no exact English equivalent: it means roughly "form," "shape," "configuration," or "organized whole." The Gestaltists argued that the mind does not register a mosaic of separate sensations that are later glued together; rather, it grasps organized wholes directly and immediately. Their rallying cry was that the whole is different from the sum of its parts . Definition Gestalt: an organized whole or configuration whose properties cannot be derived from, or predicted by, the properties of its isolated parts. The melody survives transposition to a new key even though every individual note has changed: the form, not the elements, is what we perceive. A note of precision that examiners love: the popular phrase "the whole is greater than the sum of its parts" is a loose rendering. The more faithful translation of Wertheimer's claim is that the whole is different from the sum of its parts. The organized whole possesses emergent properties, qualities that simply do not exist at the level of the components and therefore cannot be predicted by adding them up. The founding demonstration: the phi phenomenon (1912) The movement is conventionally dated to 1912, when Max Wertheimer published his study of apparent motion , the effect he labelled the phi phenomenon . The set-up is simple: two stationary lights are flashed in rapid succession, first one and then, a fraction of a second later, the other. What the observer sees is not two separate flashes but a single light moving from the first position to the second (this is the same principle that makes a strip of still film frames look like continuous motion). The crucial point is that the motion exists only in the perceived whole . There is no movement in either light considered alone; movement is a property of the configuration. Elementism, which insists that experience is built up from independent sensory atoms, cannot account for this. Wertheimer's collaborators and observers in these experiments were Wolfgang Köhler and Kurt Koffka , and the three became the founders of the school. High-yield Phi phenomenon, Max Wertheimer, 1912 is the founding study of Gestalt psychology. Apparent motion proves that the organized whole has properties (here, motion) not present in its parts, refuting structuralist elementism. The three founders Founder Signature contribution Max Wertheimer Founder of the school; the phi phenomenon (1912); later productive thinking (genuine, insightful problem-solving versus blind reproduction of memorized routines). Wolfgang Köhler Insight learning in chimpanzees, reported in The Mentality of Apes (1925); the concept of isomorphism ; carried Gestalt psychology to the United States. Kurt Koffka Chief popularizer in the English-speaking world; Principles of Gestalt Psychology (1935); applied Gestalt ideas to developmental psychology. The laws of perceptual organization The Gestaltists' most enduring legacy is their catalogue of the principles by which the perceptual system organizes a raw sensory field into coherent objects and groups. Presiding over all of them is the law of Prägnanz . Definition Prägnanz (the "law of good figure," "law of simplicity," or minimum principle ): of all the ways a stimulus could be organized, we perceive the one that is the simplest, most stable, most regular, and most economical. It is the master principle from which the other laws follow. Law / principle What it says Everyday example Prägnanz (good figure) We adopt the simplest, most regular, most stable organization available. Overlapping rings are seen as whole circles, not odd arcs. Proximity Elements close together are grouped as a unit. oo oo oo reads as three pairs, not six dots. Similarity Elements that look alike are grouped together. Rows of crosses among circles are seen as belonging together. Continuity (good continuation) We prefer smooth, continuous contours over abrupt changes. Two crossing lines are seen as two straight lines, not four bent segments. Closure We mentally fill in gaps to perceive a complete, whole figure. A broken circle is still read as a circle. Common fate Elements that move together are grouped together. A flock of birds turning in unison is seen as one flock. Figure-ground The field splits into a bounded "figure" standing out against a formless "ground." The Rubin vase/faces reversible image. Symmetry / good form Symmetrical, balanced regions are perceived as figures and as wholes. Symmetrical bracket pairs { } group as one unit. Definition Figure-ground organization: the most basic act of perceptual segregation, in which one part of the field is seen as a distinct, contoured object (the figure ) and the rest recedes into an undifferentiated background (the ground ). In reversible figures the two can spontaneously swap. Memory hook For the grouping laws remember "Pretty Cats See Clearly, Fully Content" = P roximity, C ontinuity, S imilarity, C losure, F igure-ground, C ommon fate. And keep Prägnanz at the top as the " P resident" of all the laws: simplicity rules. Insight learning (Köhler) Wolfgang Köhler, marooned on Tenerife during the First World War, studied chimpanzees, the most famous of whom was named Sultan . Placed in a cage with a banana hung out of reach and some boxes and sticks lying about, Sultan would, after a period of apparent contemplation, suddenly stack the boxes or fit two sticks together to rake in the fruit. Köhler called this insight : a sudden reorganization of the perceptual field in which the relations among the elements abruptly fall into place, the famous "aha!" moment. Crucially, once achieved, the solution was retained and could be transferred to new but structurally similar problems. Trap Wolfgang Köhler's insight learning vs. Edward Thorndike's trial-and-error. Thorndike's cats in the puzzle box learned gradually and blindly , by random fumbling that was slowly stamped in by reward (a smooth learning curve). Köhler's apes solved problems suddenly and intelligently , by grasping relationships (an abrupt, all-or-none jump). Insight = perceptual reorganization, not incremental association. Exam items love to swap these two. Isomorphism To explain why we perceive organized wholes, Wolfgang Köhler proposed the doctrine of psychophysical isomorphism : conscious perceptual experience and the underlying processes in the brain share the same structural form . The organization we experience is not imposed on a chaotic brain; it mirrors a corresponding organization in the cortical "field." Perceived form and neural form are, in this sense, isomorphic (literally "same shape"). Kurt Lewin: field theory, the bridge to social psychology Kurt Lewin extended the Gestalt insight, that elements are governed by the whole field they belong to, from perception to motivation, personality, and social behavior . He is the bridge from Gestalt perception to modern social and organizational psychology. His central construct was the life space : the totality of all the facts (needs, goals, barriers, possibilities) that influence a person at a given moment. From this came his celebrated formula: High-yield B = f(P, E) — behavior is a function of the person and the environment , taken together as an interacting field. Memorize the formula exactly. Tension systems: an unmet goal creates a state of psychological tension that presses toward resolution. The Zeigarnik effect: Lewin's student Bluma Zeigarnik showed that uncompleted tasks are remembered better than completed ones, because the unresolved tension system keeps them active in memory. Conflict types: approach-approach (two desirable goals), avoidance-avoidance (two undesirable options, "between a rock and a hard place"), and approach-avoidance (one goal with both attractive and repellent features). Group dynamics and action research: Lewin founded the systematic study of groups and championed research conducted in real-world settings to produce social change, summed up in his maxim, "There is nothing so practical as a good theory." Legacy Gestalt psychology founded the scientific study of perceptual organization and its laws are still taught essentially intact. Its emphasis on holistic mental structure fed directly into the rise of cognitive psychology and into research on problem-solving and insight . Through Lewin it seeded much of modern social and organizational psychology . Trap Do not confuse the Gestalt psychology of Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Köhler, and Kurt Koffka (a school of perception and cognition ) with Fritz Perls' Gestalt therapy (a humanistic-existential psychotherapy of the here-and-now, the empty chair, awareness). They share only the word "gestalt" and a loose holistic spirit. Perls was not one of the founders, and Gestalt therapy is not an application of the laws of perceptual organization. 5. Behaviorism Behaviorism dominated American psychology from roughly 1913 to the 1960s and remains, even now, the single most heavily tested school on Indian clinical entrances. It grew out of a frustration with structuralism and its method of introspection , which produced unreliable, unverifiable reports of private experience. The behaviorists' radical answer was to throw out the mind altogether as a subject matter and rebuild psychology as an objective natural science of behavior , governed by laws of learning that could be observed in a laboratory and applied to predict and control what organisms do. Definition Behaviorism is the school holding that psychology should study only observable, measurable behavior (stimulus-response relations), not the mind or consciousness. Its goal is to predict and control behavior, and its core mechanism is learning through conditioning . 5.1 The behaviorist manifesto: John B. Watson John B. Watson (1878-1958) is the founder of behaviorism as a formal school. In 1913 he published "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It" in Psychological Review , a paper so programmatic it is simply called the "Behaviorist Manifesto." Watson declared that psychology is "a purely objective experimental branch of natural science," whose theoretical goal is the prediction and control of behavior . He rejected consciousness, mental states, and introspection as outside the bounds of science, and demanded that psychology deal only in observable stimuli and responses. Watson's stance is best labelled methodological behaviorism : he did not deny that inner events exist, but insisted they are scientifically useless because they cannot be publicly observed. He was a fierce environmentalist , denying that heredity shapes personality and ability. His most quoted line captures this radical environmentalism: "Give me a dozen healthy infants, well-formed, and my own specified world to bring them up in and I'll guarantee to take any one at random and train him to become any type of specialist I might select... regardless of his talents, penchants, tendencies, abilities, vocations, and race of his ancestors." In 1920, with his student and later wife Rosalie Rayner , Watson ran the famous "Little Albert" experiment . A roughly 11-month-old infant ("Albert B.") was shown a white rat (initially a neutral stimulus he did not fear). Each time he reached for it, the experimenters struck a steel bar behind his head, producing a loud, frightening noise (UCS). After repeated pairings, Albert came to fear the white rat alone (a conditioned emotional response ), and the fear generalized to other furry white objects, a rabbit, a dog, cotton wool, even a Santa Claus mask. The study demonstrated that emotions like fear can be classically conditioned in humans, anchoring Watson's environmentalism. (It is also a standard ethics case study: there was no evidence Albert's fear was ever extinguished.) Watson left academia in 1920 after his affair with Rayner became a scandal and went on to a successful career in advertising , applying conditioning principles to consumer behavior. High-yield Three dates examiners love: Watson's 1913 manifesto ("Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It"), Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning (work from the late 1890s-1900s), and Little Albert 1920 (John B. Watson & Rosalie Rayner). Watson = founder of behaviorism; goal = prediction and control . 5.2 Classical conditioning: Ivan Pavlov Ivan Pavlov (1849-1936) was a Russian physiologist who won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on digestion , not for psychology. While studying salivation in dogs, he noticed they began to salivate before food touched their mouths, at the sight of the feeder or the sound of footsteps. He called these anticipatory responses "psychic secretions" and turned to studying them systematically, founding classical (Pavlovian/respondent) conditioning . In classical conditioning a neutral stimulus (a bell, originally producing no salivation) is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus (food) that automatically triggers an unconditioned response (salivation). After enough pairings, the bell alone elicits salivation, now a conditioned response to a conditioned stimulus . Element Abbreviation In Pavlov's dog Unconditioned stimulus UCS Food (meat powder) Unconditioned response UCR Salivation to food (reflexive, unlearned) Conditioned stimulus CS Bell (after pairing with food) Conditioned response CR Salivation to the bell alone (learned) Several lawful phenomena follow: Acquisition — the building of the CS-CR association across pairings. Learning is strongest when the CS slightly precedes the UCS ( forward/delayed conditioning ); contiguity (close timing of CS and UCS) is essential, and short CS-UCS intervals work best. Extinction — presenting the CS repeatedly without the UCS weakens and eventually abolishes the CR. Spontaneous recovery — after extinction and a rest interval, the CR reappears (weakly) when the CS is presented, showing extinction suppresses rather than erases learning. Generalization — stimuli similar to the CS (a higher-pitched bell) also evoke the CR. Discrimination — the organism learns to respond only to the specific CS and not to similar stimuli (the opposite of generalization). Higher-order (second-order) conditioning — a well-established CS can itself act like a UCS to condition a new neutral stimulus (e.g., pairing a light with the already-conditioned bell so the light alone evokes salivation). Watson explicitly built on Pavlov : Little Albert is classical conditioning of a fear response in a human, with the loud noise as UCS and the rat as CS. 5.3 Edwin Guthrie: contiguity and one-trial learning Edwin Guthrie (1886-1959) offered the most economical learning theory: the law of contiguity . A stimulus pattern that accompanies a response will, on its recurrence, tend to be followed by that response, no reinforcement required. Crucially, Guthrie argued the full-strength S-R bond is formed in a single pairing ( one-trial learning ); apparent gradual learning is just the building up of many independent stimulus-response connections. His practical legacy is the idea that breaking a habit means attaching the old cue to a new, incompatible response. 5.4 Edward Thorndike: connectionism and the Law of Effect Edward L. Thorndike (1874-1949) studied how animals learn by placing hungry cats in a puzzle box from which they had to escape (by pressing a lever or pulling a loop) to reach food. Cats did not "reason" their way out; they thrashed about until they stumbled on the correct response, and over trials the time to escape steadily fell. He called this trial-and-error learning and his theory connectionism , because learning is the strengthening of bonds (connections) between stimuli and responses. Thorndike's laws: Law of Effect — responses followed by a satisfying state of affairs are "stamped in" (strengthened); responses followed by discomfort are "stamped out." This is the cornerstone law. Law of Exercise — connections are strengthened by use (repetition) and weakened by disuse. (He later softened this, recognising practice without feedback does little.) Law of Readiness — learning depends on the organism's preparedness to act; acting when ready is satisfying, being blocked is annoying. High-yield Thorndike's Law of Effect is the direct conceptual ancestor of B. F. Skinner's operant conditioning. "Satisfying consequences strengthen behavior" (Thorndike) becomes "reinforcement increases behavior" (Skinner). Note that Edward Thorndike is sometimes classified under functionalism rather than behaviorism, because of his focus on the adaptive function of learning. 5.5 B. F. Skinner: radical behaviorism and operant conditioning B. F. Skinner (1904-1990) is the most influential behaviorist. Unlike John B. Watson, his radical behaviorism did not deny private events (thoughts, feelings): it accepts they exist but treats them as behavior to be explained, never as inner causes of action. Causes always lie in the environment and the organism's reinforcement history. Skinner distinguished respondent behavior (reflexive, Pavlovian, elicited by stimuli) from operant behavior, which is emitted and "operates on" the environment, controlled by its consequences . He invented the operant chamber ("Skinner box") , in which a rat presses a lever or a pigeon pecks a key to obtain food. The unit of analysis is the three-term contingency or A-B-C : an Antecedent (discriminative stimulus that signals availability of reinforcement), the Behavior (response), and the Consequence (reinforcer or punisher) that changes the future probability of that behavior. Definition Reinforcement = any consequence that increases the future probability of the behavior it follows. Punishment = any consequence that decreases it. "Positive" and "negative" do not mean good/bad: positive = add a stimulus , negative = remove a stimulus . Positive (add stimulus) Negative (remove stimulus) Reinforcement (behavior up) Positive reinforcement: add something pleasant. Give a child praise/candy for studying, studying increases. Negative reinforcement: remove something aversive. Take a painkiller and the headache stops, pill-taking increases. (Seatbelt buzzer stops when you buckle up.) Punishment (behavior down) Positive punishment: add something aversive. A spanking or a scolding for misbehaving, misbehavior decreases. Negative punishment (omission): remove something pleasant. Take away phone/TV privileges for breaking curfew, curfew-breaking decreases. Trap Negative reinforcement is NOT punishment. This is the most-missed item on these exams. Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus and therefore increases behavior (escape/avoidance). Punishment decreases behavior. If the behavior goes up, it is reinforcement, full stop, regardless of "negative." Memory hook Two questions decode the 2x2 every time: (1) Did the behavior go UP or DOWN? Up = Reinforcement, Down = Punishment. (2) Was something ADDED or TAKEN AWAY? Added = Positive, Removed = Negative. Solve them in that order and you can never confuse the cells. More Skinnerian machinery: Primary vs secondary reinforcers — primary reinforcers satisfy biological needs innately (food, water, warmth); secondary (conditioned) reinforcers acquire their power by association (money, tokens, grades, praise). Shaping (successive approximation) — reinforcing closer and closer approximations to a target behavior to build complex responses that would never occur spontaneously. Schedules of reinforcement — the rule for when responses are reinforced. Continuous reinforcement produces fast learning but rapid extinction; partial/intermittent schedules produce learning that is more resistant to extinction. Schedule Rule Response pattern Everyday example Fixed-ratio (FR) Reinforce after a set number of responses High rate; brief post-reinforcement pause Piece-rate pay (every 10 items) Variable-ratio (VR) Reinforce after a varying, unpredictable number of responses Highest, steadiest rate; most resistant to extinction Slot machines, gambling Fixed-interval (FI) Reinforce first response after a set time "Scalloped" pattern; responding rises near deadline Weekly paycheck; studying before a scheduled exam Variable-interval (VI) Reinforce first response after a varying time Slow, steady, stable rate Checking email; pop quizzes High-yield Variable-ratio (VR) produces the highest, most stable response rate and is the most resistant to extinction , which is exactly why gambling is so addictive. Mnemonic: ratio schedules give the higher response rates (you control the count), and variable schedules resist extinction (you never know when the next reward comes, so you keep going). Skinner's principles powered behavior modification : the token economy (institutional patients earn tokens, secondary reinforcers, for target behaviors, later exchanged for privileges), programmed instruction, and a wide range of clinical and educational interventions. In 1957 he published Verbal Behavior , arguing language too is learned operant behavior. In 1959 Noam Chomsky's scathing review demolished it, arguing the speed and generativity of children's language acquisition could not be explained by reinforcement and required innate cognitive structures. That critique is widely cited as a turning point that helped launch the cognitive revolution . 5.6 Neo-behaviorism: the S-O-R turn The neo-behaviorists kept the objective method but inserted the Organism (O) between Stimulus and Response, allowing unobservable intervening variables as theoretical constructs (S-O-R rather than bare S-R). Clark Hull (1884-1952) built a formal hypothetico-deductive system of learning expressed in equations. His drive-reduction theory held that learning occurs when a response reduces a biological drive (hunger, thirst), restoring homeostasis. His central formula, sEr (reaction potential) = sHr (habit strength) x D (drive) and further terms, treats habit strength and drive as intervening variables linking stimulus to response. Edward Tolman (1886-1959) championed purposive (or cognitive) behaviorism . His rats in mazes showed latent learning : rats that explored a maze without reward still learned its layout, showing a sudden drop in errors once reward was introduced, proving learning had occurred without reinforcement. He argued animals build internal cognitive maps of their environment. Tolman effectively cracked open the "black box," reintroducing internal representation and purpose, and prefigured cognitive psychology. Kenneth Spence (1907-1967), Hull's foremost collaborator, refined the Hull-Spence theory, especially work on the role of incentive motivation ( K ) and discrimination learning. 5.7 Social learning: Albert Bandura, the bridge to cognitive Albert Bandura (1925-2021) showed that much learning occurs without direct reinforcement , through observation and modeling . In the Bobo doll experiment (1961), children who watched an adult aggressively beat an inflatable Bobo doll later imitated that aggression, while those who saw a non-aggressive model did not. Children also learned vicariously : when a model was rewarded for aggression, i

title: Systems & Theories — Answer Explanations
text: Systems & Theories — Answer Explanations Every one of the 119 questions from the Systems & Theories mock, written out the way the test screen shows them: the correct answer and the theorist it belongs to up top, the concept built from scratch below, then each wrong option nailed to whose idea it actually is. Read it straight through to lock in who owns what, or jump to a school and skim the answer lines. Companion to the Systems & Theories teaching book and the mock itself. In this book History & Schools (19) Psychodynamic (36) Behavioural / Learning (13) Humanistic / Gestalt (21) Cognitive / Consciousness (12) Indian Psychology (18) History & Schools Q1 What do Herman Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud share in common? ✓ Answer: D · (a) and (c) The answer is option (d) because the question rewards seeing that two separate claims are each fully true of all three men, and stopping at one undersells what they share. To place this historically, all three belong to the late nineteenth-century emergence of psychology as a science, the era when the study of mind broke away from pure philosophy and physiology and began to use real methods. Hermann Ebbinghaus (Germany, memory research), Francis Galton (England, differential psychology), and Sigmund Freud (Austria, psychoanalysis) worked in different countries and traditions and never collaborated, yet each launched a brand-new line of inquiry on his own initiative, which is exactly what option (a) means by independent pioneers. None of them merely speculated; each invented a fresh observational method to make some part of the mind studyable, which is what option (c) adds. Ebbinghaus created the nonsense-syllable technique and used himself as sole subject to chart the forgetting curve , bringing the experimental rigour of Wilhelm Wundt 's new science to the higher process of memory. Galton pioneered the measurement of individual differences , devising questionnaires, twin studies, mental tests, and the statistical idea of correlation , seeding psychometrics and behaviour genetics. Freud developed clinical tools like free association and dream interpretation to probe the unconscious, opening the dynamic/clinical tradition that ran parallel to the academic labs. Because both the pioneer claim and the novel-method claim hold for every one of the three, the combined option is correct. Lock in: when two single options are each independently true and a 'both' choice exists, the 'both' choice usually wins, so never stop at the first correct-looking answer. Panwar key: Herman Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud, all 3 of them worked independently and were pioneers in the field of psychology. And they developed novel observational methods to study how the mind works. Why the other options are traps A. Each of them worked independently and were pioneers in the field of psychology Option (a) names their independent, pioneering originality, which is genuinely true of Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud, so it tempts you to stop early. But it captures only half of what they share and ignores option (c)'s equally true point that each invented a new observational method. Because (c) is also correct, the combined choice (d) is the complete answer, making (a) true but incomplete. B. Each of them founded a formal psychology laboratory Founding a formal psychology laboratory belongs to Wilhelm Wundt , who opened the first lab at Leipzig in 1879 ; it is the standard distractor in any history item about early figures. None of these three founded such a lab: Hermann Ebbinghaus did self-experiments, Galton ran an anthropometric measurement station, and Sigmund Freud worked clinically. So this statement is simply false of all three and cannot be what they share. C. Each of them developed novel observational methods to study how the mind works Option (c), the invention of novel observational methods, is fully true of all three (nonsense syllables, correlation, free association), so it is tempting in its own right. The catch is that it describes only their methodological side and leaves out option (a)'s equally true point about independent pioneering. Since both single claims hold, the combined option (d) is the better and more complete answer. Q2 In which year the first mental hospital in the USA was opened? ✓ Answer: B · 1753 The answer is 1753 because that is when the Pennsylvania Hospital in Philadelphia, the first hospital in the United States, opened its doors and, crucially, admitted patients with mental illness from the very start. To see why this date matters in the history of psychology, separate a general hospital from a dedicated asylum, and place the event on the historical arc of how society moved from neglect toward treatment of the mentally ill. In the colonial era, before any organised system of care, people with mental illness were typically confined at home, jailed, or left to wander; there was no public institution to receive them, and explanations of madness were still heavily moral and supernatural rather than medical. The 1753 opening sits at the very beginning of the institutional and moral-treatment story that would later run through Philippe Pinel 'unchaining' patients in France, William Tuke 's York Retreat in England, and Dorothea Dix 's mid-nineteenth-century reform crusade across America. The Pennsylvania Hospital, championed by Benjamin Franklin and physician Thomas Bond , was founded to care for the sick poor of all kinds, and among its earliest patients were several suffering from mental illness. That detail is the whole point: organised institutional care for the mentally ill in America began not inside a separate asylum but within this general hospital in 1753. Purpose-built facilities such as the Williamsburg asylum (1773), often called the first American hospital devoted solely to the mentally ill, came later, but the recognised starting line for organised treatment is the 1753 opening. Lock in the pairing: first U.S. hospital equals 1753, Philadelphia, with mental patients among its first admissions, so the answer is this general hospital and not the later dedicated asylums. Panwar key: The first hospital in the U.S. opened its doors in 1753 in Philadelphia. While it treated a variety of patients, six of its first patients suffered from mental illness. Why the other options are traps A. 1693 1693 is far too early; the American colonies had no public hospital of any kind at that point, and the care of the mentally ill was still entirely informal (home confinement or jail). The number is a near-miss decoy designed to tempt anyone who only half-remembers a late-seventeenth-century date, but no American mental hospital existed then. C. 1793 1793 is a real and memorable Philadelphia date, but it marks the catastrophic yellow-fever epidemic that devastated the city, not the founding of any hospital. The question pairs the right city with the wrong event to bait you. The Pennsylvania Hospital had already been open for forty years by 1793, so this cannot be the founding year. D. 1547 1547 is the year London's Bethlem Hospital (the infamous 'Bedlam') was granted to the City and became a dedicated asylum, in England , not the USA. It is a tempting distractor because Bethlem is the most famous early institution for the insane. But the question asks specifically about the first American mental hospital, so an English date is wrong by country. Q3 Who established the first laboratory for experimental study of psychology? ✓ Answer: C · Wundt The answer is Wundt because Wilhelm Wundt opened the first laboratory devoted to the experimental study of psychology, and that single act is conventionally treated as the founding moment of psychology as an independent science. To grasp why this is such a landmark, place it on the historical arc. Before 1879 the study of the mind belonged to two parent disciplines: philosophy , which reasoned about mind from the armchair, and physiology , which studied the body's sensory and nervous machinery (figures like Weber, Fechner and Helmholtz). There was no separate discipline that examined mental processes through controlled experiment. Wundt fused the two when he founded his laboratory at the University of Leipzig in 1879 , Germany, deliberately creating a space where conscious experience could be measured under controlled conditions, for instance by timing reactions to stimuli (mental chronometry) and training observers to report their sensations through introspection . Because he founded both the lab and a formal research programme with students (Edward Titchener, Hall, Cattell and others) who then carried the method across Europe and America, Wundt is called the father of experimental psychology , and the school he launched is structuralism (later systematised by his pupil Titchener). He thus sits at the precise hinge between the pre-scientific philosophy of mind that came before and the procession of modern schools that followed: structuralism, then functionalism, then behaviourism, Gestalt, psychoanalysis and the cognitive era. Every later force in the history of psychology defines itself in part by how it agrees with or revolts against the experimental, consciousness-studying programme Wundt began in that room in Leipzig. The fact to lock in is the trio of name, year and place: Wundt, 1879, Leipzig. If a question asks who founded the first psychology laboratory or who made psychology an experimental science, the answer is Wundt, not the physiologists or differential-psychology figures who preceded or accompanied him. Panwar key: Wilhelm Wundt opened the first laboratory of psychology in 1879, in Leipzig, Germany. Why the other options are traps A. Galton Francis Galton belongs to the same founding era and did pioneer mental testing, individual differences, and his 'anthropometric laboratory' for measuring people, which makes 'laboratory' a tempting word-match. But Galton's was a measurement station for collecting data on the public, not a research laboratory for the controlled experimental study of consciousness, and it came after Leipzig. He did not found experimental psychology. B. Weber Ernst Weber was a physiologist whose work on sensory thresholds (Weber's law, the just-noticeable difference) directly fed into the new experimental psychology, so he is a plausible-sounding 'early scientist of the mind'. However, Weber studied sensation as physiology and founded no psychology laboratory; he is a precursor to Wilhelm Wundt, not the founder of the discipline's first lab. D. Jung Carl Jung is a famous name in psychology, which makes him an easy lure, but he was a psychoanalyst who founded analytical psychology in the early twentieth century. He was born in 1875, only four years before the Leipzig lab opened, worked in the clinical/depth tradition rather than the experimental one, and founded no early experimental laboratory. Q4 American Psychological Association (APA) was founded in: ✓ Answer: A · 1892 The answer is 1892 because the American Psychological Association was founded in July of that year, and the place and people are worth fixing alongside the date. The APA was organised at Clark University in Worcester, Massachusetts, when a small group of psychologists met to create a national society to advance psychology as a science and profession. Its driving force and first president was G. Stanley Hall , himself a giant of early American psychology: he studied in Wundt's Leipzig tradition, is credited with opening one of the first U.S. psychology laboratories (at Johns Hopkins), founded the first American psychology journal, and trained many of the country's earliest psychologists, which is why he was the natural figure to convene the new body. To place this historically, the 1890s were the moment American psychology came of age and detached itself from philosophy and physiology. The discipline born in Wundt's Leipzig laboratory in 1879 had crossed the Atlantic; William James had just published his landmark Principles of Psychology (1890); structuralism and the emerging functionalism were competing for direction; laboratories were multiplying on American campuses; and practitioners needed a shared organisation for standards, communication and annual meetings. The APA filled exactly that role and has since grown into the largest professional psychology body in the world, marking the professional, institutional phase of psychology's becoming a science. The cluster to lock in is: APA, 1892, Clark University, G. Stanley Hall as first president. Watch the year carefully, because the 1892 founding is easy to blur with the dates of subsequent annual meetings, the first formal convention, or later expansions; the foundational year this question tests is 1892. Panwar key: The American Psychological Association was formed in July 1892 at Clark University, Worcester, Massachusetts, United States. Why the other options are traps B. 1893 1893 is a deliberate off-by-one decoy. It sits right next to the true founding year and is exactly the kind of near-miss that catches a candidate who recalls 'early 1890s' but not the precise digit. It is not the APA's founding year, which was 1892; treat the one-year gap as the whole trap. C. 1896 1896 is a genuinely important date in American psychology, which is what makes it dangerous: it is the year Lightner Witmer opened the first psychological clinic (at the University of Pennsylvania), launching clinical psychology. The question is counting on you to confuse two different 'firsts'. It is not when the APA was founded, so it is wrong here. D. 1897 1897 postdates the APA's 1892 founding by five years and is simply a later year offered to muddy the timeline. There is no major APA-founding event in 1897, so it functions purely as a distractor for anyone unsure whether the association formed in the early or late 1890s. Q5 What is true about Structuralism? ✓ Answer: A · Aim was to create a "periodic table" of the "elements of sensations" The answer is option (a) because the defining, signature ambition of structuralism was to build the mental equivalent of chemistry's periodic table, cataloguing the basic elements of sensation . To understand this, place the school on the historical arc. Structuralism, founded by Wilhelm Wundt in his 1879 Leipzig laboratory and systematised by his English-born American student Edward Titchener , was the very first formal school of psychology after the discipline became a science. Its core assumption was openly borrowed from the chemistry of the day: just as complex substances reduce to a finite set of chemical elements, complex conscious experience should reduce to a finite set of irreducible mental elements, namely sensations, images and affective feelings. The method for isolating these elements was trained introspection , in which disciplined observers reported the raw contents of their awareness (the quality, intensity and duration of an experience) under controlled conditions. The aim was thus both analytic and descriptive: dissect consciousness into its atoms and arrange them into an orderly table of sensory elements. Historically, structuralism was soon challenged by functionalism (which asked what the mind is for, not what it is made of) and then largely swept aside by behaviourism , which rejected the study of consciousness altogether. Historically this was the discipline's first attempt to look like a hard science, modelling itself on chemistry's success in reducing matter to elements; its eventual failure (introspective reports proved unreliable and irreproducible between laboratories) helped trigger both functionalism and the behaviourist revolt. While structuralists did also care about consciousness in a general sense, the answer the question rewards is the unique, signature goal: the periodic table of sensations. Lock this in: structuralism equals reducing consciousness to elemental sensations, which is why option (a) beats the vaguer option (b) and why the behaviourist-flavoured option (c) is simply wrong. Panwar key: Structuralism was the first approach to understanding psychology after the field was born. The aim was to understand and be able to well describe the structures of which the human mind is formed. It also aimed at creating a table of elements of sensations like the periodic table in chemistry. Why the other options are traps B. Aim was to understand the nature of consciousness Option (b), understanding the nature of consciousness, is loosely true of structuralism and so is a tempting 'safe' choice, but it is too broad and vague: it describes the general territory rather than structuralism's distinctive aim. The signature goal the key prefers is the 'periodic table of sensations' in option (a). And option (d) 'all the above' is impossible because option (c) is false, so (b) cannot be folded into a correct 'all' answer. C. Aim was to study the behaviour and not mind Studying behaviour and not the mind describes behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner), the school that explicitly rejected introspection and consciousness, which is the direct opposite of structuralism. It is placed here precisely to bait a student who has not separated the schools. Structuralism studied the mind via introspection, so this statement is false of it, and its falsity is also what sinks option (d). D. all the above 'All the above' is a tempting catch-all, but it can only be correct if every component statement is true, and option (c) (behaviour not mind) flatly contradicts structuralism. Because one of the bundled claims is false, the whole 'all the above' option collapses; this is the classic rule that a single false member kills an 'all of the above' choice. Q6 According to John Dewey, ____ is the connection between sensory stimuli and motor responses. ✓ Answer: B · Reflex arc The answer is the reflex arc because in his famous 1896 paper The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology , John Dewey took the reflex arc, the supposed connection between sensory stimulus and motor response, as his explicit subject and target of criticism. To understand the concept, start with what a reflex arc means in physiology: a stimulus excites a sensory (afferent) pathway, which connects through the nervous system to a motor (efferent) pathway, producing a response, usually diagrammed as a one-way stimulus-then-response chain. To place this historically, Dewey's paper is a founding statement of American functionalism (the Chicago school) and an early shot against the emerging stimulus-response (S-R) psychology that would harden into behaviourism under John B. Watson. The S-R view treated 'stimulus' and 'response' as two separate, basic building blocks of behaviour stitched together. Dewey argued that this carving is artificial: sensation and movement are not two detachable units but phases of one continuous, coordinated act of adaptation, in which the response loops back and reshapes how the next stimulus is even perceived (the child reaching for the candle flame is one organised act, not stimulus then separate response). Physiology, he said, implies a unity of coordinated action, whereas the old psychology wrongly treated stimulus and response as separable. This emphasis on the whole adaptive act, and on function over fixed elements, is exactly what makes the paper functionalist and a bridge toward later organism-centred and Gestalt-flavoured thinking. The fact to lock in: the term Dewey defined and then criticised is the reflex arc (the sensory-stimulus-to-motor-response connection), and his contribution was to reject its fragmentation in favour of a unified, functional act. Panwar key: John Dewey's Education theory based on his concept of functional psychology, focused on action and application. It went against the traditional concept of stimulus-response. Dewey through his theory argued that the neural circuitry of the reflex arc was being misinterpreted by behaviourist psychology which was using stimulus and response as basic units. Physiology implied a unity of coordinated action, but psychology was treating 'stimulus' and 'response' as separable. Why the other options are traps A. Efferent arc The 'efferent arc' names only the outgoing motor limb of the pathway (efferent meaning carrying signals away from the centre toward the muscles), which is genuinely part of the picture and so sounds technical and plausible. But it is just one half of the connection; the reflex arc is the whole afferent-to-efferent loop John Dewey discussed. Picking the half-term misses the unified concept he was actually targeting. C. Association arc 'Association arc' is not a term John Dewey used, and it borrows the respectable-sounding word 'association' (from associationist psychology) to seem like a real technical concept. There is no such named structure in Dewey's reflex-arc paper, so it is a pure fabrication distractor designed to tempt anyone who does not recall the exact phrase 'reflex arc'. D. Dynamic arc 'Dynamic arc' likewise is not a recognised Dewey concept; it sounds appealing because John Dewey's whole point was that the act is dynamic and continuous rather than static. The examiner is weaponising the spirit of his argument to invent a plausible-but-false label. The concept he actually named and critiqued was the reflex arc, not any 'dynamic arc'. Q7 According to Titchener, Introspection is a highly specialised form of ______ in which the psychologist attempts to study his own consciousness scientifically. ✓ Answer: D · Self observation The answer is self observation because that is precisely how Edward Titchener framed his trained method: introspection is a highly specialised form of self-observation in which the psychologist studies his own consciousness scientifically. To understand this, place Titchener and his project on the historical map. Titchener was Wundt's English-born student who carried the new German laboratory psychology to America and founded structuralism at Cornell in the 1890s, the school whose aim, inherited from Wundt's 1879 Leipzig programme, was to reduce mental life to its elemental sensations, images and affective states. Reaching those elements cannot be done by watching behaviour from outside; it requires a disciplined inward look, and Titchener characterised that look as a comparatively neutral, systematic act of observing the self , sharply distinct from casual everyday reflection. His trained observers (often called 'reagents') learned to report the raw qualities of an experience, its quality, intensity, duration and clearness, while avoiding the stimulus error , the mistake of naming the object instead of describing the bare sensation it produced (saying 'an apple' rather than 'a round red patch with these brightness and hue qualities'). So introspection for Titchener was self-observation made rigorous and scientific, a controlled report of conscious contents rather than ordinary thinking, perceiving or merely attending. Historically this very method became structuralism's fatal vulnerability: trained introspection proved unreliable and irreproducible between laboratories, with different labs reporting different 'elements', which is exactly what let behaviourism (John B. Watson, 1913) dismiss the whole enterprise as unscientific and shift psychology to observable behaviour. The distinction to lock in: Titchener's introspection is defined as a specialised form of self-observation, the neutral scientific watching of one's own conscious contents, which is why the answer is self observation and not attention, self-perception or self-thinking. Panwar key: According to Titchener, Introspection is a highly specialised form of self observation in which the psychologist attempts to study his own consciousness scientifically. Self-observation is the relatively neutral approach to study the self and was used by Edward Tichener. Why the other options are traps A. Self perception 'Self-perception' is the term from Daryl Bem's 1960s self-perception theory, the idea that we infer our own attitudes by observing our behaviour, a social-psychology concept from a completely different era and tradition. It is a tempting near-synonym because both involve the self, but Edward Titchener's structuralist method was about directly reporting the contents of consciousness, not inferring attitudes from behaviour. B. Self thinking 'Self thinking' is not a recognised technical term anywhere in structuralism's account of introspection; it is offered because it loosely echoes the idea of an inward mental act. Edward Titchener's method was deliberately distinguished from ordinary thinking, since thinking is itself one of the conscious contents to be observed, not the act of observation. The fabricated phrase is there to catch a loose match. C. Attention 'Attention' is a real and central topic in early experimental psychology (the focusing of consciousness on a stimulus), which makes it a credible decoy. But attention is an object of study, a process the introspecting observer might report on, not the act of observing one's own consciousness. Edward Titchener defined introspection as self-observation, so naming the studied process instead of the method is the trap here. Q8 The aim of Functionalism was to study ______ as it functions in adapting the ______ to its environment. ✓ Answer: B · Mind, Organism The answer is option (b), mind then organism , because the classic aim of functionalism was to study the mind as it functions in adapting the organism to its environment. To understand this, place functionalism on the historical arc and contrast it with the school it reacted against. Structuralism (Wundt's Leipzig lab and Titchener at Cornell) was the first force, asking what the mind is made of and breaking consciousness into elemental sensations through introspection. Functionalism , the distinctively American second force, was led in spirit by William James at Harvard and developed by John Dewey and James Angell at the University of Chicago around the turn of the twentieth century; it asked instead what the mind is for . This shift was driven by Charles Darwin's theory of evolution: if every biological feature exists because it aids survival, then mental processes (perceiving, remembering, feeling, willing) must also serve an adaptive purpose. The guiding question therefore became practical and biological: how do mental processes help a living creature meet the demands of its surroundings and survive? In that formula the mind is the thing studied, and the organism is what the mind serves by adapting it to its environment. This adaptive emphasis is why functionalism is often described as importing Darwinian thinking into psychology, and why it later seeded evolutionary psychology downstream and the whole tradition of applied psychology (education, industry, mental testing). The order of the blanks is exactly what the question tests: study the mind as it adapts the organism, not the reverse. Lock in the phrasing precisely: functionalism studies the mind functioning to adapt the organism to its environment. Panwar key: Functionalism was an early approach after the idea of Cartesian duality was popular. The aim was to study the mind as it functions in adapting the organism to its environment. Why the other options are traps A. Organism, Mind Option (a) uses the right two words, 'organism' and 'mind', but in the reversed order, which is exactly the trap, since careless readers grab the familiar terms without checking the slots. Functionalism studies the mind as the thing that functions to adapt the organism; making the organism adapt the mind inverts the entire logic and contradicts the Darwinian, survival-serving role functionalism assigned to mental processes. C. Thinking, Organism Option (c) narrows the first blank to 'thinking', which is tempting because thinking is an obvious mental activity. But functionalism's declared object of study was the mind in its broad sense, the whole sweep of mental processes serving adaptation, not the single faculty of thinking. Substituting one narrow process for the general subject matter makes this both too narrow and historically inaccurate. D. Attention, Individual Option (d) offers 'attention' and 'individual', both real psychology terms, which lends it a plausible feel. Attention, however, is just one specific mental process, not the overarching subject matter functionalism set out to study, and 'individual' does not match the biological framing of 'organism' adapting to its environment. The mismatch on both blanks rules it out. Q9 ______ of the American Psychological Association represents Health Psychology. ✓ Answer: B · Division 38 The answer is Division 38 because that is the APA division designated for Health Psychology , now formally called the Society for Health Psychology. To understand the answer, you need to know how the American Psychological Association is organised.
