Rather than being one undifferentiated body, the APA (founded 1892, the institutional milestone in psychology's becoming a profession) is split into numbered divisions, each representing a distinct specialty or interest area; the numbers roughly track the order in which divisions were chartered, not any ranking of importance, so they function as essentially arbitrary labels. Division 38 is devoted to the psychological dimensions of physical health and illness: how behaviour, stress, beliefs and emotions influence the onset and course of disease; how to promote healthy behaviour; and how psychologists work inside the healthcare system to prevent, treat and manage illness and disability. As a field, health psychology emerged as a recognised force in the 1970s, alongside the rise of behavioural medicine, and rests on the biopsychosocial model articulated by George Engel (1977), which holds that health and illness arise from the interplay of biological, psychological and social factors rather than biology alone, a direct challenge to the older purely biomedical model that the discipline helped overturn. The APA recognises clinical health psychology as a professional specialty, and Division 38 is its organisational home. The fact to lock in is the simple pairing: Division 38 equals Health Psychology. Because division numbers are arbitrary chartering labels rather than meaningful codes, this is purely a memory item, so anchor it firmly as 38 for health and do not let it slide into the neighbouring numbered divisions. Panwar key: Division 38 of the American Psychological Association represents Health Psychology. Under APA (American Psychological Association) clinical health psychology is a professionally recognized specialty that investigates and implements clinical services across diverse populations and settings to promote health and well-being and to prevent, treat and manage illness and disability. Why the other options are traps A. Division 16 Division 16 is the Division of School Psychology , the specialty serving children and education systems. It is a real, well-known division, which is what makes it a strong decoy, but it has nothing to do with physical health and illness. Health psychology is Division 38, so 16 is simply the wrong number attached to a different (and easily confused) applied specialty. C. Division 47 Division 47 is the Society for Sport, Exercise and Performance Psychology . It is a tempting trap because exercise and physical wellness sit close to the idea of 'health', and a hurried reader may equate sport/fitness with health psychology. But sport and exercise psychology is its own distinct division focused on athletic performance, not the biopsychosocial study of illness, which belongs to Division 38. D. Division 98 There is no Division 98 representing health psychology, or indeed any APA division numbered that high in this context; it is a pure fabrication distractor. The large, round-feeling number is offered to catch anyone with no firm recall who might gamble on a high number. The correct, real designation for health psychology is Division 38. Q10 Which of the following historical perspectives gave rise to the evolutionary perspective? ✓ Answer: D · Functionalism The answer is functionalism because the evolutionary perspective grew directly out of functionalism's central question, which was what mental processes are for . To understand the lineage, start with functionalism itself and its place on the historical arc. Founded in spirit by William James and developed by the Chicago school (John Dewey, Angell), functionalism arose in late-nineteenth-century America as a reaction against structuralism. Where structuralism dissected the contents of consciousness, functionalism, deeply shaped by Charles Darwin's theory of evolution, asked how consciousness helps an organism adapt to and survive in its environment. That made adaptation , purpose and survival value the heart of psychological explanation. Evolutionary psychology , a modern perspective that crystallised in the late twentieth century (associated with figures like Tooby, Cosmides and Buss), takes exactly this adaptive logic and pushes it further: it explains behaviours and mental traits as products of natural selection , asking how a given tendency would have improved survival and reproduction in ancestral environments. So the conceptual bridge between the two is the shared focus on function and adaptive value; functionalism interpreted thought and behaviour through their usefulness to the organism, and evolutionary psychology reframes that usefulness in terms of inherited, gene-based adaptations. The other schools, by contrast, centred quite different things and so could not have produced the adaptive logic: structuralism (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener) catalogued what consciousness contains ; psychoanalysis (Freud) explained behaviour through unconscious drives and childhood conflict; and behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) reduced it to learned stimulus-response links forged by the environment in a single lifetime. None of these placed inherited adaptive function at the centre. Functionalism alone made 'what is this mental process for, and how does it aid survival' the organising question, and evolutionary psychology simply re-rooted that question in genes and natural selection. The distinction to lock in: it is functionalism, with its Darwinian adaptive emphasis, that seeded the modern evolutionary perspective. Panwar key: Functionalism paved the way for the understanding and interpreting human evolution and behaviour from a perspective that focused on the functionality aspect of thought and behaviour, the choices and the fears that people make and have. Why the other options are traps A. behaviourism Behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) studied observable conditioned responses and explicitly banned talk of inner mental states or adaptive 'purpose', leaning on learning rather than inherited function. It is a tempting distractor because it is biological-sounding and scientific, but its whole stance, environment-driven learning over inherited adaptation, is conceptually opposed to the evolutionary emphasis on naturally selected traits, so it did not give rise to it. B. Structuralism Structuralism (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener) analysed consciousness into its elemental sensations and deliberately ignored questions of purpose, function or survival value. It is offered because it is an early foundational school, but its static, element-cataloguing aim is the exact opposite of the adaptive, functional thinking that fed evolutionary psychology. Structuralism actually provoked functionalism as a reaction, rather than seeding the evolutionary view. C. Psychoanalysis Psychoanalysis (Freud) explored unconscious drives, childhood conflict and instinctual energy. The word 'instinct' can make it feel biological and therefore evolutionary, which is the bait. But psychoanalysis explained behaviour through intrapsychic conflict and developmental history, not through the adaptive function of mental processes shaped by natural selection, so it is not the parent of the evolutionary perspective. Q11 Who is the most associated with the techniques of introspection? ✓ Answer: A · Wundt The answer is Wundt because Wilhelm Wundt is the figure most identified with the technique of introspection , having made it the signature method of the first scientific psychology. To understand this, recall what introspection meant in his hands and where it sits on the historical arc. It was not casual self-reflection but a trained, controlled, almost experimental procedure (sometimes called experimental self-observation ): observers were given a precise, repeatable stimulus and asked to report the immediate contents of their own consciousness, such as the quality, intensity and duration of a sensation, under standardised laboratory conditions, with trials repeated to check reliability. Wundt founded the first psychology laboratory at the University of Leipzig in 1879 , Germany, the act conventionally treated as psychology's birth as a science, and built his school, structuralism , around this method, using it to break conscious experience into its elemental components on analogy with chemistry. His student Edward Titchener later carried introspection to America and refined it (including the concept of the stimulus error ), but the technique is most associated with Wundt as its originator within experimental psychology. The historical contrast worth holding is the cast of other founders, each tied to a different force: William James founded functionalism and was sceptical of rigid introspection; John Watson founded behaviourism (1913) and rejected introspection outright as unscientific, demanding the study of observable behaviour instead; and Max Wertheimer founded Gestalt psychology, which studied whole perceptual forms. Indeed, introspection's eventual unreliability between laboratories is exactly what gave behaviourism its opening to dismiss the method. The fact to lock in: Wundt plus introspection plus the Leipzig 1879 lab plus structuralism form one tight cluster, so when introspection is named, the default answer is Wundt. Panwar key: Wilhelm Wundt, the founder of modern psychology, a proponent of the structuralist perspective, used the technique of introspection to understand and interpret the human mind. He started the first psychology laboratory in Leipzig, Germany. Why the other options are traps B. James William James is from the same founding generation and certainly used and discussed introspection, which makes him a credible choice. But James founded functionalism and was openly critical of the rigid, element-hunting introspection that Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener practised, favouring a more naturalistic study of the 'stream of consciousness'. He is not the figure most associated with the introspective technique ; that is Wundt. C. Watson John Watson is a strong trap precisely because his name is tightly linked to introspection, but for the opposite reason: in his 1913 behaviourist manifesto he explicitly rejected introspection as unscientific and unverifiable, insisting psychology study only observable behaviour. Choosing him reverses the relationship. He is the great opponent of introspection, not its proponent, so he is wrong here. D. Wertheimer Max Wertheimer founded Gestalt psychology , which studied whole perceptual organisations ('the whole is greater than the sum of its parts') and reacted against the atomistic, element-by-element approach that introspection served. He is offered as a famous early-school founder to tempt the unsure, but his method and aims were about perceptual wholes, not the introspective reporting of elemental conscious contents. Q12 Which among the following branches of Psychology specifically studies behaviour in relation to genetic inheritance? ✓ Answer: A · Ev

title: Amity, MA Clinical Psychology: The Entrance, Built to the Exhaustive Syllabus
text: Amity, MA Clinical Psychology: The Entrance, Built to the Exhaustive Syllabus This is the whole RCI-regulated M.A. / M.Phil Clinical Psychology entrance in one book, built to the Ultimate Exhaustive Master Syllabus you sent and taught from the ground up. Not notes about the exam: the actual content, every micro-concept built from scratch to the depth you set (the Jung breakdown, the Pinel sleep chapter), so you learn it cold, not just recognise it. The six domains follow the syllabus exactly, in its order, with the heavy core (biopsychology, advanced statistics, psychopathology) taught hardest. Two appendices add the depth off your own Amity paper. Read it cover to cover and you walk in ready. The exhaustive syllabus, in order 1 · Biopsychology & Advanced Neurosciences 2 · Advanced Statistics, Psychometrics & Research Methodology 3 · Psychopathology & Clinical Syndromes 4 · Psychological Assessment & Psychodiagnostics 5 · Psychotherapy & Clinical Interventions 6 · Foundational Psychology, Lifespan Development & Social Dynamics Appendices (off your own paper) Appendix A · PYQ Depth: Off Your Own Paper Appendix B · Indian Psychology (off your own paper) How this book is built The six domains map one-to-one onto the exhaustive master syllabus, down to the micro-concept. Each topic is taught the same way: what it is , the theory or mechanism , the names and exact criteria or numbers , a worked example , the way it shows up in the paper , and the trap . Coloured boxes flag what matters most: Definition (memorise this), High-yield (near-certain to be tested), Exam trap (the distractor built to catch you), and Memory aid (a hook). Nothing is left at a one-liner: every sub-concept is taught to the same floor. The two appendices are not on the formal syllabus: they are the concepts your own Amity paper actually tested (your Master Concept List, and the Indian-psychology cluster), kept because they are real and high-value. 1 · Biopsychology & Advanced Neurosciences This section teaches the physical machinery of the nervous system from the membrane up: how a single neuron holds a charge, fires, and recovers; how that signal jumps across the synapse; what the neurotransmitters are and how the drugs you will be questioned on act on them; and finally how the cortex and the deep brain are organised into the maps and loops that the examiners love to test. Biopsychology is the most fact-dense domain in the whole entrance, and it rewards the candidate who knows exact numbers (the resting potential is roughly −70 mV, threshold is −55 mV, the pump moves 3 sodium out for 2 potassium in) and exact names (Synaptotagmin, the Nucleus Basalis of Meynert, Brodmann area 17). Read it once for the story, then again for the numbers. Every distractor the paper throws at you is a near-neighbour of a true fact, so we will pair each mechanism with the trap that sits next to it. A. Membrane Dynamics & Electrophysiology A neuron at rest is not electrically dead; it is a charged battery held away from equilibrium by metabolic work. Understanding the resting potential, how it is built, and how it collapses into an action potential is the foundation for everything else in this section, so we build it ion by ion. Resting Membrane Potential: the gradients and the driving forces The resting membrane potential (RMP) is the steady voltage difference across the neuronal membrane when the cell is not signalling, conventionally about −70 mV (the inside is negative relative to the outside). It exists because four ions are unequally distributed across the membrane and because the membrane is selectively permeable to them. The key players, with their characteristic gradients, are: Ion Where concentrated Equilibrium potential (approx.) Resting permeability Potassium (K + ) High inside −90 mV High (leak channels open) Sodium (Na + ) High outside +60 mV Low at rest Chloride (Cl − ) High outside −65 to −70 mV Moderate Organic anions (A − : proteins, phosphates) Trapped inside n/a (impermeant) None Two forces act on every ion. The chemical (concentration) gradient pushes an ion from where it is concentrated to where it is dilute. The electrical gradient pulls an ion toward the oppositely charged compartment. The combination is the electrochemical driving force . For potassium, the concentration gradient pushes K + out (it is concentrated inside), but as positive charge leaves, the inside becomes more negative and the electrical gradient begins pulling K + back in. The voltage at which these two forces exactly balance, so there is no net flux of that single ion, is its equilibrium (reversal) potential . Because the resting membrane is far more permeable to K + than to anything else, the RMP sits close to the potassium equilibrium potential, near −90 mV, but is dragged a little more positive (to about −70 mV) by the small resting sodium leak. The Nernst equation: equilibrium for a single ion The Nernst equation calculates the equilibrium potential for one ion species from its concentration ratio across the membrane. In the form usually quoted for body temperature it is: E ion = (61 / z) × log 10 ( [ion] outside / [ion] inside ) millivolts, where z is the ionic charge (+1 for Na + and K + , −1 for Cl − ) and 61 is the constant RT/F converted to base-10 logarithms at 37°C (the value 58 to 62 is used in different textbooks; learn 61). Worked example: for potassium with roughly 5 mM outside and 140 mM inside, E K = 61 × log 10 (5/140) = 61 × log 10 (0.0357) = 61 × (−1.447) = about −88 mV. That is why the resting cell, dominated by K + permeability, rests near −90 mV. Definition The equilibrium potential of an ion is the membrane voltage at which the electrical force exactly cancels the chemical force, producing zero net movement of that ion. The Nernst equation gives it for a single ion; the GHK equation gives the resting potential when several ions are permeable at once. Exam trap Nernst handles one ion in isolation. title: RML Clinical Psychology, CET-166 · Study Material from Scratch
text: RML Clinical Psychology, CET-166 · Study Material from Scratch ABVIMS & Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital · MA Clinical Psychology (RCI) via GGSIPU · the whole entrance syllabus taught from zero, tuned to how the RML paper actually behaves. Built for Sihan, 2026-07-02. You flagged RML as the emergency, so this is the first RML drop: a complete, from-scratch study text that covers every concept the CET-166 clinical paper tests, built off the syllabus in your RML Task brief and off how past RML / IPU clinical papers actually behave. Read it top to bottom and you have covered the subject core. Every theorist is given by full name (not just a surname), every test names its author, and every therapy names who developed it, because that is exactly what this paper rewards. Now expanded to the full syllabus neighborhood (2026-07-03): not just the PYQ hot topics, but the foundational build-up, the related theories, and the adjacent subtopics the examiner can swing into, so the high-yield material still gets the most room while nothing is left as a blind spot. Every one of the 12 sections gained new ground: the surrounding reasoning types and the full mental-health-law stack, sensation and cognition and language, brain-imaging methods and behaviour genetics, prenatal-to-ageing-to-death development, the self and social cognition and attraction, biological and cognitive and Indian personality models, the history of abnormality plus culture-bound syndromes, the mental status examination and rehabilitation psychology, group and play and specific behavioural therapies, Indian test adaptations and clinical rating scales, qualitative methods and ANOVA and non-parametric statistics, and the six darshanas with Yoga and Buddhist psychology in depth. Entrance CET-166 (GGSIPU) Split 70% test + 30% interview Format large MCQ block, no negative marking 12 sections · from scratch Full-syllabus expanded 2026-07-03 6-year PYQ map 2020–2025 Companion mocks 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 How to use this. This is a teaching text, not a cheatsheet: each section builds a topic from the ground up, then flags the exact traps and matching-items RML fishes for. The green Key boxes are the must-knows, the red Trap boxes are the confusions the paper exploits, the teal Who → what boxes are the theorist / founder pairings, and the purple RML tilt boxes tell you how this specific paper phrases the question. Read the 6-year PYQ map first to set your priorities, then after each section sit the matching part of any of the six live PYQ mocks ( 2020 , 2021 , 2022 , 2023 , 2024 , 2025 ) and the weak spots map straight back here. What makes the RML paper different, baked into every section below: (1) lean harder on Indian Psychology , tested past AND present; (2) treat abnormal as ICD-deep and factual , including the older signs and eponyms DSM has dropped; (3) drill who developed which therapy and the acronyms (REBT, DBT, ACT, EMDR, MI) until reflexive; (4) by the six-year PYQ count the paper is actually carried by General/basic psychology, Assessment & tests, Statistics/Research methods, Abnormal, and Biopsychology (the top five = 65% of marks; see the PYQ map ); (5) no negative marking, so attempt everything . The syllabus, 13 sections: ★ The 6-year PYQ map (read first) 1 · Reasoning, Research Aptitude & General Awareness 2 · General & Basic Psychology 3 · Biopsychology 4 · Developmental 5 · Social 6 · Personality 7 · Abnormal (ICD-deep) 8 · Clinical Psychology 9 · Counselling & Psychotherapy 10 · Assessment & Tests 11 · Research Methods & Statistics 12 · Indian Psychology 13 · Social Work (the RML 2020 strand) ★ What actually repeats: the 6-year PYQ map (2020–2025) Everything below this heading is built from the real RML papers, all six of them : 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, which is 570 actual questions (100 each year except 2023, which had 70). Every one of those questions was tagged to a topic, the topics were counted across the six years, and the concepts that keep coming back were pulled out. So this is not a guess about what the examiner likes; it is the paper's own track record. Read this section first, let it set your priorities, then go into the twelve teaching sections knowing exactly where the marks actually live. How the marks distribute. The single table below is the whole weighting in one view: how many questions each topic drew in each of the six years, the six-year total, its share of the 570 marks, and which teaching section covers it. The bottom four rows of the ranking (cognitive, social, schools, and the rest) are still worth marks, but the top five topics, basic/general, assessment, statistics, abnormal, and biopsychology, are 65% of the entire paper on their own. That is the order to study in. Topic 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 6-yr Share Taught in General & basic psychology 3 4 10 17 38 20 92 16.1% §1–2, sensation, perception, memory, motivation, emotion, intelligence, learning Psychological assessment & tests 9 15 19 3 6 22 74 13.0% §10 Research methods & statistics 8 19 6 21 6 12 72 12.6% §11 Abnormal / psychopathology 19 13 15 1 14 8 70 12.3% §7 Biopsychology 9 6 7 7 18 18 65 11.4% §3 Developmental & child 9 18 14 2 3 8 54 9.5% §4 Counselling & psychotherapy 8 11 15 0 13 1 48 8.4% §9 Cognitive psychology 9 3 6 9 0 10 37 6.5% §2 Social psychology 16 8 8 2 2 1 37 6.5% §5 Schools & systems / applied 10 3 0 8 0 0 21 3.7% §8, §2 Every paper 100 100 100 70 100 100 570 100% the whole book Attack order, straight off the six-year data: (1) General & basic psychology and (2) Assessment & tests and (3) Research methods & statistics are the three biggest buckets, about 42% of the paper between them, and they are the most learnable (definitions, who-built-which-test, stats vocabulary), so bank them first. (4) Abnormal and (5) Biopsychology are the next tier and together add another 24%. Only after those five are solid should you spend heavily on (6) developmental, (7) therapy, (8) cognitive, (9) social, and (10) schools/systems. Personality looks like a zero in the table only because RML rarely labels a question "personality"; its content (Sigmund Freud's structure, Raymond Cattell's 16PF, Hans Eysenck's dimensions, the Big Five) is tested inside the general, abnormal and assessment buckets, so section 6 is not optional, it is spread across the others. RML tilt, confirmed by the data: two things carry across almost every year, so make them reflexive. First, "who developed what" : the paper repeatedly names a test, therapy, or theory and asks for its author (Hermann Rorschach, Henry Murray, Lee Cronbach, Albert Ellis, Aaron Beck, Jean Piaget, Erik Erikson). Second, the projective tests and the defense mechanisms , which appear in four of the six years each. If you drill only two things, drill those. The rest of this section is the concept-by-concept breakdown, topic by topic, ordered biggest bucket first. Each callout names the concept, the years it actually appeared, and the exact fact or distinction the paper fishes for. Every recurring item here has a fuller treatment in the numbered teaching sections below. Schools & Systems of Psychology, 21 questions over six years This is a small but revealing bucket. It is not "systems of psychology" in the textbook sense (structuralism, functionalism, and so on live in the General bucket). Here the recurring core is organisational / industrial behaviour, systems & family therapy, and, from 2023 onward, research software (Excel and SPSS). Learn the named theories and the named theorists, because RML asks them by name. Repeats (2020, 2023): Organisational & industrial psychology is the steadiest thread here. 2020 probed dysfunctional organisational cultures and case management premises; 2023 asked about a decentralised, empowerment-focused structure (the flat / organic structure) and about Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory. Know the two families of motivators at work. Who → what: Frederick Herzberg → Two-Factor (Motivation-Hygiene) Theory. Motivators (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement) drive genuine job satisfaction; hygiene factors (salary, supervision, working conditions, company policy) only prevent dissatisfaction and never satisfy. The 2023 question keys on "motivators that lead to job satisfaction," so pick the growth-of-the-job factors, not pay. Repeats (2020): Group development ran across several 2020 items. Bruce Tuckman's stages are the must-know: forming → storming → norming → performing → adjourning . The 2020 stem "struggle with each other over leadership and group definition" = storming ; "clarified its purpose and strategy for achieving its goals" = norming . Also seen: common group properties, formed-group characteristics, and William Shulman's group-role language. Who → what: Gregory Bateson → the double-bind theory of schizophrenia. The 2021 mother-and-son vignette (she stiffens at his embrace, then blames him for withdrawing, with no escape from the contradiction) is the classic double-bind illustration: conflicting messages on different logical levels with no way to comment on or leave the situation. The 2021 "individuals, families, and cultures given different power as creators of their realities" stem points to constructivist / narrative family therapy. Repeats (2023): Research software is a 2023 cluster worth easy marks. SPSS = the standard statistical-analysis package (tabulation, graphing, statistical tests) in psychology research; MS-Excel uses PivotTables for tabulating data and the AVERAGE function for a mean of a range. Expect one or two verbatim "which software / which function" items. General & Basic Psychology, 92 questions over six years (the biggest bucket) This is the single largest slice of the RML paper and the most scatter-shot: research methodology, motivation, memory, perception, learning, the schools of psychology, stress and health, cognitive biases, and Indian psychology all live here. The good news is that it is theorist-heavy and fact-checkable, so a map of the repeats converts directly into marks. Each year has a centre of gravity: 2022-2023 lean research methods, 2024 is a memory-perception-learning avalanche, and 2025 is almost entirely motivation, schools, and Indian psychology. Repeats (2020, 2022, 2023): Research methodology and design is the largest recurring theme in this bucket. Recurring hooks: the double-blind design (controls both participant and experimenter expectancy), confounding variables (the barbecue-vs-plain-chips flavour and the radio-on/off items both test uncontrolled confounds), sampling methods ( stratified = divide into subgroups then sample each; cluster = sample whole groups), field vs lab experiments, the literature review, hypothesis formulation, plagiarism, and referencing / citation ethics. Trap: Deductive vs inductive reasoning is asked repeatedly (2023, 2024) and students flip them. Deductive = theory first, then test with observations, general → specific; its conclusion's validity depends on the truth of its premises . Inductive = gather data, find patterns, then build a theory, specific observations → broad generalisation (qualitative research leans inductive). If the stem says "starts with a theory," it is deductive. Repeats (2021, 2024, 2025): Motivation theory is a top-three repeat and dominates 2025. Know each by its one-line signature. Abraham Maslow 's hierarchy (self-actualisation = realising full potential; belonging / love must be met before esteem) appears in both 2021 and 2025. Theory & theorist Core claim (RML one-liner) Hierarchy of Needs (Abraham Maslow) Lower needs first; self-actualisation = full potential at the top Self-Determination Theory (Edward Deci & Richard Ryan) Three needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness; intrinsic motivation = internal reward & growth Expectancy Theory (Victor Vroom) Effort → performance → outcome, and the outcome must be valued (valent) Goal-Setting Theory (Edwin Locke) Specific and difficult (challenging) goals motivate best Drive-Reduction Theory (Clark Hull) Motivation reduces internal tension to restore homeostasis Incentive Theory Behaviour pulled by external rewards / incentives Social Cognitive Theory (Albert Bandura) Self-efficacy and observational learning drive motivation Trap: Self-Determination Theory's three needs are autonomy, competence, relatedness . The 2025 "which is NOT one of the three needs" item plants a decoy (often "achievement" or "esteem"). Achievement belongs to David McClelland, not to SDT. Repeats (2020, 2024): Memory is the 2024 heavyweight and links back to 2020. The founders are the answers, so memorise the name-to-concept map below. The 2024 paper alone tests the magic number, the serial-position effect, decay theory, filter / attenuation theories, tip-of-the-tongue (Roger Brown and David McNeill, 1966), the PQRST study method, and the method of reconstruction. Concept Theorist (the answer) "Magic number" 7 ± 2 (span of short-term memory) George A. Miller Primacy-recency / serial-position effect Hermann Ebbinghaus Filter theory of attention Donald Broadbent Filter-attenuation theory Anne Treisman Self-reference effect T. B. Rogers (Rogers, Kuiper & Kirker) Decay theory of forgetting Edward Thorndike (law of disuse) RML tilt: "Tip of the tongue" is a retrieval failure (the trace is stored but momentarily inaccessible), not encoding or storage. In the PQRST study method (Preview, Question, Read, Self-recitation, Test), S = Self-recitation (actively recalling in your own words). And the 2020 "what do Hermann Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud share" item keys on their common contribution to the early study of memory / association . Repeats (2024): Perception and Gestalt organisation form a dense 2024 block. Dark adaptation = the eyes growing more sensitive to light (dim light) over time; closure = the Gestalt tendency to complete an incomplete figure; the Stroop effect = interference / selective-attention breakdown (colour word vs ink colour). Depth cues recur as a mini-family (below). 2024 depth-cue stem Monocular cue Rail tracks appear to converge Linear perspective Density of stones increases with distance Texture gradient Painted stripes on a freeway off-ramp Relative size / texture gradient Repeats (2024, 2025): Learning and conditioning span both years. Insight learning (sudden "aha" grasp of a solution) is Wolfgang Kohler's Gestalt work; shaping = reinforcing successive approximations; extinction = weakening a habit by removing all reward; stimulus generalisation vs discrimination (the furry-black-cat vs short-haired-tabby item = discrimination); a token that must be traded (five stickers) is a secondary / conditioned reinforcer . 2025 names the parent school directly: stimulus-response conditioning = behaviourism (John B. Watson, 1913). Repeats (2020, 2024, 2025): The schools of psychology and their history recur across three years. 2020 asked who first used "clinical psychology" in print ( Lightner Witmer , 1896-1907, who also opened the first psychology clinic). 2024 asked who gave "folk psychology" / Volkerpsychologie ( Wilhelm Wundt ). 2025 asked you to name whole approaches from a description. Approach (2025 stems) Signature & key figures Behaviourism Learning via stimulus-response conditioning; John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner Psychodynamic / psychoanalytic Unconscious forces & early childhood; inner drives beyond control; Sigmund Freud Humanistic Free will, growth, self-actualisation; Abraham Maslow, Carl Rogers Comparative psychology Study of animal behaviour Structuralism / founder of the field Wilhelm Wundt (first lab, 1879); "folk psychology" Repeats (2024): Stress and health cluster in 2024. Hans Selye 's General Adaptation Syndrome runs in strict order: alarm → resistance → exhaustion . Type A behaviour is the pattern most directly linked to higher coronary-heart-disease risk. Distinguish an acute stressor (short, sharp, time-limited) from a chronic one. Trap: 2024 mixes several cognitive-bias / problem-solving terms that look alike. Functional fixedness (Karl Duncker, 1945) = seeing an object only in its usual use; hindsight bias (Baruch Fischhoff, 1975) = the "I knew it all along" overestimate of past predictability; a heuristic = a rule-of-thumb shortcut for efficient search. Do not swap functional fixedness for mental set. RML tilt: Indian psychology is a live 2025 theme (five questions) and is easy to underprepare. Core points: it is rooted in Vedanta and the Indian philosophical traditions and centres on consciousness and the self ; Atman = the true self / soul (distinct from ego); it treats mental health holistically (mind-body-spirit, practices such as yoga and meditation) rather than through a purely Western symptom-and-diagnosis lens. Assessment & Tests, 74 questions over six years This topic is dominated by a handful of named tests and the reliability-validity vocabulary: the Rorschach, the MMPI (Starke Hathaway and J. Charnley McKinley, 1943), the TAT and projective logic, the reliability and validity families, and the IQ line reappear in year after year, so the recurring names below carry most of the marks. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2025): The Rorschach inkblot test is the single most-repeated item. Built by Hermann Rorschach (Swiss psychiatrist, 1921), it has 10 cards total : 5 achromatic (black and grey), 2 black-and-red, and 3 fully multicoloured, so 5 cards are coloured . It is a projective test of personality and unconscious process. RML also asks its procedure: the Enquiry (Inquiry) Phase is the second stage where the examiner returns to each blot to ask what was seen and what made it look that way (location, determinants). Who → what: Hermann Rorschach → inkblot test; Henry Murray & Christiana Morgan → Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), 1930s (1935), Harvard; Starke Hathaway & J. Charnley McKinley → MMPI; John Buck → House-Tree-Person test; Edgar Doll → Vineland Social Maturity Scale; Lee Cronbach → coefficient alpha; Alfred Binet & Theodore Simon → first intelligence test (1905); David Wechsler → WAIS/WISC. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022): The MMPI (Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory) is asked almost every early year. It is an objective, self-report inventory that measures psychopathology and personality (clinical scales plus validity scales), NOT a projective test and NOT an intelligence test. That objective-self-report identity is the fact RML fishes for. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2025): Projective tests and their techniques. A projective test uses ambiguous stimuli to draw out unconscious thoughts, motives and personality. Learn the technique labels the paper uses: the Rorschach is an association technique ; the TAT is a construction technique (the participant constructs a story); word-association is also association-based. The TAT's stories are analysed to infer needs, motives and inner conflicts (Murray's need-press theory). Trap: TAT vs Rorschach. Both are projective, but the Rorschach uses inkblots (perception/association) while the TAT uses picture cards of people in scenes and asks for a story (apperception/construction). RML asks directly for the "key difference" and for how many TAT cards are used: the full set is 31, and roughly 20 are shown in a typical session. Who → what: the reliability family. Test-retest = same test, same people, two occasions (stability over time). Inter-rater = agreement between two scorers/observers. Split-half = correlate two halves of one test, best split by the odd-even method and corrected by Spearman-Brown. Cronbach's alpha ( Lee Cronbach ) = internal consistency across all items. RML has asked each of these by definition in 2021, 2022 and 2025. Repeats (2021, 2024, 2025): Validity types. Face validity = looks like it measures the trait, on the surface. Content validity = covers the whole domain. Criterion-related validity splits into concurrent (against a criterion measured now) and predictive (against a future criterion). Construct validity = the test truly captures the theoretical construct. Trap: the 2024 and 2025 items ask which type is NOT criterion-based. Only concurrent and predictive are criterion-based; construct and content validity are separate categories, so they are the correct "NOT criterion" answers. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2025): Intelligence and IQ. Memorise the ratio-IQ formula IQ = (Mental Age ÷ Chronological Age) × 100 (MA 8, CA 10 → IQ 80). Know the test-to-author map: WAIS/WISC are Wechsler individual intelligence scales; Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices measure nonverbal fluid intelligence; the first intelligence test was built by Alfred Binet (with Theodore Simon, 1905). RML tilt: RML likes attitude-scale and rating-scale wording. A Likert scale ( Rensis Likert ) is a summated rating scale : agree-to-disagree items are summed into one score. It appears in 2020, 2022 and 2023 phrased as "summated rating scale," "attitude measurement scale," or "a Likert scale is best described as." Research Methods & Statistics, 72 questions over six years Stats repeats cluster tightly on five spines: sampling methods, scales of measurement, the ANOVA/F machinery, central tendency, and the correlation-is-not-causation logic, with hypothesis testing errors and research ethics close behind. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2023, 2025): Sampling methods, the top stats repeat. Split probability from non-probability. Convenience/accidental (whoever is easy to recruit), snowball (participants refer others), and quota/purposive are non-probability . Systematic sampling = selecting every nth person from a list. Random sampling matters because it gives every member an equal chance and makes the sample representative, which is what licenses generalisation. Repeats (2023, 2024, 2025): Scales of measurement (S.S. Stevens). Nominal = unordered categories (car colours). Ordinal = ranked. Interval = equal intervals but an arbitrary/no true zero (temperature). Ratio = equal intervals plus a true zero and counting (number of books). Trap: zero is the discriminator. The 2024 "arbitrary zero" item is the interval scale; the 2023 "equal intervals AND a true zero point" item is the ratio scale. Do not answer ratio when it says arbitrary zero. Repeats (2020, 2022, 2025): Measures of central tendency are mean, median and mode ; standard deviation is a measure of dispersion, NOT central tendency (a common "which is NOT" answer). In a negatively skewed distribution the order is mean < median < mode , so the mean sits to the left of (below) the median. For skewed data such as anxiety scores, the median is the preferred summary because it resists outliers. Who → what: the ANOVA family (2021, 2022). Ronald Fisher → ANOVA and the F-ratio , where F = between-groups variance ÷ within-groups (pooled/error) variance, so the denominator is the pooled within-group variance . As chance (error) variance falls, F rises . Post-hoc tests (Tukey's HSD, Scheffe, Duncan's multiple range, Newman-Keuls) are run only after a significant ANOVA . ANCOVA adds one assumption ANOVA lacks: a covariate statistically controlled for. Repeats (2021, 2025): Correlation is not causation. A correlational or observational study (regularly exercising adults being less depressed, meditators being less stressed) cannot establish cause because there is no manipulation and no random assignment , so third variables and reverse causation stay open. This exact reasoning is RML's favourite "why is this conclusion not appropriate" item. Who → what: matching a test to the data. Pearson's r → two continuous variables (stress vs sleep). Biserial/point-biserial → one continuous and one dichotomous variable. Non-parametric equivalents (2023): Mann-Whitney U → independent-samples t-test; Kruskal-Wallis → one-way ANOVA (3+ independent groups); Friedman → repeated-measures design. Repeats (2022, 2023): Hypothesis-testing errors. A Type I error = rejecting a true null (false positive, controlled by alpha). A Type II error = failing to reject a null that is actually false (false negative). The 2023 stem "fails to reject the null when it is actually false" is by definition Type II . RML tilt: two smaller but reliable repeats. Informed consent (2021, 2025) = telling participants the study's purpose and procedures so they can freely decide to take part. And the normal-distribution line (2021, 2022): the z-table is derived from the standard normal curve, and the bell curve was first described by Abraham de Moivre and popularised by Carl Friedrich Gauss (hence "Gaussian"). Abnormal & Psychopathology, 70 questions over six years This is the single heaviest cluster on the CET-166 paper, and it rewards flat memorisation over reasoning. RML sits close to the ICD text, loves the older eponyms and signs (Eugen Bleuler, Schneider, Janet), and returns to the same handful of anchors every year: Sigmund Freud's defense mechanisms, schizophrenia signs, the anorexia-versus-bulimia contrast, mood disorders, and dissociation. Learn these as fact lists, not as concepts to derive under time pressure. Repeats (2020, 2022, 2024, 2025): Defense mechanisms are the number-one recurring item, almost always as a clinical vignette ("name the mechanism"). Sigmund Freud's ego defenses you must recognise on sight: sublimation (channeling an unacceptable urge into an acceptable outlet, e.g. anger into kickboxing), projection (attributing your own unacceptable thoughts or impulses to others, asked twice in 2025), displacement (redirecting a feeling from a threatening target to a safer one, e.g. yelling at the dog when angry at your partner), repression (involuntary blocking of painful material from awareness), and rationalisation (excusing failure by blaming an external cause, e.g. Clare blaming a co-worker for being fired). Mechanism Core move Paper cue Sublimation Urge → socially valued outlet Anger → kickboxing class Projection Own impulse attributed to others "attributing unacceptable thoughts to others" Displacement Feeling shifted to a safer target Yells at dog / argues with husband Repression Involuntary blocking from awareness Cannot bring anxiety-provoking material to consciousness Rationalisation Self-serving excuse for a failure Blames co-worker for being fired Splitting All-good / all-bad, no middle Seen in borderline personality disorder Projective identification Melanie Klein, paranoid-schizoid Ego defense "in paranoia" Who → what: Sigmund Freud → structural model ( id runs on the pleasure principle, ego on the reality principle, superego is morality) and the topographic model (the preconscious holds accessible memories recalled at will). Asked in 2020, 2022 (Freud on alcohol dependence = oral-stage fixation) and 2025 ("component that operates on the reality principle" = the ego). Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2024): Schizophrenia recurs every one of those years. Know the positive versus negative symptom split (positive = added experiences: delusions, hallucinations; negative = lost function: flat affect, avolition, alogia, anhedonia), identical-twin concordance of roughly 50 percent , and expressed emotion (EE) = a family climate of criticism, hostility and emotional over-involvement that predicts relapse. RML also asks the ICD inclusion/exclusion criteria directly. Who → what: Kurt Schneider → First-Rank Symptoms of schizophrenia (2022 "who gave the concept", 2024 "which is NOT a first-rank symptom"). The list: audible thoughts / voices commenting or arguing, thought withdrawal-insertion-broadcasting, made (passivity) feelings, impulses and acts, and delusional perception. Anything negative-symptom (e.g. flat affect) is the classic "NOT first-rank" trap answer. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2024): Eating disorders, always framed as anorexia-versus-bulimia. Shared feature = intense fear of weight gain plus disturbed body image; the discriminator = anorexia nervosa carries markedly low body weight (and, in older criteria, amenorrhea = absence of menstrual periods), whereas bulimia nervosa runs at near-normal weight with binge eating plus compensatory behaviour (self-induced vomiting, laxatives, fasting, over-exercise). Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2024): Mood / affective disorders. Bipolar is the disorder where mood "swings from one extreme to another"; a manic episode's core pair = elevated/expansive mood plus increased energy or activity. Major depressive disorder is cued by loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia) and appetite change, NOT euphoria or specific phobias. Dysthymia (persistent depressive disorder) = milder but longer-lasting than MDD. Depression is the one the paper nicknames the " common cold of psychiatry " and the usual cause of pseudodementia . Repeats (2022, 2024, 2025): Dissociative disorders. Multiple distinct personalities within one person = dissociative identity disorder (DID). Psychodynamic theory reads dissociative symptoms as defense against trauma; dissociative amnesia is usually localised or selective, whereas generalised amnesia wipes the entire life history. RML pairs this with hysteria/conversion signs (see eponyms below). Repeats (2023, 2025): The diathesis-stress model asks the same thing twice: mental disorders arise from the interaction of a predisposing vulnerability (the diathesis, genetic or biological) with environmental stress, not from either alone. Repeats (2021, 2022, 2025): Personality disorders. They are stable, long-term, pervasive patterns. Antisocial PD = manipulation, lack of remorse, irresponsibility; obsessive-compulsive PD = driven by a need for order and control (not the same as OCD). RML tilt: The 2024 paper in particular is dense with eponyms and older signs , so bank them cold: "ambivalence" (one of Eugen Bleuler's four A's) was coined by Eugen Bleuler ; "la belle indifférence" in hysteria is attributed to Pierre Janet ; delusion of infidelity = Othello syndrome (delusional jealousy); First-Rank Symptoms = Kurt Schneider ; kleptomania is a classic French-alienist eponym. RML rewards knowing the name attached to the term, not just the term. Counselling & Psychotherapy, 48 questions over six years The therapy section is built around two obsessions RML returns to every year: who developed which therapy (founder attribution) and the mechanics of behaviour therapy and CBT . Learn the acronym-to-founder map below cold; it converts several guaranteed marks. Note that ego defense mechanisms reappear inside this section too, so the Freud grid above is doing double duty. Who → what: This is the paper's favourite therapy question type (2021, 2022, 2024 all ask it). Memorise the founder map: Therapy / concept Developer (full name) Cognitive therapy / CBT, Socratic questioning Aaron Beck REBT and the ABC model Albert Ellis DBT (distress tolerance) Marsha Linehan ACT (acceptance & commitment) Steven Hayes EMDR Francine Shapiro Motivational Interviewing (MI) William Miller & Stephen Rollnick Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) Gerald Klerman & Myrna Weissman Client-centred therapy Carl Rogers Self-efficacy Albert Bandura Systematic desensitisation Joseph Wolpe Progressive deep muscle relaxation Edmund Jacobson Individual psychology, inferiority complex Alfred Adler Collective unconscious Carl Jung Repeats (2021, 2022, 2024, 2025): The cognitive family. Aaron Beck's cognitive therapy is drilled through its methods (Socratic questioning, collaborative identification of cognitive errors such as overgeneralisation and arbitrary inference, thought records for depression). Albert Ellis's REBT is drilled through the ABC model : Activating event → Beliefs → Consequences. Keep Beck (errors/distortions) and Ellis (irrational beliefs, ABC) separate in your head; the paper baits you to swap them. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022): Behaviour therapy built on relaxation. The technique where a patient relaxes while visualising a graded hierarchy of anxiety-provoking scenes (the public-speaking vignette in 2021) is systematic desensitisation , developed by Joseph Wolpe on the principle of reciprocal inhibition / counterconditioning; the relaxation half is Edmund Jacobson's progressive deep relaxation. Repeats (2021, 2022): Operant-based methods. "Behaviour analysis" and "functional analysis" (asked verbatim, twice each) rest on the principles of operant conditioning (B.F. Skinner): behaviour is shaped by its consequences. Shaping = reinforcing successive approximations; the "Lovaas programme" = applied behaviour analysis for autism. Who → what: EMDR (2021, 2022) → Francine Shapiro, and it was developed specifically for PTSD / trauma ; the technique pairs recall of the distressing memory with bilateral eye movements. DBT and its distress tolerance module (2024) → Marsha Linehan. Trap: Defense mechanisms show up inside the therapy section, not just abnormal (2024 asked four in a row). Match them precisely: displacement (harassed at work → argues at home), projective identification in paranoia (Melanie Klein), isolation / undoing / reaction formation in OCD, and splitting in borderline personality disorder. Also do not confuse OCD's exposure treatment ERP (exposure and response prevention) with EMDR. Biopsychology, 65 questions over six years Biopsychology is the single biggest physiological load in the RML paper, and it repeats along a small set of predictable axes: which neurotransmitter goes with which disease, which lobe or structure does which job, and how the classic theories of emotion order the events. Learn the tables below cold and you clear most of the section on recognition alone. Repeats (2022, 2023, 2024, 2025): Neurotransmitter → function/disease is asked almost every year. Memorise the pairings: acetylcholine loss → Alzheimer's dementia (2022), dopamine degeneration in the substantia nigra → Parkinson's disease (2023), endorphins are the "feel-good" neurotransmitters (2024), and alcohol acts as an agonist at GABA receptors (2022). Neurotransmitter Signature link RML tests Acetylcholine Deficiency → Alzheimer's disease; muscle activation Dopamine Degeneration → Parkinson's; blocked by neuroleptics GABA Main inhibitory NT; alcohol is an agonist Endorphins "Feel-good" NT, pain relief and pleasure Serotonin / Dopamine Mood; targets of antidepressants and antipsychotics Repeats (2020, 2024): Lobe → function is a perennial. The frontal lobe handles cognitive/intellectual functioning and voluntary movement (2020, 2024), the parietal lobe interprets sensory information (2024), the occipital lobe processes vision, and the temporal lobe processes hearing and language. Lobe Main domain Frontal Voluntary movement, planning, intellect, personality Parietal Somatosensory, interpreting sensory input, spatial sense Occipital Vision Temporal Hearing, language comprehension, memory Repeats (2020, 2023, 2024, 2025): Subcortical structure → job is tested constantly. Fix these: hippocampus → consolidation of long-term memory and the site damaged in anterograde amnesia (2023, 2024); amygdala → emotion, fear and aggression, the "seat of emotion" (2023, 2025); hypothalamus → hunger/satiety centre and homeostasis (2021, 2024); medulla (brainstem) → breathing and heart rate (2023); pineal gland → melatonin and the circadian sleep-wake clock (2022, 2023). Structure Function RML fishes for Hippocampus Long-term memory consolidation; damaged in anterograde amnesia Amygdala Fear, aggression, emotional modulation of memory ("seat of emotion") Hypothalamus Satiety/hunger centre, homeostasis, links to pituitary Medulla oblongata Vital autonomic functions: breathing, heart rate Pineal gland Melatonin; circadian rhythm and sleep-wake cycle Trap: The "satiety centre" is the ventromedial hypothalamus (destroy it and the rat overeats), while the lateral hypothalamus is the hunger/feeding centre (destroy it and the rat stops eating). RML has flipped these both ways (2021, 2024). Who → what: Theories of emotion recur every cycle (2020, 2025). William James and Carl Lange (James-Lange theory): stimulus → bodily/physiological arousal → then the felt emotion ("we are afraid because we tremble"). Walter Cannon and Philip Bard (Cannon-Bard theory): arousal and emotion occur simultaneously. Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer (two-factor theory): arousal plus a cognitive label, which explains misattribution of arousal, feeling attraction when actually just aroused by fear (2020, 2025). Who → what: Paul Ekman is tied to the six universally recognised basic emotions: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust (2025 asks which one is NOT on the list, so anything like "contempt", "pride", or "love" is the answer). Repeats (2021, 2022, 2024): Alcohol-related amnesia recurs. Chronic alcoholism → Korsakoff's syndrome (thiamine/B1 deficiency), classically involving profound retrograde amnesia and confabulation (2021, 2024). Distinguish anterograde amnesia (cannot form NEW memories, hippocampal damage) from retrograde amnesia (loss of OLD memories). Who → what: Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) describes stress in three stages: alarm, resistance, exhaustion (2020). Pair this with the fight-or-flight (Walter Cannon, 1915) response, run by the sympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system with the adrenal glands (2024). Repeats (2022, 2024): Sleep architecture appears repeatedly. A normal night runs in roughly 90-minute cycles, giving about 4 to 6 NREM-REM cycles per major sleep period (2022, 2024). Know the NREM to REM progression and that REM is when vivid dreaming occurs. Who → what: Aphasia (loss of language) is the umbrella term (2020), and RML repeatedly probes Broca's aphasia: slow, laboured, non-fluent, telegraphic speech using only keywords, from damage to Broca's area in the left frontal lobe (2022, 2025). Contrast Wernicke's aphasia (fluent but meaningless speech, comprehension lost). Prosopagnosia is the specific inability to recognise faces (2024). Repeats (2024, 2025): Sensory systems and thresholds recur. The vestibular system (semicircular canals of the inner ear) senses spin and balance (2024); rods are the receptors for scotopic (dim-light) vision (2024); the human ear responds to roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (2024); and the absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity detectable 50% of the time (2025). RML tilt: The 2024 and 2025 papers lean on split-brain and imaging facts. Cutting the corpus callosum severs communication between the two hemispheres (Roger Sperry's split-brain work); the left hemisphere is typically dominant for language and analytic processing. For imaging, EEG gives the highest temporal resolution, while CT/MRI are used to view brain structure after a head injury (2025). RML tilt: The pituitary is repeatedly framed as the "master gland" that controls the other endocrine glands and regulates growth (2024). Neuroleptic (antipsychotic) drugs treat psychosis/schizophrenia and can cause tardive dyskinesia as a long-term side effect (2022, 2025). Cognitive Psychology, 37 questions over six years Cognitive Psychology in RML clusters tightly around three areas: the architecture of memory (stores, working memory, memory types), how and why we forget, and perception with its named theorists and biases. Almost every named-psychologist question in the section comes from perception or decision-making, so bind each name to its one idea. Who → what: The stage/multi-store model (Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin) runs sensory memory → short-term/working memory → long-term memory. Sensory memory holds information for the shortest duration (2020), and RML asks which store is NOT part of this model (2025). Encoding is the process that moves new information into memory (2025). Store Duration / capacity Sensory memory Shortest, under ~1 second; large raw capacity Short-term / working ~15-30 sec; ~7 items (George Miller) Long-term memory Potentially unlimited and long-lasting Who → what: Working memory (Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch) is a repeat favourite. Know its four components: the central

title: SGT University · MA Clinical Psychology Entrance · Study Material from Scratch
text: SGT University · MA Clinical Psychology Entrance · Study Material from Scratch Shree Guru Gobind Singh Tricentenary University, Gurugram · MA Clinical Psychology (RCI) · the whole general-psychology core taught from zero, packaged as one deep readable book. Built for Sihan, 2026-07-04. RML is in the bag, so this is the SGT drop. Here is the honest starting point: SGT does not publish a syllabus PDF the way RML's CET-166 does. The official line is that the entrance "syllabus will be as prescribed by SGT University as per the guidelines of the UGC," which in plain terms means a general psychology aptitude test drawn from the standard PG-psychology core, followed by a personal interview. So this book is not built off a leaked topic list; it is built off the seven areas a UGC-guideline general-psych test actually pulls from, the same base you have been grinding all cycle, just gathered into one place you can read top to bottom. Every theorist is given by full name, every test names its author, every therapy names who developed it, because that is exactly what a general-awareness paper rewards. Read it end to end and you have covered the subject core for SGT, and for every other general-psych entrance on your list. Entrance SGT MA Clinical Psychology (RCI) Two stages written test → interview No published syllabus UGC-guideline general psych 14 chapters · from scratch Exam ~11 Jul 2026, Gurugram campus Tracker SGT pattern & dates How to use this. This is a teaching text, not a cheatsheet: each chapter builds a topic from the ground up, then flags the exact traps a general-psych paper fishes for. The green Key boxes are the must-knows, the red Trap boxes are the confusions the paper exploits, the teal Who → what boxes are the theorist / founder / test pairings, and the amber Why boxes explain the mechanism so it sticks. The book now runs to fourteen content chapters: the seven core subject areas plus full stand-alone chapters on learning, memory and cognition, motivation and emotion, social psychology, personality, and intelligence, since a general-psychology paper samples every one of these. Read Section 1 first to set your priorities, then work the chapters. Because SGT has no negative-marking guidance published, treat every question as answerable and never leave a blank. Contents: 1 · How the SGT paper behaves 2 · Biopsychology & physiological 3 · Developmental 4 · Abnormal & clinical 5 · Assessment & testing 6 · Psychotherapy & counselling 7 · Statistics & research methodology 8 · General awareness & history 9 · Learning & conditioning 10 · Memory, attention & cognition 11 · Motivation & emotion 12 · Social psychology 13 · Personality 14 · Intelligence 15 · The attack plan & the interview 1 How the SGT paper behaves, and how to prep it Before any content, get the shape of the thing right, because half of prepping an entrance is knowing what you are walking into. SGT University runs its own offline entrance for the MA Clinical Psychology (RCI) programme at its Gurugram campus, in two stages: a written test followed by a personal interview . Unlike RML's CET-166, there is no standalone syllabus document, no published breakdown of number of questions, marks per question, duration, or negative marking. SGT's own pages say only that the syllabus follows UGC guidelines. That is not a gap in your prep; it is the design. A UGC-guideline general-psychology aptitude test means the paper samples broadly and shallowly across the whole PG-psychology base rather than drilling deep into one niche. Key. No published SGT syllabus is not a reason to panic; it is a reason to prep breadth over depth. The paper rewards the person who can recognise a term, a theorist, or a test from any corner of psychology, not the person who has memorised one topic to the bone. The seven areas the written test draws on Mapping the "UGC-guideline general psychology" wording onto how these general aptitude papers actually behave, the written test pulls from seven areas. This book has one section per area, in this order: # Area What it samples 2 Biopsychology / physiological Neuron, action potential, neurotransmitters, brain structures, endocrine, sensation & perception 3 Developmental Jean Piaget, Erik Erikson, Lev Vygotsky, attachment, moral & lifespan development 4 Abnormal / clinical DSM-5-TR & ICD-11, the major disorders, etiology, case vignettes 5 Assessment / testing Reliability & validity, intelligence & personality tests, projectives, Indian adaptations 6 Psychotherapy & counselling Psychoanalytic, behavioural, CBT, humanistic; who developed which therapy 7 Statistics & research methodology Descriptive & inferential stats, designs, sampling, ethics 8 General awareness / aptitude History & schools of psychology, learning, memory, social psychology, key theorists Why this order. Biopsychology and developmental are the highest-density "recognise the fact" areas in any general paper, so they lead. Assessment and therapy are where the "who made this" questions cluster, so full names are non-negotiable there. General awareness is last because it is the catch-all that ties the schools and theorists together once you have met them in the earlier sections. Trap. Do not confuse SGT's general aptitude test with a deep clinical M.Phil paper. A general-psych entrance will ask "who proposed the hierarchy of needs" (Abraham Maslow, 1943) far more often than it asks a fine-grained ICD-11 sub-code. Prep the recognisable landmarks of every area, not the deep cuts of one. How to spend the days you have Breadth pass first. Read all fourteen chapters once, front to back, so no area is a blank. That alone clears most of a general aptitude paper. Second pass on the founder boxes. The teal Who → what boxes are the single most exam-efficient thing here; a general paper is dense with "match the theorist / test / therapy to its author." Use your existing mocks as the drill. Everything on the site (the PYQ mocks, the common-section work, the bio and diagnostic sets) is the same base SGT samples. Sitting any of them is valid SGT practice. Prep the interview in parallel (Section 9): the second stage is a real gate, and it is the cheapest marks to secure because it rewards clarity about why you want clinical psychology, not more recall. 2 Biopsychology & Physiological Psychology Biopsychology (also called physiological psychology, biological psychology, or behavioural neuroscience) asks one question: how does the physical machinery of the body, above all the nervous system, produce behaviour, thought, emotion, and experience? To answer an entrance paper on this topic you must be able to build the brain from its smallest working part upward. We therefore start with the single cell, the neuron, and end with whole-brain imaging. Nothing here needs prior biology; every term is defined as it appears. 2.1 The Neuron: The Unit of the Nervous System The nervous system is built from billions of specialised cells called neurons (nerve cells) that receive, integrate, and transmit information as electrical and chemical signals. A neuron is not like an ordinary body cell; it is shaped for communication, with parts that collect signals at one end and pass them on at the other. Parts of a neuron Soma (cell body): the metabolic centre. It holds the nucleus and keeps the cell alive. Incoming signals are summed here. Dendrites: short, branching fibres that spread out from the soma like the branches of a tree (the word means "little tree"). They are the receiving surface; they collect signals from other neurons. Axon: a single long fibre that carries the outgoing signal away from the soma toward other cells. One neuron has many dendrites but usually just one axon (which may branch at its end). Myelin sheath: a fatty white insulating layer wrapped in segments around many axons. It speeds up signal conduction and stops the signal leaking. Myelin is why "white matter" is white. Nodes of Ranvier: the small unmyelinated gaps between segments of myelin. The signal jumps from node to node (see saltatory conduction). Terminal buttons (axon terminals, end feet): the swollen tips at the end of the axon branches. They store and release chemical messengers onto the next cell. Why. The neuron's shape is a receive-integrate-transmit pipeline: dendrites in, soma decides, axon out, terminals hand off. Every fact about signalling maps onto this direction of flow, so memorise the direction, not just the parts. Glial cells (neuroglia): the support staff Neurons are outnumbered by glial cells ("glia" means glue), which support, feed, insulate, and protect neurons. They do not fire signals themselves but are essential. Astrocytes: star-shaped cells that hold neurons in place, supply nutrients, mop up excess chemicals, and help form the blood-brain barrier. Oligodendrocytes: make the myelin sheath in the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord). One oligodendrocyte myelinates several axons. Schwann cells: make the myelin sheath in the peripheral nervous system (nerves outside the brain and cord). One Schwann cell myelinates one segment of one axon, and Schwann cells help peripheral nerves regenerate. Microglia: the immune cells of the nervous system; they clean up dead cells and fight infection. Trap. Papers love to swap myelin-makers: oligodendrocytes myelinate the CNS, Schwann cells myelinate the PNS. If a question mentions the brain or spinal cord, the answer is oligodendrocyte; if it mentions a peripheral nerve, the answer is Schwann. The neuron doctrine: Golgi versus Cajal In the late 1800s scientists argued whether the nervous system was one continuous web (the "reticular theory") or a set of separate cells. Camillo Golgi , an Italian physician, invented a silver-staining method (the "black reaction") that made single neurons visible, yet he believed the network was continuous. The Spaniard Santiago Ramon y Cajal used Golgi's own stain to show that neurons are separate, individual cells that merely communicate across tiny gaps. Cajal's view, the neuron doctrine , won. Who → what. Camillo Golgi → the silver stain that revealed neurons (but he backed the continuous-network theory). Santiago Ramon y Cajal → the neuron doctrine (neurons are discrete cells). They shared the 1906 Nobel Prize despite disagreeing. 2.2 Resting and Action Potentials: How a Neuron Fires The resting potential A neuron at rest is electrically charged, like a tiny battery. The inside of the axon is about −70 millivolts (mV) relative to the outside; this is the resting membrane potential . It exists because charged particles (ions) are unevenly spread across the membrane: sodium (Na+) is concentrated outside, potassium (K+) inside, and the inside carries a net negative charge. Key. Resting potential = about −70 mV, inside negative. The neuron is "polarised" and ready to fire. This imbalance is maintained by the sodium-potassium pump , a protein in the membrane that constantly pushes 3 sodium ions out for every 2 potassium ions it pulls in, using energy. Because it moves more positive charge out than in, it helps keep the inside negative. The action potential (the nerve impulse) When enough incoming signals push the membrane past a threshold (about −55 mV), the neuron fires an action potential , a rapid electrical spike that travels down the axon. It has clear phases: Depolarisation: sodium channels open, Na+ rushes in, and the inside shoots up toward +30 to +40 mV (briefly positive). Repolarisation: sodium channels close, potassium channels open, K+ flows out, and the charge drops back toward negative. Hyperpolarisation (undershoot): the charge briefly overshoots below −70 mV before the pump restores the resting state. Key. The all-or-none law : a neuron either fires a full action potential or none at all. The strength of a stimulus is coded by how often the neuron fires (frequency), not by making a bigger spike. Every spike is the same size. Refractory periods Absolute refractory period: immediately after firing, the neuron cannot fire again no matter how strong the stimulus (sodium channels are inactivated). Relative refractory period: shortly after, the neuron can fire again but only with a stronger-than-usual stimulus. Why. The refractory period forces the impulse to travel in one direction (down the axon, not backward) and sets an upper limit on firing rate. Saltatory conduction In myelinated axons the impulse does not crawl smoothly; it jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next (Latin saltare , to leap). This saltatory conduction is much faster and more energy-efficient than conduction along an unmyelinated fibre. Trap. When myelin is destroyed (as in multiple sclerosis), conduction slows and fails; saltatory conduction cannot occur without intact myelin and nodes. Do not confuse the nodes (bare gaps) with the myelin (insulation): the impulse jumps to the nodes because the myelinated stretches are skipped. 2.3 Synaptic Transmission: How Neurons Talk to Each Other Neurons do not touch. Between the terminal button of one neuron and the dendrite of the next lies a microscopic gap, the synapse (synaptic cleft). The signal crosses this gap chemically. The action potential reaches the terminal button of the presynaptic (sending) neuron. Calcium enters and causes tiny sacs called synaptic vesicles to move to the membrane. By exocytosis the vesicles fuse with the membrane and dump their neurotransmitter (chemical messenger) into the cleft. The neurotransmitter drifts across and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic (receiving) neuron, like a key in a lock. This opens channels and changes the postsynaptic cell's charge. The signal is then cleared by reuptake (the presynaptic neuron sucks the transmitter back in for reuse) or by enzymes that break it down. Excitation and inhibition EPSP (excitatory postsynaptic potential): the transmitter makes the postsynaptic cell more likely to fire (depolarises it toward threshold). IPSP (inhibitory postsynaptic potential): the transmitter makes it less likely to fire (hyperpolarises it away from threshold). Why. A neuron is a voting machine: it constantly adds up EPSPs and IPSPs arriving on its dendrites and soma (this is "summation"). Only if excitation outweighs inhibition past threshold does it fire. Behaviour is the net result of this balance across billions of cells. The discovery of neurotransmission Who → what. Otto Loewi → first proof of chemical neurotransmission. In a famous 1921 frog-heart experiment (reportedly designed in a dream) he stimulated the vagus nerve of one heart, collected its fluid, applied it to a second heart, and slowed that heart too. He named the substance "Vagusstoff" ("vagus substance"), later identified as acetylcholine , the first known neurotransmitter. Charles Sherrington → coined the term "synapse" and described reflex integration. 2.4 Major Neurotransmitters Different chemical messengers do different jobs, and many disorders and drugs work by changing one of them. Learn the function and the clinical link for each; entrance papers almost always test the link. Neurotransmitter Main function Disorder / drug link Acetylcholine (ACh) Muscle movement, learning, memory, arousal Loss of ACh neurons in Alzheimer’s disease; blocked at the junction in myasthenia gravis Dopamine Reward, motivation, voluntary movement, pleasure Too much (overactivity) linked to schizophrenia; too little (loss of cells) causes Parkinson’s disease Serotonin Mood, sleep, appetite, impulse control Low levels linked to depression and anxiety; SSRIs raise it Norepinephrine (noradrenaline) Alertness, arousal, fight-or-flight Involved in mood disorders and stress; targeted by some antidepressants GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) The main inhibitory transmitter; calms neural activity Low activity linked to anxiety and seizures; boosted by benzodiazepines and alcohol Glutamate The main excitatory transmitter; learning and memory Excess causes excitotoxicity (cell death from over-firing), implicated in stroke and seizures Endorphins Natural painkillers; pleasure and "runner’s high" Mimicked by opiate drugs (morphine, heroin), which bind endorphin receptors Key. Memorise the four highest-yield pairings: dopamine → schizophrenia (too much) and Parkinson’s (too little); serotonin → depression; GABA → anxiety (the calming brake); acetylcholine → Alzheimer’s and memory. Trap. GABA is inhibitory (the brain’s brake) and glutamate is excitatory (the accelerator). Papers reverse these constantly. Also note dopamine is the classic "two-disease" transmitter: excess → schizophrenia, deficit → Parkinson’s, which is why anti-schizophrenia drugs can cause Parkinson-like side effects. 2.5 Organisation of the Nervous System The whole nervous system splits into two great divisions: Central nervous system (CNS): the brain and the spinal cord. This is the control centre and integrator. Peripheral nervous system (PNS): all the nerves outside the CNS that connect it to the body and outside world. The PNS divides again: Somatic nervous system: carries sensory information in and controls voluntary skeletal muscles (moving your arm). Autonomic nervous system (ANS): controls involuntary functions of glands and internal organs (heartbeat, digestion). It has two opposing branches. Situation Sympathetic branch Parasympathetic branch Role "Fight or flight" (Walter Cannon, 1915) (arouses, spends energy) "Rest and digest" (calms, conserves energy) Heart rate Speeds up Slows down Pupils Dilate (widen) Constrict (narrow) Digestion Inhibited Stimulated Trap. Sympathetic and parasympathetic are opposites, but both belong to the autonomic system. A common wrong answer treats the sympathetic system as "voluntary"; it is involuntary. Voluntary muscle control is the somatic system. The spinal cord and the reflex arc The spinal cord relays messages between brain and body, but it can also act on its own in a reflex arc , a fast, automatic response that bypasses the brain. When you touch a hot stove: a sensory (afferent) neuron carries the pain signal to the spinal cord, an interneuron passes it across, and a motor (efferent) neuron orders the muscle to pull back, all before the brain even registers the pain. Why. Routing simple protective reflexes through the spinal cord alone saves the time it would take to consult the brain; the brain is informed a fraction of a second later. This is why you yank your hand away before you feel the burn. 2.6 The Brain The brain is traditionally divided into hindbrain, midbrain, and forebrain, roughly from bottom-and-back (older, survival functions) to top-and-front (newer, higher functions). Hindbrain Medulla (medulla oblongata): controls vital automatic functions, heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure. Damage is fatal. Pons: a bridge relaying signals between higher and lower brain; involved in sleep, arousal, and facial movement. Cerebellum ("little brain"): coordinates balance, posture, and smooth, well-timed voluntary movement; also involved in some learning. Damage causes clumsy, jerky movement. Midbrain A relay hub for vision and hearing reflexes and for movement. It contains parts of the reticular formation, a network running through the brainstem that controls arousal, alertness, and the sleep-wake cycle. Forebrain and the limbic system The forebrain contains the most advanced structures. Beneath the cortex sits the limbic system , the emotional and motivational core: Amygdala: the fear and emotion centre; tags experiences as threatening; central to aggression and emotional learning. Hippocampus: forms new long-term memories and supports spatial navigation. Damage causes an inability to form new memories. Hypothalamus: the body’s regulator; controls hunger, thirst, temperature, sex drive, and it commands the pituitary gland (the link between brain and hormones). Remember the "four Fs": feeding, fighting, fleeing, and sexual behaviour. Thalamus: the great relay station ; nearly all sensory information (except smell) passes through the thalamus on its way to the cortex. Trap. Do not confuse hippocampus (memory formation) with hypothalamus (drives and hormones), or thalamus (sensory relay) with hypothalamus (regulation and pituitary control). Amygdala = emotion/fear; hippocampus = memory. These four are the most-tested structures in the whole section. The cerebral cortex: four lobes The wrinkled outer layer of the forebrain, the cerebral cortex , is where perception, thought, and language happen. Each hemisphere has four lobes: Lobe Location Main function Frontal Front Planning, decision-making, personality, voluntary movement (motor cortex), speech production Parietal Top-back Touch, temperature, pain, body position (somatosensory cortex) Temporal Sides (near temples) Hearing, language comprehension, memory Occipital Back Vision (visual cortex) Language areas and hemispheric specialisation Who → what. Paul Broca → Broca’s area (in the left frontal lobe), for speech production ; damage causes Broca’s aphasia (halting, effortful speech, comprehension intact). Carl Wernicke → Wernicke’s area (in the left temporal lobe), for language comprehension ; damage causes Wernicke’s aphasia (fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension). Roger Sperry → split-brain research on hemispheric specialisation (Nobel Prize 1981). The two hemispheres are somewhat specialised (lateralisation): for most people the left hemisphere handles language, logic, and analysis, while the right hemisphere handles spatial ability, faces, and holistic processing. They are joined by the corpus callosum , a thick band of fibres. Roger Sperry studied "split-brain" patients whose corpus callosum was cut to treat epilepsy; his experiments showed the two halves could then work independently, revealing what each side does on its own. Trap. Broca = b roken, halting speech (production); Wernicke = w ordy, fluent nonsense (comprehension). Both areas are in the left hemisphere for most people. Also: each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body (contralateral control). 2.7 The Endocrine System Alongside the fast electrical nervous system runs a slower chemical one: the endocrine system , a set of glands that release hormones directly into the bloodstream to act on distant organs. Pituitary gland: the "master gland", sitting under the hypothalamus. It releases hormones that control the other endocrine glands (and it is itself controlled by the hypothalamus). Adrenal glands: release adrenaline (epinephrine) for fight-or-flight (Walter Cannon) and cortisol for stress. Thyroid gland: releases thyroxine, which sets the body’s metabolic rate. Pineal gland: releases melatonin, which regulates sleep and the day-night (circadian) cycle.
