The HPA axis and key hormones The stress response runs on the HPA axis : the H ypothalamus signals the P ituitary, which signals the A drenal glands to release cortisol. This is the body’s slow, sustained stress system. Cortisol: the main stress hormone; mobilises energy but harms health if chronically high. Adrenaline (epinephrine): the fast surge that races the heart in an emergency. Oxytocin: the "bonding" hormone; released in childbirth, breastfeeding, and social attachment. Thyroxine: controls metabolism and energy use. Melatonin: promotes sleep and tracks the light-dark cycle. Why. Nervous versus endocrine is a speed-versus-duration trade-off. The nervous system sends fast electrochemical signals down fixed wires for immediate, brief effects; the endocrine system sends slower hormones through the blood for widespread, longer-lasting effects. The hypothalamus is the bridge that lets the brain command the hormones. Trap. The pituitary is the "master gland", but it takes orders from the hypothalamus (a brain structure, not a gland in the usual sense). So the true top of the chain is the hypothalamus, which is why the same structure keeps appearing in both the brain and endocrine sections. 2.8 Sensation and Perception: The Basics Sensation is the raw detection of a stimulus by a sense organ; perception is the brain’s interpretation of that sensation into a meaningful experience. Sense organs first perform transduction : converting physical energy (light, sound, pressure) into the neural signals the brain can read. Thresholds and psychophysics Absolute threshold: the smallest amount of a stimulus a person can detect 50% of the time (e.g. a candle flame seen far away on a dark night). Difference threshold (just noticeable difference, JND): the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected. Who → what. Ernst Weber → Weber’s law: the JND is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, not a fixed amount (adding one candle to ten is noticeable; adding one to a hundred is not). Gustav Fechner → founded psychophysics and extended Weber’s work into a law relating physical stimulus strength to perceived sensation. The visual pathway Light enters the eye and lands on the retina , which holds two kinds of receptor cells: Rods: many, at the edges; work in dim light; see in black and white; give night vision. Cones: concentrated in the centre (fovea); work in bright light; give colour and sharp detail. Signals leave the eye by the optic nerve and travel to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Two classic theories explain colour vision: Who → what. Thomas Young and Hermann von Helmholtz → the trichromatic (three-colour) theory: the retina has three cone types tuned to red, green, and blue, and all colours arise from their combined activity. Ewald Hering → the opponent-process theory: colour is coded by opposing pairs (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white); one member of a pair is excited while the other is inhibited. Trap. The two colour theories are not rivals; both are correct at different stages. Trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz) operates at the cones (retina) ; opponent-process (Hering) operates later , in the retinal ganglion cells and brain. Opponent-process best explains afterimages (stare at green, look away, see red). Auditory basics Sound waves enter the ear, vibrate the eardrum, pass through three tiny bones, and reach the fluid-filled cochlea in the inner ear. Hair cells in the cochlea transduce the vibrations into neural signals sent along the auditory nerve to the temporal lobe. Pitch corresponds to the frequency of the wave and loudness to its amplitude (measured in decibels). 2.9 Research Methods in Biopsychology To study a brain we cannot open, biopsychologists use recording, imaging, and damage-based methods, plus genetics to separate nature from nurture. Recording and imaging techniques Method What it does Shows structure or function? EEG (electroencephalogram) Records electrical brain waves from scalp electrodes; excellent timing Function (activity over time) ERP (event-related potential) Averages EEG responses time-locked to a specific stimulus to isolate the brain’s reaction to it Function (precise timing) CT (computed tomography) X-ray scan giving a still picture of brain anatomy Structure PET (positron emission tomography) Tracks a radioactive tracer to show which areas use most glucose/blood Function (metabolic activity) fMRI (functional MRI) Tracks blood-oxygen flow to map active regions; good spatial detail Both, but prized for function Lesion studies Observe behaviour after a brain area is damaged or removed to infer its function Function (by loss) Trap. Sort methods by their strength: EEG and ERP have superb temporal resolution (when) but poor spatial detail (where); fMRI and PET have good spatial resolution (where) but slower timing. CT gives structure only; fMRI and PET show function. Lesion evidence shows what a region is needed for, not everything it does. Behaviour genetics Behaviour genetics studies how much of a trait comes from genes versus environment. Twin studies: compare identical (monozygotic, 100% shared genes) with fraternal (dizygotic, ~50% shared) twins. If identical twins are far more alike on a trait, genes matter more. Adoption studies: compare adopted children with both their biological and their adoptive parents to separate genetic from environmental influence. Heritability: the proportion of the variation in a trait across a population that is due to genetic differences. It ranges from 0 to 1. Trap. Heritability is about variation within a population , not about a single individual. A heritability of 0.5 does not mean "half of your intelligence comes from genes"; it means half of the differences among people in that group trace to genetic differences. This distinction is a favourite trick question. Recap. Neuron = dendrites (in) → soma (integrate) → axon/myelin (out) → terminals; oligodendrocytes myelinate the CNS, Schwann cells the PNS; Cajal’s neuron doctrine beat Golgi’s network (they shared the 1906 Nobel). Resting potential −70 mV kept by the sodium-potassium pump; the action potential is all-or-none (depolarise, repolarise), jumps node to node (saltatory). Otto Loewi proved chemical transmission (acetylcholine, "Vagusstoff"). Key transmitter links: dopamine → schizophrenia (excess) and Parkinson’s (deficit), serotonin → depression, GABA (inhibitory) → anxiety, glutamate (excitatory) → excitotoxicity, ACh → Alzheimer’s. CNS vs PNS; somatic (voluntary) vs autonomic (sympathetic fight-or-flight vs parasympathetic rest-and-digest); the spinal reflex arc bypasses the brain. Brain: medulla (vital signs), cerebellum (coordination); limbic amygdala (fear), hippocampus (memory), hypothalamus (drives + pituitary), thalamus (sensory relay); four lobes (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital); Broca (speech production) vs Wernicke (comprehension), both left; Roger Sperry’s split-brain work. Pituitary is master gland under the hypothalamus; HPA axis releases cortisol. Weber-Fechner thresholds; rods (dim, night) vs cones (colour, detail); Young-Helmholtz trichromatic (cones) plus Hering opponent-process (later, explains afterimages). EEG/ERP = timing, fMRI/PET = location, CT = structure; twin and adoption studies define heritability as population-level variation, not an individual’s fixed fraction. 2.10 Sleep, consciousness and biological rhythms Consciousness is the awareness a person has of their own thoughts, feelings and surroundings at any given moment. It is not a single fixed state but a continuum that shifts across the day and night, from alert wakefulness through drowsiness into the various stages of sleep. Sleep is not simply the switching off of the brain. It is an active, organised, rhythmic process that the body drives on a roughly 24-hour schedule, and studying it reveals how deeply behaviour is governed by biology. Biological rhythms and the circadian clock A biological rhythm is any cyclical change in a bodily process that repeats over a regular period. The most important for behaviour is the circadian rhythm , from the Latin circa (about) and dies (a day), meaning a cycle that lasts about 24 hours. The sleep-wake cycle, body temperature, and the release of many hormones all follow a circadian pattern. Rhythms shorter than a day are called ultradian (for example the stages of a single sleep cycle repeating through the night), and rhythms longer than a day are called infradian (for example the roughly monthly menstrual cycle). The internal clock that keeps the circadian rhythm running is a tiny cluster of cells in the hypothalamus called the suprachiasmatic nucleus , usually shortened to the SCN. It sits just above the point where the optic nerves cross, which is why it can receive information about light directly from the eyes. Even with no external cues the SCN keeps ticking on a cycle close to, but not exactly, 24 hours. External cues that reset the clock to the true day are called zeitgebers , a German word meaning time-givers . Light is the most powerful zeitgeber. Who → what. The SCN was identified as the master circadian pacemaker through animal lesion studies in the 1970s: destroying it abolished the regular sleep-wake and hormonal rhythms, showing that this one small structure sets the body's daily timing. When light falls on the retina, signals travel to the SCN, which then instructs the pineal gland , a small structure deep in the brain, to adjust its output of the hormone melatonin . Melatonin promotes sleepiness. In darkness the pineal gland releases more melatonin, and in bright light it releases less. This is the chemical bridge between the light of the outside world and the felt urge to sleep. Key. Light → eye → suprachiasmatic nucleus (the clock) → pineal gland → melatonin (the sleep signal). Darkness raises melatonin; light lowers it. The sleep cycle: NREM and REM Sleep is measured chiefly with the electroencephalograph , or EEG, a device that records the electrical activity of the brain through electrodes on the scalp. As a person falls asleep and moves through the night, the EEG traces out characteristic patterns of brain waves that let researchers divide sleep into distinct stages. Sleep falls into two broad kinds: NREM (non-rapid-eye-movement) sleep and REM (rapid-eye-movement) sleep. Under the modern scheme, NREM sleep is divided into three stages, N1 to N3, followed by a period of REM. One full pass through these stages takes roughly 90 minutes, and the cycle repeats four to six times a night (an ultradian rhythm). As the night goes on, the deep NREM stages shorten and the REM periods lengthen. Stage N1 (light sleep): the brief transition from wakefulness into sleep. Brain waves slow from alpha toward theta. The person is easily woken and may experience sudden jerks. Stage N2: a deeper light sleep marked on the EEG by short bursts of activity called sleep spindles and single large waves called K-complexes . Most of a night is spent here. Stage N3 (slow-wave or deep sleep): the deepest sleep, dominated by large slow delta waves. It is hardest to wake someone from this stage, and it is thought to be the most physically restorative. Sleepwalking and night terrors, when they occur, arise here. REM sleep: after the deep stages the brain returns to a fast, active pattern resembling waking. The eyes dart rapidly beneath closed lids, and the body's voluntary muscles are effectively paralysed. Most vivid dreaming happens here. EEG wave patterns Each state of consciousness has a signature brain-wave pattern, described by its frequency (how many cycles per second, measured in hertz) and amplitude (how tall the waves are). As a rough rule, the more alert and active the brain, the faster and smaller the waves; the deeper the rest, the slower and larger the waves. Wave Frequency Typical state Beta Fast (about 13 to 30 Hz) Alert, awake, actively thinking or concentrating Alpha Moderate (about 8 to 12 Hz) Awake but relaxed, calm, eyes often closed; drowsy onset Theta Slow (about 4 to 7 Hz) Light sleep, stages N1 and N2 Delta Very slow (below about 4 Hz), high amplitude Deep slow-wave sleep, stage N3 Trap. Do not confuse fast small beta waves (busy waking mind) with slow tall delta waves (deepest sleep). A common exam catch is that REM sleep shows a fast, waking-like EEG even though the person is deeply asleep and hard to wake; this mismatch is why REM is called paradoxical sleep . REM, paradoxical sleep and dreaming REM sleep is called paradoxical sleep because the brain looks awake on the EEG while the body is at its most still, the large muscles being temporarily paralysed (a state called atonia that stops us acting out dreams). Rapid eye movements, irregular breathing and heart rate, and vivid narrative dreams all belong to REM. People woken from REM report dreaming far more often and in more detail than those woken from NREM. Newborns spend a very large proportion of sleep in REM, which has led to the idea that REM supports brain development and the consolidation of memory. Theories of why we sleep There is no single agreed answer to why sleep evolved, but two broad families of theory dominate. Restorative theory: sleep serves to repair and restore the body and brain. During sleep, especially deep NREM, the body releases growth hormone, repairs tissue, clears metabolic waste, and the brain consolidates memories. On this view we sleep because sleep does necessary maintenance. Evolutionary or adaptive theory: sleep evolved to keep an animal safe and to conserve energy during the hours when it cannot forage or defend itself effectively. On this view sleep is an adaptation that reduced risk and saved calories, and different species sleep in patterns suited to their ecological niche. Common sleep disorders in brief Insomnia: persistent difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting restful sleep, despite adequate opportunity, causing daytime distress or impairment. Narcolepsy: a neurological disorder marked by overwhelming daytime sleepiness and sudden uncontrollable sleep attacks, sometimes with sudden loss of muscle tone (cataplexy) triggered by emotion, reflecting intrusions of REM-like states into wakefulness. Sleep apnoea: repeated pauses in breathing during sleep, often because the airway collapses, which briefly wakes the person again and again and leaves them unrefreshed and sleepy by day. 2.11 Behavioural genetics and evolution Behavioural genetics is the field that studies how much of the variation in behaviour and psychological traits across people can be traced to inherited biological factors versus the environment. It is the modern, evidence-based way of examining the old nature-versus-nurture question. Genes, chromosomes and DNA Inside the nucleus of almost every cell in the body are chromosomes , thread-like structures made of a molecule called DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid). Humans normally have 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs, one of each pair inherited from each parent. DNA carries the coded instructions for building and running the body, and a gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a particular product or trait. Genes are the basic units of heredity passed from parents to offspring. Key. DNA is the molecule; a gene is a stretch of DNA that codes for something; chromosomes are the long packaged strands of DNA. Genes sit on chromosomes; chromosomes are made of DNA. Genotype versus phenotype The genotype is the full set of genes an individual carries, the inherited genetic blueprint. The phenotype is the set of observable characteristics that actually appear, such as eye colour, height, or a behavioural tendency. The phenotype results from the genotype interacting with the environment. Two people can share a genotype for a trait yet differ in phenotype because of different experiences, nutrition, or circumstances. Dominant and recessive Genes often come in alternative versions called alleles . An allele is dominant if a single copy is enough to express its effect in the phenotype, and recessive if its effect appears only when two copies are present (one from each parent). This is why a recessive trait can skip generations, hidden in carriers who possess one copy but do not show it. Heritability Heritability is a statistic, expressed from 0 to 1 (or as a percentage), that estimates how much of the variation in a trait within a population is due to genetic differences among its members. It is one of the most misunderstood ideas in psychology. Trap. Heritability is about variation across a group, not about a single person. A heritability of 0.5 for a trait does NOT mean half of one individual's trait is caused by genes. It means about half of the differences between people in that population are associated with genetic differences. Heritability also depends on the environment studied and can change if conditions change. Twin and adoption studies Because we cannot ethically control people's genes or upbringing, behavioural geneticists use natural experiments. The two main designs are twin studies and adoption studies. Monozygotic twins (identical twins) develop from a single fertilised egg that splits, so they share essentially 100 percent of t

title: Effects, Phenomena, Theories & Originators
text: Effects, Phenomena, Theories & Originators One consolidated lookup for every named effect, phenomenon, illusion, theory, complex and the people behind them. The five old sweeps overlapped heavily (an "effect" carries an originator; a theory carries a theorist), so each item now lives in exactly one entry: the definition, who coined it, the classic study, and the confusable lookalike, together. Drill it both directions: cover the "Who" column and name the person; cover the description and name the term. High-yield NIMHANS / MET ask this two ways. (1) Name the "____ effect / theory / complex" and ask who proposed it (answer = a person). (2) Describe a scene/finding with no name and ask you to name it (answer = the effect/theory). Almost every trap is a same-family lookalike (halo↔horn, Pygmalion↔Golem, placebo↔nocebo, James-Lange↔Cannon-Bard, McCall's T↔Student's t). Always learn each item with its twin. In this reference Named effects (grouped) Phenomena, illusions, biases & clinical signs Theories & models (by domain) Named complexes & syndromes Who originated what — theorists Psychometrics, statistics & standard scores 1. Named effects Every named "____ effect," its originator, and the one-line hook. Grouped by domain so the good-twin / bad-twin pairs sit together. 1.1 Memory & learning effects Effect Who What it is Zeigarnik effect Bluma Zeigarnik Interrupted / unfinished tasks are remembered better than completed ones. Von Restorff (isolation) effect Hedwig von Restorff The odd-one-out item in a list stands out and is recalled best. Serial position effect Ebbinghaus (named by Murdock) First + last items in a list recalled best (= primacy + recency together). Primacy effect — First items recalled well (rehearsed into long-term store). Recency effect — Last items recalled well (still in short-term store). A delay/distractor kills recency, not primacy. Spacing (distributed practice) effect Ebbinghaus Spread-out study beats cramming for long-term retention. Testing effect — Retrieving (self-testing) cements memory better than re-reading. Generation effect Slamecka & Graf Info you generate yourself is remembered better than info you just read. Self-reference effect Rogers, Kuiper & Kirker Material related to yourself is encoded and recalled better. Misinformation effect Elizabeth Loftus Post-event misleading info distorts the original memory (eyewitness work). Picture superiority effect Allan Paivio (dual-coding) Pictures are remembered better than words. Encoding-specificity / context effect Tulving & Thomson Recall is best when retrieval cues match the encoding context (state/context-dependent memory). Levels-of-processing effect Craik & Robert Lockhart Deeper (semantic) processing → better memory than shallow (visual/acoustic). Trap Remove the delay/distractor and it's the recency end that vanishes (STM decays); primacy survives. Zeigarnik = unfinished remembered; von Restorff = distinctive remembered — don't merge them. 1.2 Attention & perception effects Effect Who What it is Stroop effect J. Ridley Stroop Slower to name ink colour when the word spells a different colour (automatic reading interferes). Cocktail-party effect Colin Cherry Selective attention to one voice in a crowd, yet you still catch your own name. McGurk effect McGurk & MacDonald What you see the mouth do changes what you hear (audio-visual speech fusion). Ventriloquist effect — Sound is mislocated toward a plausible visual source. Troxler effect (fading) Ignaz Troxler Fixate steadily and unchanging peripheral stimuli fade from awareness. Motion aftereffect (waterfall illusion) — After staring at motion, a static scene appears to drift the opposite way. Bouba/kiki effect Wolfgang Köhler (later Ramachandran) People map "bouba" to round shapes, "kiki" to spiky ones (sound symbolism). Tetris effect — Heavy repeated activity intrudes into imagery/dreams. Trap The phi phenomenon and autokinetic phenomenon are labelled "phenomena," not "effects" — they live in §2.1. Same content, the label decides where the examiner files it. 1.3 Social & expectancy effects Effect Who What it is Halo effect Edward Thorndike One good trait (e.g. looks) bleeds into an overall positive judgement. Horn(s) effect — The negative mirror of halo: one bad trait darkens the whole impression. Pygmalion (Rosenthal) effect Rosenthal & Jacobson High teacher/leader expectations → the person actually performs better (self-fulfilling prophecy). Golem effect — Low expectations → worse performance (the dark twin of Pygmalion). Hawthorne effect Elton Mayo (Western Electric studies) People change behaviour because they know they're being observed. John Henry effect Saretsky A control group tries extra hard because it knows it's the comparison (a research artefact). Mere-exposure effect Robert Zajonc Repeated exposure alone increases liking (also a persuasion lever: familiarity breeds liking). Bystander effect Latané & John Darley More onlookers → less likely any one helps (diffusion of responsibility). After Kitty Genovese. 5-step decision model: notice → interpret → take responsibility → know how → act. (Theory form in §3.6.) Ringelmann effect Max Ringelmann Per-person effort drops as group size grows (precursor to social loafing). Pratfall effect Elliot Aronson A competent person becomes more likeable after a small blunder. Spotlight effect Thomas Gilovich Overestimating how much others notice you. False-consensus effect Lee Ross Overestimating how many people share your views/choices. Lake Wobegon / above-average effect — Most people rate themselves above average (illusory superiority). Cheerleader effect — Faces look more attractive in a group than alone. Overjustification effect Lepper, Greene & Richard Nisbett Paying for an already-enjoyed activity kills the intrinsic motivation. Boomerang effect Hovland tradition (akin to Brehm) Persuasion backfires, shifting the attitude the opposite way (cousin of reactance, §3.6). Trap Same-study, different name: Pygm

title: Lookalikes — telling two close terms apart on the options
text: Lookalikes — telling two close terms apart on the options For when plain definitions aren't enough and the trap is a near-identical distractor. Each block is one confusable pair: what's the same (why both look right), what differs (line by line), and the one tell — the single thing in the stem that splits them. Read the tell, not the whole block, on exam day. Built 2026-05-25. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How to use it. The examiner picks two real, correct-sounding terms and bets you can't split them. Don't re-derive both definitions. Find the tell word in the stem (added vs removed? up vs down? before vs after? thought vs act?) and the option falls out. These are the pairs that actually bleed marks on MET/NIMHANS. Jump to: 1. Learning & conditioning 2. Developmental 3. Sensation & perception 4. Memory & cognition 5. Stats & research 6. Abnormal / clinical 7. Defense mechanisms 8. Therapy 9. Social 10. Intelligence 1. Learning & conditioning Classical conditioning vs Operant conditioning Same: both are associative learning; both show acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation and discrimination. Classical (Ivan Pavlov) Operant (B. F. Skinner) Behaviour Involuntary, reflexive (salivation, fear) Voluntary, emitted (lever press) Association Stimulus → stimulus (CS–US) Behaviour → consequence (response–reinforcer) Learner Passive, responds to a cue Active, operates on the environment Reinforcer timing Comes before/with the response Comes after the response The tell: Is the behaviour automatic and triggered by a cue that comes first (classical), or voluntary and shaped by what happens after (operant)? Any "reward / consequence / punishment" in the stem → operant. Negative reinforcement vs Punishment Same: both are operant procedures and both usually involve an aversive/unpleasant stimulus, so they read alike. Negative reinforcement Punishment Effect on behaviour Increases it Decreases it What happens Removes an aversive stimulus (take painkiller → pain gone) Adds aversive (positive) or removes pleasant (negative) "Negative" means Subtraction, not "bad" — The tell: Did the behaviour go up or down ? Up = reinforcement (negative = the bad thing was taken away ). Down = punishment. "Negative" is about removal, never about being unpleasant. Positive punishment vs Negative punishment Same: both decrease a behaviour. Positive punishment Negative punishment Operation Add something aversive (scolding, spanking) Remove something pleasant (take phone, time-out, fine) Other name — Response cost / omission The tell: Positive = something was added ; negative = something was taken away . Both still reduce the behaviour, so judge by add vs subtract, not by good vs bad. Primary reinforcer vs Secondary reinforcer Same: both strengthen behaviour when they follow it. Primary Secondary (conditioned) Why it reinforces Innately satisfies a biological need (food, water, sex, warmth) Learned value through association Learning needed? No Yes (money, tokens, praise, grades) The tell: Does it satisfy a body need directly (primary) or only because you learned it stands for something else (secondary)? Money is the classic secondary reinforcer. Shaping vs Chaining Same: both build complex operant behaviour using reinforcement. Shaping Chaining What's reinforced Successive approximations to one target behaviour Linking a sequence of already-learned behaviours Picture it Refining one act closer and closer Step 1 → step 2 → step 3 as a chain The tell: One behaviour polished step-by-step (shaping) vs several separate behaviours joined in order (chaining). Stimulus generalisation vs Stimulus discrimination Same: both describe how a conditioned response transfers (or doesn't) across stimuli. Generalisation Discrimination Response to similar cues Yes — spreads to stimuli like the CS No — only the exact CS triggers it Little Albert (John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner, 1920) Feared all furry white things Would fear only the rat The tell: Response spreads to lookalikes (generalisation) vs narrows to one exact cue (discrimination). 2. Developmental Assimilation vs Accommodation (Jean Piaget) Same: the twin processes of adaptation ; both are how a schema deals with new information. Assimilation Accommodation Schema Stays the same — new info forced into it Changes / a new one is created to fit reality Example Calls a whale a "fish" Learns a whale is a mammal, makes a new category The tell: Did the existing schema stay put (assimilation) or did it have to change (accommodation)? If the child updated their mental category, it's accommodation. Piaget vs Lev Vygotsky Same: both constructivists; both say the child actively builds knowledge rather than passively absorbing it. Piaget Vygotsky Engine of development The individual child exploring; cognition leads language Social/cultural interaction; language leads cognition Signature terms Stages, schema, assimilation/accommodation, egocentrism ZPD, scaffolding, More Knowledgeable Other, private speech The tell: Is the driver the child alone (Piaget) or a guiding social other / ZPD (Vygotsky)? Any "scaffolding" or "zone of proximal development" → Vygotsky. 3. Sensation & perception Sensation vs Perception Same: both are stages of taking in stimulus information. Sensation Perception What it is Raw detection by sense organs + transduction Brain's organisation & interpretation of it Direction Bottom-up (data in) Top-down (meaning added) The tell: Detecting the raw signal at the receptor (sensation) vs making sense of / recognising it (perception). Interpretation, meaning, recognition → perception. Absolute threshold vs Difference threshold (JND) Same: both are psychophysics thresholds (Weber/Fechner). Absolute threshold Difference threshold (JND) Detects Minimum intensity to detect a stimulus 50% of the time Smallest detectable change between two stimuli Law — Weber's law: JND is a constant proportion The tell: Detecting that one stimulu

So this pack is built differently: every block ends in the exact distinction the examiner uses to separate the two options that look identical. Read it for the contrasts, not the trivia. C.1 The schools of psychology (the "isms"), in order Almost every general paper has one "who founded / what method / which school" item. Learn them as a story: each school is a reaction to the one before it. School Core claim Method Key names Structuralism Break consciousness into its basic elements (sensations, feelings) Introspection Wilhelm Wundt (first lab, 1879), Edward Titchener Functionalism Why does the mind do what it does; its purpose and adaptation Observation, applied focus William James, Dewey, Angell Gestalt The whole is different from the sum of its parts; perception is organised Phenomenology Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler Psychoanalysis Behaviour is driven by the unconscious and early conflict Free association, dream analysis, case study Sigmund Freud, later Jung, Alfred Adler Behaviourism Study only observable behaviour; the mind is a black box Controlled experiment, conditioning John B. title: Mock Debriefs & Weak-Spot Fixes
text: Mock Debriefs & Weak-Spot Fixes Every concept you got wrong, guessed, or flagged across all the mocks (MET Mock 1, the NIMHANS PYQ-based mock, the diagnostic-baseline drills, and the MPhil/PEP sets) consolidated into one corrective read, organised by topic, not by which mock it came from. Where a miss recurred across mocks it is marked as a persistent weak spot. This is where you fix what tripped you. Nothing is cut: every corrected answer, distractor analysis, mnemonic, and exam trap from the originals lives here, merged so each concept appears once. These are your real syllabus, ranked by how often and how badly they recurred. Each links to its full fix below. Weak spot Where it recurred The fix in one line Pituitary / hypothalamus / endocrine axis NIMHANS mock (3 of 6 biopsych wrongs), diagnostic baseline FLAT PiG anterior pituitary; melatonin is pineal; cortisol is adrenal cortex , not medulla; hypothalamus integrates endocrine + autonomic Neuroanatomy: tracts, lobes, basal ganglia MET Mock 1 (6 biopsych wrongs) Corticospinal crosses at medullary pyramids; right parietal → left neglect; red nucleus is NOT basal ganglia Therapy school attribution MET Mock 1 (4 wrongs), NIMHANS (3 wrongs) Match technique → school → founder by trigger word; empty chair = Fritz Perls, musterbation = Albert Ellis, therapeutic community = Maxwell Jones Standard scores & WAIS structure Both mocks, diagnostic Subtest scaled M=10 SD=3; index M=100 SD=15; +1 SD = 84th pct; VCI + PRI = 3 core subtests each Reliability statistic ↔ concept NIMHANS, MET, diagnostic (Cohen's kappa missed twice) Kappa = inter-rater categorical; alpha/KR-20 = internal consistency; ICC = inter-rater continuous Sampling: stratified vs cluster vs non-probability MET Mock 1 + NIMHANS (quota/cluster swapped) Stratified = sample within strata; cluster = whole clusters; "can't compute sampling error" = non-probability (quota) ICD vs DSM durations NIMHANS (schizophrenia), MET (dysthymia, PTSD clusters) NIMHANS leans ICD: schizophrenia ≥1 month (ICD) vs ≥6 months (DSM); read which classification the stem names Named social-psych concepts NIMHANS (Genovese, Type D, anomie all wrong) Pure trivia: learn the named effect + its discoverer + its two-factor mechanism Sleep architecture (REM vs delta) Diagnostic (twice), MET Mock 1 (elimination) REM = atonia + wake-like EEG (paradoxical); delta/N3 = slow wave + normal tone; parasomnias (sleepwalking) are N3 "NOT / EXCEPT" negation-blindness Every mock — careless misses Underline the negation before reading options; this is your most expensive avoidable error High-yield Your self-notes are the syllabus. Every "wtf is X" / "never read this" / "don't know shit about this" you wrote on a question is a topic you had not opened. The same notes recurred across mocks, which means a gap left unfixed reappears. The NIMHANS mock sat at 71.25 vs an 80 cutoff (gap 8.75 = roughly 9 wrongs to convert); 6 of those wrongs were in biopsych alone, so fixing that one section clears the line. On MET Mock 1 your attempted-accuracy was 92% (49 right, 4 wrong) but you skipped 47 — there the gap was coverage, not accuracy. PYQ analysis of 300 NIMHANS questions (2023–25) shows Therapy + Abnormal + Biopsych together = ~49% of marks; that is where to spend time. Trap Your guessing is luck-loaded. On the NIMHANS mock you guessed ~17 times and got 14 right; that regresses toward ~50% on the real paper, so plan against a score nearer 68 than 71. A guess is only worth it on MET-style scoring (+4/−1) once you have eliminated 2+ options. Exam-day execution rules Underline NOT / EXCEPT / LEAST / ALL in the stem before reading options. Half your "knew it but got it wrong" misses are negation-blindness (the ACTH/melatonin pituitary question, the Bandura "not required" question). ~20% of NIMHANS PYQs are NOT-stems. On a NOT-question, pick the outlier , not the most familiar item. On antonym / odd-one-out items, find the outlier first. If 3 of 4 options agree in meaning, the 4th is almost always the answer (gregarious: 3 synonyms + reclusive). Read the relationship in the stem — synonym? antonym? part-whole? cause-effect? — before scanning options. Eliminate extreme-word options on RC main-idea questions: "every, always, never, all, none, only, must" are usually too strong. Pick the most general statement the passage actually supports. Hedging language ("can," "may," "in some cases," "a range of") → tone is "supportive but qualified," not absolute. If the stem names ICD, give ICD durations; if DSM, give DSM. If unspecified on NIMHANS, default to ICD (Indian exam). MET often leans DSM. Don't guess on biostats unless the RR/OR/HR/NNT table is firm. You were guessing 4–5 of 10 biostats questions — a coin flip on ~20% of NIMHANS marks. Pacing: 100 Qs / 90 min ≈ 54 sec/Q. Over 90 sec → mark and skip, return later. Don't change a first instinct unless you find a concrete reason. Last 5 minutes: never leave a blank where there is no negative marking; with −0.25, only answer if you eliminated 2 options. Length of options is not a reliable tell on the real paper — don't lean on it. NIMHANS uses heavy case-vignette stems; practise extracting the diagnostic core fast. text: History of Psychology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) History of Psychology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Source pp. 3–7 Founding lab Wilhelm Wundt, Leipzig, 1879 Themes Western timeline · Greek & 17th-c. philosophers · schools & founders · Indian psychology India Sen Gupta, Calcutta 1916 · NIMHANS What this covers. The full history of psychology as a discipline: the Western chronology from the first psychology course (1875) through positive psychology (1998), the Greek theorists (Hippocrates' humoral theory, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle) and the 17th-century philosophers who framed the mind, the major schools of psychology with their founders and "forces," the parallel history of psychology and clinical psychology in India, and the Indian systems (Yoga, Buddhism, Hinduism, Jainism, Sufism) that form Indian psychology. Contents: 1 · Western Timeline 2 · Greek Theorists 3 · 17th-Century Philosophers 4 · Major Schools of Psychology 5 · Psychology in India 6 · Clinical Psychology in India 7 · Yoga Psychology 8 · Indian Psychology 1 · Western Timeline Timeline of psychology. A winding road timeline marking psychology milestones from the first psychology course in 1875 to positive psychology in 1998. Psycho Didi notes · p. 4 The chronology below tracks how psychology developed as a formal discipline, from its first course and laboratory to the emergence of each major school. Year Milestone 1875 First psychology course, by William James on Physiological Psychology at Harvard 1879 Wilhelm Wundt established the first psychological laboratory at the University of Leipzig, Germany 1892 American Psychological Association (APA) established 1896 Structuralism 1896 Functionalism 1900 Psychoanalysis (Sigmund Freud) 1912 Gestalt psychology (Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka and Wolfgang Köhler) 1913 Behaviourism (John B. Watson, 1913) 1940s Existentialism 1954 Humanistic psychology 1956 Cognitive psychology 1998 Positive psychology Key: Wundt (1879, Leipzig) founded the first psychology lab — the conventional birth of psychology as a science. James taught the first psychology course (1875) and later founded functionalism. 2 · Greek Theorists Greek theorists. The mind-body argument followed by the key ideas of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, next to an illustrated head. Psycho Didi notes · p. 4 The Mind–Body Argument Monists: mind and body are a single entity. Dualists: mind and body are separate entities. Hippocrates — Humoral Theory Hippocrates: humoral theory. Hippocrates' four humors (black bile, yellow bile, blood and phlegm) with the temperament linked to each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 4 Hippocrates was a dualist . His humoral theory linked four bodily humors to four temperaments. Humor Temperament Character Black bile Melancholic Sad, depressed, poetic and artistic Yellow bile Choleric Fiery, energetic, and passionate Blood Sanguine Warm-hearted, cheerful, optimistic, and confident Phlegm Phlegmatic Slow, quiet, rational, and consistent Socrates Dualist. Focused on morality . Explained eudemonia : long-lasting contentment, peace and happiness comes from building virtues like honesty, generosity, kindness, altruism, etc. Plato Dualist. Allegory of the cave and allegory of the chariot . Tripartite theory of the soul: rational (mind), emotional (spirited), and appetites (pleasures). Theory of forms: forms are universals and are the purest representation of things that actually exist. Aristotle Monist. Gave the first theory of cognitive sciences ; described sensation and perception — special sensible and common sensible . Theory of associationism : law of contiguity, law of frequency, law of similarity, law of contrast. Trap: Hippocrates, Socrates and Plato were dualists ; Aristotle was a monist . The four laws of association (contiguity, frequency, similarity, contrast) belong to Aristotle. 3 · 17th-Century Philosophers 17th century philosophers. The main ideas of Descartes, Locke, Kant and Dilthey set side by side in four columns. Psycho Didi notes · p. 4 René Descartes Famously stated "cogito, ergo sum" ("I think, therefore I am"). Innatism: the mind is born with ideas and knowledge. Dualist. Believed the pineal gland to be the seat of the soul. John Locke Empiricism: all knowledge comes from the senses. Tabula Rasa: individuals are born as a blank slate and all knowledge is acquired from the external world. Rejected innatism . Immanuel Kant Rejected the soul as the subject matter of psychology. Types of knowledge: A priori knowledge: innate knowledge — rationalism. A posteriori knowledge: empiricism. William Dilthey Best known for the way he distinguished between the natural and human sciences . Wrote Ideas for a Descriptive and Analytic Psychology (1894). Who → what: René Descartes → innatism + "cogito, ergo sum" + pineal gland; Locke → empiricism + tabula rasa; Kant → a priori / a posteriori knowledge; Dilthey → natural vs. human sciences. 4 · Major Schools of Psychology Major schools of psychology. A table of nine schools of psychology, from structuralism (1896) to transpersonal (1960s), with each founder and a short description. Psycho Didi notes · p. 5 Each school is defined by its founder(s), method of study, and central focus. Several are tagged as a "force" in psychology. School (year) Founder(s) Description Structuralism (1896) Edward Bradford Titchener Aimed to discover the structural elements of the mind. Method: introspection . Emphasized basic conscious elements. Functionalism (1896) William James Assumed that thinking, like the senses, developed because it was adaptive — it contributed to our ancestors' survival. The role of consciousness is adaptation . text: Research & Statistics — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Research & Statistics Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Type I vs Type II error Parametric vs non-parametric Reliability & validity t-test / ANOVA / factor analysis Research designs What this covers. Core research methodology and statistics for the exam: key terms, the research process, variables and designs, descriptive and inferential statistics (central tendency, dispersion, t-tests, ANOVA family), factor analysis and regression, reliability and validity (with threats), standard scores, and research ethics. Original diagrams. 14 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 9 to 13) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Terms to Know · 2 · What is Research (Steps & Types) · 3 · Variables · 4 · Research Designs · 5 · Descriptive Statistics · 6 · Inferential Statistics: t-test & ANOVA · 7 · Factor Analysis & PCA · 8 · Regression & Correlation · 9 · Reliability · 10 · Validity & Threats · 11 · Standard Scores · 12 · Research Ethics 1 · Terms to Know Research and statistics terms to know. Colour-coded cards defining core research and statistics terms, arranged around a central Type I and Type II error table. Psycho Didi notes · p. 9 Type I and Type II errors. A decision table that crosses the conclusion drawn with the true state of nature and marks the two correct conclusions (one labelled power), the Type I error and the Type II error. Psycho Didi notes · p. 9 Random assignment: giving every participant an equal chance of being in an experimental or control group. Internal validity: extent to which an experiment investigates what it is supposed to. External validity: generalisability. Demand characteristics: factors that influence a participant's behaviour based on what they think the purpose of the experiment is. Observer expectancy effect: experimenter communicates expectations unintentionally (Pygmalion / Rosenthal effect). Descriptive statistics: the branch of statistics which deals with descriptions of obtained data. Inferential statistics: deals with drawing conclusions about a large group of individuals on the basis of observations of a few participants. Parameter: a measurable characteristic of a population. Confidence interval: the mean of your estimate plus and minus the variation in that estimate. Null hypothesis: the claim that the effect being studied does not exist. Alternate hypothesis: statement that suggests there is a relationship between the variables being studied. Significance level: the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true, i.e., the probability of making a Type I error. Effect size: a quantitative measure of the magnitude of the experimental effect. The larger the effect size, the stronger the relationship between the two variables. Skewness: a lopsided and asymmetrical curve because of extreme data. Kurtosis: the term used to identify the degree of steepness or shallowness of a distribution. Post hoc test: "like a post mortem." Requires two conditions: a directional hypothesis and a significant F ratio. Trap: Type I error = null hypothesis is true but we reject it (alternate is false but we accept it) → "false alarm." Type II error = null hypothesis is false but we accept it (alternate is true but we reject it) → "miss." The significance level is the probability of making a Type I error. Key: Test power is the probability that the test will reject the null hypothesis when the alternate hypothesis is true, i.e., it will not make a Type II error. Feature Parametric test Non-parametric test Assumptions Generalizable; normal probability curve; uses mean; homogeneity of variance; probability sample; large sample size Assumption-free test Test power Higher Low test power Data type Interval / ratio Nominal data only Example t-test, ANOVA Chi square 2 · What is Research (Steps & Types) Research is a systematic, controlled, empirical, critical investigation. Steps Steps of research. The eight steps of research, from identifying a research problem to reporting findings. Psycho Didi notes · p. 10 Identify a research problem Review of literature Formulate a hypothesis Research design Collect data Analyse data Interpret data Report findings 3 · Variables Variables. The definition of a variable and its types: independent, dependent, extraneous (controlled and confounding), stimulus, organismic and behavioural. Psycho Didi notes · p. 10 A variable in research is a characteristic, number, or quantity that can be measured or counted and can take on different values. Type Description Independent variable (IV) Manipulated. Dependent variable (DV) Not manipulated; changes with change in IV. Extraneous variables Controlled. Confounding variables Uncontrolled extraneous variables that affect results. Stimulus variable e.g. light (always IV). Organismic variable e.g. age. Behavioural / response variable e.g. response rate (always DV). 4 · Research Designs Research: steps, variables and types of research. A flowchart branching from types of research into experiment, observation, correlation and special designs, alongside boxes on research steps, the definition of research and variables. Psycho Didi notes · p. 10 Experiment Experiment (lab): complete control on secondary (error) variance, e.g. lab experiment. Field experiment: secondary variance just greater than lab experiment; happens in a real setting; difficult to control extraneous variables. Quasi experiment: secondary variance greatest; no random assignment; non-equivalent groups, e.g. ex post facto studies. Correlation Not causation established; only helps us understand association. Gives us the direction of the relationship. Can't control extraneous variables. Generalization is possible. Types: positive, negative, zero. Trap: Correlation is not causation. It shows association and direction but cannot control extraneous variables. Observ

Development and organization of the nervous system; the forebrain and its four lobes; the limbic system and basal ganglia; diencephalon, midbrain and hindbrain; meninges and ventricles; important Broadmann's areas; techniques to study the brain; dysfunctions of the brain by region; neurotransmitters, hormones and the endocrine glands; glial cells; the peripheral nervous system (cranial and spinal nerves); and the autonomic nervous system. A flowchart that splits the nervous system into its divisions and traces each neural tube subdivision to the brain structures, ventricles and functions that develop from it. Psycho Didi notes · p. 15 The Nervous System is divided into the Central Nervous System (CNS) and the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) . Central Nervous System (CNS) — the Brain and the Spinal Cord . Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) — includes the Autonomic Nervous System (with its Sympathetic and Parasympathetic divisions) and the Somatic Nervous System (with its Afferent and Efferent nervous systems). Enteric Nervous System — controls the smooth muscle and glandular tissue in the digestive system. Development from the neural tube The brain develops from the neural tube , forming the following divisions: Primary vesicle Sub-division Becomes Forebrain (Prosencephalon) Telencephalon Cerebral hemispheres / four lobes Diencephalon Thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus Midbrain Mesencephalon Midbrain Hindbrain (Rhombencephalon) Metencephalon Pons and cerebellum Myelencephalon Medulla Don't confuse. Afferent nerves carry sensory information toward the CNS; Efferent nerves carry motor commands away from the CNS. Similarly, the Sympathetic system drives "fight or flight" (Walter Cannon, 1915) while the Parasympathetic system drives "rest and digest." 2 · The Forebrain & the Four Lobes The forebrain contains the neocortex , which contains the primary and association cortexes . Key. In the cerebral cortex, grey matter is outside and white matter is inside . Lobe Functions Frontal Lobe Executive functioning; association; motor cortex; Broca's area (left hemisphere); metacognition Parietal Lobe Sensation; haptic memory; proprioception; the " where " pathway Occipital Lobe Awareness of visual stimuli Temporal Lobe Auditory cortex; Wernicke's area (left hemisphere); part of the hippocampus; stores declarative memories; olfactory bulb 3 · The Limbic System The limbic system. A table giving the function and dysfunction of each limbic system and basal ganglia structure, with a small brain illustration beside each name. Psycho Didi notes · p. 16 Key structures of the limbic system, their functions, and dysfunctions: Name Function Dysfunction Amygdala Fear and rage; emotional and flashbulb memory (Roger Brown and James Kulik, 1977); sense fear and aggression in others; recognize learning, memory consolidation of emotional memories Kluver-Bucy syndrome; Hyperorality; Hypersexuality Hippocampus Encoding new memory; shaped like a seahorse; located in temporal lobe Anterograde amnesia; PTSD Septum Pleasure; inhibits aggression Sham rage / Septal rage Thalamus Relay (contralateral); contains LGN, MGN, VLN, Pulvinar Extreme pain in opposite side of the body Hypothalamus Homeostasis; controls endocrine glands; eating (Lateral, Anterior, Ventromedial); sleep (Suprachiasmatic nucleus) Aphagia; Adipsia Cingulate gyrus Memories; regulate aggression — Who → what. Papez (1937) — the Papez circuit: pain information transmission; recollecting pleasant memories. Dysfunction: aggressive behaviour, shyness. Amygdala (detail) Fear and rage center Encodes emotional memories Sense fear in others Hippocampus (detail) Encode declarative memories Role in PTSD Damaged by long exposure to glucocorticoids Cingulate gyrus (detail) Transmission Important in decision making Pain Social interaction Sex Largest part 4 · The Basal Ganglia The Basal Ganglia handle motor coordination and inhibition; they prevent unnecessary motor movements and activity in the white matter of the frontal lobe. Dysfunction: tremors, involuntary muscle movements, abnormal increase in tone, difficulty initiating movements, and abnormal posture. Components of the basal ganglia: caudate , putamen , globus pallidus , substantia nigra , nucleus accumbens , and subthalamic nuclei . title: Psychopathology
text: Psychopathology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Psychopathology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Biggest chapter (PDF pp. 25–55) DSM-5-TR (2022) & ICD-11 (2022) based Full disorder coverage, every duration cutoff MSE + all diagnostic groups + named syndromes Psychopharmacology appendix What this covers. The complete psychopathology core: the 4 D's of abnormality and the history of clinical psychology; the six approaches to treatment; case history and the full Mental Status Examination (MSE); the DSM and ICD classification systems and how they differ; then every major diagnostic group in DSM-5 order — neurodevelopmental, anxiety, OCD-related, depressive (mood), bipolar/mania, schizophrenia spectrum, trauma/stressor-related, dissociative, somatic, feeding/eating, sleep-wake, sexual/gender/paraphilic, personality, substance-related, and neurocognitive disorders — plus named eponymous syndromes, culture-specific syndromes, and a psychopharmacology reference. Original diagrams. 55 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 26 to 55) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Foundations & Approaches · 2 · Case History & MSE · 3 · DSM & ICD Classification · 4 · Neurodevelopmental Disorders · 5 · Anxiety Disorders · 6 · OCD & Related Disorders · 7 · Depressive (Mood) Disorders · 8 · Bipolar & Related Disorders · 9 · Schizophrenia Spectrum & Psychotic Disorders · 10 · Trauma & Stressor-Related Disorders · 11 · Dissociative Disorders · 12 · Somatic Symptom & Related Disorders · 13 · Feeding & Eating Disorders · 14 · Sleep-Wake Disorders · 15 · Sexual Dysfunctions, Gender Dysphoria & Paraphilias · 16 · Personality Disorders · 17 · Substance-Related & Addictive Disorders · 18 · Neurocognitive Disorders · 19 · Named / Eponymous Syndromes · 20 · Culture-Specific Syndromes · 21 · Psychopharmacology Reference 1 · Foundations & Approaches to Psychopathology Different Terms Introduction to psychopathology. Boxes listing the 4 D's of abnormality, early history of humane treatment, and definitions of abnormal, psychopathology and clinical psychology. Psycho Didi notes · p. 26 Abnormal: outlining atypicality. Abnormality depends on the intensity and frequency of behaviour. Psychopathology: part of abnormality — the medical angle of the abnormal (involves neuroimaging, aetiology, diagnosis, prognosis). Clinical Psychology: application of psychological principles in the treatment of mental disorders. The 4 D's of Abnormality: Deviance (social and statistical), Distress (causing unhappiness), Dysfunction (unable to show adaptive behaviour), Danger (to oneself and others). History of Clinical Psychology History of clinical psychology. A box noting the founding of the APA, Lightner Witmer's role, and the 1952 start of the DSM and ICD-6. Psycho Didi notes · p. 26 Historically the mentally ill were tied, chained and kept in inhumane conditions. 1826 — Philippe Pinel introduced moral therapy . 1802–1887 — Dorothea Dix advocated for humane treatment. APA founded 1892 ; first president G. Stanley Hall . Lightner Witmer — founder of clinical psychology; opened the first clinic. DSM introduced in 1952 ; ICD-6 in 1952 . Current diagnosis is more spectrum-oriented. Named figures. Pinel (moral therapy), Dorothea Dix (humane treatment advocacy), G. Stanley Hall (first APA president), Lightner Witmer (founder of clinical psychology, first clinic). The Six Approaches (with pros & cons) Approaches to psychopathology. A chart linking each approach's view of abnormality to its therapies and to its pros and cons. Psycho Didi notes · p. 26 Approach View of abnormality Methods Pros Cons Biological Organic problems, biochemical imbalances Drugs, ECT, surgery Effective for those who don't respond to other treatments Side effects; neglects non-biological problems Humanistic Failure to strive towards one's potential / being out of touch with feelings Client-centred, Gestalt, Existential Recognizes positive human goals, values and needs Unsupportive; limited research Behavioural Reinforcement history, environment Desensitization, aversion, operant conditioning (B. F. Skinner), token economy, modelling, social skills training Research supports effectiveness Not long-lasting; neglects cognitive processes Psychodynamic Internal / unconscious conflicts Free association, catharsis, analysis of resistance / transference / dreams First major alternative to biological treatment; abnormal function rooted in same processes as normal function Depends on therapist's subjective interpretation Cognitive Irrational / dysfunctional thoughts REBT, CBT Considerable research support Dysfunctional thinking may not cause abnormal functioning Sociocultural Dysfunctional society — — — 2 · Case History & Mental Status Examination Case History Case history and mental status examination. A one-page overview of case history taking, from personal information and history of present illness to past, family, personal and treatment history and physical examination. Psycho Didi notes · p. 27 Four assessment techniques are used: Observation, Conversation, Exploration, Testing . Personal information: name, father's/husband's name; sociodemographic profile (age, sex, education, occupation, socio-economic status, marital status, religion, residence, mother tongue, address); source of referral; type of admission; identification marks. Informant reliability — the 5 C's (SIMS): Contact (between patient and informant), Closeness of relationship, Continuity of the account, Consistency of the verbatim, Corroborativeness between sources. History of Present Illness — the factors Factor Definition Predisposing Factors operating from early life that determine vulnerability to develop a disorder Precipitating Events that occur shortly before the onset of a disorder Perpetuating Factors due to which the disorder is maintained or aggravated Limiting Factors which limit the illness from extensive progress Modifying Factors which modify the natural or expected course of the illness Mode of onset: abrupt, acute, insidious. Course of illness: continuous, episodic, fluctuating. Progress of illness: improving, deteriorating, static. Compliance: the extent to which the patient's behaviour (taking medications, following diets, other lifestyle changes) coincides with medical recommendations. Also covered: treatment history, past history (medical & psychiatric), family history (genogram, consanguinity), personal history (birth & early development, childhood disorders, home atmosphere, scholastic/extracurricular, occupational, menstrual, sexual & marital, forensic), premorbid personality (individualized styles of dealing with the environment characteristic of a person prior to onset), and physical examination (by physician). Mental Status Examination (MSE) General appearance and behaviour. A panel of MSE parameters covering general appearance, dress, posture, eye contact, estimate of age, body build, facial expression and touch with surroundings, with the disorders each finding suggests. Psycho Didi notes · p. 28 Attitude towards the examiner. Definitions of frank, defensive, cooperative, seductive, hostile, guarded, attentive and evasive attitudes, with the disorders linked to each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 28 Rapport and motor behaviour. Six strategies and three types of rapport, followed by a grid of motor behaviour signs with their definitions and associated disorders. Psycho Didi notes · p. 29 Speech. A panel of speech parameters such as intensity, pitch, quality, reaction time, speed, ease, productivity, deviation and manner of relating, with example disorders. Psycho Didi notes · p. 30 Cognitive functions. Definitions of orientation, attention, abstract ability, intelligence, concentration and memory, with the conditions in which each is disturbed. Psycho Didi notes · p. 31 Mood and affect. Definitions of mood and affect and the dimensions of affect: quality, mobility, intensity, reactivity, communicability, appropriateness and diurnal variation. Psycho Didi notes · p. 31 Thought. A panel describing disturbances of thought under stream, form, possession and content, with definitions and linked conditions. Psycho Didi notes · p. 32 Perception. Sensory distortions (changes in intensity, quality and spatial form) and sensory deception (hallucinations in each sense). Psycho Didi notes · p. 33 Other psychotic phenomena. Definitions of somatic passivity and the made phenomena: made act, made affect and made impulse. Psycho Didi notes · p. 33 Judgement. A definition of judgement and its three types: social, personal and test judgement. Psycho Didi notes · p. 33 Insight. Intellectual versus true emotional insight and the six grades of the insight rating scale. Psycho Didi notes · p. 33 The part of clinical assessment describing the sum total of the examiner's observations and impressions of a psychiatric patient at the time of interview. General Appearance & Behaviour Parameter Finding & associations Eye contact Assesses rapport, truthfulness, insight, concentration. Partial (fleeting); Absent — complete loss (Paranoid Schizophrenia, Acute delusional disorder). Depression → lowered eyes; Anxiety → shifting gaze. Dress Appropriate (normal); Shabby (Dementia, Substance abuse); Inappropriate , e.g. rain hood on a dry day (Mania, Histrionic PD). Facial expression Depression → corners of mouth turned down, vertical furrows on brow. Anxiety → horizontal forehead creases, widened palpebral fissures, dilated pupils. May be fixed/wooden (parkinsonian drug side effects) or reflect thyrotoxicosis. Posture Depression → hunched shoulders, gaze downward. Anxiety → edge of chair, gripping sides. Agitated depression → tremulous, picking at fingernails. Mania → restlessness. Catatonia → odd postures. Estimate of age Younger than stated → Histrionic PD; Older than stated → Depression or Chronic Schizophrenia. General appearance Kempt (normal, OCPD); Overtly made up (mania/hypomania, histrionic/narcissistic PD, some schizophrenia); Unkempt/untidy (organic psychosis, dementia, substance abuse, severe depression, schizophrenia); Sickly ; Perplexed . Body-build typologies. Ernst Kretschmer: Pyknics (stocky/rounded), Leptosomes (long/linear), Athletics (broad-shouldered/muscular). William Sheldon's somatotypes: Endomorph (round, fat abdomen), Mesomorph (cubical head, muscular), Ectomorph (thin, receding chin, spindly limbs). Attitude towards the examiner Frank and Cooperative / Attentive (normal). Defensive & Guarded (Paranoid Schizophrenia, Delusional disorder). Evasive (Organic psychoses, Substance abuse). Hostile (Paranoid Schizophrenia, Antisocial PD). Seductive . Rapport A bidirectional empathetic relationship. Easily established — normal persons, Mania; Established with difficulty — Schizophrenia, Dementia, Depression; Not possible — Paranoid Schizophrenia, Dementia, Depression. Motor Behaviour (selected signs) Sign Description / association Retardation Slowness of initiation/execution — Depression Hyperactivity Increased motor activity, often with over-talkativeness Mannerisms Unusual repeated goal-directed action (e.g. odd hand movements when shaking hands) Stereotypy Repetitive, non-goal-directed action carried out uniformly Grimace Non-goal-directed facial expression; e.g. Schnauzkrampf (snout spasm) — Schizophrenia Tics Sudden involuntary twitchings — Gilles de la Tourette syndrome (SIMS) Waxy flexibility Person maintains the body position into which they are placed Negativism Verbal/non-verbal opposition to suggestion — catatonic schizophrenia Echolalia Repeating another's words — catatonic schizophrenia Echopraxia Repetition by imitation of another's movements Ambivalence Co-existence of two opposing impulses toward the same thing — Schizophrenia, borderline state, OCD Automatic obedience Undue compliance with instructions — catatonia Waxy flexibility, odd posturing, rigidity, self-injury Catatonia; self-injurious behaviour → Borderline PD Also noted: preoccupied, restless, awkward (apraxia, MR), destructive (catatonic/manic excitement), silly smiling (Mania, Hebephrenia), aggressive, perseveration, dyskinesia, dystonia, chorea, athetosis, hallucinatory behaviour, gestures, touching the examiner. Speech Intensity: excessively loud (Mania, Hypomania), abnormally soft (vocal cord palsy, Depression, Paranoid Schizophrenia). Pitch: monotonous (parietal lobe damage, chronic schizophrenia, depression). Reaction time: increased (hypothyroidism, depression, schizophrenia), decreased (Mania). Speed: very slow (depression, dementia, hypothyroidism); rapid with prolixity/flight of ideas (mania, hypomania, hyperthyroidism). Pressure of speech — increased, accelerated, hard to interrupt (Mania, Schizophrenia, cognitive disorders). Ease: hesitant (head injury, anxiety), mutism (stupor, dementia), slurring (cerebellar damage), stuttering/stammering (severe anxiety, schizophrenia), whispering (pseudobulbar palsy), muttering (schizophrenia, dementia). Deviations: rhyming/punning (mania), talking past the point ( Ganser's syndrome , schizophrenia), clang association (schizophrenia, mania), stereotypy (catatonic schizophrenia), perseveration. Cognitive Functions Orientation (time, place, person), attention, concentration, memory (immediate / recent / remote), abstract ability, intelligence (comprehension, general information, vocabulary, calculation). Thinking style Definition & association Concrete thinking Thinking bound to actual things/events & immediate experience — Schizophrenia, young children Functional thinking Abstraction relating only to functional aspects — Schizophrenia, MR Over-abstraction Excessive manifestation of a concept beyond relevance — Schizophrenia, philosophical preoccupations Mood & Affect Mood = persistent, sustained emotion colouring perception of the world. Affect = present emotional responsiveness inferred from expression. Quality: dysphoric, anxious, irritable, depressed, elevated, euphoric, elated, exalted, ecstatic, euthymic. Intensity: shallow (lack of depth), blunted (greatly diminished, uniform voice), flat (no affect displayed). Appropriateness: Paramimia — lack of unity between modes of emotional expression; Parathymia — expression opposite to what is expected (e.g. laughing at tragic news). Diurnal variation: worse in morning (endogenous depression, headache), worse in evening (anxiety, delirium/ sundowning ), worse at night (uremia). Thought Aspect Key terms Stream Acceleration, pressured speech, flight of ideas (rapid, chance connections still understandable), prolixity (ordered flight, returns to task), retardation/bradyphrenia, poverty of speech (laconic), circumstantiality (reaches point via trivia), tangentiality (oblique, never reaches point), thought blocking (sudden arrest → blank) Form Negative type (loses ability to form concept) vs positive type (false concept by blending incongruous elements): loosening of associations, derailment, neologism, over-inclusion Possession Obsession , rumination , compulsion , thought alienation — insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting, thought echo Content Worry, phobias, impulse, somatic symptoms, religious preoccupations (OCD), magical thinking, depressive cognition (worthlessness/helplessness/hopelessness), suicidal/homicidal ideas, inflated self-esteem, delusion (a false firm belief) Perception Sensory distortion — intensity: hyperaesthesia, hyperacusis, hypoacusis. Quality: Xanthopsia (yellow), Chloropsia (green), Erythropsia (red/pink). Spatial form: Micropsia (smaller), Macropsia/megalopsia (larger), Porropsia (retreat into distance without size change). Sensory deception — Hallucination: perception without an adequate external stimulus (auditory, visual, olfactory, gustatory, tactile). Delusion vs Hallucination. A delusion is a false firm belief (a disorder of thought content ). A hallucination is a perception without an adequate external stimulus (a disorder of perception ). An illusion is a misperception of a real stimulus. Don't conflate them. Other psychotic phenomena. Somatic passivity — belief that outside influences play on the body. Made phenomenon — made act (actions under external control), made affect (feelings not one's own), made impulse (impulse admitted as one's own action but not one's own drive). Judgement & Insight Judgement: social, personal, test. Insight — degree of awareness/understanding of being ill (intellectual vs true emotional insight), rated on a 6-point scale: Insight — 6-point scale: Grade 1 complete denial → Grade 2 slight awareness but denying → Grade 3 attributed to external/physical factors → Grade 4 due to something unknown in self → Grade 5 intellectual insight → Grade 6 true emotional insight. 3 · Classification — DSM & ICD The DSM The DSM. DSM editions from DSM-I to DSM-5 arranged around a history box, with the five axes, DSM-5 categories, new and eliminated disorders, and criticism. Psycho Didi notes · p. 34 Emil Kraepelin differentiated dementia praecox (a biological illness from anatomical/toxic processes) from manic depression (an episodic disorder not leading to permanently impaired brain function) as the two forms of psychosis. Edition Year Key features DSM-I 1952 Developed by the American Psychiatric Association; 100 conditions; division into psychosis & neurosis DSM-II 1962 Written in paragraphs as explanations DSM-III 1980 Multiaxial system introduced; symptomatic criteria; started aligning with ICD DSM-IV & IV-TR 1994 Five-axis system fully articulated DSM-5 2013 Multiaxial system dropped; spectrum approach; Roman numerals replaced by Arabic DSM-5-TR 2022 Latest; added prolonged grief disorder The five axes (DSM-III to IV-TR): Axis I clinical syndromes (V codes); Axis II personality disorders & intellectual disability; Axis III general medical condition; Axis IV psychosocial & environmental problems; Axis V global assessment of functioning (GAF). DSM-5 disorder categories Neurodevelopmental; Schizophrenia-spectrum & other psychotic; Bipolar & related; Depressive; Anxiety; Obsessive-compulsive & related; Trauma & stressor-related; Dissociative; Somatic symptom & related; Feeding & eating; Sexual dysfunctions; Gender dysphoria; Paraphilic disorders; Sleep-wake; Disruptive, impulse-control & conduct; Neurocognitive; Substance-related & addictive; Personality disorders. New in DSM-5: social (pragmatic) communication disorder; disruptive mood dysregulation disorder; premenstrual dysphoric disorder; hoarding disorder; excoriation (skin-picking) disorder; disinhibited social engagement disorder; binge eating disorder; central sleep apnea; sleep-related hypoventilation; REM sleep behaviour disorder; restless legs syndrome; caffeine withdrawal; cannabis withdrawal; major NCD with Lewy Body Disease; mild neurocognitive disorder. Eliminated: sexual aversion; polysubstance-related disorder. Criticism of DSM: medicalization (over-diagnosis), pharmaceutical influence, cultural and ethical concerns, comorbidity. The ICD The ICD. ICD editions arranged around a box of its uses, with the F-code categories, ICD-11 changes, an ICD-10 versus ICD-11 comparison and a Venn diagram of ICD versus DSM. Psycho Didi notes · p. 35 International Classification of Diseases. ICD-6: 1948/49. Essential for standardization, research & epidemiology, healthcare management, resource allocation, global consistency. Block ICD grouping F00–09 Organic mental disorders (neurocognitive) F10–19 Substance use disorders F20–29 Schizophrenia and related F30–39 Mood disorders F40–49 Neurotic, stress-related, somatoform disorders F50–59 Behavioural syndromes associated with physiological disturbances F60–69 Personality disorders F70–79 Intellectual disability (neurodevelopmental) F80–89 Psychological development disorders F90–98 Emotional development disorders F99 Unspecified ICD editions: ICD-9 (1977), ICD-10 (1993), ICD-11 (2022). ICD-11 eliminated acute stress disorder and gender incongruence as a personality disorder (dimensional approach instead of categorization) and added prolonged grief disorder, compulsive sexual behaviour, gaming disorder. ICD vs DSM ICD DSM Origin 1949 1952 Authoring body WHO APA Scope Broader Narrower Outlook Global American Editions 11 5 Similarities: symptoms overlap; both are authoritative guidebooks. Other differences: cultural considerations, billing/insurance, acceptance and use. ICD-10 vs ICD-11 ICD-10 ICD-11 21 disorder groupings 11 disorder groupings No harmonization with DSM Harmonization with DSM Separate grouping for childhood/adolescent-onset disorders Omits a separate childhood/adolescent grouping Categorical approach Categorical, with dimensional expansions (severity, course, specific symptoms) 14,400 codes; no extension codes 55,000 codes; extension (X) codes for signs/symptoms, causes, disorders 28 chapters 22 chapters 4 · Neurodevelopmental Disorders Neurodevelopmental disorders in DSM and ICD. Two circles comparing the neurodevelopmental disorders listed in the DSM with the ICD codes F70-79, F80-89 and F90-98. Psycho Didi notes · p. 36 Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) ADHD. A flowchart of ADHD symptoms, differential diagnosis and treatment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 36 Earlier diagnosable only up to age 7, now up to age 12 ; stays into adulthood if untreated; many comorbidities. Inattention: distractible, loses interest, keeps shifting tasks, doesn't attend to detail, loses things. Hyperactivity: impulsive, can't wait, aggressive, can't wait for turn, squirms, talks excessively. Any 6 symptoms must be met; duration ≥ 6 months. Treatment: Ritalin, amphetamine, dextroamphetamine; behavioural modification, applied behavioural analysis, shaping, chaining, token economy, response cost; Modafinil; Clonidine, venlafaxine, bupropion, SNRI. DDx: oppositional defiant, conduct disorder, aggression, depression, substance use, ASPD; problems with frontal lobe & cerebellum; difficulty copying, rapid alternating movements, right-left discrimination. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD / Pervasive Developmental Disorder) Autism spectrum disorder. A flowchart of ASD symptoms, differential diagnosis and treatment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 36 Chromosomes 2, 7, 4, 15, 19 involved. Impairment in social interaction (eye contact, social smile, attachment, expression, making friends, routine). Impairment in communication and language (delayed milestones, articulation difficulty, echolalia, verbigeration, saying "me" instead of "you"). Restrictive, repetitive, stereotyped behaviour, flapping, echopraxia; impaired theory of mind; high pain tolerance; biting/scratching/headbanging; isles of precocity (high skill in something). Treatment: Risperidone, Aripiprazole; behaviour modification. DDx: Fragile X, Phenylketonuria, Rubella, Intellectual disability, Tuberous sclerosis, asphyxia. Rett's Syndrome Rett's syndrome. A flowchart of Rett's syndrome symptoms, differential diagnosis and treatment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 36 Losing fine motor skills; head circumference decreases from 5–48 months; stereotyped movement; problems with walk/talk/eat/breathe; 75% seizures ; progressive; mostly in girls; microencephaly. A subtype of pervasive developmental disorder. Normal early development followed by partial/complete loss of speech, locomotion & hand-use skills with deceleration in head growth. Treatment symptomatic. Heller's Syndrome (Childhood Disintegrative Disorder, CDD) Heller's syndrome. The symptoms of Heller's syndrome. Psycho Didi notes · p. 37 Rare; late onset (> 3 years) of developmental delays in language, social function, motor skills. Symptoms age 2–10 years: impaired social skills, language skills, bladder control; stereotyped behaviour; microcephaly. Another neurodevelopmental disorder. Asperger's Syndrome Asperger's syndrome. The symptoms of Asperger's syndrome. Psycho Didi notes · p. 37 Mild ASD; problems with social interaction; experience emotion but can't express; restrictive, repetitive, stereotyped behaviour. Intellectual Disability (ID) Intellectual disability. A flowchart of intellectual disability covering the intro, aetiology with percentages, differential diagnosis, and mild to profound types with IQ ranges. Psycho Didi notes · p. 37 Overlaps with ADHD and Autism before 18 years; IQ below 70; spectrum approach; based on adaptive functioning in conceptual, social and practical domains; onset before 18 years . Type IQ % of ID Features Mild 50–70 85% 6th-grade academic skill; independent life; relationships possible; problem with abstract thinking Moderate 35–50 10% Limited vocabulary; needs help with self-care/social tasks; can handle money; relationships possible but little emotion Severe 20–30 5% May learn simple commands; rudimentary communication Profound 0–20 1–2% All development stunted; low age span Aetiology: genetic abnormality (5%) — chromosomal, cranial anomaly, single-gene disorder, inborn errors of metabolism ( Tay-Sachs, Lesch-Nyhan ); perinatal (10%) — infections, prematurity, birth trauma, hypoxia, kernicterus, placental abnormality, drugs; acquired physical (infections, cretinism, trauma, lead poisoning, cerebral palsy); sociocultural (15%) — deprivation; psychiatric (1–2%). DDx: deaf/dumb, deprived, speech defect, psychiatric disorder, systematic disorder, epilepsy. Global Developmental Delay Delay in development for a patient under 5 years who has not been adequately evaluated; missed developmental milestones. Specific Learning Disability (SLD) Specific learning disability. A flowchart of specific learning disability symptoms (dyslexia, dysgraphia, dyscalculia, mixed disorder) and differential diagnosis. Psycho Didi notes · p. 37 IQ is normal but poor academic score. Dyslexia — inability to read/comprehend; Dysgraphia — poor handwriting; Dyscalculia — arithmetic impairment. Tics & Tourette's (Motor Disorder) Tics/Tourette's and global developmental delay. A flowchart of tic and Tourette's symptoms and other facts, next to a short note on global developmental delay. Psycho Didi notes · p. 37 1% of young people; family history of tics or OCD. Motor tics, vocal tics, involuntary jerks; stress develops; effort goes into controlling tics. Tourette's: ≥ 2 motor and 1 vocal tic; knee-jerking responses; longer than 1 year. Vocal: barks, clicks, coughs, grunts. Coprolalia — swearing (bad-word) tics. Dopamine antagonists used for treatment. Communication Disorders Communication disorders. A flowchart branching from communication disorders to language, speech sound, childhood onset fluency and social pragmatic disorders, each with its symptoms. Psycho Didi notes · p. 37 Language disorder: problems in spoken/written/sign language; expressive & receptive; vocabulary & grammar; speaks slower & less; academic issues; can co-exist with ADHD. Speech sound (phonological) disorder: substituting/omitting sounds (e.g. "ghaspetti" for "spaghetti"); diagnosed only in first language; 2–3% of preschool children. Childhood-onset fluency (stuttering) disorder: difficulty with beginning of words; momentary panic; anxiety/frustration; occurs with consonants and initial sounds; begins 2–5 years; more in boys; ~3% of children; dopamine antagonists used. Social (pragmatic) communication disorder: don't understand what to say where; poor contextual use of speech; less practical language use, convention, turn-taking, non-verbal/implied communication; may be comorbid. 5 · Anxiety Disorders (F40–48) Anxiety (F40-48). General anxiety features, the features of neurosis, trait versus state anxiety, and motor, autonomic, cognitive, affective and other symptoms. Psycho Didi notes · p. 38 Anxiety disorders according to DSM 5. Notes on each DSM-5 anxiety disorder, from generalized anxiety disorder and phobias to selective mutism and unspecified anxiety disorder. Psycho Didi notes · p. 38 Neurosis — subjective distress; ego-dystonic; insight present; personality & behaviour preserved; absence of organicity; reaction to stress & adjustment; somatoform. Anxiety symptoms.
