Motor (tremors, restlessness, muscle twitch, fearful face); autonomic/visceral (palpitation, tachycardia, sweating, flushes, hyperventilation, chest constriction, mouth dryness, reduced micturition, mydriasis); cognitive (poor concentration, distractibility, hyperarousal, vigilance); affective (apprehension, fearfulness, inability to relax, irritability, feelings of doom); other (noise sensitivity, insomnia, increased startle response). Trait anxiety ("I often feel anxious") vs state anxiety ("I feel anxious now") — those with trait anxiety also have state anxiety. Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) Most diagnosed anxiety disorder; free-floating anxiety; for 6 months or more ; constant low arousal of the sympathetic nervous system. DDx: OCD, PTSD, mood disorder, physical causes, realistic anxiety. Treatment: benzodiazepine, SSRI, barbiturates (old), CBT, relaxation, psychodynamic therapy. Social Anxiety Disorder Severe irrational fear of evaluation; dysfunction at work and relationships; ≥ 6 months ; sometimes only due to evaluation of performance. Specific Phobia Defence mechanism: displacement . Irrational, disproportional fear of certain animals, natural environment, situations, blood/injection, others. Fear out of proportion; insight present; inability to control fear; avoidance of the object. Agoraphobia Fear of being in a place where they can't get up and leave; fear of crowded/enclosed places. Treatment: clomipramine, venlafaxine, buspirone. Panic Disorder Feelings of impending doom; hippocampus and amygdala involved; periodic, discrete bouts of panic/terror in the absence of any real threat; feels like a heart attack; should be present for more than a month . Separation Anxiety Disorder Fear that something will happen to the attachment figure if away; can happen in adults; may have vomiting; ≥ 6 months in adults, ≥ 4 weeks in children . Selective Mutism Children remain silent except before close people; normal intelligence; family history of SAD; may develop SAD in adulthood; duration > 1 month ; treatment: social skills training. Other anxiety disorders Substance-induced anxiety disorder (from exposure/withdrawal to a medication); anxiety disorder due to another medical condition ; other specified anxiety disorder (clinician specifies reason for non-fulfilment); unspecified anxiety disorder (clinician does not specify). 6 · Obsessive-Compulsive & Related Disorders OCD related disorders according to DSM 5. Four cards on body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania and excoriation disorder. Psycho Didi notes · p. 39 Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) Obsessive compulsive disorder. OCD features, obsessions, compulsions, major patterns, aetiology, treatment and DSM specifiers arranged around a central title. Psycho Didi notes · p. 39 Young-adulthood onset; most common in males; family history. Obsessions: ego-dystonic, irrational, absurd, distressing, recognised as one's own idea. Compulsions: to neutralize the obsession; not realistic; irrational; insight present; subjective; may diminish the anxiety associated with the obsession. Major patterns: contamination, pathological doubt, intrusive thought, symmetry (tics). Aetiology. Dysfunction in fronto-striatal brain circuitry ( caudate ). Defence mechanisms: reaction formation, isolation of affect, undoing . DSM specifier: with good/fair insight; with poor insight; with absent insight/delusional beliefs; tic-related. Treatment: clomipramine, antipsychotics, lithium, valproate; Exposure and Response Prevention, aversion therapy; caudectomy, cingulotomy, capsulectomy. Trichotillomania Recurrent pulling out of one's hair resulting in hair loss and bald patches; attempts to control the behaviour. Excoriation (Skin-Picking) Disorder Recurrent skin picking resulting in skin lesions; attempts to control the behaviour. ICD-11: factitious dermatitis. Hoarding Disorder Overwhelming urge to accumulate things; distressed when discarding possessions. Body Dysmorphic Disorder Preoccupied with minor body imperfections. Specify if: with muscle dysmorphia. 7 · Depressive (Mood) Disorders Mood disorders: depressive. Boxes on aetiology, physical signs, prognosis, treatment and features, with a flowchart branching to MDD, persistent depressive disorder, DMDD and PMDD. Psycho Didi notes · p. 40 Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) Duration ≥ 2 weeks. Mnemonic SIGECAPS: S leep disturbance (REM latency, early-morning awakening); low I nterest; G uilt; E nergy deficit; reduced C oncentration; reduced A ppetite; P sychomotor agitation/retardation; S uicidal ideation. Specifiers/features: with psychotic features (schizoaffective); atypical features (hypersomnia, overeating); melancholic features (in old age); catatonic features. Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia) Symptoms persist for 2 years ; no suicidal ideation; no hospitalization; symptoms never absent for longer than 2 months. MDD vs Persistent Depressive Disorder. MDD = ≥ 2 weeks, may include suicidal ideation and hospitalization. Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) = ≥ 2 years, no suicidal ideation, no hospitalization, symptoms never absent > 2 months. Double depression = MDD superimposed on dysthymia (a poor-prognosis feature). Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (DMDD) For children and adolescents; a precursor to bipolar ; sudden anger, throwing fits, tantrums; persistent negative moods; sadness translated into complete outbursts. DDx: oppositional defiant disorder. Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) Mood shifts or other dysphoria in the week or two before the menstrual period. Prognosis, subtypes & aetiology Good prognosis Poor prognosis Acute onset; typical clinical features; severe depression; well-adjusted premorbid personality; good treatment response Comorbidity with personality disorder/alcohol abuse; double depression; chronic stress; unfavourable early environment; hypochondriacal features; poor drug compliance Endogenous Exogenous Absence of any precipitating life event Due to a precipitating life event; less likelihood of psychosis; more somatic complaints; less likelihood of suicide Physical signs. Veraguth's fold — triangular fold in the nasal corner of the upper eyelid. Omega sign on the forehead. Aaron Beck's cognitive triad — negative view of self, world, future. Also: learned helplessness (Martin Seligman). Aetiology: unipolar depression concordance rate 46%; abnormality in monoamine, acetylcholine and GABA neurotransmitters; hormonal disturbances; neuroanatomical — reduced dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and increased HPA axis. Treatment: pharmacotherapy takes 3–4 weeks; maintained for 6 months (prophylactic). Tricyclic antidepressants (block reuptake of serotonin & norepinephrine, the "-pramines"; anticholinergic side effects — constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, dry mouth). SSRIs / NaSSA / SNRI (side effects: nausea, anxiety, diarrhoea). MAOIs. Antipsychotics. Therapies: CBT, mindfulness, IPT, ECT, TMS, vagus nerve stimulation, deep brain stimulation, sleep deprivation therapy, phototherapy (1500–10,000 lux). 8 · Bipolar & Related Disorders (Mania) Mood Disorders: Mania. A one-page summary of mania with boxes for aetiology and prevalence, mania versus hypomania, treatment, the DIG FAST criteria and specifiers, plus a flowchart branching into Bipolar I, Bipolar II and cyclothymic disorder. Psycho Didi notes · p. 41 Manic episode criteria — mnemonic DIG FAST: D istractibility; I mpulsivity; G randiosity; F light of ideas; A ctivity (goal-directed) increase; S leep deficit; T alkativeness. Bipolar I Requires a manic episode . Major depressive episodes common but not required for diagnosis. Bipolar II A hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode ; there has never been a full manic episode. Bipolar I vs Bipolar II — and Mania vs Hypomania. Mania (Bipolar I): lasts 1 week , accompanied by less intense depression, may have psychotic features, requires hospitalization. Hypomania (Bipolar II): lasts 4 days , accompanied by major depressive episodes, may not require hospitalization, never a full manic episode. Bipolar I needs a manic episode; Bipolar II needs hypomania + ≥ 1 MDE and no full mania. Cyclothymic Disorder Periods with hypomanic symptoms (not meeting full criteria) and depressive symptoms (not meeting full criteria) for at least 2 years , during which symptoms have not been absent for more than 2 months. Specifiers Mood-congruent psychotic features; mood-incongruent psychotic features; catatonia; peripartum onset; seasonal pattern; hypomania; mixed episodes (cycle in 7 days); anxious distress; rapid cycling; melancholic features; atypical features. Aetiology & prevalence. Bipolar disorder is the most genetically influenced disorder (74% if both parents affected). Neurotransmitters: increased dopamine activity. Genetic factors: chromosomes 18q, 22q, 21q. Mania more common in men; depression more common in women; onset 30 years and above; more in divorced/single persons. Treatment: Lithium (side effects: postural tremors [treated with beta-blockers], memory disturbance, intracranial tension, peripheral neuropathy, hypothyroidism, polyuria, diabetes; lithium toxicity — tremors, renal impairment, ataxia, delirium, increased reflexes, convulsions, vomiting, kidney issues), Valproate (acute mania), Lamotrigine (depressive), Carbamazepine, Oxcarbazepine, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, antidepressants; ECT; therapy. Treatment continued for 2 years. 9 · Schizophrenia Spectrum & Other Psychotic Disorders Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders. A grid of boxes covering positive and negative symptoms, history, types, epidemiology, prognosis, speech and catatonia, etiology, the duration rules for other psychotic disorders, and treatment. Psycho Didi notes · p. 49 History. Emil Kraepelin gave the term dementia praecox (1896); his classification: simple dementia, paranoia, catatonia, hebephrenia. Eugen Bleuler coined the term schizophrenia and gave the 4 A's : Ambivalence, Autism, Association (disturbance), Affect disturbance . Karl Kahlbaum — catatonia. Symptoms Negative symptoms: affective flattening, avolition, apathy, anhedonia, asociality, alogia. Schneider's First-Rank Symptoms (positive). Audible thoughts (1st person); voices heard arguing (3rd person); voices commenting on one's actions; thought withdrawal; thought diffusion/broadcasting; made feeling; made impulse; made actions; somatic passivity. Also: hallucinations; delusions (erotomania, grandeur, guilt, jealousy, passivity, persecution, poverty, reference, somatic, thought control). Speech disturbances: poverty of speech, echolalia, verbigeration (continual repetition of stereotyped phrases), perseveration. Catatonia (Karl Kahlbaum): agitation, cataplexy (sudden muscle weakness/paralysis), echolalia/echopraxia, exaggerated compliance, grimace, mannerism, mutism, stereotypy, posturing, waxy flexibility. Types (subtypes) Paranoid; Catatonic; Disorganized/Hebephrenic; Undifferentiated; Residual; Simple ( worst prognosis ). Also pfropfschizophrenie — schizophrenia and mental retardation coexisting. Type 1 Type 2 Ventricles Normal ventricles Dilated ventricles Damage No organic damage; no comorbidity — Medication response Good prognosis Low response to medication Duration & the psychotic-disorder family Disorder Duration Symptoms to be met Schizophrenia 6+ months All Schizophreniform disorder 1–6 months All Schizoaffective disorder 2 weeks Schizophrenia + mood disorder Delusional disorder 1 month Delusion Brief psychotic disorder 1 day and 1 night All Schizophreniform vs Schizophrenia (the classic duration trap). Schizophreniform = 1–6 months ; Schizophrenia = 6+ months — same full symptom set, only the duration cutoff differs. Brief psychotic disorder is even shorter (1 day–1 month), and schizoaffective requires both schizophrenia and a mood disorder. Etiolog

title: Psychological Testing
text: Psychological Testing — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Psychological Testing Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Neuropsychological batteries Intelligence & Indian tests Projective & objective personality tests MMPI · 16PF · NEO-PI · EPQ Test → author → what it measures What this covers. A complete tour of psychological tests for the clinical/NET syllabus: neuropsychology foundations and batteries (Halstead-Reitan, Luria-Nebraska, AIIMS, NIMHANS) plus individual neuro tests (WCST, Bender-Gestalt, Stroop, Tower tests, ROCF, CANTAB, MMSE, PGIBBD, WMS); intelligence tests (Stanford-Binet 5, Raven's, CFIT, Kaufman family, Leiter) and Indian adaptations (Bhatia's Battery, Binet-Kamat, Kulshreshtha, WAPIS, MISIC); and personality tests split into projective (Rorschach, TAT, Rosenzweig, Szondi, sentence-completion and drawing tests) and non-projective objective inventories (MMPI family, MCMI, MBTI, EPPS, Holland, MPQ, 16PF (Raymond Cattell), NEO-PI (Paul Costa and Robert McCrae), EPQ). Every test name, author, age range, subtest and cutoff is preserved. Original diagrams. 16 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 57 to 68) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Introduction to Neuropsychology · 2 · Neuropsychological Tests: goals, categories, approaches · 3 · Halstead-Reitan Battery · 4 · Other Neuropsychological Tests · 5 · Intelligence Tests · 6 · Indian Intelligence Tests · 7 · Personality Tests: overview · 8 · Projective Tests · 9 · Non-Projective Tests (Non Factor Analytic) · 10 · Non-Projective Tests (Factor Analytic) 1 · Introduction to Neuropsychology Intro to Neuropsychology. Mind map linking neuropsychology (the study of brain function and behaviour) to its history, neuroplasticity research findings and the two types of neuroplasticity. Psycho Didi notes · p. 57 Neuropsychology is the study of brain function and behaviour. Neuroplasticity Experience expectant — development according to expected growth pattern. Experience dependent — plasticity dependent on new learning, based on new experiences. History of the mind–brain question Mentalism (Aristotle) — a non-material psyche is responsible for behaviour. Dualism (René Descartes) — the body is like a machine (only controls reflex); the mind controls the machine. Materialism (Charles Darwin) — the mind is just our brain; neuroplasticity is based on evolution, the capacity to change. Research findings Florenz and Galls challenged localization: removed the cortex of 3 dogs. Young children can recover fast from brain damage (stem cells migrate). In adults, new neurons (2%) are formed in the hippocampus and striatum. Functioning improves with physiotherapy. 2 · Neuropsychological Tests: goals, categories, approaches Neuropsychological tests. Mind map of neuropsychological testing that branches into its introduction, goals, commonly named tests, categories assessed, sensitivity and specificity, and fixed versus flexible battery approaches. Psycho Didi notes · p. 57 Neuropsychological testing allows for an in-depth analysis of functional limitation associated with brain dysfunction, and is required for diagnosis by some diagnostic criteria for neurological disorders. Goals (Schaefer et al., 2023) Establish a baseline. Gauge an individual's cognitive strengths and weaknesses and aid in treatment planning. Assist in establishing diagnoses. Establish lateralization and possible etiology of brain lesions. Track progress in rehab. Determination of disability, return to work/school, driving ability or legal purposes. Categories assessed Abstract · Attention · Daily activities · Emotional Distress · Language · Memory · Motor skills · Orientation · Sensation · Perception · Visuospatial reasoning. Sensitivity and Specificity Key. Sensitivity = a test's ability to correctly identify people who have a disease. Specificity = a test's ability to correctly identify people who do not have a disease. Approaches to Neuropsychological tests Approach Description Example Fixed battery Uses the same battery of tests for every client; maintains a constant testing condition; comprehensive normative data; better psychometric properties; broader empirical base for interpretations. Halstead-Reitan Battery Flexible battery Only those measures directly related to the patient's presenting symptoms should be administered. The administered battery inherently changes with a patient's referral question. Uses a core battery of tests and techniques for clients with various syndromes; tests implemented vary based on the practitioner as well as context. Meyers Neuropsychological Battery Commonly named neuropsychological tests Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) Raven's Progressive Matrices Shipley Institute of Living Scale The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST; David Grant and Esta Berg, 1948) Proverbs The Wechsler Memory Scale (WMS) The Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure (ROCF) test The Benton Visual Retention Test (BVRT) Consonant trigrams Stroop test 3 · Halstead–Reitan Neuropsychological Test Battery Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Test Battery. Overview of the Halstead-Reitan battery with its introduction, extra information, five scales and other measures, illustrated with photos of the Booklet Category Test, Tactual Performance Test boards and a finger tapping device. Psycho Didi notes · p. 58 Founder note. The Halstead-Reitan battery arose from one of the first neuropsychology labs in America; it proposed the theory of "biological intelligence" . Introduction Created one of the first neuropsychology labs in America. First neuropsychological test to have a factor-analytic process. Was made to test head trauma. Created: 1935. Time taken: 6–8 hours. 1956: The Halstead-Reitan Test Battery begins to emerge as the premiere test battery in neuropsychology. Now it can detect tremors, cerebrovascular accidents, infections, degenerative diseases, learning disabilities, neurological disorders. Proposed theory of "biological intelligence". Extra information Total 7 scores. Removed: critical flicker fusion test, time sense test. For ages: 15+. Based on T-score value. 6-point score. Scales / Measures Category test — measures abstract reasoning and concept formation; requires the examinee to find the rule for categorizing pictures of geometric shapes. Tactual performance test (Seguin) — measures kinesthetic and sensorimotor ability; requires a blindfolded examinee to place blocks in the appropriate cutout on an upright board with the dominant hand, then non-dominant hand, then both hands; also tests for incidental memory of blocks (score: total time, memory, location). Seashore Rhythm Test — measures attention and auditory perception; requires the examinee to indicate whether paired musical rhythms are same or different. Speech sound perception test — measures attention and auditory-visual synthesis; requires the examinee to pick from four choices the written version of taped nonsense words. Finger tapping test — measures motor speed; requires the examinee to tap a telegraph-key-like lever as quickly as possible for 10 seconds. Other measures Grip strength — requires the examinee to squeeze as hard as possible; separate trials with each hand. Trail making, parts A, B — requires the examinee to connect numbers (part A) or numbers and letters in alternating order (part B) with a pencil line under pressure of time. Tactile form recognition — requires the examinee to recognize simple shapes (e.g., triangle) placed in the palm of the hand. Sensory-Perceptual Exam — requires the examinee to respond to simple bilateral sensory tasks, e.g., detecting which finger has been touched. Aphasia Screening test — tasks include naming a pictured item (e.g., fork), repeating short phrases. Supplementary: WAIS-III, WRAT-3, MMPI-2, memory tests such as Wechsler Memory Scale-III or Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test. 4 · Other Neuropsychological Tests Other Neuropsychological Tests: Luria-Nebraska, Vineland, Bender-Gestalt, WCST. Mind map of the Luria-Nebraska battery, the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, the Bender-Gestalt Test and the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, with a clock-drawing sample, Bender-Gestalt design cards, Vineland-3 materials and WCST cards. Psycho Didi notes · p. 59 Luria-Nebraska Test Battery Founder note. Luria-Nebraska — started in 1978, standardized by Golden in 1980. The AIIMS and NIMHANS batteries are based on this. 269 items (0, 1, 2 scale); T scores are used. In some areas 2 scores are assigned to the same task: speed and accuracy. Can check any organic damage. Total 14 scales: motor, rhythm, tactile, visual, receptive speech, expressive speech, writing, reading, arithmetic, memory, intellectual scales, pathognomonic — left and right hemisphere. The Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales (VABS) / Vineland Social Maturity Scale (VSMS) Founder note. Developed by American psychologist Edgar Arnold Doll (1935). Most widely used test to measure adaptive behaviour in existence; can be used from birth until death. For younger children, there is a semi-structured interview with parents. Domains: communication, daily living skills, socialization, motor skills, maladaptive behaviour (optional). Can check for Autism Spectrum Disorder, deficits in adaptation, genetic disorders, traumatic brain injury. Age 7–90: given only 3 subtests (not the motor skills subtest). Age 0–7: given all 4 subtests. The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) Founder note. Given by E.A. Berg in 1948 (60 cards); Heaton modified it in 1981 to a total of 64 cards. Order: Colour → Form → Number. Can break rapport if the client is unable to answer correctly. Bilateral prefrontal dysfunction patients are excited to give the test even if they give wrong answers. Checks for perseveration. Scored using Milner's criteria. The Bender-Gestalt Test (BGT) Founder note. Developed in 1938 by Lauretta Bender . Tests: hand-eye coordination, perseveration, prefrontal damage. Involves 13 designs for children less than 8 years and 12 designs for age 8 years and above. Memory recall process; global scoring system. Clients are given a lot of sheets, but asked to draw on only one. Visuospatial difficulties identified (lesions in right parietal lobe). Seguin Form Board Test Other Neuropsychological Tests: Seguin, BVRT, Seashore, Stroop, ROCF, CANTAB, Tower tests. Mind map of the Seguin Form Board, Benton Visual Retention, Seashore, Stroop, Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure, CANTAB and Tower tests, with a form board photo, a Stroop colour-word chart, a sample complex figure drawing and a Tower of London diagram. Psycho Didi notes · p. 60 Founder note. Indian adaptation by J. Bharatraj ; norms by S. K. Goel . Part of the Halstead-Reitan test battery (1947). Client is asked to draw the board from memory. Earlier it was used to test eye-hand / visuomotor coordination. Earlier given as 10 blocks of Gesell figures. The Benton Visual Retention Test (BVRT) Founder note. Developed by Arthur Benton . Currently: 5th edition; includes 10 designs. Clients are required to see and copy 10 designs immediately out of memory. Time taken: 5 minutes. The Seashore Test Founder note. The tests were developed by Carl E. Seashore . Used in the Halstead-Reitan Battery. 3–5 errors considered normal. Measures musical ability and cerebral function. Seashore Rhythm Test — a subtest of the Seashore Measures of Musical Talent that measures generalized cerebral function; age-related problems occur. Stroop Test Test of selective attention, response conflict and inhibition; errors indicate dysfunction. Because of conceptual primacy, colour takes longer to recognize. No age bias. For checking smaller lesions, more items need to be added. Indicative of frontal functioning; biggest test is 4 block/trial. Tower Tests Tests for frontal, planning and executive dysfunction. A measure of means-end analysis (Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, 1972). Requires the client to reach the final goal in the least number of moves possible. Test Apparatus Least number of moves possible Tower of London Utilizes balls 5 Tower of Hanoi Utilizes rings 6 Dependent on working backwards; one has to visualize; repeat-state avoidance. Checks for inhibition of conflicting responses and working memory. Prepotent: goal-subgoal conflict. The Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure Test (ROCF) Founder note. Developed by Rey in 1941; standardized by Osterrieth in 1944. Measures visuospatial construction ability, visual memory, and executive functioning by the prefrontal lobe. 3 stages: copy, immediate recall, delayed recall. Uses one-for-one diagram. Checks for: fine motor coordination, visuospatial memory, planning and organization, attention and coordination. Age-related bias may be present. Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB) Computerized test. Time taken: 40–45 mins. Checks for dementia; frontal, temporal, hippocampal dysfunction. Checks for organic as well as non-organic damage. Independent of language and not sensitive to gender. Subtests: psychomotor coordination and motor speed; reasoning and planning abilities; spatial memory; attention and vigilance. Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) Other Neuropsychological Tests: MMSE, PGIBBD, AIIMS, NIMHANS, WMS. Mind map of the Mini-Mental State Examination, the PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction, the AIIMS and NIMHANS neuropsychological batteries and the Wechsler Memory Scale. Psycho Didi notes · p. 61 Basic exam of cognitive screening; 11 items. A score of 23/30 and lesser is considered pathological. Domains: orientation, repetition, verbal recall, attention, calculation, language and visual construction. Made in 1975, standardized in 1995. Time taken: 5–10 mins. Used for people with neurocognitive disorder. Drawbacks: heavily verbal; the test has a "floor effect" (can't tell high deterioration). The Postgraduate Institute of Brain Dysfunction (PGIBBD) Founder note. Given by Prashad and Verma , 1990; 2007. Language: Hindi; available for all. For ages: 20–59 years. 19 domains. 5 subtests: PGI Memory scale: immediate, recent, very short term, long term, verbal, non-verbal. Bhatia short scale: Koh's block design, Alexander Pass Along. VAIS: 1. info, 2. digit span, 3. arithmetic, 4. verbal comprehension. Nahor Benson test: organic brain pathology. Bender Gestalt Test. The Wechsler Memory Scale (WMS) Given for the first time in 1945. 4th edition: 2009. Working memory deficits indicate frontal lobe damage; long-term memory deficits indicate temporal lobe damage. Checks for auditory, visual, visual working, immediate, and delayed memory. Does not check much of: verbal memory or verbal working memory and remote memory. Time taken: 80 minutes. Checks for neurocognitive disorders (Korsakoff). The AIIMS Neuropsychological Battery Founder note. Given by Surya Gupta , 2000 — a Hindi adaptation of the Luria-Nebraska test. Training only given by the author; very expensive. 160 items; ages 15–80 years. Used to assess cognitive function; has versions for younger individuals. Scales: motor, tactile, visual, receptive speech, expressive speech, reading, writing, arithmetic, memory, intellectual processes, left hemisphere, right hemisphere, pathognomonic. The NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery Founder note. Version used: 2004 by Dr. Rao . Inspired by Luria-Nebraska. The test is available but the manual is not. Developed on the principles of localization and lateralization. Checks for attention, visual search, mental search, psychomotor deficit, working memory (frontal lobe damage). Also checks for temporal (BVRT) and parietal lobe (BGT) damage. Includes 19 tests. Popular tests: tower test, Stroop task, complex figure, finger tapping, WCST. 5 · Intelligence Tests Intelligence Tests: history and timeline. Scroll tracing intelligence testing from anthropometry to psychometric testing, next to a timeline of milestones from 1890 to 2014. Psycho Didi notes · p. 62 History Anthropometry (Francis Galton) Chronometry — RT test (Fechner) Mental Test (Cattell) Psychometric testing (Binet) Dates and timeline Year Milestone 1890 Cattell — Mental test. 1905 1st psychometric test by Binet to identify children with special needs. 1912 Stern gave the term IQ. 1916 IQ formula; Stanford-Binet test. 1917 Army Alpha (Robert Yerkes, 1917) and Army Beta test. 1939 Wechsler Bellevue scale introduced deviation IQ. 2003 Stanford-Binet Test-5. 2004 The Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (KABC II). 2008 WAIS. 2012 WPPSI. 2014 WISC. Key. Basal age = the last level where we get all answers correct. Ceiling age = the lowest level where we get all answers correct. Stanford-Binet Test-5 Stanford-Binet Test-5. Tree diagram of the Stanford-Binet 5 showing its key facts, basal and ceiling age, and the five factor scores with the tasks under each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 62 Follows Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory; given in 2003. 10 subtests; deviation IQ used; uses factor analysis. Age: 2–85 years. 5 factor scores Fluid reasoning — matrices, absurdities, inductive reasoning. Knowledge — procedural, general knowledge, missing details, vocabulary, difficult words. Quantitative reasoning — arithmetic problem, word problem, counting. Visuospatial reasoning — puzzles, direction problems. Working memory — words, sentences, short visual info. Raven's Progressive Matrices Intelligence Tests: CAS-II, Kaufman tests and culture fair tests. Panel covering the Cognitive Assessment System-II, the three Kaufman tests (KABC, KAIT, KBIT), culture fair tests (Draw A Person, Leiter), the Culture Fair Intelligence Test and Raven's Progressive Matrices, with sample KBIT pictures and a Raven's matrix item. Psycho Didi notes · p. 63 Coloured Progressive Matrices (36 cards). Advanced Progressive Matrices (48 cards). Standard Progressive Matrices (60 cards). Power and speed test; measures Fluid Intelligence. Mean = 100; SD = 15. Culture Fair Intelligence Test (CFIT) Founder note. By Raymond Cattell . Group test; speed and power test; 3 forms; only non-verbal test. Different from other tests in reading, experience, language, speed/tempo, environmental experiences. Can be given in groups. The Kaufman Adolescent and Adult Intelligence Test (KAIT) Founder note. Kaufman tests by Alan Kaufman . Age: 11–85+. Based on Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory (fluid and crystallized intelligence) and some part of Jean Piaget's theory. Culture biased. Cognitive Assessment System-II (CAS-II) Based on PASS theory (Das, Naglieri). Only for adolescents; used for scholarship tests. Contains the Naglieri Nonverbal Aptitude test. Mean: 100, S.D.: 3. The Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (KABC) Based on PASS theory. 4 global scales: Simultaneous, Successive, Mental Processing, Achievement. Culture biased. The Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test (KBIT) Age: 4–90 years; both verbal and nonverbal. Time taken: 20 minutes. Mean: 100, SD: 15. Culture Fair Tests Draw A Person Test (DAPT) 1926; performance test to measure observation and conceptual thinking. Leiter International Performance Scale Performance test; made for African groups; elimination of verbal instruction; no time limit. Tests: reasoning, visualisation, attention, memory. 6 · Indian Intelligence Tests Indian Intelligence Tests. Tree diagram grouping Indian intelligence tests into a performance test (Bhatia's Battery), tests based on Binet's test (Binet Kamat, Kulshreshtha) and tests based on Wechsler's test (WAPIS, MISIC), with a photo of the MISIC kit. Psycho Didi notes · p. 63 Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence Given in 1940; normed for ages 11–16 years. Performance test. Includes: Koh's block design — speed and power. Alexander Pass along — speed and power. Pattern drawing — speed and power. Immediate memory: digit span — verbal and power. Picture construction. Different norms for rural and urban population. Can be only administered individually. Not completely culture fair. Binet Kamat Test Bombay Karnataka version of the Binet Simon Scale; based on the 1916 Simon Binet test. Used ratio IQ. Ages: 3–22 years, separate norms. Measures: language, reasoning, conceptual thinking, social intelligence, memory, visuomotor performance. Heavily verbal — can't check subnormal intelligence. Items are not appropriate to current times; easy to administer. Severe and profound mental retardation. Kulshreshtha Intelligence Test 1960; Hindi adaptation of the Stanford-Binet (Lewis Terman, 1916) test. Ages: 2–22 years; each age level = 6 items. Verbal and performance tests; uses ratio IQ. Tests based on Wechsler's test Wechsler Adult Performance Intelligence Scale (WAPIS) Founder note. Made by Prabha Ramalingaswami (1974). 11 subtests (from WAIS): 6 verbal, 5 non-verbal. Picture completion and picture arrangement have been modified. Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) Founder note. Arthur J. Malin of Nagpur reformed Wechsler's scales. Ages: 6–15 years; 2–2.5 years. 11 subtests: 6 verbal: i. information, ii. general comprehension, iii. arithmetic, iv. analogy and similarity, v. vocabulary, vi. digit span. 5 non-verbal: i. block design, ii. picture completion, iii. object assembly, iv. symbol coding, v. maze. 7 · Personality Tests: overview Personality Tests. Tree diagram of personality assessment showing an introduction timeline and four types (personality inventories, non projective tests, projective tests, observation), with the California Personality Inventory, Bell's Adjustment Inventory and observational tests in boxes below. Psycho Didi notes · p. 64 Projective tests began in 1800. 1st test: Word Association test — Francis Galton, Emil Kraepelin, Carl Jung . 1916: Carl Jung's first standardized word association test. 1917: 1st objective test — Woodworth's Personal Data Sheet. Types / categories of personality assessment Observational tests — rating scales and interview technique. Rating scales: judgement about personality in some categories. Interviews: structured and unstructured. Personality inventories (self-report: forced choice). Non-projective tests , Observation . Bell's Adjustment Inventory 1934; to diagnose adjustment problems. Home: satisfaction/dissatisfaction; health: shyness, introversion. Student form and occupation form; 140 Qs. Adapted in Indian languages. California Personality Inventory 1957, 1987; work-related inventory. Measures behaviour in the organizational setting. 8 · Projective Tests Projective Tests: association techniques and construction tests. Page splitting projective tests into association techniques and construction tests, covering the Word Association Test, Rorschach Inkblot Test, Blacky's Picture Test, Thematic Apperception Test and Rosenzweig Picture Frustration Study. Psycho Didi notes · p. 65 Association techniques Rorschach Inkblot Test Founder note. 1921, by Herman Rorschach ; he created it while playing klexography. Projective vs objective. The Rorschach is a projective association technique studying unconscious thoughts, unlike objective self-report inventories (MMPI, 16PF). Scoring is subjective and system-dependent (Exner etc.), not criterion-keyed. Administration: 10 cards, 7×10 inches, shown one at a time in sequence. Card Theme i Paranoia ii Violence, communication, dominance iii Sexual preference iv Father card v Hostility, castration complex, schizophrenia vi Intimate relationships vii Mother card viii Emotions / complex situations ix Uncertainty / ambiguity x Life situation / oral fixation Phases: Performance proper. Enquiry: ask what, why, where it was seen. Testing the limits: done to give participants with weird responses another chance. Studies unconscious thoughts. Average number of responses: 20–25; per card: 3–5. Focus on: content of the story, feeling or tone, subject's behaviour apart from the responses. Scoring system: Levey, Beck S., Hertz, Klopfer, Exner (1974). Latest scoring system by Exner : 1993. Scoring based on: location, determinant, form quality, content, popular responses. Blacky's Picture Test Based on Sigmund Freud's psychosexual stages; for children ages 5 and older; 11 cartoon stimuli. In addition to requesting a story for each card, the examiner also presents multiple-choice questions based on stages of psychosexual development. Word Association Test Founder note. Also known as free association technique. First systematically described by Francis Galton (1879); introduced into the psychological laboratory by Wilhelm Wundt ; first applied to the study of abnormality by Emil Kraepelin ; adapted for use as a projective technique by Carl Jung . Construction tests Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) Founder note. Given by Henry Murray and Christina Morgan (1935, 43); based on Murray's theory of personology. Can be both idiographic and nomothetic. 19 cards, for male, female, boys, girls; total cards that can be given: 20. Blank card: Card no. 16. Bellack's scoring system is used. Analysis: Hero · Needs of the hero · Thema · Outcome. Needs of the hero: Needs motivated by desire for power, property, prestige, knowledge, creativity: achievement, acquisition, aggression, construction, counteraction, dominance, exposition, recognition, understanding. Needs motivated by affection, admiration, sympathy, love, dependence: affiliation, deference, nurturance, sex, succorance. Needs motivated by desire for freedom, change, excitement, play: autonomy, change/travel adventure, excitation/dissipation, play. Miscellaneous needs: abasement, blame avoidance, cognizance, harm avoidance, passivity, rejection, retention, sentience. Presses: Press of deprivation: acquisition, retention. Press descriptive of an empty, alien, or rejecting environment: lack of things/opportunities/friends, human support; loss; rejection; uncongenial environment. Press of coercion and restraint: dominance; imposed task, duty or training. Press descriptive of a hostile aggressive environment: aggression. Press of danger, injury, death: affliction, death of hero, physical danger, physical injury. Press of friendliness, sympathy, respect, dependent, love: affiliation, deference, nurturance, sex, succorance. Miscellaneous press: birth of offspring, claustrum, cognizance, example, exposition, luck. 3 levels of interpretation: descriptive level, interpretive level, diagnostic level. Rosenzweig Picture Frustration Study Consists of 24 cartoon pictures each portraying two persons in a frustrating situation. Responses are scored as to whether, and to what degree, they indicate that the subject exhibits aggression towards the source of the frustration; assumes blame or guilt as the cause of frustration; or justifies, minimizes or denies the frustration. The score is based on a total of nine factors derived from combinations of three types of aggression and three directions of aggression. Three types of aggression: obstacle dominance, ego defense, need persistence. Three directions of aggression: extragression, imagression, intragression. What to ask: current situation; thoughts and feelings of the character; preceding events; outcome. Choice or ordering tests: Szondi Projective Tests: choice or ordering, completion and expressive tests. Page linking projective tests to choice or ordering tests (Szondi), completion tests (Sentence Completion, Sack's Sentence Completion) and expressive tests (House Tree Person, Draw A Man, Kinetic Family Drawing). Psycho Didi notes · p. 66 Founder note. Developed by Leopold Szondi in 1935. Intended to reveal a person's innermost suppressed traits, the parts of yourself you have pushed down into your subconscious. Number of photos: 48. The test involves looking at a series of 48 photos of people with distinct expressions on their faces. The patient picks the friendliest faces and the unfriendliest, the idea being that a person identifies with like people and that their choices from the pictures would represent traits of themselves. Completion tests Sentence Completion Test Semi-projective. 1940: first given by Rohde and Hidreth . Sack's Sentence Completion Test Founder note. By Joseph M. Sacks . Developed to explore specific clusters of attitudes or significant areas of an individual's life. Number of items: 60. 4 subscales: family, sex, relationships, self concepts — each measured on 15 different attitudes such as fears, guilt, and goals. A rating sheet with the four appropriate stems rearranged under the 15 attitude headings allows a clinician to rate the examinee's responses on a continuum that ranges from no significant disturbance to severely disturbed. Expressive tests House Tree Person Test (HTP) Asks for the drawing of a house, a tree, and a person, in order to evaluate them together and globally. Person: who is the person; how old he is; what does he do best; what does he like least. Tree: what kind of tree it is; how old it is; what season it is; has someone tried to cut it down; who waters it; does it have enough light to grow. Usually administered on children. Draw A Man Test Founder note. Goodenough , 1926. Scoring: Chen-Sea (2000). Patients are given a blank piece of paper (8.5×11) entitled "Draw an Entire Man" and a pencil, and are asked to draw an entire man from memory. Kinetic Family Drawing Founder note. Burns and Kaufman , 1970. Helps assess a child's self-concept and family dynamics. The child is asked to draw a picture of their family, including themselves, "doing something". 9 · Non-Projective Tests (Non Factor Analytic) Non-Projective Tests (Non Factor Analytic): MMPI family, MCMI, MBTI. Boxed fact cards for the MMPI, MMPI-2, MMPI-II-RF, MMPI-A, MMPI-3, the Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory and the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator. Psycho Didi notes · p. 67 Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) Founder note. Given by Hathaway & McKinley (1989); ages 18 and above. 567 items. 1943: 1st test of validity scales. 1989: Revision. MMPI-A published in 1992. Uses the criterion keyed method (criterion validity). T scores. Time taken: 40–45 minutes. Validity Scales CNS — cannot say. L — Lie scale. F — Infrequency scale, faking bad (1st half). K — Defensiveness / Evasiveness. Fb — Faking bad (last half). VRIN — Variable Response Inconsistency. TRIN — True Response Inconsistency. F-K — Honesty of test. S — Superlative self presentation. Fp — Faking psychopathology in a clinical setting. Fs — Overreporting somatic symptoms. Why it matters. People scoring high on the K scale show high adjustment, insight, higher socioeconomic status, education. People scoring low on the K scale: masochistic tendencies. Clinical Scales Hs — Hypochondriasis D — Depression Hy — Hysteria Pd — Psychopathic deviate Mf — Masculinity Femininity Pa — Paranoia Pt — Psychasthenia Sc — Schizophrenia Ma — Hypomania Si — Social Introversion Other Scales 28 Harris-Lingoes subscales. Content scales: Butcher, Graham, Williams & Ben-Porath (1990). Content component scales (Ben-Porath & Sherwood, 1993). Personality Psychopathology Five scales (PSY-5; Harkness et al., 2002). Restructured clinical scales (Tellegen et al., 2003). Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory 2 (MMPI-2) Validity scales and clinical scales: same as MMPI. Version Author / Year Age Items Scales MMPI Hathaway & McKinley 18+ 567 Validity + Clinical MMPI-2-RF (restructured form) 2008 18+ 338 50 (an alternative to MMPI-II, not a total replacement) MMPI-A Adolescents 14–18 478 Validity and clinical same as MMPI-2; additionally F1 & F2 scales and other subscales MMPI-3 Yossef Ben-Porath & Auke Tellegen (2020) — 335 52 Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory (MCMI) Founder note. Given by Theodore Millon . 4th edition based on DSM-5. 5th grade reading level; made for age 18+. 195 true or false questions. Time taken: 25–30 mins. Scales 15 personality pattern scales. 10 clinical syndrome scales. 5 validity scales: 3 modifying indices, 2 random response indicators. 45 Grossman personality facet scales. Clinical scales — severe SS — thought disorder CC — major depression PP — delusional disorder A — generalized anxiety H — somatic symptom N — Bipolar D — Persistent depression B — Alcohol use T — Drug Use R — PTS Validity Scales X — disclosure Y — desirability Z — debasement V — invalidity W — inconsistency Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) Founder note. By Isabel Myers and Katherine Briggs ; made by the theoretical method (Carl Jung). Highly used by organizations. Interest inventory: Ipsative (every single option has the same value). Types: extroversion vs introversion; sensing vs intuiting; thinking vs feeling; judging vs perceiving. Criticism: little scientific evidence; weak validity; incomprehensive and vague. Allport, Vernon & Lindzey — Study of Values Scale Non-Projective Tests (Non Factor Analytic): Study of Values, EPPS, Holland, MPQ. Boxed fact cards for the Allport, Vernon and Lindzey Study of Values scale, the Edwards Personal Preference Schedule, Holland's Interest Inventory with a RIASEC hexagon, and the Multiphasic Personality Questionnaire. Psycho Didi notes · p. 68 Ipsative; given in 1931. Based on six value orientations: theoretical, economic, aesthetic, social, political, religious. 240 points; interest inventory. Edwards Personal Preference Schedule (EPPS) Founder note. By Ellen Edwards ; derived from Murray's theory. Interest inventory: ipsative. Validity scales: social desirability, consistency. 225 items; used in vocational training. Based on Murray's needs: Achievement, Deference, Order, Exhibition, Autonomy, Affiliation, Intraception, Succourance, Dominance, Abasement, Nurturance, Change, Endurance, Heterosexuality, Aggression. Holland's Interest Inventory Based on Holland's Theory of Vocational Types or the RIASEC model. Vocational Types: Realistic (R), Investigative (I), Artistic (A), Social (S), Enterprising (E), Conventional (C). Multiphasic Personality Questionnaire (MPQ) Founder note. Developed by Murthy (1964); the Indian version of MMPI-2. Age: 18 and above. 100 statements, forced choice type. 2 validity scales: K scale, Repressor Sensitiser. 7 clinical scales: Anxiety, Manic, Psychopathic deviation, Depression, Paranoid, Schizophrenia, Hysteria. 10 · Non-Projective Tests (Factor Analytic) Non-Projective Tests (Factor Analytic): 16 PF, EPQ, NEO-PI. Fact cards for Cattell's 16 PF (traits, 16 source traits, types of data), the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire and the NEO-PI. Psycho Didi notes · p. 68 16 PF Founder note. By Raymond Cattell ; made using factor analysis. Type of traits: temperamental, ability, dynamic (bipolar). Surface traits are a combination of source traits. Oblique design used for factor analysis. Gave the specification equation R = f(S,P). Identified 11 second-order factors. Used multiple abstract variance analysis to measure heritability of traits. 16 source traits Warmth · Reasoning · Emotional stability · Dominance · Liveliness · Rule conscious · Social boldness · Sensitivity · Vigilance · Abstractness · Privateness · Apprehension · Open to change · Self reliance · Perfection · Tension. Types of data Key. Objective measurement: the participant should not know what is being measured. L data — D, J, K, P factors are a part of L data. Q data T data Global 5 scale — created out of second-order factors. Response style scales: acquiescence; impression management (narcissists will show a lot of social desirability); infrequency. NEO-PI Founder note. By Paul Costa and Robert McCrae ; based on the five factor model / big five model. Year: 1978. No lie scale, no validity scales. Number of items: 240; orthogonal rotation used. Three versions: NEO-PI (1985), NEO-PI-R (1992), NEO-PI-3 (2005). Domains measured by NEO-PI: Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism, Openness, Conscientiousness. Each domain has 6 facets. The psychoticism scale of EPI correlates negatively with agreeableness and conscientiousness scales. Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ) Founder note. By Hans Eysenck . Theory: Type → Trait → Habit → S-R (smallest). Focuses on nature (biological disposition) only. 108 items; current version: EPQ-R (1985). Can measure 22 personality disorders. Three dimensions (PEN): Psychoticism – Impulse control (gave this dimension after working at Maudsley hospital). Extroversion – Introversion. Neuroticism – Emotional Stability. 4th dimension: Lie scale. Reliability vs validity check. Note the distinct validity-scale families across objective tests: MMPI (Starke Hathaway and J. Charnley McKinley, 1943) uses criterion-keyed validity scales (L, F, K, VRIN, TRIN…); MCMI uses X/Y/Z/V/W; EPPS uses social desirability + consistency; MPQ uses K + Repressor-Sensitiser; the 16PF uses response-style scales (acquiescence, impression management, infrequency); NEO-PI has no validity/lie scales, whereas the EPQ (Hans Eysenck and Sybil Eysenck, 1975) adds a Lie scale as its 4th dimension. Don't confuse a validity scale (detects faking) with a clinical/content scale (measures the trait).

title: Psychological Interventions
text: Psychological Interventions — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Psychological Interventions Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Psychodynamic → Sigmund Freud Behaviour therapy: 3 wings CBT waves 1–3 Humanistic & existential Stress, coping & counselling What this covers. The full sweep of psychological interventions: psychodynamic psychotherapy (Freud, defence mechanisms, transference) and transactional analysis (Eric Berne); behaviour therapy across its classical-conditioning, operant and modelling wings; the three waves of cognitive-behaviour therapy (Beck's CT and Ellis's REBT, then DBT, MBCT, MBSR (Jon Kabat-Zinn, 1979) and ACT with other third-wave therapies); EMDR (Francine Shapiro); gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls) and its many techniques; humanistic and existential therapy (Carl Rogers, Karl Jaspers, Sartre, Viktor Frankl, Irvin Yalom); stress and coping models; and the principles of counselling and guidance. Original diagrams. 25 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 70 to 80) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Psychodynamic Psychotherapy · 2 · Transactional Analysis · 3 · Behaviour Therapy · 4 · Cognitive-Behaviour Therapy (Waves 1–3) · 5 · EMDR · 6 · Gestalt Therapy · 7 · Humanistic & Existential Therapy · 8 · Stress and Coping · 9 · Counselling and Guidance 1 · Psychodynamic Psychotherapy Psychodynamic psychotherapy: Freud. Infographic page on Freud with his photo, early life, career, important therapy processes, defence mechanisms, dreams and dream work, and an illustration of a client on a couch with a therapist. Psycho Didi notes · p. 70 Psychodynamic psychotherapy → Sigmund Freud. Worked with Joseph Breuer (the case of Anna 'O' ); influenced by Jean-Martin Charcot (hypnosis) and Breuer (catharsis). Freud — early life & career Was his mother's favourite child; observed his own life; was attracted to his mother and scared of his father. Started teaching at the University of Vienna in 1873. Died in Britain from jaw cancer. Career milestones: cocaine exploration; influence of Jean-Martin Charcot (hypnosis) and Josef Breuer (catharsis); movement from resistance to suggestion → concentration technique → free association; publication of Studies on Hysteria . Defence mechanisms Defence Core idea Repression Keeping unpleasant memories or thoughts buried in the unconscious. Primal : innately part of the Id. Proper : unacceptable derivatives of original id impulses. Denial Refusing to recognise an unpleasant reality. Rationalization Creating a socially acceptable excuse to justify unacceptable behaviour. Reaction formation Not acknowledging unacceptable impulses and over-emphasising their opposite. Projection Transferring one's unacceptable qualities or impulses to others. Important processes Process Meaning Resistance Reluctance to discuss certain topics; conscious defence mechanisms. Transference The patient projects feelings meant for others onto the therapist. Counter-transference The therapist develops emotional reactions towards the patient. Working through Discussing emotionally charged material over many therapy sessions. Trap — transference vs counter-transference. Transference = patient → therapist (patient projects feelings for others onto the therapist). Counter-transference = therapist → patient (therapist develops emotional reactions towards the patient). Dreams Manifest content: the clearly identifiable stories, characters, events and actions. Latent content: the unconscious thoughts, desires, fears and conflicts. Dream work Mechanism Function Condensation Condensing multiple thoughts into a single dream element or symbol. Displacement Shifting emotional significance from one object to another. Symbolization Representing an action or idea through symbols. Secondary revision Rationalizing latent content. 2 · Transactional Analysis Transactional analysis: Eric Berne. Introduction and four types of analysis beside three circles showing the Parent ego (nurturing and critical), Adult ego and Child ego (free and adapted). Psycho Didi notes · p. 71 Transactional Analysis → Eric Berne. Transactional Analysis is a psychotherapeutic method characterised by a creative combination of cognitive and psychodynamically oriented psychotherapy, enriched by aspects of communication therapy and gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls) processes. Types of analysis Structural analysis: individual personality analysis. Transactional analysis: dialogue analysis. Game analysis: saying something and meaning something else (analysis of ulterior transactions). Script analysis: compulsive, rigid transactions that people act out compulsively. Ego states Parent ego — Nurturing parent and Critical parent. Adult ego. Child ego — Free child and Adapted child. Transactions Transactions. Three Parent-Adult-Child diagrams with arrows showing complementary, crossed and ulterior transactions between two people. Psycho Didi notes · p. 71 Complementary transactions. Crossed transactions. Ulterior transactions — e.g. saying "You don't love me" while meaning "You love my brother so much!" 3 · Behaviour Therapy Behaviour therapy: introduction, applications and features. Introduction and assumptions of behaviour therapy, its applications and fields of use, and its key features, with a small illustration of three people. Psycho Didi notes · p. 72 Behaviour therapy is the application of experimentally derived principles of learning to the treatment of psychological disorders. Assumptions An empirical approach. Most behaviour is learned and therefore can be unlearned. Maladaptive behaviours are learned in the same manner as adaptive ones. The historical account of the development of a problem behaviour is less relevant than the present factors. It rejects the assumptions of traditional trait theory. Features Focus on present factors. Functional assessment and behavioural analysis. Recognition of individual–e

title: Health Psychology, Ethics & Laws
text: Health Psychology, Ethics & Laws — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Health Psychology, Ethics & Laws Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Health-behaviour models (HBM, TPB, TTM) Levels of prevention APA Ethics Code (Principles A–E) Mental Healthcare Act 2017 RCI & RPWD Acts What this covers. Two linked areas. First, Health Psychology : epidemiology basics, the levels of prevention (primordial, primary, secondary, tertiary), and the major health-behaviour and illness models (Health Belief Model, Theory of Planned Behaviour, Transtheoretical Model, biopsychosocial model (George Engel, 1977)). Second, Psychology in Practice — Ethics & Laws : the APA General Principles and Ethical Standards, and the history of Indian mental-health legislation from the colonial Lunacy Acts through the RCI Act, the disability acts, and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 and its 2022 amendment. Original diagrams. 8 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 82 to 85) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: Health Psychology · Ethics & Laws Health Psychology Epidemiology and disease measures Epidemiology. Definition of epidemiology with morbidity, incidence, prevalence and mortality, under an illustration of two researchers with a magnifying glass. Psycho Didi notes · p. 82 Epidemiology is the study of the frequency, distribution and causes of infectious and non-infectious disease in a population. Its core measures are: Term Meaning Morbidity The number of cases of a disease that exist at some given point in time. Incidence The number of new cases at some given point of time. Prevalence The total number of existing cases at some given point of time. Mortality The number of deaths due to particular causes. Don't confuse. Incidence counts only new cases; prevalence counts all existing cases (new + old). Morbidity is about illness; mortality is about death. Levels of prevention Types of prevention. Diagram branching from types of prevention to primordial, primary, secondary and tertiary prevention, each with examples and an icon. Psycho Didi notes · p. 82 Level Focus Primordial prevention Inhibit the emergence of risk factors in the form of environmental, economic, social, and behavioral conditions and cultural patterns of living, etc. Primary prevention Awareness programs, psychoeducation, vaccination, wearing a helmet. Secondary prevention Early detection and treatment; reversal of problems/damage. Tertiary prevention Only management, since reversal is not possible; stopping further progression of problems. Key. Order by when they act: Primordial (before risk factors even appear) → Primary (before disease) → Secondary (early disease, still reversible) → Tertiary (established disease, manage and limit progression). Health-behaviour models Biopsychosocial model of health. Venn diagram of biological, psychological and social or environmental factors that overlap around mental health. Psycho Didi notes · p. 82 Health belief model, TTM and theory of planned behaviour. Notes on the six constructs of the health belief model, the six stages of the transtheoretical model, and the three components of the theory of planned behaviour. Psycho Didi notes · p. 82 The Health Belief Model (HBM) Given by Rosenstock . It explains health behaviour through six constructs : Perceived susceptibility — a person's subjective perception of the risk of acquiring an illness or disease. Perceived severity — a person's feelings on the seriousness of contracting an illness or disease. Perceived benefits — a person's perception of the effectiveness of various actions available to reduce the threat of illness or disease. Perceived barriers — a person's feelings on the obstacles to performing a recommended health action. Cue to action — the stimulus needed to trigger the decision-making process to accept a recommended health action. Self-efficacy (Albert Bandura, 1977) — the level of a person's confidence in his or her ability to successfully perform a behaviour. Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) Given by Icek Ajzen ; earlier called the Theory of Reasoned Action . According to this theory, a health behaviour is the direct result of a behavioural intention . Behavioural intentions are themselves made up of three components: Attitudes toward the specific action — beliefs about the outcomes of the behaviour (e.g. "if I change my diet, I will lose weight, improve my health, and be more attractive") and evaluations of those outcomes (e.g. "being healthy and looking good are desirable"). Subjective norms regarding the action — normative beliefs (e.g. "my family and friends think I should change my diet") and motivation to comply (e.g. "I want to do what they want me to do"). Perceived behavioural control — e.g. "I will be able to change my diet". Transtheoretical Model of behaviour change (TTM) Given by James Prochaska . It posits that health behaviour change involves progress through six stages of change : Precontemplation Contemplation Preparation Action Maintenance Termination Biopsychosocial model of health Health and illness are understood as the product of interacting biological, psychological, and social factors, rather than biology alone. Model → author. Health Belief Model → Rosenstock Theory of Planned Behaviour (formerly Theory of Reasoned Action) → Ajzen Transtheoretical Model (TTM) → James Prochaska Don't confuse. HBM's self-efficacy vs TPB's perceived behavioural control — both are about confidence to perform the behaviour but belong to different models. TPB's older name is the Theory of Reasoned Action (which lacked perceived behavioural control). Ethics & Laws APA Ethical Principles and Code of Conduct APA code of conduct: introduction. Banner title and introduction describing the parts of the APA Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct. Psycho Didi notes · p. 84 APA preamble and five general principles. The preamble

title: Cognitive Psychology
text: Cognitive Psychology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Cognitive Psychology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Sensation & perception Attention & SDT Learning & conditioning Memory models & forgetting Intelligence & creativity Thinking · problem solving · language What this covers. The whole cognitive block: how a stimulus becomes a perception (Gestalt organization, constancies, motion and depth cues, colour and sound theories, top-down vs bottom-up perception), theories of attention and signal detection, classical and operant conditioning (B. F. Skinner) plus cognitive/social learning, the multi-store, working-memory and levels-of-processing (Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart, 1972) models, forgetting and memory distortion, the major theories of intelligence and creativity, thinking and concept formation, problem-solving heuristics and cognitive biases, and theories of language development. Original diagrams. 107 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 87 to 107) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Sensation & Perception · 2 · Colour & Sound Perception · 3 · Attention · 4 · Classical & Operant Conditioning · 5 · Cognitive & Social Learning · 6 · Memory Models · 7 · Forgetting & Memory Distortion · 8 · Intelligence · 9 · Creativity · 10 · Thinking & Concepts · 11 · Problem Solving, Reasoning & Decision-Making · 12 · Language Development 1 · Sensation & Perception Process and types of perception. Flow from stimulation to transduction, sensation, attention and perception, with arrows splitting perception into top-down and bottom-up types. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 The perceptual sequence runs stimulation → transduction → sensation → attention → perception . Perception can be driven two ways: Top-down — expectation driven (knowledge and context shape what we perceive). Bottom-up — stimulus / data driven (the raw sensory input drives perception). Top-down vs bottom-up. Top-down = expectation/knowledge driven (constructivist, e.g. Gregory). Bottom-up = stimulus/data driven (direct/ecological, e.g. Gibson). Endogenous attention is top-down; exogenous attention is bottom-up. Gestalt psychology Gestalt psychology. Notes on the phi phenomenon, the six laws of organization and Pragnanz, with an overlapping rings drawing for Pragnanz. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Core dictum: the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Key ideas include the Phi phenomenon and the law of Prägnanz — every stimulus pattern is seen so that the resulting structure is as simple as possible. Max Wertheimer — founder of Gestalt perception; described the Phi phenomenon , a type of stroboscopic motion , best seen at a time interval of 30 to 200 milliseconds . Laws of Perceptual Organization Law Principle Proximity Objects physically close together are grouped together. Continuity Stimuli falling along the same plane tend to be grouped together. Closure We fill in small gaps so objects are still perceived as whole. Similarity Stimuli resembling one another tend to be grouped together. Common region Stimuli in a common area or ground are grouped together. Common fate Objects moving in a similar direction are grouped together. Perceptual Constancy Perceptual constancy. Definitions of colour or brightness constancy, size constancy and shape constancy. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Colour / brightness constancy — perceiving colour or brightness as constant despite changes in lighting. Size constancy — perceiving an object as the same size regardless of its distance from the observer. Shape constancy — perceiving an object as maintaining its shape despite changes in orientation. Apparent (Illusory) Motion Apparent motion and the autokinetic effect. Definition of apparent motion and the autokinetic effect found by Muzafer Sherif (1935). Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Induced motion. Definition of induced motion with a photo of the moon behind drifting clouds as the example. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Phi phenomenon, motion parallax and stroboscopic effect. Three panels on the phi and beta phenomena with critical flicker fusion, motion parallax with a train passenger drawing, and the stroboscopic effect with a multi-exposure dancer photo. Psycho Didi notes · p. 87 Perception of motion when there actually is none. Autokinetic effect — a stationary point of light appears to move in a dark room. Found by Muzafer Sherif (1935) . Induced motion — motion of one object causes a nearby stationary object to appear to move (e.g. clouds moving past the moon make the moon appear to race through the clouds). Phi phenomenon — an optical illusion in which stationary objects shown in rapid succession, past the threshold at which they can be perceived separately, appear to move. Temporal threshold: 30–200 ms . Beta phenomenon — similar to the phi phenomenon but usually circular motion. Critical Flicker Fusion Frequency — the frequency at which a flickering light appears steady; the threshold where separate/discontinuous images seem to fuse. Motion parallax — as we move, nearby objects appear to glide rapidly past us while more distant objects move more slowly (extremely far objects such as the moon seem to move away from you). Stroboscopic effect — a rapid succession of still images or lights creates the illusion of motion. Depth & Distance Cues Depth perception and the visual cliff. Visual cliff apparatus drawing next to notes on binocular cues (convergence, retinal, vertical and horizontal disparity, horopter) and monocular cues. Psycho Didi notes · p. 88 Monocular cues Cue Description Accommodation Change in the lens shape as the eye focuses. Interposition (overlap / partial occlusion) A closer object cuts off the view of part or all of a more distant one. Relative size The closer of two same-size objects casts a larger image on the retina. Texture gradient Closer objects have a coarser, more distinct texture; far objects appear more densely packed / smooth. Aerial / atmospheric perspective Closer objects appear sharper than more distant, hazy objects. Relative height / elevation Objects closest to the horizon appear farthest; the lowest objects in the field of vision seem closest. Linear perspective Parallel lines (e.g. edges of sidewalks) seem to converge in the distance. Relative brightness The closer of two identical objects reflects more light to your eyes. Binocular cues Binocular convergence — depth cue based on the inward movement of the eyes as they focus on nearby objects. Retinal disparity — the slight difference in the images seen by each eye, used by the brain to perceive depth. Vertical disparity — due to the image falling on a different place in the retina. Horizontal disparity — due to the difference in angles at which the eyes are placed. Horopter — the imaginary line at which an object placed there produces no disparity. Eleanor Gibson & Richard Walk — the Visual Cliff depth-perception experiment on 3–6 month-old babies; concluded that depth perception is innate . Perceptual Set Perceptual set. Bruner and Goodman (1947) coin study notes, with a coin and a same-size cardboard disc showing that the coin loomed larger. Psycho Didi notes · p. 88 Refers to the influence of values on perception. Jerome Bruner & Goodman (1947) — coins were perceived as larger than same-size cardboard discs, and more so by poor children than rich children. Because coin size correlates with value, valuable coins "loomed larger" in perception even when the cardboard was the same size. Top-Down Theories of Perception Top-down theories of perception. Three columns on Gregory's processing theory, template matching theory and prototype theory. Psycho Didi notes · p. 88 Constructivist theory (Processing theory) — proponent Richard Gregory (1970) . Perception is a hypothesis based on prior knowledge; we actively construct our perception of reality from the environment and stored information. Higher-order thinking is involved. Template Matching theory — a template is an internal construct that, when matched by sensory stimuli, leads to recognition of an object. "Lock and key" idea of pattern recognition; the object must match the template exactly . Prototype theory (Eleanor Rosch, 1975) — an alternative to template matching. A prototype for each object is stored in memory; a pattern is checked against the prototype and recognised if resemblance is found. Not as rigid as templates. Shortcoming: does not account for exceptions. Bottom-Up Theories of Perception Bottom-up theories of perception. Notes on Gibson's direct perception, feature detection theory, Biederman's geon theory and Selfridge's pandemonium model with its four demons. Psycho Didi notes · p. 88 J. J. Gibson — Direct (Ecological) Perception : the information in the stimulus itself is the important element; learning and cognition are unnecessary because there is enough information in the environment to make an interpretation. Constraints — a barrier in the environment that helps perception. Affordance — a mediator in the environment that helps perception. Light feedback — from the reflection of light we decide whether to move forward or backward. Feature Detection theory — object recognition is high-order processing preceded by a step in which complex incoming stimuli are identified according to simpler features. Irving Biederman (1987) — Geon theory (aka recognition by components ): the human information-processing system has a limited number of simple geometric shapes ( geons , "geometric ions") that combine to form meaningful objects. Identifying an object from its geons = the principle of componential recovery ; each geon's unique set of Non-Accidental Properties gives geons the property of discriminability . Oliver Selfridge — Pandemonium Model ("pandemonium" = a very noisy, chaotic place). Four kinds of demons: image demons (sensation) → feature demons (feature separation) → cognitive demons (compare with memory) → decision demons (perception). 2 · Theories of Colour & Sound Perception Vision — photoreceptor cells Vision. Labelled human eye anatomy diagram with notes on rods and cones, properties of colour, opponent process and trichromatic theories, dark vs light adaptation and the visual pathway. Psycho Didi notes · p. 89 Rods Cones Vision Achromatic, night vision (scotopic) Chromatic vision (photopic) Number ~120 million ~6–8 million Photopigment Rhodopsin (from vitamin A) Photopsin Activated Only in low-light / scotopic vision Bright light; types L, M, S cones Visual pathway: Photoreceptors → Horizontal cells → Bipolar cells → Amacrine cells → Ganglion cells → Optic nerve → Optic chiasm → Optic tract → Lateral geniculate nucleus → Primary visual cortex. Properties of colour Visible spectrum of light: 380 to 760 nm . Hue — the actual colour seen. Saturation — concentration of colour. Brightness — intensity of light. Young–Helmholtz — Trichromatic theory of colour : the retina has three types of colour receptor, each especially sensitive to red, green or blue ; stimulating combinations produces all other colours. Ewald Hering — Opponent-Process theory : three sets of opponent retinal processes enable colour vision — red–green, yellow–blue, white–black . If one colour of a pair is perceived, the other cannot be. Explains afterimages . Dark vs Light adaptation Light adaptation Dark adaptation Transition Rod → cone dominance Cone → rod dominance Mechanism Photopigment bleaching; pupil constriction Chemical changes in photoreceptors; pupil dilation Photosensitivity Low High Time Takes less time Takes more time (rods must be regenerated) Audition Audition. Labelled ear anatomy diagram with notes on properties of sound, the auditory pathway, place theory, frequency theory and the volley principle. Psycho Didi notes · p. 89 Properties of sound Audible frequency: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz . Amplitude — height of the sound wave; determines loudness. Frequency — waves per second; determines pitch. Timbre — quality of sound. Hermann von Helmholtz — Place theory : we hear different pitches because different sound waves trigger activity at different places along the cochlea's basilar membrane. Best explains high pitches . Rinne & Rutherford (1880) — Frequency theory : the brain reads pitch by monitoring the frequency of neural impulses travelling up the auditory nerve. Does not explain sound sensing above 1000 Hz. Best explains low pitches . Key — Volley principle (Ernest Wever and Charles Bray, 1930). Supports frequency theory: neurons fire in alternating rapid succession so that, combined, they achieve a frequency above 1000 waves per second. Auditory pathway: Pinna → Auditory canal → Tympanic membrane → Hammer (Malleus) → Anvil (Incus) → Stirrup (Stapes) → Cochlea → Auditory nerve → Cochlear nerve → Superior olivary complex → Lateral lemniscus → Inferior colliculus → Medial geniculate body → Auditory cortex. Other senses Proprioception. Proprioception branching into kinesthetic and vestibular senses, each with a stick-figure illustration. Psycho Didi notes · p. 89 Kinesthetic / Proprioception — sense of body position and movements. Vestibular — sense of head positioning (parietal lobe); semi-circular canals and cerebellum involved. 3 · Theories of Attention Attention is the concentration of mental activity that lets you take in a limited portion of the vast stream of information available from both your sensory world and your memory. Sequence: sensation → attention → perception . Types of attention (source) Introduction to attention. Definition of attention, the sensation to attention to perception sequence, and exogenous (bottom-up) vs endogenous (top-down) attention. Psycho Didi notes · p. 90 Hierarchical model of attention. Sohlberg and Mateer pyramid of attention levels from focused at the base through sustained, selective and alternating to divided at the top, with definitions and the determinants of vigilance. Psycho Didi notes · p. 90 Exogenous — controlled by the stimulus; bottom-up. Endogenous — the brain internally decides what is important; top-down. Sohlberg & Mateer (1987, 1989) — Hierarchical model of attention : focused → sustained → selective → alternating → divided. Focused attention — ability to focus attention on a stimulus. Sustained attention (vigilance) — ability to attend to a stimulus/activity over a long period. Determinants: sensory factor, temporal certainty, spatial certainty, clarity of stimuli. Selective attention — ability to attend to a specific stimulus in the presence of distracting stimuli. Alternating attention — ability to shift focus between two or more stimuli. Divided attention (multitasking) — ability to attend to different stimuli at the same time. Signal Detection Theory (SDT) Signal detection theory. SDT notes with a two by two table of hit, correct rejection, false alarm and miss for liberal and conservative responders. Psycho Didi notes · p. 90 Wesley W. Peterson & Theodore G. Birdsall — Signal Detection Theory : detection of a signal depends on sensitivity and response bias . Sensitivity (d′) = number of hits − number of false alarms. Signal present Signal absent Responds "yes" Hit (correct) False alarm (incorrect) Responds "no" Miss (incorrect) Correct rejection (correct) For a liberal participant the receiver-operating (ROC) curve peaks towards the right; for a conservative participant it peaks towards the left. Theories of Selective Attention Theories of selective attention. Notes on Cherry, Broadbent's filter model and Treisman's attenuation model, with flow diagrams of the selection filter and the attenuator. Psycho Didi notes · p. 90 Late selection model. Deutsch and Deutsch notes with a flow diagram where messages pass physical analysis and semantic analysis before the attended message reaches awareness and response. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Multimode attention theory and perceptual load. Notes on Johnston and Heinz's three-stage multimode theory and Lavie and Tsal's perceptual load theory. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Feature integration theory. Treisman and Gelade notes with a diagram of colour and orientation feature maps feeding a map of locations, plus example displays of a colour singleton search and a conjunction search. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Spotlight theory of attention. Spotlight theory notes with a circular blurred-text illustration marking the focus, fringe and margin. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Shortcomings of selective attention. Definitions of inattentional blindness and change blindness. Psycho Didi notes · p. 91 Selective attention is tested with a shadowing / dichotic listening task. Colin Cherry (1953) — early selection model : no overlap in dichotic listening; we do not understand a stimulus before we perceive it. Donald Broadbent (1958) — Filter model (a bottleneck model): we filter information right after we notice it, at the sensory level. Anne Treisman (1980) — Attenuation model : explains the cocktail-party phenomenon . Instead of blocking stimuli out, the filter merely weakens the strength of stimuli other than the target. Deutsch & Deutsch (1963) — Late Selection model : stimuli are filtered out only after being analysed for both their physical properties and their meaning. Johnston & Heinz (1978) — Multimode attention theory : attention is a flexible system that selects a stimulus at three stages — (1) sensory representations created, (2) semantic representations created, (3) both sensory and semantic representations enter consciousness. More processing requires more mental effort. Lavie & Tsal (1994) — Perceptual Load theory : perception is a limited-capacity process that proceeds automatically until that capacity is filled. Anne Treisman & Garry Gelade (1980) — Feature Integration Theory (FIT) : explains how an individual combines pieces of observable information about an object to form a complete perception. Two kinds of visual search: feature search (fast, pre-attentive, primitive features) and conjunction search (slower, effortful; targets defined by a conjunction of features). Eriksen & St James (1986); Michael Posner et al. — Spotlight theory of attention : people can attend to only one region of space at a time. Inspired by William James , attention has a focus (central area extracting high-resolution information where attention is directed), a fringe (extracts information more crudely, extending over a specified area), and a margin (the cut-off between them). Shortcomings of selective attention Inattentional blindness (Arien Mack and Irvin Rock, 1998) — people fail to see things that are actually there. Change blindness — inability to detect changes in objects or scenes being viewed. 4 · Classical & Operant Conditioning Key — definition. Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour as a result of experience. Two basic kinds of learning Introduction to learning.
