Definition of learning and the split into non-associative learning (habituation, sensitization) and associative learning (classical and instrumental conditioning). Psycho Didi notes · p. 92 Non-associative learning (short term) — learning about a single stimulus: Habituation — a decreased behavioural response to an innocuous stimulus. Sensitization — an increase in a behavioural response to an intense stimulus. Associative learning (long term) — learning relationships among events: classical conditioning and instrumental (operant) conditioning . Classical Conditioning Strength of conditioning. Delayed, trace, simultaneous and backward conditioning, each drawn as CS and UCS arrows showing their timing. Psycho Didi notes · p. 92 Classical conditioning and principles of conditioning. Pavlov notes with a before, during and after conditioning dog illustration, the five principles with dog examples, and a first-order vs second-order conditioning table. Psycho Didi notes · p. 92 Contiguity and contingency. Rescorla's view that the CS must predict the US, with positive, negative and zero contingency. Psycho Didi notes · p. 92 Major points to be remembered. Summary list of classical conditioning features: reflex based, respondent, passive, S-S type, and the amygdala's role. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Classical conditioning and biological preparedness. Notes on biological preparedness with the Garcia and Koelling rat diagram and a cues by consequences table for sweet and click cues. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Ivan Pavlov (1897) — first researched classical conditioning: a previously neutral stimulus becomes associated with another stimulus through repeated pairing. Based on three broad principles: Contiguity — nearness in space and time. Contingency — prediction power. Blocking — a CS blocks conditioning with another neutral stimulus. Principles of conditioning Principle Meaning Example (Pavlov's dog) Acquisition CS & US repeatedly paired so CS acquires US properties. Dog learns to salivate to the bell. Extinction CS presented without US; CR fades and disappears. Dog stops salivating to the bell. Spontaneous recovery After extinction & rest, CS again produces a faint CR. Dog salivates again on hearing the bell. Generalization CR shown to stimuli similar to the CS. Dog salivates to other bell-like noises. Discrimination CR shown only to the CS, not to similar stimuli. Dog salivates only to the specific bell. Second-order (higher-order) conditioning — once a CS elicits a CR, that CS can briefly be used as a US to condition a response to a new stimulus. Strength / timing of conditioning Type Timing (CS vs US) Note Delayed Bell rings and, while still ringing, food is presented. Conditioning occurs the fastest . Trace CS, then a short break, then the US. — Simultaneous CS and US presented at the same time. — Backward US presented first, followed by the CS. E.g. taste aversions in pregnancy / chemotherapy. Contiguity and Contingency Robert Rescorla — conditioning involves cognitive components. The CS must be a reliable predictor of the US (contingency); mere temporal contiguity is not enough. Positive contingency — CS predicts the presence of the UCS → excitatory conditioning . Zero contingency — no pattern, so no learning takes place. Negative contingency — CS predicts the absence of the UCS → inhibitory conditioning . Classical conditioning & biological preparedness Animals and humans are biologically prepared to make certain connections more easily (e.g. learned taste aversions can be learnt in a single trial). John Garcia & Robert Koelling (1966) — rats more readily learned certain associations: food more likely to become CS for nausea ; noise more likely to become CS for shock . Key — classical conditioning at a glance. Totally based on reflexes ; response is elicited by the stimulus (also called respondent conditioning ); passive learning; reflexes can be conditioned or unconditioned; magnitude of response matters; it is an S–S type of conditioning. The amygdala (lateral nucleus) organizes emotional responses provoked by aversive stimuli. Operant Conditioning Operant conditioning introduction. Thorndike and Skinner notes with a drawing of Thorndike's cat puzzle box and a labelled Skinner box. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Reinforcement and punishment. Two by two table of positive and negative reinforcement and punishment, defined as adding or removing pleasant or unpleasant stimuli. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Principles of operant conditioning. Acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization and discrimination, each with a rat and bar example. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Shaping and chaining. Definitions of shaping and chaining with a chain-link icon. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Reinforcement schedules. The two basic schedule types, continuous and partial, and when each works better. Psycho Didi notes · p. 93 Schedules of reinforcement. Tree of the four partial schedules (fixed ratio, variable ratio, fixed interval, variable interval) with a learning over time graph showing a separate line for each schedule. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Learning and maintaining fear. Two-stage account of fear: classical conditioning or escape learning first, then instrumental avoidance learning. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Edward Thorndike — learning theory leading to operant conditioning (B. F. Skinner); used a cat in a puzzle box ( trial-and-error learning ). His theory is called associationism / connectionism . Three laws: law of readiness , law of practice/exercise , and the law of effect (behaviour followed by pleasant consequences is repeated; behaviour followed by unpleasant consequences is stopped). B. F. Skinner (1937) — coined the term operant conditioning . The Skinner box delivers food via a lever/disk; the food is a reinforcer and giving it is reinforcement . Operant/instrumental conditioning = learning the relationship between responses and outcomes (an S–R association). Principles of operant conditioning Acquisition — the rat learns to press the bar for food. Extinction — the rat unlearns the bar–food connection and stops pressing. Spontaneous recovery — after extinction and rest, the rat presses the bar again. Generalization — the rat presses other objects that look like the bar. Discrimination — the rat learns to press only a particular bar. Reinforcement & Punishment Positive (add) Negative (remove) Reinforcement (increases behaviour) Deliver a pleasant stimulus after the response (add pleasant). Remove an unpleasant/aversive stimulus after the response (remove unpleasant). Punishment (reduces behaviour) Deliver an unpleasant/aversive stimulus after the response (add unpleasant). Remove a pleasant stimulus after the response (remove pleasant). Negative reinforcement ≠ punishment. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant to increase a behaviour; punishment reduces a behaviour. Don't confuse "negative" (remove) with "punishment" (weaken). Shaping and Chaining Shaping — reinforces the steps used to reach the desired behaviour. Chaining — animals are taught to perform a number of responses successively to get a reward. Reinforcement schedules Two basic types: Continuous (rewarded every time; better for learning new behaviour) and Partial (better once behaviour is learnt; more resistant to extinction ). Schedule Reinforcement provided... Fixed ratio After a fixed number of responses. Variable ratio After a number of responses that varies unpredictably. Fixed interval After a fixed amount of time since the last reinforcement. Variable interval After an amount of time that varies unpredictably since the last reinforcement. Learning and maintaining fear (two-factor) Stage 1 — classical conditioning / escape learning: through repeated pairing of the warning light (CS) and shock (UCS), the animal learns the light predicts the shock and shows a conditioned fear response (CR) to the light alone. Stage 2 — instrumental conditioning / avoidance learning: successful reduction of the aversive stimulus reinforces and strengthens the avoidance behaviour. It gives temporary relief, but the long-run consequences of avoidance are detrimental. 5 · Cognitive & Social Learning Learned Helplessness Learned helplessness. Maier and Seligman two-stage experiment notes with a drawing of the shuttle box, its warning light, electrified grid floor and barrier. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Cognitive approach to learning. Notes on Woodworth's S-O-R approach and Kohler's insight learning with chimpanzees. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Martin Seligman — cognitive approach to learning: control over the outcome of behaviour is as important for learning as contiguity and contingency. Experiment — Maier & Seligman (1976): Stage 1: some dogs learn that whether they receive a shock depends on their own behaviour; other dogs learn they have no control over the shock. Stage 2: both groups placed in a shuttle box; a tone signals an imminent shock, and the dog must jump the barrier to avoid it. Found: control dogs learn the response rapidly; yoked dogs do not. They had learned that shocks were uncontrollable, and this non-control made avoidance learning impossible → learned helplessness . Robert Woodworth — S–O–R approach : to predict the response we must know not only the stimulus but also the organism stimulated; human motivations and conscious decisions play an important part in behaviour. Wolfgang Köhler (1925) — Insight learning , studied on chimpanzees: insight occurs when one suddenly realises how to solve a problem. Learning happens in a sudden way due to insight, not gradual strengthening of the S–R connection. Social Learning Theory Social learning theory. Bandura notes with the attention, retention, motor reproduction and motivation sequence and three Bobo doll conditions: reinforced, not reinforced and punished model. Psycho Didi notes · p. 94 Albert Bandura — Social Learning Theory (aka observational learning ): learning is achieved by mentally rehearsing and then imitating the observed actions of models. An S–O–R theory. Process of learning (sequence): attention → retention → motor reproduction → motivation. Bobo doll experiment — conditions: model hits doll and is reinforced (vicarious reinforcement), model hits doll and is not reinforced , model hits doll and is punished (vicarious punishment). Key. Learning occurs in all three conditions irrespective of reinforcement; however, reproduction of behaviour was dependent on reinforcement. Tolman's Purposive Behaviourism Tolman's purposive behaviourism. Tolman and Honzik latent learning notes with a graph of maze errors over 17 daily trials for rewarded, never-rewarded and delayed-reward rat groups. Psycho Didi notes · p. 95 Edward Tolman — Purposive behaviourism (aka latent learning, expectancy, place learning, sign-stimulus theory). Experiment: Tolman & Honzik (1930) . Group A — reinforced on each trial; Group B — never reinforced; Group C — reinforced only on day 11. Found: Group C had actually learnt the maze without reinforcement ( latent learning ) but showed it once reinforcement appeared. The rats developed a cognitive map — a mental representation of the maze. Components of learning: the significate (desired outcome/goal), the sign (stimulus prompting action), and means–end relations (the learner's internal thought process). Field Theory Field theory. Lewin's field theory notes with a life space diagram (person, driving and restraining vectors, barrier, goal) and the four types of conflict. Psycho Didi notes · p. 95 Kurt Lewin (1930) — Field Theory , based on Gestalt psychology, an S–O–R approach: a person's psychological state affects their social field and vice versa. "Field" = the totality of a person's experiences, needs and topography; field forces (intrinsic or extrinsic) drive behaviour. Types of conflict Conflict Description Vacillation / equilibrium Approach–approach Two goals, both valued. Low vacillation, low equilibrium. Avoidance–avoidance Two goals, both undesirable; running away is more likely. More vacillation and equilibrium. Approach–avoidance One goal has both positive and negative vectors. Highest vacillation; equilibrium stage very long. Double approach–avoidance Multiple goals each with positive and negative vectors. Conflict resolved more easily when equilibrium is less. 6 · Theories of Memory Introduction to memory. Definition of memory as the capacity to register, store and recover information, with a brain and clock icon. Psycho Didi notes · p. 96 Key — definition. Memory is our capacity to register, store and recover information over time — the persistence of learning over time. It is a complex mental system involving multiple stages of information processing. Early models Models of memory: early models. Primary memory (William James) and secondary memory (Waugh and Norman, 1965) with what each holds. Psycho Didi notes · p. 96 In the mid-1960s researchers proposed two structures of memory: Primary memory — proposed by William James ; holds temporary information currently in use. Secondary memory — proposed by Waugh & Norman (1965) ; holds information permanently or for a very long time. Sperling & iconic memory George Sperling and iconic memory. Iconic memory notes with the Sperling (1960) letter grid figure comparing whole report and partial report. Psycho Didi notes · p. 96 George Sperling — iconic memory : a type of visual memory lasting only a fraction of a second. Sensory memory capacity is much larger than believed. In Sperling's test, partial report was more successful than whole report; iconic memory capacity is 9–12× that of STM . Multi-Store Model Multi-store model. Atkinson and Shiffrin flow diagram from sensory memory through selective attention and encoding to STM and LTM, with maintenance and elaborative rehearsal and retrieval loops. Psycho Didi notes · p. 96 Richard Atkinson & Richard Shiffrin (1968) — Multi-Store (modal) Model : information passes from one storage system to the next in a fixed order — Sensory memory → STM → LTM . Store Duration Capacity Notes Sensory memory 1–4 sec Limited, but more than STM Subtypes: iconic (visual), echoic (auditory), haptic (touch). Short-term memory (STM) 18–30 sec 7 ± 2 Temporary storage; gate to LTM; prone to forgetting. Long-term memory (LTM) Very long / permanent Unlimited Reached via elaborative rehearsal ; accessed by retrieval. Flow: Sensory memory → (selective attention → encoding) → STM → (maintenance rehearsal keeps it in STM; elaborative rehearsal moves it) → LTM. George Miller (1956) — the magic number 7 ± 2 : the average number of items held in short-term memory. Emphasized recoding / chunking of information. Working Memory Model The working memory model. Baddeley and Hitch diagram with the central executive above the episodic buffer, fed by the visuo-spatial sketchpad and the phonological loop with its articulatory subsystem. Psycho Didi notes · p. 97 Alan Baddeley & Graham Hitch (1974) — Working Memory Model : temporarily holds and manipulates information during cognitive tasks. Memory span is determined by the speed with which we rehearse information. Component Role Central executive (master subsystem) Takes information from everywhere and integrates it; determines what goes into LTM. Visuo-spatial sketchpad (slave subsystem) Handles visual and spatial information; aids motor movement (1–2 sec). Phonological loop (slave subsystem) Holds verbal/acoustic information (1–4 sec); the articulatory subsystem performs subvocal rehearsal. Episodic buffer Integrates information across the subsystems and links to LTM (added later). STM vs Working memory. STM (Atkinson–Shiffrin) is a passive store (~7±2 items, 18–30 sec). Working memory (Baddeley–Hitch) is an active system that holds and manipulates information via a central executive plus slave subsystems. Levels of Processing Model Levels of processing model of memory. Craik and Lockhart notes with a table of processing depth from shallow (structural) through mid level (phonetic) and deep (semantic) to deepest (personally relevant). Psycho Didi notes · p. 97 Fergus Craik & Robert Lockhart (1972) — Levels of Processing model : information is more likely remembered when processed at a deep level. There is only one memory system. Depth Level Type of processing Shallow Structural Physical appearance of the word. Mid-level Phonetic Sound of the word. Deep Semantic Meaning of the word. Deepest Personally relevant Self-referent processing. Short-term memory testing Short-term memory. Notes on Miller's magic number 7 plus or minus 2 and chunking, and the Brown-Peterson trigram task. Psycho Didi notes · p. 97 Brown–Peterson task — a test of STM using a trigram ; the trigram was forgotten within 15–18 to 30 seconds when rehearsal was prevented. Tulving's model of Long-Term Memory Endel Tulving's model of long-term memory. Tree splitting LTM into declarative (semantic, episodic) and non-declarative (procedural, priming, conditioning, non-associative) memory with brain areas for each. Psycho Didi notes · p. 97 Other memory types. Short definitions of autobiographical, eidetic and flashbulb memory beside a light bulb icon. Psycho Didi notes · p. 97 Endel Tulving (1972) — model of long-term memory; distinguished episodic vs semantic memory within declarative memory. LTM type Subtype About Brain area Declarative (explicit) hippocampus-dependent Semantic Facts Cortex Episodic Events Cortex Non-declarative (implicit) hippocampus-independent Procedural (skills) Motor skills Basal ganglia, motor cortex, cerebellum Conditioning Learned associations Cerebellum Non-associative Habituation, sensitization — Priming (semantic) Facilitated processing Cortex Other memory types Autobiographical memory — LTM related to the self (semantic + episodic). Eidetic memory — photographic memory; children have it better. Flashbulb memory (Roger Brown and James Kulik, 1977) — vivid memory of emotionally arousing, surprising events; a strong autobiographical subtype. 7 · Forgetting & Memory Distortion Hermann Ebbinghaus. Ebbinghaus's nonsense syllable self-testing, the early drop and later levelling off of retention, and the method of savings. Psycho Didi notes · p. 98 Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885) — systematically tested his own memory of lists of nonsense syllables . Found a huge drop in retention soon after learning that eventually levelled off (the method of savings ); emphasized overlearning / revision . Retrieval types Types of retrieval. Tree of three retrieval types: recall (no cue, hardest), recognition (cued, easiest) and relearning (most sensitive measure). Psycho Didi notes · p. 98 Retrieval Note Recall Without a cue — the hardest . Cued recall Easier than free recall. Recognition Easiest. Relearning The most sensitive measure of learning. Neural basis Long-term potentiation. LTP notes with a drawing comparing a normal and a potentiated synapse, showing the presynaptic terminal, synaptic cleft, receptors and dendritic spine. Psycho Didi notes · p. 98 Long-term depression. Definition of LTD as the long-term weakening and pruning of unused synaptic connections. Psycho Didi notes · p. 98 Long-Term Potentiation (LTP; Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo, 1973) — persistent strengthening of a synaptic connection lasting minutes to hours; based on the Hebbian principle ("neurons that fire together, wire together"). NMDA glutamate receptors are necessary for memory formation; AMPA receptors — dendrites double their contact surface by splitting in two; terminal buttons release more neurotransmitter after potentiation; nitric oxide acts as a catalyst. In the lab, a high-frequency electric charge is applied to the pre-synaptic neuron. Long-Term Depression (LTD) — long-term weakening of a synaptic connection; prunes unused synapses, trimming unimportant connections and leaving only the salient connections strengthened by LTP. Theories of forgetting Decay theory of forgetting. Decay theory in two points beside an illustration of a brain breaking into fragments. Psycho Didi notes · p. 98 The serial position curve. Serial position notes with a U-shaped recall curve labelling the primacy effect, the recency effect and the interference at the low middle. Psycho Didi notes · p. 98 Interference theory of forgetting. Bergstrom's interference theory with definitions of proactive and retroactive interference and two factors for forgetting. Psycho Didi notes · p. 99 Decay theory — forgetting is an automatic process; the engram for the information disappears. Interference theory — supported by the serial-position curve. Serial Position Curve Represents the probability of recall of a word given its serial position in a list. Primacy effect — superior recall of words at/near the beginning of a list (into LTM); disrupted by proactive interference . Recency effect — superior recall of words at/near the end of a list (still in STM); disrupted by retroactive interference . John Bergström (1892) — Interference theory of forgetting . title: Personality & Motivation
text: Personality & Motivation — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Personality & Motivation Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Sigmund Freud · Carl Jung · Karen Horney · Alfred Adler · Erich Fromm Humanistic & Existential Murray's Personology Motivation: drive, arousal, need theories nAch · ERG · Self-Determination What this covers. The major approaches to personality — psychoanalytic/psychodynamic (Freud), the neo-Freudians and analytical psychology (Jung, Horney, Adler, Fromm), humanistic (Carl Rogers), existential and transpersonal approaches (Heidegger, Rollo May, Wilber), and Murray & Morgan's personology — followed by the theories of motivation (instinct, arousal, drive-reduction, and the need theories of Abraham Maslow, Alderfer, David McClelland, Edward Deci & Richard Ryan, and Zuckerman). Original diagrams. 18 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 109 to 115) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Psychoanalytic & Psychodynamic (Freud) · 2 · Neo-Freudian & Analytical Psychology · 3 · Humanistic Approach (Rogers) · 4 · Existential & Transpersonal Approaches · 5 · Personology (Murray & Morgan) · 6 · Theories of Motivation & Emotion 1 · Psychoanalytic & Psychodynamic (Freud) Approaches to personality: psychodynamic (Freud). Freud's topographical model drawn as an iceberg, beside notes on life and death instincts, the id, ego and superego, three types of anxiety and the defence mechanisms. Psycho Didi notes · p. 109 Theory → Theorist. Psychosexual / psychodynamic personality theory → Sigmund Freud . Freud — the psychodynamic model Sigmund Freud used a topographical model of the mind and held that behaviour springs from innate instincts and unconscious conflict. Life and death instincts — both are innate: Life instinct (eros) — libidinal energy that pushes us to function; survival-related instincts. Death instinct (thanatos) — instincts to hurt; destructive energy. The Id, Ego and Superego Structure Principle Develops in Id Pleasure principle — seeks immediate gratification Oral phase Ego Reality principle Anal phase Superego Morality principle Phallic stage The superego consists of two parts: Ego ideal — rewards ideal behaviour. Conscience — punishes with guilt. Three types of anxiety (Freud) Anxiety Nature Description Realistic anxiety Realistic fear The fear of an actual item. Moral anxiety Social fear Fear of punishment; represented by shame and guilt. Neurotic anxiety Nervous fear The fear of being overwhelmed; feeling that you are about to lose it; fear of the id taking over. Defence mechanisms Repression — keeping unpleasant memories or thoughts buried in the unconscious. Primal: innately part of the id. Proper: unacceptable derivatives of original id impulses. Denial — refusing to recognize an unpleasant reality. Rationalization — creating a socially acceptable excuse to justify unacceptable behaviour. Reaction formation — not acknowledging unacceptable impulses and over-emphasizing their opposite. Projection — transferring one's unacceptable qualities or impulses to others. Displacement — diverting one's impulses to a more acceptable target. Sublimation — channelling socially unacceptable impulses into acceptable activities. Regression — reverting to immature ways of responding. Identification — enhancing self-esteem by imagining or forming alliances with others. Intellectualization — ignoring troubling emotional aspects by focusing on abstract ideas or thoughts. Suppression — actively choosing to ignore something to do what is better and more important at the moment. Key. Id = pleasure principle (oral); Ego = reality principle (anal); Superego = morality principle (phallic), made of the ego ideal (rewards) and conscience (guilt). Repression is the "primal" defence; suppression is conscious, repression is unconscious. 2 · Neo-Freudian & Analytical Psychology Jung — Analytical Psychology Jung: analytical psychology. A comparison of Freud and Jung on the role of libido, the forces that influence personality and the unconscious. Psycho Didi notes · p. 109 Jung's structure of the psyche, energy principles and archetypes. A circle split into ego, personal unconscious and collective unconscious with arrows to their features, plus Jung's energy principles, psychological types and major archetypes. Psycho Didi notes · p. 110 Theory → Theorist. Analytical psychology → Carl Jung . Point of difference Sigmund Freud Jung Role of libido Sexual energy Broad psychic energy Forces that influence personality Present in the past only Present in the past as well as the future The unconscious Personal unconscious Personal and collective unconscious Structures of the psyche: Ego — is in control of itself; the conscious mind. Personal unconscious — accessible once in a while; personal memories that have lost their intensity. Collective unconscious — shared memories (patterns of behaviour), motifs, primordial patterns. Contains complexes , formed if a collective unconscious element completely takes over our personality. Energy principles: The principle of opposites — every wish or feeling has its opposite. The principle of equivalence — there is a constant amount of energy in our psyche. The principle of entropy — redistribution of energy within our psyche. Four functions: thinking, feeling, sensing, intuiting. Psychological types — attitudes: introversion / extraversion; rational / irrational. Archetypes and the anima/animus: Anima — the female archetype in the male psyche. Animus — the male archetype in the female psyche. Syzygy — anima and animus (Carl Jung) together. Self — finding a balance between the different aspects of ourselves. Persona — a mask, a facade to meet society's demands; a compromise between your needs and society's demands. Shadow — deepest, darkest instincts; comparable to the id. Other major archetypes: Joker , Wise Old Man , Hero , Witch , Villain . Horney Hor

text: Social Psychology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Social Psychology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Attribution & biases Cognitive dissonance (Leon Festinger, 1957) Persuasion & social influence Conformity · Compliance · Obedience Helping · Proxemics What this covers. The core of social psychology as it appears in MPhil Clinical and UGC NET JRF papers: a timeline of landmark thinkers and studies, attribution theory and its many biases, Harold Kelley's covariation model, cognitive dissonance (Leon Festinger, 1957) and attitude change, the Elaboration Likelihood Model (Richard Petty and John Cacioppo, 1986), the three types of social influence (compliance, conformity, obedience) with their techniques and classic experiments, social norms, prosocial helping (the decision stage model), and proxemics (personal space zones). Original diagrams. 16 diagrams from the Psycho Didi PDF (pages 122 to 123) sit under the section they belong to, exactly as drawn. Tap one to open it full size and zoom in. Contents: 1 · Timeline of Social Psychology · 2 · Attribution & Attributional Biases · 3 · Kelley's Covariation Model · 4 · Cognitive Dissonance · 5 · Attitude Change (Elaboration Likelihood Model) · 6 · Social Influence: Compliance, Conformity, Obedience · 7 · Social Norms · 8 · Prosocial Behaviour & Helping · 9 · Proxemics (Personal Space) 1 · Timeline of Social Psychology Timeline of social psychology. A winding road timeline marking key social psychology figures and studies from 1917 to 1994. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Key figures and landmark studies that shaped the field, in chronological order. Year Figure Contribution 1917 John Dewey The need for social psychology 1935 Muzafer Sherif Conformity studies 1940s — Field theory (Kurt Lewin) 1950s Solomon Asch Conformity study 1954 Gordon Allport Nature of prejudice 1959 Erving Goffman Presentation of self 1961 Serge Moscovici Social representation 1963 Stanley Milgram Obedience study 1965 William Glasser Choice theory 1968 Robert Zajonc Mere exposure effect 1971 Philip Zimbardo Stanford Prison experiment 1971 Elliot Aronson Jigsaw classroom 1972 Spence and Helmreich Attitude towards women 1977 Brown and Kulik Flashbulb memories 1994 Ignacio Martín-Baró Liberation psychology 2 · Attribution & Attributional Biases Attribution. Notes defining attribution and its two categories, dispositional and situational. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Attribution refers to the way in which people assign responsibility for certain outcomes. Typically attribution falls into two categories: Dispositional (individual) — assumes that the cause of a behaviour or outcome is internal. Situational — assigns the cause to the environment or external conditions. Watch the biases. Several attributional biases are easily confused. The fundamental attribution error (Lee Ross, 1977) is about judging others , while the actor–observer bias and self-serving bias concern how we explain our own actions. Learn the direction (internal vs external) each one pulls. Types of attributional bias Flexible attribution. A list of attributional biases, each with a one-line definition. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Flexible attribution — a general label for the shifting, motivated way people assign causes. Fundamental attribution error — when judging the behaviour of others, people are more likely to overestimate the role of dispositional attributes and to underestimate the role of the situation. Self-serving bias — seeing the cause of actions as internal when the outcomes are positive and external when the results are negative. Actor–observer bias — we tend to attribute our own actions to the situation. Optimism bias — we like to believe that bad things happen to other people, but not to ourselves. Just-world belief ( M. J. Lerner ) — a belief that the world is essentially fair and just (leads to victim blaming). Self-fulfilling prophecy — because person A expects person B to achieve or fail, person B is likely to do just that. Positive: Rosenthal / Pygmalion effect Negative: Golem effect 3 · Kelley's Covariation Model Kelley's Covariation Model (1967). A table showing the levels of consensus, consistency and distinctiveness that lead to an internal or an external attribution. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Covariation model → Harold Kelley (1967). Explains whether we make an internal or external attribution based on three kinds of information: consensus, consistency, and distinctiveness. Information Internal attribution External attribution Consensus Low High Consistency High High Distinctiveness Low High 4 · Cognitive Dissonance Cognitive dissonance. Notes on Festinger's cognitive dissonance, the minimum justification effect, the types of dissonance and the ways to reduce it. Psycho Didi notes · p. 122 Cognitive dissonance → Leon Festinger. Cognitive dissonance refers to the tension that results from holding conflicting beliefs, attitudes, opinions, or values, or when our actions do not coincide with these cognitions. Key — minimum justification effect. Dissonance is experienced when external rewards are not adequate to justify behaviour. Therefore: Large reward = small attitude change Small reward = large attitude change Types of cognitive dissonance Free choice — when you liked both options. Forced choice — when you dislike both options. Methods of reducing dissonance Changing one's attitude Changing one's behaviour Trivialization 5 · Attitude Change (Elaboration Likelihood Model) Elaboration Likelihood Model. A table comparing the central and peripheral routes by audience, processing effort and how long the attitude change lasts. font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:.03em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--muted)} body.drill .qa.open .q::after{content:""} The Full Manipal Viva Sheet 141 questions with model answers, word for word, in the order a clinical psychology panel actually walks through them. Built 6 Aug 2026 for the MAHE / MCHP M.A. Clinical Psychology department session on 7 August 2026 , App No 126202084. This is the answers page. The logistics, the slot finder and tonight's checklist are on the Manipal sheet . Questions 141 Format Q → model answer → the follow-up Answer length 20 to 40 seconds Drill mode hides every answer Every answer here is built to one shape, because that shape is what gets marked: definition, then theorist, then example . Say the definition in one clean sentence. Name who it comes from. Give one concrete instance, preferably from a real client or your own data. Then stop talking. A panel asking a viva question wants to know whether you own the concept, not whether you can talk for two minutes about it. The commonest way to lose marks in an oral is to answer correctly and then keep going until you say something wrong. Drill mode: off Reveal all Drill mode hides every answer. Read the question, say it out loud, then tap the card to check yourself. Jump to: 0 · The shape of an answer 1 · Openers 2 · Definitions Bank 3 · Core definitions 4 · MSE and assessment 5 · Psychometrics 6 · Psychopathology 7 · Therapy schools 8 · Development and psychodynamics 9 · Ethics and law 10 · Stats and methods 11 · Dissertation defence 12 · Vignettes 13 · Curveballs and the close 0 · The shape of an answer Question type Structure Length "What is X?" Definition in one sentence → theorist and year → one example → stop. 15 to 20 seconds "Difference between X and Y?" Name the dimension they differ on first, then one line each. Never list X fully then Y fully. 20 seconds "How would you manage this case?" Safety first → what you would rule out → assessment → provisional formulation → intervention → supervision. 45 to 60 seconds "Why do you think that?" Give the reasoning, then name what would change your mind. Panels mark for the second half. 20 seconds Something you do not know "I'm not certain, sir. My understanding is ___, but I'd want to check that before I state it." Then stop. 8 seconds Your three anchors. The M.Sc (you have the theory), the 250+ YourDOST clients across roughly 473 sessions (you are not theory-only), the dissertation with 214 participants analysed in SPSS by you (you can do research). Any question you have not prepared for, walk it back to one of those three. You are never empty-handed. 1 · Openers Tell us about yourself. "Good morning sir, good morning ma'am. I'm Mohammed Sihan. I did my M.Sc in Clinical Psychology at Jain Deemed-to-be University, Bangalore, 2022 to 2024. Alongside and since, I've been working as a counsellor on YourDOST, an online mental health platform, where I've carried over 250 individual clients across roughly 473 sessions, mostly anxiety, low mood, relationship distress and academic stress. My dissertation was a quantitative study on pornography consumption in relation to personality, aggression and sexual compulsivity in Indian young adults, 214 participants, Spearman correlations and logistic regression in SPSS. What I want next is structured clinical training under supervision, in a hospital setting, with real assessment and real diagnostic work. That's why I applied here." Forty-five seconds, all evidence, and it ends by handing them the next question. You control the follow-up instead of waiting for it. Why clinical psychology? "Three reasons, one personal, one academic, one professional. Personally, the work I've done on YourDOST is the only work I've done where I finish a session more awake than I started it. Academically, my M.Sc pulled me towards psychopathology and assessment specifically, the diagnostic side rather than the purely supportive side. Professionally, I keep running out of road with real clients: I can stabilise someone and do CBT work on a thought loop, but when there's an obsessive-compulsive presentation or a possible bipolar pattern underneath, my role is to refer, not to assess and formulate. I don't want to keep stopping at the referral." One personal line, one academic, one professional, and no sob story. The third reason is the one only somebody with real caseload hours can give. Why Manipal? Why this department? "Because of the setting. MAHE is one of the few places where clinical psychology training sits inside a full teaching hospital system, so it isn't classroom-only, there's actual patient contact and multidisciplinary work alongside psychiatry. Second, MCHP has a long-standing training tradition and dedicated faculty in the department, so supervision isn't an afterthought. Third, the structure of this programme specifically: a two-year MA with supervised practicum and a dissertation, on the RCI track, rather than a degree that leaves me academically qualified and professionally unlicensed. I sat the MET, I'm in the interview band, this is my first choice." Concrete without faking insider knowledge. Do not invent faculty names, centre names or accreditation claims. Vague-but-true beats specific-but-wrong when you are talking to the people who run the department. You already have an M.Sc in Clinical Psychology. Why a second master's? "The M.Sc gave me the academic base and the research training, and I've used both, I ran a full quantitative dissertation off it. What it didn't give me was supervised clinical practice inside a hospital, and that's the piece the RCI-recognised route provides. I'm not repeating a degree, I'm adding the supervised clinical training and the professional recognition my present qualification doesn't carry." Own it in the first sentence. Any hesitation here reads as "he couldn't get in anywhere else." What have you read recently? "Marsha Linehan's Building a Life Worth Living . It's her memoir, and what struck me is that DBT came out of her own experience of being on the wrong side of the treatment, being the patient nobody could hold. It changed how I think about validation. Before that I read it as a technique you apply before you get to the change work. She writes it as the thing that makes change possible at all, and I notice the difference in my own sessions when I skip it." Name one real book, one sentence on why, and make the why about your practice. Do not name a textbook, and do not name something you have not actually read, because the next question is always "what did you make of it?" What are your strengths? "Two. First, volume of contact hours, over 250 clients, which means I've built the reflex of sitting with distress without rushing to fix it. Second, I'm comfortable with data. I did my own SPSS analysis rather than handing it to someone, so when I read a paper I read the method section, not just the abstract." What is your weakness? "My clinical exposure is heavily weighted to online counselling with a relatively high-functioning population. I haven't worked on a ward, and I haven't sat with severe mental illness in an acute phase. I know the psychopathology academically, but I haven't seen most of it. That's precisely the gap this programme fills, and it's the honest answer rather than saying I work too hard." A real weakness that the programme fixes. Never give a disguised strength, panels have heard "I'm a perfectionist" a hundred times and it costs you credibility for the rest of the interview. Where do you see yourself in five years? "Working as a clinical psychologist in a hospital or an institutional setting, RCI registered, with a caseload that includes assessment and not only therapy. I'd like to still be doing research alongside it, in behavioural addiction and impulse control, which is where my dissertation sat. Longer term I'd want to supervise, but I'm aware that's a decade of clinical hours away, not five years." What if you don't get in here? "I'd reapply. I've also sat for the other RCI-track entrances this cycle, so I have parallel options, but the plan doesn't change: supervised clinical training, then registration. I've built a year of preparation around this and I'd spend another one on it if I had to." No desperation, no bluffing that you have nowhere else to go, and no implying you have a better offer. Steady is the right register. Why should we take you over the other candidates? "I won't compare myself to people I haven't met, sir. What I'd say is that I come in with three things already done: a master's in this exact subject, a completed quantitative dissertation I analysed myself, and 250-plus clients of real contact hours. Most applicants have one of those. So I need the clinical supervision from you, not the basics." 2 · Definitions Bank: the general concepts These are the ordinary psychology words, not the clinical ones. Every viva has a stretch where they stop asking about you and start asking "what is personality", "what is intelligence", "define learning". It is the cheapest section of the interview to win and the easiest to fumble, because you know all of this and will still ramble if you have not fixed the wording in advance. One shape for all twenty-nine: the definition in one line, the theorist attached, then the follow-up they always ask . Say the definition. Name the man. Stop. Let them ask the follow-up, and have it ready. The one mistake here. Answering "what is personality" with a list of theories. They asked for the definition, not the syllabus. Give the sentence, give the name, then be quiet. If you open with Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Alfred Adler and Gordon Allport, you have told the panel you cannot separate a definition from a topic, and they will keep pushing until you say something wrong. Define personality. "Personality is the dynamic organisation within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine his characteristic behaviour and thought. That's Allport, and it's worth quoting because every word in it is doing work: dynamic, so it changes; organisation, so it's a system and not a list of traits; psychophysical, so it's mind and body together; and characteristic, so it's what's consistent about the person across situations." Trait versus type, or nomothetic versus idiographic. Trait approaches treat personality as continuous dimensions everyone sits somewhere on, so Gordon Allport, Raymond Cattell's sixteen factors, Hans Eysenck's three, the Big Five. Type approaches sort people into discrete categories, so William Sheldon's somatotypes, Carl Jung's introvert and extravert, Type A and Type B. Traits describe, types classify, and the modern evidence is dimensional, which is why the Big Five survived and typologies did not. Nomothetic means studying variables across large samples to find general laws, which is what a trait questionnaire does. Idiographic means studying the individual case in depth, which is what Allport himself argued for with personal dispositions and the case study. Say clinical work needs both: the psychometrics are nomothetic, the formulation is idiographic. Quoting Allport verbatim is the single highest-yield sentence in this whole section. They know the quote. Getting it word for word says trained, not read-up. Define intelligence. "Intelligence is the global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, to think rationally and to deal effectively with his environment. That's Wechsler. Global, because it's an aggregate rather than one ability, and effectively, because it's judged by how well the person handles the world, not by what's inside his head." The models, in order. Charles Spearman's two-factor theory: every task loads on general ability, g, plus a specific factor s, and g is what the positive manifold in the correlations is telling you. L. L. Thurstone rejected a single g and gave seven primary mental abilities, verbal comprehension, word fluency, number, space, memory, perceptual speed and reasoning. Raymond Cattell split g into fluid intelligence, reasoning with novel material, which peaks early and declines, and crystallised, accumulated knowledge, which holds up. Howard Gardner's multiple intelligences: eight relatively independent intelligences including musical, bodily-kinaesthetic and the two personal ones, criticised because they're closer to talents than to measured abilities. Robert Sternberg's triarchic: componential or analytic, experiential or creative, and contextual or practical, which is the one IQ tests miss. If they want the modern answer, say the Cattell-Horn-Carroll model is the one current test batteries are actually built on. Define memory. "Memory is the set of processes by which information is encoded, stored and retrieved. Three stages, and a failure at any one of them looks like forgetting from outside. The classic structural account is Richard Atkinson and Shiffrin's multi-store model, 1968: sensory register, short-term store, long-term store, with rehearsal moving material across." Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch replaced short-term memory with working memory, because short-term store as a passive box couldn't explain how people hold and manipulate at the same time. Four components: the phonological loop for verbal and acoustic material, with a store and an articulatory rehearsal process; the visuospatial sketchpad for visual and spatial material; the central executive, an attentional controller that allocates resources and doesn't store anything itself; and the episodic buffer, added in 2000, which binds information from the subsystems and long-term memory into single episodes. On long-term memory use Endel Tulving: declarative or explicit, splitting into episodic, events with a time and place, and semantic, facts; against non-declarative or implicit, which is procedural skills, priming and conditioning. Anterograde amnesia is the clinical proof of the split, HM lost episodic learning and kept procedural learning. What is cognitive dissonance? "Cognitive dissonance is the psychological discomfort a person feels when they hold two inconsistent cognitions, and that discomfort motivates them to change an attitude or a behaviour to reduce it. Festinger, 1957. The classic demonstration is Festinger and J. Merrill Carlsmith, 1959: subjects paid one dollar to say a boring task was interesting rated it as more enjoyable than subjects paid twenty dollars, because twenty dollars is a sufficient external justification and one dollar isn't, so the only way to resolve it is to decide you actually liked the task." Where it shows up clinically. It's the engine of motivational interviewing: you deliberately develop discrepancy between the person's behaviour and their own stated values, and let the dissonance do the work rather than arguing with them. It also explains post-decisional regret, effort justification, and why insight alone doesn't change behaviour, because the cheaper route to reducing dissonance is usually to change the cognition rather than the act. Define learning. "Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour or behavioural potential that results from experience or practice. Kimble's definition, and the qualifiers are the whole answer: relatively permanent, so it excludes fatigue and drug effects; potential, because learning can occur without being performed; and from experience, so it excludes maturation." The distinction they want is learning versus performance, and it's Tolman's. His rats in the latent learning study formed a cognitive map of the maze with no reward, and it showed only when reward was introduced, so learning had happened without being performed. After that, name the types: classical conditioning, operant conditioning, observational learning through Bandura's Bobo doll, insight learning through Wolfgang Köhler, and verbal learning through Ebbinghaus. Define motivation. "Motivation is the internal process that initiates, directs and sustains goal-directed behaviour. It's inferred, never observed, you see the behaviour and infer the drive behind it. The classical account is Hull's drive-reduction theory: a physiological need creates a drive state, behaviour that reduces the drive is reinforced." Why drive reduction isn't enough, and what replaced it. It can't explain curiosity, exploration or play, where organisms increase arousal rather than reduce it, which is what the optimal arousal theories and the Yerkes-Dodson law handle. Then the hierarchy of needs, Abraham Maslow: physiological, safety, belongingness and love, esteem, self-actualisation, with the lower needs prepotent. Then the split that matters clinically, Edward Deci and Richard Ryan's self-determination theory: intrinsic motivation from autonomy, competence and relatedness against extrinsic motivation from external reward, and the over-justification effect, where rewarding an intrinsically motivated behaviour reduces it. David McClelland's need for achievement, affiliation and power is the one to add if they're asking in an organisational frame. Define emotion. "An emotion is a complex reaction pattern with three components: a subjective feeling, a physiological arousal response, and a behavioural or expressive response. So it's what you feel, what your body does, and what shows on your face." The four theories, and the order they came in is the answer. James-Lange: the bodily change comes first and the emotion is your perception of it, you're afraid because you run. Cannon-Bard: the thalamus sends signals to cortex and body simultaneously, so feeling and arousal are parallel, not sequential, because visceral changes are too slow and too undifferentiated to produce distinct emotions. Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer's two-factor theory: emotion is undifferentiated arousal plus a cognitive label taken from the situation, which is the adrenaline study with the confederate. Lazarus: cognitive appraisal comes first, primary appraisal asks is this a threat to me, secondary asks can I cope with it, and the emotion follows the appraisal. Say the Lazarus line last, because appraisal is what CBT operates on. If they ask mood versus emotion, mood is longer, lower in intensity and usually without a clear object; emotion is short, intense and directed at something. Define perception. "Perception is the process of organising and interpreting sensory information so that it has meaning. Sensation is the raw registration of the stimulus by the receptor, perception is what the brain makes of it, which is why the same retinal image can be seen two ways in an ambiguous figure." Bottom-up versus top-down. Gibson's direct or bottom-up theory says the optic array contains enough information for perception without inference, and there's no need for the brain to add anything. Gregory's constructivist or top-down theory says perception is an active hypothesis built from fragmentary sensory data plus stored knowledge, which is why illusions happen, the hypothesis is wrong. The reconciliation is that Gibson works for rich viewing conditions and Gregory works for poor, degraded or ambiguous ones. Add the Gestalt organising laws, figure and ground, proximity, similarity, closure, continuity and common fate, and add perceptual constancy, size, shape, colour and brightness, which is what makes the illusions work. Define attention. "The best definition is still William James: 'It is the taking possession by the mind, in clear and vivid form, of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought.' Operationally, attention is the selective allocation of limited processing capacity to some stimuli at the expense of others." The filter models, in sequence. Donald Broadbent's early selection: a filter at the sensory stage selects on physical characteristics and blocks the unattended channel completely, which fails because people hear their own name on the unattended ear, that's the cocktail party effect and Neville Moray's demonstration. Anne Treisman's attenuation: the filter weakens rather than blocks, so unattended material still gets through if its threshold is low, and your own name has a permanently low threshold. Deutsch and Deutsch's late selection: everything is analysed for meaning and the selection happens at the response stage. Daniel Kahneman moved from filters to a capacity model, attention as a limited pool of resources allocated flexibly. Clinically, name the types: sustained, selective, divided, alternating, and say that sustained attention is what a digit vigilance test measures and divided attention is what a Trails B measures. Define consciousness. "Consciousness is awareness of oneself and of the environment, and of one's own mental processes. It's the one every definition struggles with, so give the two dimensions clinicians use: level of consciousness, meaning arousal, which runs from alert through drowsy, confused, stuporous to comatose; and content of consciousness, meaning what you're aware of. William James described it as a stream, continuous, always changing, personal and selective." Sigmund Freud's topographic model against the clinical assessment of consciousness. Freud: conscious, what's in awareness now; preconscious, what can be brought into awareness; unconscious, what's actively kept out and reaches you only through dreams, slips and symptoms. Clinically, altered states are sleep, dreaming, hypnosis, meditation and drug states, and the pathological alterations are delirium, which is a clouding with fluctuating attention, and the dissociative states, where consciousness is intact in level but split in content. Do not merge the two vocabularies, one is psychodynamic and the other is neuropsychiatric. Define attitude. "An attitude is a learned predisposition to respond in a consistently favourable or unfavourable manner towards a given object, person or situation. Allport, 1935, called it the most distinctive and indispensable concept in social psychology. Three components, the ABC model: affective, what you feel about it; behavioural or conative, how you tend to act; cognitive, what you believe about it." Do attitudes predict behaviour? Mostly weakly, which is LaPiere's classic finding, and the answer is the theory of planned behaviour, Icek Ajzen: behaviour follows intention, and intention comes from attitude, subjective norm and perceived behavioural control. For attitude change go to persuasion, the elaboration likelihood model, Richard Petty and John Cacioppo: the central route works through argument quality and produces durable change, the peripheral route works through cues like attractiveness and produces change that doesn't last. Leon Festinger's dissonance is the other route to change, and measurement is Thurstone, Likert and the semantic differential of Osgood. Define self-concept. "Self-concept is the organised, consistent set of perceptions and beliefs a person holds about himself. Rogers, and for him it has three parts: self-image, what you see yourself as; self-esteem, how much you value yourself; and the ideal self, what you wish you were." Congruence and incongruence, and it's the whole of Rogerian theory. When self-concept and experience match, the person is congruent and functioning; when experience is inconsistent with the self-concept, it's distorted or denied, and that incongruence is what produces anxiety and defensiveness. It arises from conditions of worth, positive regard given conditionally in childhood, so therapy supplies unconditional positive regard to dissolve them. If they want the wider literature: William James split it into the I, the knower, and the Me, the known, with material, social and spiritual selves; Cooley's looking-glass self and Mead's generalised other make it social; Markus calls the units self-schemas; and Higgins's self-discrepancy theory says an actual-ideal gap produces dejection and depression while an actual-ought gap produces agitation and anxiety. Define stress and coping. "Stress is a state of psychological and physiological tension that arises when the demands on a person are appraised as taxing or exceeding their resources. That's Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model, and the word appraised is the point: stress is not in the event, it's in the relationship between the person and the event. Coping is the constantly changing cognitive and behavioural effort to manage those demands." Hans Selye and the two-way split of coping. Selye's general adaptation syndrome is the physiological account, three stages, alarm with sympathetic activation and the HPA axis firing, resistance where the body sustains a high level of arousal, and exhaustion where the resources deplete and disease appears. He also separated eustress, facilitative stress, from distress. Lazarus is the cognitive account: primary appraisal asks is this harm, threat or challenge, secondary appraisal asks what can I do about it, and reappraisal updates both. Coping splits into problem-focused, changing the stressor, which works when the situation is controllable, and emotion-focused, changing the response to it, which works when it isn't, plus avoidance coping, which is the one that predicts poor outcomes. Add social support as a buffer and the Holmes and Rahe scale as the measurement. Define adjustment. "Adjustment is the continuous process by which a person alters his behaviour, or his environment, to achieve a more harmonious relationship between himself and his surroundings. It's a process and an outcome at the same time: adjustment as achieving a state of balance, and adjustment as the ongoing effort of getting there." Adjustment versus adaptation, and where maladjustment becomes a diagnosis. Adaptation is the biological term, changes in the organism that improve survival, largely species-level and evolutionary. Adjustment is the psychological term, individual and lifelong, and can be by changing the self, alloplastic versus autoplastic if they want the pair. Clinically, when the response to an identifiable stressor is out of proportion or impairs functioning within three months of onset, that's adjustment disorder, and in DSM-5-TR it now sits in the trauma- and stressor-related disorders chapter, not on its own. The healthy markers are realistic perception, ability to deal with stress, positive self-image, ability to express feelings and good interpersonal relations. Define creativity. "Creativity is the ability to produce work that is both novel and appropriate, so original and useful in its context, because novelty alone is just oddness. Guilford is the name to attach: he separated convergent thinking, which converges on the one correct answer and is what IQ tests measure, from divergent thinking, generating many possible answers, which is what creativity requires." How you measure it, and does it correlate with intelligence. Measurement is E. Paul Torrance, the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking, scored on four dimensions: fluency, the number of ideas; flexibility, the number of different categories; originality, how statistically rare they are; and elaboration, the detail added. Process is Wallas's four stages, preparation, incubation, illumination and verification. And the relationship with intelligence is the threshold hypothesis: intelligence and creativity correlate up to roughly an IQ of 120 and are largely independent above it, so a high IQ is necessary but not sufficient. Define aptitude. "Aptitude is the potential or capacity of a person to acquire a specific skill or knowledge with training. It's predictive: it tells you what someone could learn, not what they've already learned." Aptitude versus achievement versus intelligence, and this is a three-way distinction they like because most candidates blur it. Aptitude looks forward, potential to acquire; achievement looks backward, what has already been acquired through instruction; intelligence is the general capacity underlying both, broader and less tied to a specific domain. The catch, and say it, is that the distinction is about the purpose of the test rather than the item content: the same item can serve as an aptitude item or an achievement item depending on whether you're predicting or measuring attainment. Examples are the Differential Aptitude Test, the General Aptitude Test Battery and the Minnesota Clerical Test. Define temperament. "Temperament is the biologically based, constitutional style of behaviour, the how of behaviour rather than the what or the why, present from infancy and relatively stable. It's the raw material personality is built on: temperament is what you're born with, personality is what experience makes of it." Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess, the New York Longitudinal Study. Nine dimensions, activity level, rhythmicity, approach or withdrawal, adaptability, threshold of responsiveness, intensity of reaction, quality of mood, distractibility, and attention span and persistence. Those cluster into three types: the easy child, about forty per cent; the difficult child, about ten; and the slow-to-warm-up child, about fifteen, with the rest not classifiable. The concept that matters clinically is goodness of fit, outcomes depend on the match between the child's temperament and the demands and style of the caregiver, not on temperament alone, so a difficult temperament isn't a prognosis. Add Buss and Plomin's EAS model, emotionality, activity and sociability, and Jerome Kagan's behavioural inhibition, which is the temperamental precursor of later anxiety disorder. Define conditioning. "Conditioning is the process of learning associations. Classical conditioning, Pavlov, is learning an association between two stimuli, so a neutral stimulus paired repeatedly with an unconditioned stimulus comes to elicit a conditioned response. Operant conditioning, Skinner, is learning an association between a behaviour and its consequence, so behaviour is shaped by what follows it." The difference, said properly, is respondent versus emitted behaviour: in classical conditioning the response is elicited and involuntary, and the stimulus comes before the behaviour; in operant it is emitted and voluntary, and the consequence comes after. Then give the classical processes: acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation, discrimination and higher-order conditioning. And name the clinical applications, because that's the real reason they ask: systematic desensitisation and flooding are counter-conditioning, aversion therapy is classical, token economy and contingency management are operant, and Watson's Little Albert plus O. Hobart Mowrer's two-factor theory, classical acquisition of the fear and operant maintenance by avoidance, is the model behind every phobia. Define reinforcement. "A reinforcer is any consequence that increases the probability of the behaviour it follows. Skinner, and note the definition is functional, not descriptive: something is a reinforcer only if the behaviour actually goes up, which is why chocolate isn't a reinforcer for a child who dislikes chocolate." Positive versus negative reinforcement versus punishment, and it is the single commonest confusion in a viva. Positive means adding a stimulus, negative means removing one, and reinforcement always increases behaviour while punishment always decreases it. So negative reinforcement is removing something aversive to increase behaviour, taking the painkiller to remove pain, and it's not punishment. Then the schedules: continuous reinforcement gives fast acquisition and fast extinction; of the partial schedules, fixed ratio, variable ratio, fixed interval and variable interval, variable ratio produces the highest and steadiest rate and is the most resistant to extinction, which is the gambling answer. Add the Premack principle, a higher-frequency behaviour reinforces a lower-frequency one, and primary versus secondary reinforcers. What are defence mechanisms? "Defence mechanisms are unconscious strategies used by the ego to reduce the anxiety that arises from conflict between the id, the superego and reality. Sigmund Freud introduced the idea, Anna Freud systematised it in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence , 1936. Two features define them: they operate unconsciously, and they distort reality to some degree." Are they pathological? No, and that's the answer they're testing. George Vaillant's hierarchy is the way to say it: pathological defences, denial and delusional projection; immature, projection, acting out, passive aggression, regression and fantasy; neurotic, repression, reaction formation, displacement, intellectualisation, rationalisation and undoing; and mature, sublimation, altruism, humour, suppression and anticipation. Suppression is conscious and mature, repression is unconscious, and that pair is a favourite. Defences are pathological only by rigidity, by level, and by whether they're used where a more adaptive one was available. Repression is the primary defence, the one all the others are built on. Define insight. "Insight has two entirely separate meanings and you should say so before you answer. In learning, insight is the sudden reorganisation of the perceptual field that produces a solution, without trial and error, which is Köhler's work with Sultan the chimpanzee stacking boxes to reach the banana, and it's the Gestalt objection to Thorndike. In clinical work, insight is the patient's awareness that he is ill and that his experiences are the product of that illness." Grade the clinical one, because that's what they want. The traditional six grades run from complete denial of illness, through some awareness of being ill but blaming it on others or on physical causes, to intellectual insight, awareness of being ill and of the psychological causes, and finally true or emotional insight, where the awareness actually changes behaviour. David's 1990 model is the modern one and easier to defend: three components, recognition of illness, the ability to relabel unusual mental events as pathological, and compliance with treatment. Insight is a dimension, not a yes or no, and it's poorest in mania and in schizophrenia, better in depression and typically retained in the anxiety disorders and OCD, which is why obsessions are ego-dystonic. What is transfer of learning? "Transfer of learning is the effect of previous learning on the learning or performance of a new task. Thorndike's identical elements theory is the explanation: transfer occurs to the degree the two tasks share identical elements, which is why learning Latin doesn't improve general reasoning, against the old formal discipline view." The types. Positive transfer, prior learning helps, learning Spanish after Italian. Negative transfer, prior learning interferes, driving on the other side of the road. Zero transfer, no effect. Then direction: proactive transfer, earlier learning affecting later, and retroactive, later learning affecting the retention of earlier. Also lateral transfer, applying it to a task of similar difficulty, against vertical transfer, applying it to a higher-order task. Judd's generalisation theory is the alternative to Edward Thorndike, transfer occurs through the general principle understood rather than the shared elements, and Judd's water-jet experiment is the demonstration. Say why it matters: it's the whole rationale for homework in CBT, therapy is worthless if it doesn't transfer out of the room. Define forgetting. "Forgetting is the failure to retrieve information that was previously encoded and stored. Ebbinghaus mapped it with nonsense syllables and gave the forgetting curve: loss is very rapid in the first hour and then levels off, which is why spaced repetition works and cramming doesn't." The theories, and the honest ranking. Trace decay, the memory fades with time through disuse, weak because time alone doesn't predict loss, what you do in the interval does. Interference, which is the best-supported: proactive interference, old learning disrupting new, and retroactive, new learning disrupting old. Retrieval failure or cue-dependent forgetting, Endel Tulving, where the trace is intact but the cue is missing, and the encoding specificity principle, plus state-dependent and context-dependent recall, are the evidence for it. Motivated forgetting or repression, Sigmund Freud, where anxiety-laden material is kept out of awareness, which is clinically important and experimentally weak. And organic causes, so anterograde and retrograde amnesia. If they push on where the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon fits, it's the proo

title: Your Therapeutic Style — interview-ready
text: Your Therapeutic Style — interview-ready This is your clinical voice, pulled straight from your own YourDOST session work. Every quote in a purple box is something you actually typed or said to a real client; every blue box is an answer you can give out loud in an interview, built from that same material. Nothing here is textbook-borrowed. When they ask "what's your therapeutic approach?" you don't have to perform a school you don't practise: you have a real, distinctive style and the language to describe it. Source + method are at the bottom. The one-line answer: you're an integrative, state-driven therapist with a person-centred relational base and a CBT / behavioural spine : you stabilise before you explore, validate before you intervene, and you pick the technique off the client's emotional state in the moment rather than off a manual. Your caseload line (say this with confidence): "I've carried hundreds of clients over the past year on YourDOST." That is your real number, and now it's documented, not a guess. The whole export was re-read end to end this time, every chat in the YD project, and 254 distinct named clients were individuated from it (plus another 79 real client sessions where the platform didn't preserve a usable name), across 473 session-instances. The earlier "~30" was never your caseload; it was just how many the first quick pass could separate. The real, evidenced floor is 254 named clients. So you no longer have to split "the number from you, the evidence from the sessions." Both come from the sessions now: say "hundreds over the year," and if they push for a figure, " over 250 individual clients , the full list is documented." The full client roster is the receipt: name, presenting focus, the techniques you used, session count, risk flag, all of it. 1 Your approach 2 Go-to interventions 3 Specific techniques 3b Named techniques — mechanics + PI lines 3c Most difficult case — walkthrough 4 Relationship + formulation 5 Strengths & growth edges 6 Interview answers 7 Source & method 1 · Your approach / modality, as the sessions actually show it You are not a single-school therapist, and that's a strength, not a hedge: the sessions show a deliberate, repeatable logic for when you use what . The spine is cognitive-behavioural (you name automatic thoughts, loops, triggers, and you set small behavioural homework), the relational stance is person-centred (validate first, collaborative, never directive), and you reach for ACT/compassion/solution-focused moves when they fit the moment. The defining feature: you're state-driven, not modality-driven. You don't run "CBT clients" and "person-centred clients." You read the client's level of overwhelm and switch: • Overwhelmed / flooded → containment + supportive holding • Stuck in a thought → gentle CBT / ACT reframing • Ambivalent about change → motivational interviewing (roll with resistance) • Functionally stuck → behavioural activation + problem-solving • Self-critical → compassion-focused ("what would you tell a friend?") You've actually codified this. Your own session framework is built on two named gears: A) DEFAULT MODE (use when client is stable enough to talk) … B) CONTAINMENT MODE (override default when client is overwhelmed) … Goal: Stabilize the nervous system, not solve the problem. your YD session framework, written out for yourself The CBT spine is unmistakable in your own words to clients: Sometimes our thoughts and emotions follow an automatic loop over time and it becomes important to break that loop. We can definitely look into it to Akashdeep (anxiety) For now, the goal is not to stop the voice, but to change your response to it. When it shows up, pause and say (even mentally) — "This is my old critical voice, not reality." to Vaisakh (inner critic / self-worth) It would be important to identify certain automatic thoughts that we may have that doesnt allow us to accept these thoughts. to Levi But it's always delivered on a person-centred footing: warmth and validation come first , the cognitive work comes after the client feels understood. I understand.. Feel free to start wherever you would like to. We can also start with what is bothering you the most at the moment as well if youd like to Levi — letting the client lead Why this is the honest read: across the transcripts the constant isn't a technique, it's the sequence — validate, normalise, then explore, then reframe, then one small action. You reuse the moves of several schools, but you sequence and simplify them around the client's capacity in the moment. That is textbook integrative, humanistic-CBT practice, and you can say so with examples. 2 · Your go-to interventions These are the moves that recur in almost every session, in roughly the order you deploy them. Validation + normalisation (your most frequent move) You lead with it, every time, in plain undramatic language. Thats completely understandable… anyone in that situation would feel tired. recurring across clients The care and responsibility you showed during such a difficult period speaks about your empathy and strength to the marriage-distress client Strength-spotting / restoring agency You consistently hand the client back evidence of their own competence, and you reframe "failures" as data. The relapse is actually evidence that you can change the pattern, and one relapse doesn't erase that progress. to Akashdeep I don't see those six years as foolish. You stayed because you believed it would work. to Nuzhat (breakup) despite loss and pressure, you still have a strong drive for self improvement and growth, that part of you hasn't disappeared, it's just been waiting. to the identity/career client Psychoeducation — simple, relevant, never a lecture You translate the mechanism into everyday language so the symptom stops feeling like a personal failing.
